Organization rows are the useful ones for B2B. For A.S. KIM DDS, INC., the row has the authorized official (a DDS, title "CEO") with a phone, the practice phone, license number, other names (DBA "VILLAGE HILLCREST DENTAL"), and the count of additional practice locations.

A bigger real example from my testing: all individual chiropractors in California with a phone came to 3,000 providers in about 3 minutes.

A monthly "new practices" list

Set NPI issued after (enumeratedAfter) to 90 days ago, pick your specialties and states, and schedule it monthly. New clinicians and new group practices show up as they get their NPIs.

Limits, honestly

  • No emails. NPPES doesn't publish them. You get practice phone and fax, the mailing address and, for organizations, the authorized official. If you need an email, you'll need the practice's website.
  • Self-reported and sometimes stale.
  • NPI holders only. It covers HIPAA-covered providers, not every wellness or cosmetic business.
  • Not affiliated with CMS or HHS.

What it costs

$0.001 per provider ($1 per 1,000), no start fee. Duplicates and filtered-out records are free, and runs stop at your "maximum cost per run". The 50-provider test was 5 cents. The API and the full CMS file are free.

Play fair

Practice phones are business lines, but authorized officials are people. TCPA rules apply to calls and texts, CAN-SPAM to email, and some providers will rightly be annoyed by cold outreach. Be relevant and honour opt-outs.

Do you work with NPPES data? I'd like to hear how you deal with stale records, so tell me in the comments.

title: Cómo evitar vender inventario inexistente: actualización condicional en SQLite
description:
Cómo evitar vender inventario inexistente: actualización condicional en SQLite

Una venta debería descontar existencias solo si queda cantidad suficiente. El clásico patrón «leer stock, restar y guardar» puede fallar cuando dos operaciones se ejecutan casi a la vez.

El problema y el alcance del ejemplo

La ficha de POSManager: TPV y Caja Ventas resume su función así: «TPV y caja para comercios: controla ventas, stock y tickets desde el móvil.» POSManager describe cobros, ventas, tickets y control de stock. Para estudiar una decisión de diseño vinculada al inventario, usamos una actualización SQL condicionada dentro de una transacción. No estamos describiendo la base de datos real del producto.

Cómo reproducir la idea

Puedes ejecutarlo con Python 3, que incluye SQLite. Guarda el archivo como venta.py y ejecútalo. La base está en memoria para que cada prueba comience desde cero.

import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE productos(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, stock INTEGER NOT NULL)")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE ventas(producto INTEGER, cantidad INTEGER)")
db.execute("INSERT INTO productos VALUES(1, 3)")
db.commit()

def vender(producto, cantidad):
    if cantidad <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Cantidad inválida")
    with db:  # transacción y rollback automático ante error
        cur = db.execute(
            "UPDATE productos SET stock=stock-? WHERE id=? AND stock>=?",
            (cantidad, producto, cantidad),
        )
        if cur.rowcount != 1:
            raise ValueError("Stock insuficiente o producto inexistente")
        db.execute("INSERT INTO ventas VALUES(?, ?)", (producto, cantidad))

vender(1, 2)
print("Stock restante:", db.execute("SELECT stock FROM productos").fetchone()[0])
try:
    vender(1, 2)
except ValueError as e:
    print("Venta rechazada:", e)

Qué demuestra el código

La condición stock >= ? se verifica en la misma instrucción que descuenta inventario. Si ninguna fila fue modificada, la venta no se inserta. La transacción relaciona los dos efectos: movimiento de stock y registro de venta.

Pruebas recomendadas

Deberías obtener stock 1 tras la primera venta y rechazo de la segunda. Prueba vender 0 unidades y un identificador desconocido. Comprueba que la tabla de ventas contiene únicamente una fila.

Límites que conviene reconocer

La prueba no modela devoluciones, cobros, sincronización offline, precios, impuestos ni múltiples dispositivos con inventarios divergentes. En un sistema distribuido la transacción local no resuelve por sí sola conflictos entre terminales.

Qué aprendemos

El stock es una invariante de negocio; conviene protegerla en la operación de escritura, no solo mediante validaciones en la interfaz.

Contexto y enlaces del autor

El tema se relaciona con las funciones declaradas públicamente de POSManager: TPV y Caja Ventas, una aplicación Android de AppInitDev. El código anterior es un ejemplo independiente: no se ha inspeccionado el repositorio privado ni se afirma que sea la implementación interna de la app. La referencia aparece al final para ofrecer contexto, no como requisito para completar el tutorial.

  • Google Play: POSManager: TPV y Caja Ventas
  • Página de la aplicación: https://posmanager.appinitdev.com/
  • Sitio del desarrollador: AppInitDev

title: How artificial intelligence is changing our shopping this holiday season
description:
New retail data shows AI-driven shopping research jumped 200% year-over-year, with half of consumers utilizing AI assistants during purchasing.

Salesforce projects chat agents will drive 20% of global web traffic, reflecting shifting developer and architectural demands in e-commerce platforms.

AI assistants are taking a central role in product search, with predictions that 20% of global e-commerce traffic will come from such systems. For brands, this requires a change in strategy: classic search engine optimization (SEO) is no longer enough. It is necessary to provide structured and constantly updated data on product prices, features and availability, so that digital assistants can reliably identify and recommend them.

At the same time, businesses are investing in specialized “AI shopping agents” for their own platforms, which handle needs such as order updates, returns, loyalty programs and customer service. Salesforce predicts that by Cyber ​​Week 2026, one in three e-commerce sites will have its own personalized AI agent. The data shows that companies that adopted such technology last holiday season recorded a 6,2% sales growth rate, compared to 3,9% for those that did not have such tools.

In the social media space, “social commerce” is now growing nine times faster than traditional e-commerce, with the younger generation (Gen Z) leading the way in using these channels for shopping. Despite this digital shift, the physical store remains a key factor: 77% of consumers plan to shop in physical locations, while 79% use their mobile phone in-store to compare prices or search for information. Overall, 38% of the value of holiday sales is estimated to come from hybrid shopping journeys, which combine digital research with physical presence.

title: Alternative Storage Providers — Signed User Files and Retention Recovery
description:
Short answer: choose the recovery contract before comparing storage rates. For a B2B SaaS product storing user files that must remain available until an explicit deletion deadline, Backblaze B2 is the easiest place to run a free-tier experiment, Wasabi is a storage-focused option without a free tier, and AWS S3 is the broad ecosystem baseline. The right choice depends on what happens after a timeout, a rate limit, or a worker crash.

The implementation I would ship starts with one invariant: each document has a stable application ID, and every write attempt uses it. The database owns the document state and deletion deadline. Object storage owns bytes. A worker reconciles the two, uses private access, and returns a presigned URL when a user needs to download a document.

For a team considering an alternative platform, Infrai is a narrower fit: one key and one bill can cover storage beside other backend services, while its public discovery surface describes request schemas and runnable examples. I would validate the storage contract before committing a signed-document workflow to it: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/storage/answers/store-user-uploaded-documents-%63%68%65%61%70%65%73%74-backend-option-d/

Retries are part of the data model.

The failure path is part of the storage decision

A client can disconnect after the service has accepted the final bytes. A rate limit can arrive after a multipart session has created state. A worker can time out while the object exists but the metadata row still says uploading.

I start with the application identity rather than the provider's object key. The key can contain a version or a random suffix, but the database decides which object is current. That gives retries a destination without asking a provider to infer intent, and it prevents a second attempt from silently replacing a signed file.

The deletion deadline belongs in the database and worker queue. A lifecycle rule is a useful second line of defense, not the only legal or product record. The shortest lifecycle supported by this storage surface is 1 day, and unfinished multipart fragments do not have an automatic cleanup rule, so abandoned sessions need an explicit worker path.

Here is the small policy test I would run before connecting a provider adapter. The fake client makes this runnable as-is. Its stable idempotency key, status-aware retry, and Retry-After handling are the parts worth carrying into production.

import time
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class UploadResult:
    object_key: str
    request_id: str


class RetryableUploadError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, status: int, retry_after: float | None = None):
        self.status = status
        self.retry_after = retry_after


class FakeObjectStore:
    def __init__(self):
        self.calls = 0

    def put(self, object_key, payload, idempotency_key):
        self.calls += 1
        if self.calls == 1:
            raise RetryableUploadError(429, retry_after=0.01)
        return UploadResult(object_key, idempotency_key)


def put_with_recovery(store, object_key, payload, document_id, max_attempts=4):
    key = f"signed-document:{document_id}"
    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        try:
            return store.put(object_key, payload, key)
        except RetryableUploadError as error:
            if error.status != 429 or attempt == max_attempts - 1:
                raise
            delay = error.retry_after if error.retry_after is not None else 2**attempt
            time.sleep(delay)
    raise RuntimeError("unreachable")


store = FakeObjectStore()
result = put_with_recovery(
    store, "signed/contract-1842.pdf", b"example bytes", "contract-1842"
)
print(result.object_key, result.request_id, store.calls)

The 429 branch is only half the point. Every attempt carries the same identity. A real adapter must surface non-2xx responses, honor Retry-After, and distinguish a timeout from a confirmed rejection. Ignoring the response body is how a useful upload becomes an incident.

Which alternative storage providers offer a free tier for storing user files safely?

Option Useful starting point Main boundary
Backblaze B2 Free-tier experiments and S3-compatible migration Validate access-request and bandwidth behavior
Wasabi Predictable storage-focused operation No free tier for experimentation
AWS S3 Broad ecosystem and a familiar control case Calculate storage, bandwidth, and operations
Infrai One key and one bill across backend services Private signed storage when limits fit

Backblaze B2 and Wasabi are the strongest cost-conscious alternatives here, with different experiments in mind. B2 is useful for a free-tier trial and offers competitive pricing on additional storage and access requests. Wasabi has a low flat-rate storage model, but the lack of a free tier makes experimentation a paid exercise. Both provide S3-compatible APIs, which reduces migration work, but compatibility does not make their retry, deletion, and bandwidth behavior identical.

AWS S3 is the baseline I would keep in the comparison. It is the control case for compatibility, surrounding tooling, and organizational familiarity. Its bill still needs to be calculated across storage, bandwidth, and operations; that calculation matters especially for a file-sharing product with large downloads.

Test all three with the same 10 GB fixture set, retry schedule, and download pattern. Record completion, recovery after a dropped connection, rate-limit behavior, deletion timing, and the application work required to reconcile an object with its database row. This is a test plan, not a claimed benchmark.

Infrai belongs in a narrower part of the decision. Its positioning is one key and one bill across backend services, so a team that already uses several backend capabilities does not have to gather credentials across a dozen provider dashboards or reconcile a pile of invoices. The second advantage is operationally relevant here: the API is plain REST, and its public discovery surface exposes request schemas and runnable examples; documented capabilities have examples in 10 languages. A Python service can inspect the contract and send HTTP without adding a storage SDK, while another service can use the same platform convention.

My recommendation is explicit: try Infrai for a workflow that values one backend key and bill plus a self-describing REST contract, using private signed-document storage only when its storage boundaries fit. Choose B2 when a low-friction trial is the deciding constraint, Wasabi when its storage-focused model fits the workload, and S3 when ecosystem breadth is the priority.

The limitation is a selection criterion. The storage surface has no public or public-read ACL, so it does not fit permanent public links, image hosting, or static-site hosting. It has no object versioning or object lock, so it is not the sole control for immutable, finance-grade retention. There is no If-Match conditional write, so strict concurrent updates need queue or database coordination. Browser-direct uploads cannot be configured through an independent CORS route, so that transfer boundary needs separate handling. A storage specialist is the better choice for those cases.

The database decides.

How should the recovery and deletion contract be tested?

I use a short failure matrix. Kill the connection during a large upload and verify resume or a safe new attempt under the same document identity. Force a 429 and verify exponential backoff rather than a tight loop. Crash the worker after storage succeeds but before the database transaction finishes; a reconciler should make one deliberate decision. Run deletion twice and make the second pass harmless.

Inspect what can actually be queried. Listing supports prefix filtering, but server-side metadata search is not available. Keep tenant ownership, signer, document state, and deletion deadline queryable in the database rather than assuming object metadata can be searched later.

For multipart work, keep an upload record with the provider upload ID, document ID, expected size, checksum policy, and state transitions. Clean up abandoned sessions through a worker. When a presigned URL is returned, do not send the service authorization header to that URL; the URL is the transfer authorization.

The checklist belongs beside the adapter: stable document identity, private access, database-owned deadlines, status-aware retries, idempotent consumers, reconciliation, and a provider-specific large-file test. Add an audit event for each state transition. Then measure bandwidth and operations with representative sharing traffic.

For the private write, the adapter can keep the verified route and transport rules in one small function. It uses an environment variable, an explicit method, a stable idempotency key, and a complete URL. The live request schema should still be checked before choosing payload fields.

import os
import time
from urllib.error import HTTPError, URLError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def put_private_object(bucket, key, payload, document_id, attempts=4):
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/documents/signed%2Fcontract-1842.pdf"
    # Copyable request shape: curl -X PUT 'https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/documents/signed%2Fcontract-1842.pdf' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY' -H 'Idempotency-Key: signed-document:contract-1842' -H 'Content-Type: application/octet-stream' --data-binary @signed/contract-1842.pdf
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        request = Request(
            url,
            data=payload,
            method="PUT",
            headers={
                "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
                "Idempotency-Key": f"signed-document:{document_id}",
                "Content-Type": "application/octet-stream",
            },
        )
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=60) as response:
                if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"storage returned HTTP {response.status}")
                return response.read()
        except HTTPError as error:
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == attempts - 1:
                raise RuntimeError(error.read().decode("utf-8", "replace")) from error
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt)
        except URLError:
            if attempt == attempts - 1:
                raise
            time.sleep(2**attempt)


put_private_object("documents", "signed/contract-1842.pdf", b"document", "contract-1842")

The request is deliberately private. A download path should ask the service for a presigned URL, then use that URL as the transfer authorization; it should not attach the Infrai bearer token to the returned URL. The application still decides who may access the document and when the database state allows deletion.

One more failure is easy to miss. Suppose the final part arrives, the storage response is delayed, and the worker retries while the first request is still being processed. Without a stable key, the database can point at one object while a second object consumes space, or a late response can overwrite the state written by the retry. With a stable document ID, the reconciler has something concrete to compare: the expected object key, the recorded provider request, the byte count, and the deletion deadline.

That does not remove every provider-specific decision. It makes the decision visible, testable, and boring to operate after a network failure, which is exactly what a retention workflow needs.

Further reading

  • OWASP, File Upload Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • AWS, Amazon S3 User Guide: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Welcome.html
  • Backblaze, B2 Cloud Storage: https://www.backblaze.com/cloud-storage
  • Wasabi, Wasabi Hot Cloud Storage: https://wasabi.com/cloud-storage-pricing/
  • Infrai, Storage bucket discovery: https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.bucket.create

title: How One Flash Decoder Made Robots 5 Faster—See the Numbers
description:
VFlash — Why Parallel Visual‑Planning Is Finally Leaving the Lab

Lead:

“A 30 ms visual‑planning latency on a single RTX 4090” reads like a brag in a marketing deck, but the numbers in the latest VFlash pre‑print prove the claim. The method replaces the slow, token‑by‑token generation that has haunted vision‑language models for years with a single‑shot “flash” of spatial primitives.

If you watch any robotics demo from the past six months, you’ll notice a subtle shift: the camera feed no longer lags behind the robot’s motion. That shift stems from VFlash’s parallel primitive decoding and KV‑cache sharing, two tricks that squeeze out both speed and memory.

Below I break down how the technique works, why it matters for real‑time systems, and what the market will likely do with a tool that finally lets perception and planning share the same millisecond budget.

The Case Study: From Autoregressive Bottleneck to Flash Planning

Imagine a warehouse robot that must locate a red box, compute a grasp pose, and then drive to a drop‑off zone—all while the conveyor belt keeps moving.

A traditional pipeline looks like this:

  1. Vision encoder extracts image tokens.
  2. Autoregressive decoder spits out a language‑style plan: “go to (x₁,y₁), then (x₂,y₂)…”.
  3. Planner translates the token list into joint trajectories.

Each decoding step re‑runs the attention mechanism, builds a new key‑value (KV) cache, and forces the system to wait for the previous token’s probability distribution. On a 30 Hz control loop, that latency adds up to 80–120 ms—far too much for dynamic environments.

VFlash rewrites the loop:

  1. Encoder stays the same, feeding a rich visual embedding into a shared KV cache.
  2. Plan template (e.g., “move to the red cup”) arrives as a short textual cue.
  3. Flash decoder treats the required primitives—grasp point, approach vector, target box—as slots in a single forward pass. It reads the shared KV cache, writes the coordinates for all slots simultaneously, and returns a compact tensor of (x, y, z, confidence) values.

Because the decoder never iterates token by token, it finishes in a single GPU kernel launch. The KV cache, built once per frame, serves every primitive, cutting memory usage by roughly 30 % (see the table in the brief).

The result? The robot receives a complete 3‑D plan in ≈12 ms, well within a 30 Hz loop, and can start moving while the next camera frame arrives.

The Meat: Hard Numbers That Matter

Metric Autoregressive Baseline (Flamingo‑3B) VFlash (Flash‑Primitive Decoding)
Inference time (10‑primitive plan) 68 ms (RTX 4090) 11 ms
GPU memory (KV cache) 4.2 GB 2.9 GB
Endpoint error (RoboTHOR) 2.4 cm 2.5 cm
AP on VQA‑Plan 42.1 % 45.3 %
Throughput increase (ABB pick‑and‑place pilot) – +18 % parts/hr
Planning frequency (NVIDIA System‑1 demo) 5 Hz 30 Hz

Key stat: VFlash delivers a 5–7× speed‑up with ≤1 % accuracy loss on standard robotics benchmarks.

Why the speed boost happens

  1. Parallel slot prediction – The decoder predicts all primitives in one matrix multiplication instead of a sequential softmax loop.
  2. Shared KV cache – Each primitive reads the same attention keys and values; the model avoids re‑computing attention for every step.
  3. Reduced token vocabulary – By treating coordinates as continuous outputs rather than discrete tokens, the softmax overhead disappears.

The memory reduction follows the same logic: one cache per frame versus one per token.

Real‑world latency gains

  • Industrial cobot (ABB, 2026 pilot): end‑to‑end perception‑to‑action latency dropped from 95 ms to 28 ms, allowing the arm to handle faster conveyor speeds.
  • Autonomous driving stack (NVIDIA System‑1 on Orin X): trajectory generation time fell from 120 ms to 18 ms, enabling a 30 Hz planning loop in dense city traffic.
  • Drone swarm (AirSim + ROS2 simulation): formation re‑configuration time cut in half when each UAV exchanged flash plans instead of iterative consensus messages.

These figures prove that VFlash does not merely win academic benchmarks; it reshapes the latency budget that real systems can afford.

The Pivot: Risks and Open Questions

No technology arrives without trade‑offs. VFlash’s design choices raise several concerns that engineers should weigh before shipping.

1. Loss of Fine‑Grained Control

Because VFlash outputs a fixed‑size set of primitives, it cannot dynamically extend the plan mid‑inference. Complex tasks that require conditional branching (e.g., “if obstacle, replan”) still need a fallback autoregressive module or a secondary planner.

Mitigation: Hybrid pipelines that invoke VFlash for the bulk of the plan and fall back to a lightweight autoregressive decoder when the environment triggers an exception.

2. Sensitivity to Template Quality

The decoder relies on a plan template—a short textual cue that defines the primitive set. Poorly phrased templates (e.g., ambiguous language, missing object qualifiers) can degrade the cross‑modal consistency loss, leading to higher endpoint error.

Mitigation: Use a small, supervised prompt‑tuning stage on the target domain. Early experiments on the VQA‑Plan benchmark show a +3 % AP gain after just 200 labeled examples.

3. Scaling to Hundreds of Primitives

Current results focus on 5–15 primitives per frame, suitable for most manipulation and navigation tasks. Scaling to hundreds (e.g., dense scene graphs for AR) would inflate the output tensor and could saturate GPU memory despite KV sharing.

Mitigation: Hierarchical flashing—first predict coarse region primitives, then flash detailed sub‑primitives only for regions of interest.

4. Hardware Dependence

The biggest speed gains appear on high‑end GPUs (RTX 4090, Orin X). Edge devices like the Jetson Nano still benefit from KV‑cache sharing, but the absolute latency hovers around 30 ms, which may be borderline for sub‑10 ms control loops.

Mitigation: Model quantization (int8) combined with TensorRT optimizations can shave another 5–8 ms on the Nano, according to NVIDIA’s internal benchmarks.

The Outlook: Where VFlash Could Go Next

1. Cloud‑Edge Inference APIs

Companies building Robotics‑as‑a‑Service platforms can expose VFlash as a low‑latency endpoint. Clients send a camera frame plus a textual template; the service returns a flash plan in under 15 ms. The memory savings allow multi‑tenant GPU usage, reducing cost per inference.

2. Integration with Foundation Models

Large vision‑language foundations (e.g., System‑1, LLaVA‑2) already provide robust encoders. Adding a flash decoder as a plug‑in layer turns any pre‑trained VLM into a real‑time planner without retraining the entire backbone. Early open‑source experiments on HuggingFace show a +12 % reduction in planning error when the start pose feeds directly into the decoder slots.

3. Cross‑modal Consistency as a Training Standard

The cross‑modal primitive loss that VFlash introduced aligns language commands with continuous coordinates. If the community adopts this loss, future VLMs might output structured plans by default, making flash decoding a natural extension rather than a specialized add‑on.

4. Safety‑Critical Certification

Because VFlash reduces latency and memory usage, verification teams can run more exhaustive Monte‑Carlo simulations within the same compute budget. This could accelerate certification for autonomous vehicles and medical robots, where deterministic timing matters as much as accuracy.

Closing Thoughts

VFlash does not rewrite the fundamentals of visual perception, but it re‑architects the bridge between perception and action. By collapsing a sequence of token predictions into a single parallel burst, the method clears a path for truly real‑time visual planning. The data from the November 2026 pre‑print, the ABB pilot, and NVIDIA’s System‑1 demo all point to the same conclusion: speed gains now outweigh the tiny accuracy penalty.

Engineers who care about latency should start prototyping flash decoders today, even if they later fall back to an autoregressive safety net for edge cases. The market signals—RaaS contracts demanding sub‑20 ms loops, AV platforms hunting for 30 Hz planners—suggest that the next wave of commercial robotics will lean heavily on parallel visual‑planning.

If you can get a flash plan out of a camera in under a dozen milliseconds, you already own the timing advantage most competitors still chase with slower, token‑by‑token pipelines. The question now is not whether VFlash works, but how quickly the ecosystem can integrate it into production stacks.

title: Node.js Retrieval Architecture for Healthcare Appointment Citation Tracing
description:
Healthcare appointment assistants should use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that can be traced back to a URL or document identifier. The answer is not “put every clinic document in one vector index.” A scheduler needs a small, reviewable evidence set: current appointment policy, location details, and the exact record that justified each sentence.

Short answer: map each user-visible answer to a retrieval contract, retrieve a bounded candidate set, rerank it for relevance and freshness, and return citations with the context; keep writes and deletes deliberate so an outdated appointment policy cannot survive in the collection.

How can a healthcare appointment assistant make retrieval citations auditable?

Start with the output, not the embedding model. For every answer field, define the evidence it is allowed to use. “Earliest available visit” might require a scheduling record with an observed timestamp; “bring a referral” might require a policy document and its effective date. The contract should carry source_url, document_id, updated_at, and a collection name alongside the text chunk. A model can then explain uncertainty instead of blending two clinics’ rules.

The contract also gives the reranker a boundary. Fetch, for example, a fixed top-k candidate set from the appointment-policy collection, then score lexical match, semantic relevance, and freshness in a separate stage. Do not let a broad web result silently outrank an internal policy. In a payment or ledger service I would insist on the same discipline: an audit trail is more useful than a clever score when someone asks why a result was shown.

Keep the query bounded. Set a deadline for each source, cap retries, and return a partial answer with visible citations when a slow source misses its budget. This is an exactly-once mindset applied to reading: one request should produce one reproducible evidence bundle, even if a downstream call is retried.

That boundary is where a gateway can help early.

For a team prototyping this workflow, Infrai is a reasonable place to put the collection call: its REST surface means the same HTTP contract can be used from Go, Node.js, or a service written in another language, while one key covers adjacent backend capabilities. The choice still leaves citation metadata and clinical authorization in your application, where reviewers can inspect them.

How should chunking and freshness shape the appointment search?

Chunk by the unit a reviewer can approve. A clinic’s cancellation rule, a same-day booking rule, and a holiday schedule should not share one giant chunk merely because they live in one PDF. Preserve headings and effective dates in metadata, and keep a stable document_id when the source is re-indexed. Small chunks improve citation precision; overly small chunks lose the conditions that make a rule safe to apply.

Freshness needs an explicit policy. On ingestion, upsert a changed document with a new content hash, then remove records for documents that were deleted upstream. A nightly job can catch drift, but an event-driven update is preferable for appointment availability. Retain the old identifier in an audit log rather than leaving its vector searchable. The cost is storage and review work; the benefit is that a clinician can reconstruct the evidence used at a particular time.

Audit trails matter.

Consider a policy PDF that changes at 09:00 while a patient is asking about a 10:30 visit. The ingestion worker should write the new hash, effective timestamp, and source URL before the retriever is allowed to use that version; a concurrent query can then either cite the previous version explicitly or wait for the new one, but it must not silently mix clauses from both. Store the retrieval request, candidate identifiers, reranker scores, and final citations with the assistant response. When a reviewer later sees “arrive 15 minutes early,” they can identify the exact page and revision, reproduce the bounded query, and determine whether the rule was current. This record is not busywork: it is the evidence that separates a correct correction from a mysterious change in model behavior. It also gives operations a clean place to measure stale-document hits without exposing patient data in debug logs.

Comparing integration paths for citation tracing

The practical choice is less about a leaderboard and more about how many moving parts your team must operate. Pinecone offers a hosted vector workflow with a focused SDK surface. Weaviate provides an open-source and hosted option with schema features. Elasticsearch is attractive when an existing search cluster already owns analyzers, filters, and operational dashboards. A single backend gateway can reduce credential and client sprawl, but it does not remove the need for a retrieval contract or a deletion policy.

Option Setup and credentials Citation and freshness work Good fit Trade-off
Pinecone Hosted index and one vendor credential; SDK-led integration Metadata is available, while application code must enforce source tracing and re-index rules Teams wanting a focused managed vector service A separate search stack may still be needed for lexical constraints
Weaviate Hosted or self-managed deployment with schema configuration Rich object metadata supports identifiers and timestamps Teams comfortable owning a schema-backed vector store More deployment choices mean more operational decisions
Elasticsearch Often already present in the platform; familiar auth and query tooling Strong filters and text search help bound candidates; vector freshness remains your pipeline’s job Organizations standardizing on one search cluster Vector tuning can compete with existing cluster workloads
Infrai One REST API and one key can cover vector calls and adjacent backend capabilities, without installing an SDK The same application contract can call collection and record operations while retaining its own citation metadata Teams reducing integration friction across a mixed backend It is not suitable when you need Elasticsearch-specific analyzers or a deeply customized vector index; stick with Elasticsearch there

The reason to try Infrai here is contract stability: you can keep the application’s HTTP boundary while changing the service behind a capability, instead of rewriting every language client. Its broad, self-describing discovery surface also makes a first integration easier to inspect. That convenience is an integration advantage, not proof that its ranking is superior. Your mileage may vary when governance requires a specialist’s on-prem controls.

A minimal collection lifecycle in Go

The write path below creates an explicit collection. Production code should add an idempotency key to every mutating request, record the response request ID, and apply exponential backoff for 429 responses while honoring Retry-After. The API key stays outside source control.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    payload := map[string]any{
        "name": "appointment-policy",
        "metadata": map[string]string{"purpose": "citation-tracing"},
    }
    body, _ := json.Marshal(payload)
    req, _ := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/collection/create", bytes.NewReader(body))
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "appointment-policy-2026-09-01")

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 5 * time.Second}
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    data, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
        panic("rate limited; retry with exponential backoff and Retry-After")
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("collection create failed: %s", data))
    }
    fmt.Println(string(data))
}

The collection name is intentionally boring. That makes it easy to audit, and it leaves the medically meaningful fields in your own contract rather than hiding them in a vendor-specific schema. For deletion, use the documented vector delete operation after a source-of-truth deletion event; never treat a failed fetch as permission to erase records.

The request is a POST to https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/collection/create with Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY; the Go sample makes those choices explicit.

Where the design should stop

This architecture is a poor fit for a team that needs millisecond-level, feature-rich lexical queries over a large existing corpus, or for a compliance program that mandates a particular self-hosted engine. Elasticsearch may be the better choice in those cases. It is also not a substitute for appointment-system authorization: retrieval can cite a policy, but the scheduling service must still check identity, consent, and slot ownership before confirming a visit.

I am not sure any static chunk size will remain optimal as clinic policies evolve; measure citation misses and stale-document hits against a labeled review set, then adjust chunk boundaries deliberately. The important invariant is simpler: every answer has bounded evidence, every evidence item has a traceable origin, and every index change is auditable.

Teams that want to validate the collection contract can start with the vector retrieval guide, then compare its boundary with their own authorization and retention rules.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/index.html

title: ThreatsDay: 20 Vulnerabilities & Breaches Exposing Enterprise Blind Spots
description:
Originally published on satyamrastogi.com

A single stolen credential can compromise multiple systems. Trusted configurations become attack vectors. Patch delays spanning months to years leave critical infrastructure exposed. We break down 20 critical incidents.

Executive Summary

ThreatsDay's latest threat briefing exposes a troubling pattern: attackers don't need sophistication when defenders leave low-hanging fruit dangling. From Apache OFBiz remote code execution to DreamHost credential compromise and DeFi site hijacking, the attack surface remains vast and painfully slow to remediate. Organizations face a compounding problem: rapid vulnerability discovery outpacing patch deployment, privilege escalation through trusted settings abuse, and lateral movement enabled by credential reuse across systems.

This briefing consolidates 20+ incidents spanning the week, revealing systemic weaknesses in perimeter defense, credential hygiene, and incident response timelines.

Attack Vector & MITRE Framework

Initial Access & Exploitation

Apache OFBiz RCE: CVE-class vulnerability enabling T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application). Attackers gained unauthenticated RCE against improperly patched OFBiz instances, likely through REST API endpoints or XML deserialization flaws.

DreamHost Credential Breach: T1589 (Gather Victim Identity Information) combined with T1110 (Brute Force). Compromised credentials enable T1078 (Valid Accounts) for lateral movement across hosting infrastructure.

DeFi Site Hijacking: T1195 (Supply Chain Compromise) or T1583 (Acquire Infrastructure). Attackers redirected DNS records or compromised domain registrar access, enabling T1556 (Modify Authentication Process) for phishing and fund theft.

Privilege Escalation & Persistence

Trusted Settings Abuse: T1548 (Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism). Attackers exploit admin console defaults, RBAC misconfigurations, and overprivileged service accounts to lock legitimate users out while maintaining persistence.

File Copy Operations: T1570 (Lateral Tool Transfer) and T1005 (Data from Local System). Simple cp, scp, or WebDAV requests move malicious payloads between systems without triggering endpoint detection.

Technical Deep Dive

Apache OFBiz RCE Mechanics

OFBiz instances running versions prior to the patched release are vulnerable to unauthenticated RCE through malformed requests to service endpoints. The vulnerability stems from improper input validation in XML/JSON parsing routines. Attackers craft payloads using ObjectInputStream gadget chains or OGNL expression injection, leading to arbitrary code execution as the web service user account.

Kill chain: Reconnaissance (shodan/censys for OFBiz banners) → Payload delivery (HTTP POST to /webtools/control/) → Code execution (reverse shell or command execution) → Lateral movement.

DreamHost Breach Analysis

Compromised credentials likely sourced from:

  • Password reuse across services (victims' prior breaches)
  • Phishing campaigns targeting shared hosting administrators
  • Insider threat or former employee access

Once inside DreamHost control panels, attackers could:

  • Modify DNS records for customer domains
  • Access SSH keys and API tokens
  • Pivot to customer-hosted applications
  • Maintain persistence through backdoored control panel plugins

Impact scope: Multi-tenancy architecture means a single compromised account can affect hundreds of customer sites.

DeFi Site Hijacking Techniques

DNS takeover: Registrar account compromise or expired DNSSEC keys allowed attacker control of A/CNAME records, redirecting victims to phishing replicas.

Wallet theft: Cloned UI captures private keys or approves malicious token transfers via signature requests.

Liquidity pool manipulation: Attackers with site access injected smart contract calls draining pools or minting tokens.

Patching Delay Problem

A critical red flag: some vulnerabilities taking 12+ months to reach patch deployment. Why?

  1. Coordinated disclosure timelines: Vendors often delay public patches 90+ days post-notification
  2. Legacy system complexity: Critical infrastructure running unsupported versions (EOL software)
  3. Change management friction: Enterprise approval processes for security patches requiring extensive testing
  4. Fragmented vendor ecosystem: Organizations managing patches across 50+ vendors without centralized tracking

During this window, attackers freely exploit known vulnerabilities against unpatched instances. This is not a CVSS problem-it's an operational maturity problem.

Detection Strategy

Network Level

  • Monitor for OFBiz requests to /webtools/control/ with POST payloads containing serialized objects or XML entities
  • Alert on DNS record changes for high-value domains (real-time zone file monitoring)
  • Detect unusual DreamHost API calls from non-corporate IP ranges

Host Level

  • Hunt for ObjectInputStream or OGNL expression patterns in application logs
  • Monitor service account file operations (unexpected cp/scp to sensitive directories)
  • Track authentication failures followed by successful admin logins from same source

Application Level

  • Log all credential usage and cross-reference with threat feeds for compromised passwords
  • Implement behavior analytics for DeFi transaction patterns (unusual gas spending, token approvals)
  • Monitor domain registrar API logs for unauthorized DNS changes

SIEM/EDR Rules 

Rule: OFBiz RCE Attempt
Condition: HTTP_METHOD=POST AND URL CONTAINS "/webtools/" AND (PAYLOAD CONTAINS "ObjectInputStream" OR PAYLOAD CONTAINS "rO0AB")

Rule: Lateral File Transfer
Condition: PROCESS=scp OR PROCESS=cp AND DESTINATION=/root OR DESTINATION=/home AND SOURCE_CONTEXT=non-admin

Rule: DreamHost Credential Misuse
Condition: LOGIN_SOURCE != CORPORATE_IP_RANGE AND LOGIN_SUCCESS AND NEXT_ACTION=ZONE_FILE_MODIFY

Mitigation Roadmap

Immediate (0-7 days)

  1. Patch Apache OFBiz: Update to patched version; if impossible, firewall /webtools/ endpoints
  2. Credential reset: Force password change for all DreamHost/shared hosting admin accounts
  3. MFA enforcement: Require TOTP/FIDO2 for registrar and hosting control panels
  4. DNS monitoring: Enable DNSSEC and configure alerts for unexpected zone changes

Short-term (1-4 weeks)

  1. Incident response drill: Simulate DeFi site hijacking; test SOC response time
  2. File integrity monitoring: Deploy FIM on critical servers to detect unauthorized copies
  3. Vulnerability assessment: Scan for other OFBiz instances; inventory EOL software
  4. Credential hygiene audit: Check for password reuse across services (breach database cross-reference)

Long-term (1-6 months)

  1. Patch management SLA: Reduce time-to-patch for critical vulns from 12+ months to 30 days
  2. Zero-trust architecture: Assume no credential is trustworthy; enforce device posture + context-aware access
  3. Supplier risk program: Include patch velocity in SLA negotiations with vendors
  4. Immutable infrastructure: Container-based deployments reduce attack surface for file copy exploits

Key Takeaways

  1. Credentials are keys to the kingdom: A single compromised account cascades across multi-tenant systems. Implement graduated privilege, session isolation, and anomaly detection.

  2. Patching delays are unacceptable risk: 12+ months between vulnerability disclosure and deployment is operational negligence. Enforce 30-day SLAs for critical patches.

  3. Trusted settings are attack amplifiers: Admin defaults, overprivileged service accounts, and weak RBAC are easier to exploit than zero-days. Audit before patching.

  4. Simple techniques beat complex tools: cp and credential reuse require no malware; focus defensive effort on access control, not just detection.

  5. DeFi sites inherit web2 risks: DNS hijacking, registrar compromise, and phishing remain effective despite blockchain claims. Site security is orthogonal to smart contract security.

Related Articles

  • Zyxel Switch Zero-Day: CVE-2026-107441 OOB Write RCE
  • DigiCert Data Breach: Server Migration Exposes PKI Credentials
  • CWPdoor Linux Backdoor: Trojanized Web Server Supply Chain Attack
  • French Blood Service Cyberattack: SCADA Manipulation & Supply Chain Risk
  • Google Disrupts 1.3M-Device XCPE Botnet: Videostrong Backdoor Analysis

References

  • MITRE ATT&CK: T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application
  • MITRE ATT&CK: T1078 Valid Accounts
  • NIST Cybersecurity Framework: Respond
  • CISA: Vulnerability Disclosure Best Practices
  • OWASP: Authentication Cheat Sheet

title: How to Learn from Incident Postmortems (Without Forgetting the Fix by Next Outage)
description:
The outage is over. The graph is green again. Someone drops a postmortem link in Slack with five action items and a timeline that took two hours to write.

You open it. You nod. You react with 👀. Two months later the same class of failure shows up, and nobody can find the sentence that said "always set a timeout on that client." The doc still exists. The lesson does not.

That is the postmortem problem. Teams get better at writing them than at keeping the useful bits warm in people's heads.

Why the PDF and the wiki page both fail

A good postmortem is long on purpose. Timeline, impact, root cause, contributing factors, what went well, what did not. That length is right for the incident review meeting. It is wrong for the Tuesday six weeks later when you are about to ship a similar retry loop.

People treat the link as memory. Links are storage. Memory is the one or two constraints you can still say out loud when someone asks "what did we learn last time?"

Reading the full write-up again rarely happens. It feels like homework after a fire. So the action items rot in Jira, the doc sits in Confluence, and the next on-call inherits vibes instead of rules.

Pull out the rule, not the novel

Right after the review, while the argument is still sharp, capture the postmortem the same way you would save anything else you mean to keep. Browser save, share sheet, or Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+S if you use a Chrome extension. One library beats three Slack bookmarks and a Notion page you will never search under pressure.

What you need from that page is small. A short TL;DR. A handful of key takeaways. The one rule that would have prevented the repeat. Write that rule in your own words on a note card: "outbound HTTP to payments must have a 3s timeout and circuit breaker" beats a polished paragraph about "resilience."

I park those extractions in Recl. Share the postmortem URL or a screenshot of the action list, get a short summary and takeaways, drop a one-line "your note" while the review is fresh, and let the save land under a topic instead of a flat "incidents" dump.

Skip re-reading the full timeline in that first window. You just lived it. You need the portable rule, not another hour inside the document.

Put the lesson on a schedule you will actually open

Saving is not remembering. Incident knowledge fades between on-call rotations. You ship for a month, then blank on why that queue had a poison message policy.

Passive re-reading of the same Confluence page feels responsible and still leaves you stuck when a similar alert fires at 2 a.m. What helps is retrieval: close the doc and ask yourself what the timeout was, which dashboard lied, and which runbook step was missing. Wrong answers mark the fuzzy edge.

A light loop works. A few days later, a nudge asks whether you still remember this one. Answer from memory. If you blank, open the takeaway card, not the twenty-page write-up. On Sunday evening, a short weekly quiz over what you saved that week keeps a few rules warm without turning memory into a second job.

That is the Recall side of Recl. Nudges stay short on purpose. You are keeping a handful of incident rules warm enough that they show up before the next similar deploy, not memorizing every paragraph of every postmortem.

Any system that captures the rule and schedules a revisit works. Spaced repetition fits timeouts and ownership the same way it fits flashcards. The point is a reason to see the lesson again before the next outage asks for it.

Ask your library when the pager is loud

The real test is not the review meeting. It is a half-remembered incident from last quarter while a new alert is screaming.

Instead of scrubbing Slack for the old thread, ask your library. In Recl that means asking a question and getting an answer from your own saves, with sources, so you can jump straight to the takeaway that named the missing timeout. You pull from material you already chose to keep.

If you want to see how a clean takeaway card reads, browse library.recl.app. Your own postmortems still matter more. The point is a version you will open when the graph is red, not when you have an afternoon to re-read.

Folders and auto topics help here. Keep "payments timeouts" separate from "deploy rollbacks" so you are not scrolling a graveyard of every SEV-2 from last year.

A loop you can run after every review

  1. Capture the postmortem URL or the action list the same day as the review.
  2. Write one rule in your own words. If you cannot name a rule, the write-up did not finish its job.
  3. Keep the takeaways short enough to open under stress.
  4. Revisit on a light schedule. Fail the quiz honestly. Re-read your sentence, not the whole timeline.
  5. Before the next similar change, ask your library first instead of hoping Slack search remembers.

You do not need every postmortem you have ever starred. You need three rules from the last few months that you can still teach a new teammate at 1 a.m.

Postmortems fail as learning tools when the document becomes the product. Make the portable rule the product. Save it once. Bring it back on purpose. The next outage will still hurt. It does not have to hurt the same way twice.

Asutosh builds Recl — save what matters, recall it forever. Summaries, library topics, and spaced recall for the docs and videos you'd otherwise forget.

title: Cosa sono Loop e Graph in osFoundry e quando usare l'uno o l'altro?
description:
Sono le 18:40 e l'assistente AI ti ha appena detto che i test che fallivano sono stati sistemati. Li lanci tu. Due sono ancora rossi. Potresti incollare di nuovo l'output e chiedere ancora, oppure affidare il lavoro a qualcosa che si ferma solo quando il test runner gli dà ragione. La mattina dopo una collega del marketing ti fa una domanda diversa: una cosa del genere potrebbe controllare tre siti della concorrenza ogni giorno feriale prima che lei arrivi?

Entrambi i lavori stanno nello stesso angolo di osFoundry, sotto due voci di menu vicine: Loop e Graph.

Due modi per far lavorare gli agenti senza stargli dietro

Un Loop è un modo riutilizzabile per far lavorare un team di agenti verso un obiettivo. Mette insieme una rosa di agenti, un obiettivo scritto a parole semplici, un modo per verificare se l'obiettivo è raggiunto, limiti rigidi (quanti round, quanti fallimenti di fila prima di arrendersi) e, se vuoi, un trigger come una pianificazione. Lavora a round, valuta ogni round rispetto all'obiettivo e si ferma da solo. Un Graph è un programma di workflow salvato, per quando il percorso non è fisso: può diramarsi in base a un risultato, rifare una parte finché non passa, distribuire il lavoro a più agenti contemporaneamente, fermarsi per un'approvazione umana e chiamare altri graph. Tutti e due si trovano nella barra laterale principale dell'app desktop di osFoundry, prima Loop e subito sotto Graph, e la distinzione in una riga che dà l'app stessa è quella da ricordare: un Loop segue sempre lo stesso percorso, un Graph decide il suo percorso strada facendo.

Cosa vedi mentre un Loop è in esecuzione

Questa è una sessione Loop già conclusa (i test e i nomi dei file sono dati di esempio). Le parti da conoscere:

  • La colonna delle sessioni a sinistra. Ogni esecuzione di un Loop è una sessione a sé, con uno stato sotto. Qui "Verified" significa che l'ultimo round ha superato il controllo, non che l'AI l'ha detto.
  • La striscia dei round in cima alla colonna centrale. "Round 3 of 4", più il controllo usato ("Runs npm test — a zero exit code means done") e un contatore dei fallimenti di verifica consecutivi, che è ciò che ferma un loop che non va da nessuna parte.
  • La scheda Rounds. Una riga per round con quanti criteri ha soddisfatto ("1 of 3 met", "2 of 3 met", "3 of 3 met"). Apri un round per vedere esattamente quali criteri sono passati.
  • L'inspector a destra, con le schede Goal, Trigger e Hooks.
  • Pause e Cancel sopra i pannelli, per quando vuoi che si fermi subito e non al controllo successivo.

Caso 1: uno sviluppatore che vuole i test davvero verdi

Chi: uno sviluppatore che lavora da solo, a fine giornata, con una suite JavaScript rossa e un assistente che continua a cantare vittoria.

Apri Loop e premi New session. La finestra New loop run elenca loop pronti all'uso, e cercando "JS suite" trovi Get the JS suite green. Prima di avviarlo, la scheda a destra ti dice come si comporta: Who runs it (un agente debugger che guida tre specialisti di test), How it stops (al massimo 4 round, si ferma dopo 3 fallimenti di fila) e How it grades itself (esegue npm test, e solo un exit code zero vale come finito).

In Start it scegli Run once now invece di Just add it, selezioni il progetto e la cartella in cui devono lavorare gli agenti e premi Run it now. Poi apri la scheda Rounds e guardi. Nell'esecuzione di esempio, il primo round ha soddisfatto uno dei tre test, il secondo due e il terzo tutti e tre; a quel punto il loop si è fermato da solo e la sessione è stata segnata come Verified.

Quello che ottieni non è un messaggio in chat che dice di aver risolto, ma un registro round per round di quale test è passato e quando, valutato dal tuo test runner. Nella stessa lista ci sono loop per suite Python, Go, Rust e Java, errori di tipo, lint e test instabili.

Caso 2: chi fa marketing e vuole un report sulla concorrenza ogni giorno feriale

Chi: una persona del marketing o del prodotto che controlla a mano i siti dei concorrenti e non scrive codice.

Nella stessa finestra New loop run, la sezione in alto si chiama "Start here — these need nothing set up", e lì c'è Watch the competitors, perché cerca solo sul web e non tocca mai i tuoi file. In Goal for this run scrivi chi tenere d'occhio e cosa cercare (per esempio prezzi, nuove funzionalità e assunzioni), scegli Run once now e premi Run it now. Il primo report elenca solo ciò che è cambiato, con data e fonte su ogni riga, e le affermazioni di un'azienda su se stessa sono segnate come non verificate.

Per renderlo ricorrente, apri la scheda Trigger e premi Add a schedule. La finestra Run this on a schedule offre dei preset (Every 30 min, Hourly, Daily 09:00, Weekdays 09:00), mostra la riga cron e le prossime tre esecuzioni, e fa due domande pratiche: cosa fare se un'esecuzione è ancora in corso quando tocca alla successiva (Skip it, oppure Wait, then run) e cosa fare se il computer era in standby (Up to an hour late, Up to 12 hours late o However late).

Dopo Save schedule, la scheda Trigger mostra "On a schedule" con l'orario della prossima esecuzione. Lei si ritrova un report pronto ogni mattina dal lunedì al venerdì, senza aprire un terminale. Le pianificazioni girano mentre l'app desktop è aperta, ed è a questo che serve l'impostazione di recupero.

Caso 3: un team lead il cui workflow deve diramarsi

Chi: un responsabile che vuole che ogni file di una modifica grande venga revisionato separatamente, poi un unico report unificato, con un via libera umano prima di qualsiasi cosa irreversibile.

Qui un Loop non ha più la forma giusta. Un Loop ripete lo stesso piano a ogni round, mentre il responsabile ha bisogno di un revisore per file, poi di un passaggio di merge e a volte di una pausa per l'approvazione. Questo è un Graph.

Apri Graph e premi il pulsante più accanto alla lista. Create a Graph offre due strade: Start with a working graph (un programma sicuro ed eseguibile che poi adatti) oppure Choose a starter. Gli starter sono esempi completi di schemi comuni, ognuno con una breve nota su quando usarlo. Review each item, then merge esegue un agente per elemento in parallelo e poi un unico passaggio di merge. Triage and route classifica un input una volta e lo manda a esattamente uno specialista. Propose, ask, then apply elabora una modifica, si ferma ad aspettare la risposta di una persona e agisce solo con un sì.

Il programma in sé è codice, non un diagramma drag-and-drop, perché diramazioni e retry limitati sono vero flusso di controllo. Di solito lasci che Maestro o un agente lo scriva o lo modifichi, e gestisci ciò che conta ogni giorno in Configure session: Maximum agents at once, un avviso sui token, un Hard token ceiling, l'input predefinito e quale agente e modello usa ogni passaggio.

Quando parte, il pannello di esecuzione ha tre schede. Run mostra i passaggi in diretta e puoi usare Pause, Resume o Cancel. Se il graph arriva a un passaggio di approvazione, una scheda ti chiede Approve o Decline, e il resto del lavoro in parallelo va avanti mentre aspetta. Changes elenca i file che l'esecuzione ha creato o modificato, e alcune di queste modifiche si possono annullare. History elenca le esecuzioni precedenti, così un'esecuzione fallita e quella che l'ha sistemata stanno una accanto all'altra. Il responsabile ottiene una revisione ripetibile le cui esecuzioni e modifiche ai file si possono ispezionare in seguito. I graph si possono leggere nel browser, ma per eseguirli serve l'app desktop.

Dove Loop e Graph si passano il testimone

Nessuna delle due funzioni lavora da sola. Gli agenti nel Team roster di un Loop arrivano da Agent team e Agent Registry, e il loop stesso è un preset riutilizzabile che puoi versionare in osStudio, quindi alzare una soglia di qualità o un limite di retry lascia uno storico invece di una modifica silenziosa. Un Graph riceve un identificatore stabile quando viene creato proprio perché loop e altri graph possano chiamarlo: un Loop pianificato può quindi avviare un Graph con diramazioni alle 9:00. In Message, loop e graph possono essere membri di un canale accanto a persone e singoli agenti, così i loro aggiornamenti arrivano nella stanza abituale del team. Per approfondire la parte di pianificazione, vedi pianificare agenti con cron e i trigger degli agenti.

Le domande di chi inizia

Un Loop non è solo un cron job?
No. La pianificazione è solo una parte opzionale. Un Loop è un team più un obiettivo più un controllo, con limiti di round, e tiene un registro dei criteri soddisfatti in ogni round. Puoi eseguirne uno una volta a mano e non dargli mai un trigger.

Se anche un Loop può eseguire agenti in parallelo, perché dovrei usare Graph?
Il parallelismo non è la differenza. Scegli Graph quando il passo successivo dipende dal risultato del precedente: indirizzare a uno specialista, ripetere solo la parte che è fallita, aspettare il sì di una persona o chiamare un altro workflow. Se ogni esecuzione segue gli stessi passi, un Loop è più semplice.

Un loop può girare all'infinito e bruciarmi il budget API?
Ogni loop pronto all'uso ha un tetto di round e si ferma dopo un numero fisso di fallimenti consecutivi, e la scheda mostra entrambi prima di partire. I graph hanno Maximum agents at once e un Hard token ceiling nelle impostazioni di sessione.

Devo scrivere codice?
Per i Loop no: ne scegli uno e imposti obiettivo e trigger nelle finestre di dialogo. Il programma di un Graph è codice, ma puoi partire da uno starter, lasciare che Maestro o un agente lo modifichi e cambiare input, limiti e agenti per passaggio senza toccare il programma.

Puoi provarli entrambi nell'app desktop da osfoundry.io/it/download.

title: skills: A Chinese Translation of google/skills, and What the Repo Actually Contains
description:
google/skills is a repository of Agent Skills for Google products and technologies, including Google Cloud. It has 22,761 stars, is written primarily in Python, and ships under Apache-2.0. It is a skill collection, not a runnable application — the skills are Markdown-and-assets bundles that an AI agent loads when a task touches Google Cloud IAM, GKE, BigQuery, Gemini API, and similar surfaces.

A Chinese translation of the repository was published today: yangshun2005/skills-cn. It has zero stars at the time of writing. That number is not the point; the point is that the README, the skill descriptions, and the navigation structure are now readable in Chinese, which changes how quickly a Chinese-speaking developer can decide whether a given skill is relevant before installing it.

What an Agent Skill is, concretely

An Agent Skill is a directory with a SKILL.md file plus whatever supporting files the skill needs. The file describes when the skill applies and what procedure the agent should follow. When you install skills into an agent, you are not adding code that runs on its own — you are adding context the agent can pull in when a request matches.

That distinction matters for how you evaluate the repo. Reading the skill list is the actual work. Installing is one command.

Installing

The install path goes through npx:

npx skills add google/skills

If npx is not on the machine, install Node.js first — it bundles both npm and npx.

The command is interactive. You pick which skills to install (one or all), which target agent to configure, and whether the install is project-scoped or global. It is not a single-shot install of everything, which is deliberate: the repo is large enough that installing all of it would flood an agent's context with skills irrelevant to your work.

Updating:

npx skills update

This refreshes installed skills to their latest versions and offers to remove skills that are no longer present upstream. Read that prompt. If a skill you depend on was renamed or restructured, the removal option will take it out.

The skill inventory

The repository groups skills into three broad areas.

Google Cloud onboarding. Three skills cover the entry path: authentication and authorization (IAM), a foundation-builder recipe, and an onboarding walkthrough. If you are new to a Google Cloud project and want an agent to help you get oriented, these are the first ones to install.

Multi-product solution skills. This is the largest group and the most interesting one. It includes a solution architecture workflow, multi-agent security via Agent Gateway, agentic analytics across cloud providers and data types, a borderless open data lakehouse pattern, build-and-deploy-agents guidance, a data science workflow solution, dynamic hybrid search on AlloyDB, real-time bidirectional multimodal streaming, migration of AI workloads to GKE Inference, enterprise search RAG with GKE and AlloyDB, and a secure n-tier serverless web app pattern. There is also a "Google skill finder" skill in the developers group, which is a meta-skill for locating the right skill.

AI/ML platform operations. Skills for agent access auditing, alert configuration, endpoint management, an evaluation flywheel, and GenAI inference on the agent platform.

The names are long and specific. That is a feature. A skill called "使用 GKE 和 AlloyDB 的企业搜索 RAG" tells you in the title whether it applies to your architecture. A skill called "RAG helper" would not.

Why the Chinese version is worth the trouble

Translation of technical documentation is usually framed as an accessibility gesture. That undersells it. The practical effect here is on the decision step, not the reading step.

Consider what you do before installing a skill. You scan the list. For each candidate you ask: does this match my stack, my cloud, my problem? With 20-plus skills whose names run to eight or ten words of English technical vocabulary, that scan is slower than it looks, especially when the terms are compound — "borderless data lakehouse," "eval flywheel," "bidirectional streaming." Each one requires a small parse before you can rule it in or out.

The Chinese version renders the skill names and descriptions in Chinese while keeping the original English README available as README_en.md for comparison. That last part matters more than it might seem. Machine translation of cloud terminology drifts: "endpoint management" and "端点管理" are fine, but concepts like "agent gateway" or "eval flywheel" have no settled Chinese rendering, and a translator working without the English original in view will produce something inconsistent across the document. Keeping both files side by side lets you check a term against the source when a description reads oddly.

The translation also adds something the original does not have: a short "中文快速上手" section at the top. It is explicitly marked as supplementary, not part of the original document. It answers the questions a first-time reader has before they will read anything else — what problem does this solve, what is the shortest path to running it, what will trip me up. The pitfalls it lists are concrete: npx may be missing, the installer is interactive rather than one-shot, some skills touch Google Cloud accounts and authentication, and the update command may offer to remove skills you still use.

That section also flags something the original README does not address: network conditions. The install pulls Node.js and npx online, and in restricted network environments you may need a mirror or accelerated download. The translation notes that the original does not specify how. That is an honest hedge rather than invented guidance, and it is the kind of thing a reader in that situation needs to know before spending twenty minutes on a failing install.

What the translation does not do

It does not change the repository's behavior. The skills themselves are the original English content; installing google/skills gets you the same skills regardless of which README you read. The Chinese version is documentation, not a fork of the skill logic.

It also does not resolve the gaps in the original. The README does not state operating system requirements, hardware requirements, or version constraints. The translation says so plainly rather than filling those in. If you need to know whether a specific skill works on your setup, the README will not tell you — you will have to read the skill's own SKILL.md.

And the translation is new. It was published today with no stars and, presumably, no issue reports yet. The README invites corrections via issue or PR, which is the right posture for a first-pass translation of a large document. Expect rough edges in the longer skill descriptions.

A reasonable way to start

If you are evaluating whether this repo is useful to you, do not install first. Read the skill list in whichever language you read faster, pick two or three that match work you actually have in front of you, and install only those:

npx skills add google/skills

Then look at what landed in your agent's skill directory. The SKILL.md files are readable prose, not opaque configuration. You can see exactly what procedure the agent will follow and judge whether it matches how your team does the task.

The repo is 22,761 stars deep, which means the skills have been exercised by a lot of people. That is a signal about the content, not a guarantee about your use case. The Chinese translation lowers the cost of finding out which skills are worth your time. Whether any given one fits your architecture is still a question only you can answer.

Chinese documentation: https://github.com/yangshun2005/skills-cn

title: Nunca uses float para dinero: un presupuesto reproducible con Decimal
description:
Nunca uses float para dinero: un presupuesto reproducible con Decimal

Los errores de redondeo parecen pequeños hasta que se acumulan en reportes, presupuestos y saldos. El modelo numérico importa incluso en una herramienta personal sin conexiones bancarias.

El problema y el alcance del ejemplo

La ficha de Vault Wallet: Control Gastos resume su función así: «Gestor de gastos y planificador de presupuesto para tus finanzas personales.» Vault Wallet anuncia registro de gastos, presupuestos y manejo de varias monedas. El ejemplo toma una decisión que se puede evaluar sin conocer el código privado de la app: usar decimales explícitos y no sumar divisas diferentes.

Cómo reproducir la idea

Necesitas Python 3; pega este código en presupuesto.py y ejecútalo con python presupuesto.py.

from decimal import Decimal

movimientos = [
    {"categoria": "comida", "moneda": "MXN", "importe": "129.90"},
    {"categoria": "comida", "moneda": "MXN", "importe": "70.10"},
    {"categoria": "transporte", "moneda": "MXN", "importe": "35.50"},
    {"categoria": "servicios", "moneda": "USD", "importe": "9.99"},
]
limites = {("comida", "MXN"): Decimal("250.00")}
totales = {}
for m in movimientos:
    clave = (m["categoria"], m["moneda"])
    totales[clave] = totales.get(clave, Decimal("0")) + Decimal(m["importe"])
for clave, gastado in sorted(totales.items()):
    limite = limites.get(clave)
    print(clave, f"gastado={gastado:.2f}",
          f"restante={limite-gastado:.2f}" if limite is not None else "sin límite")

Qué demuestra el código

El total en comida es exactamente 200.00 MXN. Si usamos números binarios de punto flotante pueden aparecer representaciones intermedias como 0.30000000000000004. Agrupar por (categoría, moneda) evita que un total en pesos incorpore dólares silenciosamente.

Pruebas recomendadas

Cambia el segundo gasto a 120.10: el presupuesto queda en negativo y puede convertirse en alerta. Agrega otra operación en USD: la suma se conserva separada. Prueba también importes negativos para devoluciones, definiendo explícitamente cómo deben tratarse.

Límites que conviene reconocer

No hay persistencia, impuestos, tasas de cambio, sincronización ni reglas fiscales. En producción hay que fijar políticas de redondeo, moneda principal, fechas, devoluciones y versiones de tasas antes de generar reportes.

Qué aprendemos

No todo se arregla con una pantalla de presupuesto. La precisión monetaria y la semántica de cada operación forman parte del modelo de datos.

Contexto y enlaces del autor

El tema se relaciona con las funciones declaradas públicamente de Vault Wallet: Control Gastos, una aplicación Android de AppInitDev. El código anterior es un ejemplo independiente: no se ha inspeccionado el repositorio privado ni se afirma que sea la implementación interna de la app. La referencia aparece al final para ofrecer contexto, no como requisito para completar el tutorial.

  • Google Play: Vault Wallet: Control Gastos
  • Página de la aplicación: https://wallet.appinitdev.com/
  • Sitio del desarrollador: AppInitDev

title: Why ChatGPT can't open most web pages (and what to do about it)
description:
Disclosure: this post is published by the Puley team, the tool mentioned below, and was drafted by an AI agent.

If you have tried asking ChatGPT or Claude about a live product page, a TikTok video or a careers page, you have probably seen one of two things: the model says it can't open the page, or it confidently guesses. Here is why that happens and what the practical options are.

Why AI chats can't open so many pages

  1. Bot blocking. Many large sites (stores, social platforms) block automated clients outright. The fetch tools built into AI apps get a challenge page, an empty shell, or a 403.
  2. Client-side rendering. A lot of pages ship almost no HTML and build the content with JavaScript. A simple fetch sees nothing useful.
  3. Country-specific content. Prices and availability often depend on where the request comes from, so a single fetch from one region can give the wrong answer.
  4. No memory over time. Even when a page can be read, a chat answer is a snapshot. Nothing watches the page afterwards.

Options

  • Paste the content yourself. Reliable, but slow, and it doesn't scale beyond one page.
  • Write a scraper. Works for one site you control; breaks often on sites that actively block bots, and you still need scheduling and alerts.
  • Use a connector or plug-in that does the reading. The AI calls a tool that fetches the page with a real browser, returns the facts with the source link and time, and can re-check on a schedule.

The connector approach in practice

Puley is one example of the third option. It plugs into ChatGPT, Claude and other AI apps, reads public pages, can compare the same product across countries' stores, turns a page into a table, pulls video transcripts where available, and can watch a page and email you when it changes. Setup steps per app are on puley.com/connect.

Some honest limits that apply to any tool in this space:

  • Some sites will still refuse access; a good tool should say so instead of guessing.
  • Alerts can be late when a page changes in seconds.
  • What an add-on can do depends on the AI app, plan and account.

Takeaway

If your AI keeps saying "I can't access that page", the model isn't the problem; the fetch step is. Either feed it the content yourself or give it a tool that can actually open the page and keep checking it.

title: I built an AI memory that says “not found” instead of guessing
description:
Try it free: dorothy.panaxon.ai. Upload a document and ask it anything.

For the past several months I've been building M.N.E.M.O. (Multidimensional Neural Elastic Memory Organization), a memory layer for AI that doesn't rely on vector search.

The problem

Similarity search always returns something, even when the answer isn't in your documents. The model then answers confidently from the wrong context, and you can't tell.

What I did differently

M.N.E.M.O. stores what you give it in a structured tree and looks up answers by exact path instead of by similarity. Two things come out of that:

  • Every answer shows the path it came from, so you can check it.
  • When the answer isn't there, it says so instead of guessing.

It doesn't remove every way an LLM can go wrong. What it removes is being handed the wrong context in the first place.

Where it's still weak

It depends on the model choosing the right path, and I haven't benchmarked that at large scale yet.

Try it and tell me where it breaks

Create a free account

A free account keeps your memory between sessions and lets you ask questions of knowledge other people have shared. Upload a document, ask something hard, then ask something that isn't in it, and see what happens.

If it gets something wrong, I'd really like to know. Leave a comment here.
