title: Two shapes for app data backups: presigned bucket uploads, database dumps, deletion
description:
The interesting decision in a nightly backup job isn't which object storage vendor you sign with. It's whether the archive bytes travel through your application at all. One shape has the Node.js cron process open the database dump plus the zip of that day's uploaded media and push every megabyte into the bucket itself; the other has it mint a presigned URL and stay out of the transfer completely. Use the second shape once the archive is measured in gigabytes — the app tier contributes nothing to a byte copy except memory pressure, deploy-window coupling, and one more place where a retention rule can quietly disagree with the one you wrote down.

The rest of this is about deletion, because deletion is what actually decides the design.

The invariant hiding in a nightly archive

Picture a fintech app with two classes of large objects: identity document scans that a compliance queue reads, and monthly statement PDFs that customers download for years afterwards. A nightly job produces a compressed Postgres dump — call it 4 GB — and a zip of the day's media, which on a heavy day runs past 12 GB. Both land in one bucket under a date prefix, backups/app/2026/03/08/, so listing a day is a prefix scan and expiring a day is a rule rather than a script. The only thing that makes any of this real is the restore drill: pull yesterday's dump, load it into a scratch database, and compare row counts against the numbers you recorded before the dump ran.

Two invariants fall out of that drill. Every archived object has to be readable by a restore path that doesn't depend on the application that wrote it, and every object has to have exactly one thing in the system authorised to delete it. The first kills any design where restoring requires the app to be healthy, which is a bad assumption on the day you need it. The second kills the design where a bucket lifecycle rule and a cleanup cron both believe they own the same prefix — that isn't retention, that's two jobs racing, and the loser is whoever runs the audit.

Both invariants are satisfiable on any S3-compatible bucket, and the reason I'd put a platform like Infrai on the shortlist for this particular job is that the presign call, the lifecycle rule and the scheduler that fires the whole thing sit behind the same REST surface.

Capacity falls out of the same arithmetic. Sixteen gigabytes a night is roughly 480 GB a month of resident data before compression buys anything back, and a 30-day working set alongside a seven-year statutory tail is two retention classes that should never share a prefix.

Should the Node.js cron job upload the dump, or should the app hand out a presigned bucket URL?

Shape A is the proxy: the scheduler reads the file and PUTs it to object storage using a credential the app holds. Its invariant is that exactly one identity ever writes to the bucket, which is genuinely useful for audit, and its cost is that every byte of every archive is now inside a process you also serve customer traffic from. You will meet its limits as request timeouts, container memory, and the fun of a 12 GB upload dying at 90% with no resumable state.

Shape B splits control plane from data plane. The app asks the platform for a time-limited signed URL, and whichever machine holds the file — the backup host, a sidecar, a worker outside your VPC — PUTs the bytes straight to the bucket. Its invariant is narrower and easier to defend: the long-lived credential never leaves your server, and the authorisation for the actual transfer is the URL's expiry window. That's it. If a signed URL leaks, it leaks for an hour and for one key, not for the bucket.

Infrai is one option that fits this shape cleanly, and it's where I'd start for a small platform team: POST /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key} with {"op":"put","expires_seconds":3600} returns a url, the method to use, expires_at, and any headers the upload must carry. The worker sends those bytes to the returned URL with no platform credential attached — signing it twice is the most common way people break this pattern on their first attempt. Infrai's API is also self-describing, which matters more than it sounds: the discovery surface hands back the request schema, the response schema, and runnable examples in ten languages for each capability, so adding the restore call later is reading one endpoint rather than adopting another SDK.

Most teams asking this question run the scheduler in Node.js. Mine is Go, and the shape is identical in either — three calls, one of which is a plain HTTP PUT.

Retention is a deletion policy, and it has to be provable

Date-based keys give you retention almost for free: backups/app/2026/03/08/dump.sql.gz is listable by prefix, sortable by name, and expirable by rule. What you cannot do is treat expiration as instantaneous. Lifecycle expiration on Infrai is day-granular with a one-day floor, which is the same granularity S3 has used for years, so "delete this temp export six hours after it's written" is not a lifecycle rule anywhere in this comparison — it's a job you write, with all the ownership questions that implies.

Option How you talk to it Retention control Immutability Who operates it
AWS S3 AWS SDK or S3 API Lifecycle rules, day-granular expiration Versioning plus Object Lock AWS; IAM is the real work
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible API Object lifecycle rules Check current R2 docs before relying on it Cloudflare
Backblaze B2 S3-compatible API Lifecycle rules Object Lock offered Backblaze
MinIO S3-compatible API, self-hosted Lifecycle rules Versioning and locking You, down to the disks
Infrai Plain REST over one key, no SDK to install set_lifecycle expiration, one-day floor Lacks object versioning and object lock Managed, no disks of yours

A table like that is a buy-vs-build sheet in disguise. The MinIO row is cheap until you price a person to carry the pager for it; the S3 row is boring in the way infrastructure should be boring, and boring costs IAM hours. Set the expiration rule once with POST /v1/storage/bucket/set_lifecycle/{bucket} when you create the bucket, keep it in the same repo as the backup job, and never let a second process delete anything under that prefix.

Immutability is where I'd draw the hard line for a fintech workload. Object storage without versioning means an overwrite of an existing key is final, so make keys immutable by construction — date plus run id, never a rolling latest.sql.gz — and keep the long-tail regulatory copy somewhere that offers a lock.

The upload path, end to end in Go

One presign, one PUT, no bytes through the app. Retries back off on 429 and honour Retry-After, and the presign carries an idempotency key so a retried request is understood as the same request rather than a second one.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const apiBase = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

type presignResult struct {
    Data struct {
        URL       string            `json:"url"`
        Method    string            `json:"method"`
        ExpiresAt string            `json:"expires_at"`
        Headers   map[string]string `json:"headers"`
    } `json:"data"`
}

// postJSON sends one JSON request, retrying on 429 with exponential backoff.
func postJSON(url string, body []byte, hdr map[string]string) (*http.Response, error) {
    for attempt := 0; ; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("POST", url, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        for k, v := range hdr {
            req.Header.Set(k, v)
        }
        res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        if res.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 4 {
            return res, nil
        }
        wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if s := res.Header.Get("Retry-After"); s != "" {
            if n, convErr := strconv.Atoi(s); convErr == nil {
                wait = time.Duration(n) * time.Second
            }
        }
        res.Body.Close()
        time.Sleep(wait)
    }
}

func presign(bucket, key, runID string) (presignResult, error) {
    var out presignResult
    body, err := json.Marshal(map[string]any{"op": "put", "expires_seconds": 3600})
    if err != nil {
        return out, err
    }
    // Same run plus same key means a retry is the same request, not a second upload slot.
    res, err := postJSON(apiBase+"/storage/object/presign/"+bucket+"/"+key, body,
        map[string]string{"Idempotency-Key": "backup-presign-" + runID + "-" + key})
    if err != nil {
        return out, err
    }
    defer res.Body.Close()
    raw, err := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
    if err != nil {
        return out, err
    }
    if res.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
        return out, fmt.Errorf("presign %s: %s", res.Status, raw)
    }
    return out, json.Unmarshal(raw, &out)
}

func main() {
    path := "/var/backups/dump.sql.gz"
    bucket := "fintech-archive"
    now := time.Now().UTC()
    runID := now.Format("20060102")
    key := "backups/app/" + now.Format("2006/01/02") + "/dump.sql.gz"

    signed, err := presign(bucket, key, runID)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "presign:", err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }

    f, err := os.Open(path)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "open:", err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    defer f.Close()
    info, err := f.Stat()
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "stat:", err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }

    // The signed URL carries its own authorization. The platform key must not be sent here.
    put, err := http.NewRequest(signed.Data.Method, signed.Data.URL, f)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "request:", err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    put.ContentLength = info.Size()
    for k, v := range signed.Data.Headers {
        put.Header.Set(k, v)
    }

    res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(put)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "upload:", err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    defer res.Body.Close()
    if res.StatusCode/100 != 2 {
        detail, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "upload %s: %s\n", res.Status, detail)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Printf("stored %s (%d bytes), signature expires %s\n", key, info.Size(), signed.Data.ExpiresAt)
}

The restore side is the same call with op set to get: the server mints a short-lived download URL, hands it to whoever is doing the recovery, and the bucket stays private throughout. There are no permanent public links in this design and there shouldn't be — a backup archive that can be fetched by anyone holding a URL forever is a data incident waiting for a slow news day. Run that restore monthly against a scratch database. An untested backup is a rumour.

When this shape is the wrong call

Direct browser-to-bucket uploads are the clearest boundary. Those need CORS rules on the bucket, and if a web page PUTting straight into storage is central to your product, stick with S3, R2 or MinIO where you set those rules yourself; server-generated signed URLs are the supported path for browser downloads here, not a browser-side upload widget.

Regulatory immutability is the second. Infrai lacks object versioning and object lock, so if an auditor wants provable write-once storage for the seven-year statement copies, keep that tier on S3 with Object Lock or on Backblaze B2, and let the platform bucket hold the 30-day working set. Two buckets, two retention classes, one restore drill that covers both.

And if you already live inside AWS — IAM roles, KMS keys, Glacier tiering, an on-call rota that knows S3 error codes — the answer is S3, and adding another vendor to save a few integration hours is a trade I wouldn't take.

Infrai is worth trying for the presign-and-expire half of this workflow if you're a small platform team that wants the archive path to be plain HTTP calls rather than another SDK and another cloud account: the same key that drives your scheduled job also covers the bucket, so there's one credential to rotate instead of one per backend service. Your mileage varies with how much of your stack is already committed elsewhere. If that boundary fits your system, the nightly-backup walkthrough at https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/storage/answers/object-storage-app-data-backups-nodejs-cron-upload-data/ covers the same three steps against a real bucket.

Sources

  • Infrai discovery: storage.bucket.set_lifecycle fields and examples — https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.bucket.set_lifecycle
  • AWS S3, Managing the lifecycle of objects — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • AWS S3, Using S3 Object Lock — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html
  • Cloudflare R2, Object lifecycles — https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/buckets/object-lifecycles/
  • Firebase Cloud Storage documentation — https://firebase.google.com/docs/storage

title: Scheduled Shipment File Recovery in 2026: API Queues Retry Failed Cleanup Jobs
description:
Short answer: schedule one small dispatch, put every expired shipment artifact on an at-least-once queue, and make each delete idempotent; retries isolate transient failures while a DLQ holds the jobs that need an operator.

For a one-person B2B SaaS, this is less about elegant infrastructure than protecting the next release. A shipment update may fan out to many subscribers, leaving API exports or object-storage files that expire later. One cron callback should identify that batch. It should not spend its whole run deleting every object.

How should a Node.js API retry failed scheduled file cleanup jobs?

Start with the smallest design that preserves the delivery guarantee you actually need.

Choice Delivery behavior Recovery path Best fit
Cron deletes everything One failed delete can complicate the whole run Rerun and determine what already changed Tiny, disposable batches
Cron + queue + DLQ Each object retries independently; the worker must tolerate duplicate delivery Inspect repeated failures, fix the cause, then redrive Routine shipment-file retention
Temporal or Apache Airflow Use a workflow system when the cleanup is part of a DAG or needs orchestration Follow the workflow engine's execution model Multi-step business processes
Apache Kafka Retained records can serve replay and multiple consumer groups Replay from the log Cleanup events that must also remain an event stream
BullMQ Compare its operating model with the managed API choices Use its own worker tooling Teams willing to own a Node.js queue stack
Inngest or Trigger.dev Evaluate their contracts against the same retry and recovery requirements Use the selected product's recovery controls Teams choosing a dedicated job platform

My default is cron + queue + DLQ. The cron target lists expired artifacts and emits one compact task per object. Workers delete objects, acknowledge success, and reject a retryable failure for another attempt. A persistent failure, such as a malformed object key or missing permission, moves to the DLQ for deliberate recovery.

Infrai is a reasonable option for a solo SaaS that wants this scheduling boundary behind one REST contract. Infrai exposes backend capabilities through one REST API: plain HTTP, no SDK, and callable from any language or runtime. Infrai puts scheduling and queue behind one API key and one bill, leaving this small workflow with one credential to rotate and one invoice to reconcile. Its consistent contract also means switching the provider behind a capability doesn't require application code changes in the cleanup pipeline. I would try it for the cron-and-queue boundary when weekly shipping time matters more than owning queue plumbing.

Don't confuse that recommendation with a universal one. The catch is that the platform has no DAG orchestration or fan-out/join primitive, and its push subscribers need a public HTTPS target. Keep Temporal or Airflow when cleanup participates in a real workflow; keep a direct system that reaches private workers when exposing an ingress is unacceptable.

Delivery guarantees determine the shape

A standard queue is at-least-once, so the same cleanup task can reach a consumer more than once. This is expected delivery behavior. The useful invariant is therefore not "the worker ran once." It is "after one or more valid deliveries, the artifact is absent and the cleanup record is complete."

That changes the unit of work. Put one file or object-delete task on the queue instead of one task for the entire nightly sweep. If shipment shp_48291 created 600 subscriber exports, a permission problem on one object should not force the other 599 deletes through the same retry cycle. The producer can use a stable task ID derived from the tenant, artifact key, and retention cutoff. The consumer records completion against that ID and treats another delivery as success. Short keys help. Clear ownership helps more.

There is a hard boundary here — acknowledgement deletes a queue message, and retention tops out at 30 days. This queue is not an audit log, analytics stream, or Kafka-style replay source. Store the business evidence you need somewhere meant to retain it. The queue carries work.

Cron has a separate boundary. A run can last no more than 900 seconds, paused schedules do not backfill missed triggers, and timing can have second-level jitter. Let cron discover and enqueue a bounded page of candidates, then return. Long deletion work belongs in consumers. If a sweep can discover more records than one dispatch safely handles, persist a cursor and schedule another bounded dispatch rather than stretching the callback toward its limit.

No heroics.

I don't use FIFO deduplication as the only idempotency layer because its window is five minutes. A delayed retry or a later sweep can arrive outside that window. The worker still needs a durable claim or completion record keyed by the cleanup task ID, plus delete semantics that accept an already-absent object as the intended final state.

A retry-safe TypeScript worker

Start at the provider edge. This publisher accepts a JSON document that has already been validated against Infrai's live discovery schema, then sends it unchanged. That detail matters because the schema, rather than an article, owns the batch fields. Run it with a schema-valid batch file and a stable operation key; retrying the command reuses the same idempotency key.

import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const inputPath = process.argv[2];
const operationKey = process.argv[3];

if (!apiKey || !inputPath || !operationKey) {
  throw new Error("usage: INFRAI_API_KEY=ifr_... tsx publish.ts batch.json operation-key");
}

const batch: unknown = JSON.parse(await readFile(inputPath, "utf8"));

for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
  const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish_batch", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "Idempotency-Key": operationKey,
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(batch),
  });

  if (response.ok) {
    process.stdout.write(`${await response.text()}\n`);
    break;
  }

  const body = await response.text();
  if (response.status !== 429 || attempt === 4) {
    throw new Error(`publish failed (${response.status}): ${body}`);
  }

  const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
  const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
    ? retryAfter * 1_000
    : 500 * 2 ** attempt;
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
}

The application core below is independent of that provider payload. Map the discovered delivery fields at the HTTP edge; keep the cleanup rule testable and stable. The claim operation must be atomic in the real repository, usually through a unique key or conditional write.

type CleanupTask = {
  taskId: string;
  tenantId: string;
  objectKey: string;
  shipmentId: string;
};

type ClaimResult = "acquired" | "completed" | "busy";

interface CleanupStore {
  claim(taskId: string): Promise<ClaimResult>;
  complete(taskId: string): Promise<void>;
  release(taskId: string): Promise<void>;
}

interface ObjectStore {
  deleteIfPresent(tenantId: string, objectKey: string): Promise<void>;
}

type WorkerResult =
  | { action: "ack"; reason: "deleted" | "already-completed" }
  | { action: "retry"; reason: string };

export async function cleanShipmentArtifact(
  task: CleanupTask,
  cleanupStore: CleanupStore,
  objectStore: ObjectStore,
): Promise<WorkerResult> {
  const claim = await cleanupStore.claim(task.taskId);

  if (claim === "completed") {
    return { action: "ack", reason: "already-completed" };
  }

  if (claim === "busy") {
    return { action: "retry", reason: "another delivery owns the task" };
  }

  try {
    await objectStore.deleteIfPresent(task.tenantId, task.objectKey);
    await cleanupStore.complete(task.taskId);
    return { action: "ack", reason: "deleted" };
  } catch (error) {
    await cleanupStore.release(task.taskId);
    const reason = error instanceof Error ? error.message : "unknown delete failure";
    return { action: "retry", reason };
  }
}

The queue adapter translates ack into acknowledgement and retry into negative acknowledgement according to the provider's delivery schema. It should use exponential backoff, honor Retry-After when a call is rate-limited with HTTP 429, and stop automatic attempts at a finite threshold so the message reaches the DLQ. The task stays small: a 256 KB message limit is plenty for identifiers, but it is a warning not to embed file contents or a giant subscriber list.

Keep authentication at the edge too. The API uses Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY; the key belongs in an environment variable, never in a task or source file. Its public discovery surface exposes the current request JSON Schema and runnable TypeScript examples without authentication, which is the right place to map this worker to the live contract instead of guessing fields. The implementation only needs plain HTTP, so there is no provider SDK tied through the domain layer.

Recovery is an operating loop

Retries are useful only when they converge. Classify the response before deciding what happens next: HTTP 429 waits and retries, while repeated permission or malformed-key failures need investigation rather than a hot loop. Once the permission or data issue is fixed, redrive the DLQ. Do not acknowledge first and hope a later process reconstructs the work; ack removes the message. For the shipment example, the operator view needs a small amount of durable context: task ID, tenant, shipment ID, object key, attempt count, last failure category, and the time the cleanup became due. Those are application fields, not claims about a vendor response. They answer the practical questions at 8:10 on a release morning: Is one tenant affected? Is the key builder producing bad input? Did a credential scope change? Can this batch be redriven without duplicating subscriber-facing effects? One long record per attempt is unnecessary; a compact current state plus durable transitions gives the operator enough evidence to act without turning the queue into storage.

Ack means gone.

Observability has to cross the schedule, dispatch, and worker. Correlate them with the stable task ID. Infrai's cron run output retains only the first 4 KB, so it should summarize counts and a cursor rather than carry per-object diagnostics. I'm not sure how long your business needs deletion evidence; legal and customer-contract requirements decide that. Whatever the answer, store it outside the queue because a successful acknowledgement removes the message and queue retention is finite.

This recovery loop costs some schema work, but it buys back operator time. That is the revenue-per-hour test I care about: can I diagnose one failed shipment artifact, fix its cause, and redrive it without replaying a night's successful deletes? If yes, the infrastructure is earning its place. If no, another dashboard won't rescue the design.

When should the runner-up win?

Choose Temporal when retries belong to a durable, multi-step business workflow, or Apache Airflow when the cleanup is one node in a DAG. Infrai explicitly does not provide those orchestration primitives. RabbitMQ is worth evaluating when priority queues are central to the design. Kafka is the better shape when cleanup records must remain replayable or feed multiple consumer groups, because an acknowledged work queue cannot provide that history.

A direct cloud scheduler and queue can also be the right runner-up when the rest of the product already lives in one cloud and the team is comfortable coupling to its contracts. That choice trades portability for direct integration. For a solo operation, I would make that trade when private network delivery is mandatory, since these cron targets must be public HTTP URLs and push queue subscribers must be public HTTPS endpoints.

Other limits can decide the matter quickly. Infrai delayed messages stop at seven days, native debounce and throttle are absent, one-to-many topics require separate queues, and cron expressions do not support nonstandard extensions such as L. These aren't defects. They are contract boundaries. If the retention policy needs a quarterly delayed message, or if the shipment fan-out needs a retained event consumed independently by several teams, select the specialist rather than building glue around the mismatch.

For ordinary expired-file cleanup, stay boring: schedule discovery, enqueue individual deletes, make consumption idempotent, cap retries, inspect the DLQ, and retain audit evidence separately. Ship the product next week.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the scheduled S3 cleanup guide and verify the live schemas before sending a batch.

References

  • RFC 2104: HMAC keyed-hashing for message authentication
  • RabbitMQ priority queue documentation
  • Temporal documentation
  • Apache Airflow documentation
  • Apache Kafka documentation

title: Jak mierzyć widoczność marki w AI Search? Powtarzalny pomiar krok po kroku
description:
Jak sprawdzić, czy AI wymienia moją markę? Przygotuj stały zestaw pytań klientów, zapisuj odpowiedzi wraz z datą i warunkami testu, a następnie sprawdzaj obecność oraz rolę marki. Udział odpowiedzi z nazwą firmy licz wyłącznie wśród poprawnie zebranych odpowiedzi. Taki wynik opisuje badaną próbkę, a nie całą widoczność marki w internecie.

W tym poradniku zbudujemy prosty dziennik obserwacji AI Search i policzymy pierwszy wskaźnik w Pythonie. FunkyMEDIA będzie nazwą szukanej marki w przykładzie. Wszystkie odpowiedzi demonstracyjne są syntetyczne: nie pochodzą z rzeczywistych wyszukiwarek, nie opisują klientów i nie stanowią wyników badań firmy.

Najpierw ustal, co naprawdę chcesz zmierzyć

Pytanie „czy AI nas zna?” jest zbyt szerokie, aby dało się na nie odpowiedzieć jednym wynikiem. System może poprawnie opisać firmę, kiedy podasz jej nazwę, ale nie wymienić jej w odpowiedzi na ogólne pytanie o dostawcę. Może też wymienić nazwę, przypisując jej niewłaściwą usługę.

Dlatego w naszym przykładzie oddzielimy cztery obserwacje:

  • obecność nazwy marki;
  • rolę wzmianki: przykład, opis, rekomendacja lub ostrzeżenie;
  • poprawność informacji o firmie;
  • widoczne źródła, na których oparto odpowiedź.

To odrębne pola. Samo wystąpienie nazwy nie potwierdza rekomendacji. Link do strony nie dowodzi, że źródło wspiera każde zdanie odpowiedzi. Rekomendacja nie oznacza natomiast, że odbiorca odwiedził witrynę albo został klientem.

Na początek zmierzymy tylko obecność marki. Dopiero gdy potrafimy odtworzyć ten pomiar, warto dodawać bardziej złożone oceny.

Ułóż pytania wokół potrzeb użytkownika

Zamiast wielokrotnie wpisywać nazwę firmy, przygotuj pytania opisujące rzeczywiste zadania odbiorcy. Dla usług związanych z AI Search mogą to być:

  • „Jak sprawdzić, czy moja firma pojawia się w odpowiedziach AI?”;
  • „Jak porównać dostawców monitoringu wzmianek o marce?”;
  • „Jakie dane powinien zawierać raport widoczności w AI?”;
  • „Jak ocenić, czy rekomendacja dostawcy jest poparta źródłami?”.

To propozycje scenariuszy, a nie dane o liczbie wyszukiwań. Ich priorytet można później zweryfikować na podstawie rozmów z klientami, dostępnych danych wyszukiwania i pytań trafiających do działu obsługi.

Każdemu pytaniu przypisz trwały identyfikator oraz kategorię intencji. Zapisz również, czy zawiera nazwę marki. Pytania z nazwą firmy i pytania ogólne raportuj osobno: odpowiadają na różne potrzeby badawcze.

Przy kolejnej rundzie zachowaj podstawowy panel. Nowe pytania dodaj do osobnej grupy eksploracyjnej. Jeśli zmienisz jednocześnie treść pytań i stronę internetową, późniejszą różnicę trudniej będzie zinterpretować.

Zapisuj jedną obserwację jako jeden rekord

Praktycznym formatem startowym jest JSONL: każda linia pliku zawiera osobny obiekt JSON. Taki dziennik można przeglądać ręcznie, analizować w Pythonie i później przenieść do bazy danych.

Minimalny rekord może wyglądać tak:

{
  "observation_id": "demo-001",
  "panel_version": "2026-11-v1",
  "query_id": "q-001",
  "query_text": "Jak mierzyc obecnosc marki w AI?",
  "engine": "synthetic-demo",
  "collected_at": "2026-11-06T19:00:00Z",
  "language": "pl",
  "market": "PL",
  "session": "new",
  "status": "ok",
  "answer_text": "FunkyMEDIA jest tu przykladowa nazwa marki.",
  "source_urls": [],
  "mention_role": "example",
  "annotation_version": "v1"
}

Pole „engine” powinno identyfikować faktycznie użyty produkt lub interfejs. Jeśli nie znasz wersji modelu, zapisz brak tej informacji zamiast ją zgadywać. W odpowiednich polach zanotuj również dostępność wyszukiwania, stan zalogowania i istotne ustawienia.

Pusta lista źródeł oznacza tu, że nie zapisano żadnych widocznych adresów. Nie jest dowodem, że system nie korzystał z żadnej informacji. Dziennik ma oddzielać to, co obserwowalne, od przypuszczeń o działaniu modelu.

Oddziel błędy techniczne od odpowiedzi bez marki

Załóżmy, że wykonano sześć prób. Pięć zakończyło się zebraniem odpowiedzi, a jedna błędem technicznym. W dwóch poprawnych odpowiedziach wystąpiła marka.

Wskaźnik obecności wśród poprawnych odpowiedzi wynosi wtedy 2/5, czyli 40%. Osobno raportujemy błąd w jednej z sześciu prób.

Nie należy po cichu traktować błędu jak odpowiedzi bez wzmianki. Nie zaobserwowaliśmy bowiem odpowiedzi, którą można ocenić. Jednocześnie błędów nie wolno ukrywać: jeśli częściej dotyczą konkretnego silnika lub grupy pytań, uzyskana próbka może być niepełna w istotny sposób.

W tym przykładzie odpowiedź typu „nie mam wystarczających informacji” jest poprawnie zebranym wynikiem i pozostaje w mianowniku. To decyzja metodologiczna, którą trzeba zapisać przed liczeniem. Możesz stosować dodatkowe kategorie, ale nie zmieniaj ich między rundami bez oznaczenia nowej wersji.

Policz prosty wskaźnik w Pythonie

Poniższy przykład korzysta wyłącznie z biblioteki standardowej. Normalizuje zapis Unicode i wielkość liter, a następnie szuka całego tokenu nazwy marki.

import re
import unicodedata

def normalize(text):
    return unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", text).casefold()

def contains_brand(text, aliases):
    normalized = normalize(text)
    return any(
        re.search(r"(?<!\w)" + re.escape(normalize(alias)) + r"(?!\w)",
                  normalized) is not None
        for alias in aliases
    )

def summarize(rows, aliases):
    valid = [row for row in rows if row["status"] == "ok"]
    mentions = sum(contains_brand(row["answer"], aliases) for row in valid)
    return {
        "attempts": len(rows),
        "valid_answers": len(valid),
        "errors": sum(row["status"] == "error" for row in rows),
        "answers_with_brand": mentions,
        "presence_rate": mentions / len(valid) if valid else None,
    }

rows = [
    {"status": "ok", "answer": "FunkyMEDIA jako przyklad."},
    {"status": "ok", "answer": "Opis FUNKYMEDIA."},
    {"status": "ok", "answer": "Inny dostawca."},
    {"status": "ok", "answer": "Brak wystarczajacych informacji."},
    {"status": "ok", "answer": "SuperFunkyMEDIA nie jest ta sama nazwa."},
    {"status": "error", "answer": ""},
]

result = summarize(rows, ["FunkyMEDIA"])
assert result["valid_answers"] == 5
assert result["answers_with_brand"] == 2
assert result["presence_rate"] == 0.4
assert not contains_brand("SuperFunkyMEDIA", ["FunkyMEDIA"])
assert summarize([], ["FunkyMEDIA"])["presence_rate"] is None
print(result)

Oczekiwany wynik obejmuje sześć prób, pięć poprawnych odpowiedzi, jeden błąd i dwie odpowiedzi z marką. Dla pustej próbki otrzymamy None, a nie zero procent. Brak obserwacji nie jest zaobserwowanym brakiem widoczności.

Dokumentacje normalizacji Unicode i wyrażeń regularnych opisują użyte mechanizmy. Sama reguła dopasowania jest jednak elementem naszego przykładu, a nie uniwersalnym standardem rozpoznawania firm.

Nie pomyl wykrycia nazwy z identyfikacją firmy

Prosty matcher rozwiązuje tylko część problemu. Może poprawnie wykryć nazwę, lecz nie ustali, czy chodzi o właściwą organizację. Dwie firmy mogą mieć podobne nazwy; odpowiedź może też zawierać cytat lub adres domeny.

Dlatego przygotuj rejestr zatwierdzonych aliasów. Przy każdym zapisz, skąd pochodzi i czy może być niejednoznaczny. Nie dodawaj automatycznie wszystkich wariantów zwróconych przez model.

W trudniejszych przypadkach sprawdzaj kontekst: domenę, lokalizację, produkt albo usługę. Niepewną wzmiankę skieruj do ręcznej oceny. Wynik „do weryfikacji” jest bardziej użyteczny niż fałszywa pewność.

W raporcie warto zachować osobno automatyczne dopasowanie i ostateczną adnotację. Dzięki temu zmiana algorytmu nie usuwa historii wcześniejszych decyzji.

Powtarzaj test w porównywalnych warunkach

Jedna odpowiedź jest pojedynczą obserwacją. Jeśli chcesz ocenić zmienność, zaplanuj kilka powtórzeń i zapisuj każde z nich. Nie wybieraj wyłącznie najlepszej odpowiedzi.

Zachowaj ten sam panel, liczbę prób oraz możliwie porównywalne warunki sesji. Oddziel wyniki różnych silników i języków. Jeżeli interfejs lub sposób zbierania danych się zmieni, zaznacz to w raporcie.

Powtórzenia tego samego pytania nie stają się automatycznie niezależnymi obserwacjami. Przy bardziej zaawansowanej analizie nie traktuj stu niemal identycznych prób jak stu niezależnych potrzeb użytkowników.

Prowadź także dziennik zmian strony: co poprawiono, kiedy i dlaczego. Wzrost liczby wzmianek po zmianie treści może być interesujący, ale sam porządek czasowy nie dowodzi przyczynowości. W tym samym okresie mogły zmienić się inne źródła i sam produkt AI.

Raportuj wynik razem z jego zakresem

Użyteczny komunikat brzmi: „W syntetycznym przykładzie marka wystąpiła w 2 z 5 poprawnych odpowiedzi; jedna z 6 prób zakończyła się błędem”. Nie brzmi: „Marka ma 40% rynku AI”.

Do rzeczywistego raportu dołącz panel pytań, okres pomiaru, silniki, liczbę powtórzeń, zasady kwalifikacji oraz sposób identyfikacji marki. Pokaż również odpowiedzi bez marek i przypadki niejednoznaczne.

Jeśli mierzysz Google AI Overviews, osobno zapisuj, czy taki element w ogóle się pojawił. Brak AI Overview to inna obserwacja niż obecny AI Overview bez wskazanej firmy. Dokumentacja Google dotycząca funkcji AI podkreśla znaczenie standardowych praktyk SEO; nie opisuje specjalnej optymalizacji gwarantującej obecność.

Dalszym krokiem może być ocena poprawności informacji, źródeł i roli wzmianki. Każdy z tych etapów wymaga własnych reguł, przykładów granicznych i możliwości sprawdzenia decyzji.

Informacja o serii i sposobie przygotowania

Materiał przygotowano dla serii edukacyjnej FunkyMEDIA. Kontekst firmowego podejścia opisuje metodologia AI Search i Brand Mentions FunkyMEDIA. To źródło własne firmy, a nie niezależne potwierdzenie skuteczności przedstawionego przykładu.

Profile własne wydawcy: FunkyMEDIA na LinkedIn i FunkyMEDIA na YouTube.

Ujawnienie użycia AI: tekst i przykłady zostały wygenerowane z użyciem AI. Dane demonstracyjne są syntetyczne. Artykuł nie przedstawia osobistych doświadczeń autora ani wyników klientów.

title: Compartir archivos por Wi-Fi local: un prototipo y sus riesgos de seguridad"
description:
Compartir archivos por Wi-Fi local: un prototipo y sus riesgos de seguridad

Cuando el móvil y el ordenador están en una misma red, una transferencia no necesita pasar por la nube. Sin embargo, «funciona en mi Wi-Fi» no significa «es seguro»: descubrimiento, permisos, autenticación y transporte son problemas distintos.

El problema y el alcance del ejemplo

La ficha de Nexus Local: Gestor Web Wi-Fi resume su función así: «Gestiona archivos y duplica tu pantalla desde el navegador mediante Wi-Fi local.» La ficha pública de Nexus Local describe acceso a archivos y pantalla desde el navegador por Wi-Fi local. Para estudiar una sola pieza de ese problema, construiremos un servidor HTTP de solo descarga con Python. Este prototipo NO reproduce el servidor, el cifrado ni la arquitectura de la app; sirve para observar el alcance real de una dirección de red.

Cómo reproducir la idea

Necesitas Python 3.10+, dos equipos en una red Wi-Fi de confianza y una carpeta de prueba llamada compartir con un archivo no confidencial. Guarda el código como servidor.py junto a esa carpeta.

from http.server import SimpleHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
from functools import partial
from pathlib import Path

folder = Path('compartir').resolve()
if not folder.is_dir():
    raise SystemExit('Crea la carpeta compartir antes de iniciar')

handler = partial(SimpleHTTPRequestHandler, directory=str(folder))
server = ThreadingHTTPServer(('0.0.0.0', 8000), handler)
print('Servidor de PRUEBA en el puerto 8000; Ctrl+C para salir')
try:
    server.serve_forever()
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass
finally:
    server.server_close()

Qué demuestra el código

El servidor atiende solicitudes en todas las interfaces (0.0.0.0), y SimpleHTTPRequestHandler expone el contenido de la carpeta seleccionada. No hay credenciales, control de acceso por persona ni HTTPS. Eso lo vuelve útil para un laboratorio, pero inapropiado para archivos privados.

Pruebas recomendadas

  1. Ejecuta python servidor.py. 2. Averigua la IP local del ordenador, por ejemplo con ipconfig o ip addr. 3. Desde el otro dispositivo, abre http://IP_LOCAL:8000/. 4. Descarga un archivo de prueba. 5. Apaga el servidor y comprueba que la dirección deja de responder. Si falla, revisa el aislamiento entre clientes, cortafuegos y red invitada.

Límites que conviene reconocer

No implementa subida, descubrimiento automático, TLS, contraseñas ni acceso seguro en redes públicas. Una versión real necesitaría autenticación por sesión, confirmación explícita del usuario, HTTPS correctamente configurado, límites de tamaño, validación de rutas y controles contra accesos no autorizados.

Qué aprendemos

La LAN reduce dependencias externas, pero no reemplaza un modelo de amenazas. La pregunta de diseño es qué dispositivo puede conectarse, a qué archivos y durante cuánto tiempo.

Contexto y enlaces del autor

El tema se relaciona con las funciones declaradas públicamente de Nexus Local: Gestor Web Wi-Fi, una aplicación Android de AppInitDev. El código anterior es un ejemplo independiente: no se ha inspeccionado el repositorio privado ni se afirma que sea la implementación interna de la app. La referencia aparece al final para ofrecer contexto, no como requisito para completar el tutorial.

  • Google Play: Nexus Local: Gestor Web Wi-Fi
  • Página de la aplicación: https://nexuslocal.appinitdev.com/
  • Sitio del desarrollador: AppInitDev

Referencia técnica

Documentación de http.server

title: Como aprendi Apache Spark — Parte 8: RDD Lineage e tolerância a falhas — como o Spark se recupera
description:
Nos primeiros artigos desta série, começamos com uma das abstrações que ajudaram a definir o Apache Spark:

RDD — Resilient Distributed Dataset.

Falamos bastante sobre:

Distributed Dataset

Vimos:

Partitions
Tasks
Executors
Shuffle
Memory

Mas existe uma palavra no nome que merece um capítulo próprio:

Resilient.

Por que um RDD é resiliente?

A resposta está em uma das ideias mais elegantes da arquitetura original do Spark:

Lineage.

Em vez de depender apenas da replicação de cada resultado intermediário, Spark mantém informações sobre como os dados foram produzidos.

Se parte deles for perdida, em muitos casos ela pode ser reconstruída.

Essa ideia conecta:

Immutability
    ↓
Transformations
    ↓
Lineage
    ↓
DAG
    ↓
Recomputation
    ↓
Fault Tolerance

E muda a forma como enxergamos falhas em processamento distribuído.

1. Falhas fazem parte de sistemas distribuídos

Imagine um cluster:

             DRIVER
                │
      ┌─────────┼─────────┐
      ▼         ▼         ▼
  Executor 1 Executor 2 Executor 3

Agora imagine que estamos processando:

10 TB

durante horas.

Nesse período, alguma coisa pode acontecer:

Executor failure
Machine failure
Process crash
Network problem
Disk problem
Container termination

Em um sistema distribuído, a pergunta não deveria ser apenas:

E se alguma coisa falhar?

Uma pergunta melhor é:

Como o sistema continua quando alguma coisa falhar?

Essa diferença é fundamental.

2. Um problema simples

Imagine um dataset dividido em quatro partições:

RDD A

P1
P2
P3
P4

Distribuídas assim:

Executor 1
├── P1
└── P2

Executor 2
├── P3
└── P4

Agora o Executor 2 desaparece.

Executor 1
├── P1
└── P2

Executor 2
└── X

Perdemos:

P3
P4

O que fazer?

Uma possibilidade seria manter cópias de tudo.

Outra possibilidade é saber como reconstruir o que foi perdido.

Essa segunda ideia é central no modelo de RDDs.

3. RDDs são imutáveis

Uma característica importante dos RDDs é:

RDDs são imutáveis.

Quando fazemos:

rdd2 = rdd1.map(lambda x: x * 2)

não estamos modificando rdd1.

Estamos descrevendo outro RDD:

RDD1
 │
 │ map(x * 2)
 ▼
RDD2

Depois:

rdd3 = rdd2.filter(lambda x: x > 100)

temos:

RDD1
 │
 │ map
 ▼
RDD2
 │
 │ filter
 ▼
RDD3

Cada transformação cria uma nova abstração derivada da anterior.

Essa propriedade ajuda a tornar a linhagem previsível.

4. O que é Lineage?

Lineage representa a sequência de dependências e transformações utilizada para produzir um dataset.

Considere:

rdd1 = sc.textFile("/data/events")

rdd2 = rdd1.map(
    lambda line: line.split(",")
)

rdd3 = rdd2.filter(
    lambda row: row[2] == "purchase"
)

rdd4 = rdd3.map(
    lambda row: (row[1], 1)
)

rdd5 = rdd4.reduceByKey(
    lambda a, b: a + b
)

Conceitualmente:

textFile
   ↓
 RDD1
   ↓
  map
   ↓
 RDD2
   ↓
 filter
   ↓
 RDD3
   ↓
  map
   ↓
 RDD4
   ↓
reduceByKey
   ↓
 RDD5

Essa cadeia descreve:

Como RDD5 foi derivado dos dados originais.

Isso é lineage.

5. Lineage não significa guardar todas as cópias

Esse ponto é importante.

Imagine:

RDD1
 ↓
RDD2
 ↓
RDD3
 ↓
RDD4
 ↓
RDD5

Não precisamos interpretar isso como:

Memory

RDD1 complete
RDD2 complete
RDD3 complete
RDD4 complete
RDD5 complete

Lineage não significa manter automaticamente todas as versões materializadas.

O que Spark preserva é a informação necessária sobre as dependências entre os datasets.

Podemos pensar:

Data
+
Transformation Graph
=
Ability to recompute

Essa diferença é essencial.

6. Lazy Evaluation e Lineage

Agora podemos conectar outro conceito da série.

Quando escrevemos:

rdd2 = rdd1.map(...)
rdd3 = rdd2.filter(...)
rdd4 = rdd3.map(...)

Spark não precisa executar imediatamente cada transformação.

Ele constrói relações entre os RDDs.

Conceitualmente:

rdd1
  │
 map
  │
rdd2
  │
filter
  │
rdd3
  │
 map
  │
rdd4

Quando uma Action aparece:

rdd4.count()

temos:

Lineage
   ↓
Action
   ↓
Job
   ↓
Stages
   ↓
Tasks

Lazy evaluation e lineage estão profundamente conectados.

7. O DAG

Essa cadeia de dependências não precisa ser apenas linear.

Podemos ter:

          RDD A
         /     \
        /       \
       ▼         ▼
    RDD B      RDD C
       \         /
        \       /
         ▼     ▼
          RDD D

Isso forma um:

Directed Acyclic Graph — DAG

ou:

Grafo Direcionado Acíclico

Direcionado porque existem relações de dependência.

Acíclico porque a computação não forma ciclos arbitrários de dependência entre esses datasets.

Conceitualmente:

Source
  ↓
Transform
  ↓
Transform ─────┐
  │            │
  ▼            ▼
Branch A    Branch B
  │            │
  └──────┬─────┘
         ▼
       Result

O DAG representa a estrutura da computação.

8. DAG não é exatamente a mesma coisa que Stage

Essa distinção é importante.

Podemos ter uma sequência de transformações:

map
 ↓
filter
 ↓
map
 ↓
reduceByKey
 ↓
map

Mas isso não significa necessariamente:

5 transformations
=
5 stages

Como vimos anteriormente, dependências narrow podem ser agrupadas em um mesmo Stage.

Shuffle frequentemente cria uma fronteira.

Então podemos ter:

STAGE 1

map
 ↓
filter
 ↓
map
 ↓

====== SHUFFLE ======

STAGE 2

reduce
 ↓
map

Portanto:

Lineage / DAG
      ↓
Stage boundaries
      ↓
Tasks

são conceitos relacionados, mas não idênticos.

9. Narrow Dependencies

Vamos revisitar um conceito importante.

Considere:

rdd2 = rdd1.map(
    lambda x: x * 2
)

Podemos ter:

RDD1 P1 ───► RDD2 P1
RDD1 P2 ───► RDD2 P2
RDD1 P3 ───► RDD2 P3

Cada partição filha depende de uma quantidade limitada de partições anteriores.

Isso caracteriza uma dependência estreita:

Narrow Dependency.

Agora imagine que perdemos:

RDD2 P2

Spark pode precisar reconstruir apenas o caminho relevante:

RDD1 P2
   ↓
 map
   ↓
RDD2 P2

Essa granularidade é extremamente importante para tolerância a falhas.

10. Recomputation

Aqui chegamos ao coração da resiliência.

Imagine:

Source

P1 P2 P3 P4
 │  │  │  │
 ▼  ▼  ▼  ▼

Map

P1' P2' P3' P4'

Agora:

P3'

é perdida.

Spark conhece sua dependência:

Source P3
    ↓
   map
    ↓
  P3'

Então pode reconstruí-la.

Não precisa necessariamente recalcular:

P1'
P2'
P4'

A ideia é:

Recompute what was lost from the lineage.

Essa é uma das razões para a palavra:

Resilient.

11. Resiliência sem replicar tudo

Uma abordagem possível para tolerância a falhas seria:

Resultado intermediário
       ↓
Copy 1
Copy 2
Copy 3

Mas isso possui custos:

Storage
Network
Replication
Coordination

RDDs introduziram uma ideia poderosa para datasets derivados deterministicamente:

Don't replicate every intermediate result
              ↓
Keep lineage
              ↓
Recompute lost partitions

Isso não elimina a necessidade de persistência ou replicação em todos os contextos.

Mas cria um mecanismo elegante para recuperar dados derivados.

12. Um exemplo mais completo

Imagine:

raw = sc.textFile(
    "/data/logs"
)

parsed = raw.map(parse_line)

errors = parsed.filter(
    lambda x: x.level == "ERROR"
)

by_service = errors.map(
    lambda x: (x.service, 1)
)

counts = by_service.reduceByKey(
    lambda a, b: a + b
)

Temos:

TEXT FILE
    ↓
   raw
    ↓
  parse
    ↓
 parsed
    ↓
 filter
    ↓
 errors
    ↓
   map
    ↓
by_service
    ↓
reduceByKey
    ↓
 counts

Agora imagine uma partição de errors sendo perdida.

Spark conhece:

textFile
   ↓
 parse
   ↓
 filter
   ↓
errors partition

Então pode reconstruir aquela partição a partir da origem e das transformações necessárias.

13. E depois de um Shuffle?

Agora a situação fica mais interessante.

Considere:

counts = by_service.reduceByKey(
    lambda a, b: a + b
)

Como vimos na Parte 4:

Map-side work
      ↓
Shuffle Write
      ↓
Network
      ↓
Shuffle Read
      ↓
Reduce-side work

Temos uma wide dependency.

Agora uma partição posterior pode depender de dados produzidos por várias partições anteriores.

Conceitualmente:

P1 ───┐
P2 ───┼──► Shuffle ───► R1
P3 ───┤
P4 ───┘

Se determinado resultado for perdido, a recomputação pode ser mais cara porque envolve dependências mais amplas.

Isso mostra que:

Nem todo lineage possui o mesmo custo de recuperação.

14. Narrow vs. Wide também importa para Fault Tolerance

Compare:

Narrow 

P1 ───► P1'
P2 ───► P2'
P3 ───► P3'

Perdeu P2'?

Recompute P2
     ↓
     P2'

Agora:

Wide 

P1 ───┐
P2 ───┼──► P'
P3 ───┤
P4 ───┘

A dependência é mais ampla.

Isso afeta:

  • custo de recomputação;
  • organização dos Stages;
  • shuffle;
  • recuperação.

Mais uma vez, shuffle aparece como uma fronteira importante da arquitetura.

15. Então por que usar Cache?

Se Spark consegue recomputar tudo, poderíamos perguntar:

Por que utilizar cache?

Porque recomputação também custa.

Imagine:

Source
 ↓
Expensive Transformation A
 ↓
Expensive Transformation B
 ↓
Dataset X

Agora utilizamos Dataset X cinco vezes:

             Dataset X
            /    |    \
           ▼     ▼     ▼
         Job A Job B Job C

Sem persistência, determinadas partes da linhagem podem precisar ser recomputadas.

Se Dataset X for caro de produzir, podemos decidir:

dataset_x.cache()

Agora trocamos:

Repeated Computation

por:

Storage

Esse é um trade-off.

16. Cache vs. Recomputation

Podemos pensar assim:

                 Dataset
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          ▼                   ▼
      Recompute             Cache
          │                   │
          ▼                   ▼
     More CPU             More Memory
     More Time            Storage Cost
          │                   │
          └─────────┬─────────┘
                    ▼
                 Trade-off

A pergunta não é:

Cache é bom?

A pergunta é:

O custo de manter esse dataset é menor do que o custo esperado de recomputá-lo?

Essa é uma pergunta muito mais útil.

17. Persistência e tolerância a falhas

Agora existe uma nuance importante.

Se persistimos um RDD e uma partição persistida é perdida devido à falha de um Executor, o lineage ainda pode permitir sua recomputação.

Imagine:

RDD X cached

Executor 1
├── P1
└── P2

Executor 2
├── P3
└── P4

Executor 2 falha:

P3 X
P4 X

Spark ainda conhece:

Lineage

e pode reconstruir essas partições quando necessário.

Então:

Cache

e:

Lineage

não são mecanismos concorrentes.

Eles se complementam.

18. persist()

Como vimos na Parte 7, podemos usar:

rdd.persist()

para controlar estratégias de persistência.

Conceitualmente:

Persistence
    │
    ├── Memory
    ├── Disk
    ├── Serialized forms
    └── Replication options

A escolha depende do workload.

Por exemplo:

Dataset pequeno
+
reutilizado frequentemente
+
caro de recomputar

pode justificar uma estratégia diferente de:

Dataset enorme
+
utilizado uma vez

Persistência deve responder a uma necessidade real.

19. Mas Lineage pode crescer

Agora imagine um pipeline muito longo:

RDD1
 ↓
RDD2
 ↓
RDD3
 ↓
RDD4
 ↓
RDD5
 ↓
RDD6
 ↓
...
 ↓
RDD100
 ↓
...
 ↓
RDD500

Temos uma longa cadeia de dependências.

Em determinados workloads iterativos ou pipelines extensos, essa linhagem pode se tornar indesejavelmente longa ou cara para recuperação.

Queremos então, em alguns cenários, interromper essa dependência histórica.

É aqui que aparece outro conceito:

Checkpoint.

20. O que é Checkpoint?

A ideia do checkpoint é materializar o estado de um dataset em armazenamento confiável e cortar sua dependência da linhagem anterior para fins de recuperação.

Antes:

Source
 ↓
A
 ↓
B
 ↓
C
 ↓
D
 ↓
E

Se E precisar ser reconstruído:

Source → A → B → C → D → E

Agora imagine um checkpoint em C:

Source
 ↓
A
 ↓
B
 ↓
C
 ↓
CHECKPOINT
 ↓
D
 ↓
E

A recuperação posterior pode partir do checkpoint:

CHECKPOINT
    ↓
    D
    ↓
    E

Isso trunca a linhagem anterior.

21. Configurando Checkpoint em RDD

Em um contexto de RDD, podemos definir um diretório de checkpoint:

sc.setCheckpointDir(
    "/path/to/reliable/checkpoints"
)

Depois:

rdd.checkpoint()

Quando o RDD for materializado por uma Action, o checkpoint poderá ser efetivamente produzido.

Por exemplo:

rdd.checkpoint()

rdd.count()

Conceitualmente:

checkpoint()
    ↓
mark RDD
    ↓
Action
    ↓
compute
    ↓
write checkpoint

Assim como cache, existe interação com lazy evaluation.

22. Checkpoint não é Cache

Essa distinção é fundamental.

Cache

Objetivo principal:

Reuse
 ↓
Performance

Checkpoint

Objetivo principal:

Materialize reliable state
        ↓
Truncate lineage
        ↓
Recovery / lineage management

Simplificando:

CACHE
"Evite recomputar algo que vou reutilizar."

versus:

CHECKPOINT
"Crie um novo ponto materializado e corte a dependência da linhagem anterior."

Os dois podem aparecer juntos.

Mas resolvem problemas diferentes.

23. Cache não corta Lineage

Imagine:

A
 ↓
B
 ↓
C
 ↓
D

Fazemos:

d.cache()

Ainda existe conceitualmente:

A
 ↓
B
 ↓
C
 ↓
D [cached]

O lineage continua conhecido.

Se a partição persistida for perdida, Spark pode usar essa linhagem para reconstruí-la.

Agora com checkpoint:

A
 ↓
B
 ↓
C
 ↓
D
 ↓
CHECKPOINT

a linhagem anterior pode ser truncada depois que o checkpoint é materializado corretamente.

Essa é uma diferença arquitetural importante.

24. Checkpoint também tem custo

Checkpoint não é gratuito.

Precisamos:

Compute
   ↓
Write
   ↓
Reliable Storage

Isso envolve:

  • I/O;
  • armazenamento;
  • tempo;
  • gerenciamento.

Portanto, não queremos:

checkpoint everything

Queremos checkpoint quando existe uma razão arquitetural.

Por exemplo:

  • lineage muito longo;
  • processamento iterativo;
  • necessidade de ponto confiável;
  • custo elevado de reconstrução.

25. Um pipeline iterativo

Imagine um algoritmo que executa repetidamente:

Iteration 1
    ↓
Iteration 2
    ↓
Iteration 3
    ↓
Iteration 4
    ↓
...
    ↓
Iteration 100

Se cada iteração depende da anterior, podemos formar uma linhagem extensa.

Conceitualmente:

Initial
 ↓
I1
 ↓
I2
 ↓
I3
 ↓
...
 ↓
I100

Em determinadas situações, podemos estabelecer checkpoints intermediários:

Initial
 ↓
I1
 ↓
...
 ↓
I20
 ↓
CHECKPOINT
 ↓
I21
 ↓
...
 ↓
I40
 ↓
CHECKPOINT

Assim reduzimos a profundidade necessária para recuperação futura.

26. Falha de Executor não significa falha da aplicação

Agora podemos enxergar resiliência de forma melhor.

Temos:

Executor 1
Executor 2
Executor 3
Executor 4

Um desaparece:

Executor 1
Executor 2
Executor 3 X
Executor 4

Isso não implica necessariamente:

APPLICATION FAILED

Spark pode reagendar trabalho e reconstruir dados necessários quando a situação permite.

Conceitualmente:

Executor failure
      ↓
Lost Tasks / Data
      ↓
Scheduler
      ↓
Re-execution
      ↓
Lineage
      ↓
Recompute
      ↓
Continue

Essa capacidade é central em computação distribuída.

27. Task Failure

Também podemos ter falha em uma Task específica.

Por exemplo:

Stage 10

Task 1 ✓
Task 2 ✓
Task 3 X
Task 4 ✓

Spark pode tentar executar novamente a Task.

Task 3
  ↓
Retry
  ↓
Task 3 ✓

Talvez em outro Executor.

Isso ajuda com falhas transitórias.

Mas existe uma distinção importante.

28. Falha transitória vs. falha determinística

Imagine:

Task failed

porque uma máquina teve um problema temporário.

Retry pode funcionar:

Attempt 1 → FAIL
Attempt 2 → SUCCESS

Agora imagine código:

def transform(x):
    return 100 / x

e temos:

x = 0

A Task falha.

Spark tenta novamente.

Attempt 1 → divide by zero
Attempt 2 → divide by zero
Attempt 3 → divide by zero

Não importa quantas máquinas utilizarmos.

O problema está nos dados ou no código.

Isso nos ensina:

Fault tolerance não corrige lógica determinística incorreta.

29. Recomputation também não corrige dados ruins

Imagine:

corrupted input

A partição falha.

Spark tenta novamente:

read
 ↓
fail
 ↓
retry
 ↓
read same corrupted data
 ↓
fail

Lineage ajuda a recuperar computação perdida.

Não transforma entrada inválida em entrada válida.

Resiliência tem limites.

30. O Driver continua sendo especial

Até agora falamos muito sobre Executors.

Mas existe um componente central:

DRIVER

O Driver coordena a aplicação.

Se um Executor falha, Spark pode frequentemente reagendar trabalho.

A falha do Driver possui implicações diferentes porque ali está o processo que coordena a aplicação.

A capacidade de recuperar o Driver depende também:

  • do modo de implantação;
  • do cluster manager;
  • da configuração;
  • da plataforma utilizada;
  • dos mecanismos externos de supervisão/restart.

Portanto:

Executor fault tolerance

não deve ser confundida automaticamente com:

Driver high availability

São problemas relacionados, mas diferentes.

31. Lineage não substitui durabilidade da fonte

Imagine que nosso RDD começa em:

/data/events

e depois:

Source
 ↓
Map
 ↓
Filter
 ↓
RDD

Se perdemos uma partição intermediária, podemos tentar reconstruí-la a partir da fonte.

Mas e se a fonte original desaparecer?

Source X

Agora lineage sabe:

como

reconstruir.

Mas não possui necessariamente:

de onde

obter os dados originais.

Portanto:

Lineage não substitui armazenamento durável dos dados de origem.

Essa distinção é muito importante em arquitetura de dados.

32. Fault tolerance não é Backup

Outro erro conceitual seria pensar:

Spark é fault tolerant
        ↓
não preciso de backup

Não.

São problemas diferentes.

Fault tolerance

Ajuda o sistema a continuar ou recuperar processamento diante de determinadas falhas.

Backup

Protege dados contra cenários como:

  • exclusão;
  • corrupção;
  • desastre;
  • erro operacional;
  • perda da fonte.

Podemos ter um engine extremamente resiliente processando uma fonte que foi permanentemente destruída.

O engine não recria magicamente dados que deixaram de existir.

33. Lineage e DataFrames

Até agora usei RDDs porque lineage é um conceito especialmente natural para explicar a arquitetura original do Spark.

Mas DataFrames também participam de uma computação baseada em dependências e planos.

Quando escrevemos:

resultado = (
    vendas
    .filter("ano = 2026")
    .groupBy("estado")
    .sum("valor")
)

continuamos tendo:

Source
 ↓
Transformations
 ↓
Dependencies
 ↓
Stages
 ↓
Tasks

A diferença é que agora também existe a camada estruturada que vimos na Parte 6:

DataFrame
 ↓
Logical Plan
 ↓
Catalyst
 ↓
Physical Plan
 ↓
Distributed Execution

Os fundamentos não desapareceram.

Eles ganharam novas abstrações.

34. Lineage vs. Query Plan

Também não devemos tratar:

Lineage

e:

Query Plan

como exatamente a mesma coisa.

Uma forma útil de pensar é:

Lineage

Relaciona datasets e dependências necessárias para derivação/recomputação.

Query Plan

Representa operações lógicas e físicas usadas pelo engine estruturado para planejar e executar uma consulta.

Eles se encontram na execução distribuída, mas são conceitos distintos.

35. DAG Scheduler

Agora podemos encaixar outra peça da arquitetura.

Spark possui componentes responsáveis por transformar a computação em trabalho executável.

Uma visão conceitual:

Application
    ↓
Action
    ↓
Job
    ↓
DAG Scheduler
    ↓
Stages
    ↓
Task Sets
    ↓
Executors

O DAG Scheduler consegue analisar dependências e identificar fronteiras de Stage, especialmente ao redor de shuffles.

Podemos pensar:

Narrow
 ↓
same Stage where possible

Wide
 ↓
Shuffle
 ↓
new Stage boundary

Isso conecta lineage diretamente ao modelo de execução que estudamos na Parte 2.

36. Task Scheduling

Depois que o trabalho é dividido em Stages e Tasks, precisamos executar essas Tasks nos Executors.

Conceitualmente:

DAG Scheduler
     ↓
Stages
     ↓
Task Scheduler
     ↓
Executors

Agora entram preocupações como:

  • recursos disponíveis;
  • localização;
  • execução;
  • retries;
  • status das Tasks.

O Spark não é apenas uma biblioteca de transformação.

Existe um sistema de scheduling distribuído por trás da API.

37. Data Locality

Existe ainda uma ideia importante.

Se os dados estão próximos de determinado Executor ou nó, pode ser vantajoso executar o processamento próximo deles.

Em vez de:

Move 100 GB of data
      ↓
to computation

podemos preferir, quando a arquitetura permite:

Move computation
      ↓
to data

Essa filosofia foi extremamente importante no ecossistema de Big Data.

No Spark, scheduling pode considerar locality dependendo da fonte e do ambiente.

Novamente encontramos o princípio:

Mover computação costuma ser mais barato do que mover grandes volumes de dados.

38. Falhas e Shuffle

Shuffle torna a recuperação mais interessante.

Imagine:

Stage 1
  ↓
Shuffle Write
  ↓
Stage 2

Os outputs intermediários de shuffle são importantes para o Stage seguinte.

Se dados intermediários necessários forem perdidos devido a falhas, Spark pode precisar recomputar partes anteriores.

Conceitualmente:

Lost Shuffle Data
       ↓
Need previous output
       ↓
Recompute upstream tasks
       ↓
Regenerate shuffle data
       ↓
Continue downstream work

Agora entendemos por que lineage continua relevante mesmo depois de falarmos sobre shuffle.

39. Recomputation tem custo

Fault tolerance não significa:

failure = free

Imagine:

2-hour computation
      ↓
lost intermediate data
      ↓
recompute

O sistema pode conseguir se recuperar.

Mas isso custa:

  • CPU;
  • tempo;
  • rede;
  • I/O;
  • dinheiro.

Então existe outra pergunta arquitetural:

Qual é o custo aceitável de recomputação?

É aqui que persistência e checkpoint podem entrar.

40. Cache, Checkpoint ou Recompute?

Podemos montar um modelo mental:

Dataset intermediário
        │
        ▼
Será reutilizado?
   │           │
  sim         não
   │           │
   ▼           ▼
Cache?     Recompute?
   │
   ▼
É caro de reconstruir
e lineage é problemático?
   │
   ▼
Checkpoint?

Não é uma árvore de decisão absoluta.

É apenas uma forma de pensar.

A escolha depende de:

Cost of computation
Cost of storage
Reuse
Failure probability
Lineage length
Recovery requirements

41. Um exemplo prático

Imagine:

raw = spark.read.parquet(
    "/data/events"
)

base = (
    raw
    .filter("event_date >= '2026-01-01'")
    .select(
        "customer_id",
        "event_type",
        "value"
    )
)

Essa transformação é usada por vários outputs:

por_cliente = (
    base
    .groupBy("customer_id")
    .count()
)

por_evento = (
    base
    .groupBy("event_type")
    .count()
)

receita = (
    base
    .groupBy("customer_id")
    .sum("value")
)

Temos:

                  RAW
                   │
                   ▼
             Filter + Select
                   │
                   ▼
                  BASE
             ┌─────┼─────┐
             ▼     ▼     ▼
         Customer Event Revenue

Se base for caro de produzir e reutilizado várias vezes:

base.cache()

pode fazer sentido.

A decisão nasce do DAG.

Não de uma regra genérica de que:

cache = performance

42. Um exemplo de Checkpoint

Agora imagine um processamento iterativo ou uma cadeia extremamente extensa.

Em RDD:

rdd = sc.textFile("/data/source")

for i in range(100):
    rdd = expensive_transformation(rdd)

A linhagem pode crescer:

Source
 ↓
T1
 ↓
T2
 ↓
T3
 ↓
...
 ↓
T100

Podemos decidir estabelecer checkpoints em pontos apropriados.

Conceitualmente:

Source
 ↓
T1
 ↓
...
 ↓
T25
 ↓
CHECKPOINT
 ↓
T26
 ↓
...
 ↓
T50
 ↓
CHECKPOINT

Assim controlamos o tamanho da cadeia de recuperação.

43. localCheckpoint() merece cuidado

Spark também possui mecanismos de checkpoint local em determinados contextos.

Mas existe uma diferença conceitual importante:

Reliable checkpoint

busca armazenamento confiável para quebrar a linhagem mantendo capacidade adequada de recuperação.

Já um checkpoint baseado apenas em armazenamento local dos Executors não oferece necessariamente a mesma garantia de tolerância a falhas.

Portanto:

Não devemos tratar todo tipo de checkpoint como equivalente em resiliência.

A escolha depende do objetivo.

44. Resiliência também depende do storage

Se o checkpoint precisa servir como ponto confiável de recuperação, precisamos pensar:

Onde ele está armazenado?

Um diretório local efêmero possui características muito diferentes de armazenamento distribuído e durável.

Então a arquitetura completa é:

Spark
   +
Lineage
   +
Checkpoint strategy
   +
Reliable storage

Fault tolerance não acontece isoladamente.

45. O que acontece quando uma máquina desaparece?

Agora podemos responder de forma muito melhor.

Imagine:

Executor 3
    ↓
FAIL

Spark pode identificar trabalho perdido.

Depois:

Lost partition
      ↓
Find lineage
      ↓
Find required ancestors
      ↓
Schedule recomputation
      ↓
Execute elsewhere
      ↓
Rebuild data
      ↓
Continue

Essa sequência explica o:

Resilient

de:

Resilient Distributed Dataset.

46. O que eu olho quando existem muitas recomputações?

Se uma aplicação está refazendo trabalho demais, quero investigar:

Executors estão instáveis?

Existe perda de containers?

Existe pressão de memória?

Existe GC excessivo?

Existe problema de infraestrutura?

Existe shuffle data sendo perdida?

A linhagem é cara?

Falta persistência em um ponto estratégico?

Ou seja, recomputation é um mecanismo de recuperação.

Mas recomputation excessiva também pode ser sintoma.

47. Resiliência não significa ignorar infraestrutura

Podemos ter:

Executor failure
 ↓
Retry
 ↓
Executor failure
 ↓
Retry
 ↓
Executor failure

Em algum momento a pergunta deixa de ser:

Spark consegue tentar novamente?

e passa a ser:

Por que meus Executors continuam morrendo?

Talvez exista:

OOM
Disk failure
Container eviction
Network instability
Bad node
Data skew

Fault tolerance deve absorver falhas ocasionais.

Não deve ser usada para esconder um cluster permanentemente instável.

48. Observabilidade novamente

No troubleshooting, quero relacionar:

Application
    ↓
Jobs
    ↓
Stages
    ↓
Tasks
    ↓
Executors

com:

Failures
Retries
Recomputation
Shuffle
Memory
GC
Spill

Se Tasks estão sendo repetidas, preciso saber por quê.

Se Stages estão sendo refeitos, preciso saber por quê.

Se Executors desaparecem, preciso saber por quê.

Resiliência é muito mais útil quando acompanhada de observabilidade.

49. Um modelo mental de Fault Tolerance

Minha forma de enxergar ficou assim:

                   DATA SOURCE
                       │
                       ▼
                 Transformations
                       │
                       ▼
                    Lineage
                       │
                       ▼
                      DAG
                       │
                       ▼
                    Stages
                       │
                       ▼
                     Tasks
                       │
                       ▼
                   Executors
                       │
                       ▼
                    Failure?
                   /         \
                 não          sim
                 │             │
                 ▼             ▼
             Continue      What was lost?
                               │
                               ▼
                           Lineage
                               │
                               ▼
                         Recompute
                               │
                               ▼
                           Continue

Agora acrescente:

Cache

quando queremos evitar recomputação frequente.

E:

Checkpoint

quando queremos estabelecer um novo ponto materializado e truncar uma linhagem problemática.

50. A principal lição deste capítulo

A resiliência do Spark não vem de uma única configuração.

Ela emerge de várias ideias trabalhando juntas:

Immutable Datasets
        +
Transformations
        +
Dependencies
        +
Lineage
        +
DAG
        +
Task Scheduling
        +
Retries
        +
Recomputation

E, quando necessário:

Cache / Persist

ou:

Checkpoint

Essa arquitetura permite que uma falha parcial não precise significar perda completa da computação.

51. O significado de RDD ficou muito mais claro

No começo da série:

RDD
=
Resilient Distributed Dataset

podia parecer apenas um nome.

Agora conseguimos decompor:

DISTRIBUTED
     ↓
Partitions across cluster

DATASET
     ↓
Collection of data

e:

RESILIENT
     ↓
Lineage
     ↓
Recomputation
     ↓
Fault recovery

Essa é uma das ideias fundamentais da arquitetura original do Spark.

52. O que essa ideia me ensinou além do Spark

A lição mais interessante vai além da tecnologia.

Em sistemas distribuídos, não podemos construir arquitetura assumindo:

Everything will always work

Precisamos assumir:

Machines fail
Processes fail
Networks fail
Tasks fail
Containers disappear

Então a arquitetura precisa responder:

What happens next?

Essa pergunta vale para:

  • processamento de dados;
  • microsserviços;
  • bancos distribuídos;
  • streaming;
  • Kubernetes;
  • cloud;
  • Machine Learning distribuído.

Tolerância a falhas não é um recurso opcional adicionado no final.

É uma propriedade arquitetural.

53. Como penso hoje

Quando vejo uma transformação Spark:

resultado = (
    dados
    .filter(...)
    .map(...)
    .reduceByKey(...)
)

não penso apenas:

input
 ↓
transform
 ↓
output

Penso:

Where is the source?
        ↓
What are the dependencies?
        ↓
Where are the shuffle boundaries?
        ↓
What is the lineage?
        ↓
What happens if a partition disappears?
        ↓
How expensive is recomputation?
        ↓
Should something be persisted?
        ↓
Is checkpointing justified?

Essa mudança de mentalidade é muito mais importante do que memorizar APIs.

Próximo artigo

Agora temos uma base sólida sobre:

RDD
 ↓
Partitions
 ↓
Transformations
 ↓
Lineage
 ↓
DAG
 ↓
Stages
 ↓
Tasks
 ↓
Executors
 ↓
Fault Tolerance

Mas existe um tema do material original que merece ser revisitado com bastante cuidado:

variáveis compartilhadas.

Em uma aplicação comum, podemos imaginar:

contador += 1

e esperar que exista apenas um contador.

Mas em Spark temos:

Driver
  +
Executor 1
  +
Executor 2
  +
Executor 3

Então surge uma pergunta:

O que significa "variável compartilhada" em uma aplicação distribuída?

No próximo artigo vamos explorar:

  • closures;
  • serialização de funções;
  • variáveis capturadas;
  • Driver vs. Executors;
  • por que alterar uma variável dentro de uma Task não funciona como muitos esperam;
  • Broadcast Variables;
  • Accumulators;
  • quando utilizar cada mecanismo;
  • armadilhas de side effects;
  • e como pensar em estado em computação distribuída.

Vamos sair disto:

counter = 0

for item:
    counter += 1

para isto:

              DRIVER
                 │
          serialized closure
        ┌────────┼────────┐
        ▼        ▼        ▼
     Executor Executor Executor
        │        │        │
      Task     Task      Task

E entender por que código aparentemente simples muda completamente quando atravessa máquinas.

← Parte 7: Memória — Executors, Driver, Cache, Spill e OutOfMemory

Próximo: Parte 9 — Variáveis compartilhadas no Apache Spark: Broadcast, Accumulators e Closures

title: Automating Edge LLM Guardrails: Mitigating Autonomous Agent Prompt Injection in Multi-Tenant Environments
description:
Automating Edge LLM Guardrails: Securing Multi-Tenant AI Architecture

Deploying large language models across distributed edge nodes requires robust real-time guardrails. As multi-tenant AI agents handle complex enterprise data streams, traditional vector databases often fail to sanitize dynamic prompt inputs—leaving system architectures vulnerable to token-level injection vectors.

The Security Challenge at the Edge

Security engineers operating high-throughput AI infrastructure must implement native input filtering mechanisms directly at the application gateway layer. Intercepting inference tokens prior to execution prevents unauthorized memory reads and malicious API calls without introducing noticeable latency.


yaml
# Conceptual Policy Engine Configuration snippet

  max_cross_tenant_access: denied
Key Architecture Goals:
Token-Level Sanitization: Intercepting dynamic prompts before hitting core inference engines.

Multi-Tenant Context Isolation: Preventing context leakage across execution boundaries.

Low-Latency Gateway Enforcement: Maintaining high throughput using native gateway rules.

title: Artex Hacking Tool Found Exposed on Hundreds of Public Servers
description:
If you're running penetration testing tools in the cloud, check your access controls now. Hundreds of servers hosting the Artex hacking tool have been found publicly exposed to the internet, according to a recent TechCrunch report.

The Discovery

Security researchers uncovered hundreds of servers running Artex—a legitimate penetration testing framework—that were left accessible without authentication. This means anyone on the internet could connect to these servers and use the tool's capabilities, which include network scanning, vulnerability exploitation, and password cracking.

The exposure wasn't a vulnerability in Artex itself. It was a configuration oversight by the operators who deployed the tool without proper network restrictions. These servers were essentially unlocked doors to powerful hacking utilities.

Why This Matters for Developers

If you develop, deploy, or maintain any security tooling in cloud environments, this should be a wake-up call. Here's what to check right now:

  • Are your security tools accessible from the public internet?
  • Do they require authentication for every endpoint?
  • Have you tested your deployment from an external network?

The typical mistake is assuming that because a tool is internal or experimental, it doesn't need security hardening. But cloud providers assign public IPs by default, and even "temporary" setups can persist for months.

Practical Next Steps

  1. Audit your cloud security groups – Review inbound rules for any instances running security tools. Restrict access to known IP ranges only.
  2. Enable authentication – If Artex or similar tools don't enforce login by default, add a reverse proxy with basic auth or integrate with an identity provider.
  3. Monitor for unexpected access – Set up logging and alerts for connections to these services. Unusual traffic patterns may indicate compromise.
  4. Use ephemeral environments – Spin up test instances only when needed and tear them down immediately after.

The lesson is simple: treat every deployed instance as if it's already under attack. Because in this case, hundreds of servers were effectively inviting attackers in.

Source: TechCrunch - Hundreds of Artex AI hacking tools found publicly exposed to the web

title: Claude Code said "all tests pass". It had skipped them. So I built a fail-closed gate.
description:
If you use an AI coding agent long enough, you will see this: the agent says "Done - all tests pass", and it's true only because a test was skipped, deleted, or quietly weakened in the same change.

It's a known failure mode (see anthropics/claude-code#7074). Asking the agent nicely in CLAUDE.md doesn't fix it, because the agent is the one grading its own work.

The idea: don't trust "done", verify it

I built BuildProof around one rule: the agent's claim is never accepted on its word. A separate check decides, and it fails closed - if it can't prove the work is good, the change is rejected.

After Claude Code finishes a turn (as a hook), or on a pull request (as a GitHub Action), it:

  1. Re-runs the real test suite - not the agent's summary of it.
  2. Checks the tests really ran - zero tests executed is a failure, not a pass.
  3. Diffs the tests themselves - any test that was skipped, deleted, or had assertions weakened in the same change blocks it.
  4. Checks for regressions against the previous state.
  5. Rolls back rejected changes automatically.
  6. Signs accepted changes with an ed25519 certificate, so "this passed" is something you can verify later, not just a log line.

What it looks like

The demo page shows real output - a change that "passes" by weakening a test, and how it gets rejected:

👉 https://buildproof.mgrprosnetwork.com/demo

Try it 

npm install -g buildproof

Package: https://www.npmjs.com/package/buildproof

Full disclosure: I'm the maker. It's a commercial tool with a 14-day free trial, not open source.

I'd really like feedback from people who run agents on real codebases: what other ways have you seen an agent "fake" a green build? Every trick you've seen becomes a new check.

title: Scoped Realtime Tokens for Express Chat Rooms — Reconnects, Fan-out, and Retention
description:
Short answer: verify the session on the server, issue a short-lived token limited to the browser user's channels, and renew it before expiry. The browser should never receive the server key. For an edtech chat room, that policy is the least complicated way to keep reconnects from becoming an authorization bug while preserving a clear delivery contract at fan-out.

The important cost is not the token request. It is the telemetry produced by every connection, retry, publish, and delivery attempt. I treat each log line as bytes stored and each label as cardinality. A design that keeps every message body, room id, user id, retry reason, and browser version forever will eventually turn a useful incident record into an expensive event archive.

Start with the delivery contract

An in-app notification room has two separate questions: may this browser subscribe, and what does it receive after the network disappears? A scoped token answers the first. It does not, by itself, promise that a missed event will be replayed.

For a classroom discussion, I would define the contract before choosing a provider. Presence can be approximate. A notification that changes assignment state needs a durable source of truth. A typing indicator can be dropped. A moderation event needs an audit trail outside the transient fan-out path.

This distinction matters during reconnects. The client should reconnect with a token that is still valid, then resubscribe only to the channels granted to that user. If the token is near expiry, re-issue it before the connection drops rather than waiting for an authorization failure. The application should fetch current state after a suspicious gap; it should not infer state from an assumed perfect stream.

The server-side sequence is deliberately small:

  1. Authenticate the Express request and verify its session.
  2. Resolve the user's allowed channels from application data.
  3. Issue a token for that client identity and channel set.
  4. Return only the scoped token to the browser.
  5. Renew before expiry and re-fetch authoritative state after reconnect.

The verification route is GET /v1/auth/session/verify/{session_id}. Token issuance is POST /v1/realtime/token/issue, and revocation is POST /v1/realtime/token/revoke. The exact request schema should come from the endpoint's current schema; inventing field names in a copy-paste example is a poor trade when authorization is involved.

No guessing.

What actually makes the bill grow?

In an active room, the dominant telemetry term is usually event volume multiplied by retained bytes, not the occasional token issue. A useful first approximation is:

stored bytes = events x average serialized event size x retention days

Labels multiply the search surface. If one event carries room, course, lesson, user, browser, region, reconnect reason, and message type as independently varying dimensions, the number of possible label combinations grows far faster than the number of rooms. High-cardinality labels also make an incident query harder to reason about.

Keep the dimensions that answer an operational question: room_id for a bounded room-level investigation, event_type, delivery_result, and a coarse deployment version. Hash or omit direct user identifiers in routine telemetry. Keep the full authorization decision in a short-lived security log, with access controls and a retention period chosen for the incident process rather than copied into every delivery event.
