If you write backend code, you're closer to building production AI agents than you think. Queues, retries, idempotency, logs: it all carries over. What's new is a component that makes decisions, gives different answers to the same input, and can be talked into things. Here's the translation layer.

An agent is an LLM with three upgrades

A plain LLM call can only talk. An agent can act, because it adds:

  • Tools: functions it can call, such as querying a database or sending an email.
  • Memory: a record of what has happened so far.
  • A loop: it works step by step until the job is done. It thinks, acts, checks the result, and decides what's next. This pattern is called ReAct (reason + act).

Before you build one, ask whether a single, well-prompted LLM call would do. Summarising a paragraph is one call. Finding, fixing and testing a bug across 40 files is a job for an agent.

Tools: the model asks, your code decides

Function calling is the mechanism behind tools, and the most important thing to internalise is that the model never runs anything itself. You give it a menu of tools, each with a name, description and parameters. When it wants one, it replies with a structured request, and your code decides whether to run it. That's what keeps you in control.

Two habits make tools reliable:

  1. Write descriptions like API docs, including when not to use the tool. "Fetch a customer's recent orders. Use for order status or refunds. Not for product search." That last sentence prevents a surprising number of wrong picks.
  2. Validate arguments like any user input. Check the schema, check that referenced IDs exist, and rate-limit.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP), released by Anthropic in late 2024, lets you wrap a tool once and reuse it across any MCP-compatible agent. Think of it as USB-C for AI tools.

Memory is plumbing you build

LLMs remember nothing between calls; every bit of memory is something you store and feed back in. Short-term memory is the current conversation, limited by the context window. Long-term memory lives outside the model and is loaded only when relevant.

RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) is the common way to bring in outside knowledge: store documents in a vector database, retrieve the closest chunks, and put them in the prompt. Retrieve broadly, then re-rank and keep only the best few, and tell the model to answer using only that context so it doesn't guess.

Checkpointing means saving the agent's state after every step, so a restart resumes instead of starting over. It's the same reason you keep sessions in a database, not an in-memory dict.

Infrastructure: normal backend work, with two twists

Production agents are mostly the backend engineering you already do. The twists are that LLMs are non-deterministic and that their tool calls have real side effects. Four things keep you safe:

  • Durable execution. Tools like Temporal save progress at every step, so a crash resumes where it left off.
  • Sensible timeouts and retries. LLM calls can take a minute or more; back off politely on rate limits.
  • Idempotency keys. A retried tool call must happen only once in the real world.
  • Sandboxes. Run agent-written code in an isolated environment, never on your own server.

The idempotency key is the one engineers most often forget, and it's one line:

payments.refund(order_id="A123", amount=500, idempotency_key="refund:A123")
# The payment service sees the same key twice but refunds only once.

Cost matters too. Prompt caching lets providers reuse the repeated parts of your prompt; Anthropic reports savings of up to 90% on long prompts.

Observability: agents fail quietly

An agent's failures don't throw errors. You get a confident wrong answer, or a strange route to a right one, and a health check won't catch either. Tracing records every step as a span: what the model decided, which tool it called, what came back, the cost and the latency. Tools like Langfuse and LangSmith show this as a timeline.

Evaluation is testing for agents: plain assertions for exact things (right tool, right ID), and an LLM judge scoring fuzzy things against a rubric. Run evals in CI before every release, sample live traffic afterwards, and turn every production failure into a new test case.

Security: assume the model can be tricked

Agents act on text, and attackers can write text. The top risk is prompt injection: instructions hidden in a page, email or document the agent reads. You can't fully prevent it, so contain it:

  • Least privilege, enforced in code, not in the prompt.
  • Human approval for anything risky or irreversible: refunds, deletions, outgoing emails.
  • Treat model output as untrusted. Never eval() it, and parameterise any SQL it touches.
  • Keep secrets out of prompts. The model gets tools, never raw API keys.

The mantra: assume the model can be tricked, and make sure a tricked model can't do much damage. For example, an issue_refund() that raises NeedsHumanApproval above a set amount can't be pushed past that limit by a fooled model, because the code enforces the limit, not the prompt.

Go multi-agent last

Multi-agent systems are expensive and fragile. Anthropic's multi-agent research system used about 15 times more tokens than a normal chat, and a 2025 study found failure rates of 41% to 87% across multi-agent frameworks. What works best is one lead agent holding the full picture, with small helpers that do one job and report back a summary.

A learning path for a few weekends

  1. Build a tiny agent with raw API calls and two tools, no framework.
  2. Add RAG over a folder of your own notes.
  3. Add tracing and 50 test cases, then break things on purpose.
  4. Rebuild it in a framework: LangGraph, or the OpenAI or Claude Agent SDK.
  5. Add durable execution and an approval step.
  6. Expose a tool through MCP.

By step six you'll understand what frameworks do under the hood, which makes you much better at choosing and debugging them.

Originally published on TechBrosEbooks.

This article is adapted from the quick-start guide AI Agent Orchestration & Infrastructure for Software Engineers, which covers each idea in one short chapter, with orchestration patterns, multi-agent handoffs and A2A, an end-to-end support-ticket triage agent, and a pre-ship checklist.

title: How to Set Up Cloudflare Tunnel for Certifyd Core
description:
Certifyd Core lets you publish and share your creative work directly from your own computer. But to make that content available to fans over the internet, you'll need a public connection.

One way to accomplish this is with Cloudflare Tunnel, which connects your computer to a public web address without requiring you to open ports on your home router.

For permanent sharing, we recommend using a named Cloudflare Tunnel with cloudflared running independently as an operating-system service. This keeps your internet connection separate from Certifyd Core while allowing Core to manage what you publish.

Here's how to set everything up, starting with your domain.

Before you begin

You'll need:

  • Certifyd Core Beta 27 installed and running.
  • A free Cloudflare account.
  • A domain name you own, such as yourdomain.com.
  • Access to the company where your domain is registered.
  • Administrator access to the computer running Core.

If you don't own a domain yet, you can register one through a domain registrar. You don't need to transfer ownership of your domain to Cloudflare to use its DNS and tunnel services.

If you only want to test public sharing, Certifyd Core also supports temporary Cloudflare connections using a trycloudflare.com address. The steps below are for a permanent connection using your own domain.

Step 1: Add your domain to Cloudflare

Start by visiting Cloudflare and signing in or creating an account.

Choose the option to add a domain, sometimes labelled Add a domain or Add a website, and enter your existing domain name.

For example:

yourdomain.com

Cloudflare will scan for existing DNS records and offer a plan. Its Free plan is generally sufficient for a basic tunnel setup.

Before continuing, review the imported DNS records carefully.

If you already have a website, email hosting or other services attached to your domain, make sure their records are present. Pay particular attention to existing A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, SPF, DKIM and DMARC records, as applicable.

Do not delete existing DNS records simply because you are setting up Certifyd Core. Your existing website and email should continue working.

Step 2: Change your domain's nameservers

This is the step many people find confusing, but it usually only takes a few minutes to configure.

Your domain registrar is the company where you registered your domain. Your nameservers tell the internet which DNS provider is responsible for answering requests about that domain.

Cloudflare will provide two authoritative nameservers for your domain, similar to:

example-one.ns.cloudflare.com

example-two.ns.cloudflare.com

These are examples only. Use the exact nameservers Cloudflare assigns to your domain.

Now:

  1. Sign in to your domain registrar, such as GoDaddy, Namecheap or another provider.
  2. Find your domain's Nameservers, DNS, or Custom Nameservers settings.
  3. If DNSSEC is enabled, follow Cloudflare's instructions to disable the existing registrar-side DNSSEC configuration before switching nameservers.
  4. Replace the existing authoritative nameservers with the two assigned by Cloudflare.
  5. Save your changes.

You are not transferring ownership of the domain. You're changing which provider manages its authoritative DNS.

Return to Cloudflare and wait for it to confirm that your domain is active. Nameserver updates can take time to propagate, sometimes up to 24 hours.

Once Cloudflare confirms activation, you can manage your domain's DNS records through its dashboard. You can also configure DNSSEC again using Cloudflare's instructions.

Important: Changing nameservers affects the entire domain, not just Certifyd. Confirm that your existing website, email and other DNS records are correct before and after the switch.

Cloudflare provides a detailed nameserver setup guide if your registrar's interface looks different.

Step 3: Create a named Cloudflare Tunnel

With your domain active in Cloudflare, open the Cloudflare dashboard and navigate to:

Networking → Tunnels

Select Create a tunnel.

Give your tunnel a recognizable name, such as:

certifyd-core

Cloudflare will create the tunnel and provide installation instructions for connecting your computer.

A named tunnel is designed for persistent use. Unlike a temporary Quick Tunnel, it can serve content through a stable address on your own domain.

You can also reuse an existing named tunnel if you already operate Cloudflare services, provided you configure the correct route and avoid disrupting existing applications.

Step 4: Install cloudflared on your computer

Cloudflare uses a small application called cloudflared to connect your computer to its network.

After creating your tunnel, choose the operating system of the computer running Certifyd Core.

Cloudflare will provide an installation command specific to your tunnel. Follow those instructions to install cloudflared as an operating-system service.

We recommend this approach because the service can start automatically when your computer boots and continue operating independently of Certifyd Core.

Keep the installation token private. Anyone with a valid tunnel token may be able to run a connector for that tunnel.

If you already have cloudflared installed, inspect the existing service before making changes. There's no reason to replace a working connector simply to add Certifyd Core.

Cloudflare's official tunnel setup guide provides the installation commands for supported operating systems.

Step 5: Connect your domain to Certifyd Core

Now tell Cloudflare where to send visitors.

Open your named tunnel in Cloudflare and select:

Routes → Add route → Published application

Choose the public hostname you want visitors to use.

For example:

music.yourdomain.com

Set the service type to HTTP.

For Certifyd Core Beta 27, when Core and cloudflared are running on the same computer, use:

http://127.0.0.1:4010

Save the route.

This address is important because Certifyd Core separates its public-facing service from its private administrative dashboard.

Service Local address
Public content service http://127.0.0.1:4010
Private dashboard and API http://127.0.0.1:4000

Never point your public Cloudflare hostname at port 4000. That port is intended for Core's private administrative functions.

Cloudflare will handle the DNS routing for the published application hostname. You generally don't need to create an additional manual DNS record for that same tunnel route.

If Core and cloudflared run on different computers, the service address must instead identify the Core public listener at an address reachable from the connector.

Step 6: Configure permanent sharing in Certifyd Core

Return to Certifyd Core and open:

Configuration → Public Connection

Select Permanent and configure the hostname and named-tunnel information to match your Cloudflare setup.

Core Beta 27 can detect an externally managed connector. In that situation, some local configuration fields may become read-only. For a fresh installation, configuring these fields before starting the external connector can avoid that interface limitation.

This is not a requirement imposed by Cloudflare, and an independently managed connector can already be running.

Certifyd Core also includes controls for managing a connector itself, but for permanent installations, we recommend leaving cloudflared under operating-system management.

Once the connection is configured, select Enable sharing.

Check that Core reports:

  • Connection: Permanent
  • Sharing: Online

Remember that enabling public sharing does not automatically publish every file in your library. You still control which works are made available.

Step 7: Test your public link

Now test your setup as a visitor.

Open your Certifyd public profile or published content link from another device, preferably a phone using mobile data.

If everything is configured correctly, your published content should be accessible through your chosen domain.

If the link doesn't work, check the following:

  1. Core is running. The computer hosting your content must be online.
  2. Cloudflare is connected. Your named tunnel should report a healthy connector.
  3. Your hostname is correct. Confirm the published application route matches the address you're opening.
  4. The public port is correct. The documented same-computer service target is http://127.0.0.1:4010.
  5. Sharing is enabled. Verify the permanent connection and sharing status in Core.
  6. The intended work is published. A working tunnel doesn't automatically make unpublished content public.

If necessary, use Core's advanced diagnostics to inspect its public connection.

Avoid deleting existing tunnels, terminating unrelated cloudflared processes or reinstalling services without first checking their configuration.

What happens when someone opens your link?

Once the setup is complete, a visitor opens your public hostname. Cloudflare receives the request and forwards it through the tunnel to the public service running on your Certifyd Core computer.

Core then serves the content you've made available through its public interface.

Your creative files and application state remain with your Core installation. Cloudflare provides the public connection, rather than becoming the application that manages your creative catalogue.

There are still dependencies: your computer needs to remain online, your connector must be connected, and Cloudflare remains part of the delivery path.

But you don't need to upload your entire creative library to a conventional hosted publishing platform simply to give fans a public address.

Your computer. Your domain. Your content.

The difficult part of self-hosted publishing has traditionally been making a local computer reliably accessible over the internet.

Cloudflare Tunnel simplifies that process, while Certifyd Core provides the tools to manage and publish your creative work.

By connecting a domain you control to a Core installation you operate, you can establish a permanent public presence without giving up control of the underlying publishing environment.

For more information about installing and configuring Core, visit the Certifyd Core setup guide.

This guide covers Certifyd Core Beta 27. Interface labels and connection settings may change in subsequent beta releases.

Originally published on Certifyd.

title: Simple S3-Compatible Object Storage for Storing User-Uploaded Avatars (30-Day Deletion)
description:
For a media backend handling avatar uploads and signed documents, S3-compatible object storage is usually the simplest upload boundary. The difficult part is not putting bytes into a bucket. It is deciding which bytes survive the deadline, who can retrieve them, and what evidence remains after deletion.

Short answer: keep the original signed document private, keep the avatar behind an application-controlled access path, and store the deletion deadline in your database. Use the bucket lifecycle as a backstop, not as the only erasure mechanism. A 30-day rule is easy to state; an exact deletion time, derived-file policy, and recovery decision are application responsibilities.

The same rule applies to a user avatar, although the retention outcome differs. An avatar may live as long as the account needs it. A signed document may have a fixed end date. Do not let the shared upload code silently give both objects the same lifetime.

For this workflow, Infrai is a plausible platform boundary: its private object storage can sit beside other backend capabilities behind one REST API and one key. That keeps the application contract focused on object keys and retention records while the service behind it can change. The deletion decision still stays in the application.

What is the 30-day retention bill actually keeping?

Start with retained bytes, not upload calls. For each signed file, count the source document, preview images, extracted text, failed multipart fragments, and any audit material that the service deliberately stores. A 4 MB source with a 600 KB preview and 200 KB of extracted text is already a 4.8 MB retention decision before copies and abandoned uploads enter the picture.

The dominant term changes when derivatives stop surviving for the full document window. Keep the signed original until its deadline. Delete a preview or extracted text earlier when the product does not need it. This is a useful trade: a later dispute may require regenerating a preview from the retained source, but it does not require retaining every convenient derivative forever.

The retention ledger should contain the bucket, object key, received time, deletion deadline, object type, and deletion result. It belongs in a database because lifecycle rules have a one-day minimum granularity, while a business deadline may be precise to the second. A worker can read that ledger and retry a delete without treating “already gone” as a new failure.

The timestamp is not the whole record. Suppose a signed contract arrives at 14:37:12 UTC and the media service creates a preview, a text extraction, and a moderation artifact. The ledger needs to connect those derived keys to the source and state which one may be deleted first. If the worker deletes the source before it records the result, the next retry must understand that the object is already absent. If a queue message is delivered twice, the second consumer must not create a new derivative or extend the deadline. If an operator changes the deadline, the audit record should explain who made the change and why. These are ordinary data-handling details, but they decide whether a deletion report is evidence or a guess assembled from bucket listings after the fact. The storage service can hold the bytes; it cannot infer the business relationship between an avatar, a signed original, and the temporary files produced while processing them.

That boundary matters.

What do I deliberately stop keeping? Usually temporary output and abandoned multipart pieces. The cost is operational: an engineer may need to regenerate a preview or investigate a missing intermediate artifact. That is a visible cost. Keeping undocumented copies is a hidden one.

Should I use S3-compatible object storage for storing user-uploaded avatars?

The comparison should focus on retention controls and processor boundaries, not on SDK preference. AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, and Backblaze B2 all expose S3-compatible access, but they are not interchangeable once the record needs a particular recovery or residency control.

Option Useful fit Boundary to verify
AWS S3 A specialist choice when mature lifecycle, versioning, Object Lock, and regional controls matter Versioned copies and retention policies can make deletion more involved than deleting one current key
Cloudflare R2 A reasonable choice when the delivery and operations boundary already sits with Cloudflare Confirm the regional and compliance model for signed records, rather than assuming edge reach means residency
Backblaze B2 Straightforward object storage with an S3-compatible API and lifecycle rules Check the required replication, region, and integration controls for the media service
Infrai storage A fit when private objects need to sit beside other backend capabilities behind one platform boundary No public-read ACL, versioning, Object Lock, If-Match conditional writes, cross-region automatic replication, or self-service CORS route

Infrai is the interesting middle option for a team that wants the storage contract to stay portable while the surrounding backend changes. Its storage capability uses an S3-compatible interface, and the platform exposes storage alongside other backend capabilities through one REST API, one key, and one base URL. Swapping the service behind that boundary does not require changing the application’s retention ledger.

The second advantage is less glamorous but practical during review: the discovery surface is public and self-describing, with request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples. Documented capabilities have examples in 10 languages. That reduces the friction of checking a storage-to-worker handoff across a Python service, a scheduled runtime, or a different team’s implementation; nobody has to infer the request contract from a client library. The platform has 295 routes across 20 modules, but breadth is not a retention guarantee.

Here is the smallest server-side upload shape I would validate against the live schema. It assumes the bucket already exists, keeps the object private, reads the key from an environment variable, and treats rate limiting as a retryable response.

import os
import time
from pathlib import Path

import requests


def put_private_avatar(bucket, key, filename):
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
        "Content-Type": "application/octet-stream",
        "Idempotency-Key": f"avatar:{bucket}:{key}",
    }
    body = Path(filename).read_bytes()

    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.request(
            "PUT",
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/example-bucket/user-123-avatar",
            headers=headers,
            data=body,
            timeout=30,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
            time.sleep(min(delay, 30))
            continue
        if not 200 <= response.status_code < 300:
            raise RuntimeError(f"upload failed: {response.status_code} {response.text}")
        return response.json()
    raise RuntimeError("upload remained rate-limited after retries")

This is a private object write, not a public image URL. For browser-direct transfer, use a presigned URL and keep the platform Authorization header away from that returned URL. The application should still validate the avatar type and associate the resulting key with its user record.

This is where the recommendation needs a hard edge. The limitation is concrete: Infrai storage does not provide public URLs for these objects, so it is unsuitable for a permanent public image host or static-site asset bucket. It also does not provide object versioning or WORM-style Object Lock. An accidental overwrite is therefore not recoverable from storage history. Strict concurrent writes need coordination in a database or queue because there is no If-Match conditional write. Choose AWS S3 or another specialist when any of those controls is mandatory.

How should the application enforce deletion rather than hope for it?

Give the application ownership of the deadline. At upload time, create a private object key that does not encode a public identity, write the retention record in the same application transaction as the upload intent, and make retrieval go through an authorization decision. If direct transfer is needed, issue a presigned URL for the appropriate operation. The client must never send the platform Authorization header to that returned URL.

The storage API can create a bucket and put an object through the verified storage routes, including POST /v1/storage/bucket/create and PUT /v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}. Those route names are enough to establish the boundary; the request schema should come from the live capability documentation rather than from a guessed payload in an article.

The deletion worker then follows a small state machine:

  1. Select records whose deadline has passed and claim them with a lease.
  2. Delete the object by its stored bucket and key.
  3. Record the response and mark the ledger entry deleted when the object is gone.
  4. Retry transient failures with backoff, keeping the operation idempotent.
  5. Reconcile the ledger against object listings using prefix filtering, without pretending object metadata is server-searchable.

Lifecycle remains useful as a second line of defense. It can catch a worker that was disabled, but it cannot replace the database when the shortest rule is one day and the product promise is an exact deletion deadline. Multipart fragments also have no automatic cleanup rule, so abandoned uploads need an explicit operational policy.

The privacy boundary deserves equal attention. There is no browser-configurable standalone CORS route available for self-service direct uploads, even though the bucket model has a cors_rules field. If a browser must upload directly, test the chosen integration path before making it the default. A server-mediated upload is slower to design but keeps the credential and authorization decision in a familiar place.

Where does a specialist provider win?

Use AWS S3 or another specialist when the record requires WORM protection, object history, cross-region automatic replication, or a contractual residency guarantee. Those are not details that a general backend surface should be assumed to supply. A runtime API does not create an audio or document residency commitment, and a deletion timestamp is not contractual proof that every processor copy disappeared.

Cloudflare R2 is a better boundary when the organization already operates its delivery controls there and its regional requirements fit. Backblaze B2 deserves consideration when its lifecycle and region model match the service. Infrai is a reasonable choice for a media backend that wants private S3-compatible objects, one REST boundary for adjacent backend work, and a self-describing contract that is easy to inspect across languages. The application must still own the deadline, access policy, region decision, and deletion evidence.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the private upload and retention-ledger part of an avatar or signed-document workflow when portability and a single backend interface matter, and keep a specialist provider in the design when versioning, immutable retention, replication, or contractual residency is mandatory. That is the line between a convenient storage abstraction and a compliance control.

The operational checklist is short. Classify originals and derivatives. Choose the region before accepting a file. Record an explicit deadline. Keep access private. Make deletion retries safe. Test that a presigned response does not become a permanent public URL. Record the result.

If that boundary matches your system, start with the storage capability documentation and verify the access, region, and deletion assumptions before adoption.

Further reading

  • Infrai official documentation
  • Infrai guide: React file uploads to object storage
  • MDN: Content-Disposition response header
  • Amazon S3 Object Lock
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility
  • Backblaze B2 S3-compatible API

title: Que unos agentes limpien la deuda técnica que marca Sonar costó $44. Poder fiarnos del resultado, $520.
description:
En el artículo anterior contaba cómo montamos un quality gate sobre el diff para el código que escriben los agentes. Eso protege el código nuevo, pero deja fuera la deuda que ya existía. Este artículo va de esa deuda.

Hablo de una app Ionic grande y con algunos años de vida, con la deuda que acumula cualquier proyecto así: sobre todo code smells de mantenibilidad que Sonar marca y que nunca entran en un sprint, porque la deuda siempre pierde contra un evolutivo en el planning.

Un workflow de Claude Code con 246 subagentes limpió casi toda esa deuda y subió bastante la cobertura de tests, en una PR de más de mil ficheros. Fueron 19 horas de reloj y unos $600 en tokens. Yo le dediqué un par de horas como mucho. La PR lleva semanas mergeada y no hay ningún bug ni revert atribuidos a ella.

El dato que más me sorprendió está en el título: los agentes que arreglaban el código y escribían los tests costaron unos $44. Todo lo demás se fue en poder fiarse del resultado. De esa parte va el resto, con cifras por capa, porque en mi opinión es la que casi nadie publica.

Qué estaba optimizando

Que un agente sepa cambiar un || por un ?? ya lo sabemos. La pregunta de verdad es otra: si al final tengo una PR de más de mil ficheros escrita por una IA, ¿cómo la apruebo? Nadie va a leer ese diff, y una PR que no se puede revisar es vibe coding descontrolado.

Así que el objetivo no era cuántas incidencias se cerraban. Era llegar a una PR que una persona pudiera aprobar sin leer el código y sin que aparecieran regresiones después. La revisión humana no desaparece: pasa de leer líneas a comprobar las pruebas de cada cambio y leer con calma los pocos que alteran el comportamiento.

El equipo de Claude Code cuenta algo parecido: optimizan el mínimo tiempo humano de revisión que no aumente reversiones ni incidentes. Aquí lo aplico a un caso concreto, una limpieza masiva, y añado lo que ellos no publican: cuánto cuesta cada capa de verificación y cuántos de sus hallazgos son reales.

Un lote, de principio a fin

Darle la lista de incidencias a una sola sesión no funciona: no cabe en un contexto, no paraleliza y no deja rastro por cambio. Los workflows de Claude Code son un script JavaScript que lanza subagentes. La diferencia con pedirle a un agente que los lance es que el control de flujo es código: qué se paraleliza, qué se revisa y qué pasa si algo falla no depende de que un modelo se acuerde.

La unidad de trabajo es el lote. Un script reparte el escaneo de Sonar en 52 lotes por carpeta, pesando incidencias, líneas sin cubrir y specs que faltan. Un lote tiene esta forma (simplificado):

{
  "id": "14",
  "scope": "src/app/common/validators",
  "agentType": "angular-implementer",
  "specsToCreate": 3,
  "files": [
    {
      "path": "src/app/common/validators/greater-than.validator.ts",
      "needsSpec": true,
      "issues": [
        {"rule": "typescript:S6606", "line": 16, "coverage": "covered"},
        {"rule": "typescript:S6582", "line": 28, "coverage": "covered"}
      ]
    }
  ]
}

El implementer sigue una escalera de garantías en cada fichero:

  1. Si no tiene spec, escribe una de caracterización que pase sobre el código sin tocar. Fija lo que el código hace hoy, no lo que debería hacer.
  2. Si la línea que va a cambiar no está cubierta (el campo coverage), añade antes un test que fije su salida.
  3. El refactor tiene que ser equivalente.
  4. Si el cambio es intencionado porque hay un bug real, lleva un test que pasa de rojo a verde y una nota con la prueba manual.
  5. Si algo queda en rojo, revierte ese cambio y lo marca como skipped. No se debilita ningún test.

En el historial de ese lote queda así, de más antiguo a más nuevo:

test(validators): caracterizar emailValidator y su regex
test(validators): caracterizar greaterThan y lessThan validators
refactor(validators): quitar escape innecesario en regex de email
refactor(validators): usar ?? y optional chaining en greaterThan y lessThan

-    const value = control?.value?.toString() || ''
+    const value = control?.value?.toString() ?? ''
-    if (compareControl && compareControl.invalid) {
+    if (compareControl?.invalid) {

Cada lote deja una nota con cuatro secciones: cambios de comportamiento, TODOs pendientes, falsos positivos y skipped. Un cambio de comportamiento anotado tiene esta pinta:

getData(): signature ?? '' sustituye a signature ? signature : ''. Idéntico para null, undefined, '' y cualquier string. Difiere solo para 0/false, que no puede llegar desde el componente que lo llama.

Hay más de 150 notas así, listadas en la PR. El patrón no es perfecto: en tres casos el test y el cambio tuvieron que ir en el mismo commit, porque el test ya llamaba a la API nueva, y la nota lo dice.

Una advertencia sobre la cobertura: sube unos 20 puntos, pero la mayor parte son tests de caracterización, que fijan también los bugs que el código ya tuviera. Sube la red para detectar cambios, no la confianza en que el comportamiento sea el correcto.

Cuánto cuesta fiarse, capa por capa

Cada capa de verificación encontró cosas que las anteriores no habían visto. Esta es la tabla que me habría gustado leer antes de empezar: cuántos hallazgos entregó cada capa, cuántos eran reales y cuánto costó, a precios de lista de la API con la caché de 1 hora de Claude Code.

Capa Agentes Hallazgos Reales Coste aprox. $ por hallazgo real
Implementers (arreglo + tests) 66 — — 44 $ —
Revisores por lote (Sonnet) 124 sin medir 1 bloqueante 30 $ 30 $
Integración, gates y reescaneo 5 6 incidencias nuevas 6 39 $ 7 $
E2E contra preproducción 1 10 fallos 0 regresiones 10 $ —
Auditoría con otro modelo (Fable) 8 30 7 69 $ 10 $
/code-review al máximo 31 15 13 375 $ 29 $

El plan, el autofix mecánico y la sesión principal suman otros 34 $. Total: unos 600 $.

Lo que leo en la tabla:

  • Arreglar es barato; verificar, no. El 7 % del gasto fue en hacer el cambio. El resto, en poder demostrar que el cambio era correcto.
  • La capa más cara encontró el fallo más grave. Un agente cambió una regex por otra con lookbehind para contentar a Sonar, y el lookbehind no existe en Safari antes de la 16.4: en dispositivos antiguos habría roto un formulario. Ningún test unitario lo ve, porque los tests corren en Chrome. Lo encontró el /code-review al máximo, antes del merge y después de que todas las capas anteriores dieran el visto bueno.
  • La precisión varía mucho. La auditoría con otro modelo acertó en el 23 % de sus hallazgos; el code-review, en el 87 %. Cada hallazgo se confirmaba o se refutaba con un test antes de tocar código, así que los falsos positivos costaron tokens, pero no cambios.
  • De los revisores por lote no sé si compensan. Pararon un bloqueante real, pero no medí cuántos de sus hallazgos no bloqueantes se aplicaron. Es lo primero que mediría la próxima vez.
  • La verificación también hay que verificarla. El reescaneo final cazó 6 incidencias nuevas que habían metido los propios arreglos del code-review.

No probé a repetir el mismo revisor, así que no puedo decir que no sirva. Lo que sí vi es que cada cambio de modelo o de corte (por lote, por área, por ángulo) sacó cosas nuevas.

Sobre los tokens: el 97,7 % de la entrada fue lectura de caché. Cada turno de un agente relee su contexto entero, así que lo que se paga es el número de turnos, no el tamaño del cambio. Por eso el code-review, con buscadores que encadenan cientos de turnos, es la capa más cara. Elegir el modelo por rol (Haiku para implementar UI, Sonnet para servicios y revisores, Opus para el plan y la integración) fue lo que más contuvo el coste. Con una suscripción de Claude Code lo que se paga es la cuota, no estas cifras.

Qué hace el revisor humano

La PR no pide leer el diff. Pide esto, en este orden:

  1. Elegir commits refactor(...) al azar y comprobar que el test(...) anterior toca el mismo fichero y pasa sobre el código de antes.
  2. Leer todas las notas de cambios de comportamiento, que van en el primer comentario de la PR. Son lo único que debería cambiar algo, y cada una dice por qué es equivalente o qué cambia.
  3. Leer con calma los pocos puntos marcados para revisión particular: los cambios que se revirtieron a propósito y por qué, los que necesitan prueba manual en varios navegadores y los TODOs que se borraron y deberían ser tickets.
  4. Revisar la lista de bugs que los agentes encontraron y no tocaron, porque estaban fuera de alcance.
  5. Pasar el ciclo de regresión manual.

El punto 1 es por muestreo; el 2, completo. Si el muestreo encuentra un refactor sin su test previo, la confianza en el resto cae y toca revisar el lote entero.

Un Sonar en local como oráculo

Es la pieza que más subestimé. Nuestro Sonar es Community Build, que no tiene ramas, así que analizar la rama en el servidor pisaría el análisis de la rama principal. Levanté un SonarQube Community en Docker con los perfiles de fábrica y comprobé que reproducía exactamente la misma línea base que el servidor.

Con eso el plan sale de datos y no de intuición, y cada fase mide su trabajo con la misma vara que usará el CI. Si vas a pedirle a unos agentes que mejoren una métrica, dales la forma de medirla ellos mismos.

Lo que salió mal

Un agente hizo push, abrió una PR y movió el ticket de Jira. Nadie se lo pidió. Tenía instalada una skill para terminar ramas y la siguió hasta el final. La PR salió con el gate en rojo, porque era un snapshot a medias. Ahora los prompts prohíben cualquier acción externa y los worktrees tienen un pushurl inválido:

git config --worktree remote.origin.pushurl no-push://bloqueado

Prohibirlo en el prompt no basta, hay que impedirlo.

Reanudar el run relanzó lotes que ya estaban hechos. resumeFromRunId reutiliza el prefijo más largo de llamadas que no han cambiado. Con dos carriles dentro de un parallel(), el orden no es estable, las claves de caché de los revisores no coincidieron y volvió a lanzar lotes terminados. Lo paré al minuto. Para continuar un run a medias, me ha funcionado mejor escribir un script nuevo solo con lo pendiente. Por eso fueron cuatro runs y no uno.

Los carriles iban desequilibrados. Repartí los lotes por orden y uno de los carriles terminó horas antes que el otro. La versión que dejé en el repo los alterna y deja las deprecaciones, que son lo más pesado, para el final.

Datos de prueba. Al escribir specs, los agentes tienden a reutilizar valores que ven en el código en lugar de inventarlos. El code-review lo marcó y se sustituyeron por datos sintéticos. Ahora hay una regla explícita en las instrucciones del repo, pero ninguna comprobación automática.

Las prohibiciones viven en el prompt. Pedí no usar NOSONAR, eslint-disable, @ts-ignore, as any ni it.skip, y justificar cada falso positivo en sonar-project.properties. Se cumplió, pero lo vigilaban los revisores, no el gate. Es el mismo error que el del push, solo que esta vez no explotó.

Un arreglo que no arreglaba nada. Un agente anotó como bug corregido un cambio que, con los datos reales de entrada, no tenía ningún efecto. Un test en verde puede estarlo por el motivo equivocado.

Casos de QA duplicados. Para la regresión manual, Claude creó en la herramienta de test 7 casos que ya existían. Los existentes no estaban enlazados a requisitos ni tenían tags. Cuando le señalé la carpeta de plantillas, reutilizó 40 y creó uno solo para lo que de verdad faltaba. Un agente solo reutiliza lo que puede encontrar; si no, se inventa la regresión.

Cambios que ningún test reproduce. Algunos arreglos de seguridad que pide Sonar dependen del navegador y no se pueden probar en un test unitario que corre en Chrome. Esos se marcan en la PR y se validan a mano en cada navegador antes del merge.

Cómo aplicarlo en tu repo

Nada de esto depende de Sonar ni de Claude Code. Sirve para cualquier cambio masivo hecho por agentes: deprecaciones, un salto de versión, una regla de lint nueva.

Antes de lanzar nada

  • Monta un oráculo que reproduzca la métrica del CI en local y comprueba que da la misma línea base que el servidor.
  • Reparte el trabajo en lotes pequeños por carpeta y elige el modelo por rol: barato para implementar, otro distinto para auditar.
  • Bloquea por infraestructura cualquier acción externa: push, PRs, tickets. No basta con prohibirlo en el prompt.
  • Deja escrita la regla de datos de prueba sintéticos antes de que el primer agente escriba un fixture.
  • Ten la regresión manual localizable: casos en carpetas por funcionalidad, enlazados a requisitos y con tags.

En cada lote

  • Escalera de garantías: caracterización, test de la línea, refactor equivalente, rojo → verde solo para bugs reales y revertir lo que quede en rojo.
  • Un commit test(...) antes de cada refactor(...).
  • Una nota por lote con cambios de comportamiento, TODOs, falsos positivos y skipped.
  • Nada que esconda el problema (NOSONAR, eslint-disable, as any, it.skip), y que lo compruebe el gate, no solo el revisor.

Antes de abrir la PR

  • Gates completos y reescaneo con el oráculo, también después de aplicar los arreglos de la auditoría.
  • E2E repitiendo cada fallo sobre la rama base, para separar regresiones de lo que ya fallaba.
  • Al menos una revisión con otro modelo y otra con otro corte (por área, por ángulo). Cada hallazgo se confirma o se refuta con un test antes de tocar código.
  • Presupuesta la verificación: aquí costó más de diez veces lo que el arreglo.

En la PR y después

  • La descripción lleva las notas de comportamiento, los puntos de revisión particular, lo revertido y los bugs encontrados sin tocar.
  • La revisión humana es por muestreo de commits, lectura completa de las notas y QA.
  • Mide reversiones y bugs atribuidos a la PR, y qué aportó cada capa, para recortar la siguiente vez.

Lo que todavía no sé

  • Si los revisores por lote compensan sus 30 $, porque no medí cuántos de sus hallazgos no bloqueantes se aplicaron.
  • Si lotes más pequeños o un code-review menos exhaustivo habrían dado la misma garantía por menos dinero.
  • Cuánto tardó de verdad la revisión humana de la PR. No lo cronometré, y es justo la métrica que todo esto pretende bajar.

El workflow ha quedado en el repo, parametrizado para repetirlo con otras migraciones masivas. La próxima ejecución me dirá si lo aprendido aquí se sostiene.

Si has hecho algo parecido, me interesa sobre todo cómo lo revisó tu equipo y cuánto te costó cada capa de verificación. Es el dato que menos se publica y el que más ayuda a decidir.

title: I built a live mess-menu app for my university — here's the stack and why it stuck
description:
Every hostel student at my university wakes up to the same question: what's the mess serving, and is it worth walking down for?

The "official" answer was a PDF that nobody kept up to date. So I built the thing I actually wanted — a fast page that tells you today's food, with serving times, and lets students rate each meal so you know what you're walking into.

👉 Live: https://nustmessmenu.oddmancy.com

What it does

  • Today — breakfast, lunch and dinner with serving timings, at a glance.
  • This week — the full weekly menu so you can plan around the good days.
  • Ratings & reviews — students rate each meal, so "chicken karahi" with a 4.5 reads very differently from one with a 1.8.

No login. No ads. Free.

The stack

Deliberately boring, because boring is reliable:

  • React + TypeScript on the frontend.
  • Cloudflare Workers serving it from the edge — cheap, globally fast, and it shrugs off traffic spikes (which mattered more than I expected — more on that another day).
  • A small backend for the menu + review data.
  • Tailwind for styling.
  • SEO done properly: server-rendered content, a real sitemap, and structured data — so when someone searches the mess menu, the site actually shows up instead of a stale link.

What I learned

The engineering here is trivial. The part that made it stick was removing exactly one daily friction for a few thousand people. The ratings turned a lookup tool into something students check and contribute to — that loop is what keeps it alive.

If you're building something small, that's the bar worth aiming for: not "impressive," just "used every single day."

Try it

If you're a student (or just curious how the edge setup feels), take a look and leave a review on today's meals:

https://nustmessmenu.oddmancy.com

Happy to go deep on the Cloudflare Workers + SEO setup in the comments if anyone's interested.

title: Edtech Agent Errors: How to Attribute 2 Calls Before Posting Failures
description:
Attribute each model call to its tutoring run before posting the error; otherwise, the failure record can explain what broke while leaving the cost of the failed lesson invisible. TL;DR: preserve the original exception, attach a bounded run identifier and per-call evidence, and verify delivery separately from the lesson outcome. Keep accounting evidence when error delivery is disabled.

The implementation question often starts with a Node.js catch block and an HTTP client such as axios. The useful contract is an explicit POST with message, stack, environment, and context. This guide demonstrates that capture-and-post boundary in Go, using an edtech agent loop whose operational question is which calls a failed lesson paid for.

What page fired, and which tutoring run paid for it?

Start the postmortem with the page, its triggering condition, and the affected run identifiers. An error event doesn't establish that someone was paged, that a learner was affected, or that an expensive call caused the failure. Those are separate pieces of evidence. A dashboard that makes error counts look calm offers little comfort if retries keep consuming model calls after the lesson has failed, especially when the only accounting record is attached to the final exception and omits earlier successful work.

Count the successful call.

Consider a synthetic tutoring run with 2 calls: one proposes a hint, and the next checks the answer. The example labels their costs as unknown rather than inventing charges. In production, preserve available cost metadata at each call boundary, together with the step, attempt, elapsed duration, and provider request identifier. A missing cost is unknown, not zero. Keep the authoritative ledger in normal application persistence; an error event carries only a small diagnostic snapshot.

Use opaque identifiers. Student names, answers, prompts, and access tokens don't belong in this diagnostic snapshot. Restricting the context makes investigation less convenient, but a support engineer can follow the run identifier through authorized application records without copying a learner's lesson into every downstream error system.

How should capturing and posting errors to an error tracking API preserve tutoring costs?

Save this program as capture.go and run it with go run capture.go. It uses the standard library and sends traffic only to a local test receiver. That receiver deliberately returns one rate-limit response before accepting the event. Its empty success response is a fixture, not a claim about a hosted API's response envelope.

The context keys are application-owned example data. The stack is collected at capture time, so a real application should preserve frames closer to the original failure when later wrapping or asynchronous delivery would lose them. A Node.js implementation should preserve the original error's message and stack before serializing its payload.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/http/httptest"
    "os"
    "runtime/debug"
    "strconv"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type Event struct {
    Message string `json:"message"`
    Stack string `json:"stack"`
    Environment string `json:"environment"`
    Context map[string]any `json:"context"`
}

func retryDelay(value string, fallback time.Duration) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if when, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if delay := time.Until(when); delay > 0 { return delay }
        return 0
    }
    return fallback
}

func post(client *http.Client, target, key, eventID string, body []byte) error {
    deadline := time.Now().Add(3 * time.Second)
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 2; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, target, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil { return err }
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", eventID)
        if key != "" { req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key) }
        response, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("capture delivery: %w", err) }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(response.Body, 4096))
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return readErr }
        if response.StatusCode >= 200 && response.StatusCode < 300 { return nil }
        if response.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 1 {
            return fmt.Errorf("capture status %d: %s", response.StatusCode, data)
        }
        delay := retryDelay(response.Header.Get("Retry-After"),
            time.Duration(1<<attempt)*100*time.Millisecond)
        if delay > time.Until(deadline) {
            return errors.New("capture retry exceeds delivery budget")
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
    return errors.New("capture attempts exhausted")
}

func main() {
    var mu sync.Mutex
    requests, accepted := 0, 0
    firstID := ""
    receiver := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        mu.Lock()
        defer mu.Unlock()
        if r.Method != http.MethodPost { w.WriteHeader(405); return }
        var event Event
        if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&event); err != nil {
            http.Error(w, err.Error(), 400); return
        }
        if event.Message == "" || event.Stack == "" || event.Context["run_id"] != "lesson-demo-17" {
            http.Error(w, "missing attribution evidence", 400); return
        }
        requests++
        id := r.Header.Get("Idempotency-Key")
        if requests == 1 { firstID = id }
        if id == "" || id != firstID {
            http.Error(w, "unstable event identity", 400); return
        }
        if requests == 1 {
            w.Header().Set("Retry-After", "1")
            http.Error(w, "fixture rate limit", 429); return
        }
        accepted++
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)
    }))
    defer receiver.Close()

    original := errors.New("synthetic answer-check failure")
    event := Event{
        Message: original.Error(), Stack: string(debug.Stack()),
        Environment: "local-fixture",
        Context: map[string]any{
            "run_id": "lesson-demo-17",
            "failed_step": "answer-check",
            "calls": []map[string]any{
                {"step": "hint", "attempt": 1, "cost_status": "unknown"},
                {"step": "answer-check", "attempt": 1, "cost_status": "unknown"},
            },
        },
    }
    body, err := json.Marshal(event)
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    if os.Getenv("CAPTURE_DISABLED") == "1" {
        fmt.Println("delivery disabled; lesson outcome:", original)
        return
    }
    err = post(&http.Client{Timeout: time.Second},
        receiver.URL+"/v1/errors/capture", os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"),
        "lesson-demo-17-answer-check-event-1", body)
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    mu.Lock()
    defer mu.Unlock()
    if requests != 2 || accepted != 1 { panic("delivery verification failed") }
    fmt.Println("verified: 2 delivery attempts, 1 acceptance; lesson outcome:", original)
}

A stable identity covers retries of this particular event. Generate a new identity for a different failure, and persist it alongside a queued event if delivery must survive a restart. The fixture rejects its first request before acceptance; the final count verifies this sequence, not a remote deduplication guarantee. Transport errors surface instead of triggering blind retries.

The demo doesn't implement a durable ledger or background queue. Its purpose is narrower: make the exception snapshot and delivery behavior inspectable before introducing student traffic. Production accounting persistence belongs before the sender, so disabling that sender cannot erase the record of successful model work. The fallback starts at 100ms; the fixture asks for 1000ms through Retry-After. These are test settings, not observed service latency.

Verify attribution and rehearse rollback

The acceptance line confirms two delivery attempts and one acceptance while preserving the synthetic lesson failure. Inspect the serialized event locally: both call entries must survive, attempt numbers must remain unchanged, and the retry must preserve the event identity. A duplicated ledger entry is an accounting error even if the dashboard shows one tidy error group.

Retain evidence.

Measure agent latency around the actual loop with a monotonic elapsed-time measurement, then measure delivery latency separately. Don't add the receiver's deliberate one-second backoff to learner-facing model duration. Reconcile costs against available per-call metadata and retain provider request identifiers for mismatches. If the failing response lacks usable billing evidence, label the attribution incomplete and reconcile later; assigning zero manufactures certainty precisely where the postmortem needs evidence.

For rollback, set CAPTURE_DISABLED to 1 in the process environment and run the same program. It should report delivery disabled and preserve the same lesson outcome without sending a request. The local receiver's in-memory records are disposable. Production accounting records aren't.

Before rollout, repeat the exercise with an invalid payload and a receiver that stays rate-limited. Require delivery to stop under the retry policy while the lesson is never executed again. This sample allows two attempts, honors Retry-After when the requested wait fits, and stops rather than retrying early when it exceeds the three-second retry-wait budget. That budget isn't a strict end-to-end deadline; each HTTP request has its own timeout. A production worker needs a durable failure path and independent monitoring for undelivered events.

Choose the receiver by the evidence it preserves

Successful delivery proves transport acceptance. It doesn't prove that the next incident will reach the pager. Keep notification ownership, trace investigation, and missed-job detection as explicit requirements rather than assuming an error dashboard covers them.

Option Useful fit for this tutoring workflow Trade-off to evaluate
Sentry An error-focused Node.js integration is a useful starting point when exception context drives investigation. Validate run identifiers and cost evidence separately; an exception alone cannot account for earlier successful calls.
Datadog Consider an application monitoring workflow when investigation needs broader service context. Evaluate the instrumentation scope and correlation work alongside the small capture contract; broader coverage adds integration decisions.
Grafana Consider a telemetry investigation workflow when the team already works from shared operational views. Prove error-to-run navigation and choose the supporting telemetry components explicitly. A dashboard alone isn't a cost ledger.
OpenTelemetry Its logs signal provides a standards reference for associating records with execution context. Correlation identifiers don't establish billing evidence or an operational paging policy.

These are evaluation criteria, not findings from a comparative benchmark. The documentation below provides starting points for reproducing the same exercise; no latency ranking or automatic agent-cost accounting claim follows from this example.

Infrai combines a self-describing REST API with a single key and unified billing: one key, one bill across 20 modules. Public discovery supplies schemas and runnable examples, so wiring capture starts with inspecting a capability rather than learning a new SDK; sharing the credential across backend capabilities reduces handoffs between the tutoring runtime and its error sender. Its specified per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request metadata supports the ledger when the application preserves that evidence at each call boundary. The trade-off is workflow ownership: keep paging in a separately owned process, use a trace investigation tool when span-tree navigation is required, and use a heartbeat monitor such as Healthchecks for lesson-processing jobs that never run. Posting an exception doesn't satisfy those requirements.

Choose the receiver that passes the failure exercise while leaving a reconcilable ledger. Ask what page fired. Then ask which calls the failed lesson paid for.

References

  • OpenTelemetry logs signal concepts
  • Sentry Node.js documentation
  • Datadog application monitoring documentation
  • Grafana documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation

title: Cloud Storage Provider Explained — 3 Scalable App Data Backup Choices
description:
Short answer: Choose AWS S3 or Google Cloud Storage for a scalable app data backup when strong SDK documentation is the deciding factor; consider Infrai when one REST surface across backend services matters more than storage-only features.

Cloud object storage for application backups has no universal winner. For an e-commerce app serving generated reports to authenticated customers, AWS S3 and Google Cloud Storage are the safest starting points when SDK documentation is the primary constraint. Both provide documented SDKs for major programming languages, which matters when a custom backup worker must stay maintainable.

A third shape can make sense when the main pain is coordinating backend services: Infrai exposes storage through one REST API and one credential, with public discovery and runnable examples in 10 languages. It is not a replacement for every object-storage feature. Large-file throughput, regional availability, recovery guarantees, browser delivery, and concurrency rules still decide the outcome.

Which cloud storage provider fits a scalable app data backup?

Start with the artifact, not the provider logo. A report might be a 4 MB CSV today and a 900 MB compressed export next quarter. The customer should authenticate with the application, while the application controls access to the object. That rules out public buckets, permanent public URLs, and provider secrets in browser code.

The minimum workflow is concrete: write a report, keep it private, identify it by a stable customer-and-report key, and return it only after the application checks authorization. The backup path also needs bucket and file management APIs, plus a regional footprint close to the app's users. A well-documented SDK cannot compensate for a region choice that makes every large download cross a long network path.

That distinction matters.

The awkward part is overwrite behavior. If two workers produce the same report key, an unconditional write can replace an earlier object. Strict mutual exclusion therefore needs queue or database coordination when the storage layer does not offer an If-Match conditional write. That is a design decision, not a detail to postpone.

Three provider shapes, three sensible boundaries

AWS S3 is the conventional default for a storage-first team that wants extensive SDK support and a mature object-storage ecosystem. It fits when storage primitives and provider-native tooling are the center of gravity. The trade-off is provider coupling, so portability should be tested rather than assumed.

Google Cloud Storage is the other clear first choice here. Its documented SDKs also support major programming languages. It fits well when the app already lives in Google Cloud and the regional API location matches its customer base. A good SDK reduces integration friction; it does not make cross-provider migration automatic.

Cloudflare R2 is a useful third product to evaluate when an S3-compatible workflow or a different delivery boundary matters. Compatibility is not equivalence. Verify the exact large-object behavior, regional assumptions, SDK examples, and recovery controls your report archive needs.

Infrai occupies a different position. It puts backend services behind one REST API and one key, which can reduce credential and billing coordination for a solo builder. Its storage vendor coverage includes R2 and S3 but not GCS; it also has no cross-region automatic replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool. Use it when a consistent backend interface matters more than a storage-only control plane.

Choice Best fit Boundary to verify
AWS S3 Storage-first backup with extensive SDK support Regional placement and provider coupling
Google Cloud Storage Google-aligned app with documented SDK integration Regional API availability and migration assumptions
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible workflow worth evaluating Large-object behavior and recovery controls
Infrai One REST surface for several backend services No GCS coverage, replication, or bulk migration

Do not turn this into a benchmark. No runtime latency or throughput measurement belongs here without a controlled test using your report sizes, customer geography, and concurrency.

A small implementation that keeps access private

The implementation boundary should be boring: the worker chooses the object key, the storage adapter writes privately, and the application later mediates access. This TypeScript is the policy layer, not a pretend provider SDK.

type ReportJob = {
  customerId: string;
  reportId: string;
  format: "csv" | "json";
};

type BackupPlan = {
  objectKey: string;
  acl: "private";
  delivery: "signed-only";
};

export function planReportBackup(job: ReportJob): BackupPlan {
  if (!job.customerId || !job.reportId) {
    throw new Error("customerId and reportId are required");
  }

  return {
    objectKey: `reports/${job.customerId}/${job.reportId}.${job.format}`,
    acl: "private",
    delivery: "signed-only",
  };
}

The provider adapter should use the selected provider's documented SDK and produce a signed URL only after authorization. Keep the provider authorization header on the server-side request; never send it to the returned presigned URL. Store credentials through a secrets-management system, not source control or browser code.

Here is the smallest Infrai-shaped write adapter for a private report. It uses the verified storage object-put route, sends raw report bytes, checks the response, and backs off on rate limiting. The caller still needs to issue a presigned read through its storage adapter after authorization.

const baseUrl = ["https://api", "infrai.cc/v1"].join(".");

export async function putPrivateReport(
  bucket: string,
  key: string,
  reportBytes: Uint8Array,
): Promise<void> {
  const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(
      `${baseUrl}/storage/object/put/${encodeURIComponent(bucket)}/${encodeURIComponent(key)}`,
      {
        method: "PUT",
        headers: {
          Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
          "Content-Type": "application/octet-stream",
          "Idempotency-Key": `report-${bucket}-${key}`,
          "X-Object-ACL": "private",
        },
        body: reportBytes,
      },
    );

    if (response.ok) return;
    if (response.status !== 429 || attempt === 3) {
      throw new Error(`Report upload failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("Retry-After"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) && retryAfter > 0
      ? retryAfter * 1000
      : 2 ** attempt * 250;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
  }
}

Measure it.

For large reports, measure the full path: upload duration, download duration, retry behavior, memory use, and concurrent jobs. Test an object larger than the usual report, because a design that works for a small CSV can fail once serialization, buffering, and customer download overlap. The useful number is your workload's p95 completion time by region, not a generic vendor claim.

Where the convenient option stops

Infrai's storage surface is not a public-file platform. There is no public or public-read ACL, so static website hosting, permanent public links, and image-hosting patterns are out of scope. There is no object versioning or object lock, so an accidental overwrite is not automatically recoverable and an immutable, finance-grade archive needs an external design.

There is also no If-Match conditional write. Coordinate competing writers in a queue or database if the report key must be mutually exclusive. Browser direct uploads require care because there is no independent set-CORS route that customers can configure themselves. Lifecycle expiration has a one-day minimum, multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and metadata cannot be searched server-side beyond prefix filtering. These are manageable constraints for an authenticated report service; they are poor fits for WORM retention, rich object search, or self-service browser uploads.

The same discipline applies to S3, Google Cloud Storage, and R2: read the current contract for the operations you actually need. SDK documentation is a selection criterion, not a recovery plan.

My selection rule

Choose AWS S3 or Google Cloud Storage when the job is a storage-first backup system and strong SDK documentation is decisive. Pick between them using existing cloud placement, regional API availability, and the provider-specific operations your worker needs.

Evaluate Cloudflare R2 when S3-compatible access is useful, but validate large-object behavior and recovery before committing. Evaluate Infrai when one REST surface and one credential across backend services reduce meaningful integration work, while accepting the storage limits above.

Before shipping, run a matrix with the real report sizes: one writer, two competing writers, a retry, an interrupted upload, and a customer download from each target region. Keep the object private in every case. That test tells you more than a leaderboard.

Further reading

  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Google Cloud Storage documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet
