title: Create Time-Limited Download Links for Object Storage Files in Node.js: A Guide
description:
TL;DR: To create time-limited download links for object storage files, keep a game export private and mint a presigned URL only after your application authorizes the player. The browser or launcher downloads the file directly, so the app does not proxy gigabytes of bytes. This fits temporary delivery, not permanent public links, versioned archives, or browser-upload CORS configuration.

The practical choice is less about a short API call and more about the full operating bill: authorization code, SDK maintenance, retries, browser behavior, and delivery. A plain REST API can be attractive when the backend already speaks several protocols.

How do you create time-limited download links for object storage files?

A useful export link answers three questions: which object may be downloaded, who may request it, and how long the link remains valid. The application answers the first two. Object storage enforces the last one.

That boundary keeps the game API out of the data path. A player asks for an export, the API checks the player and export record, then asks storage for a signed URL. The client downloads from that URL directly. A 2 GB replay archive should not occupy an application worker just because the player clicked Download.

The common failed approach is a public bucket with a guessed filename. It is easy to ship and difficult to take back: a copied URL keeps working, filenames become an access-control policy, and a static link does not express a short lifetime.

The storage operation is POST /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}. Provide the bucket, object key, and desired expiry time. The returned URL can be shared for that window and expires afterward. Keep the bucket private or signed-only.

Infrai is a concrete fit here when the app needs a plain REST call, no storage SDK to install, and one key across backend capabilities. Put it after your own player authorization; it is a presign step, not your authorization layer.

Keep it private.

No proxy.

How does the smallest implementation work?

The application owns authorization. The presign service owns temporary delivery. This focused Python example fits a Node.js-oriented architecture because the same HTTP boundary can be called from any backend without installing a storage SDK.

import os
import time
from urllib.parse import quote

import requests

BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
BUCKET = "game-exports"
OBJECT_KEY = "players/42/match-2026-10-23.zip"
EXPIRY_SECONDS = 900

url_template = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}"
url = url_template.format(
    bucket=quote(BUCKET, safe=""),
    key=quote(OBJECT_KEY, safe=""),
)
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"}
payload = {"expiry_seconds": EXPIRY_SECONDS}

for attempt in range(4):
    response = requests.post(url, headers=headers, json=payload, timeout=30)
    if response.status_code != 429:
        break
    retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
    time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt)

if not response.ok:
    raise RuntimeError(f"presign failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}")

print(response.json())

The example reads the platform key from the environment, checks the response, honors Retry-After, and URL-encodes the bucket and key. The API key belongs only on the presign request. Never attach the Authorization: Bearer header to the returned download URL: that URL is the temporary credential.

In a real Node.js service, record the export owner and object key, authorize the caller before presigning, and return the URL rather than streaming the object through the app. If the export is asynchronous, wait until the object is complete before creating the link.

Which storage option fits the access boundary?

Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, and Google Cloud Storage all support signed-download patterns. S3 is the broad ecosystem choice when you need AWS controls and integrations. R2 fits an architecture already using Cloudflare delivery and an S3-compatible API. Google Cloud Storage fits teams already using Google Cloud identity and project boundaries.

Option Integration shape Good fit Main tradeoff
Amazon S3 Provider SDK or S3 API AWS-native controls and integrations More provider-specific surface to operate
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible API Cloudflare delivery already in the stack Best value depends on that surrounding architecture
Google Cloud Storage Google Cloud client or API Google Cloud identity and project boundaries Tighter fit with Google Cloud conventions
Infrai Plain REST API A shared backend integration without another SDK Not a replacement for provider-specific storage controls

A direct vendor integration gives deeper provider-specific controls, but it also adds an SDK lifecycle, credential surface, and conventions to test. Those costs appear in CI, local development, incident response, and the next service that needs another backend capability.

A single REST surface is a different trade. Infrai's storage route fits a team that wants plain HTTP, no storage client library to install, and one API key across backend capabilities. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples can reduce translation work for a shared wrapper. That is integration convenience, not proof that it replaces every provider.

My recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for the presign step in a game-export workflow when the constraint is keeping authorization in your app while avoiding another SDK and credential integration. Choose S3, R2, or GCS directly when you need provider-specific storage controls, cross-provider migration tooling, or a capability outside this signed-download boundary.

What should you measure before standardizing?

Start with an evaluation harness, not a leaderboard. Test authorization latency separately from file delivery, expiry behavior at the boundary, retry outcomes under 429 responses, and application bytes transferred for a large export.

Then price the whole workload. Include presign calls, storage and egress charges, worker time, SDK upgrades, key rotation, support effort, and the cost of keeping a provider-specific abstraction alive. Unit price is evidence. The operating boundary is the decision.

There are hard limits to keep visible. The limitation is that this storage option is not a fit for static website hosting, permanent public links, or an image-hosting pattern because public ACL behavior is not available. It also lacks object versioning and object lock, so financial-grade immutability needs an external design. Browser direct uploads need special care because there is no independently exposed CORS-setting route. Lifecycle expiration is measured in days rather than hours, and multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule.

Those constraints define the pattern. For private, temporary game exports, authorization stays close to the product while large-byte delivery moves to object storage.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage documentation and verify expiry behavior in your own evaluation harness.

Further reading

  • Infrai documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • Google Cloud Storage signed URLs: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls
  • MDN, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS

title: Fix Presigned Object Storage Export Filenames and Content-Type
description:
Short answer: keep every tenant export private, set the object's Content-Type and Content-Disposition metadata before issuing a fresh presigned download link, and verify that metadata with a HEAD request before handing the URL to a browser.

For a developer tool that stores product images and generates tenant-scoped PDF or CSV exports, this is an access-control decision before it is a browser quirk. A signed link authorizes one object for a bounded period; it should not be asked to repair metadata that was wrong when the export was written. My operational recommendation is to make metadata validation a release condition for the export job, then sign only the validated object. This keeps the failure domain small and gives the service an observable checkpoint instead of leaving users to report that a file opened in a tab with an opaque name.

Compare browser symptoms with stored object state

The browser has three inputs that matter here: the URL, the stored media type, and the stored content disposition. If a CSV or PDF opens inline, or the save dialog proposes the wrong filename, inspect the object metadata first. The reliable repair is to set the correct Content-Type and Content-Disposition at upload time or immediately afterward, before generating another presigned link.

Don't make the object public to sidestep this. Public URLs aren't available in the storage path discussed here, and a permanent public link would weaken tenant isolation anyway. Generate a fresh signed link after the metadata checkpoint passes, and never attach the API bearer token when the client follows that returned URL.

This is also where integration shape starts to matter. Infrai is a reasonable option for a platform team that wants to put the object, correct its metadata, inspect it, and create a presigned link through plain HTTP without installing or tracking a storage SDK. With Infrai, one key and one bill cover storage plus other backend capabilities, which removes separate credentials and invoice reconciliation from the export service. I would try it for private, tenant-scoped exports when that small REST surface and a short path to the first working download matter more than provider-specific storage controls.

How should presigned object storage PDF and CSV exports set the filename and content-type?

Treat the object key, download filename, and media type as separate values. An object key is an internal storage address. The filename is user-facing metadata. The media type describes the bytes. Coupling all three to a string such as tenant-42/report-final.pdf tends to survive the happy path and fail later, when a customer chooses Q3 revenue, final.pdf or a name containing non-ASCII characters.

The smallest useful integration test is a HEAD check against the exact object that will be signed. This runnable Go program keeps credentials in the environment, makes the method explicit, surfaces non-success bodies, and backs off on 429 while honoring an integer Retry-After value:

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    bucket, objectKey := os.Getenv("STORAGE_BUCKET"), os.Getenv("STORAGE_OBJECT_KEY")
    apiKey := os.Getenv("STORAGE_API_KEY")
    if bucket == "" || objectKey == "" || apiKey == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "set STORAGE_BUCKET, STORAGE_OBJECT_KEY, and STORAGE_API_KEY")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    endpointTemplate := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/head/{bucket}/{key}"
    endpoint := strings.NewReplacer(
        "{bucket}", url.PathEscape(bucket),
        "{key}", url.PathEscape(objectKey),
    ).Replace(endpointTemplate)
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }

        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(res.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "head failed: %s: %s\n", res.Status, body)
            os.Exit(1)
        }

        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }

    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "head remained rate-limited after four attempts")
    os.Exit(1)
}

Set Content-Type and Content-Disposition through the documented input for POST /v1/storage/object/set_metadata/{bucket}/{key}. Pull the request schema from the public discovery document rather than freezing a guessed client struct; the discovery surface is self-describing and its documented capabilities include runnable Go examples. That gives the implementation a machine-readable contract without adding an SDK dependency. After the metadata update succeeds, run the HEAD check and only then create the download link. I am not sure which characters your customers will put into export names, and nobody can settle that from a unit test fixture alone, so include spaces, Unicode, commas, quotes, and long names in browser-level checks. Your mileage may vary across browsers, especially around how a filename is displayed, but the stored metadata should remain the invariant.

Small detail. Big blast radius.

Compare the metadata checkpoint with the browser result

Make the export job observable as a sequence: write the object privately, set metadata, read the object head, issue the signed URL, and record the outcome against the tenant export request. The storage SLO should measure successful, correctly named downloads rather than merely successful object writes; otherwise a green upload metric can hide a broken user journey.

A compact pre-release runbook is enough:

  1. Generate one PDF and one CSV for a non-production tenant fixture.
  2. Confirm the HEAD result carries the intended media type and attachment disposition before signing.
  3. Download each signed URL in the browsers you support, without the API authorization header.
  4. Repeat with a filename containing spaces, Unicode, punctuation, and a deliberately long basename.
  5. Confirm that one tenant cannot obtain a link for another tenant's object and that the application issues a fresh link rather than storing a permanent public URL.

Should rollback rewrite the object?

Rollback should be boring. Stop issuing new links for the affected export type, restore the last known-good exporter configuration, correct the object metadata, verify it with HEAD, and then issue replacement links. Do not overwrite the only copy of a regulated export on the assumption that object versioning will recover it; this surface has no object versioning or object lock. For strict recovery requirements, retain an external source of truth or choose storage with the required retention controls.

One more gate: alert on the metadata-validation failure rate and the age of unclaimed exports, then review stored volume against the lifecycle floor. A service that can generate exports faster than users consume them needs a capacity plan even when every request returns successfully.

Compare managed REST with direct storage providers

The buy-versus-build question isn't “which service can store a PDF?” All five options can sit in a design conversation; the useful comparison is which operational boundary the platform team is willing to own. I use the following decision table as a capacity-planning prompt, not as a feature scorecard:

Option Best fit for this export path Integration and on-call trade-off
Infrai A private signed-download flow where plain REST and fewer application credentials are the priority Small client surface; accept the capability boundaries listed below
AWS S3 directly A team already committed to AWS-specific storage controls and operations Keep the provider integration, signing model, credentials, and lifecycle policy in your service boundary
Cloudflare R2 directly A team whose delivery path and operations already center on Cloudflare Favor direct provider control over a shared multi-provider API
Google Cloud Storage directly A team that requires GCS or has standardized its platform around Google Cloud Use the specialist directly because GCS is outside this managed storage surface
MinIO, self-hosted A team that deliberately wants to own storage capacity and failure recovery Maximum infrastructure ownership, including upgrades, capacity headroom, and the storage SLO

The catch is that the managed layer is not suitable for static website hosting, permanent public image links, or a public-read ACL. It also isn't the right control plane when the requirement includes object versioning, object lock or WORM retention, strict conditional writes with If-Match, cross-region automatic replication, GCS or B2 coverage, metadata search, or hour-level lifecycle expiry. Browser-direct uploads that depend on self-service CORS configuration should stay with a specialist as well. Stick with AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, Google Cloud Storage, or a deliberately operated MinIO deployment when one of those provider-specific controls is a hard requirement rather than a possible roadmap item.

How should export volume affect capacity planning?

For the developer-tools scenario, I would keep product-image delivery and tenant export delivery as separate policy classes even if the bytes share a provider. Exports contain tenant data, have a clear request-to-generation lifecycle, and need auditable issuance of short-lived access; images may have different cache and retention needs. The managed lifecycle floor is one day, multipart fragments do not have an automatic cleanup rule, and list operations filter by prefix rather than server-side metadata. Those constraints should feed the capacity model: budget for abandoned multipart data, pick object prefixes that support tenant-scoped inventory, and use a queue or database if concurrent writers require strict coordination. No amount of prettier download code removes those responsibilities.

If this boundary fits the service, start with the storage documentation and validate the metadata contract against a disposable tenant export.

References

  • Amazon S3 object lifecycle management
  • Cloudflare Workers documentation

title: The A2A CLI on Azure: One Client for Container Apps, Agent Framework and Localhost
description:
This article provides a step by step guide to running A2A agents on Azure and driving them with the A2A CLI. A Rust agent on the official A2A Rust SDK runs in Azure Container Apps. A Microsoft Agent Framework agent on an Azure OpenAI model runs in Container Apps behind Entra ID and hands its work to the Rust agent. Both also run on a laptop, and one set of a2a commands checks all four.

https://github.com/xbill9/rust-dev/tree/main/a2a-agentframework-azure

The A2A CLI drove all four endpoints with the same commands, and 19 of 19 checks passed. Every hop speaks A2A 1.0: the Rust SDK serves it, Agent Framework serves it, and the Agent Framework agent calls the Rust agent with the A2A 1.0 Python client. On Azure the CLI needs one extra flag, an Entra ID bearer token, which az login already provides. Model access, registry pulls and the token all run on Entra ID, with no API key anywhere.

What Is Being Built?

Agent Where it runs A2A Model
mersenne-agent (Rust) laptop, port 8304 1.0, JSON-RPC and REST none
mersenne-agent (same image) Container Apps, 0.25 vCPU, 0.5 GiB 1.0, JSON-RPC and REST none
Agent Framework coordinator laptop, port 8309 1.0, JSON-RPC and REST gpt-5.4-mini on Azure OpenAI
Agent Framework coordinator (same code) Container Apps, Entra ID auth 1.0, JSON-RPC and REST gpt-5.4-mini on Azure OpenAI 
a2a CLI ──► Container Apps auth (Entra ID token) ──► Agent Framework Agent ──Entra ID──► Azure OpenAI gpt-5.4-mini

Step 3 — The Tool Calls the Rust Agent With the A2A 1.0 Python Client

Agent Framework's A2A package is built on a2a-sdk 1.x, the same protocol version as the Rust agent. The tool sends a data part and reads the Rust agent's structured report straight from the reply:

value = Value()
value.struct_value.update({"count": count})
request = SendMessageRequest(message=Message(
    role=Role.ROLE_USER, message_id=os.urandom(16).hex(), parts=[Part(data=value)],
))
async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=60) as http:
    client = await create_client(
        RUST_AGENT_URL, ClientConfig(streaming=False, httpx_client=http))
    async for event in client.send_message(request):
        task = event.task if event.HasField("task") else None
        for artifact in (task.artifacts if task else []):
            for part in artifact.parts:
                if part.HasField("data"):
                    report = MessageToDict(part.data)
                elif part.HasField("text"):
                    summary = part.text

The tool refuses a reply whose requested or found differs from the count the model asked for, and the instructions tell the model to quote the agent's own reply line. The model picks N; the Rust agent does the counting and the timing. Data parts cross a protobuf Struct, so integers arrive as floats and the tool reads them with int().

Step 6 — One Reply, One Artifact

Agent Framework's OpenAI client streams a reply as text deltas, then sends one more update holding the whole text under the same message id. One streamed reply, every text update:

1 msg_02d7537ef107 'Found'
2 msg_02d7537ef107 ' first'
...
21 msg_02d7537ef107 ' 7'
22 msg_02d7537ef107 'Found first 4 Mersenne primes in 0.0026ms.\n2, 3, 5, 7'
# last update repeats everything streamed before it under the same message_id: True

A2AExecutor appends every update to one artifact, which leaves the reply in the task twice. WholeTextA2AExecutor lets the closing update replace the artifact, so streaming clients see the deltas and the finished task holds the reply once, as a single text part:

class WholeTextA2AExecutor(A2AExecutor):
    async def handle_events(self, item, updater, streamed_artifact_ids=None, default_artifact_id=None):
        if isinstance(item, AgentResponseUpdate):
            key = item.message_id or default_artifact_id or ""
            text = "".join(c.text for c in item.contents if c.type == "text" and c.text)
            so_far = self._streamed.get(key, "")
            if text and so_far and text == so_far:
                del self._streamed[key]
                if streamed_artifact_ids is not None:
                    streamed_artifact_ids.discard(key)  # next add_artifact replaces
            elif text:
                self._streamed[key] = so_far + text
        await super().handle_events(item, updater, streamed_artifact_ids, default_artifact_id)

Targets take turns, one call each per round, so drift during the run lands on every target alike. Every reply is checked, and the statistics come from the script (results/summary-20261106.txt). The Rust agent's own compute time is a fraction of a millisecond on both machines, so the 153.7 ms between the laptop and Container Apps medians is the network and TLS. A coordinator call is an Azure OpenAI call plus a nested A2A call to a Rust agent. The Container Apps coordinator's median sits 55.2 ms above the laptop's, and both ranges span more than a second: the model call sets the time, and where the coordinator runs moves it by less than the spread between calls.

So, Which One?

For an agent with no model in it, Container Apps is the short path: one container app with external ingress, a public HTTPS address and no client changes. Every call costs the network trip, 153.7 ms here, on top of a computation that takes a fraction of a millisecond.

For an agent built around a model, the same Container Apps environment hosts it behind Entra ID with built-in authentication and no code in the agent. The CLI adds one flag, and az login supplies the token. The model call sets the response time, wherever the agent runs.

For talking to any of them, the A2A CLI is the one client. With Agent Framework on A2A 1.0, the agents talk to each other with the Python SDK and the laptop talks to all of them with the CLI, over one protocol version end to end.

Summary

The goal of this article was to show that the A2A CLI drives the same agents on a laptop and on Azure Container Apps with the same commands. The key to the solution was A2A 1.0 on every hop, Entra ID for every credential, and one set of checks run against every endpoint. The results were:

  • 🟢 19 of 19 CLI checks passed across four endpoints: card, send, stream, REST and data parts on the Rust agent; card, send, stream, REST and a 401 without a token on the coordinator
  • 🟢 Agent Framework serves A2A 1.0 with JSON-RPC and REST, and its tool calls the Rust 1.0 agent with the a2a-sdk 1.x client
  • 🟢 The Container Apps coordinator's calls reached the Container Apps Rust agent, confirmed in its log
  • 🟢 No API keys and no registry password: Entra ID for the model, the image pull and the CLI's token
  • ⚠️ The coordinator needs WholeTextA2AExecutor, or each reply lands in the task twice
  • ⚠️ The async Azure credential needs aiohttp pinned; nothing else installs it
  • ⚠️ Container Apps added 153.7 ms per Rust agent call over the laptop; the coordinators' medians differ by 55.2 ms, inside a spread of more than a second

Scope: one laptop (13th Gen Intel Core i7-1360P, Linux), one Azure region (eastus2), one replica of each app at 0.25 vCPU and 0.5 GiB, one model (gpt-5.4-mini), measured on 2026-11-06. Timing used N=10 with 20 calls per target, one run per comparison. Every Azure figure includes the trip from the laptop. Both apps kept one replica running, so cold starts were not measured; cost, gRPC, task commands, push notifications and load were not tested.

The strategy for running A2A agents on Azure and driving them with the A2A CLI was validated with an incremental step by step approach.

title: How to Fix Delayed Webhook Message Queue Timeout Issues with Node.js — 2026 Guide
description:
Short answer: use a delayed message queue with bounded retries, then send the fallback email through the same replaceable adapter; this keeps webhook timeout issues from becoming shipment-state corruption.

For this queue-to-email handoff, Infrai is worth trying when one credential and one REST API matter more than specialist workflow features. Its public, self-describing discovery surface supplies schemas and runnable examples, so a Python or Node.js adapter does not need an SDK just to learn the contract.

A marketplace should put shipment fan-out behind a queue, bound each webhook attempt, and make mail fallback idempotent. Cron should trigger work; a worker should consume it. Cron runs are limited to 900 seconds, queue delays to 604800 seconds, retention to 30 days, and standard queues are at-least-once.

Keep it boring.

How should a message queue handle timeout issues when delivering delayed webhooks?

Set a subscriber timeout below the queue and cron trigger SLA. Log endpoint, attempt, elapsed time, status, and reason. A timeout is uncertain delivery, not proof of shipment failure. An exhausted attempt belongs in a dead-letter queue. HMAC signing protects event integrity; RFC 2104 specifies the construction.

import hashlib
import hmac
import os
import time


def signed_headers(event_id: str, body: bytes) -> dict:
    digest = hmac.new(os.environ["WEBHOOK_SECRET"].encode(), body, hashlib.sha256)
    return {"X-Delivery-Id": event_id, "X-Signature": digest.hexdigest()}


def deliver(event: dict, subscriber: dict, attempts: int = 4) -> bool:
    body = subscriber["serialize"](event)
    headers = signed_headers(event["shipment_event_id"], body)
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        result = subscriber["deliver"](body, headers, timeout_seconds=10)
        if result.delivered:
            return True
        if attempt + 1 < attempts:
            time.sleep(min(60, 2 ** attempt))
    return False

The 10-second budget is an application choice. Honor Retry-After for 429 responses. Never acknowledge before the final delivery decision.

The failure I want in the test plan is a subscriber that accepts the TCP connection and then stalls. That case is easy to miss because connection metrics look healthy while the queue lease keeps aging. Record the delivery id before the request, measure the whole request rather than only connection setup, and classify the result as retryable until the attempt budget expires. A 429 with a server delay is different from a malformed response, but both need a durable outcome. After the last attempt, preserve the original shipment event and subscriber identity in the DLQ record. Otherwise a redrive becomes a manual reconstruction exercise, which is how duplicate shipment notices slip into production.

Short timeouts are useful only when the evidence survives them.

How does the shipment event reach mail without a second credential?

The queue worker and mail fallback can share one REST base URL and one Authorization: Bearer value. The application owns payload schemas and policy; this adapter keeps both routes replaceable.

import os
import requests

HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"}


def post(url: str, payload: dict, key: str) -> dict:
    response = requests.post(url, headers={**HEADERS, "Idempotency-Key": key}, json=payload, timeout=15)
    if response.status_code == 429:
        raise RuntimeError("retry this idempotent request after Retry-After")
    if not response.ok:
        raise RuntimeError(f"request failed: {response.status_code} {response.text}")
    return response.json()


def consume_then_email(consume_payload: dict, email_payload: dict, event_id: str) -> dict:
    consumed = post("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/consume", consume_payload, event_id + ":consume")
    email_payload["shipment_event_id"] = event_id
    sent = post("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/batch/send", email_payload, event_id + ":email")
    return {"consumed": consumed, "email": sent}

An alternative such as Inngest plus Resend means two signups, two credential sets, and glue for event handoff, retry state, and observability. A single-key design still means one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface.

Which replacement boundary survives a provider change?

Keep publish_event, consume_delivery, and notify_subscribers stable. Store shipment event id, delivery id, and subscriber id in every attempt. Inspect persistent timeouts in the DLQ and redrive only after fixing the cause. Redrive can deliver again, so idempotency remains mandatory; FIFO deduplication lasts only five minutes.

Option Best fit Limitation Migration cost
One-key scheduling plus email One credential and REST contract Seven-day delay, 30-day retention, public HTTPS targets Keep route adapters and discovery schemas
BullMQ with Redis Existing Redis and Node.js workers Redis operations remain yours Coupled worker and queue semantics
Inngest Event-driven workflows Its execution model becomes central Translate workflow steps and retry state
SQS plus SES AWS-governed systems Separate IAM and service contracts More provider-specific adapters

BullMQ is sensible when Redis is already a platform service. Inngest or Temporal is better for a DAG or fan-out join. SQS plus SES fits AWS ownership. A specialist also wins for Kafka-style replay, multiple consumer groups, private-network delivery, debounce, throttle, or a join primitive.

Test a slow public endpoint, a 429 with Retry-After, malformed output, and a never-ending endpoint. Assert bounded retries, late acknowledgement, DLQ placement, and delivery-id preservation after redrive. One timeout must not block another subscriber.

Paused cron triggers are not backfilled, and trigger timing has second-level jitter. Run-history output is limited to 4KB, so durable diagnostics belong in application logs. If the marketplace can retain its event, delivery id, retry policy, and subscriber record while changing queue vendors, the integration is replaceable.

Teams with a marketplace shipment fan-out and a small adapter surface should try Infrai for the queue-to-email handoff because one key and a self-describing REST contract reduce credential and schema glue.

If this boundary fits, start with the Infrai capability index and verify current schemas.

References

  • RFC 2104
  • Amazon SQS visibility timeout
  • BullMQ retries
  • Inngest retries
  • Capability discovery index

title: Developer Changelog Retrieval Architecture: Go Pipelines for Citation Tracing
description:
Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives every handoff to generation. For a developer changelog tracker, that shape gives better citation tracing than asking one vector index to answer an unbounded question, while keeping latency predictable enough for an interactive B2B SaaS workflow.

The invariant I care about is simple: every sentence shown to a user must be explainable by a small, stable set of changelog records. A retrieved chunk without its document id, release date, and canonical URL is not evidence; it is only text that happened to score well.

Infrai can sit behind this contract when a team wants vector operations and other backend services behind one REST surface. That is an integration decision, not a retrieval strategy.

Start with the retrieval contract

Before selecting a database, map the user-visible answer to a contract. A question such as “What changed in the payments SDK after version 3.4?” should produce claims, each claim should carry source ids, and each source id should resolve to the exact changelog revision that was indexed. The contract also states what happens when evidence is weak: return “not enough evidence” instead of silently expanding the search window.

I model that contract explicitly in Go. The types are deliberately boring because auditability beats cleverness here.

package retrieval

import "time"

type Citation struct {
    DocumentID string
    Revision   string
    URL        string
    Published  time.Time
}

type Evidence struct {
    ChunkID   string
    Text      string
    Citations []Citation
    Score     float64
}

type Answer struct {
    Text     string
    Evidence []Evidence
    Abstain  bool
}

The discovery call below keeps the client honest about paths and schemas. It uses the same bearer key as the eventual vector request, and it treats rate limiting as a normal control-flow branch.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func discovery(ctx context.Context) ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 200 * time.Millisecond
            if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(value); parseErr == nil {
                    wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery rate limit persisted after retries")
}

The ingestion side enforces the other half of the contract. A changed changelog gets a new revision and is re-indexed deliberately; a deleted record is removed from its collection, rather than left as a stale citation that can reappear in a top-k result. Keep a manifest of document id, revision, checksum, and collection membership so reconciliation is a queryable operation, not a late-night grep.

What should a developer changelog tracker retrieve, and how?

There are two viable system shapes. The first is a single-stage vector search: embed each chunk, ask for the top k, and pass the results to the answer model. It is easy to launch, but metadata filters, version boundaries, and citation completeness all become prompt conventions. Those conventions drift.

The second is staged retrieval. First, resolve structured constraints such as product, version range, and publication date. Next, run a bounded lexical or vector query inside the matching collection. Finally, rerank a small candidate set and attach immutable citation metadata before generation. This design adds one hop, yet it makes the important invariants executable: a slow source cannot block the user flow, and a result outside the requested release window cannot sneak in because it was semantically similar.

For a changelog tracker, I choose the staged shape. Set an explicit timeout for each stage, retry only transient transport failures with exponential backoff, and cap both candidate count and total context bytes. A 300 ms budget is an example policy, not a measured guarantee; your mileage may vary, so record stage timings and tune the budget against a labeled evaluation set.

The citation assembler should be deterministic. Sort evidence by the selected ranking key, de-duplicate on document id plus revision, and preserve the original URL. If generation retries, it receives the same evidence list. That is the retrieval equivalent of an exactly-once mindset: the answer may be regenerated, but its supporting records do not mutate underneath it.

Where a unified REST surface fits

Infrai is a reasonable option when the team wants vector operations alongside other backend capabilities behind one REST API, one key, and one bill. That removes a concrete operating burden for a small tracker: credentials and invoice reconciliation do not spread across separate service dashboards. Its public discovery surface and consistent HTTP interface also make it practical to call from Go without installing a vendor SDK, while keeping the retrieval code portable.

In this architecture, use a named vector collection per corpus or tenant boundary, then keep query limits in your application contract. Collection lifecycle is explicit: create with POST /v1/vector/collection/create, remove obsolete data with DELETE /v1/vector/delete, and retain the manifest as the audit record. The exact request schema should be generated from the service discovery document at implementation time; do not infer fields from a prose example.

Infrai is worth trying for teams that need a compact, HTTP-first vector layer and expect to combine it with several backend services under the same operational account. It is not the right choice when your organization requires a deeply specialized search platform, on-premise controls that your procurement process mandates, or an existing Elastic operating model with mature query DSL and observability. Stick with a specialist in those cases.

A fair comparison of the system shapes

The product choice follows the invariant, not the other way around. Here is how common options map to this workflow:

Option Strength for changelog retrieval Citation-tracing cost Good fit when
Elastic / Elasticsearch Mature lexical search, filters, and operational tooling You design revision metadata and evidence assembly Your team already runs Elastic and needs rich boolean queries
Pinecone Managed vector index with straightforward scaling Application still owns version scoping and immutable citations You want a focused hosted vector service
Weaviate Vector plus schema-oriented objects and modules Schema discipline is required to keep revisions unambiguous You prefer an object model around documents and chunks
Infrai vector API Plain REST access with a broad backend surface under one key You still own the retrieval contract and evaluation harness You want fewer service integrations around a staged design

No row removes the need for an evaluation set. Retrieval quality is a property of chunking, filters, embeddings, and ranking together; it is not a vendor checkbox. Latency is likewise a system budget, so measure p95 per stage after you have representative changelog traffic.

Roll out with evidence, then tighten the boundary

Start with a small labeled set of real tracker questions. Label whether the expected release appears, whether each answer claim has a resolvable citation, and whether the system abstains when the release is absent. Run the same set against both the single-stage baseline and the staged pipeline. Keep the baseline until the staged version wins on citation recall without violating your latency budget.

During migration, dual-write only changed documents, compare manifests, and delete records that no longer exist in the source repository. Log request id, collection, query bounds, candidate ids, and final citations; avoid logging secrets or full customer documents. That audit trail is useful during incident review and keeps compliance conversations concrete.

Small detail, large consequence: a citation points to a revision, not merely a URL.

The final decision rule is conditional: choose staged retrieval whenever citation tracing and release scoping are product requirements; choose a single-stage index only for a narrow prototype whose users can tolerate weaker provenance. The architecture should make that trade-off visible before a model writes a confident sentence. If this boundary fits your system, the vector retrieval guide is a practical place to inspect the collection workflow.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/query-dsl.html
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/get-started/overview
  • https://docs.weaviate.io/weaviate
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

title: A Guide to SaaS Signup CNAME Upsert Recovery and Rollback
description:
Customer-owned zones preserve control over a customer's mail identity; platform-owned zones give the application a place where it can automate changes directly. TL;DR: commit the tenant reservation and a durable provisioning intent together, then reconcile DNS outside the signup transaction. Treat CNAME upsert and rollback as recoverable operations, and track SPF, DKIM, and DMARC separately before declaring the mail setup ready.

For a hypothetical B2B SaaS signup, I would put cedar.app.example in a platform-owned zone while the customer keeps customer.example and its mail policy. Suppose the CNAME write times out after the signup has committed. My first postmortem question would be: what page fired? A failed request counter does not establish whether the record exists, and a green signup dashboard does not establish that the customer's mail authenticates. This is a worked scenario, not an account of a production incident.

Preserve the evidence.

The invariant I would extract is that an unknown DNS outcome must retain an owner and a recovery path. An HTTP response should not decide who owns the next attempt.

Should a tenant subdomain be provisioned inside the signup transaction?

The reader asking for a Node.js example that provisions a tenant subdomain inside the signup transaction is asking for a useful guarantee: either the tenant gets its name or the system can explain and recover the incomplete signup. Implement that guarantee as explicit application state. The minimal implementation below uses Go; the transaction boundary is the same design concern in a Node.js service.

Use one local transaction to reserve the tenant label, record its generation, and insert a provisioning job. Require uniqueness on the reserved name. If the transaction fails, neither reservation nor job should become visible; if it commits, a worker has durable work even when the client disconnects. Those are requirements for the storage implementation, not guarantees supplied by calling a function named Commit.

The tempting alternative is to hold the database transaction open while making the DNS request. That couples signup latency to the external request without providing a shared commit protocol: a timeout still leaves the caller unable to distinguish a rejected write from an accepted write whose response was lost. Rolling back the local row at that moment would throw away useful recovery information. This is a design failure worth preventing before it appears in a postmortem.

Return a provisioning state.

A practical proposed lifecycle is reserved, dns_pending, dns_ready, and mail_pending, followed by ready only when the product's documented checks pass. Record terminal rejection separately from retryable uncertainty. Keep the status visible to the customer so that another click on signup does not become an accidental second provisioning request.

Zone ownership determines who can finish the job

With a platform-owned application zone, the worker can own the desired CNAME and its repair process. With a customer-owned zone, the application needs either authorized automation or an explicit customer action; issuing instructions is not evidence that those instructions have been applied. Keep that distinction in the state model, because a worker cannot retry its way into authority over someone else's zone.

For the example tenant, the application route and the customer's mail identity are separate resources. A successful CNAME upsert for cedar.app.example must not satisfy the mail-readiness check for customer.example. DMARC evaluates alignment with the domain in the message's visible From field, using authenticated SPF or DKIM identifiers; a web-routing record is not that evidence. RFC 7489 describes this distinction and the policy-discovery process.

For customer-domain mail, make the requested SPF authorization and DKIM signing configuration specific to the sending arrangement, then inspect DMARC policy and alignment with that customer's intended From domain. Avoid publishing universal TXT examples that claim to fit every sender. An SPF-authenticated identifier can differ from the visible From domain, and a DKIM signature can verify without its signing domain aligning with that From domain. Either aligned authentication path can satisfy DMARC; requiring both to pass would be a separate product policy, not the DMARC rule.

There is a consequential trade-off here. A platform-controlled mail identity can reduce the number of customer DNS actions, but it changes the identity under which messages are sent; preserving the customer's identity requires coordinating records and verification in the customer's zone. Choose that boundary deliberately. It cannot be settled by a generic successful-provisioning badge.

Authentication is not an inbox guarantee. RFC 7489 leaves message disposition subject to receiver policy, so report what was checked rather than promising delivery from a DNS result.

Make an uncertain upsert safe to repeat

The following is a compilable boundary sketch for a reconciliation worker, not a DNS provider SDK. Its storage and DNS adapters must implement the stated contracts. The signup handler must already have committed the reservation and job atomically, and the adapter must restrict writes to the zone and records this application is authorized to manage.

package provisioning

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
)

type Intent struct {
    TenantID   string
    Generation int64
    Name       string
    Target     string
}

type Store interface {
    // Load the current committed intent, never an old queue payload.
    Current(context.Context, string) (Intent, error)
    // Compare generation atomically; a stale result must not mark ready.
    MarkDNSReady(context.Context, string, int64) error
}

type DNS interface {
    // Serialize with replacement and cancellation for this tenant.
    // Repeating the same intent must converge without duplicate records.
    // Reject a generation older than the latest accepted generation.
    // A nil result means the desired authoritative record was verified.
    EnsureCNAME(context.Context, Intent) error
}

func Reconcile(ctx context.Context, s Store, dns DNS, tenantID string) error {
    intent, err := s.Current(ctx, tenantID)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("load DNS intent: %w", err)
    }
    if err := dns.EnsureCNAME(ctx, intent); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("reconcile DNS generation %d: %w",
            intent.Generation, err)
    }
    if err := s.MarkDNSReady(ctx, intent.TenantID, intent.Generation); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("record DNS verification: %w", err)
    }
    return nil
}

The interface comments carry the difficult part.

A database comparison before an external write is insufficient if cancellation or replacement can race that write. Route those operations through the same serialized controller, or implement equivalent fencing in the adapter; do not assume the DNS service understands the generation field. If that contract cannot be enforced, this sketch is incomplete for concurrent replacement. Consider generation 7 waiting on a DNS call while generation 8 requests cancellation: checking a database flag before the first call would not stop its late completion. The controller must finish or resolve the earlier operation before applying the newer intent, and it must retain uncertain work across restart. A generation number in a log line cannot provide that ordering by itself.

Don't discard uncertainty.

A read timeout or an upsert timeout returns an error and leaves the job recoverable. If the record was written but MarkDNSReady failed, the next attempt loads the current intent and verifies the desired record again. Schedule retries with bounded backoff, retain attempt history, and expose persistent failure for investigation. The code intentionally defines no arbitrary retry count that would quietly turn an uncertain outcome into abandonment.

Test the boundaries that change recovery decisions: an accepted write followed by a lost response, a failed readiness update after verification, and a cancellation racing a worker. Also test an unexpected existing record. Treat it as an ownership conflict requiring investigation unless the controller can establish that it owns the record; an upsert must not become permission to overwrite unrelated configuration.

Rollback is another desired state

Do not make the timeout handler issue an unconditional delete. In the hypothetical incident, that delete could remove the record the first request successfully created; after a replacement, it could also remove the newer tenant configuration. Model cancellation as a new generation with an explicit cleanup intent, and keep the reservation until the controller has established the cleanup outcome.

For a newly allocated record, cleanup means removing only configuration whose ownership is established. For an update to an existing managed record, compensation may instead mean restoring the prior desired value. Preserve that value before the change. Customer-owned mail policy deserves its own boundary: cancelling a web signup is not sufficient reason to delete the customer's SPF or DMARC policy.

Operationally, measure the age of committed intents awaiting verification, recovery attempts, and ownership conflicts. Define pages around an actionable breach of the signup promise, with the tenant, name, generation, and last observed result attached. A dashboard counting successful API calls would miss the precise gap this design is meant to expose: accepted work without a verified outcome.

The smallest useful incident timeline has three separate observations. Preserve their timestamps:

Observation What it establishes What remains open
Local commit The reservation and job were saved together DNS outcome
Authoritative record verification The desired routing record was observed Customer mail authentication
Mail-authentication check The tested message's authentication and alignment results Receiver disposition

Diagnose from those observations before assigning blame to propagation or telling the customer to repeat setup.

This workflow is unnecessary when signup only reserves an application identity and no DNS change is required. If customer administrators must publish all records manually, use a pending-verification workflow with clear instructions rather than pretending the worker can perform the write. If the platform already uses a preconfigured routing arrangement, first establish whether a per-tenant CNAME is required at all.

The operational acceptance rule remains modest: retain enough state to recover uncertain writes, establish who controls each record, and make readiness describe the checks actually completed. Mail authentication and application routing should each have evidence of their own.

References

RFC 7489 supplies the DMARC authentication-alignment, policy-discovery, and receiver-policy details used here, especially Sections 3 through 6. The transaction lifecycle, controller contracts, and recovery tests are proposed implementation requirements for this example.

Sources

  • https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7489

title: O Fim do "Timeout" Silencioso: Padrões de Design para Filas de Alta Disponibilidade em Vendas
description:
Você termina de orquestrar um novo fluxo de captura de leads. Os webhooks estão mapeados, os payloads JSON batem perfeitamente com o esquema do banco de dados e o teste local retorna um status de sucesso em menos de 200 milissegundos. Você aprova o deploy para produção. Uma semana depois, a equipe de marketing escala a campanha, o tráfego atinge o pico esperado e o diretor de vendas avisa que contatos qualificados estão sumindo do pipeline. Ao investigar os logs do servidor, você encontra um cemitério de requisições derrubadas.
Essa é a dura realidade de depender de integrações síncronas diretas em operações comerciais críticas.
A Armadilha das Integrações Ponto a Ponto
Quando subimos instâncias auto-hospedadas de automação — como um motor n8n rodando em contêineres Docker em um VPS na DigitalOcean — a abordagem padrão de engenharia quase sempre é mapear a entrada de dados e apontar um nó HTTP diretamente para o CRM ou para o banco PostgreSQL da empresa. Operamos sob a premissa perigosa de que o servidor de destino estará sempre com baixa latência e pronto para receber a carga.
No mundo real, CRMs corporativos impõem limites rigorosos de requisições simultâneas e bancos de dados sofrem picos de lentidão durante horários comerciais ativos. Se um webhook tenta empurrar um novo lead exatamente no milissegundo em que o servidor de destino está processando queries internas pesadas, a requisição HTTP trava. Em poucos segundos, a plataforma de origem corta a conexão por esgotamento de tempo.
O resultado é um timeout silencioso. O sistema falha nos bastidores, nenhum alerta crítico é disparado para a equipe comercial e a oportunidade de negócio simplesmente evapora na rede sem deixar rastros.
Desacoplando a Ingestão do Processamento
Depender de lógicas de retry configuradas na própria origem raramente resolve a raiz do problema. Bombardear um servidor que já está gargalado com requisições repetidas apenas agrava a latência da infraestrutura. Para proteger dados transacionais de alto valor, o paradigma arquitetônico precisa mudar: é obrigatório parar de tratar o roteamento de leads como uma chamada telefônica síncrona e começar a tratá-lo como uma fila de mensagens de alta disponibilidade.
A solução estrutural exige o desacoplamento total. O momento de recebimento do webhook deve ser isolado do seu processamento final através de uma camada de buffer intermediária. A única função primária dessa infraestrutura é interceptar a requisição instantaneamente, devolver um 200 OK para a origem liberando a conexão de forma segura, e reter o payload. A partir desse momento, os dados são orquestrados e entregues ao destino final em um ritmo controlado, respeitando a capacidade real de absorção do servidor.
O Middleware como Roteador Comercial
Construir, conteinerizar e manter esse barramento de eventos tolerante a falhas do zero consome um tempo precioso que as equipes de desenvolvimento poderiam aplicar no produto principal. É para resolver exatamente essa quebra de resiliência sem adicionar overhead de manutenção que plataformas de roteamento dedicado como o Zapflux são implementadas na arquitetura.
Atuando como um middleware focado puramente no tráfego comercial, a ferramenta serve como o amortecedor vital entre os canais imprevisíveis de captura front-end e os bancos de dados rígidos de backend. Ela absorve o impacto de picos massivos de tráfego, gerencia a retenção das mensagens e garante a sincronização estrita dos dados apenas quando os sistemas de destino estão saudáveis e prontos.
Engenharia de vendas escalável significa aceitar a premissa básica de que APIs externas inevitavelmente vão falhar, impor rate limits ou apresentar lentidão. Ao substituir conexões frágeis de ponta a ponta por uma camada de roteamento estruturada, eliminamos o risco da perda de pacotes e garantimos que a fricção técnica nunca seja a responsável por uma venda perdida.
Como vocês costumam arquitetar a tolerância a falhas quando precisam integrar webhooks de alto volume com bancos de dados e CRMs legados em produção?

title: Equinix opens SG6: server eligibility belongs in the AI rack delivery plan
description:
Equinix announced the opening of SG6 in Singapore on November 6. Its English release states that the first phase provides 8 MW of capacity and approximately 1,550 cabinets, with up to 20 MW of IT capacity at full build-out.

For technical buyers, another detail deserves attention. The company's Japanese announcement says customer IT servers deployed at SG6 must have recognized energy-efficiency certification or demonstrate equivalent efficiency, in connection with Singapore standard SS 715:2025.

My operational reading is that server eligibility should be resolved before equipment ships. The opening creates a new placement option. A successful deployment still needs agreement on the particular hardware, its facility interfaces and the evidence required for acceptance.

Resolve the hardware evidence before ordering

Ask the operator what documentation it accepts for the exact server configuration being proposed.

A useful submission should identify the server model, installed components and relevant certification or equivalent evidence. Have the hardware supplier explain which configurations the documentation covers. Ask the operator how it handles changes after approval, including a substituted component or a revised server build.

This is a proposed procurement process, not an interpretation of every requirement in the standard. Obtain the applicable admission criteria directly from Equinix and assign responsibility for resolving any uncertainty.

The practical objective is to avoid discovering a documentation gap after the hardware has arrived.

Match cooling capabilities to the actual rack

Equinix describes SG6 as supporting high-density AI infrastructure with liquid-cooling capabilities. That facility-level description is a starting point for the interface discussion.

For the proposed deployment, request the supported temperature, flow and pressure ranges, coolant requirements and physical connection details. Confirm where responsibility passes between the facility, coolant distribution equipment and the servers.

Include the residual air-cooled load in that discussion. Ask the server supplier to identify heat that remains outside its liquid-cooling path and have the operator confirm how that heat will be handled in the intended placement.

Record those answers against the equipment list. A change in the rack design should trigger an interface review before installation.

Keep power reservations and operating assumptions together

The announced phase capacity does not specify the allocation available to an individual customer.

My recommendation is to review the contracted power alongside the rack's expected behavior. Agree on the planning basis for normal operation, peak demand and any permitted load changes. Confirm how the installation is expected to behave during maintenance or a supply-path event.

Have the operator and hardware supplier review the same assumptions. Differences between their documents should be resolved while the design can still change.

This is also a useful point to identify the telemetry each party will receive. A shared record of power and cooling conditions can help distinguish an equipment issue from an interface problem during commissioning.

Treat the PUE figure as a design target

Equinix says SG6 is designed for a Power Usage Effectiveness of 1.20 and is targeting Green Mark Platinum certification. Those are design and certification targets in the opening announcement.

For an operational comparison, ask what measured information will become available and under which reporting boundary. Record the period, facility loading and relevant operating conditions alongside the result.

Keep that facility metric separate from the application's useful work. A workload acceptance exercise should also measure the service outcomes the customer needs, such as latency, throughput and completion time, under an agreed configuration.

That provides a clearer basis for deciding whether the deployment meets its objectives than treating a design figure as a measured result for a particular workload.

Agree on acceptance before production traffic

A practical next step is a joint readiness review covering hardware eligibility, electrical service, cooling interfaces and installation responsibilities.

Turn unresolved items into explicit prerequisites for delivery or commissioning. Agree on the test workload, the evidence to retain and the people authorized to accept the result. Include the escalation route for an issue that crosses the facility and server support boundaries.

The SG6 opening is the new development. For an AI infrastructure team considering the site, the immediate work is to connect that opportunity to an approved hardware configuration and a documented acceptance process. That makes the eventual move from delivery to production easier to assess and manage.

title: Hangfire Alternative in .NET: Why I Replaced It With BackgroundService and Channel
description:
The first version of this site was an ASP.NET Core MVC app with Hangfire wired in: a dashboard at /hangfire, five recurring jobs, ten places in the code that called BackgroundJob.Enqueue, and a second SQL Server database just to hold Hangfire's job tables. When I rewrote the backend as a separate Web API, I didn't bring Hangfire with me. The API that serves this page runs two BackgroundService classes fed by System.Threading.Channels, and one WHERE clause does the work of the every-minute job.

This isn't a "Hangfire is bad" post. Hangfire is a good library. It's a post about checking which jobs actually needed it, because for this site the answer was none of them.

The short version: Use Hangfire (or Quartz.NET) when a job must survive a restart, retry on its own, or be visible on a dashboard. If the work is in-process, short-lived and fine to lose on a crash, a BackgroundService with a bounded Channel is built into .NET, needs no extra database, and is about 60 lines. A job that only "flips something on at a certain time" often needs no job at all: filter by time in the query.

What Hangfire was doing on the old site

The setup was the standard one from Hangfire's docs, with SQL Server storage on its own connection string:

// Program.cs of the old MVC site (connection string name only - the value lives in config)
var hangfireConnectionString = builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("HangfireConnection");

builder.Services.AddHangfire(c => c
    .SetDataCompatibilityLevel(CompatibilityLevel.Version_180)
    .UseSimpleAssemblyNameTypeSerializer()
    .UseRecommendedSerializerSettings()
    .UseSqlServerStorage(hangfireConnectionString, new SqlServerStorageOptions
    {
        QueuePollInterval = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(15),
        DisableGlobalLocks = true,
    }));
builder.Services.AddHangfireServer();

// ...and after app.Build():
RecurringJob.AddOrUpdate("check-scheduled-posts",
    () => blogPostService.PublishScheduledPostsAsync(),
    "* * * * *");

Here is every job it had, and what each one became in the new API:

Hangfire job (old site) Schedule What replaced it
check-scheduled-posts Every minute Nothing runs. The query filters on ScheduledAt <= now
daily-backup 02:00 daily The hosting panel's scheduled backup, outside the app
update-sitemap Recurring A Next.js route handler that regenerates at most once an hour
cleanup-expired-comments, cleanup-old-logs Recurring Dropped. The only cleanup left is inside a worker loop (below)
Fire-and-forget: welcome and reset emails, newsletter sends, image optimisation, analytics Enqueued per request Emails are sent inside the request. Page views go through a Channel

When I checked the API's database on 2 November, it had 31 tables and none of them belonged to Hangfire. The separate Hangfire database is only referenced by the old app's config.

Why I didn't keep it

Three reasons, in the order they mattered.

The database is on remote shared hosting. Every query this site makes crosses the internet to a shared SQL Server. Hangfire's SQL Server storage polls its queue table, and with QueuePollInterval at 15 seconds that's 5,760 polls a day per worker, whether or not there's any work, plus the heartbeat and recurring-job checks. On a dedicated server nobody would notice. On a shared host with a round trip on every call, it's background load for nothing.

Most of the jobs didn't need a scheduler. The every-minute job looked for posts whose publish time had passed and flipped them live. But a post doesn't have to be flipped. If every public query asks "is this post published and is its time in the past?", the post becomes visible at the right moment on its own:

// A post is live when it is published AND its scheduled time has passed.
// EF Core translates this to a WHERE clause, so "publishing on schedule" needs no job at all.
public static Expression<Func<BlogPost, bool>> IsLive(DateTime utcNow) =>
    p => p.IsPublished
         && p.PublishedAt != null
         && (p.ScheduledAt == null || p.ScheduledAt <= utcNow);

The API's public post queries (lists, tags, authors, the single post) all go through that expression. There's no job to fail, no minute of lag, and nothing to monitor.

A second database is a second thing to back up, restore and secure. When this site's main database was restored from a backup on 29 October, I had to work out which posts the restore had wiped. With Hangfire's state in another database, a restore of one without the other leaves jobs that point at rows that no longer exist. One database is simpler.

The replacement: BackgroundService plus a bounded Channel

The job that most needed to run in the background was the cheapest one: counting page views. Writing a view row on every post request meant the reader waited on a remote INSERT before the post came back. Now the endpoint drops an event on a channel and returns:

public readonly record struct PostViewEvent(int PostId, string? IpAddress, string? UserAgent);

public sealed class ViewTracker
{
    private readonly Channel<PostViewEvent> _channel = Channel.CreateBounded<PostViewEvent>(
        new BoundedChannelOptions(10_000)
        {
            // Under a spike, lose a few analytics rows rather than block a request.
            FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.DropWrite,
            SingleReader = true,
        });

    public ChannelReader<PostViewEvent> Reader => _channel.Reader;

    // Called from the GET /posts/{slug} endpoint. Never awaits, never touches the database.
    public void Track(PostViewEvent view) => _channel.Writer.TryWrite(view);
}

A BackgroundService reads the channel, waits up to 5 seconds or 200 events, and writes the batch in one go:

public sealed class ViewTrackerWorker(
    ViewTracker tracker,
    IServiceScopeFactory scopeFactory,
    ILogger<ViewTrackerWorker> logger) : BackgroundService
{
    private static readonly TimeSpan FlushInterval = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5);
    private const int MaxBatch = 200;

    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        var buffer = new List<PostViewEvent>(MaxBatch);
        while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            try
            {
                // Wait for the first event, then collect more for up to 5 seconds or 200 items.
                if (!await tracker.Reader.WaitToReadAsync(stoppingToken)) break;
                using var window = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(stoppingToken);
                window.CancelAfter(FlushInterval);
                try
                {
                    do
                    {
                        while (buffer.Count < MaxBatch && tracker.Reader.TryRead(out var view))
                            buffer.Add(view);
                    } while (buffer.Count < MaxBatch && await tracker.Reader.WaitToReadAsync(window.Token));
                }
                catch (OperationCanceledException) when (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
                {
                    // The 5-second window ran out - the normal path.
                }

                await FlushAsync(buffer, stoppingToken);
                buffer.Clear();
            }
            catch (OperationCanceledException) when (stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
            {
                break;
            }
            catch (Exception ex)
            {
                // One bad batch must not kill the loop - an unhandled exception here stops the
                // service, and since .NET 6 it stops the whole host by default.
                logger.LogError(ex, "Failed to flush post views");
                buffer.Clear();
                await Task.Delay(FlushInterval, stoppingToken);
            }
        }
    }

    private async Task FlushAsync(List<PostViewEvent> buffer, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // A BackgroundService is a singleton; DbContext is scoped. Make a scope per batch.
        using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope();
        var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<ApplicationDbContext>();

        db.PostViews.AddRange(buffer.Select(v => new PostView { BlogPostId = v.PostId, ViewedAt = DateTime.UtcNow }));
        await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);

        // One UPDATE per post, not one per view.
        foreach (var group in buffer.GroupBy(v => v.PostId))
        {
            var n = group.Count();
            await db.BlogPosts.Where(p => p.Id == group.Key)
                .ExecuteUpdateAsync(s => s.SetProperty(p => p.ViewCount, p => p.ViewCount + n), ct);
        }
    }
}

Registration is two lines. The tracker is a singleton so the endpoint and the worker share the same channel:

builder.Services.AddSingleton<ViewTracker>();
builder.Services.AddHostedService<ViewTrackerWorker>();

The second worker, for the site's real-user speed data, is the same pattern with a 20,000-event channel and 300-event batches. It also deletes rows older than 90 days, once a day, from inside the same loop. That one check replaced the two cleanup jobs I had in Hangfire.

Details that matter

  • Bounded, not unbounded. Channel.CreateUnbounded grows until the process runs out of memory if the database is down for long. A bound plus DropWrite loses analytics rows instead, which is the right failure for a view counter.
  • Catch everything inside the loop. Since .NET 6, an unhandled exception in ExecuteAsync stops the host by default (BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior.StopHost). One failed batch shouldn't take the API down.
  • Create a scope per batch. Hosted services are singletons and DbContext is scoped. Injecting the context directly into the worker either fails at startup or keeps one context alive forever.
  • Batch the UPDATE too. ExecuteUpdateAsync runs one UPDATE ... SET ViewCount = ViewCount + n per post in the batch, not one per view.

What I gave up

This only works because I accepted these, on purpose:

  • Anything in the channel is lost on a restart or crash. Up to 5 seconds of page views. For a view counter that's fine. For a payment webhook or an order email it is not.
  • No retries. Hangfire retries a failed job automatically (10 attempts by default). My worker logs the error and drops the batch.
  • No dashboard. Failures show up in the log, not on a page.
  • Emails run inside the request. A contact form submission waits for two SMTP sends before the visitor sees "sent". At this site's volume that's acceptable. With a slow mail server or real traffic, it wouldn't be, and that is the first thing I'd move back to a queue.
  • Scheduled posts aren't announced when they go live. The API pings IndexNow when a post is saved, but only if it's already live. A post scheduled for tomorrow becomes visible tomorrow through the query filter, and nothing tells Bing. I submit those by hand. A scheduler would have handled that.
  • IIS can stop the worker. A BackgroundService lives inside the app pool. If IIS idles the pool out, the worker stops until the next request. That's harmless for work that's created by requests, but a daily timer won't fire on a site nobody visited. Hangfire on IIS has exactly the same problem, which is why its docs tell you to configure the app to always run.

Hangfire vs Quartz.NET vs BackgroundService

Hangfire Quartz.NET BackgroundService + Channel
Survives a restart Yes (storage: SQL Server, Redis and others) Yes, with the ADO.NET job store No
Automatic retries Yes No, you handle it in the job No, you write it
Dashboard Built in Not built in No
Cron schedules Yes Yes, the strongest of the three PeriodicTimer for fixed intervals
Extra storage Its own tables (or database) Its own tables, if persistent None
Cost Free (LGPL), Pro is paid Free (Apache 2.0) Built into .NET

If you only need a recurring job and can live with it not running while the app is down, PeriodicTimer covers it without a library:

// Generic example, not from this site: a daily job without Hangfire.
public sealed class NightlyCleanup(IServiceScopeFactory scopes, ILogger<NightlyCleanup> logger) : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        using var timer = new PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan.FromHours(24));
        do
        {
            try
            {
                using var scope = scopes.CreateScope();
                var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
                var cutoff = DateTime.UtcNow.AddDays(-90);
                await db.Logs.Where(l => l.At < cutoff).ExecuteDeleteAsync(stoppingToken);
            }
            catch (Exception ex) when (ex is not OperationCanceledException)
            {
                logger.LogError(ex, "Nightly cleanup failed");
            }
        } while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(stoppingToken));
    }
}

When I'd still pick Hangfire

  • Work that must not be lost: payments, order confirmations, anything a customer would notice was missing.
  • Jobs that call flaky third-party APIs and need retries with backoff.
  • More than one server, where only one of them should run a job.
  • A team that needs to see and re-run failed jobs without reading logs.

If none of those apply, look at each job and ask whether it needs a scheduler at all, or just a query that checks the time. I wrote more about how the MVC site became a separate API and front end in the migration post, and about keeping the API fast on remote hosting in the Web API performance post.

FAQ

What is a good Hangfire alternative in .NET Core?

For in-process work that can be lost on a restart, the built-in BackgroundService with a bounded System.Threading.Channels queue needs no library and no database. For persistent, cron-scheduled jobs, Quartz.NET is the usual free alternative. Hangfire is still the easiest choice when you need retries and a dashboard.

Hangfire vs BackgroundService: which should I use?

Use BackgroundService when the work is short, created by requests and fine to lose on a crash, such as view counters or log batching. Use Hangfire when a job must survive restarts, retry on failure or be visible on a dashboard, such as emails tied to orders or payments.

Hangfire vs Quartz.NET: what is the difference?

Hangfire is built around fire-and-forget and delayed jobs with automatic retries and a built-in dashboard. Quartz.NET is a scheduler first, with the most flexible cron and calendar triggers, but no built-in dashboard and no automatic retries. Both can persist jobs to a database.

How do I make a background task queue in ASP.NET Core?

Register a singleton that wraps a bounded Channel, write to it from your endpoints with TryWrite, and read from it in a BackgroundService registered with AddHostedService. Create a DI scope per batch to get a DbContext, and catch exceptions inside the loop so one failure does not stop the host.

Does Hangfire need its own database?

No. Hangfire can store its tables in your application's database, under its own HangFire schema, or use a separate database or Redis. Either way it adds tables that have to be backed up and kept in step with your data.

Do I need a job to publish scheduled blog posts?

Not necessarily. If every public query filters on the scheduled time, for example ScheduledAt <= now, the post appears at the right moment with no job. A job is only needed if something else must happen at that moment, such as notifying search engines or sending emails.

Will a BackgroundService keep running on IIS?

Only while the application pool is running. IIS stops idle pools by default, which stops hosted services too. Work created by requests is fine, but timers need the app pool set to always running, the same requirement Hangfire has on IIS.
