title: Prevent Spoofed Orders in Next.js Telegram Mini Apps using Server-Validated MainButton Checkout
description:
Shipping an e-commerce storefront inside a Telegram Mini App using Next.js App Router seems straightforward until untrusted client state compromises your checkout process. Front-end developers frequently rely on window.Telegram.WebApp.initDataUnsafe to identify the user and send cart totals directly from the client to an API route. Because initDataUnsafe can be mutated by anyone opening your app in a standard browser or using browser developer tools, accepting unverified user IDs or total prices from the front end allows users to modify invoice amounts, impersonate other customer accounts, or execute unverified orders.

Building a robust Telegram Mini App shop requires verifying the raw initData payload using an HMAC-SHA256 signature on the server, calculating cart prices strictly from stored backend database values, controlling Telegram's native MainButton across React render lifecycles, and accounting for renderer discrepancies between iOS WebViews and Telegram Desktop.

Validating Telegram initData in Next.js Route Handlers

When a client triggers a checkout flow, the application must pass the raw window.Telegram.WebApp.initData query string to a Next.js App Router Route Handler (app/api/checkout/route.ts). Never pass pre-parsed JSON objects from initDataUnsafe. The raw string contains key-value pairs sorted alphabetically and signed by Telegram using a secret key derived from your Bot Token.

If your API route receives a list of product IDs and quantities, it must recalculate the total price on the server side using your application's product catalog. Once verified, the route calls Telegram's createInvoiceLink Bot API endpoint to return a native payment link back to the front end.

Here is how to validate initData and generate an invoice link securely in a Next.js Route Handler:

// app/api/checkout/route.ts
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server';
import crypto from 'crypto';

interface CartItem {
  id: string;
  quantity: number;
}

const PRODUCT_CATALOG: Record<string, { name: string; priceInCents: number }> = {
  'item_1': { name: 'Developer Mug', priceInCents: 1500 },
  'item_2': { name: 'Mechanical Keyboard', priceInCents: 12000 },
};

function verifyTelegramInitData(initDataRaw: string, botToken: string) {
  const params = new URLSearchParams(initDataRaw);
  const hash = params.get('hash');
  if (!hash) return { isValid: false, user: null };

  params.delete('hash');

  const dataCheckArray: string[] = [];
  for (const [key, value] of params.entries()) {
    dataCheckArray.push(`${key}=${value}`);
  }
  dataCheckArray.sort();
  const dataCheckString = dataCheckArray.join('\n');

  const secretKey = crypto
    .createHmac('sha256', 'WebAppData')
    .update(botToken)
    .digest();

  const calculatedHash = crypto
    .createHmac('sha256', secretKey)
    .update(dataCheckString)
    .digest('hex');

  if (calculatedHash !== hash) {
    return { isValid: false, user: null };
  }

  const authDate = parseInt(params.get('auth_date') || '0', 10);
  const now = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);
  if (now - authDate > 86400) {
    return { isValid: false, user: null }; // Reject auth_date older than 24 hours
  }

  const userRaw = params.get('user');
  const user = userRaw ? JSON.parse(userRaw) : null;

  return { isValid: true, user };
}

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  try {
    const body = await request.json();
    const { initData, items } = body as { initData: string; items: CartItem[] };

    const botToken = process.env.TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN;
    if (!botToken) {
      return NextResponse.json({ error: 'Server configuration error' }, { status: 500 });
    }

    const { isValid, user } = verifyTelegramInitData(initData, botToken);
    if (!isValid || !user) {
      return NextResponse.json({ error: 'Invalid signature or expired session' }, { status: 401 });
    }

    // Recalculate cart total on server
    let totalAmount = 0;
    const invoicePrices = [];

    for (const item of items) {
      const product = PRODUCT_CATALOG[item.id];
      if (!product) {
        return NextResponse.json({ error: `Invalid product ID: ${item.id}` }, { status: 400 });
      }
      const itemTotal = product.priceInCents * item.quantity;
      totalAmount += itemTotal;
      invoicePrices.push({
        label: `${product.name} x${item.quantity}`,
        amount: itemTotal,
      });
    }

    if (totalAmount === 0) {
      return NextResponse.json({ error: 'Cart is empty' }, { status: 400 });
    }

    // Request invoice link from Telegram Bot API
    const response = await fetch(`https://api.telegram.org/bot${botToken}/createInvoiceLink`, {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        title: 'Order Checkout',
        description: `Order for Telegram User ID ${user.id}`,
        payload: JSON.stringify({ userId: user.id, timestamp: Date.now() }),
        provider_token: process.env.PAYMENT_PROVIDER_TOKEN || '',
        currency: 'USD',
        prices: invoicePrices,
      }),
    });

    const data = await response.json();
    if (!data.ok) {
      return NextResponse.json({ error: data.description || 'Failed to create invoice' }, { status: 500 });
    }

    return NextResponse.json({ invoiceUrl: data.result });
  } catch (err) {
    return NextResponse.json({ error: 'Internal server error' }, { status: 500 });
  }
}

If an attacker manipulates the cart payload in the browser or sends a fake HTTP request, the route fails at the signature check stage or re-computes the price from server records. The front end never sends prices; it only sends product identifiers and quantities.

Syncing the MainButton and Cart State in React

Telegram provides a native UI button pinned to the bottom of the Mini App container via Telegram.WebApp.MainButton. Integrating MainButton inside a React dynamic application often introduces event listener memory leaks, duplicate payment requests, or visual desynchronization when cart items change.

A common implementation flaw occurs when developers bind Telegram.WebApp.MainButton.onClick inside a component without unbinding previous listeners on state changes. Every re-render attaches another listener callback, causing a single tap on the button to execute multiple fetch calls to /api/checkout simultaneously.

To prevent this, sync MainButton state inside a dedicated React useEffect block, managing visibility, text, and event listener cleanup explicitly:

// components/CartCheckout.tsx
'use client';

import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

interface CartItem {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  priceInCents: number;
  quantity: number;
}

export default function CartCheckout({ items }: { items: CartItem[] }) {
  const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(false);

  const totalCents = items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.priceInCents * item.quantity, 0);

  useEffect(() => {
    const tg = window.Telegram?.WebApp;
    if (!tg || !tg.MainButton) return;

    if (items.length === 0) {
      tg.MainButton.hide();
      return;
    }

    tg.MainButton.setText(`CHECKOUT ($${(totalCents / 100).toFixed(2)})`);
    tg.MainButton.show();

    if (isLoading) {
      tg.MainButton.showProgress(false);
      tg.MainButton.disable();
    } else {
      tg.MainButton.hideProgress();
      tg.MainButton.enable();
    }

    const handleMainButtonClick = async () => {
      setIsLoading(true);
      try {
        const response = await fetch('/api/checkout', {
          method: 'POST',
          headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
          body: JSON.stringify({
            initData: tg.initData,
            items: items.map(i => ({ id: i.id, quantity: i.quantity })),
          }),
        });

        const result = await response.json();
        if (!response.ok) {
          tg.showAlert(result.error || 'Checkout failed');
          return;
        }

        // Open native payment modal via invoice link
        tg.openInvoice(result.invoiceUrl, (status) => {
          if (status === 'paid') {
            tg.showAlert('Payment successful!');
            // Clear cart or redirect user
          } else if (status === 'failed') {
            tg.showAlert('Payment failed or canceled.');
          }
        });
      } catch (err) {
        tg.showAlert('Network error occurred during checkout.');
      } finally {
        setIsLoading(false);
      }
    };

    tg.MainButton.onClick(handleMainButtonClick);

    return () => {
      tg.MainButton.offClick(handleMainButtonClick);
    };
  }, [items, totalCents, isLoading]);

  return (
    <div className="p-4">
      <h2 className="text-lg font-bold">Your Cart</h2>
      {items.length === 0 ? (
        <p>Cart is empty.</p>
      ) : (
        <ul className="divide-y">
          {items.map((item) => (
            <li key={item.id} className="py-2 flex justify-between">
              <span>{item.name} x{item.quantity}</span>
              <span>${((item.priceInCents * item.quantity) / 100).toFixed(2)}</span>
            </li>
          ))}
        </ul>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

Calling tg.MainButton.offClick(handleMainButtonClick) inside the clean-up return statement guarantees that old event listeners are removed whenever items or isLoading changes.

Fixing iOS and Desktop Telegram WebView Render Quirks

Developing Mini Apps in modern browsers does not prepare your interface for Telegram's underlying WebViews. Android, iOS, and Telegram Desktop interpret viewports, color themes, and navigation stack updates in radically different ways.

1. Viewport Height Truncation on iOS

Standard CSS rules like height: 100vh break inside iOS Telegram WebViews. iOS WebViews calculate 100vh based on the full screen size including obscured areas behind native top bars and bottom gesture controls. This causes the bottom portion of your Next.js application—often the cart action area—to render below the visible fold.

Telegram provides window.Telegram.WebApp.viewportStableHeight and CSS variables injected directly into the document root. Set up your layout using dynamic CSS custom properties rather than hardcoded 100vh rules.

2. BackButton Routing Synchronization

Next.js App Router relies on next/navigation to manage client routing. However, Telegram native apps expect the top-left BackButton to open and close depending on view depth. If the user navigates from the product catalog into a detail page, your React code must explicitly call Telegram.WebApp.BackButton.show() and register a click listener that calls router.back().

3. Desktop Theme Mismatches

Telegram Desktop allows users to set custom light, dark, and high-contrast themes. If your application relies exclusively on standard Tailwind dark modes or prefers-color-scheme, the Mini App interface will clash with Telegram's surrounding window chrome. Telegram passes current color tokens through window.Telegram.WebApp.themeParams.

Here is a dedicated Client Component setup that resolves viewport height calculations, binds BackButton to Next.js navigation, and syncs color themes:

// components/TelegramInitializer.tsx
'use client';

import { useEffect } from 'react';
import { useRouter, usePathname } from 'next/navigation';

declare global {
  interface Window {
    Telegram?: {
      WebApp?: any;
    };
  }
}

export default function TelegramInitializer() {
  const router = useRouter();
  const pathname = usePathname();

  useEffect(() => {
    const tg = window.Telegram?.WebApp;
    if (!tg) return;

    // Tell Telegram client the Mini App is initialized
    tg.ready();
    tg.expand();

    // Fix iOS viewport height bug using native dynamic viewport variables
    const updateViewport = () => {
      if (tg.viewportStableHeight) {
        document.documentElement.style.setProperty(
          '--tg-viewport-height',
          `${tg.viewportStableHeight}px`
        );
      }
    };

    tg.onEvent('viewportChanged', updateViewport);
    updateViewport();

    return () => {
      tg.offEvent('viewportChanged', updateViewport);
    };
  }, []);

  // Handle Telegram native BackButton sync with Next.js router
  useEffect(() => {
    const tg = window.Telegram?.WebApp;
    if (!tg || !tg.BackButton) return;

    if (pathname !== '/') {
      tg.BackButton.show();
      const handleBack = () => {
        router.back();
      };
      tg.BackButton.onClick(handleBack);

      return () => {
        tg.BackButton.offClick(handleBack);
      };
    } else {
      tg.BackButton.hide();
    }
  }, [pathname, router]);

  return null;
}

In your root layout (app/layout.tsx), apply the dynamic CSS variable to your master wrapper container to protect against layout clipping on iOS devices:

// app/layout.tsx
import TelegramInitializer from '@/components/TelegramInitializer';
import Script from 'next/script';
import './globals.css';

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <head>
        <Script
          src="https://telegram.org/js/telegram-web-app.js"
          strategy="beforeInteractive"
        />
      </head>
      <body
        className="bg-[var(--tg-theme-bg-color,#fff)] text-[var(--tg-theme-text-color,#000)]"
        style={{ minHeight: 'var(--tg-viewport-height, 100vh)' }}
      >
        <TelegramInitializer />
        {children}
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}

Server Verification of Telegram Invoice Webhooks

After a user completes payment inside the Telegram payment UI via openInvoice, Telegram sends asynchronous webhooks (pre_checkout_query and successful_payment) to your bot backend to confirm settlement. Never fulfill physical goods or mark orders as paid solely based on the front-end openInvoice status callback, as network disconnections or client-side tampering can spoof front-end callbacks.

Your bot's webhook endpoint must handle pre_checkout_query updates by verifying stock availability and responding to Telegram within 10 seconds. When Telegram confirms payment capture, it posts a successful_payment update containing the payment charge ID.

Secure your Next.js webhook Route Handler using the X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token header to guarantee that incoming updates originate from Telegram's servers:

// app/api/webhook/route.ts
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server';

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  const secretToken = request.headers.get('x-telegram-bot-api-secret-token');
  if (secretToken !== process.env.TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET) {
    return NextResponse.json({ error: 'Unauthorized webhook request' }, { status: 401 });
  }

  const update = await request.json();
  const botToken = process.env.TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN;

  // Step 1: Approve or decline pre-checkout query
  if (update.pre_checkout_query) {
    const queryId = update.pre_checkout_query.id;
    const payload = JSON.parse(update.pre_checkout_query.payload);

    // Check database to ensure inventory exists for payload.userId
    const isItemInStock = true;

    await fetch(`https://api.telegram.org/bot${botToken}/answerPreCheckoutQuery`, {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        pre_checkout_query_id: queryId,
        ok: isItemInStock,
        error_message: isItemInStock ? undefined : 'Item went out of stock.',
      }),
    });

    return NextResponse.json({ ok: true });
  }

  // Step 2: Confirm final payment success
  if (update.message?.successful_payment) {
    const payment = update.message.successful_payment;
    const payload = JSON.parse(payment.invoice_payload);
    const telegramPaymentChargeId = payment.telegram_payment_charge_id;

    // Mark order as paid in database using idempotency on telegramPaymentChargeId
    console.log(`Order completed for user ${payload.userId}. Charge ID: ${telegramPaymentChargeId}`);

    return NextResponse.json({ ok: true });
  }

  return NextResponse.json({ ok: true });
}

Rejecting untrusted secret tokens, calculating invoice pricing strictly on Next.js server handlers, and synchronizing MainButton and BackButton events inside React guarantees your store runs securely across iOS, Android, and Desktop Telegram WebViews.

title: Auto-Open Swagger UI on Spring Boot Startup (Linux, Windows & macOS)
description:
Every time I restart my Spring Boot service during development, I repeat the same ritual:

  1. Wait for startup to finish.
  2. Scroll the console to find the Swagger URL.
  3. Copy it.
  4. Paste it into the browser.

A hundred times a day. So I automated it.

In this post I'll show a small CommandLineRunner bean that auto-opens Swagger UI in your default browser, works identically on Linux, Windows, and macOS, and fails gracefully on headless servers (Docker, CI, remote VMs).

The whole thing is ~60 lines of pure JDK code. No extra dependencies.

What it does

  • Detects the OS at runtime via System.getProperty("os.name")
  • Uses xdg-open on Linux, open on macOS, and cmd /c start on Windows
  • Falls back to java.awt.Desktop#browse if the CLI tool is missing
  • Silently skips on headless machines (no crashes)
  • Toggleable via application.yml — set openProject.isOpen: false in prod
  • Prints a clickable link in the console for good measure

1. Configuration

Add a small block to application.yml:

openProject:
  isOpen: true
  web:
    openUrl: "http://localhost:8080/swagger-ui/index.html"

2. The BrowserLauncher bean 

package com.gama.swagger.config;

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

import java.awt.Desktop;
import java.net.URI;
import java.util.Locale;

@Component
public class BrowserLauncher implements CommandLineRunner {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(BrowserLauncher.class);

    @Value("${openProject.isOpen:true}")
    private boolean isOpen;

    @Value("${openProject.web.openUrl}")
    private String openUrl;

    @Override
    public void run(String... args) {
        if (!isOpen) {
            log.info("Auto-open browser disabled (openProject.isOpen=false).");
            return;
        }

        String os = System.getProperty("os.name", "").toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);
        log.info("Detected OS: {}", os);

        try {
            if (os.contains("win")) {
                // Windows: cmd /c start "" <url>  (the empty "" is the window title)
                Runtime.getRuntime().exec(new String[]{"cmd", "/c", "start", "", openUrl});
            } else if (os.contains("mac")) {
                Runtime.getRuntime().exec(new String[]{"open", openUrl});
            } else if (os.contains("nux") || os.contains("nix") || os.contains("aix")) {
                if (isCommandAvailable("xdg-open")) {
                    Runtime.getRuntime().exec(new String[]{"xdg-open", openUrl});
                } else {
                    log.warn("xdg-open not found. Install it: sudo apt install xdg-utils");
                    fallbackDesktopBrowse();
                }
            } else {
                log.warn("Unrecognized OS '{}' — trying Desktop.browse fallback", os);
                fallbackDesktopBrowse();
            }
            log.info("Attempted to open browser: {}", openUrl);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            log.warn("Could not auto-open browser: {}", e.getMessage());
        }
    }

    /** Last-resort attempt using the Java Desktop API (works when a GUI is present). */
    private void fallbackDesktopBrowse() {
        try {
            if (Desktop.isDesktopSupported()
                    && Desktop.getDesktop().isSupported(Desktop.Action.BROWSE)) {
                Desktop.getDesktop().browse(new URI(openUrl));
                log.info("Opened via Desktop.browse fallback.");
            } else {
                log.warn("No GUI available — please open manually: {}", openUrl);
            }
        } catch (Exception ex) {
            log.warn("Desktop.browse fallback failed: {}", ex.getMessage());
        }
    }

    private boolean isCommandAvailable(String cmd) {
        try {
            Process p = new ProcessBuilder("which", cmd)
                    .redirectErrorStream(true)
                    .start();
            return p.waitFor() == 0;
        } catch (Exception e) {
            return false;
        }
    }
}

3. Print a clickable link in the console

Most modern terminals (GNOME Terminal, Konsole, iTerm2, Windows Terminal, IntelliJ's console, VS Code's terminal) auto-detect URLs. Just log the full URL from main:

@SpringBootApplication
public class SwaggerApplication {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(SwaggerApplication.class);

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var context = SpringApplication.run(SwaggerApplication.class, args);

        String port = context.getEnvironment().getProperty("server.port", "8080");
        String ctx  = context.getEnvironment().getProperty("server.servlet.context-path", "");

        log.info("Swagger UI: http://localhost:{}{}/swagger-ui/index.html", port, ctx);
    }
}

title: No Threads, Still Races: Two awaits Can Corrupt State a Java Lock Would Have Guarded
description:
• Book: Kotlin and Java to TypeScript
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

An account holds 100. Two requests arrive at the same moment, each asking to withdraw 80. Your TypeScript service approves both, pays out 160, and records a final balance of 20.

If you came from a JVM codebase, you would have wrapped that method in synchronized without thinking. Then someone told you Node runs your JavaScript on a single thread, and the lock instinct went quiet. The single thread is real. The safety you inferred from it is not, and the gap sits at every await in your code.

Where "single-threaded" stops protecting you

The Node.js docs say it plainly: the event loop gives Node non-blocking I/O "despite the fact that a single JavaScript thread is used by default". That thread runs one job at a time, and MDN's execution model page spells out what you get from it: "whenever a function runs, it cannot be preempted and will run entirely before any other code runs."

The catch is what counts as one run. An async function does not run in one piece. MDN's await reference describes what happens at each await: "Control exits the function and returns to the caller. When the awaited expression's value is resolved, another microtask that continues the paused code gets scheduled."

So an async function with two awaits is three jobs, and any other job can run between them. The same page adds the detail that catches people: "Even when the used promise is already fulfilled, the async function's execution still pauses until the next tick." Awaiting a cached value, or await null, still hands the thread to whoever is queued next.


One thread, many turns: every await is a door another task can walk through.

Reproduce it: two withdrawals, one balance

Save this as race.ts. Node 22.18+ and 23.6+ strip types by default, so node race.ts runs it; on older versions use tsx: npx tsx race.ts.

let balance = 100;

const sleep = (ms: number) =>
  new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function withdraw(id: string, amount: number) {
  const current = balance; // check...
  if (current < amount) {
    console.log(`${id}: declined`);
    return;
  }
  await sleep(10); // fraud check, DB call, anything
  balance = current - amount; // ...then act
  console.log(`${id}: approved, balance ${balance}`);
}

async function main() {
  await Promise.all([withdraw("A", 80), withdraw("B", 80)]);
  console.log(`final balance ${balance}`);
}

main();

Trace it by hand. withdraw("A", 80) runs synchronously until its await: it reads 100, passes the check, starts a 10 ms timer and returns a pending promise. withdraw("B", 80) runs next, before A resumes, because A is parked on that timer. B also reads 100 and passes. When the timers fire, A writes 100 - 80 and B writes its own stale current minus 80. Both log "approved", both write 20, and main reports a final balance of 20.

That is two bugs in one function. The check-then-act lets both requests through, and the read-modify-write turns two debits into one. Swap sleep(10) for await Promise.resolve() and the trace does not change, because the continuation still goes through the microtask queue.

What synchronized would have done

Here is the same method in Java, guarded the way a JVM developer guards it by reflex:

class Account {
  private long balance = 100;

  synchronized boolean withdraw(long amount)
      throws InterruptedException {
    long current = balance;
    if (current < amount) return false;
    Thread.sleep(10); // the same fraud check
    balance = current - amount;
    return true;
  }
}

Oracle's tutorial on intrinsic locks gives the rule: "As long as a thread owns an intrinsic lock, no other thread can acquire the same lock. The other thread will block when it attempts to acquire the lock." The sleep does not loosen that, since per the Thread.sleep Javadoc "the thread does not lose ownership of any monitors." Thread B waits at the method entry, reads 20 after A returns, and gets false. A ReentrantLock with the documented lock(); try { ... } finally { unlock(); } idiom gives you the same outcome.

The reason this works in Java is that the thread itself waits, holding the lock while it waits. In TypeScript nothing waits. The await gives the only thread away, so a lock has to be something that outlives the await: a promise the next caller is forced to wait on.

Two notes for the JVM side. First, Java's own async code has the same hole: a synchronized method releases its lock "when the method returns", per the same tutorial, so one that returns a CompletableFuture is unlocked before the future completes. Second, TypeScript has an advantage here. In Java, a thread can be preempted between any two statements. In JavaScript, only the awaits are interleaving points, so you can find every one of them by reading the function.

Same race, cache edition

The pattern shows up anywhere you read shared state, await, then write it. A lazy cache fill is the usual one (loadUser is your database call):

const cache = new Map<string, User>();

async function getUser(id: string): Promise<User> {
  const hit = cache.get(id);
  if (hit) return hit;
  const user = await loadUser(id); // every miss lands here
  cache.set(id, user);
  return user;
}

Fifty concurrent requests for a cold key all miss before the first load returns, so you get fifty database queries instead of one. The quieter bug is the stale write. Request one misses and starts loading the old row. An update lands, writes the database and calls cache.delete(id). Then request one's load resolves and cache.set puts the old row back, where it stays until the next invalidation.

Four fixes that fit TypeScript

1. Keep the critical section free of awaits. Do the slow part first, then check and write in one synchronous block. Run-to-completion guarantees nothing interleaves inside it.

async function withdraw(id: string, amount: number) {
  await sleep(10); // slow part first
  if (balance < amount) return false;
  balance -= amount; // check and write, no await between
  return true;
}

Both calls finish their sleep, then A takes the balance to 20 and B sees 20 and declines. The rule to carry around: read shared state after your last await, and write it before your next one.

2. A promise-chain mutex, about 15 lines. When the await has to sit inside the critical section, make each caller wait on the promise of the caller before it.

class Mutex {
  #tail: Promise<void> = Promise.resolve();

  async run<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
    const prev = this.#tail;
    let release = () => {};
    this.#tail = new Promise<void>((resolve) => {
      release = () => resolve();
    });
    await prev;
    try {
      return await fn();
    } finally {
      release();
    }
  }
}

const lock = new Mutex();
const withdrawSafe = (id: string, amount: number) =>
  lock.run(() => withdraw(id, amount));

Wrap the racy withdraw from race.ts and A runs to the end while B waits on A's promise, then B reads 20 and declines. The finally releases the lock even when fn throws, the same job finally { unlock(); } does in Java.

Two differences from ReentrantLock matter. This mutex is not reentrant: calling lock.run from inside a function already holding lock waits on itself forever. And there is no timeout. If you want timeouts and semaphores, async-mutex ships them, and its README makes the same point this post does: JavaScript is single-threaded, but its async execution model "allows for race conditions." For per-account locking, keep a Map<string, Mutex> keyed by account id.


A promise-chain mutex: each caller holds the next one's key until it finishes.

3. Single-flight for cache fills. Cache the in-flight promise, not only the finished value, so concurrent misses share one load. Go developers know this as singleflight, "a duplicate function call suppression mechanism."

type User = { id: string; name: string };
declare function loadUser(id: string): Promise<User>;

const cache = new Map<string, User>();
const inflight = new Map<string, Promise<User>>();

function getUser(id: string): Promise<User> {
  const hit = cache.get(id);
  if (hit) return Promise.resolve(hit);
  const running = inflight.get(id);
  if (running) return running;
  const p: Promise<User> = loadUser(id)
    .then((user) => {
      if (inflight.get(id) === p) cache.set(id, user);
      return user;
    })
    .finally(() => {
      if (inflight.get(id) === p) inflight.delete(id);
    });
  inflight.set(id, p);
  return p;
}

function invalidate(id: string) {
  cache.delete(id);
  inflight.delete(id); // a late fill can no longer write back
}

getUser is not async on purpose: the cache lookup, the in-flight lookup and inflight.set all happen in one synchronous run, so no second caller can slip between them. The inflight.get(id) === p checks fix the stale write. Once invalidate drops the entry, the old load still resolves for whoever awaited it, but it no longer writes to the cache. Failed loads are not cached, because finally clears the entry either way.

4. A database row lock when the state lives outside the process. Everything above guards one Node process. Run three replicas and each has its own Mutex, so the balance needs a lock where it lives. In Postgres, the shortest version is a conditional update:

import pg from "pg";

const pool = new pg.Pool();

async function withdrawDb(id: string, amount: number) {
  const { rowCount } = await pool.query(
    `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - $1
     WHERE id = $2 AND balance >= $1`,
    [amount, id],
  );
  return rowCount === 1;
}

Under Read Committed, Postgres's default, a second concurrent update on the same row waits for the first to commit, then "the search condition of the command (the WHERE clause) is re-evaluated to see if the updated version of the row still matches." The second withdrawal sees 20, fails balance >= 80, and rowCount comes back 0.

When the decision needs application logic between the read and the write, take the lock explicitly with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside a transaction. The Postgres docs say it blocks other transactions' UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT FOR UPDATE on those rows "until the current transaction ends."

async function withdrawLocked(id: string, amount: number) {
  const client = await pool.connect();
  try {
    await client.query("BEGIN");
    const { rows } = await client.query(
      "SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE",
      [id],
    );
    const balance = Number(rows[0].balance);
    if (balance < amount) {
      await client.query("ROLLBACK");
      return false;
    }
    await fraudCheck(id, amount); // awaits are safe here
    await client.query(
      "UPDATE accounts SET balance = $1 WHERE id = $2",
      [balance - amount, id],
    );
    await client.query("COMMIT");
    return true;
  } catch (err) {
    await client.query("ROLLBACK");
    throw err;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
}

node-postgres is explicit that you "must use the same client instance for all statements within a transaction", which is why this checks out one client instead of calling pool.query. Here fraudCheck stands in for your own slow step. This is the closest thing TypeScript has to the Java version: the lock survives the await because it lives in the database, and the database does not care what your thread is doing. Keep that window short, since every other withdrawal on the row queues behind it.

If this was useful

Moving from the JVM to TypeScript, the syntax comes quickly. The habits take longer: some quietly stop applying, like reaching for a lock, and some still apply in a new shape. Kotlin and Java to TypeScript is written for that move, including the jump from coroutines and threads to async/await.

If you are coming from Java or Kotlin, start with Kotlin and Java to TypeScript and pick up The TypeScript Type System when the types get interesting. If you already write TypeScript daily, TypeScript Essentials and The TypeScript Type System are the core path, and TypeScript in Production is for anyone shipping it at work.

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

title: A Vibe Coding Workflow That Ships: Plan, Code, Test, Deploy
description:
You've used an AI coding assistant a few times. Sometimes you got something great; sometimes you got something terrible; and you're not sure which to expect next. The difference is rarely the model. It's the workflow around it.

Let's get the honest version out of the way: AI won't turn you into a 10x engineer. It makes typing about 10x faster and thinking maybe 1.2x faster. Most of this job is thinking, so the gain is smaller than the demos promise, but it's real. The actual shift is that you spend less time producing code and more time specifying and verifying it.

The loop: plan, code, test, deploy, with a verify after each

This isn't a new lifecycle. It's the four stages you already know, with an assistant plugged into each, plus one step that matters more than anything else: verify after every stage.

Skip it and errors compound forward. A made-up requirement in planning becomes a wrong function, then a test that certifies the wrong function is correct, and now it's in production. Catching it in planning costs a minute. Catching it after release costs an afternoon.

The other thing that decides whether this works is how much you ask for at once. Ask for "a user management system" and you'll get 800 lines you'll skim and merge without understanding. Ask for "the POST /users handler, validation only, no database calls yet" and you get 40 lines you can read properly in two minutes.

If you can't verify the output in five minutes, you asked for too much.

Context is the whole game

Your assistant isn't stupid; it's working blind. It can't see your repo conventions, your team's decisions or your production constraints. Almost everything it gets wrong for apparently silly reasons traces back to something you knew and it didn't.

  • Write the project rules file once. Most AI coding tools read one from the repo root: stack, conventions, and things not to do. Ten minutes writing it saves correcting the same three mistakes forty times.
  • Paste the real thing. The actual schema, real sample data, the exact error message, not a paraphrase from memory.
  • Say "follow the patterns in this file". Paste an existing file from your codebase. A real file is unambiguous where a prose style guide is vague, and this one habit kills most convention drift.

Plan: ask for questions before you ask for a plan

Planning doesn't feel like progress, which is why engineers skip it. It's also the stage that pays best. Don't ask for a plan; ask to be interrogated:

I need to add recurring expenses to our tracker. Before proposing
anything, ask me the 7 questions that most affect the design. Number them.

You'll get questions like: what happens to future instances when someone deletes the series? What does a monthly rule starting on the 31st do in February? Some you'd have thought of. Some you'd have discovered three days later with the feature half-built.

Then harvest edge cases, grouped by data model, calendar and timezone, user actions and failure recovery, and triage them yourself into now, later and not doing. That triage is your spec. Ask for trade-offs, never for the answer: you know your team and your deadline, and the model doesn't.

On a CSV export feature, this step surfaced CSV injection: a user names an expense =HYPERLINK("http://evil.com","click"), a colleague opens the export in Excel, and it's a live formula. One prompt, forty seconds, and a vulnerability that never shipped.

Code: small batches, and read before you run

Match the mode to the task. Autocomplete is for the line you were already going to write. Chat is for self-contained units such as one function or one migration. Agents are for mechanical sweeps with a clear finish line, like a rename everywhere. The more judgement a task needs, the smaller the batch should be.

Work skeleton first: types, signatures and file layout before any function bodies. Then implement one unit at a time: implement, read, run, and commit at every green point. Scan every block that comes back with four questions:

  1. Does it do what I asked, not what it decided would be nicer?
  2. What did it invent? Check that every import and method actually exists.
  3. Where does it break? Empty, null, zero, negative, enormous, concurrent.
  4. Can I explain every line? If not, learn it or delete it.

And follow the two-strikes rule. If the second attempt at the same fix didn't work, the third won't either. The model has locked onto a wrong mental model, so reset with a fresh framing or write it yourself.

Test: from the spec, never from the code

This is where AI helps most and hurts most. The mistake almost everyone makes once: pointing it at finished code and saying "write tests for this". It reads your implementation and writes tests asserting that your code does exactly what it currently does, bugs included. You now own a suite that locks your bug in place, plus a green CI badge.

The fix is one sentence: generate tests from the rules, and keep the implementation off-limits.

Write tests for calculateRefund. Here are the business rules — do not
look at my implementation.
- Full refund if cancelled more than 7 days before the event
- 50% between 7 days and 24 hours
- Nothing within 24 hours
- The 2% processing fee is never refunded
- Refunding an already-refunded booking throws AlreadyRefundedError
Include boundary cases at exactly 7 days and exactly 24 hours,
with hardcoded expected values.

"Hardcoded expected values" matters more than it looks. If a test computes the expected number with the same formula as your code, it's running your bug twice and checking the results match.

Before you trust a suite, sabotage it: flip a comparison operator on purpose. If nothing goes red, your tests are decoration. And read the assertions: expect(save).toHaveBeenCalled() tells you far less than expect(saved.amount).toBe(4750).

Deploy: self-review first, and say what to skip

Run the AI over your diff before you ask a human, and tell it what to ignore:

Review this diff as a senior engineer on this codebase. Focus on unhandled
error paths, race conditions, N+1 queries and missing validation. Cite line
numbers. Skip style nits — the linter handles those.

Leave out the last line and you'll get twelve comments about variable names and nothing about the transaction you forgot to roll back. The AI is good at null paths, off-by-one errors and unclosed resources. It's blind to whether the feature is a good idea, which is why humans stay in the loop.

PR descriptions and changelogs are free money. In incidents, ask for ranked hypotheses plus a command that would confirm or rule out the top one, rather than an answer. And scrub emails, tokens and account IDs from logs before pasting them anywhere.

title: that lovable + supabase research is wild (and what a free outside check can actually see)
description:
ok so people are freaking out about the crissy field lovable writeup and… yeah. the numbers are rough.

they looked at 159,041 lovable projects. 34,545 used supabase. 24,664 of the ones they dug into were already shipping database records on first page load with no login. that alone is not automatically a bug — some of that data is meant to be public. they then made additional read-only requests with the same public key and found emails in 10,560 tables across 7,403 of those sites, plus examples that go past contact forms (passports, chat messages, tickets).

full piece, including their limitations section: https://www.crissyfield.de/research/lovable-en/

two caveats from their writeup that more people should repeat:

  1. “data on first paint” ≠ “confirmed leak.”
  2. the ~30% figure is not a confirmed leak rate for all lovable apps. it only applies to the 24,664 sites they examined more closely, the sample came from common crawl, and they only pulled parts of each dataset.

what i keep telling people building with lovable / cursor / bolt / v0: the scary part usually isn’t “i leaked the supabase anon key.” that key is supposed to be in the browser. the scary part is missing or wide-open row level security. a public anon key is not a secret. a service_role key in client code is.

what an outside check can (and can’t) see

i built hackorbroke.com for that launch moment. one polite, read-only pass against a live url you own.

from the outside it fetches your homepage and a few same-site scripts; looks for supabase urls + anon / service_role tokens in browser-visible code; treats service_role in client code as a hard fail; treats a normal anon key as “expected, but go verify RLS” — because it does not query your tables; and checks boring stuff people skip (.env, .git/config, robots/sitemap, headers, http→https, obvious ai spend traps).

drop a public github repo in and it also does a static code read: migrations that never enable rls, write policies open to everyone, supabase functions with verify_jwt = false next to the service role, server routes that call paid ai apis with no sign-in / rate limit. still no live db reads, no password guessing, no exploit testing.

that’s the honest limit. crissy field went further than a pre-launch checker should. an outside scan is the “did i leave the door labeled?” check — not a pentest, not a guarantee, and not a claim that every unauthenticated route is a bug. some public endpoints are intentional.

what to do this week if you shipped a lovable + supabase app

  1. open supabase → table editor. every table with personal data needs rls on, with policies that match how users sign in.
  2. rotate anything that was ever a service_role in the client.
  3. assume “data on first paint” is public unless you can explain why it shouldn’t be.
  4. run a free outside scan anyway. it’s free, redacts secrets, and gives a fix prompt you can paste back into lovable / cursor.

i’m not dunking on lovable. the gap is the same one every weekend app has: auth and access rules are easy to forget when the ui looks done.

short version: public anon key ≠ safe database. rls is the product.

soft ask: paste your preview or prod url into https://hackorbroke.com, check the box that you own it, and run the free scan before real users land. if something’s loud, fix that first. if it’s quiet, still stare at the rls toggles.

title: Sensitive Data Discovery in Python: Build a PII Scanner That Validates, Not Just Matches
description:
Before you can encrypt, mask, or delete personal data, you need to know where it lives. That sounds obvious until someone asks “which of our 400 tables hold card numbers?” and the honest answer is a shrug. GDPR Article 30 expects a controller to keep a record of processing that describes “the categories of personal data”, and you cannot write that record from memory.

That is the job of sensitive data discovery: scan the stores you own, find columns that hold PII, and label them. The usual first attempt is a folder of regexes. It finds everything, including order numbers, timestamps, ZIP+4 codes and SKUs, and after a week nobody reads its report.

In this post we build a small scanner in Python that does the boring parts properly:

  1. Walks a SQLite database and a folder of CSV exports.

  2. Samples each column with reservoir sampling (bounded memory, reproducible).

  3. Finds candidates with regexes, then validates them: Luhn and network prefixes for cards, ISO 7064 mod-97 for IBANs, SSA rules for SSNs, libphonenumber for phones.

  4. Uses the column name as a second signal and computes a confidence score per column.

  5. Writes a data inventory in JSON and Markdown with classification labels and masked examples.

  6. Compares the result with Microsoft Presidio on the same samples.

Versions: Python 3.13, Faker 40.44.0, phonenumbers 9.0.42, pytest 9.2.0, and for the comparison presidio-analyzer 2.2.366 with spaCy 3.8.18 and en_core_web_sm 3.8.0. All test data is synthetic (seeded Faker), and every output block below is copied from a real run.

What a column-level scanner needs

Discovery for analytics, as the PixelPlex guide describes it, is about finding patterns and insights in data. Discovery for privacy asks a narrower question about each column: “does this hold a data type that law, contracts or policy say we must protect?” Answering it per column, not per value, is the key design decision. A single cell can look like anything. Two hundred cells from the same column rarely lie.

Stage What it does Why it matters
Walk List tables/files and columns Coverage: you only classify what you enumerate
Sample Up to 200 non-empty values per column Bounded cost per column, no full-table scans
Detect Cheap regex finds candidates Fast, high recall
Validate Checksums and numbering rules Removes look-alikes
Score Hit ratio + column-name signal A column decision, not a cell decision
Report Labels, confidence, masked examples Something a human can review and act on

Step 1. Synthetic data with traps

make_data.py builds shop.db with three tables and two CSV exports. Real PII is mixed with values that a lazy regex will misread:

Column Real content Looks like
orders.order_number 16 random digits a card number
app_events.device_serial 16 random digits a card number
orders.sku US48XKQ93821PZ7A style codes an IBAN
payments.batch_ref 000-, 666-, 9xx- codes an SSN
customers.created_at, zip, app_events.app_version dates, ZIP+4, versions phone numbers
orders.card_masked **** **** **** 1234 a card column by name only
customers.notes free text, some with an email or phone mostly harmless text
leads.contact half emails, half phones two entity types in one column

Listing: make_data.py (full) 
"""Generate a synthetic SQLite database and CSV exports for the scanner demo.

Every value comes from Faker (seeded) or random.Random (seeded). No real PII.
"""
import csv
import random
import sqlite3
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

from faker import Faker

SEED = 42
# Fixed ranges: relative ones like "-30d" would change the data every day.
START, END = datetime(2024, 1, 1), datetime(2026, 1, 1)
DATA = Path(__file__).parent / "data"


def digits(rng: random.Random, n: int) -> str:
    return "".join(rng.choice("0123456789") for _ in range(n))


def main() -> None:
    fake = Faker("en_US")
    Faker.seed(SEED)
    rng = random.Random(SEED)
    DATA.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    (DATA / "exports").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    db_path = DATA / "shop.db"
    db_path.unlink(missing_ok=True)

    con = sqlite3.connect(db_path)
    con.executescript(
        """
        CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, full_name TEXT, email TEXT,
            phone TEXT, ssn TEXT, zip TEXT, created_at TEXT, notes TEXT);
        CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_number TEXT, customer_id INTEGER,
            amount REAL, sku TEXT, card_masked TEXT, placed_at TEXT);
        CREATE TABLE payments (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, card_number TEXT,
            iban TEXT, batch_ref TEXT, company_code TEXT);
        """
    )

    customers = []
    for i in range(1, 401):
        note = fake.sentence(nb_words=10)
        roll = rng.random()
        if roll < 0.08:
            note += f" Prefers email: {fake.free_email()}"
        elif roll < 0.16:
            note += f" Call back on {fake.phone_number()}"
        customers.append((i, fake.name(), fake.email(), fake.phone_number(), fake.ssn(),
                          fake.zipcode_plus4(), fake.date_between(START, END).isoformat(), note))
    con.executemany("INSERT INTO customers VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?)", customers)

    orders = []
    for i in range(1, 1201):
        sku = (rng.choice(["US", "DE", "FR", "GB"]) + digits(rng, 2)
               + "".join(rng.choice("ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789") for _ in range(12)))
        orders.append((i, digits(rng, 16), rng.randint(1, 400), round(rng.uniform(5, 900), 2),
                       sku, "**** **** **** " + digits(rng, 4),
                       fake.date_time_between(START, END).isoformat(timespec="seconds")))
    con.executemany("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?)", orders)

    payments = []
    for i in range(1, 401):
        batch_ref = f"{rng.choice(['000', '666', str(rng.randint(900, 999))])}-{digits(rng, 2)}-{digits(rng, 4)}"
        payments.append((i, rng.randint(1, 400), fake.credit_card_number(), fake.iban(),
                         batch_ref, "CP-" + digits(rng, 6)))
    con.executemany("INSERT INTO payments VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?)", payments)
    con.commit()
    con.close()

    with open(DATA / "exports" / "leads.csv", "w", newline="") as fh:
        w = csv.writer(fh)
        w.writerow(["lead_id", "name", "contact", "company", "bank_acct"])
        for i in range(1, 301):
            contact = fake.company_email() if rng.random() < 0.5 else fake.phone_number()
            w.writerow([i, fake.name(), contact, fake.company(), fake.iban()])

    with open(DATA / "exports" / "app_events.csv", "w", newline="") as fh:
        w = csv.writer(fh)
        w.writerow(["event_id", "device_serial", "app_version", "event", "ts"])
        for i in range(1, 601):
            w.writerow([fake.uuid4(), digits(rng, 16),
                        f"{rng.randint(1, 12)}.{rng.randint(0, 9)}.{rng.randint(0, 99)}.{rng.randint(1000, 9999)}",
                        rng.choice(["open", "tap", "purchase", "close"]),
                        fake.date_time_between(datetime(2025, 12, 1), END).isoformat(timespec="seconds")])

    print(f"wrote {db_path.relative_to(DATA.parent)}: customers=400 orders=1200 payments=400")
    print("wrote data/exports/leads.csv (300 rows), data/exports/app_events.csv (600 rows)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Output:
# wrote data/shop.db: customers=400 orders=1200 payments=400
# wrote data/exports/leads.csv (300 rows), data/exports/app_events.csv (600 rows)

Faker is seeded, but its docs warn that results are not guaranteed to be stable across patch versions, so the version is pinned to the patch level in requirements.txt.

Step 2. The “before”: regex only

The scanner has a --naive flag that keeps the regexes and turns off validators and the name signal. This is what many homegrown PII detection scripts look like:

python -m pii_scan --db data/shop.db --csv data/exports --naive

[naive] columns=31 findings=31 confirmed=23 review=8
  app_events.event_id        CREDIT_CARD  review    conf=0.01 valid=1% regex=1%
  app_events.device_serial   CREDIT_CARD  confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  app_events.device_serial   PHONE        confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  app_events.app_version     PHONE        confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  app_events.ts              PHONE        confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  leads.contact              CREDIT_CARD  review    conf=0.01 valid=0% regex=0%
  leads.contact              EMAIL        confirmed conf=0.53 valid=53% regex=53%
  leads.contact              PHONE        review    conf=0.47 valid=47% regex=47%
  leads.bank_acct            IBAN         confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  leads.bank_acct            PHONE        confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  customers.email            EMAIL        confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  customers.phone            CREDIT_CARD  review    conf=0.05 valid=5% regex=5%
  customers.phone            PHONE        confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  customers.ssn              US_SSN       confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  customers.ssn              PHONE        confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  customers.zip              PHONE        confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  customers.created_at       PHONE        confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  customers.notes            CREDIT_CARD  review    conf=0.01 valid=0% regex=0%
  customers.notes            EMAIL        review    conf=0.09 valid=9% regex=9%
  customers.notes            PHONE        review    conf=0.07 valid=8% regex=8%
  orders.order_number        CREDIT_CARD  confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  orders.order_number        PHONE        confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  orders.sku                 IBAN         confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  orders.placed_at           PHONE        confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  payments.card_number       CREDIT_CARD  confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  payments.card_number       PHONE        confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  payments.iban              IBAN         confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  payments.iban              PHONE        confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  payments.batch_ref         US_SSN       confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%
  payments.batch_ref         PHONE        confirmed conf=1.00 valid=100% regex=100%

23 columns “confirmed”, and only 7 of them really hold PII. The phone regex fires on timestamps, ZIP+4 codes, app versions, SSNs, IBANs and card numbers. The card regex is certain that order numbers and device serials are payment cards. orders.sku is “100% IBAN”. A report like this gets ignored, and then the one real finding in it gets ignored too.

Step 3. Validators

Each detector is a pair: a regex that finds candidates and a function that rejects look-alikes. Here is the whole module:

"""PII detectors: a candidate regex plus a validator that rejects look-alikes."""
from __future__ import annotations

import re
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Callable
import phonenumbers

# ---------- validators ----------

def luhn_ok(number: str) -> bool:
    """Luhn mod-10 check over a string of digits."""
    total = 0
    for i, ch in enumerate(reversed(number)):
        d = int(ch)
        if i % 2 == 1:
            d *= 2
            if d > 9:
                d -= 9
        total += d
    return total % 10 == 0


def card_ok(raw: str) -> bool:
    num = re.sub(r"[ -]", "", raw)
    if not num.isdigit() or not 12 <= len(num) <= 19:   # Maestro goes down to 12 digits
        return False
    if len(set(num)) == 1:            # 0000000000000000 passes Luhn, it is not a card
        return False
    # Major networks start with 2-6; 1800/2131 are 15-digit JCB prefixes that Faker generates.
    if num[0] not in "23456" and not num.startswith(("1800", "2131")):
        return False
    return luhn_ok(num)


def iban_ok(raw: str) -> bool:
    s = raw.replace(" ", "").upper()
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[A-Z]{2}\d{2}[A-Z0-9]{11,30}", s):
        return False
    rearranged = s[4:] + s[:4]
    as_int = "".join(str(int(c, 36)) for c in rearranged)   # A=10 ... Z=35
    return int(as_int) % 97 == 1


SSN_BLOCKLIST = {"078-05-1120", "219-09-9999"}   # numbers the SSA lists as misused/advertising


def ssn_ok(raw: str) -> bool:
    m = re.fullmatch(r"(\d{3})-(\d{2})-(\d{4})", raw)
    if not m:
        return False
    area, group, serial = m.groups()
    if area in ("000", "666") or area.startswith("9"):
        return False
    if group == "00" or serial == "0000":
        return False
    return raw not in SSN_BLOCKLIST


def email_ok(raw: str) -> bool:
    local, _, domain = raw.rpartition("@")
    if not local or local.startswith(".") or local.endswith(".") or ".." in local:
        return False
    labels = domain.split(".")
    if len(labels) < 2 or not labels[-1].isalpha():
        return False
    return all(lbl and not lbl.startswith("-") and not lbl.endswith("-") for lbl in labels)


def phone_matches(text: str, region: str = "US",
                  leniency=phonenumbers.Leniency.VALID) -> list[str]:
    """libphonenumber's matcher instead of a regex. VALID = real ranges, POSSIBLE = right length."""
    return [m.raw_string for m in phonenumbers.PhoneNumberMatcher(text, region, leniency=leniency)]


def phone_weight(text: str) -> float:
    if phone_matches(text):
        return 1.0
    if phone_matches(text, leniency=phonenumbers.Leniency.POSSIBLE):
        return 0.5        # right length, but not in an assigned range: half credit
    return 0.0


# ---------- detector table ----------

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Detector:
    entity: str
    label: str                     # classification label for the inventory
    pattern: re.Pattern            # cheap candidate finder (the "naive" scanner uses only this)
    validate: Callable[[str], bool]
    name_hints: frozenset[str]     # column-name tokens that count as a signal


DETECTORS = [
    Detector("CREDIT_CARD", "Restricted",
             re.compile(r"\b(?:\d[ -]?){11,18}\d\b"), card_ok,
             frozenset({"card", "cc", "pan", "ccnum", "credit"})),
    Detector("US_SSN", "Restricted",
             re.compile(r"\b\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}\b"), ssn_ok,
             frozenset({"ssn", "social", "tin", "taxid"})),
    Detector("IBAN", "Restricted",
             re.compile(r"\b[A-Z]{2}\d{2}[A-Z0-9]{11,30}\b"), iban_ok,
             frozenset({"iban", "bank", "acct", "account"})),
    Detector("EMAIL", "Confidential",
             re.compile(r"[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}"), email_ok,
             frozenset({"email", "mail", "contact"})),
    Detector("PHONE", "Confidential",
             re.compile(r"\+?\d[\d\s().-]{7,}\d"), lambda s: phone_weight(s) > 0,
             frozenset({"phone", "mobile", "tel", "cell", "msisdn", "contact"})),
]


def name_tokens(column: str) -> set[str]:
    """'customerEmail' -> {'customer', 'email'}; 'cc_num' -> {'cc', 'num'}."""
    spaced = re.sub(r"([a-z0-9])([A-Z])", r"\1 \2", column)
    return {t for t in re.split(r"[^A-Za-z0-9]+", spaced.lower()) if t}


def value_hit(det: Detector, value: str, validate: bool) -> tuple[bool, float]:
    """Return (regex_hit, validated weight 0..1) for one cell value."""
    candidates = det.pattern.findall(value)
    if not candidates:
        return False, 0.0
    if not validate:
        return True, 1.0
    if det.entity == "PHONE":
        return True, phone_weight(value)
    return True, float(any(det.validate(c) for c in candidates))

What each validator buys you:

  • Cards. The Luhn check digit (ISO/IEC 7812-1) catches all single-digit typos, but a random number passes it one time in ten. That is what the test test_luhn_accepts_one_in_ten_random_numbers pins down. A network prefix check (first digit 2 to 6) halves the survivors again. Note the bounds: payment card numbers can be 8 to 19 digits, Maestro goes down to 12, and the Mastercard 2221–2720 range has been live since October 2016.
  • IBAN. Move the first four characters to the end, turn letters into numbers (A=10 … Z=35), and the result mod 97 must be 1. A random string passes about once in 97.
  • SSN. The SSA has not issued area numbers 000, 666 or 900–999, and no group of digits can be all zeros. Two famous sample numbers, 078-05-1120 from a 1938 wallet insert and 219-09-9999 from a 1940 pamphlet, go on a blocklist.
  • Phone. Instead of a regex, phonenumbers.PhoneNumberMatcher (a port of Google’s libphonenumber) scans the text. Its default leniency VALID accepts only numbers in assigned ranges. POSSIBLE only checks that the length is right, so it gets half credit.

Column names are split into tokens (customerEmail becomes customer, email) and compared as whole words.

explain_fp.py shows what each layer removes on the trap columns:

CREDIT_CARD: regex -> Luhn -> Luhn + network prefix
  orders.order_number        regex 200/200 (100%)  luhn  22/200 ( 11%)  +prefix  13/200 (  6%)
  app_events.device_serial   regex 200/200 (100%)  luhn  19/200 ( 10%)  +prefix  10/200 (  5%)
  payments.card_number       regex 200/200 (100%)  luhn 200/200 (100%)  +prefix 200/200 (100%)

IBAN: regex -> ISO 7064 mod-97
  orders.sku                 regex 200/200 (100%)  mod-97   0/200 (  0%)
  payments.iban              regex 200/200 (100%)  mod-97 200/200 (100%)

US_SSN: regex -> area/group/serial rules
  payments.batch_ref         regex 200/200 (100%)  rules   0/200 (  0%)
  customers.ssn              regex 200/200 (100%)  rules 200/200 (100%)

PHONE: regex -> libphonenumber VALID
  customers.created_at       regex 200/200 (100%)  valid   0/200 (  0%)
  customers.zip              regex 200/200 (100%)  valid   0/200 (  0%)
  app_events.app_version     regex 200/200 (100%)  valid   0/200 (  0%)
  orders.order_number        regex 200/200 (100%)  valid   0/200 (  0%)
  customers.phone            regex 200/200 (100%)  valid  86/200 ( 43%)

Look at orders.order_number. Even after Luhn and the prefix check, 13 of 200 order numbers are “valid card numbers”. That is not a bug in the validator, it is arithmetic: 10% pass Luhn by chance, and about half of those start with 2 to 6. No per-value rule can fix this. The fix is to decide at the column level.

Step 4. Walk and sample SQLite and CSV 

"""Walk data sources and yield a bounded, reproducible sample per column."""
from __future__ import annotations

import csv
import random
import sqlite3
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Iterable, Iterator


@dataclass
class ColumnSample:
    source: str       # "sqlite:shop.db" or "csv:exports/leads.csv"
    table: str
    column: str
    values: list[str]  # non-null, stringified
    rows_seen: int


def reservoir(values: Iterable, k: int, rng: random.Random) -> tuple[list[str], int]:
    """Algorithm R: uniform sample of k non-empty values in one pass, O(k) memory."""
    sample: list[str] = []
    n = 0
    for v in values:
        if v is None or str(v).strip() == "":
            continue
        n += 1
        if len(sample) < k:
            sample.append(str(v))
        else:
            j = rng.randrange(n)
            if j < k:
                sample[j] = str(v)
    return sample, n


def scan_sqlite(path: Path, k: int, seed: int) -> Iterator[ColumnSample]:
    con = sqlite3.connect(f"file:{path}?mode=ro", uri=True)   # read-only: a scanner never writes
    try:
        tables = [
            r[0]
            for r in con.execute(
                "SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table' AND name NOT LIKE 'sqlite_%' ORDER BY name"
            )
        ]
        for table in tables:
            cols = [r[1] for r in con.execute(f'PRAGMA table_info("{table}")')]
            for col in cols:
                rng = random.Random(f"{seed}:{table}:{col}")
                cur = con.execute(f'SELECT "{col}" FROM "{table}"')
                values, n = reservoir((r[0] for r in cur), k, rng)
                yield ColumnSample(f"sqlite:{path.name}", table, col, values, n)
    finally:
        con.close()


def scan_csv_dir(root: Path, k: int, seed: int) -> Iterator[ColumnSample]:
    for path in sorted(root.rglob("*.csv")):
        with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as fh:
            reader = csv.DictReader(fh)
            columns = reader.fieldnames or []
            rows = list(reader)          # fine for exports; stream per column for multi-GB files
        rel = path.relative_to(root.parent)
        for col in columns:
            rng = random.Random(f"{seed}:{rel}:{col}")
            values, n = reservoir((r.get(col) for r in rows), k, rng)
            yield ColumnSample(f"csv:{rel}", path.stem, col, values, n)

Three decisions here:

  • Read-only connection. file:...?mode=ro with uri=True makes SQLite open the database read-only. A scanner that runs against production copies should not be able to write, even by accident.
  • Reservoir sampling (Algorithm R). One pass, $k$ values in memory, every value has the same chance of being picked, and you do not need to know the row count first. LIMIT 200 would give you the oldest 200 rows, which on a table where a column was repurposed last year tells you nothing about today.
  • Per-column seeds. random.Random(f"{seed}:{table}:{col}") makes each run reproducible, so two scans of unchanged data produce identical inventories and diffs show only real changes.

Step 5. Score columns, not cells 

"""Score every (column, entity) pair and decide what goes into the inventory."""
from __future__ import annotations

import statistics
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass

from .detectors import DETECTORS, Detector, name_tokens, value_hit
from .sources import ColumnSample

CONFIRM_AT = 0.6     # confidence needed for status "confirmed"
REVIEW_AT = 0.2      # below this a finding is dropped (unless the column is free text)
MIN_TEXT_HITS = 3    # free-text columns: this many validated hits -> "review"


@dataclass
class Finding:
    source: str
    table: str
    column: str
    entity: str
    label: str
    status: str            # confirmed | review
    confidence: float
    hit_ratio: float       # validated hits / sampled values
    regex_ratio: float     # raw regex hits / sampled values (what a naive scanner sees)
    sampled: int
    rows_seen: int
    name_signal: bool
    free_text: bool
    examples: list[str]    # masked, never raw values


def is_free_text(values: list[str]) -> bool:
    if not values:
        return False
    return statistics.median(len(v) for v in values) > 30 and \
        sum(" " in v for v in values) / len(values) > 0.5


def mask(value: str) -> str:
    if "@" in value:
        local, _, domain = value.partition("@")
        return f"{local[:1]}***@{domain}"
    keep = 4 if len(value) > 8 else 2
    return "*" * (len(value) - keep) + value[-keep:]


def score(det: Detector, col: ColumnSample, validate: bool) -> Finding | None:
    n = len(col.values)
    if n == 0:
        return None
    regex_hits, valid_hits = 0, 0.0
    examples: list[str] = []
    for v in col.values:
        r, ok = value_hit(det, v, validate)
        regex_hits += r
        valid_hits += ok
        if ok and len(examples) < 2:
            examples.append(mask(v) if len(v) < 40 else mask(v[-24:]))
    name_signal = validate and bool(name_tokens(col.column) & det.name_hints)
    hit_ratio = valid_hits / n
    # 80% of the weight on what the data says, 20% on what the column is called.
    confidence = round(min(1.0, 0.8 * hit_ratio + 0.2 * name_signal), 2) if validate else round(hit_ratio, 2)
    free_text = is_free_text(col.values)
    if not validate:
        status = "confirmed" if hit_ratio >= 0.5 else ("review" if regex_hits else None)
    elif confidence >= CONFIRM_AT:
        status = "confirmed"
    elif confidence >= REVIEW_AT or (free_text and valid_hits >= MIN_TEXT_HITS):
        status = "review"
    else:
        status = None
    if status is None:
        return None
    return Finding(col.source, col.table, col.column, det.entity, det.label, status,
                   confidence, round(hit_ratio, 3), round(regex_hits / n, 3), n, col.rows_seen,
                   name_signal, free_text, examples)


def scan_columns(columns, validate: bool = True) -> list[Finding]:
    findings = []
    for col in columns:
        for det in DETECTORS:
            f = score(det, col, validate)
            if f:
                findings.append(f)
    return findings


def to_dicts(findings: list[Finding]) -> list[dict]:
    return [asdict(f) for f in findings]

The confidence formula is deliberately simple:

confidence = 0.8 * validated_hit_ratio + 0.2 * column_name_signal
  • 0.6 or more is confirmed, 0.2 to 0.6 is review, below that the finding is dropped.
  • A name alone gives 0.2, which lands in review. That is how orders.card_masked shows up: the name says card, the values are masked, and a person should confirm the masking is real.
  • A column where half the values are valid cards stays in review if it is called ref, and becomes confirmed if it is called cc_num. The test test_column_name_breaks_the_tie checks exactly this.
  • Free text is different. If the median value is longer than 30 characters and most values contain spaces, three or more validated hits are enough for review, because PII in notes is sparse by nature. Without the “free text” condition, the 13 Luhn-valid order numbers would have triggered this rule too.

Step 6. The inventory report 

"""CLI: python -m pii_scan --db data/shop.db --csv data/exports [--naive]"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import itertools
from pathlib import Path

from .report import build_inventory, to_json, to_markdown
from .scanner import scan_columns, to_dicts
from .sources import scan_csv_dir, scan_sqlite


def main() -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Sensitive data discovery for SQLite + CSV")
    ap.add_argument("--db", type=Path, action="append", default=[])
    ap.add_argument("--csv", type=Path, action="append", default=[])
    ap.add_argument("--sample", type=int, default=200, help="values sampled per column")
    ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=7)
    ap.add_argument("--naive", action="store_true", help="regex only: no validators, no name signal")
    ap.add_argument("--out", type=Path, default=Path("out"))
    args = ap.parse_args()

    columns = list(itertools.chain(
        *(scan_sqlite(p, args.sample, args.seed) for p in args.db),
        *(scan_csv_dir(p, args.sample, args.seed) for p in args.csv)))
    findings = to_dicts(scan_columns(columns, validate=not args.naive))
    mode = "naive" if args.naive else "validated"
    inv = build_inventory(findings, len(columns), mode)
    args.out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    (args.out / f"inventory_{mode}.json").write_text(to_json(inv))
    (args.out / f"inventory_{mode}.md").write_text(to_markdown(inv))

    print(f"[{mode}] columns={len(columns)} findings={inv['findings']} "
          f"confirmed={inv['confirmed']} review={inv['review']}")
    for t in inv["tables"]:
        for c in t["columns"]:
            print(f"  {t['table'] + '.' + c['column']:<26} {c['entity']:<12} {c['status']:<9} "
                  f"conf={c['confidence']:.2f} valid={c['hit_ratio']:.0%} regex={c['regex_ratio']:.0%}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Listing: pii_scan/report.py (full) 
"""Turn findings into a data inventory: JSON for machines, Markdown for humans."""
from __future__ import annotations

import json
from collections import defaultdict

LABEL_RANK = {"Public": 0, "Internal": 1, "Confidential": 2, "Restricted": 3}


def build_inventory(findings: list[dict], columns_scanned: int, mode: str) -> dict:
    tables: dict[tuple[str, str], dict] = defaultdict(lambda: {"label": "Internal", "columns": []})
    for f in findings:
        t = tables[(f["source"], f["table"])]
        t["columns"].append(f)
        # A table inherits the most sensitive label among its confirmed columns.
        if f["status"] == "confirmed" and LABEL_RANK[f["label"]] > LABEL_RANK[t["label"]]:
            t["label"] = f["label"]
    return {
        "mode": mode,
        "columns_scanned": columns_scanned,
        "findings": len(findings),
        "confirmed": sum(f["status"] == "confirmed" for f in findings),
        "review": sum(f["status"] == "review" for f in findings),
        "tables": [{"source": s, "table": t, **v} for (s, t), v in sorted(tables.items())],
    }


def to_json(inv: dict) -> str:
    return json.dumps(inv, indent=2)


def to_markdown(inv: dict) -> str:
    out = [
        f"# Sensitive data inventory ({inv['mode']})",
        "",
        f"Columns scanned: {inv['columns_scanned']} | findings: {inv['findings']} "
        f"(confirmed {inv['confirmed']}, review {inv['review']})",
        "",
    ]
    for t in inv["tables"]:
        out += [
            f"## {t['source']} / {t['table']} - {t['label']}",
            "",
            "| column | entity | status | confidence | valid hits | regex hits | name signal | example |",
            "|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|",
        ]
        for c in sorted(t["columns"], key=lambda c: -c["confidence"]):
            out.append(
                f"| {c['column']} | {c['entity']} | {c['status']} | {c['confidence']:.2f} | "
                f"{c['hit_ratio']:.0%} | {c['regex_ratio']:.0%} | {'yes' if c['name_signal'] else 'no'} | "
                f"{(c['examples'] or [''])[0]} |"
            )
        out.append("")
    return "\n".join(out)

From 23 confirmed columns to 7, and the 7 are exactly the columns with real PII. All 16 false confirmations are gone, and nothing real was lost: the leads.contact phone finding moved to review because only a third of that mixed column are valid phone numbers, while the same column is confirmed as EMAIL.

Each table gets the highest label among its confirmed columns (Restricted for cards, SSNs and IBANs, Confidential for emails and phones, Internal otherwise). A slice of the JSON inventory:
