Un cliente que no se actualiza no conoce los códigos nuevos. Es la objeción de verdad y la respuesta no es negarla: el síntoma es que un error nuevo sale como la frase genérica del default(), y en una app que nadie actualiza, para siempre. Por eso el message del servidor sigue en el contrato aunque este cliente no lo pinte: la jerarquía es catálogo propio, texto del servidor, frase genérica. Usar el segundo escalón es elegir a conciencia una degradación —inglés a quien no lo lee— antes que no decir nada.

Y lo que esto no es. No es un sistema de internacionalización: no hay diccionario global ni claves, la frase es un valor dentro de la excepción. Tampoco valida formularios ni sustituye al log. Y no pide que el servidor deje de redactar, sino que lo que redacte vaya al log y a los clientes que no conocen el código.

Para quién no es, y para quién sí

Si la API tiene un solo cliente, en un solo idioma, y sus errores son los que el usuario no puede arreglar, el catch del principio es la respuesta correcta: las clases espejo del cliente serían deuda sin contrapartida. Ese caso es más común de lo que parece.

El balance se invierte con cuatro condiciones: dos o más clientes sobre la misma API; dos o más idiomas; errores con datos que el usuario necesita para arreglar algo; y un código que ya consume alguien fuera de tu repositorio. Con dos de las cuatro, el contrato se paga solo.

Y hay una posición contraria bien documentada que conviene conocer antes de copiar nada de esto. La guía de diseño de API de Google, AIP-193, exige los parámetros con nombre —"any request-specific information which contributes to the Status.message […] must be represented within metadata"— y aun así manda la frase ya traducida desde el servidor, en un LocalizedMessage que "should be localized to a user-specified locale where possible". No es que una de las dos esté equivocada: son dos fronteras distintas. Google escribe para APIs públicas con clientes que no controla, y ahí el servidor no puede dar por hecho que al otro lado haya un catálogo; esto es un backend que sirve a una pantalla que sí se controla.

La regla práctica: si el texto del error lleva un dato dentro, el dato viaja por el contrato y la frase se queda en el cliente.

El código

El contrato, el filtro, las excepciones del envío y del transportista, los espejos y un catálogo por operación están en este proyecto de ejemplo, contra @nestjs/common 12.3.3. Las respuestas del servidor están fijadas en archivos que comprueban los dos lados: el servidor, que la aplicación real las produce, y el cliente, que con esas mismas respuestas redacta la frase que toca en cada operación. Son 25 tests, y dos de ellos enseñan las dos mitades del errorCode de la v12: el código llega al cliente y los datos no.

Hablemos

¿Preguntas, feedback o una visión distinta? Me encantaría leerte. Me encuentras aquí:

  • GitHub — hgomezrobaina
  • LinkedIn — Héctor Gómez Robaina
  • X — @hgomezrobaina

title: Understanding Local AI (1): The Economics of Personal AI
description:
Training in the Cloud, Running at Home

Your next computer could change what you are willing to pay for an AI subscription.

The Economics of Personal AIWhen you buy a powerful computer, you expect it to do the work. You paid for the processor, the memory, and the electricity. Yet when you open a cloud AI assistant, much of that hardware waits while another computer generates the answer.

There are good reasons for this. Large models can need more resources than a personal device can provide. But the balance can change as computers improve and models become more efficient.

That raises a business question as much as a technical one: what happens to the AI subscription when the customer already owns a computer capable of doing the job?

Apple offers a particularly interesting case. It sells the hardware, controls the operating system, and can put an assistant directly into the applications people already use.

My thesis is that local AI could become another reason to buy a better computer — and, for some users, a reason to cancel a separate AI subscription.

Apple has already started

This is not a proposal for Apple to enter a field it has ignored.

Its 2026 Apple Foundation Models family includes both local and server-based models. Apple describes AFM 3 Core Advanced as a 20-billion-parameter model designed for its more capable silicon, with only part of the model active for each request. [1]

What does “20 billion parameters” mean?Parameters are numerical settings adjusted during training. Together, they shape how a model processes information and generates answers. Twenty billion parameters means twenty billion of these learned values — not twenty billion facts or stored answers.*More parameters generally require more storage, but the number alone does not tell you how capable a model is. In a sparse model like this one, only selected parts participate in each computation. That reduces the work needed to generate an answer, although the other parameters still need to be stored.*Apple and Google also announced a multi-year collaboration using Gemini models and Google’s cloud technology as a foundation for the next generation of Apple Foundation Models. [2]

So the ingredients already exist: external technology and computing resources, models adapted to Apple’s products, and a combination of local and cloud execution.

The open question is how much everyday work can move onto the device — and what that does to the economics.

Training and serving customers are different bills

Developing a capable model is expensive. Training requires computing resources, data, experimentation, and people who know what they are doing. Renting infrastructure changes how a company pays for that work; it does not make the work free.

Then comes another bill: running the model whenever customers use it.

A cloud assistant needs resources to answer requests throughout the day. More usage means more work, although the cost of each request depends on the model, hardware, and how efficiently the service operates.

Local inference changes who supplies those resources. The customer’s computer generates the answer. The provider still pays for development, distribution, updates, and support, but it does not have to supply server inference for that local request.

Apple could therefore sell a device that performs useful AI work while also reducing the amount of that work Apple must serve centrally.

That is the business opportunity. The computation still happens, but the customer has already bought the machine that performs it.

Deliver the model, then let the device work

The basic approach is straightforward: develop models centrally, optimise them for supported hardware, and distribute them to devices. Updated models could arrive alongside operating-system updates or as separate downloads.

Making a model smaller takes more than putting it in a ZIP file. Quantisation reduces the precision used to store its numerical values. Distillation trains a smaller model using guidance from a larger one. These approaches can reduce resource requirements, with tradeoffs that need testing.

Apple has already documented aggressive quantisation in its on-device models. [3]

The user does not need to understand any of that. The useful experience is receiving an update and finding that the computer can now do more.

Over time, capable local assistance could become something buyers expect from the operating system, much as they expect search, dictation, and a web browser.

Local does not have to mean open

Open-weight models already let people download model weights and run them on suitable hardware. Mistral, for example, publishes models for this purpose. The permissions attached to those releases depend on the individual licence. [4]

Apple does not have to adopt that distribution model for its own proprietary technology. It could deliver an optimised model as a controlled component of the operating system, accessible through Siri and supported application interfaces, without offering a freely reusable model download.

Apple already provides developer access to its on-device model through the Foundation Models framework. Access to a model’s capabilities and publication of its weights are different things. [5]

Compression and protection also serve different purposes. Compression makes a model practical to store and run. Access controls and protected packaging can make unauthorised reuse harder; they do not guarantee that weights delivered to a user-controlled device can never be extracted.

The commercial point remains: Apple could distribute local capability as part of a paid device and software ecosystem, then replace or improve the model through subsequent updates. It would not need to give everyone an unrestricted copy to run on competing hardware.

Open-weight models make local AI available to people willing to choose and install them. Apple’s opportunity is to make comparable everyday usefulness part of the computer’s normal experience, with deployment, integration, and updates handled for the user.

The next Mac versus the next subscription renewal

Consider a future Mac generation — an “M7,” purely as a scenario, not a claim about an announced product.

Suppose its local assistant handles the tasks for which you currently pay a cloud service: rewriting text, explaining code, summarising documents, translating messages, and answering everyday questions.

You might still find a cloud assistant better at difficult research or complex programming. But if you rarely need those capabilities, would you keep paying every month?

Apple would not have to reproduce every feature of ChatGPT to change that decision.

Apple can earn money without charging for every answer

A cloud service can sell access to its models. A hardware company can also sell the device that makes those models useful.

If better local AI encourages buyers to choose more memory, upgrade an older machine, or stay within the platform, Apple has potential ways to benefit beyond a standalone assistant subscription.

This is my strategic interpretation, not a disclosed Apple financial forecast.

It also creates a tension for customers. AI might help them avoid a subscription while encouraging a more expensive hardware purchase. And local execution does not prevent Apple or another developer from charging for the software itself.

“Runs on your computer” and “included in the purchase price” are separate promises.

The operating system may matter as much as the model

A personal assistant becomes useful when it can work with your documents and applications, subject to the permissions you grant it.

That gives an operating-system vendor an important opportunity. It can make AI available where the task already happens, without requiring the user to move everything into a separate chat window.

For many everyday jobs, convenient integration and reliable execution may matter more than having the highest-scoring model.

Local processing also offers a practical privacy benefit: tasks completed entirely on the device need not send their contents to a remote model. But an assistant can still use online search, connected services, or cloud fallback. The application’s actual behavior matters more than a “local AI” label.

Why the cloud will still have a role

A model fitting in memory does not mean it runs comfortably alongside everything else. Response speed, long documents, power consumption, and heat all affect the experience. A desktop with substantial memory and a thin laptop running on battery face different limits.

Cloud systems keep improving too. They can offer capabilities that remain beyond personal hardware, while serving users who prefer inexpensive devices.

Apple’s own architecture includes server models for demanding work, which makes its present approach hybrid. [1]

My forecast is that more routine requests will become practical locally, while remote services retain value for tasks that benefit from greater resources. That does not guarantee lower total data-center demand: wider adoption and more ambitious tasks could outweigh the work moved onto devices.

The subscription will need a stronger reason to exist

The important change would be in what customers consider worth paying for.

If a capable assistant comes with the computer and handles their daily needs, a separate subscription becomes a purchase for additional capabilities. Providers would have to earn it through better results, specialised tools, collaboration, or access to services the local assistant cannot replace.

For Apple, that could turn AI capability into hardware value. For cloud providers, it could make everyday assistance harder to sell on its own.

We are used to asking whether a personal computer can run a large model. The more consequential question may soon be:

Can it do enough that you stop paying someone else to run one for you?

Sources and further reading

Current product descriptions are distinguished from the author’s forecasts. The hypothetical M7 scenario does not imply announced specifications, pricing, or capabilities.

  • Apple: Introducing the Third Generation of Apple’s Foundation Models
  • Google and Apple: Joint Statement, January 12, 2026
  • Apple: Foundation Language Models Tech Report 2025
  • Mistral: Introducing Mistral 3
  • Apple: Foundation Models Framework

title: 🛠️ Database Connection Pooling: The Hidden Bottleneck That Can Bring Your Application Down
description:
Imagine this.

Your application has been running perfectly for weeks. APIs are responding quickly, database queries are working and everything looks healthy.

Then, suddenly:

  • API requests start taking several seconds.
  • Some requests time out, while others never seem to complete.
  • New database operations stop working.
  • Restarting the application temporarily fixes everything.
  • A few minutes or hours later, the same problem returns.

You check the database. It's running.

You check the application. No obvious crash.

You check the logs and find something like:

Error: context deadline exceeded
Error: connection pool exhausted
Error: timeout acquiring connection

One possible reason?

Your application has run out of available database connections.

This is where database connection pooling becomes extremely important.

Connection pooling is one of those concepts that developers often configure once and forget about. But an incorrectly configured pool, or connections that are never released, can gradually bring an otherwise healthy application to a halt.

In this article, we'll go beyond what connection pooling is. We'll understand how it works, how connections get stuck, how to reproduce pool exhaustion, how to debug it in a real application and which practices help prevent these problems in production.

We'll use Go's database/sql package for practical examples, but the concepts apply to most backend technologies.

1. First, why do we need a database connection pool?

Let's start with a basic question.

What happens when an API needs to execute a database query?

At a high level, the application needs a connection to the database, sends a query, receives the result and then releases the connection for reuse.

Opening a brand-new database connection for every request is expensive.

Establishing a connection can involve:

  • A network connection between the application and database.
  • Authentication.
  • Database session initialization.
  • TLS negotiation, if configured.
  • Other database and driver-specific setup.

Now imagine an application receiving 500 requests simultaneously.

If every request independently opens a new database connection, we could end up creating hundreds of connections unnecessarily.

That introduces overhead and can overwhelm the database server.

Instead, we use a connection pool.

A connection pool maintains a collection of reusable database connections. When an application needs a connection, it borrows one from the pool. Once the operation is finished, the connection is returned so another operation can use it.

Think of it like a shared collection of resources:

  1. A request needs a database connection.
  2. The pool provides an available connection.
  3. The request executes its database operation.
  4. The connection is released back to the pool.
  5. Another request can reuse it.

The important part is that the application doesn't need to establish a new physical connection for every query.

One important distinction: A connection pool is not the same as a database connection.

The pool manages connections. Your application borrows and returns them as database operations require.

2. How connection pooling works in Go

Go makes connection pooling particularly interesting because database/sql manages the pool for us.

Consider this example:

db, err := sql.Open("postgres", connectionString)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

defer db.Close()

A common misconception is that sql.Open() immediately establishes a database connection.

It doesn't necessarily do that.

sql.Open() creates a *sql.DB handle, which manages a pool of connections. Actual connections are typically established when they're needed.

If you want to verify that the database is reachable during application startup, use PingContext():

ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(
    context.Background(),
    5*time.Second,
)
defer cancel()

if err := db.PingContext(ctx); err != nil {
    log.Fatalf("database connection failed: %v", err)
}

Also, notice something important:

*sql.DB is designed to be long-lived and shared across goroutines.

You generally create one database handle during application startup and reuse it throughout the application's lifetime.

You should not create a new sql.DB inside every API handler.

For example, avoid this:

func GetUsers(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    db, err := sql.Open("postgres", connectionString)
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "Database error", 500)
        return
    }

    defer db.Close()

    // Execute query...
}

Why?

Because every handler creates its own pool. Instead of sharing a controlled number of connections, you end up with multiple independent pools.

This can cause:

  • Unnecessary connection creation.
  • Too many connections on the database server.
  • More resource consumption.
  • Difficult-to-manage connection limits.

A better approach is to initialize the pool once and inject the shared *sql.DB into your repository or service layer.

type UserRepository struct {
    db *sql.DB
}

func NewUserRepository(db *sql.DB) *UserRepository {
    return &UserRepository{
        db: db,
    }
}

Now every repository operation uses the same pool.

3. Understanding the connection pool configuration

Go provides several methods to control the pool.

These are worth understanding properly because setting them without understanding their impact can create production issues.

SetMaxOpenConns 

db.SetMaxOpenConns(25)

This defines the maximum number of open connections that the pool can have at a time.

For example, if the maximum is 25:

  • Up to 25 connections can be open.
  • If all 25 are busy, additional operations wait.
  • When a connection becomes available, a waiting operation can use it.

This is one of the most important settings because it controls how many concurrent database operations can hold connections from that pool.

SetMaxIdleConns 

db.SetMaxIdleConns(10)

This defines the maximum number of connections that can remain idle in the pool.

Why keep idle connections?

Because creating a new connection takes time. Keeping a reasonable number of connections available can reduce the overhead of establishing new ones.

But don't confuse idle connections with unused resources that are automatically closed immediately. Idle connections can remain open until they are reused or removed by pool lifecycle rules.

SetConnMaxLifetime 

db.SetConnMaxLifetime(30 * time.Minute)

This sets the maximum amount of time a connection may be reused.

Once a connection reaches its lifetime, it becomes eligible for removal and replacement.

Why is this useful?

  • Database infrastructure may rotate connections.
  • Network devices may terminate long-lived connections.
  • Cloud database environments may have connection lifecycle constraints.
  • Long-lived sessions can accumulate server-side state.

This does not mean an active query is forcibly interrupted exactly when the lifetime expires. The pool applies connection lifetime rules as connections are returned and reused.

SetConnMaxIdleTime 

db.SetConnMaxIdleTime(5 * time.Minute)

This controls how long an idle connection can remain unused before it becomes eligible for closure.

For example, imagine your application receives heavy traffic during the day but very little traffic at night.

You might not need to keep every previously opened connection around during idle periods.

This setting helps the pool clean up connections that have been sitting unused.

Putting everything together

A basic configuration might look like this:

func NewDatabase(dsn string) (*sql.DB, error) {
    db, err := sql.Open("postgres", dsn)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

    db.SetMaxOpenConns(25)
    db.SetMaxIdleConns(10)
    db.SetConnMaxLifetime(30 * time.Minute)
    db.SetConnMaxIdleTime(5 * time.Minute)

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(
        context.Background(),
        5*time.Second,
    )
    defer cancel()

    if err := db.PingContext(ctx); err != nil {
        db.Close()
        return nil, err
    }

    return db, nil
}

These values are examples, not universal production defaults. Your actual configuration should depend on database capacity, application concurrency, query behavior, number of instances and workload.

We'll come back to sizing later.

4. The real problem: How does an application run out of connections?

Now let's get to the interesting part.

Suppose your application has the following configuration:

db.SetMaxOpenConns(5)

That means the pool can have at most five open connections.

Imagine five API requests are executing database operations simultaneously.

All five connections are occupied.

Now a sixth request arrives.

What happens?

It waits until one of the existing operations releases a connection.

This is expected behavior.

But what if those five connections are never released?

The sixth request keeps waiting.

The seventh request keeps waiting.

Eventually, requests start timing out and your application appears to be stuck.

This is called connection pool exhaustion.

The database itself might still be healthy. The problem is that your application cannot obtain a connection from its own pool.

Let's look at the most common reasons.

5. Common causes of connection leaks and pool exhaustion

Problem 1: Forgetting to close query rows

This is one of the easiest mistakes to make.

Consider:

func GetUsers(db *sql.DB) error {
    rows, err := db.Query("SELECT id, name FROM users")
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    for rows.Next() {
        var id int
        var name string

        if err := rows.Scan(&id, &name); err != nil {
            return err
        }

        fmt.Println(id, name)
    }

    return nil
}

Looks perfectly fine, right?

But there's an issue.

We never close rows.

A Rows object can hold a database connection while the result set is being consumed. If it isn't closed, the connection may remain unavailable to other operations.

A safer implementation:

func GetUsers(db *sql.DB) error {
    rows, err := db.Query("SELECT id, name FROM users")
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer rows.Close()

    for rows.Next() {
        var id int
        var name string

        if err := rows.Scan(&id, &name); err != nil {
            return err
        }

        fmt.Println(id, name)
    }

    return rows.Err()
}

Three important things are happening here:

  1. defer rows.Close() ensures cleanup when the function returns, including error paths.
  2. rows.Err() checks whether iteration ended because of an error.
  3. The connection can be returned to the pool once the result set is closed and the operation is finished.

A practical rule: Whenever you call Query() and receive *sql.Rows, close it.

Also, remember that QueryRow() behaves differently: it represents a single-row result and doesn't require you to call Close().

Problem 2: Not completing database transactions

Transactions are another common source of connection exhaustion.

Consider:

func UpdateUser(db *sql.DB) error {
    tx, err := db.Begin()
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    _, err = tx.Exec(
        "UPDATE users SET status = ? WHERE id = ?",
        "active",
        10,
    )

    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    return nil
}

What's wrong here?

We started a transaction but never committed or rolled it back.

A transaction holds its underlying connection until it is completed.

If this happens repeatedly, connections can remain occupied and the pool can eventually become exhausted.

A safer pattern:

func UpdateUser(db *sql.DB) error {
    tx, err := db.Begin()
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    defer tx.Rollback()

    _, err = tx.Exec(
        "UPDATE users SET status = ? WHERE id = ?",
        "active",
        10,
    )
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    if err := tx.Commit(); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    return nil
}

Why defer Rollback() if we're going to commit?

Because it provides cleanup for every early return.

After a successful commit, the deferred rollback simply returns an error indicating that the transaction has already completed. It's safe to ignore that result in this cleanup pattern.

The important thing is that every transaction should have a clearly defined completion path.

Never start a transaction and leave its lifecycle uncertain.

Problem 3: Starting another database operation inside a transaction

Here's a subtle issue that can be particularly confusing.

Imagine your pool has only one connection:

db.SetMaxOpenConns(1)

Now consider:

func UpdateAndFetch(db *sql.DB) error {
    tx, err := db.Begin()
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer tx.Rollback()

    _, err = tx.Exec(
        "UPDATE users SET status = ? WHERE id = ?",
        "active",
        10,
    )
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    var name string

    err = db.QueryRow(
        "SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = ?",
        10,
    ).Scan(&name)

    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    return tx.Commit()
}

Can you spot the problem?

The transaction already holds the only available connection.

But the next query uses db.QueryRow(), which tries to acquire a connection from the pool.

There are no available connections.

The transaction is waiting for the query to finish and the query is waiting for the transaction's connection to become available.

Neither can proceed.

This is a deadlock-like situation caused by exhausting the pool.

The fix is simple: execute queries that belong to the transaction through tx, not through db.

err = tx.QueryRow(
    "SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = ?",
    10,
).Scan(&name)

This is an especially important distinction:

  • db.Exec() / db.Query() acquire connections from the pool.
  • tx.Exec() / tx.Query() use the connection already reserved by that transaction.

Problem 4: Long-running queries

Not every pool exhaustion issue is caused by a connection leak.

Sometimes, connections are being released correctly, but database operations are taking too long.

Imagine:

  • Your pool has 20 connections.
  • 20 requests execute slow database queries.
  • Each query takes 15 seconds.
  • Another 100 requests arrive during that period.

Those new requests must wait for connections.

The application may appear unresponsive even though no connection has leaked.

Common reasons include:

  • Missing database indexes.
  • Queries scanning too many rows.
  • Unnecessary joins.
  • Lock contention.
  • Large result sets.
  • Database CPU or I/O saturation.
  • Slow network communication.

This is why increasing MaxOpenConns isn't always the solution.

If the database is already struggling, allowing more concurrent queries may make things worse.

The right approach is to investigate query execution time, database load and lock waits.

Problem 5: Queries without timeouts

Consider:

rows, err := db.Query(
    "SELECT id, name FROM users",
)

What happens if the database takes too long to respond?

Without a suitable context deadline, the operation may wait longer than the caller can reasonably tolerate.

Use context-aware operations:

ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(
    context.Background(),
    3*time.Second,
)
defer cancel()

rows, err := db.QueryContext(
    ctx,
    "SELECT id, name FROM users",
)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
defer rows.Close()

A context deadline gives the operation a time limit and allows cancellation to propagate through the database driver where supported.

Be careful, though: a timeout is not a substitute for closing rows or completing transactions.

You need both proper resource cleanup and sensible deadlines.

6. Let's reproduce connection pool exhaustion

Theory is useful, but let's actually see what happens.

We'll intentionally create a small pool and hold connections for a few seconds.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "database/sql"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    db, err := sql.Open("postgres", "your-connection-string")
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer db.Close()

    db.SetMaxOpenConns(2)
    db.SetMaxIdleConns(2)

    for i := 1; i <= 5; i++ {
        go func(id int) {
            ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(
                context.Background(),
                10*time.Second,
            )
            defer cancel()

            start := time.Now()

            conn, err := db.Conn(ctx)
            if err != nil {
                fmt.Printf(
                    "Worker %d failed: %v\n",
                    id,
                    err,
                )
                return
            }
            defer conn.Close()

            fmt.Printf(
                "Worker %d acquired connection in %v\n",
                id,
                time.Since(start),
            )

            time.Sleep(5 * time.Second)

            fmt.Printf("Worker %d released connection\n", id)
        }(i)
    }

    time.Sleep(12 * time.Second)

    stats := db.Stats()

    fmt.Printf("Open: %d\n", stats.OpenConnections)
    fmt.Printf("In use: %d\n", stats.InUse)
    fmt.Printf("Idle: %d\n", stats.Idle)
    fmt.Printf("Wait count: %d\n", stats.WaitCount)
    fmt.Printf("Wait duration: %v\n", stats.WaitDuration)
}

Here, we're deliberately limiting the pool to two connections while starting five workers.

What should happen?

  1. The first two workers acquire connections.
  2. The remaining three workers wait.
  3. When one of the first workers closes its connection, a waiting worker can acquire it.
  4. The process continues until all workers finish or their contexts expire.

Notice this line:

defer conn.Close()

It returns the reserved connection to the pool.

For this demonstration, we're using db.Conn() to reserve a connection explicitly. In normal application code, you generally use QueryContext, ExecContext, or a transaction and let database/sql manage connection acquisition.

Try changing the sleep duration, pool size and context timeout. You'll get a much better understanding of how pool contention behaves.

7. How to debug connection pool exhaustion in a real application

Now imagine this happens in production.

The API is slow, requests are timing out and the database pool is fully occupied.

Where do you start?

Don't immediately increase the connection limit or restart the application.

First, collect evidence.

Step 1: Check pool statistics

Go provides a very useful method:

stats := db.Stats()

It returns a DBStats structure containing information about the pool.

Some important fields:

Field What it tells you
OpenConnections Currently open connections
InUse Connections currently checked out
Idle Connections currently idle
MaxOpenConnections Configured maximum
WaitCount Total number of waits for a connection
WaitDuration Total time spent waiting for connections

Let's log them:

func LogDBStats(db *sql.DB) {
    stats := db.Stats()

    log.Printf(
        "DB Pool | Open: %d | InUse: %d | Idle: %d | MaxOpen: %d | WaitCount: %d | WaitDuration: %v",
        stats.OpenConnections,
        stats.InUse,
        stats.Idle,
        stats.MaxOpenConnections,
        stats.WaitCount,
        stats.WaitDuration,
    )
}

Call this periodically or expose these values through your application's metrics endpoint.

Now imagine you see:

DB Pool | Open: 25 | InUse: 25 | Idle: 0 |
MaxOpen: 25 | WaitCount: 1200 | WaitDuration: 45s

What does this tell us?

  • All 25 connections are currently occupied.
  • There are no idle connections available.
  • Other operations have been waiting for connections.
  • The pool is experiencing contention.

This is a strong indication that the pool is under pressure.

But don't jump to the conclusion that connections are leaking.

The same pattern can be caused by slow queries, long transactions, high request concurrency, or actual leaks.

Important: WaitCount and WaitDuration are cumulative counters. They aren't necessarily the number of requests waiting right now.

For meaningful monitoring, compare their values over time. For example, calculate the increase in WaitCount and WaitDuration over each monitoring interval.

Step 2: Check whether connections are being released

This is where you investigate the code.

Search for:

  • db.Query() without rows.Close().
  • Transactions without a commit or rollback.
  • Early returns before cleanup.
  • Long-running queries.
  • Database operations inside loops.
  • Connections reserved using db.Conn() without Close().
  • Rows that remain open while unrelated work is performed.

Pay special attention to functions that execute multiple database operations.

For example:

rows, err := db.QueryContext(ctx, query)
if err != nil {
    return err
}

// Some processing...

if someCondition {
    return nil
}

If rows.Close() is missing, that early return can leave the result set open.

Using defer rows.Close() immediately after successfully acquiring rows is a much safer pattern.

Step 3: Check the database server itself

Your application metrics tell you what is happening inside the pool.

But they don't tell you everything about the database.

You should also investigate the database server.

For PostgreSQL, you can inspect active sessions using:

SELECT
    pid,
    usename,
    state,
    wait_event_type,
    wait_event,
    query_start,
    NOW() - query_start AS query_duration,
    query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = current_database()
ORDER BY query_start;

Look for:

  • Long-running queries.
  • Sessions waiting on locks.
  • Unexpectedly high numbers of active sessions.
  • Sessions in idle in transaction state.

That last state is particularly interesting.

An idle in transaction session means a transaction has started but is currently not executing a query and has not been completed.

Such transactions can hold locks and other resources and can contribute to connection pressure.

For MySQL, you can inspect current sessions using:

SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST;

Look at the connection count, query duration and session state.

These checks help distinguish application-side connection leaks from database-side performance or locking problems.

Step 4: Check query latency and acquisition time separately

This is a debugging detail worth remembering.

A database operation can be slow for two very different reasons:

  1. It took a long time to acquire a connection.
  2. It acquired a connection quickly, but the query itself took a long time.

These should be measured separately.

For example:

start := time.Now()

rows, err := db.QueryContext(ctx, query)
acquireAndExecuteDuration := time.Since(start)

if err != nil {
    return err
}
defer rows.Close()

log.Printf(
    "Query call duration: %v",
    acquireAndExecuteDuration,
)

This measures the time spent obtaining a connection and executing the query call until it returns its rows. It is not necessarily the full time spent consuming the result set.

For more detailed observability, instrument:

  • Connection acquisition duration.
  • Query execution duration.
  • Rows iteration duration.
  • Transaction duration.
  • Connection pool wait statistics.

This makes it much easier to identify where the time is actually going.

Step 5: Don't use application restarts as the permanent fix

Restarting an application can temporarily solve a pool exhaustion issue because closing the database handle releases its connections.

But if the underlying bug remains, it will happen again.

A restart is a recovery action, not a root-cause fix.

The goal should be to identify why connections are staying occupied and correct that behavior.

8. How should you choose the connection pool size?

This is one of the most common configuration questions.

Should MaxOpenConns be 10, 25, 50, or 100?

There is no universal answer.

It depends on your workload and database capacity.

Let's take an example.

Suppose your database server allows 200 connections.

Your architecture has:

  • 3 application instances.
  • 1 background worker service.
  • 1 scheduled job service.
  • Database administration and migration connections.

If every application instance configures:

db.SetMaxOpenConns(100)

Then your three application instances alone could potentially open 300 connections.

That's already more than the database's total connection limit.

Remember:

The connection limit applies to the database server, not just one application instance.

A better way to think about it:

Database connection budget
    |
    +-- Application instance 1
    +-- Application instance 2
    +-- Application instance 3
    +-- Background workers
    +-- Scheduled jobs
    +-- Migrations and administration
    +-- Operational reserve

The total possible connections across all these consumers must fit within the database's available capacity.

You should also leave room for database maintenance and other operational needs.

What factors should influence the pool size?

1. Number of application instances

A pool size of 25 across four instances can potentially mean 100 connections.

2. Query execution time

Long-running queries occupy connections longer, increasing contention.

3. Request concurrency

A large number of concurrent requests doesn't automatically mean you need an equally large database pool. Many requests may not need the database simultaneously.

4. Database capacity

The database must be able to handle the number of concurrent queries efficiently.

5. Background jobs

Workers and scheduled tasks also consume connections and must be included in your calculations.

6. Connection limits of your database infrastructure

Managed databases, self-hosted databases and connection proxies may impose different limits.

A practical approach

Start with a conservative pool size.

Then:

  1. Load test realistic traffic.
  2. Monitor InUse, Idle, WaitCount and WaitDuration.
  3. Check query latency and database CPU.
  4. Identify whether connection waits are caused by slow queries or insufficient pool capacity.
  5. Increase the limit gradually if the database has capacity.
  6. Repeat the load test and compare results.

Don't increase the pool size simply because requests are waiting.

More connections can increase database contention and make the situation worse.

The objective isn't to maximize the number of connections.

It's to find a balance between application concurrency and database capacity.

9. Best practices for production applications

Let's put the important practices together.

1. Create one shared database pool

Initialize *sql.DB during application startup and reuse it.

Avoid creating a new pool for every request or repository operation.

2. Always close query rows 

rows, err := db.QueryContext(ctx, query)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
defer rows.Close()

Do this immediately after successfully obtaining rows.

3. Always complete transactions

Use a clear commit or rollback path.

A deferred rollback is a useful safety net for early returns.

4. Use context-aware database operations

Prefer:

db.QueryContext(ctx, query)
db.ExecContext(ctx, query)
db.BeginTx(ctx, nil)

Use sensible deadlines based on the operation and API requirements.

5. Don't hold connections longer than necessary

Avoid performing unrelated work while holding:

  • Open result sets.
  • Transactions.
  • Reserved connections.

For example, don't make an external HTTP request while holding a database transaction unless that is an intentional and carefully designed requirement.

6. Monitor pool statistics

Expose connection pool metrics and alert on sustained saturation, increasing wait time and unusual connection usage.

7. Monitor the database too

Application metrics alone aren't enough.

Track database CPU, memory, query latency, locks, active sessions and connection usage.

8. Size pools across all application instances

Don't configure every instance independently without considering the total database connection budget.

9. Use query timeouts and appropriate indexes

A slow query can occupy a connection just as effectively as a leaked connection.

Optimize the query instead of blindly increasing the pool.

10. Test under concurrency

A database operation that works perfectly in a single-request test may behave very differently under concurrent load.

Load testing and integration testing can expose resource lifecycle problems before production does.

10. A few misconceptions worth clearing up

Misconception 1: Increasing MaxOpenConns always fixes connection exhaustion.

Not true. If connections are leaking or queries are too slow, increasing the limit may only delay the problem or overload the database.

Misconception 2: sql.Open() immediately creates a database connection.

Not necessarily. It creates a pool handle. Use PingContext() when you need to verify connectivity.

Misconception 3: Idle connections are bad.

Not necessarily. Idle connections are reusable resources. The problem is keeping more of them than your workload or infrastructure needs.

Misconception 4: Every connection leak is caused by forgetting rows.Close().

No. Unfinished transactions, reserved connections that aren't closed, slow operations and other resource-lifecycle issues can also cause pool exhaustion.

Misconception 5: A healthy database means the application can always query it.

Not true. Your application's local connection pool can be exhausted even when the database server itself is healthy.

Misconception 6: MaxOpenConns should match the number of API requests.

No. Many API requests don't execute database queries simultaneously. Pool sizing should be based on actual database concurrency and server capacity.

11. Your production debugging checklist

If your application suddenly starts timing out while communicating with the database, here's a practical checklist to follow.

  • [ ] Check whether InUse has reached MaxOpenConnections.
  • [ ] Check whether Idle is consistently zero.
  • [ ] Compare WaitCount and WaitDuration over time.
  • [ ] Check for missing rows.Close() calls.
  • [ ] Check whether transactions are always committed or rolled back.
  • [ ] Look for reserved connections that aren't closed.
  • [ ] Identify long-running queries.
  • [ ] Inspect database locks and idle in transaction sessions.
  • [ ] Separate connection acquisition time from query execution time.
  • [ ] Check total connections across all application instances.
  • [ ] Review context deadlines and query timeouts.
  • [ ] Load test the fix before deploying it.

This checklist won't automatically identify every possible issue, but it gives you a systematic place to start instead of randomly changing pool configuration.

Final thoughts

Database connection pooling is not just about setting MaxOpenConns and MaxIdleConns and moving on.

It's about understanding how your application acquires, uses and releases database connections.

A missing rows.Close(), an unfinished transaction, or a query that takes much longer than expected can occupy connections and eventually prevent the rest of your application from accessing the database.

The interesting part is that the database might be completely healthy while your application is unable to execute another query.

That's why connection pool monitoring, proper resource cleanup, query optimization and realistic pool sizing are all important parts of building reliable backend systems.

If there's one thing I'd like you to take away from this article, it's this:

Don't just monitor whether your database is up. Monitor whether your application can actually get a connection to use it.

Because sometimes, the problem isn't that your database stopped working. It's that your application ran out of ways to talk to it.

💬 Have you ever debugged a connection pool exhaustion issue in a production application?

What was the actual root cause - a connection leak, a long-running query, an unfinished transaction, or something else?

I'd love to hear about real-world debugging experiences in the comments.

Happy debugging! 🚀

title: 48-Hour Field Notes: My Per-Call Timeout Was Longer Than the Job Window Itself
description:
I spent two nights watching a nightly job call a model once per queue row, and the failure was never the model. It was arithmetic: a fixed 120-second timeout per attempt, three attempts, and a scheduler window that closed long before the last row was reached. Why do we budget time per request but almost never per job? Here is what I tried, what broke, and the clamp I would repeat.

The setup I actually ran

  1. A queue table with one row per item, where each row needed one model call plus schema validation.
  2. A worker loop that pulled rows in order and wrote a status column after each successful call.
  3. A constant per-call HTTP timeout of 120 seconds, three attempts, and a wall-clock window enforced outside the worker.
  4. A fake-clock test suite that ran before any live call, because I wanted the failure in milliseconds, not hours.

That naive loop looked perfectly reasonable in isolation, and that is exactly why it survived review. Ask yourself what the scheduler sees when every attempt eats its full timeout:

# the version I shipped first, and regretted
def process_naive(items, post):
    for item in items:
        for attempt in range(3):
            try:
                return post(item, timeout=120)   # fixed, forever
            except TimeoutError:
                continue
        return None

If sixty rows each burn three 120-second timeouts, the worst case is six hours inside a window measured in minutes. The process gets killed mid-row, so the row in flight has an unknown outcome while every earlier row looks fine. Nothing downstream can tell those two situations apart without reading logs by hand.

The fix: one deadline, passed down, with a reserve

Instead of a constant timeout, I pass a single monotonic deadline into the worker and derive each call's timeout from what is actually left. Three rules carry the whole change, and none of them is clever:

  • Clamp: timeout = min(cap, deadline - now - reserve).
  • Refuse: if the clamped value drops below a floor, do not start the call at all.
  • Record: log the granted timeout next to each result so you can audit the arithmetic later. 
# budget.py  (needs Python 3.10+ for the union type)
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Budget:
    deadline: float        # time.monotonic() value for the whole job
    reserve: float = 45.0  # seconds held back for checkpoint + clean exit
    floor: float = 3.0     # never start a call with less usable time than this
    cap: float = 120.0     # no single call may exceed this

    def call_timeout(self, now: float) -> float | None:
        remaining = self.deadline - now - self.reserve
        if remaining < self.floor:
            return None
        return min(self.cap, remaining)

The reserve is the part everyone skips, and it is the part that keeps the run honest under pressure. I hold back enough seconds for the final checkpoint write, the status flush, and a clean exit before the scheduler's axe falls. Ask yourself how long your cleanup really takes when the database is busy, not when it is idle. My first reserve was too small, and the last row never got its status write at all.

The loop that defers instead of overrunning 

# worker.py
import time
from budget import Budget

def run(queue, call_model, checkpoint, budget, clock=time.monotonic):
    done, deferred = [], []
    for item in queue:
        timeout = budget.call_timeout(clock())
        if timeout is None:
            deferred.append(item["id"])
            continue
        try:
            result = call_model(item, timeout=timeout)
        except TimeoutError:
            checkpoint(item["id"], status="pending", detail="deferred")
            deferred.append(item["id"])
            continue
        checkpoint(item["id"], status="done", result=result)
        done.append(item["id"])
    return done, deferred

A deferred item is not a failure, and treating it as one is how you end up retrying into a closed window. The next run picks it up because the checkpoint still says pending, so the job converges across windows instead of dying inside one. Is that slower? Yes, deliberately, and it is the only version where the final row count means anything.

A reproducible test with no network at all 

# test_budget.py
from budget import Budget
from worker import run

class FakeClock:
    def __init__(self, t=0.0): self.t = t
    def __call__(self): return self.t
    def advance(self, seconds): self.t += seconds

def test_clamp_shrinks_as_the_window_closes():
    clock = FakeClock(0.0)
    b = Budget(deadline=100.0, reserve=40.0, floor=5.0, cap=30.0)
    assert b.call_timeout(clock()) == 30.0     # 60 usable, cap wins
    clock.advance(40.0)
    assert b.call_timeout(clock()) == 20.0     # 20 usable, remaining wins
    clock.advance(20.0)
    assert b.call_timeout(clock()) is None     # 0 usable, refuse

def test_slow_model_defers_instead_of_overrunning():
    clock = FakeClock(0.0)
    b = Budget(deadline=10.0, reserve=4.0, floor=2.0, cap=3.0)
    granted, writes = [], []
    def call_model(item, timeout):
        granted.append(round(timeout, 2))
        clock.advance(timeout)                 # pretend the call used it all
        return {"ok": True}
    done, deferred = run(
        [{"id": i} for i in range(5)],
        call_model,
        checkpoint=lambda item_id, **kw: writes.append((item_id, kw["status"])),
        budget=b,
        clock=clock,
    )
    assert granted == [3.0, 3.0]
    assert done == [0, 1]
    assert deferred == [2, 3, 4]
    assert writes == [(0, "done"), (1, "done")]

Run it with python -m pytest -q test_budget.py, and both tests finish in milliseconds. They fail loudly the moment someone "simplifies" the clamp back into a constant, which is the reason I keep them in the repo. A fake clock is cheaper than a night of watching timestamps scroll past at 3am.

What broke in the first 48 hours

  • I used time.time() first, and one NTP step made the remaining budget jump backwards into absurd timeouts.
  • My reserve was smaller than the checkpoint write under contention, so the last row was processed but never recorded.
  • The deadline was computed once before the loop, so "remaining" never actually moved during the run.
  • Deferred rows were logged as errors, which paged me for a job that was, by its own definition, healthy.

Each of those is a one-line fix and a two-hour investigation, which is roughly the usual ratio for this kind of plumbing.

Where MonkeyCode came in

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

I ran the worker on MonkeyCode's free server option and pointed call_model at its free model access, which let me exercise the clamp against a real endpoint before paying for any infrastructure. Both of those availability claims are operator-supplied and can change, so read the current terms yourself rather than planning around my notes. The clamp code does not care which endpoint answers, which is precisely the point of testing it separately.

If you want to rehearse this yourself, start with the fake-clock tests, then do one supervised run against a free endpoint and watch the granted timeouts shrink as the window closes.

Who should not use this approach

  • Workloads with sub-second calls, where a three-second floor never triggers and the extra branch is just noise.
  • Non-idempotent side effects, because deferring a half-applied write is worse than an honest timeout.
  • Jobs that must complete inside a single window for correctness; split the work instead of stretching the budget.
  • Pipelines where the scheduler already hands you a per-item deadline you can read directly.
  • Anything that needs a latency guarantee, since a budget is an accounting tool and not an SLA.

Checklist before the next run

  1. Compute the worst case as items × attempts × cap, then compare it against the window out loud.
  2. Pick the reserve from measured cleanup time, not from optimism about the database.
  3. Assert the clamp and the refusal path in a fake-clock test.
  4. Log granted timeout, elapsed time, and remaining-at-start for every single call.
  5. Treat deferred rows as pending forever, and never as errors that trigger a page.

Two nights of field notes bought me one arithmetic identity, a small test file, and a job that now ends before its window does. Isn't that a better trade than another round of guessing at why the last rows look weird?

title: Just about anyone can rent access to White House IP addresses
