title: Refactor a Messy Repo With a Diff Budget and One Frozen Seam
description:
Most messy-repo refactors fail at review time, not at compile time. The diff grows, the reviewer guesses, and the team merges risk. The smallest safe change is a frozen seam plus a hard diff budget.

The rule: freeze behavior before you move code

  1. Pick one runtime seam. A seam is a function call you can test without the UI or database.
  2. Write a characterization test at that seam. Use real inputs, not invented ones.
  3. Record the current output, including quirks.
  4. Set a diff budget. Example: 20 changed production lines, two production files, zero deleted tests.
  5. Change one thing. Run the contract test and the budget check.
  6. Stop if the budget fails. Split the change.

This is not a purity rule. It is a review-capacity rule. AI coding tools make large patches cheap to produce. Review capacity did not grow with patch size.

The code below is a minimal example, not a report from a production repository.

Step 1: Find a seam you can test in one minute

Use git grep and coverage. Pick a function with a narrow input and a visible output. Avoid the function with ten globals.

git grep -n 'def send_receipt' -- app
python -m pytest --cov=app.receipts --cov-report=term-missing tests/ -q

The example function reads a clock, a setting, and a mailer. That is three hidden dependencies. You do not refactor all three at once.

# app/receipts.py
from datetime import datetime
from django.conf import settings
from .mail import send_mail

def send_receipt(order):
    if order.total <= 0:
        return 'skipped'
    body = f'Order {order.id} total {order.total} at {datetime.now().isoformat()}'
    if settings.DRY_RUN:
        return 'dry-run'
    send_mail(order.email, 'Receipt', body)
    return 'sent'

Step 2: Write the contract test before the change

Pin the current behavior with a test that calls only the public function. Use monkeypatch for the clock, setting, and mailer. The test is boring on purpose.

# tests/test_receipts_contract.py
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from types import SimpleNamespace
import pytest
import app.receipts as receipts

class FixedDateTime(datetime):
    @classmethod
    def now(cls, tz=None):
        return cls(2026, 11, 7, 12, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc)

@pytest.fixture
def order():
    return SimpleNamespace(id='A-17', total=42, email='buyer@example.test')

def fail_mail(*args):
    raise AssertionError('mail sent')

def test_positive_order_sends_receipt(monkeypatch, order):
    sent = []
    monkeypatch.setattr(receipts, 'datetime', FixedDateTime)
    monkeypatch.setattr(receipts.settings, 'DRY_RUN', False, raising=False)
    monkeypatch.setattr(receipts, 'send_mail', lambda *args: sent.append(args))
    assert receipts.send_receipt(order) == 'sent'
    assert sent == [('buyer@example.test', 'Receipt', 'Order A-17 total 42 at 2026-11-07T12:00:00+00:00')]

def test_zero_total_is_skipped(monkeypatch, order):
    order.total = 0
    monkeypatch.setattr(receipts, 'send_mail', fail_mail)
    assert receipts.send_receipt(order) == 'skipped'

def test_dry_run_does_not_send(monkeypatch, order):
    monkeypatch.setattr(receipts, 'datetime', FixedDateTime)
    monkeypatch.setattr(receipts.settings, 'DRY_RUN', True, raising=False)
    monkeypatch.setattr(receipts, 'send_mail', fail_mail)
    assert receipts.send_receipt(order) == 'dry-run'

This test is a contract, not a unit test of helpers. It survives the extraction. It also gives you a failure oracle.

Step 3: Prove the test can fail

Run the test once. Then change one branch and run it again. The test must fail. Revert the branch.

python -m pytest tests/test_receipts_contract.py -q
# temporarily change 'skipped' to 'sent'
python -m pytest tests/test_receipts_contract.py -q  # must fail
git checkout -- app/receipts.py

A passing test with no failure history is a weak gate. One mutation is enough for this check. Keep it small and revert it immediately.

Step 4: Add a diff budget script

The budget turns review capacity into a command. The numbers are examples. Pick a budget your team can review in one sitting.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
'''Fail a refactor diff that is too large to review.'''
import argparse
import subprocess
import sys

def parse_numstat(text):
    prod_files, prod_lines, deleted_tests = [], 0, 0
    for row in text.splitlines():
        add, delete, path = row.split('\t', 2)
        if path.startswith('tests/'):
            if delete != '-' and int(delete) > 0:
                deleted_tests += int(delete)
            continue
        if path.startswith('scripts/') or path.endswith('.md'):
            continue
        prod_files.append(path)
        if add != '-' and delete != '-':
            prod_lines += int(add) + int(delete)
    return prod_files, prod_lines, deleted_tests

def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument('--max-lines', type=int, default=20)
    p.add_argument('--max-files', type=int, default=2)
    p.add_argument('--base', default='HEAD')
    a = p.parse_args()
    text = subprocess.check_output(['git', 'diff', '--numstat', a.base], text=True)
    files, lines, deleted_tests = parse_numstat(text)
    print(f'production files={len(files)} lines={lines} deleted_test_lines={deleted_tests}')
    if len(files) > a.max_files or lines > a.max_lines:
        print('BUDGET EXCEEDED: split the refactor before review.', file=sys.stderr)
        return 1
    if deleted_tests > 0:
        print('BUDGET EXCEEDED: deleted test lines.', file=sys.stderr)
        return 1
    return 0

if __name__ == '__main__':
    raise SystemExit(main())

Run it before and after the change. Include new files with git add -N so the diff sees them.

git add -N app/receipts.py
python scripts/diff_budget.py --max-lines 20 --max-files 2
Signal Example threshold Action
Production files changed > 2 Split the change
Production lines changed > 20 Stop and review
Deleted test lines > 0 Reject
Contract test failures > 0 Revert

This table is a guardrail, not a correctness proof. A small diff can still be wrong. A large diff is harder to review, so it needs a different plan.

Step 5: Make the smallest safe change

Inject the clock, setting, and mailer with defaults. Existing call sites keep working. The contract test stays unchanged.

# app/receipts.py after one seam change
from datetime import datetime
from django.conf import settings
from .mail import send_mail

def send_receipt(order, *, now=None, dry_run=None, mailer=None):
    if order.total <= 0:
        return 'skipped'
    now = now or datetime.now
    dry_run = settings.DRY_RUN if dry_run is None else dry_run
    mailer = mailer or send_mail
    body = f'Order {order.id} total {order.total} at {now().isoformat()}'
    if dry_run:
        return 'dry-run'
    mailer(order.email, 'Receipt', body)
    return 'sent'

This patch touches one function and adds no call-site edits. The test can now pass an explicit clock later. That is a separate change.

If the patch changes a call site, reject it. If it reformats the file, reject it. If it renames helpers, reject it. The point is one seam, not a cleanup pass.

Step 6: Put a constrained model behind a stop condition

MonkeyCode is the project behind this outreach. Its operator describes it as an open-source project and states that the offer includes free model access and a free server option, including 10 million free tokens. Verify current terms before you rely on them.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The product is relevant here only as a constrained patch runner. The workflow still stands without it. Use it to draft a unified diff from three inputs: the target file, the contract test, and the budget.

Use a narrow prompt:

Return a unified diff only.
Change one function in app/receipts.py.
Do not touch call sites, comments, imports, or formatting.
Preserve behavior for all existing callers.
The patch must fit 20 changed lines and 2 production files.

Then run the two gates in a clean environment:

python -m pytest tests/test_receipts_contract.py -q
python scripts/diff_budget.py --max-lines 20 --max-files 2

The free server option is useful for that clean run. The free model access is useful for the draft. Neither replaces the test or the budget. The model is not the authority.

If you test this workflow, run the two commands on the free server and keep the budget output with the diff.

Who should not use this workflow

  • Teams with no runnable test harness. You cannot freeze behavior you cannot execute.
  • Code that cannot leave your network. Use local tooling only.
  • Cross-module dependency cycles. That needs a design change, not one seam.
  • Regulated code with strict provenance rules. Get approval before using any external service.
  • Teams that need an SLA. A free option is not a support contract.

Limitations

A diff budget is a review guardrail, not a correctness proof. Characterization tests freeze current behavior, including current bugs. Fix bugs in a separate change. AI-generated patches can be syntactically valid and behaviorally wrong. Free offers can change, so verify the terms yourself. The budget numbers are examples, not universal constants.

The win is not a cleaner repo in one day. The win is a reviewable change with a failure oracle. Start with one seam, one contract test, and one budget check.

title: Route Agent Patches to the Cheapest Gate That Can Catch Them
description:
Route Agent Patches to the Cheapest Gate That Can Catch Them

The cheapest reliable verification for an agent patch is a function of the diff's shape, not of who wrote it. Most review pipelines miss this and run the entire matrix on everything. That is not rigor. It is a way of postponing a decision until the queue decides for you.

Patch volume went up. Reviewer attention did not. The only sustainable response is to spend expensive gates where they can actually fail, and cheap gates everywhere else.

The failure mode: uniform verification

A one-line docstring edit and a lockfile bump currently cost the same wall-clock time. Both wait behind the same suite. Both get the same treatment.

The result is predictable. The suite gets slower, the queue gets longer, and people start merging on red because "it's probably the flaky one." Any of that sound familiar? Uniform verification does not buy safety — it buys the habit of ignoring failures.

A patch router fixes the ordering, not the tests. It answers one question before anything runs: what is the minimum set of gates that could plausibly catch a defect in this diff?

Four signals that actually change the gate set

Diff size alone is a weak proxy. These signals are stronger, and all four are extractable with git diff alone.

Signal Why it changes the tier
Production files changed with no test file changed Nothing in the diff demonstrates the new behaviour was exercised
Assertions added vs. removed Tests edited without a new assertion are often tests edited to pass
Dependency or CI surface touched Blast radius leaves the repo; local gates cannot see it
Change size on production files A 4-line change and a 400-line change fail differently

Note what is not on the list: commit message, model name, author confidence. None of those are evidence.

The router

Reference implementation below, standard library only, no benchmark claims attached. It reads a diff range and prints the tier plus the gate list.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""triage.py - emit the cheapest verification tier that can catch this diff.

Usage: python3 triage.py [base_ref]   (default: HEAD~1)
Output: JSON on stdout.
"""
import json
import re
import subprocess
import sys

TEST_PATH = re.compile(
    r"(^|/)(tests?|spec|__tests__)(/|$)"
    r"|(_test\.py$|^test_.*\.py$|\.test\.[jt]sx?$|\.spec\.[jt]sx?$)"
)
SRC_PATH = re.compile(r"\.(py|ts|tsx|js|jsx|go|rs|java|kt|rb|php|cs)$")
DEP_PATH = re.compile(
    r"(^|/)(package-lock\.json|pnpm-lock\.yaml|poetry\.lock"
    r"|requirements.*\.txt|pyproject\.toml|go\.sum|Cargo\.lock)$"
)
CI_PATH = re.compile(
    r"(^|/)(\.github/workflows/|\.gitlab-ci\.yml|Makefile|tox\.ini|noxfile\.py)"
)
ASSERT_LINE = re.compile(r"\+(?!\+\+).*\b(assert\b|expect\s*\(|require\.\w+\()")

GATES = {
    0: ["lint"],
    1: ["lint", "unit-suite"],
    2: ["lint", "unit-suite", "property-checks", "fixture-lock"],
    3: ["lint", "unit-suite", "property-checks", "fixture-lock",
        "order-permutations", "freeze-audit", "human-signoff"],
}


def git(*args):
    return subprocess.run(("git",) + args, capture_output=True,
                          text=True, check=True).stdout


def numstat(base):
    rows = []
    for line in git("diff", "--numstat", base, "HEAD").splitlines():
        add, dele, path = line.split("\t", 2)
        rows.append({"path": path,
                     "add": 0 if add == "-" else int(add),
                     "del": 0 if dele == "-" else int(dele)})
    return rows


def signals(rows, base):
    src = [r for r in rows
           if SRC_PATH.search(r["path"]) and not TEST_PATH.search(r["path"])]
    tst = [r for r in rows if TEST_PATH.search(r["path"])]
    added = removed = 0
    for line in git("diff", "-U0", base, "HEAD", "--").splitlines():
        if ASSERT_LINE.match(line):
            added += 1
        elif line.startswith("-") and not line.startswith("---") \
                and ASSERT_LINE.match("+" + line[1:]):
            removed += 1
    return {
        "prod_files": len(src),
        "test_files": len(tst),
        "src_churn": sum(r["add"] + r["del"] for r in src),
        "asserts_added": added,
        "asserts_removed": removed,
        "deps_changed": any(DEP_PATH.search(r["path"]) for r in rows),
        "ci_changed": any(CI_PATH.search(r["path"]) for r in rows),
    }


def tier(s):
    if s["deps_changed"] or s["ci_changed"]:
        return 3, "dependency or CI surface moved"
    if s["prod_files"] and not s["test_files"]:
        return (2 if s["src_churn"] > 30 else 1), "production change, no test change"
    if s["prod_files"] and s["test_files"]:
        if s["asserts_added"] == 0:
            return 3, "tests edited but no assertion added"
        if s["asserts_removed"] > s["asserts_added"]:
            return 3, "more assertions removed than added"
        return 2, "production and test change together"
    if s["test_files"]:
        return 1, "test-only change"
    return 0, "docs or comments only"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    base = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "HEAD~1"
    sig = signals(numstat(base), base)
    t, why = tier(sig)
    print(json.dumps({"tier": t, "reason": why,
                      "gates": GATES[t], "signals": sig}, indent=2))

Run it before you run anything else:

python3 triage.py origin/main

Sample output for an agent patch that edited three tests and removed two assertions without adding any:

{
  "tier": 3,
  "reason": "tests edited but no assertion added",
  "gates": ["lint", "unit-suite", "property-checks", "fixture-lock", "order-permutations", "freeze-audit", "human-signoff"],
  "signals": {"prod_files": 0, "test_files": 3, "src_churn": 0, "asserts_added": 0, "asserts_removed": 2, "deps_changed": false, "ci_changed": false}
}

That path escalates on purpose. A patch that only touches tests and only removes assertions is the exact shape you want a human to look at.

Wire it in, in five steps

  1. Land triage.py in scripts/ and make it a one-liner in your CI job, before the test step.
  2. Make the runner read the JSON and short-circuit. Tier 0 runs lint and stops.
  3. Keep tier 3 as a blocking human gate. Do not let it auto-merge on green.
  4. Log tier and reason next to every build. After two weeks you will know whether the thresholds match your repo.
  5. Tune the 30 in src_churn > 30 from that log, not from intuition.

The runner itself is boring, which is the point:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
python3 scripts/triage.py "${1:-HEAD~1}" > /tmp/plan.json
cat /tmp/plan.json
tier=$(python3 -c 'import json;print(json.load(open("/tmp/plan.json"))["tier"])')
case "$tier" in
  0) ./scripts/lint.sh ;;
  1) ./scripts/lint.sh && ./scripts/test.sh ;;
  2) ./scripts/lint.sh && ./scripts/test.sh \
       && ./scripts/properties.sh && ./scripts/fixture-lock.sh ;;
  *) ./scripts/full-matrix.sh ;;
restart_placeholder
esac

Where a free model tier actually fits

One step in this workflow is high-volume, low-stakes, and wrong a lot: drafting the candidate property list for a tier-2 patch. That is a good job for a free model tier, because every draft is validated by an executable check before it counts.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The second fit is the runner. Tier 0 and tier 1 gates are cheap and should never queue behind the main CI fleet, so an always-on free server running the fast path is a reasonable use of one. Both availability claims — the free model access and the free server option — come from the project operator; check the current terms on the project page yourself before you plan capacity around them.

What must stay outside the model's hands: the tier decision, the pass/fail verdict, and the human sign-off. Those are the parts where a plausible wrong answer is expensive.

Property checks by patch shape

A property that cannot be executed is not a property. Keep the list short, executable, and tied to the diff.

Patch shape Property to try first Cheap check
Pure transform Round-trip: decode(encode(x)) == x 200 generated inputs
Parser or tokenizer Never raises on arbitrary bytes; returns a result or a typed error 1k fuzz iterations
State machine No transition lands outside the declared state enum Enumerate all edges
Adapter around an external API Every timeout path returns the documented error type Stub the client, inject failure
Cache or memo layer Read-after-write never returns a stale value for the same key Handler-level test

If tier 2 cannot produce at least one executable property for the changed file, that is itself a signal. It usually means the patch boundary is unclear, not that the code is safe.

Freezes need an expiry the router can read

An unexpiring flaky-test freeze is just a deleted test with extra ceremony. Give each record an owner and a date, and let the router see it.

{
  "test": "tests/test_billing.py::test_proration_rounding",
  "owner": "finley",
  "reason": "upstream FX feed returns stale rates after 22:00 UTC",
  "frozen_at": "2026-10-30",
  "expires": "2026-11-13"
}

Add one rule on top of the router: if any freeze record whose test path overlaps the diff has an expires in the past, force tier 3. Expired freezes are not noise. They are unverified claims that nobody has revisited.

Limitations and who should not use this

The heuristics read diff shape, not semantics. A four-line change to an auth check can be more dangerous than a 400-line refactor, and this router will happily assign it tier 1. Reviewers are still the last gate.

Path regexes break on monorepos with co-located tests (foo.test.ts next to foo.ts in the same directory is fine; __tests__ with a custom convention is not). Adjust the patterns before you trust the tier. The assertion counter is a lexical match and will miss custom assertion helpers.

Skip this approach if you have a mandatory full-matrix policy you cannot change, if your suite is fast enough that running everything is genuinely cheap, or if you work in a domain where every diff needs full review regardless of shape. In those cases the router adds a layer without removing work.

Start narrow

Run the router in log-only mode for a week. Compare the tier it would have assigned against what you actually ran. You will find two or three misroutes, fix the regexes, and then the short-circuit is safe to turn on.

If you want to try it with a free model drafting the property lists and a small always-on machine running the tier-0 and tier-1 path, the project page for MonkeyCode lists the current free model access and free server option — verify the terms there first, and start with tier 1 on a repository you already trust.

title: Receipt Messaging: Comparing Email and SMS API Providers Through Retention Costs
description:
For a developer tools service sending an order receipt after payment settles, compare email and SMS APIs by the work required to preserve and reconcile evidence. The working budget should include message attempts, integration maintenance, retained notification records, and investigation time. A send request is only one part of that budget.

TL;DR: Choose the integration whose acknowledgment, retry, and status semantics require the least application code to explain what happened to each settled order. Keep an application-owned receipt identity and a bounded audit trail. Evaluate email and SMS separately before deciding whether maintaining both channels earns its operational cost.

Consider an explicitly hypothetical retention calculation: one receipt generates three attempt records, each occupying 2 KB in the application's chosen representation. Retaining those records for 30 days requires 180 KB-days per receipt, excluding indexes, replicas, and backups. Cutting that window to 10 days reduces the modeled footprint to 60 KB-days; preventing one unnecessary attempt reduces it to 120 KB-days at the original window. Neither number is a provider quote or a benchmark. In this model, the retention window is the larger multiplier, although actual billing and engineering effort require separate measurements.

Count the evidence.

What does the receipt bill actually buy?

The useful comparison starts with a settled order, not a list of messaging features. Define the desired outcome as a receipt associated with the correct settlement, sent to the intended recipient through the chosen channel, with enough evidence to investigate an ambiguous result. Then account for the effort required to reach that outcome: implementing the integration, reviewing its security boundaries, maintaining templates, processing status events, handling uncertain attempts, and answering support questions after detailed records expire. For a backend team accustomed to reconciling ledgers, this is a familiar accounting problem, except that the external communication cannot be treated as an atomic ledger entry.

Storage is measurable; investigation effort needs observation. Record both during the integration exercise rather than pretending that a short request example establishes total effort.

The arithmetic above deliberately isolates retained attempt data. It does not establish that storage dominates a real deployment's costs. The engineering question is which term dominates your proposed design, and whether the integration exposes enough information to measure it without retaining entire message bodies indefinitely. If initial adapter work dominates instead, shortening retention will barely change the decision. This distinction keeps price from becoming a substitute for understanding the system.

How should teams compare email and SMS API providers for receipts?

For this workload, “best provider” should mean the smallest justified integration burden under explicit receipt requirements. Evaluate candidates against the same acceptance exercise, and attach a documentation reference or a recorded test result to every completed comparison cell. An unknown remains an unknown; it should not quietly become an affirmative feature claim.

Contract to establish Email integration exercise SMS integration exercise Work to count
Meaning of acceptance Identify precisely what the send acknowledgment establishes Identify precisely what the send acknowledgment establishes Application states needed beyond acknowledgment
Uncertain request outcome Determine the documented handling of a lost response Determine the documented handling of a lost response Duplicate prevention and investigation code
Status evidence Map documented status events to internal receipt states Map documented status events to internal receipt states Authentication, deduplication, and reconciliation logic
Retention boundary Establish what evidence remains after local expiry Establish what evidence remains after local expiry Support procedures and retained sensitive data

This is a comparison method, not a claim that all APIs implement those contracts identically. For each candidate, inspect the scope and expiry of any documented idempotency mechanism, the meaning of its status fields, and the available reconciliation interface. A candidate that needs fewer translation rules may reduce integration effort, but a candidate with a longer evidence history may simplify investigations. Those benefits can conflict.

Keep channel choice separate from failover policy. Sending an SMS merely because an email request timed out creates another external action before the first action's outcome is understood. Require a deliberate business rule for that transition, including what the recipient should see if both messages arrive. Automatic escalation otherwise turns uncertainty into additional retained evidence and potentially duplicated communication.

Reduce duplicated evidence at the settlement boundary

An exactly-once mindset begins with an application invariant: one logical receipt identity per settled order and receipt purpose. It does not require claiming exactly-once delivery to a human. For an illustrative developer tools purchase, an order such as order_tools_42 can have one logical receipt record and multiple separately identified attempts; a repeated settlement notification should resolve to that same logical receipt rather than manufacture another receipt identity.

Design the settlement transition to persist a durable notification intent within the same transaction boundary where that is available. Where settlement evidence crosses systems, define a reconciliation procedure before promising atomic behavior. The receipt worker then processes the durable intent, records an attempt, and associates any external identifier with that attempt. A unique application identity protects the local invariant; whether it also prevents a repeated external send depends on the external API's documented contract.

The dangerous gap is small: the send may have succeeded while the worker failed to record its response. A local uniqueness constraint cannot establish what happened outside the database. Mark that attempt as uncertain, preserve its correlation evidence, and follow the integration's documented recovery path. Retrying blindly would make the audit trail longer without making the original outcome clearer.

Keep uncertainty explicit.

The following Go example makes the retention model executable. Its inputs are the hypothetical assumptions from the opening; the calculation excludes infrastructure overhead and says nothing about actual provider charges.

package main

import "fmt"

func retainedKBdays(attempts, kbPerAttempt, days int64) int64 {
    return attempts * kbPerAttempt * days
}

func main() {
    fmt.Println(retainedKBdays(3, 2, 30)) // 180 KB-days
    fmt.Println(retainedKBdays(3, 2, 10)) // 60 KB-days
    fmt.Println(retainedKBdays(2, 2, 30)) // 120 KB-days
}

Store the receipt identity, settlement reference, attempt identity, template version, timestamps, external correlation identifier when available, and status transitions needed for reconciliation. Treat recipient addresses and message contents as separate retention decisions. Keeping a template version helps explain which rendering rules applied, but it cannot reconstruct a historical message if the input data has changed or expired. That loss matters when choosing how much evidence to preserve.

Make the integration prove its maintenance cost

Before deployment, exercise duplicate settlement input, a lost send response, repeated status events, and a late status event after local detail expires. These are proposed test cases, not reported incidents. For each case, inspect the resulting receipt record and ask whether a support engineer can explain the outcome without consulting unstructured logs or sending the message again to see what happens.

Make the release small enough to reconcile manually. Observe outstanding intents, uncertain attempts, duplicate events suppressed, and receipts awaiting reconciliation; define what each counter measures so that a healthy request-success rate cannot conceal an accumulating queue. Include a rollback procedure for the worker and template release, with a clear rule for intents already claimed. The integration-effort comparison should count these deployment and maintenance obligations alongside the initial adapter implementation.

There is also a compliance boundary. RFC 8058 specifies a one-click unsubscribe mechanism for list email, including the List-Unsubscribe and List-Unsubscribe-Post fields and associated authentication requirements. It does not establish the legal classification of a particular receipt, provide SMS consent rules, or set a universal retention period. Keep transactional receipt content and any proposed promotional content distinguishable, and obtain the applicable policy decision before treating one channel's unsubscribe behavior as sufficient for another channel or message purpose.

An audit trail supports an investigation. It does not certify compliance.

Decide what expires before selecting the API

Set separate retention rules for message bodies, recipient details, attempt records, and the underlying financial records. Tie each rule to an operational need and the applicable requirements; the illustrative 10-day and 30-day windows above are analytical assumptions, not retention recommendations. Include indexes, backups, exports, and copies in the deletion design, or the apparent reduction in the primary record store will misrepresent what remains.

The trade-off is explicit: compact metadata reduces retained detail but limits historical reconstruction. This design is not suitable for a workflow that must reproduce the exact receipt after its body and inputs expire; that workflow needs a separately governed content archive. The limitation is evidentiary, and adding another channel does not remove it.

For a receipt service, a defensible decision rule is to prefer the candidate that satisfies the required channel and evidence contracts with the fewest maintained states, recovery paths, and sensitive-data copies. Document any deliberate exception, such as accepting more adapter work to obtain evidence needed for a specific support obligation. No ranking survives a change in those obligations.

The final retention decision should name the evidence the team will stop keeping. If rendered bodies and recipient snapshots expire while compact attempt metadata remains, support can still trace the logical receipt and its recorded transitions, but may lose the ability to reproduce its exact wording and destination at send time. That is the investigation cost of the smaller archive. Accept it explicitly, and keep any legally required financial evidence under its own retention policy.

Further reading

References:

  • RFC 8058, Signaling One-Click Functionality for List Email Headers: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8058

title: I Built a 400-Item Front-End Checklist (and Taught My AI Assistant to Use It)
description:
Most launch bugs aren't exotic. They're the basics — a missing meta description,
a blocking script, a form without labels — missed because nobody had a list.

So I built one, and made it free: the Front-End Checklist.
Try it: https://checklist.shinningtechservices.com/

The bugs that ship are boring

I've spent years shipping front-end work across banking, healthcare, and
government. The pattern never changes: the bugs that slip through to production
are almost never clever edge cases. They're the checklist items nobody checked —
the alt text, the tap target, the meta tag, the label on the form field.

A list doesn't make you a better developer. It makes the boring stuff
impossible to forget. That's the whole idea.

What the checklist covers

400 items across 13 sections — accessibility, performance, SEO, security,
privacy, testing, and more. Every item has a priority, documentation links,
and suggested tools, so it's a work plan, not just a wall of text.

The audit engine

Paste any public URL and the audit runs up to 246 automatic checks. You get a
score, and failures sorted High, Medium, Low, each with the evidence behind it.

Some results are flagged "verify" — heuristics, not certainties. A machine can
tell you a label is missing; it can't tell you whether the label makes sense.
The score is a starting point for a human, not a verdict.

From audit to work plan

One click ticks every passing item straight into your checklist, so the audit
becomes the work plan. Export the report as Markdown or PDF, or share a link.

Checklist progress saves on your device. No account needed.

The agent skill and MCP server

There's a free agent skill for Claude Code, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot, and an
MCP server on npm:

npm i -g frontend-checklist-mcp

Your AI assistant can audit a page, explain each failure, fix the code, and
re-audit. Audit → explain → fix → re-audit, in one loop. Free API, no key.

What it can't do (honest limits)

Single page only. No JavaScript execution. No Core Web Vitals, and no
real-device or screen-reader testing. It catches the checkable basics; the
rest still needs a human and a real browser.

One note: audit runs are logged (URL, score, time) for analytics.

What's next

The checks still missing, a CLI, CI plans — and contributions. It's open
source (MIT) at Github

It audited my own agency site at 88% — the remaining failures are mine to fix,
and they're on my list. I'd genuinely like to know what it misses. What
checks would you add, and which ones shouldn't be automatic?

title: Test Redis Streams Producers and Consumers with Signadot Sandboxes
description:
Read this tutorial on Signadot docs.

Sandboxes route a request to the right version of a service by its routing key, which travels in request headers. A Redis stream breaks that chain: nobody calls a consumer, it reads entries on its own. So the routing key has to travel inside each stream entry, and every consumer, baseline and sandboxed alike, has to decide whether an entry is meant for it.

This tutorial deploys a small Python app to your Kubernetes cluster. A producer appends messages to the Redis stream demo:messages, and a consumer reads the stream and calls a notifier. You fork each of the three services into a sandbox, bundle them in a route group, and watch each message reach exactly the right version of each service, on one shared Redis and one shared stream.

Full source: signadot/examples/selective-consumption-with-redis-streams/python

How Redis Streams changes the isolation problem

Deploy a changed consumer next to the baseline and leave everything else alone, and the two end up in the same consumer group. Within a group, Redis hands each entry to whichever consumer calls XREADGROUP next, without looking at the routing key, so the sandbox silently takes a share of everyone's work and acknowledges it. The example avoids that in four steps:

  1. A consumer group per sandbox. The baseline reads through demo-consumers; a sandbox reads through demo-consumers-<routing key>, created at $ so it sees new entries only. Every group receives every entry.
  2. The routing key inside the entry. Stream entries have no headers, so the producer adds the OpenTelemetry context (traceparent and baggage) to each entry as extra fields, and the consumer reads it back out.
  3. A check per entry, on both sides. Each consumer asks the Signadot Routes API which routing keys belong to sandboxes of the consumer Deployment. The baseline skips those keys; a sandbox processes only its own key and the keys of route groups it is in.
  4. An acknowledgement for every entry. Processed or skipped, every entry gets an XACK, so nothing stays pending.

The Redis Streams integration guide covers the reasoning in depth, along with the alternative of a stream per sandbox and the operational details.

What you will deploy

Everything runs in the redis-streams-demo namespace:

  • producer (port 4000): POST /api/publish appends a message to the stream demo:messages. It also serves the demo UI and an event log, GET /api/events, that shows which workload handled each step of a message.
  • consumer: reads demo:messages through a consumer group and calls the notifier for each message it processes. It has no Service, because nothing calls it.
  • notifier (port 4001): POST /api/notify records a notification.
  • redis: Redis 7.4, holding the stream and the demo's event log.

The three services run from one image, and the first argument picks which one starts (python main.py producer, consumer or notifier). The producer and notifier Deployments carry the sidecar.signadot.com/inject: "true" annotation, so DevMesh can route the requests they receive to a sandbox. The consumer does not need it: no request ever reaches the consumer, and which copy handles an entry is decided by consumer groups and the per-entry check instead.

The files that matter:

selective-consumption-with-redis-streams/python/
├── app/                  # the three services: plain redis-py, Flask and requests
├── platform_redis/       # everything Signadot-specific
│   ├── client.py         # Redis: XADD with the OpenTelemetry context
│   ├── consumer.py       # StreamConsumer: groups, per-entry check, XACK, recovery
│   └── routes.py         # Routes API client
├── k8s/                  # Redis and the three Deployments
├── signadot/
│   ├── sandboxes/        # consumer.yaml, notifier.yaml, producer.yaml
│   └── routegroups/      # redis-streams-demo.yaml
├── Dockerfile
└── main.py

Before you begin

Info: Prerequisites

  • A Kubernetes cluster with the Signadot Operator installed.
  • The Signadot CLI, logged in with signadot auth login.
  • kubectl pointed at that cluster, and jq.
  • Docker, and a container registry your cluster can pull from.

1. Build the image

The three services run from one image. Build it and push it to your registry:

git clone https://github.com/signadot/examples.git
cd examples/selective-consumption-with-redis-streams/python

export IMAGE=docker.io/your-user/redis-streams-demo-python:latest  # your registry
docker build -t $IMAGE .
docker push $IMAGE

Note: Any registry your cluster can pull from works

docker.io/your-user/... is a placeholder. When you build images of your own services this way, push them to a private repository and give the cluster pull access to it, for example with an image pull secret.

If your cluster's nodes have a different CPU architecture than your machine (for example an Apple silicon Mac and an x86 cluster), add --platform linux/amd64 to docker build. On a local cluster that runs images straight from your Docker daemon, you can skip the push.

2. Deploy the demo

Point the manifests at your image, then deploy Redis and the three services:

sed -i.orig "s|image: redis-streams-demo-python:latest|image: $IMAGE|" k8s/*.yaml

kubectl create namespace redis-streams-demo
kubectl apply -f k8s/
kubectl -n redis-streams-demo wait --for=condition=available deploy --all --timeout=180s

The sed command keeps the original manifests as k8s/*.yaml.orig, which kubectl apply ignores.

The consumer's Deployment tells the Routes API which baseline workload it is, and only reports ready once it can actually route (k8s/consumer.yaml):

k8s/consumer.yaml

          env:
            # Which baseline workload this is, for the Signadot Routes API.
            - name: SIGNADOT_BASELINE_KIND
              value: Deployment
            - name: SIGNADOT_BASELINE_NAME
              value: consumer
            - name: SIGNADOT_BASELINE_NAMESPACE
              valueFrom:
                fieldRef:
                  fieldPath: metadata.namespace
          # Ready once the consumer group exists and routing rules are loaded.
          readinessProbe:
            exec:
              command: ["cat", "/tmp/ready"]
            periodSeconds: 2

So when kubectl wait returns, the consumer group demo-consumers exists and the consumer has its first answer from the Routes API. A sandbox forked from this Deployment inherits the same variables, and the Signadot Operator adds SIGNADOT_SANDBOX_NAME and SIGNADOT_SANDBOX_ROUTING_KEY through the sandbox downward API.

3. How the code carries the routing key

The app code is plain redis-py, Flask and requests. Everything Signadot-specific lives in platform_redis/, a thin wrapper over redis-py of the kind a platform team would ship, so app developers don't have to think about sandboxes.

The application code

The producer uses platform_redis.Redis, a drop-in redis.Redis (app/producer.py):

app/producer.py

redis_client = platform_redis.Redis.from_url(REDIS_URL, decode_responses=True)
...
entry_id = redis_client.xadd(STREAM, message, maxlen=10_000, approximate=True)

The consumer hands a handler to platform_redis.StreamConsumer (app/consumer.py). The handler receives the entry's application fields and calls the notifier with plain requests:

app/consumer.py

def handle(entry_id, fields):
    message = {"id": fields.get("id", ""), "body": fields.get("body", "")}
    if PROCESSOR_VERSION == "v2":
        message["body"] = message["body"].upper()
    events.record(f"Consumed message from {STREAM} with processor {PROCESSOR_VERSION}: "
                  f"\"{message['body']}\"", message)
    # The requests instrumentation adds the entry's baggage (and routing key)
    # to this call.
    requests.post(f"{NOTIFIER_URL}/api/notify", json=message, timeout=10).raise_for_status()


def main():
    redis_client = platform_redis.Redis.from_url(REDIS_URL, decode_responses=True)
    consumer = platform_redis.StreamConsumer(
        redis_client, stream=STREAM, group=CONSUMER_GROUP, name=socket.gethostname(),
        on_ready=lambda: pathlib.Path("/tmp/ready").touch())
    consumer.run(handle)

PROCESSOR_VERSION is the "change" this tutorial tests: v1 keeps the message body as is, and v2 uppercases it.

Carrying the key on every hop

Underneath, OpenTelemetry carries the routing key on every hop. No tracing backend is involved: the instrumentation alone propagates the W3C trace context and baggage.

  • HTTP: the Flask and requests instrumentation read and forward the baggage header, which holds sd-routing-key.
  • Into Redis: stream entries have no headers, so platform_redis.Redis.xadd adds the OpenTelemetry context (traceparent and baggage) to the entry as extra fields.
  • Out of Redis: StreamConsumer reads the context back from those fields and makes it current while the handler runs, so the handler's call to the notifier carries the key too.

Selective consumption

StreamConsumer also decides which consumer processes each entry:

  • The baseline reads through the group demo-consumers. A sandbox reads through its own group, demo-consumers-<routing key>, created at $ so it sees new entries only. Every group gets every entry.
  • It asks the Signadot Routes API which routing keys belong to sandboxes of the consumer Deployment. The baseline skips those keys; a sandbox processes only its own key and the keys of route groups it is in.
  • It acknowledges (XACK) every entry, processed or skipped, so nothing stays pending.

How platform_redis works, after the walkthrough, goes through the code that does this.

4. Send a message without a routing key

Connect your machine to the cluster, so that cluster service names resolve locally (this asks for your password):

export CLUSTER=my-cluster  # your cluster's name, from: signadot cluster list
signadot local connect --cluster=$CLUSTER

Note: Use signadot local connect, not kubectl port-forward

Port-forwarding sends traffic straight to a pod and bypasses DevMesh, so a request carrying the producer sandbox's routing key would stay on the baseline producer. signadot local connect sends your requests through the cluster's services, where DevMesh routes them.

Publish a message:

PRODUCER=http://producer.redis-streams-demo.svc:4000
curl -X POST $PRODUCER/api/publish -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"messageID": "m1", "messageBody": "hello m1"}'

Every service writes what it did to an event log that the producer serves. Define a helper that shows which workload handled each step of a message:

trail() {
  curl -s $PRODUCER/api/events | jq -r --arg id "$1" '.events[]
    | select(.context.message.id == $id)
    | "\(.context.baselineWorkload.name) (\(.context.sandboxName | if . == "" then "baseline" else . end)): \(.logEntry)"'
}
trail m1

Output

producer (baseline): Publishing message to Redis stream demo:messages
consumer (baseline): Consumed message from demo:messages with processor v1: "hello m1"
notifier (baseline): Sent notification: "hello m1"

The event log is a second stream, demo:event-log, that exists only for this helper and the demo UI. Each event records the workload's baseline name and, in a sandbox, the sandbox name.

5. Create the sandboxes

Each sandbox forks one service. The consumer sandbox also sets PROCESSOR_VERSION=v2, the "change" under test, which uppercases message bodies (signadot/sandboxes/consumer.yaml):

name: redis-streams-consumer
spec:
  description: "consumer sandbox for the Redis Streams demo (processor v2)"
  cluster: "@{cluster}"
  labels:
    demo: redis-streams
  forks:
    - forkOf:
        kind: Deployment
        namespace: redis-streams-demo
        name: consumer
      customizations:
        env:
          # The change under test: v2 uppercases message bodies.
          - name: PROCESSOR_VERSION
            value: v2
  defaultRouteGroup:
    endpoints:
      - name: producer
        target: http://producer.redis-streams-demo.svc:4000

The fork runs the same image as the baseline. In a real change it would run your branch's image instead. Every sandbox exposes the producer as an endpoint, so each one gets a preview URL for the demo UI. The route group bundles all three sandboxes under one routing key, by matching their demo: redis-streams label.

signadot sandbox apply -f signadot/sandboxes/consumer.yaml --set cluster=$CLUSTER
signadot sandbox apply -f signadot/sandboxes/notifier.yaml --set cluster=$CLUSTER
signadot sandbox apply -f signadot/sandboxes/producer.yaml --set cluster=$CLUSTER
signadot routegroup apply -f signadot/routegroups/redis-streams-demo.yaml --set cluster=$CLUSTER

Save the routing keys:

CONSUMER_KEY=$(signadot sandbox get redis-streams-consumer -o json | jq -r .routingKey)
NOTIFIER_KEY=$(signadot sandbox get redis-streams-notifier -o json | jq -r .routingKey)
PRODUCER_KEY=$(signadot sandbox get redis-streams-producer -o json | jq -r .routingKey)
GROUP_KEY=$(signadot routegroup get redis-streams-demo -o json | jq -r .routingKey)

6. Send messages with routing keys

Define a helper that publishes with a routing key in the baggage header, as a preview URL or the Signadot browser extension would:

publish() {
  curl -s -o /dev/null -X POST $PRODUCER/api/publish -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -H "baggage: sd-routing-key=$2" -d "{\"messageID\": \"$1\", \"messageBody\": \"hello $1\"}"
}

The consumer sandbox

The sandboxed consumer takes the message and runs v2. The baseline consumer skips it, and the notifier call goes back to the baseline notifier:

publish m2 $CONSUMER_KEY; sleep 1; trail m2

Output

producer (baseline): Publishing message to Redis stream demo:messages
consumer (redis-streams-consumer): Consumed message from demo:messages with processor v2: "HELLO M2"
notifier (baseline): Sent notification: "HELLO M2"

The notifier sandbox

The baseline consumer processes the message, and its call to the notifier lands on the sandbox: the routing key made it through Redis.

publish m3 $NOTIFIER_KEY; sleep 1; trail m3

Output

producer (baseline): Publishing message to Redis stream demo:messages
consumer (baseline): Consumed message from demo:messages with processor v1: "hello m3"
notifier (redis-streams-notifier): Sent notification: "hello m3"

The producer sandbox

The request goes to the sandboxed producer, which publishes to the same stream as the baseline, and the baseline consumer handles the entry:

publish m4 $PRODUCER_KEY; sleep 1; trail m4

Output

producer (redis-streams-producer): Publishing message to Redis stream demo:messages
consumer (baseline): Consumed message from demo:messages with processor v1: "hello m4"
notifier (baseline): Sent notification: "hello m4"

The route group

All three sandboxes handle the message:

publish m5 $GROUP_KEY; sleep 1; trail m5

Output

producer (redis-streams-producer): Publishing message to Redis stream demo:messages
consumer (redis-streams-consumer): Consumed message from demo:messages with processor v2: "HELLO M5"
notifier (redis-streams-notifier): Sent notification: "HELLO M5"

What each message did

Together, the five messages cover every combination:

Routing key producer consumer notifier
none (m1) baseline baseline (v1) baseline
consumer sandbox (m2) baseline sandbox (v2) baseline
notifier sandbox (m3) baseline baseline (v1) sandbox
producer sandbox (m4) sandbox baseline (v1) baseline
route group (m5) sandbox sandbox (v2) sandbox

The consumer groups and logs

Look at the stream's consumer groups:

kubectl -n redis-streams-demo exec deploy/redis -- redis-cli XINFO GROUPS demo:messages

There are two groups, demo-consumers and demo-consumers-<consumer key>, and both show pending 0: each group received every entry and acknowledged the ones it skipped. The baseline consumer's log shows each decision:

kubectl -n redis-streams-demo logs deploy/consumer | grep -E "processing|skipped"

Output

... processing 1792725846853-0 (routing key None)
... skipped 1792725891917-0 (routing key fv51lmqum5pts)
... processing 1792725892981-0 (routing key x8nxnyx7xcndj)
... processing 1792725894049-0 (routing key cv8sn8btqsjmw)
... skipped 1792725895106-0 (routing key srud7xvwuckny)

Your entry IDs and routing keys will differ. In order, these are m1 through m5: the baseline processes the message with no key, skips the consumer sandbox's key, processes the notifier and producer sandboxes' keys (neither of those sandboxes forks the consumer), and skips the route group's key, because the route group includes the consumer sandbox.

The sandboxed consumer's log is the mirror image:

kubectl -n redis-streams-demo logs -l signadot.com/sandbox-routing-key=$CONSUMER_KEY --tail=-1 | grep -E "processing|skipped"

7. Try it in the UI

The producer serves a UI that shows each message's trail as it happens. Open http://producer.redis-streams-demo.svc:4000 (it resolves while signadot local connect is running) and use the Signadot browser extension to pick a sandbox or the route group. You can also open the preview URL that signadot sandbox apply printed for each sandbox.

8. Clean up

Delete the route group and the sandboxes:

signadot routegroup delete redis-streams-demo
signadot sandbox delete redis-streams-consumer
signadot sandbox delete redis-streams-notifier
signadot sandbox delete redis-streams-producer

Redis doesn't remove a consumer group when its consumer goes away, so the consumer sandbox's group is still on the stream. With a Redis you keep, delete it yourself:

kubectl -n redis-streams-demo exec deploy/redis -- \
  redis-cli XGROUP DESTROY demo:messages demo-consumers-$CONSUMER_KEY

Then remove the demo and disconnect:

kubectl delete namespace redis-streams-demo
signadot local disconnect

How platform_redis works

Everything Signadot-specific is in three small files in platform_redis/.

Context in and out of entries

platform_redis.Redis overrides a single method. This is the whole of platform_redis/client.py:

platform_redis/client.py

class Redis(redis.Redis):
    def xadd(self, name, fields, *args, **kwargs):
        # Stream entries have no headers, so the W3C trace context and baggage
        # (which holds the Signadot routing key) travel as extra fields.
        carrier = {}
        propagate.inject(carrier)
        return super().xadd(name, {**fields, **carrier}, *args, **kwargs)

The OpenTelemetry Redis instrumentation does neither half of this: it only creates spans for Redis commands. That is why the wrapper exists. StreamConsumer reads the context back out, as shown below.

The consumer group

platform_redis/consumer.py picks the consumer group. A sandbox never joins the baseline's group:

platform_redis/consumer.py

        # Never join the baseline's group from a sandbox: within a group each
        # entry goes to only one consumer, regardless of routing key.
        if self.in_sandbox:
            self.group = f"{group}-{self.rules.sandbox_routing_key}"
        else:
            self.group = group

and creates it at the right place in the stream:

platform_redis/consumer.py

        # A sandbox starts at "$" (new entries only) instead of replaying the
        # stream; the baseline starts at "0" so nothing published before its
        # first start is missed.
        start = "$" if self.in_sandbox else "0"

Each entry

For each entry it reads, it extracts the context, decides whether the entry is meant for this workload, runs the handler with the entry's context current, and acknowledges the entry either way:

platform_redis/consumer.py

            ctx = propagate.extract(fields)
            routing_key = baggage.get_baggage(ROUTING_KEY, ctx)
            app_fields = {k: v for k, v in fields.items()
                          if k not in propagate.get_global_textmap().fields}
            if not self._should_process(routing_key):
                log.info("skipped %s (routing key %s)", entry_id, routing_key)
                return
            log.info("processing %s (routing key %s)", entry_id, routing_key)
            # Make the entry's context current, so the handler's outbound
            # calls carry the routing key.
            token = context.attach(ctx)
            ...
        finally:
            # Acknowledge processed and skipped entries alike, or they stay in
            # this group's pending entries list forever.
            self.client.xack(self.stream, self.group, entry_id)

The routing decision

The decision itself is in platform_redis/routes.py. A background thread polls the Routes API every 5 seconds for the routing rules of the consumer Deployment, and keeps two sets: the keys that route to any sandbox of it, and the keys that route to this sandbox (its own key and the keys of route groups it belongs to). The same check runs in the baseline and in a sandbox:

platform_redis/routes.py

    def should_process(self, routing_key):
        if self.in_sandbox:
            # Process only what is routed to this sandbox.
            return routing_key is not None and (
                routing_key == self.sandbox_routing_key or routing_key in self._own_keys)
        # Baseline: process everything except what a sandbox has claimed.
        return routing_key not in self._sandbox_keys

An entry with no routing key, or with a key that belongs to a sandbox of some other service, stays with the baseline consumer.

Pending entries

StreamConsumer also recovers entries left pending. At startup it reads its own pending entries (XREADGROUP with ID 0), and once a minute it uses XAUTOCLAIM to take over entries that another consumer, such as a pod that was replaced, read but never acknowledged.

Behavior and tradeoffs

  • Every group reads every entry. The data is stored once, but each sandboxed consumer reads the whole stream and skips most of it, so read load on Redis grows with the number of sandboxed consumers.
  • A failed handler drops its entry. StreamConsumer acknowledges every entry, including one whose handler raised an exception, so the failure is logged and the entry is not retried.
  • Routing changes reach the baseline within one poll. A sandbox knows its own routing key from the moment it starts, but the baseline learns about it on its next Routes API poll, up to 5 seconds later. In that window an entry with the new key can be processed by both.
  • A consumer needs the Routes API to start. It reads nothing, and stays not ready, until its first Routes API answer. After that it keeps the last rules it fetched if a refresh fails.
  • Sandbox consumer groups outlive their sandboxes. Destroy them with XGROUP DESTROY, as in Clean up.
  • decode_responses=True is required. StreamConsumer refuses a redis-py client created without it.
  • Pipelined XADD carries no context. Only platform_redis.Redis.xadd adds the context fields, so entries appended with pipeline().xadd(...) have no routing key and go to the baseline.

The integration guide covers these in more detail, along with leftover consumers, trimming, and how Redis Pub/Sub differs.

Adapt this to your stack

  1. Ship the wrapper in your shared code. Copy platform_redis/ into your platform library, or port its three pieces to your language: an XADD that adds the OpenTelemetry context, a Routes API client with a polling cache, and a stream consumer that picks the group, checks and acknowledges every entry, and recovers pending ones.
  2. Use it in your services. Producers create their client with platform_redis.Redis instead of redis.Redis. Consumers replace their XREADGROUP loop with StreamConsumer(...).run(handler); the handler receives the entry ID and the application fields.
  3. Instrument HTTP. Use the OpenTelemetry instrumentation for your HTTP server and client libraries, as app/otel.py does for Flask and requests, so the routing key reaches the producer and leaves the consumer.
  4. Set the baseline identity (SIGNADOT_BASELINE_KIND, SIGNADOT_BASELINE_NAME, SIGNADOT_BASELINE_NAMESPACE) on every consumer Deployment. Without it, StreamConsumer processes every entry, which is what you want in a cluster without Signadot.
  5. Enable DevMesh on the services that receive requests, as the producer and notifier Deployments do.
  6. Destroy a consumer sandbox's group in whatever deletes the sandbox.

Frequently asked questions

How do you test a Redis Streams consumer without a separate Redis?

Fork the consumer into a sandbox that reads the shared stream through a consumer group of its own. Every group receives every entry, the routing key travels inside each entry as OpenTelemetry baggage, and both the baseline and the sandboxed consumer check each entry against the Signadot Routes API, so exactly one of them processes it. Nothing about Redis or the stream is duplicated.

Which services does this tutorial run in sandboxes?

All three, one sandbox each: the producer, the consumer, and the notifier the consumer calls. The consumer sandbox sets PROCESSOR_VERSION=v2, which uppercases message bodies, as the change under test, and a route group bundles the three sandboxes under one routing key. Redis and the stream demo:messages stay shared with the baseline throughout.

How can I tell which version of a service handled a message?

Every service records each step in the demo's event log, and the tutorial's trail helper prints, per message, which workload handled each step: baseline or the sandbox's name. Each consumer also logs a processing or skipped line for every entry, with its routing key, and XINFO GROUPS shows one consumer group for the baseline and one for the consumer sandbox, each with nothing pending.

Do I need a container registry to follow this tutorial?

You need an image your cluster can pull. The tutorial builds one image for all three services and pushes it to your registry; the Docker Hub name in the commands is a placeholder. If the registry is private, the cluster needs pull access to it, for example through an image pull secret. On a local cluster that runs images straight from your Docker daemon, you can skip the push. If you build on an Apple silicon Mac for an x86 cluster, add --platform linux/amd64 to docker build.

How do I apply this to my own Redis Streams services?

Ship the platform_redis wrapper, or a port of it, in your shared code. Producers create their client with platform_redis.Redis instead of redis.Redis, consumers replace their XREADGROUP loop with StreamConsumer(...).run(handler), and consumer Deployments set SIGNADOT_BASELINE_KIND, SIGNADOT_BASELINE_NAME and SIGNADOT_BASELINE_NAMESPACE. Add OpenTelemetry instrumentation for your HTTP server and client so the routing key reaches the producer and leaves the consumer.

Can I use kubectl port-forward instead of signadot local connect?

Not for this tutorial. kubectl port-forward sends traffic straight to a pod and bypasses DevMesh, so a request carrying the producer sandbox's routing key would stay on the baseline producer. signadot local connect sends requests through the cluster's normal service routing, where DevMesh can route them.

See also

  • Redis Streams integration guide: the problem and both isolation patterns, in depth
  • Message Queue Isolation: the other brokers
  • Kafka: the same patterns on Kafka
  • Testing Microservices with RabbitMQ: selective consumption on a different broker
  • Header-Based Routing
  • Sandbox specification

title: Cassette the Tool Layer and Replay Agent Runs Offline
description:
You cannot replay a model. You can replay everything the model was handed, and that turns out to be enough for most agent bugs. The trick is to move the recording boundary down one layer: not the prompts, not the completions, but the tool calls and their results.

Most teams instrument the wrong surface. They save full transcripts, then discover that a transcript is a story about tokens, while the bug lives in what a tool returned at step seven. Re-run the same task and the model writes a different story, so the diff is unreadable and the failure is unreproducible. Tool-layer replay removes that noise by making the environment deterministic while leaving the model free to vary.

Record at the boundary, not at the top

A cassette is an append-only JSONL file of (tool, normalized args) -> result records, plus the ordered key sequence of the run. The key is a hash, so reordering JSON keys or reformatting a path does not break a match.

# cassette.py - record and replay the tool layer only
import hashlib, json
from pathlib import Path


def key(tool: str, args: dict, schema_version: str = "v1") -> str:
    blob = json.dumps(
        {"v": schema_version, "tool": tool, "args": args},
        sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"),
    )
    return hashlib.sha256(blob.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]


class Cassette:
    def __init__(self, path: str, mode: str = "record"):
        assert mode in {"record", "replay"}
        self.path, self.mode = Path(path), mode
        self.calls: list[str] = []
        self._seen: dict[str, dict] = {}
        if mode == "replay":
            for line in self.path.read_text().splitlines():
                rec = json.loads(line)
                self._seen[rec["key"]] = rec["result"]

    def call(self, tool: str, args: dict, fn, schema_version: str = "v1"):
        k = key(tool, args, schema_version)
        self.calls.append(k)
        if self.mode == "replay":
            if k not in self._seen:
                raise KeyError(f"cassette miss: {tool} {k}")
            return self._seen[k]
        result = fn(**args)
        with self.path.open("a") as f:
            f.write(json.dumps({"key": k, "tool": tool, "result": result}) + "\n")
        return result

Two details matter more than they look. First, schema_version is part of the key, so renaming a field or narrowing a parameter fails loudly at replay instead of silently serving a stale answer. Second, drop wall-clock fields from stored results before writing. Keep ordering; discard absolute time. A created_at inside a cassette guarantees a noisy diff on every run and teaches reviewers to ignore diffs.

Redaction happens on the way in, not on the way out. Hash or truncate anything credential-shaped before the record is written, because cassettes get committed, copied to laptops, and pasted into issues.

The debug loop

Record once against live tools. Replay as many times as you want with the network unplugged.

# 1. capture a baseline run (real tools, real side effects - use a sandbox)
python -m agent.run --cassette runs/base.jsonl --task task-07 > /dev/null

# 2. replay it offline; any cassette miss is a behavior change
python -m agent.run --cassette runs/base.jsonl --replay --task task-07

# 3. compare call paths, not prose
diff <(jq -r .key runs/base.jsonl) <(jq -r .key runs/candidate.jsonl)

The third command is the useful one. It prints a sequence of opaque hashes, which sounds useless until a step shifts and you can see exactly where: identical for nine calls, then a divergence, then a call that never appears in the baseline. That is a call-path diff, and it is stable in a way that text diffs are not. You are comparing decisions to act, not sentences about acting.

A cassette miss is not an error to swallow. Treat KeyError as the signal: the agent asked a question the baseline never asked, which is either a real behavior change or a gap in your recording. Both are worth a human look, and both are cheap to review because the key points at one tool and one argument set.

What repeats and what does not

Text transcripts answer "what did the model say". Cassettes answer "what did the run depend on". The second question generalizes: the same recording can be replayed by a rewritten prompt, a different model, or a refactored loop, and the call path tells you whether the behavior moved.

Situation Tool-layer cassette Why
Flaky third-party API in a failing step Good fit The flake becomes a fixture
Prompt or model swap Good fit Call-path diff is model-agnostic
Latency regression Poor fit Cassettes hide real timing by design
Tool schema migration Good fit, versioned keys Misses surface compatibility breaks
Multi-tenant auth bugs Poor fit Live tokens and live permissions are the subject
Model quality evaluation Poor fit You are freezing the environment, not judging answers

That table is the honest boundary. Replay is a regression and reproduction tool, not an evaluation harness, and it will lie to you about performance because every replay is fast.

Where the harness runs

A replay proxy is only useful if it is always reachable and free to hit while you debug, which is the unglamorous reason I run this harness on MonkeyCode's free server option and call models through its free model access, both supplied by the operator. The server hosts the cassette endpoint and the tiny diff service; the model access covers the recording runs and the occasional live check when a cassette miss needs a fresh answer. That keeps the loop usable on a laptop with no API budget and no key juggling in CI.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

I did not benchmark the free tier here, and quotas, hardware, and longevity are things you should confirm with the provider yourself before depending on them. If you already have paid infrastructure and a locked-down network boundary, the value is the cassette format and the diff, not the hosting.

Limitations to accept up front

Cassettes rot. A tool whose output legitimately changes every day - prices, timestamps, generated IDs - needs normalization before it goes into the store, or the recording is a one-shot artifact. Side effects still happen on the record pass, so record inside a sandbox with disposable credentials and a throwaway namespace; replay is safe precisely because it never calls out.

Also accept that a cassette cannot prove a run was correct. It proves the run took the same shape as a previous run. Pair it with an assertion about the final artifact, or you will happily certify a regression for its consistency.

Start with one task, record it, and break one tool on purpose to watch the miss fire. If the diff reads cleanly on that toy failure, you have a debug loop worth keeping.

title: Kenapa du dan Finder menampilkan ukuran folder yang berbeda
description:
Jalankan du -sh pada sebuah folder lalu bandingkan dengan ukuran di Finder, dan hasilnya sering berbeda, kadang sampai beberapa gigabyte. Tidak ada yang salah. Keduanya menjawab pertanyaan yang berbeda: berapa panjang file-nya, dan berapa banyak ruang disk yang ditempatinya. Saat disk penuh, hanya yang kedua yang penting, dan menghitungnya dengan benar butuh lebih dari sekadar menjumlahkan st_size.

Aturan di bawah ini adalah yang diikuti layar Disk pada aplikasi desktop osFoundry. Scanner-nya adalah fungsi Rust pendek di atas std::fs, dan logika yang sama muat dalam sekitar 40 baris Python. Semua angka berasal dari folder uji di volume APFS dengan blok alokasi 4 KB.

Hitung blok, bukan byte

st_size adalah panjang file. st_blocks adalah jumlah satuan 512 byte yang dialokasikan sistem file untuknya, berapa pun ukuran blok sebenarnya dari volume. Scanner di aplikasi memakai yang kedua secara default:

fn allocated_bytes(meta: &fs::Metadata, apparent: bool) -> u64 {
    if apparent {
        return meta.len();
    }
    #[cfg(unix)]
    {
        use std::os::unix::fs::MetadataExt;
        meta.blocks().saturating_mul(512)
    }
    #[cfg(not(unix))]
    {
        meta.len()
    }
}

Tiga file di folder uji menunjukkan alasannya:

File st_size st_blocks × 512
small.txt (2 byte teks) 2 4,096
sparse.img (dipotong jadi 1 GiB, tidak pernah ditulisi) 1,073,741,824 0
big.bin (200 MiB data) 209,715,200 209,715,200

File sekecil apa pun tetap memakai satu blok penuh, sehingga folder berisi 100.000 file kecil di disk bisa beberapa ratus megabyte lebih besar daripada jumlah byte-nya. File sparse kebalikannya: disk VM, file database, dan beberapa unduhan memesan panjang yang besar tetapi hanya memakai blok untuk bagian yang sudah ditulis. du di macOS menghitung blok; du -A menampilkan ukuran semu (apparent size). Kotak Apparent size di aplikasi melakukan peralihan yang sama.

Jangan ikuti link, jangan keluar dari volume

Scanner yang mengikuti symbolic link bisa menghitung folder yang sama dua kali, atau berputar tanpa henti pada link yang menunjuk ke folder induknya sendiri. Scanner yang masuk ke drive yang di-mount akan menambahkan file dari disk lain ke total disk ini. Aplikasi membaca tiap entri dengan symlink_metadata, yang menggambarkan link itu sendiri, bukan targetnya, dan membandingkan ID perangkat dengan folder tempat pemindaian dimulai:

if child_meta.file_type().is_symlink() || !same_device(root_meta, &child_meta) {
    continue;
}

same_device membandingkan st_dev, yaitu pemeriksaan yang sama seperti du -x atau find -xdev.

Hard link dan clone

Hard link adalah satu file dengan beberapa nama. Di folder uji, setelah ln big.bin hard.bin, ls -l menampilkan dua file 200 MiB, tetapi du menghitung datanya sekali saja karena ia mengingat setiap pasangan (st_dev, st_ino) yang pernah dilihat ketika st_nlink di atas 1. Scanner apa pun yang menjumlahkan blok seharusnya melakukan hal yang sama. Cadangan Time Machine pada disk HFS+ dan beberapa package manager banyak memakai hard link.

Clone APFS lebih sulit. cp -c big.bin clone.bin (atau Duplicate di Finder) membuat file kedua yang berbagi blok dengan aslinya sampai salah satunya berubah. Tiap file punya inode sendiri, st_blocks sendiri, dan jumlah link 1, sehingga du menghitung 400 MiB untuk pasangan itu. Diukur dengan df sebelum dan sesudah, clone memakai 0 KB ruang kosong, sedangkan cp biasa untuk file yang sama memakai 204.984 KB. Tidak ada field POSIX yang menunjukkan pembagian blok ini, jadi total berbasis blok melebih-lebihkan ruang yang kembali saat clone dihapus. Untuk folder penuh proyek duplikat atau pustaka foto, df sebelum dan sesudah adalah satu-satunya pemeriksaan yang bisa diandalkan.

Versi Python

Aturan yang sama, hanya dengan pustaka standar:

import os
import stat
import sys

def usage(root):
    root_dev = os.lstat(root).st_dev
    seen = set()
    allocated = apparent = 0
    skipped = 0
    stack = [root]
    while stack:
        path = stack.pop()
        try:
            entries = list(os.scandir(path))
        except OSError:
            skipped += 1
            continue
        for e in entries:
            try:
                st = e.stat(follow_symlinks=False)
            except OSError:
                skipped += 1
                continue
            if stat.S_ISLNK(st.st_mode) or st.st_dev != root_dev:
                continue
            if stat.S_ISDIR(st.st_mode):
                stack.append(e.path)
                continue
            if st.st_nlink > 1:
                key = (st.st_dev, st.st_ino)
                if key in seen:
                    continue
                seen.add(key)
            allocated += st.st_blocks * 512
            apparent += st.st_size
    return allocated, apparent, skipped

if __name__ == "__main__":
    alloc, appar, skipped = usage(sys.argv[1])
    print(f"on disk  {alloc / 2**30:8.2f} GiB")
    print(f"apparent {appar / 2**30:8.2f} GiB")
    if skipped:
        print(f"skipped  {skipped} unreadable entries")

Pada folder uji, skrip ini mencetak 0,39 GiB di disk dan 1,39 GiB apparent, sama dengan du -sk (409.604 KB) dan du -sAk. Pada pohon source code 14 GiB, hasilnya sama dengan du -sk sampai dua angka desimal. Simpan jumlah entri yang dilewati: di macOS, folder yang dilindungi izin privasi (Mail, Messages, Safari) tidak bisa dibaca tanpa Full Disk Access, dan total yang diam-diam melewatkannya terlihat lebih lengkap daripada kenyataannya.

Aplikasi menjaga hasilnya cukup kecil untuk digambar. Setiap folder menyimpan 36 anak terbesarnya, dan sisanya dijumlahkan menjadi satu node "Other items", sehingga membuka folder node_modules dengan seribu paket menampilkan 36 kotak dan satu kotak lagi untuk sisanya, bukan seribu kepingan kecil.

Menghapus dengan aman

Risiko sebenarnya dari alat disk ada di langkah menghapus. Aplikasi memindahkan item ke Trash sistem dengan crate trash, bukan menghapusnya dengan unlink, dan memeriksa setiap path sebelum memindahkan apa pun:

if !target.starts_with(&root) || target == root || home.as_ref() == Some(&target) {
    return Err("Cannot move a scan root or home folder to Trash".into());
}
if mount_points
    .iter()
    .any(|mount| target == *mount || target.parent() == Some(mount.as_path()))
{
    return Err("Cannot move a volume or its top-level items to Trash".into());
}

Path dikanonikalisasi lebih dulu, jadi .. atau symbolic link tidak bisa menyelipkan target di luar folder yang dipindai. Pilihan yang berisi satu folder bertanda di dalam folder bertanda lainnya juga ditolak, karena begitu folder induk masuk Trash, path anaknya tidak ada lagi dan batch akan gagal di tengah jalan.

Aplikasi desktop ini gratis di halaman unduh osFoundry.

title: I'm a product designer, and I built a 20+ screen AI video studio in Lovable. Here's what I learned
description:
I'm a senior product designer with 12+ years in fintech and B2B SaaS, not a developer. Over the last few weeks I built Reelpilot, a front-end template for an AI-assisted video creator studio, using Lovable.

It has 20+ screens: a dashboard, content library, analytics, a record and upload flow, a "Create with AI" flow, and a five-step editor that goes from edit to publish. It works in light and dark mode and on mobile.

👉 Live demo: https://reelpilot-story-to-screen.lovable.app/

Here's the design thinking behind it, and what I learned along the way.

The core idea: AI suggests, the creator decides

Most AI tools either do too little or take over completely. For creators, the second one is scary. It's their name on the video.

So I set one rule for every AI feature: it has to be visible, explained, editable and labelled. In practice, that turned into four patterns.

  1. Confidence labels

Every AI suggestion for a title, description, tags or category shows high, medium or low confidence. A low-confidence category suggestion tells the creator "double-check this one" without them having to guess.

  1. "Why suggested"

Each suggestion can be expanded to explain its reasoning. On the thumbnail screen, every AI-picked frame has a "why this frame" note. Trust goes up a lot when the AI shows its work.

  1. Accept, edit or reject

Nothing is applied automatically. Every suggestion has three clear actions, and editing is treated as just as normal as accepting.

  1. Labels that can't be removed

If a video includes AI-generated scenes, the publish screen shows an "AI-generated content" label that the creator can't switch off. It's a small detail, but it shows the product takes honesty seriously.

Designing the states nobody designs

The happy path is easy. The interesting work was in the in-between states:

Upload drops halfway. The upload pauses at 62%, says the connection was lost, confirms the draft is saved, and offers "Resume upload". There's even a demo toggle to simulate the network drop.
A/B testing thumbnails. The result doesn't just name a winner. It says how confident the test is ("95% confident this is real, not luck"), so creators don't overreact to noise.
Publishing with warnings. The publish screen lists things to check, each with a "Fix" link that jumps straight back to the right spot in the editor, but it still lets you publish if you choose to.
What I learned building in Lovable as a designer
Go screen by screen, flow by flow. Asking for one complete flow at a time and reviewing it carefully worked far better than asking for the whole app at once.
Be specific about states. Lovable builds what you describe. Empty, loading, error and success states only appeared when I asked for them.
Review like a design QA. After each build I went through every screen and sent back a list of fixes, just as I would with an engineering team.
Simulated data is enough to test the UX. No backend was needed to feel whether a flow made sense.
The stack

React, TypeScript, TanStack Start, Vite, Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui. All front end, with sample data.

Try it

👉 Live demo: https://reelpilot-story-to-screen.lovable.app/

If you're building an AI or creator tool and want a head start on the front end, the full source code is available here: https://lalitadeshmukh.gumroad.com/l/reelpilot-template

I'd love feedback, especially on the AI trust patterns. How do you handle AI suggestions in your products?
