title: I Import 11 Packages I Never Declared; Seven Vanish on an Upgrade
description:
I sat down to upgrade this blog's dependencies. Ordinary work: astro was one
minor behind, and @astrojs/mdx was a whole major behind — I had 7.0.5,
the registry had 8.1.3. Before touching anything I opened the release notes,
as I always do. Astro's 8.0.0 entry says:

If you haven't explicitly installed a Markdown processor, you don't need to
do anything.

I hadn't installed one. So for me this was a no-action major. I was going to
run the upgrade and move on.

I didn't. Because I tried the upgrade in a scratch directory first, and the
first step of my publishing pipeline died before reading its second line:

Error [ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND]: Cannot find package 'js-yaml'
  imported from .../scripts/render-article.mjs

js-yaml is not in my package.json. None of the eleven third-party
packages that file imports is; js-yaml only blows up first because it comes
first. All of them work today — because Astro brings them along in its own
tree and npm spreads everything into the root of node_modules. The upgrade
changes Astro's tree, and seven of the eleven disappear.

What this was measured on: macOS 26 (Darwin 25.6.0, arm64), Node v22.16.0,
npm 10.9.2, repository pin a3c41e82 (6 Nov 2026). Everything was measured
in this blog's own repository and in isolated lab directories under /tmp; the
main node_modules tree was never modified.

My first count was wrong

My first job was answering "how many are there". I wrote a forty-line scanner:
walk every .ts/.mjs/.astro/.mdx file in the repository, collect every bare
specifier inside import and require, compare against what package.json
declares.

The scanner found 32 undeclared packages. Reading the list was a relief,
because the list contained these:

dart:async        (2 files)
package:flutter   (2 files)
fmt               (2 files)
aws-sdk           (2 files)

fmt is a Go package. package:flutter is a Dart package. None of this is my
code — those are example lines inside the code blocks of the blog's own
articles. The scanner walked every content file on the blog and took each code
sample for a real import. Of the 3,079 files it scanned, 2,821 were content;
92% of the measurement was irrelevant, and 19 of the 32 packages it reported
came purely from article code blocks — the Go and Dart lines above, but also
innocent-looking JavaScript names like express and redis.

This is not my first fall into that trap on this blog — I have written the same
sentence four times before, and one of them was in an
alt-text audit
where the pattern ^#{1,6}\s counted shell comments inside code blocks as
headings. The mechanism is identical; only the scanner changed. Four times is
apparently not enough to learn something, and all four times it bit me in the
same place: code blocks.

I narrowed the scan to scripts/ and ran it again. The real numbers:

Measurement Value
Files scanned 97
Packages declared in package.json 20
Third-party packages imported 20
Undeclared 13

Eleven of the thirteen live in a single file: scripts/render-article.mjs. The
other two are @mdx-js/mdx (in two separate validation scripts) and
node-html-parser.

Node never looks at dependencies while resolving

Why do these thirteen imports not fail? The answer is in Node's resolution
algorithm. The PACKAGE_RESOLVE step in the
ESM documentation walks up the filesystem
for a bare specifier:

While parentURL is not the file system root … Let packageURL be the URL
resolution of "node_modules/" concatenated with packageName, relative to
parentURL.

So when scripts/render-article.mjs asks for js-yaml, Node checks
scripts/node_modules/js-yaml, then node_modules/js-yaml, then the parent
directory's node_modules, all the way to the filesystem root. First match
wins.

What the documentation does not contain matters more: no step of the
algorithm reads the dependencies field of package.json. It reads
exports, main, imports, name, type. It does not read dependencies.
As far as resolution is concerned, a declaration is no more binding than a
comment.

How the package reaches the root is npm's business. npm's own
folders documentation
describes it as an optimization: "Since version 3, npm hoists dependencies
by default." The page offers no guarantee that every transitive dependency
will be reachable from the root. What it offers is a default behaviour, and the
difference between those two things is exactly this article's subject.

In this repository: the lockfile holds 755 package entries, 687 of them at
the root and only 68 nested. Alongside the 20 packages I declared, there are
667 more on the same shelf that I never declared. Every one of them is one
import line away, and none of them will tell me when it leaves.

When npm does not hoist: the 68 exceptions in my own tree

If "no guarantee" sounds theoretical, the counter-example sits in my own tree.
When npm cannot place a package at the root it puts it under its dependent
instead, and that happens on version conflicts. Here is the count for this
repository: 52 packages are installed at more than one version. Examples:

chokidar                  4.0.3  and  5.0.0
readdirp                  4.1.2  and  5.0.0
@astrojs/internal-helpers 0.10.2 and  0.11.0
@astrojs/markdown-remark  7.2.2  and  7.3.1

In each conflict one version goes to the root and the other stays nested. So
hoisting is not a rule that always fires; it is an optimization applied when
there is no conflict — and which version wins the root is not determined by any
line I wrote.

When I write import 'js-yaml' I take a dependency on an install artifact. And
that artifact is shaped not by my declarations but by the relationships among
packages I never declared.

Who carries them: ownership chains from the lockfile

Which declared package brings which? I first tried reading npm ls, and the
tree output drowned in deduped lines. The better route: compute each declared
package's dependency closure from the packages map in package-lock.json.

Package Direct dependent Contained in the closure of
remark-gfm @astrojs/mdx @astrojs/mdx
remark-smartypants @astrojs/mdx @astrojs/mdx
unist-util-visit @astrojs/mdx mdx, node, astro
@mdx-js/mdx @astrojs/mdx @astrojs/mdx
shiki astro mdx, node, astro
js-yaml astro mdx, node, astro
github-slugger astro @astrojs/mdx, astro
unified — mdx, node, astro
remark-parse — @astrojs/mdx
remark-rehype — @astrojs/mdx
rehype-stringify — @astrojs/mdx
remark-mdx — @astrojs/mdx
node-html-parser rettiwt-api rettiwt-api

The five packages in the middle of the table are not a direct dependency of
any declared package — they sit two or more levels deep. For them to be at the
root, npm has to hoist across two tiers, which it is under no obligation to do.

The last row is its own story. The only package that brings
node-html-parser is rettiwt-api, this blog's Twitter client. I borrow my
HTML parser from my social-posting library. The day I post to Twitter some
other way, my render-comparison script will find itself unable to parse HTML.
There is no conceptual link between these two; the only link is that they
happen to sit in the same directory.

The upgrade experiment: four installs, the same eleven imports

To turn the theory into a measurement I started with two clean directories.
Each one declares exactly two packages and nothing else:

# lab-now: the versions this repo has today
npm i astro@7.3.5 @astrojs/mdx@7.0.5

# lab-next: the pending upgrade
npm i astro@latest @astrojs/mdx@latest   # 7.4.7 + 8.1.3

Then I tried to resolve, one by one with import(), the eleven packages
render-article.mjs needs:

=== lab-now  (astro 7.3.5 + @astrojs/mdx 7.0.5) ===
RESOLVED 11/11
packages at root (scopes expanded): 307

=== lab-next (astro 7.4.7 + @astrojs/mdx 8.1.3) ===
RESOLVED 4/11
MISSING: remark-parse, remark-rehype, rehype-stringify,
         remark-gfm, remark-mdx, remark-smartypants, js-yaml
packages at root (scopes expanded): 188

Seven of eleven gone. My explanation was ready: @astrojs/mdx's dependency
list shrank. The registry data supports it — 7.0.5 declares 14
dependencies (@astrojs/markdown-remark, @mdx-js/mdx, remark-gfm,
remark-smartypants, unist-util-visit, rehype-raw, hast-util-to-html
and others), while 8.1.3 declares 3: @astrojs/internal-helpers,
@astrojs/markdown-satteri, es-module-lexer.

The explanation looked right, but I had upgraded two packages together and
never separated what each one did. So I set up two more labs, this time
changing one thing at a time:

Install Resolved Lost
astro 7.3.5 + mdx 7.0.5 (today) 11/11 —
astro 7.4.7 + mdx 7.0.5 (minor only) 11/11 —
astro 7.3.5 + mdx 8.1.3 (major only) 5/11 6 remark/rehype packages
astro 7.4.7 + mdx 8.1.3 (both) 4/11 those six + js-yaml

The table refuted half of my explanation. The major does take six packages
away, true. But the package in my error message, the js-yaml from this
article's first line, disappears in neither change on its own. The reason:
js-yaml had two separate providers. astro@7.3.5 declares it directly
(js-yaml: ^4.3.2), and @astrojs/mdx@7.0.5 brings it a second time through
the @astrojs/markdown-remark chain. Upgrade the minor and the first provider
goes while the second holds; upgrade the major and the second goes while the
first holds. Upgrade both and I cut away both legs at once.

Writing this annoys me, because it strengthens my own thesis: no release note
could have protected me here. The major's note says nothing about js-yaml,
because the major alone does not remove it. The minor has no note at all;
minors do not get one. The breakage lives at the intersection of two changes,
and only I could have seen that intersection — for which I would have had to
write down somewhere that I use those packages.

The four survivors are worth a look too, because they also survived by
accident: unified now arrives via @astrojs/internal-helpers; shiki and
github-slugger come straight from astro; and unist-util-visit arrives by
two routes — mdast-util-to-hast and retext-smartypants. That last one is a
text package; the fact that my tree-walking package can also come from
there says plenty about how much of this rests on coincidence.

One experiment along the way was wasted. To see the same result by disabling
hoisting, I copied the repository's own package-lock.json into a third lab
directory and ran npm ci --install-strategy=nested. The layout did not
change: 516 directories were still at the root, and only 30 nested
node_modules appeared. I did not chase down why the flag was ineffective,
because the table above already answered the real question with real versions.
I am writing up the experiment that failed too — assuming a measurement
measures what you expect is the most expensive habit in this line of work, and
it caught me twice in this one article.

End to end: real script, real error

So the labs would not stay abstract, I copied scripts/render-article.mjs into
both directories unchanged — along with src/lib/blog-frontmatter-schema.mjs,
because the script imports it by relative path — and handed it a real article
file: tutorials/3583-commite-not-yazdim-klon-hicbir-notu-getirmedi.mdx.

In lab-now the script did what it should: parsed the frontmatter, extracted
that post's 16 headings, produced HTML.

In lab-next the output was:

node:internal/modules/package_json_reader:256
  throw new ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND(packageName, fileURLToPath(base), null);

Error [ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND]: Cannot find package 'js-yaml'
  imported from .../lab-next/scripts/render-article.mjs

On the first import line, before reading a single character of MDX. I should
say what this script is, because it is not some helper tool:

  • package.json's prebuild step runs scripts/migrate-content.mjs, which imports renderArticle from render-article.mjs. Every build goes through this file.
  • deploy-only.yml, content-generate.yml, translate-archive.yml and runner-selftest.yml call migrate-content.mjs directly — so they reach render-article.mjs indirectly, through that import.
  • deploy/content-fast-deploy.sh — the build-free fast publishing path — runs the same line.
  • One of the two files importing @mdx-js/mdx is validate-mdx-staged.ts, one of the hard gates that blocks a commit.

Note this: the name render-article.mjs appears in none of those
workflows. Grepping for the link does not work; it sits behind one import line
and only shows up if you follow the call chain.

Had I run the upgrade and pushed, the blog would have stopped publishing new
posts, and the first thing to tell me would have been a red deploy run. tsc
stays silent, because this is not a type error. The tests stay silent, because
none of the 17 test files under scripts/tests/ looks at dependency
declarations.

I read the release note wrong

I do not want to be unfair to the release note. The 8.0.0 entry's main change
opens like this:

Moves MDX file processing to the Markdown processors. … If you haven't
explicitly installed a Markdown processor, you don't need to do anything.

And it continues — this is the part I skipped on first reading — by saying
plainly: if you use unified(), move @astrojs/markdown-remark to 7.3.0 or
later. So the note does address unified() users, and unified() is exactly
what I use. What failed to warn me was not the note but the sentence I formed
while reading it: I thought "I never installed a markdown processor", when in
fact I had not installed one but was using it.

The first sentence is still perfectly true for someone using Astro as Astro.
MDX files are now delegated to the markdown processor; the default processor is
Sätteri, and anyone who wants the remark/unified chain installs
@astrojs/markdown-remark themselves — 8.1.3 now asks for it as a
peerDependency, which is to say it expects you to declare it.

My situation is different. I do not use that chain through Astro's
configuration; I build the unified() chain in my own script and borrow the
packages from Astro's node_modules. Astro telling me "you don't need to do
anything" is correct, because Astro does not know I use those packages too.
There is no way for it to know: I never declared them.

There is an interesting contrast here with the
dependency confusion piece.
There the danger was that the name I asked for fetched the wrong package —
right name, wrong source. Here the danger is the reverse: the name and the
source are both right, but I never said I wanted it. In the first case an
attacker does something; in the second nobody does anything, a maintainer tidies
up their own dependencies, and my pipeline falls over.

I wrote the gate, and it went red on my own repository

The lasting fix has two parts: declare the missing packages, and stop them from
accumulating silently again. The second part is forty lines:

// scripts/tests/declared-imports.test.mjs

const SCAN = ['scripts', 'src/lib', 'src/components', 'src/pages'];
const EXT = new Set(['.ts', '.tsx', '.js', '.mjs', '.cjs', '.astro']);
const SPEC =
  /(?:^|[\s;{(=])(?:import\s+(?:[\w*{},\s]+\s+from\s+)?|export\s+[\w*{},\s]+\s+from\s+|require\s*\(\s*|import\s*\(\s*)['"]([^'"]+)['"]/g;

function walk(dir, out = []) {
  let ents;
  try { ents = readdirSync(dir); } catch { return out; }
  for (const e of ents) {
    const p = path.join(dir, e);
    if (statSync(p).isDirectory()) { if (e !== 'node_modules') walk(p, out); }
    else if (EXT.has(path.extname(e))) out.push(p);
  }
  return out;
}

test('every bare import must be declared in package.json', () => {
  const pj = JSON.parse(readFileSync('package.json', 'utf8'));
  const declared = new Set([
    ...Object.keys(pj.dependencies || {}),
    ...Object.keys(pj.devDependencies || {}),
    ...Object.keys(pj.optionalDependencies || {}),
  ]);
  const offenders = new Map();
  for (const base of SCAN) {
    for (const file of walk(base)) {
      for (const m of readFileSync(file, 'utf8').matchAll(SPEC)) {
        const s = m[1];
        if (/^[./]/.test(s)) continue;
        if (/^(node|astro|virtual):/.test(s)) continue;
        const name = s.startsWith('@')
          ? s.split('/').slice(0, 2).join('/')
          : s.split('/')[0];
        if (declared.has(name)) continue;
        if (!offenders.has(name)) offenders.set(name, []);
        offenders.get(name).push(file);
      }
    }
  }
  const lines = [...offenders].map(
    ([n, f]) => `  ${n}  <- ${f[0]}${f.length > 1 ? ` (+${f.length - 1})` : ''}`,
  );
  assert.equal(
    offenders.size,
    0,
    `${offenders.size} undeclared packages are imported:\n${lines.join('\n')}`,
  );
});

Two details matter. src/content is not in the SCAN list — that is
precisely what produced the wrong count of 32 above, the code blocks inside
articles. And the skip list carries the node:, astro: and virtual:
prefixes; those are not packages but a Node builtin, an Astro virtual module
and a Vite virtual module respectively.

I ran the gate against its own repository:

not ok 1 - every bare import must be declared in package.json
  error: |-
    13 undeclared packages are imported:
      node-html-parser  <- scripts/_compare-render.mjs
      @mdx-js/mdx  <- scripts/generate-content.ts (+1)
      js-yaml  <- scripts/render-article.mjs
      ...
    13 !== 0

The gate went red on its first run, which is what you want from a gate. If your
first measurement after writing a rule comes back green, check your measurement
rather than the rule.

Declaring has a cost too

The first part — declaring what is missing — sounds like a one-command job. You
read the installed versions and write them into package.json:

for p in js-yaml unified remark-parse remark-mdx remark-gfm \
         remark-smartypants remark-rehype rehype-stringify \
         unist-util-visit shiki github-slugger \
         @mdx-js/mdx node-html-parser; do
  printf '%s@%s\n' "$p" \
    "$(node -p "require('./node_modules/$p/package.json').version")"
done

The ./node_modules/ prefix is mandatory here. Write
node -p "require('unified/package.json')" instead and eight of the thirteen
lines fail with ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED: unified, the remark-*
packages and rehype-stringify publish an exports map, and that map does not
expose the ./package.json path. Reading the file by path sidesteps the gate.
(I wrote this line without the prefix the first time, and eight lines of the
output came back as stack traces.)

There is a decision here, and I would like to pick the easy side but cannot:
the moment I declare these packages I also own their upgrades. Right now
shiki going from 4.0.2 to 4.6.0 is none of my business, because I use
whatever Astro brings. Declared, it means thirteen new lines, thirteen new
Renovate PRs and thirteen new "will this minor break something" questions.

It is still the right trade. Because in today's arrangement those questions do
not disappear, they are merely not asked of me — Astro's maintainers answer
them on my behalf, and when their answers change I learn it from a red deploy
run rather than a release note.

When writing the versions I prefer exact pins over ^, because these thirteen
are not tools I picked but tools I inherited; a range buys me nothing here. This
repository already pins astro, @astrojs/mdx and @astrojs/node exactly,
for a reason from the same family: upgrading those three separately can produce
a build that passes tsc and then dies when the server boots.

Before you write forty lines: existing tools and the structural fix

I wrote the test above myself, but presenting it as "the right way" would be
dishonest — especially in an article about a hand-rolled regex scanner giving
the wrong answer. There are three real alternatives.

A lint rule. eslint-plugin-import's
import/no-extraneous-dependencies
does exactly this job, and its documentation defines it as: "Forbid the import
of external modules that are not declared in the package.json's
dependencies, devDependencies, …". It works off a real parser, not my
regex. Two conditions: the packages have to be installed, and type imports are
ignored by default. If you already run ESLint, this is the way; this repository
does not, which is why I wrote the forty lines.

Inventory tools. depcheck and knip find both undeclared imports and the
reverse direction — packages declared but never used. This repository has
thirteen candidates in that direction too (@astrojs/check, tailwindcss,
tsx and other config-driven packages), which is a good illustration of why
such a tool still needs human judgement.

The structural fix. The lasting answer is to change package managers.
pnpm's documentation names the problem directly:
"When installing dependencies with npm or Yarn Classic, all packages are
hoisted to the root of the modules directory. As a result, source code has
access to dependencies that are not added as dependencies to the project."
pnpm builds a "non-flat" layout instead, symlinking only the project's direct
dependencies into the root directory. In that tree my thirteen imports would
have failed on day one, without waiting for an upgrade.

If you take one thing from this article, look at your package manager before
you write the gate test. The gate catches the symptom; the layout removes the
problem.

And there is a dimension that gets too little airtime: an undeclared package is
invisible on the security side too, not only at upgrade time. The scope of
npm audit, the SBOM you generate, the PRs Dependabot opens and the emergency
version pin you would apply with overrides — all of them read the declaration
list. If a package your code actually runs is missing from that list, a
vulnerability advisory for it has no path to reach you. The cost of my thirteen
packages is not thirteen Renovate PRs; it is thirteen unreviewed supply-chain
items.

Three questions to ask your own repository

  1. How many packages are at the root of node_modules, and how many in package.json? Get the first with ls node_modules | grep -vc '^\.' and the second from the length of your declaration list. The gap is the number of packages you can import silently. That command says 515 for me while the lockfile counts 687 entries at the root; the difference comes from scoped packages, since everything under @astrojs shows up as a single directory. Count it either way, and there is a crowd standing next to my 20.
  2. Which of your files are on the production path, and what do they import? An undeclared import in a helper tool is annoying; the same import on the deploy path stops publishing. To map the critical path, start from the lifecycle steps in package.json and from your workflows: 
   # 1) lifecycle steps: prebuild, postinstall, prepare...
   node -p "JSON.stringify(require('./package.json').scripts, null, 2)"
   # 2) scripts called directly by CI and deploy
   grep -rhoE 'node scripts/[a-z0-9._-]+' .github/workflows/ deploy/ \
     | sort -u
   # 3) everything those files import — packages AND neighbouring scripts
   grep -rhoE "from '[^']+'" scripts/migrate-content.mjs \
     scripts/render-article.mjs | sort -u

In the third step, do not filter out the relative paths; that is precisely
the line showing the chain. For me, the from './render-article.mjs' line
in migrate-content.mjs's output was the only clue leading to a file whose
name never appears in any workflow.

  1. Have you tried a major upgrade in an isolated directory before doing it? Two npm i calls and an import() loop take two minutes. For me those two minutes stood in for a publishing outage.

A note on the
Renovate dependency automation
side as well: in a repository with automated upgrades enabled, this failure
arrives through the merge of a PR you never looked at. Without a gate test,
automation does nothing but accelerate this class of error.

A frozen tree is a delay, not a protection

This blog is fine today. Because npm ci reads the lockfile, and the lockfile
reconstructs the 7.0.5 tree exactly — including the thirteen packages I never
declared. The break arrives with the first command that regenerates that lock.

With one exception. The server installs with npm ci --omit=dev, and
node-html-parser is marked dev: true in the lockfile — the package that
brings it, rettiwt-api, is a development dependency. So the production tree
holds twelve of the thirteen, not thirteen; the script using the thirteenth
cannot run on the server anyway. I was not looking for this; it fell out while
reading the lockfile for something else entirely. Every package you leave
undeclared turns into a delayed question like that one.

I want to state the distinction plainly, because I spent years treating the two
as the same thing: a lockfile is a freezer; a declaration is a contract. The
freezer carries yesterday's tree into today; it does not tell you why anything
is in there. The contract says "I want this package", and if nobody brings it
tomorrow, npm stops and tells you. My thirteen packages were in the freezer and
absent from the contract. The day I opened the freezer I was going to learn all
of their freshness at once.

The good news is that this is a measurable gap. It is not a code smell or an
architectural preference; it is a hole you can find and close by comparing two
lists. On my side the next job is clear — declare the thirteen packages with
exact versions and move the gate into scripts/tests/. The upgrade comes after
that; in the universe where I reversed the order, this article would be the one
the blog could not publish.

Official Sources

The @astrojs/mdx version comparison in the body is based on registry data for
7.0.5 and 8.1.3 read on 6 November 2026; the list below points to the current
form of the same documents.

  • Node.js ESM — PACKAGE_RESOLVE and bare specifier resolution
  • withastro/astro — @astrojs/mdx CHANGELOG, the 8.0.0 entry
  • withastro/astro#17262 — moving MDX processing to the Markdown processors
  • Astro Docs — @astrojs/mdx, the processor option and the Sätteri default

title: Email and Phone Normalization: Common Mistakes
description:
A contact lookup finds no match because one phone number includes spaces and another does not. The obvious response is to clean every value aggressively. That can introduce a different problem: changing a valid identifier into the wrong one.

Normalization should produce a consistent representation while retaining the original input when there is a justified need to inspect it.

Separate normalization from validation

Normalization changes representation. Validation checks whether a value meets an expected structure. Neither proves that a person owns an email address or phone number.

A syntactically valid address can still be unreachable. A well-formatted phone number can belong to a different person. Treat ownership verification as a separate process.

Be careful with email addresses

Trim accidental surrounding whitespace. Normalize the domain according to a defined policy. Do not assume every provider treats dots, plus-addressing, or letter case in the local part identically.

For example, stripping the plus suffix from every address may collapse identifiers that your application should retain separately. Provider-specific behavior is not a universal email rule.

If your business uses a case-insensitive email matching key, document that decision and keep it separate from the delivery address. Avoid inventing transformations merely to increase the match rate.

Ask for country context for phones

A national phone number without a country is ambiguous. Capture country context explicitly when necessary, then use a maintained phone-parsing library with current numbering metadata.

Keep extensions separate. Do not guess a country from an advertising campaign, browser language, or salesperson preference.

International formatting can make comparisons easier, but formatting success still does not establish ownership or active service.

Keep a clear data contract

Field Purpose
Original input Restricted troubleshooting, if retention is justified
Normalized value Consistent display or delivery
Matching key Documented comparison policy
Verification status Separate evidence of ownership

Avoid writing contact information into general analytics events or unprotected logs. Apply retention and access controls to any original values you retain.

Test edge cases deliberately

Test surrounding whitespace, international numbers, missing country context, extensions, shared inboxes, and addresses with plus suffixes. Include values your parser cannot confidently interpret.

An uncertain value should produce a clear correction request or review path. Silently guessing creates convincing-looking data that may route communication to the wrong destination.

A good normalization process makes matching more consistent without claiming more certainty than the input supports.

title: Stop Paying AWS to Talk to Itself: When to Use VPC Endpoints Instead of a NAT Gateway
description:
If you’re running EC2 instances or Lambda functions in private subnets, they may still need to reach services such as Amazon S3, Amazon ECR, and Amazon CloudWatch. A common setup sends that traffic through a NAT Gateway. It works, but it can add charges you didn’t expect.

A NAT Gateway has an hourly charge and a per-GB data processing charge. When traffic to supported AWS services passes through it, those processing charges can add up even though you’re accessing AWS services.

Where VPC endpoints help

A VPC endpoint lets resources in your VPC reach a supported service without routing that traffic through a NAT Gateway. There are two useful types:

  • Gateway endpoints support Amazon S3 and DynamoDB. There’s no additional hourly or data processing charge for the endpoint itself. If your workloads access S3 through a NAT Gateway, an S3 gateway endpoint is a good first place to look.
  • Interface endpoints support services including Amazon ECR and CloudWatch. They have hourly charges per Availability Zone and data processing charges, so adding one does not automatically save money. Check which services your workload uses, how much traffic goes to each, and the endpoint charges in your Region before deciding.

VPC endpoints don’t replace every use of a NAT Gateway. Your workloads may still need one for other outbound traffic. The goal is simpler: identify traffic that can use a gateway or interface endpoint, then compare the costs before changing your network design.

title: The Default Redshift Serverless Setting That Was Quietly Costing Us $2,700 a Month
description:
A client of mine spun up a new Amazon Redshift Serverless workgroup, pointed their nightly ELT job at it, and moved on. Three weeks later the AWS bill landed and the Redshift line item was almost four times what they'd modeled. Nobody had touched a knob. The workgroup was still running the base capacity the console picked for them when they clicked "Create": 128 RPUs, on all day, whether anyone was querying or not.

That's the trap with Redshift Serverless. It removes the "how big should this cluster be" question at setup time, but it doesn't remove the need to answer it, it just moves that question to your first bill.

What an RPU actually buys you

A Redshift Processing Unit (RPU) is a bundle of compute and memory, 16 GB of memory per RPU. Base capacity is what a workgroup runs at when idle-but-warm, and Redshift Serverless scales up from there automatically under load. You're billed per second, with a 60-second minimum, at $0.375 per RPU-hour in us-east-1 (check the pricing page for your region, it varies). Storage is separate: Redshift Managed Storage runs $0.024/GB-month in that same region.

Base capacity isn't a free-form number. The allowed steps are:

  • 4 to 8 RPUs, in steps of 4
  • 8 to 512 RPUs, in steps of 8
  • 512 to 1024 RPUs, in steps of 32 (1024 RPU is only available in a handful of regions; most cap at 512)

And your storage ceiling is tied to that number: 4 RPU tops out around 32 TB of managed storage, 8 to 16 RPU gets you up to 128 TB, and anything past that needs 32+ RPU regardless of how light your actual compute needs are.

Finding out what you're actually using

Before you touch the base capacity, measure. Redshift Serverless gives you two system views for exactly this:

-- Total elapsed query time over the window you care about
SELECT
    date_trunc('hour', start_time) AS hour,
    count(*) AS query_count,
    sum(datediff(millisecond, start_time, end_time)) AS total_elapsed_ms
FROM sys_query_history
WHERE start_time >= dateadd(day, -7, current_date)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

-- Actual RPU-hours consumed, which is what you're billed on
SELECT
    date_trunc('day', start_time) AS day,
    sum(charged_seconds) / 3600.0 AS rpu_hours,
    sum(charged_seconds) / 3600.0 * 0.375 AS approx_cost_usd
FROM sys_serverless_usage
WHERE start_time >= dateadd(day, -7, current_date)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

Run that for a representative week before you change anything. If your workgroup is sitting at 128 RPUs but sys_serverless_usage shows you rarely scale past what an 8 or 16 RPU base would cover, you've found your answer.

Right-sizing it

Once you know your number, drop the base capacity with the CLI:

aws redshift-serverless update-workgroup \
  --workgroup-name my-analytics-wg \
  --base-capacity 32

One important restriction: update-workgroup only accepts one changeable parameter per call. You can't set --base-capacity and --port in the same request.

If your workload is spiky rather than steady, consider AI-driven scaling instead of a fixed base. It's now the default for new workgroups, and it dynamically adjusts capacity within a base range of 8 to 512 RPU using a price-performance slider:

aws redshift-serverless update-workgroup \
  --workgroup-name my-analytics-wg \
  --price-performance-target Level=25,Status=ENABLED

Level 1 optimizes hardest for cost, 100 optimizes hardest for speed, 50 is the balanced default. AWS's own TPC-DS benchmarking found the Balanced setting delivered roughly 2x the performance of Optimized-for-Cost for about 3% more spend, which is a genuinely good trade if your workload has any concurrency to it at all.

Where this requires care

A few things bit me or people I work with, worth knowing before you change anything:

  • The default is not conservative. The console pre-fills 128 RPU for a new workgroup. That's fine for a real production data warehouse and wildly oversized for a dev/test workgroup or a new pipeline you're still validating.
  • Storage limits move with base capacity. If you drop to 8 RPU to save money and your dataset creeps past 128 TB, you'll hit a hard wall and have to bump the base back up, not just add storage.
  • Scaling up is automatic, scaling back down is not guaranteed to be instant or even automatic in every case, particularly at the lowest tiers. Watch sys_serverless_usage after a load spike, don't assume the meter resets itself the moment the query finishes.
  • AI-driven scaling has a recommended floor. AWS's own guidance says it isn't a great fit under roughly 32 base RPU (though the platform-level minimum to enable it has been lowered over time), so for genuinely small workloads a fixed base capacity is often simpler and cheaper to reason about.
  • Set a usage limit regardless of which mode you pick. RPU-hour limits with an alert or hard cutoff action are the actual safety net, right-sizing your base is preventive, a usage limit is what stops a runaway query from becoming a surprise invoice.

My take

Serverless billing rewards the same discipline provisioned clusters always demanded, it just hides that fact behind a friendlier setup wizard. The teams getting burned aren't picking the wrong number, they're not picking a number at all and letting the default stand. Pull a week of sys_serverless_usage, pick a base capacity that matches your actual p50 workload, lean on AI-driven scaling for the spikes, and set a hard usage limit as a backstop. That's maybe twenty minutes of work against a bill that otherwise compounds silently for months.

Further reading

  • Scaling capacity in Amazon Redshift processing unit (RPU)
  • Compute capacity for Amazon Redshift Serverless
  • Billing for Amazon Redshift Serverless
  • Unlock the power of optimization in Amazon Redshift Serverless (AWS Big Data Blog)
  • Amazon Redshift Serverless AI-driven scaling is now the default for new workgroups

title: 3,000+ stock pages that never call an API at request time
description:
I run Stockinsky, a small site that writes paid AI research reports on listed companies. Most companies will never get a paid report, but people still search for them by name. So I added a free page for every stock: ten years of financials, a red-flag checklist, dividend history and the latest close.

There are now about 2,000 China A-share pages, plus around 530 Hong Kong and 530 U.S. ones. Here is how they are built, and the one incident that shaped the design.

The rule: a page view never touches an upstream API

The first version fetched data when someone opened a page and cached the result. That works fine for people. It does not work for crawlers. A search engine bot can open hundreds of stock pages in a few minutes, and every cache miss turns into several requests to free market-data endpoints.

Then I made it worse myself. I ran a bulk measurement script on the production server, and the quote provider started rate-limiting the server's IP. Live quotes on the site broke for real users. The site and my batch job shared one IP, so the batch job took the site down with it.

After that I set one rule: the server only reads files. All fetching happens on my own machine.

Snapshots, one JSON file per stock

A local script builds one JSON file per stock:

data/stock-snapshot/A/688981.json
data/stock-snapshot/HK/...
data/stock-snapshot/US/...

Each file holds:

  • finance: ten years of revenue, net profit, ROE, gross margin, operating cash flow;
  • risk: a slimmed-down red-flag checklist (goodwill, cash and debt both high, share pledges, audit opinion, regulator inquiries...), each with the value, the rule and the source;
  • dividends: cash dividend per share for the last ten years;
  • quote: the close, change and market cap on the day the snapshot was built, with that date shown on the page.

The script then syncs the files to the server, which renders pages from disk. A crawler can open every page on the site and not a single upstream request goes out.

Being polite to free endpoints

The data sources are free public endpoints, so the build is deliberately slow:

  • Concurrency 2 by default, capped at 3. Each stock needs about 8–10 requests and takes roughly 12 seconds, so 1,000 stocks take about an hour and a half.
  • Shared data is fetched once per run. Quotes for the whole market come from about 100 batch requests, and the dividend table from about 20, instead of one call per stock.
  • Resumable. Snapshots newer than 7 days are skipped, so an interrupted run just starts again. One stock failing is logged and does not stop the others.

Slow is fine here. These numbers change once a quarter, not once a minute.

Thin pages get noindex, not a 404

Free endpoints time out, and some stocks come back with gaps. Some are suspended for months. Instead of hiding those pages, I gate what goes into the sitemap:

// a page enters the sitemap only if it passes indexable():
// enough data, not long suspended, snapshot not too old.
// Pages that fail still open normally, but carry noindex.

Visitors who land on any stock still get whatever data exists. Search engines are only asked to index the pages that are actually useful.

A timezone bug worth sharing

Snapshot dates were cut from toISOString(), which is UTC. The market data is in Beijing time (UTC+8), so a snapshot built before 8 a.m. local time was labelled with the previous day. Nothing crashed. The page just showed the wrong "as of" date. Format dates in the market's own timezone, not UTC.

Why no LLM on these pages

The site already uses LLMs for paid reports, so this was a deliberate choice:

  • Cost. Generating text for 3,000 stocks every week would be paid by the site, for pages that earn nothing directly.
  • Trust. Numbers that come straight from filings, with the source next to them, beat a fluent paragraph that is probably right.

So the free pages are purely mechanical: the same inputs always give the same page. The model only runs when a user asks for a full report.

What I would do again

  1. Separate the machine that fetches data from the machine that serves pages, even for a tiny site.
  2. Treat crawlers as a load pattern you design for, not an afterthought.
  3. Let missing data lower indexability instead of breaking the page.

Here is an example page: SMIC (688981). The free pages for China A-shares are in Chinese for now; the English site covers U.S. and Hong Kong stocks.

I built Stockinsky. The data comes from public disclosures and may lag or contain errors; company filings are the final word. Nothing here is investment advice.

title: Your AI Can Code. Why Does It Keep Building the Same Landing Page?
description:
Ask an AI coding tool for a “modern SaaS landing page.”

You can almost see the result before it finishes generating:

A giant centered headline. One word in a purple gradient. Three feature cards. A glowing button. Something blurry floating in the background for reasons nobody can explain.

The code probably works. The layout is responsive. The button even has a hover state.

Congratulations. You've built a website for a product that could be absolutely anything.

I don't think the solution is to write a 900-word prompt containing the word premium seven times. The problem starts earlier: we're asking AI to make design decisions without giving it anything meaningful to decide from.

Let's fix that with one fictional product, a few concrete constraints, and an example you can steal for your next React project.

The problem isn't the gradient

There's nothing inherently wrong with gradients, centered headlines, or cards. Plenty of excellent websites use them.

The problem is using them before you know what the page needs to communicate.

Imagine two products:

  • A tool that turns screen recordings into reproducible bug reports.
  • A portfolio platform for experimental 3D artists.

Both need a landing page. Both could use React and Tailwind. But if both open with the same centered headline and three cards, the layout is doing almost no work.

For the bug-report tool, a real example report is probably more persuasive than a decorative illustration. For the artist platform, a full-bleed visual might be the entire argument.

Same stack. Different story. Different layout.

That's the part the prompt needs to explain.

Start with the thing you're actually selling

Let's use the fictional bug-report product as an example. We'll call it Repro. It turns a screen recording into a bug report with clear reproduction steps.

A vague prompt would be:

Build a clean, modern landing page for Repro. Make it premium and add smooth animations.

There is almost nothing here for an AI editor to make a good design decision with.

This is the version I'd actually hand it:

PRODUCT
Repro turns screen recordings into bug reports with
clear steps to reproduce the issue.

AUDIENCE
Frontend engineers and small product teams.

ONE THING TO UNDERSTAND
A recording goes in. A usable bug report comes out.

PRIMARY ACTION
See a sample bug report.

VISUAL DIRECTION
Technical but approachable. Editorial typography.
Off-white background, dark text, one restrained accent.

HERO COMPOSITION
Left: short headline, explanation, one primary CTA.
Right: a realistic sample bug report, not an abstract graphic.
The preview should be the main visual proof.

AVOID
Generic three-card hero, decorative blobs,
gradient headline, stock illustrations.

RESPONSIVE BEHAVIOR
On mobile, stack copy before the sample report.
Keep the CTA visible without horizontal scrolling.

BEFORE CODING
Propose three clearly different compositions.
Explain the trade-off of each in two sentences.
Wait for a choice before writing JSX.

Notice what's missing: a long list of trendy effects.

Notice what's there: a reason for every major element to exist.

Don't ask for a prettier page. Ask for three different pages.

This is an underrated step.

If you ask for one layout, you get one layout. Then you spend the next ten prompts trying to talk the model out of its first idea.

Instead, ask for three compositions with actual differences:

Direction What changes When it makes sense
Product-first A large sample report takes up most of the hero The interface explains the value quickly
Editorial Big typography, narrow copy, small annotated preview The message needs a strong point of view
Workflow-first Recording, processing, and output shown in sequence The transformation is the product's selling point

Then choose one.

Not because the model declared it “the best option,” but because you can explain why it serves the content.

If all three proposals are the same layout with different border radii, send them back. That's not three directions. That's one direction wearing three jackets.

Put proof in the hero, not decoration

Here's a deliberately small React + Tailwind example for Repro. The right side is a sample output, not a glowing mystery object.

export default function Hero() {
  return (
    <section className="bg-[#F7F7F5] px-6 py-20 text-zinc-950 md:py-28">
      <div className="mx-auto grid max-w-6xl items-center gap-14 md:grid-cols-2">
        <div>
          <p className="mb-5 text-sm font-medium text-zinc-500">
            For teams that ship software
          </p>
          <h1 className="max-w-xl text-5xl font-semibold leading-[1.06] tracking-tight md:text-6xl">
            Less explaining bugs. More fixing them.
          </h1>
          <p className="mt-6 max-w-md text-lg leading-8 text-zinc-600">
            Turn a screen recording into a report your teammate
            can actually reproduce.
          </p>
          <a
            href="#sample-report"
            className="mt-8 inline-flex min-h-11 items-center rounded-lg bg-zinc-950 px-5 py-3 text-sm font-medium text-white hover:bg-zinc-800 focus-visible:outline-2 focus-visible:outline-offset-2 focus-visible:outline-zinc-950"
          >
            See a sample report
          </a>
        </div>

        <article
          id="sample-report"
          aria-label="Example bug report"
          className="rounded-xl border border-zinc-200 bg-white p-6 shadow-sm"
        >
          <div className="flex items-center justify-between gap-3">
            <span className="text-xs font-semibold uppercase tracking-wider text-zinc-400">
              Bug report #142
            </span>
            <span className="rounded-full bg-amber-50 px-3 py-1 text-xs font-medium text-amber-800">
              Needs review
            </span>
          </div>
          <h2 className="mt-6 text-xl font-semibold">
            Save button doesn't respond
          </h2>
          <p className="mt-2 text-sm text-zinc-500">
            Example output from a screen recording
          </p>
          <ol className="mt-6 list-inside list-decimal space-y-3 text-sm text-zinc-700">
            <li>Open account settings</li>
            <li>Change the display name</li>
            <li>Click Save</li>
          </ol>
          <p className="mt-6 border-t border-zinc-100 pt-4 text-sm text-zinc-700">
            <strong>Observed:</strong> No confirmation appears.
          </p>
        </article>
      </div>
    </section>
  );
}

Is this the most visually exciting hero on the internet? No. It isn't supposed to be.

But you can answer three important questions immediately:

  1. What does the product do?
  2. Who is it for?
  3. What will I see if I click?

That's already a stronger starting point than a beautiful layout that explains nothing.

Now comes the actual design work: refine the typography, make the preview look like the real product, tune the spacing, and decide whether anything needs to move at all.

Give the model something better than a blank canvas

Another useful trick is to work from editable components with an intentional composition rather than asking for every section from scratch.

You can use your own design system, a collection of components you've built, or a library you like. The important thing is that the editor can inspect the structure and you can change the code.

This is part of why we're building Systra Tools, a React + Tailwind component library that can also be accessed through MCP in compatible AI editors. The idea is to give the editor actual section implementations to work from, then adapt them to the content instead of hoping a vague prompt produces an interesting composition.

There's a catch, though: a good component doesn't automatically make a good page.

If you drop five spectacular sections onto one page with no shared typography, spacing, or pacing, you haven't created a design system. You've created a very expensive-looking argument between five sections.

Choose fewer things. Make them belong together.

The five-minute test before you ship

Before spending another hour polishing the hover animation, try this:

1. Hide the logo. Could the hero belong to a completely different product? If yes, add something specific: a meaningful preview, real language, or a product-specific interaction.

2. Read only the headline and CTA. Can someone understand the benefit and the next step? “Revolutionize your workflow” and “Get Started” are not doing much work here.

3. Look at the page in grayscale. Can you still see the hierarchy? If everything relies on an accent color, the composition may be weaker than it looks.

4. Open it on your phone. Does the most convincing proof disappear below three screens of decorative spacing? Move it up.

5. Turn the animation off. Does the page still make sense? If not, motion may be hiding a content problem rather than solving one.

One more rule: if the layout looks better after removing an effect, you are allowed to remove it. The CSS will recover.

Good AI-assisted design still needs decisions

AI can generate the first pass faster than most of us can open a new Figma file. That's useful.

But speed doesn't decide what matters on the page. It doesn't know which part of a product deserves the spotlight unless you tell it.

So next time the model gives you the familiar gradient headline and three cards, don't just type “make it more creative.”

Give it a real audience, a real job for the page, and a reason to choose one layout over another. Ask for competing compositions. Put proof where the decoration would normally go.

The goal isn't to make AI produce more UI. It's to make the UI say something.

What's one change you've made to your AI workflow that noticeably improved the design? I'm curious whether it's references, tighter constraints, better components, or something else entirely.

title: Large CSV PDF Export Timeout: Object Storage URL Retry and Range Runbook
description:
When a large CSV or PDF export times out in a browser, treat the file and its download URL as two different operational objects. Generate the export asynchronously, upload it completely, validate its size and content type, and only then issue a presigned URL with enough lifetime for the slowest expected connection. If the user retries an old link, mint a fresh URL; do not regenerate an object that is already complete.

Short answer: object storage is a good delivery boundary for large exports, but the timeout investigation belongs in the retry policy, URL expiry window, and object validation path.

Find the boundary before changing the client

A browser's “download failed” message does not identify which stage timed out. Record three state transitions: export generation finished, upload finished, and the link was issued. Keep the expected byte count and content type with the export job. A link should never be published while the producer is still writing, because a user can then receive a partial artifact and reasonably assume storage lost data.

Check the state.

The first check is cheap: inspect object headers before releasing the link. A size mismatch points back to generation or upload. Matching metadata with an expired URL points to delivery credentials. Matching metadata with a live URL and a slow transfer points to client retries, connection throughput, or range support. Those are separate SLOs and should have separate alerts. In a busy export queue, this distinction prevents a delivery retry from consuming another generation slot: the job record can remain ready while the service refreshes credentials, and a producer alert can stay quiet until the byte check actually disagrees. That separation also makes capacity reviews more honest, because generation workers, object storage egress, and browser retry traffic are different budgets with different failure curves.

For capacity planning, estimate a minimum URL lifetime from object bytes divided by a conservative client throughput, then add time for queueing and a user who pauses and resumes the download. There is no universal duration; mobile networks and corporate proxies make the tail wide. Your mileage may vary.

How should a browser retry a slow CSV or PDF download?

The application should return a ready export record, not a promise that a web request will finish. The browser downloads directly from the signed URL and keeps the platform bearer key out of that request. If the URL expires, ask the application for another URL tied to the same export ID. If a connection breaks, resume with a byte range only when the response demonstrates that range recovery is available; otherwise restart the transfer with a fresh URL.

Keep retries bounded. An infinite loop can turn one weak connection into unbounded egress while making availability dashboards look healthy. Verify the final byte count before marking the download complete, so a truncated CSV is not mistaken for a valid report and a PDF viewer does not mask a short tail.

HTTP response headers also affect the browser experience. Set a filename deliberately with Content-Disposition, and ensure the content type matches the generated artifact; see the MDN reference for the header's filename rules. A fresh credential is a delivery action. Rebuilding the export is a production action. They need different retry budgets.

Validate the object before issuing a credential

The verified metadata route is GET /v1/storage/object/head/{bucket}/{key}. This small Go check uses an environment variable for authentication, makes the method explicit, honors Retry-After on 429 responses, and surfaces non-success bodies instead of assuming a 200 response. It is a readiness check, not a download implementation.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 3 || os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY") == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: INFRAI_API_KEY=... go run main.go BUCKET KEY")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    u := url.URL{Scheme: "https", Host: "api.infrai.cc", Path: strings.Join([]string{
        "", "v1", "storage", "object", "head", os.Args[1], os.Args[2],
    }, "/")}

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, u.String(), nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "object check failed: %s: %s\n", resp.Status, body)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }

    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "object check remained rate limited after four attempts")
    os.Exit(1)
}

Compare the returned metadata with the export record before calling GET /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}. The presign response is then handed to the browser as a disposable credential. Do not reuse a URL after its expiry, and do not issue one until the upload-complete state is durable.

Which storage boundary fits the runbook?

The managed-versus-direct decision should follow on-call ownership and required controls. Infrai's relevant advantage here is a plain REST API: any runtime that can send HTTP can use the same contract, with no storage SDK or client-library version to maintain. That is useful for a platform team supporting Go, Node.js, and browser-facing services.

The catch is capability scope. Infrai does not provide public-read ACLs, object versioning or object lock, If-Match conditional writes, a standalone CORS configuration route, cross-region replication, or bulk cross-cloud migration. Lifecycle expiry has a one-day minimum, and provider coverage lists R2, S3, OSS, and COS rather than GCS or B2. It is not suitable for a static website, permanent public links, WORM retention, or strict compare-and-swap writes; choose a native provider or an external coordination layer for those requirements.

Option Fits this download runbook when Prefer another option when
Infrai managed REST API One HTTP contract and low SDK maintenance matter Public ACLs, WORM, versioning, GCS/B2, or self-managed CORS are required
Amazon S3 directly The platform already operates S3-native controls Provider-neutral access is the stronger constraint
Cloudflare R2 directly R2 placement and native ownership are deliberate A shared managed boundary reduces integration work
Alibaba OSS or Tencent COS directly Regional placement and provider controls dominate The team wants to avoid provider-specific client lifecycle
Backblaze B2 directly B2 is a fixed placement requirement The design depends on Infrai's listed provider set

Verify, observe, and roll back

Before rollout, test a known-size export on a throttled connection. Wait for upload completion, compare headers, issue the link, interrupt a transfer, and test both range resume and full restart. Let a test link expire, request a new one, and confirm the export ID and byte count remain unchanged.

In production, track ready-to-link latency, metadata mismatches, URL refreshes, completed bytes, and retry exhaustion against explicit SLOs. A rise in refreshes with stable generation latency suggests an expiry or throughput budget problem; mismatched metadata belongs to the producer path.

Rollback should change delivery policy without changing the artifact. Stop issuing the new link format, route new requests through the last known delivery path, and leave valid private objects untouched. If expiry sizing changed, restore the prior policy for newly issued URLs and let already signed URLs expire naturally. Keep the export identity, expected size, and completion record immutable during the rollback.

References

  • Infrai AI-readable capability index
  • MDN: Content-Disposition response header
  • Backblaze B2 pricing
