title: Self-Hosted Video Conferencing: 9 Best Platforms
description:
Self-hosted video conferencing allows organizations to run video meetings on infrastructure they control instead of relying entirely on a third-party conferencing provider. Companies can deploy conferencing software in their own data centers, private clouds, or customer-managed hosting environments to control server access, network connectivity, user authentication, and the storage of meeting-related information.

The main benefits are infrastructure control, data sovereignty, customization, integration with existing IT systems, and the ability to communicate within private networks. Self-hosted video conferencing is particularly relevant to enterprises, government agencies, healthcare institutions, universities, and businesses with strict security or operational requirements. However, it also introduces responsibility for server maintenance, capacity planning, security updates, and service availability.

Popular self-hosted video conferencing solutions include Jitsi Meet, Nextcloud Talk, OpenTalk, BigBlueButton, OpenVidu Meet, Pexip Infinity, TrueConf Server, LiveKit, and MiroTalk. These products serve different purposes: some provide complete meeting environments, others specialize in education or corporate communications, while developer-oriented platforms offer the infrastructure required to build custom video applications.

Self-Hosted Video Conferencing at a Glance

Requirement What to know
Best for open-source browser meetings Jitsi Meet and other ready-to-use WebRTC applications
Best for unified workplace communication TrueConf Server and Nextcloud Talk
Best for education and training BigBlueButton
Best for existing SIP/H.323 equipment Pexip Infinity and TrueConf Server
Best for embedded video applications OpenVidu Meet and LiveKit
Best for structured meetings OpenTalk
Best for flexible WebRTC deployment MiroTalk
Best for isolated networks Platforms with verified offline licensing and independent internal services
Main benefits Infrastructure control, data sovereignty, customization, and private-network communication
Main responsibilities Capacity planning, security, updates, monitoring, backups, and recovery

The main difference between self-hosted and cloud video conferencing is who operates the conferencing environment. Public cloud services normally provide ready-made meeting applications with vendor-managed infrastructure. Self-hosted systems give organizations control over how conferencing servers are configured, maintained, and integrated with their existing networks.

That control is valuable when communication must follow internal IT policies, use existing authentication systems, or remain available in restricted networks. It does not automatically guarantee lower costs or stronger security. The outcome depends on the product, its dependencies, the deployment architecture, and the organization's technical capabilities.

What Is Self-Hosted Video Conferencing?


Self-hosted video conferencing is a communication model in which an organization deploys and operates video meeting software on infrastructure under its administrative control.

The software typically handles meeting creation, participant authentication, audio and video communication, screen sharing, and optional services such as recording or streaming. Users connect through desktop applications, mobile clients, browsers, or compatible conference room equipment.

Unlike conventional Software as a Service platforms, self-hosted systems allow organizations to manage the application environment, determine where communication services operate, and establish their own network and storage policies.

Self-hosting does not necessarily require physical servers inside a company's office. A conferencing application installed on customer-managed cloud instances may also qualify as self-hosted. The defining factor is who controls and operates the application.

How Does Self-Hosted Video Conferencing Work?


A typical self-hosted conferencing platform includes signaling services, media infrastructure, authentication, and client applications.

When a participant joins a meeting, the application establishes a session through the conferencing environment. Signaling services coordinate connections, while media components transmit or process audio and video according to the platform's architecture.

Some systems forward media streams between participants. Others decode and combine streams before transmitting them to receiving devices. Peer-to-peer applications may establish direct connections when network conditions permit.

Recording, transcription, streaming, monitoring, and directory integration can require additional services. Consequently, installing the conferencing interface is only one part of preparing a production environment.

A basic Jitsi Meet deployment, for example, differs considerably from an enterprise installation of Pexip Infinity or TrueConf Server, although all three can operate on privately managed infrastructure.

Self-Hosted vs. On-Premises vs. Private Cloud

These terms describe related but different aspects of deployment.

Deployment model Infrastructure location Who manages the application? Typical use case
Public cloud SaaS Provider infrastructure Service provider Everyday meetings with minimal administration
Self-hosted on-premises Organization's data center Organization or contracted operator Internal communication and infrastructure control
Self-hosted private cloud Dedicated private infrastructure Organization or contracted operator Flexible private deployment
Self-hosted public cloud Customer-managed cloud instances Organization or contracted operator Custom hosting without owning physical servers
Managed private deployment Dedicated hosting environment Managed service provider Infrastructure separation with outsourced operations
Isolated-network deployment Network without public internet connectivity Organization or authorized operator Restricted and autonomous communication

An on-premises conferencing system is generally self-hosted, but a self-hosted system does not have to be on-premises.

A dedicated vendor-managed instance is not necessarily equivalent to customer-operated software. Businesses should establish who controls administrative access, upgrades, backups, encryption keys, and the underlying operating environment before selecting a deployment model.

Why Do Organizations Choose Self-Hosted Video Conferencing?


The primary reason is the ability to align communication infrastructure with internal technical, security, and operational requirements.

Data Sovereignty and Infrastructure Control

Self-hosting allows organizations to determine where conferencing servers and associated storage systems operate.

This can be important for businesses that need meeting recordings, employee information, and communication services to remain within a particular jurisdiction or approved infrastructure environment. The company can select the data center, establish storage policies, and define who is authorized to administer the system.

Data sovereignty, however, depends on more than server location. Backups, telemetry, support access, external authentication, and third-party integrations must also be considered.

Communication Within Private Networks

Some organizations restrict access to public communication services because of security policies or operational requirements.

A suitable self-hosted conferencing platform can support meetings across a corporate LAN, private WAN, or VPN. In supported configurations, the system may also operate without public internet connectivity.

This is relevant to industrial facilities, research institutions, government agencies, and companies operating restricted networks. Whether a particular product can operate autonomously must be verified through its licensing and technical documentation.

Integration With Existing IT Infrastructure

Businesses may need conferencing software to work with corporate directories, authentication providers, monitoring systems, firewalls, and existing conference room equipment.

Platforms supporting LDAP, Active Directory, SSO, SIP, or H.323 can simplify integration with established infrastructure. For example, an enterprise may want employees to use their existing accounts while connecting professional conference room terminals to the new system.

These capabilities vary between products and licensing editions, so compatibility should be tested for the intended deployment.

Customization and Application Development

Open-source solutions and developer-oriented conferencing platforms allow organizations to create custom interfaces, automate meeting workflows, and integrate live communication into their own applications.

A software company may embed customer consultations into its portal, while an enterprise might connect video meetings with internal scheduling or technical support systems.

The degree of customization depends on the product. A programmable media framework offers extensive development freedom, while a ready-to-use enterprise suite may provide a more complete interface and supported administration tools.

Greater Control Over Operating Costs

Self-hosting changes how conferencing expenses are allocated. Instead of paying only recurring subscriptions, an organization may invest in server resources, software licenses, maintenance, and internal administration.

For companies with existing infrastructure and predictable concurrency, this model can be economical. For smaller teams without technical resources, the additional operational workload may outweigh the benefits.

The financial decision should be based on total cost of ownership rather than the initial software price.

Self-Hosted Video Conferencing Statistics and Infrastructure Trends in 2026


Reliable public statistics specifically measuring global adoption of self-hosted video conferencing platforms are limited. Most enterprise technology surveys track broader categories such as cloud computing, collaboration applications, and communication services. Consequently, general cloud adoption figures should not be interpreted as direct evidence of how many organizations operate private conferencing servers.

According to Eurostat's February 2026 publication, 52.7% of EU enterprises purchased cloud computing services in 2025, compared with 45.3% in 2023 and 17.8% in 2014. The survey covered enterprises with at least ten employees or self-employed persons in specified economic activities.

Enterprise infrastructure indicator Result Relevance to conferencing infrastructure
EU enterprises purchasing cloud services in 2014 17.8% Shows the earlier level of enterprise cloud adoption
EU enterprises purchasing cloud services in 2023 45.3% Establishes the growth of cloud-based business infrastructure
EU enterprises purchasing cloud services in 2025 52.7% Demonstrates widespread use of cloud services
Cloud users purchasing email services 85.2% Communication software is frequently delivered through cloud services
Cloud users purchasing office software 71.7% Collaboration tools are strongly represented in enterprise cloud usage
Cloud users purchasing file storage 71.5% Data storage remains an important infrastructure consideration
Cloud users purchasing computing power for their own software 28.2% Some enterprises use hosted resources to run applications they manage

What These Statistics Mean for Self-Hosted Conferencing?

The figures do not demonstrate whether the use of self-hosted video conferencing is increasing or decreasing. They show that businesses operate in environments where vendor-managed cloud services, privately managed applications, and internal infrastructure can coexist.

A company may use SaaS for routine meetings while operating a separate conferencing system for sensitive communication. Another organization may deploy its own conferencing application on rented cloud servers. The relevant decision is therefore not simply whether to use cloud infrastructure, but which conferencing workloads require direct administrative control.

Insight 1: Self-Hosting Is an Operating Model, Not a Physical Location
A conferencing system does not become less self-hosted because it runs in a rented data center.
The more useful questions concern control. Who manages the application? Who can access server configuration? Where are recordings stored? Who controls upgrades? Which external services are necessary for normal operation?
A customer-managed cloud instance may provide substantial operational control. Conversely, a server physically located in an office but completely administered by an external provider may provide less direct control.
Infrastructure ownership, application administration, data sovereignty, and service availability should be evaluated as separate requirements.

Best Self-Hosted Video Conferencing Platforms

There is no universal best self-hosted video conferencing platform because the products address different communication scenarios.

Some provide complete employee-facing meeting environments. Others integrate conferencing with corporate messaging and file management. Developer-oriented solutions provide media infrastructure and APIs but may require organizations to build their own user interfaces.

The following nine platforms offer documented self-hosted deployment options.

Self-Hosted Video Conferencing Software Comparison

Platform Main specialization Deployment approach Best for
Jitsi Meet Open-source browser conferencing Customer-managed servers IT teams and customizable meeting environments
Nextcloud Talk Messaging, meetings, and documents Nextcloud infrastructure with additional media services Organizations using Nextcloud
OpenTalk Structured meetings and moderation Enterprise on-premises deployment Enterprises and public institutions
BigBlueButton Interactive virtual classrooms Self-hosted Linux infrastructure Education and training
OpenVidu Meet Embeddable conferencing application Customer-managed servers or cloud instances Software developers and SaaS providers
Pexip Infinity Enterprise conferencing and interoperability Private, public cloud, or hybrid deployment Organizations with professional video equipment
TrueConf Server Corporate messaging and private conferencing On-premises Windows or Linux servers Enterprises and restricted networks
LiveKit Programmable real-time media infrastructure Self-hosted or managed infrastructure Developers building custom applications
MiroTalk WebRTC conferencing applications Self-hosted P2P, SFU, or broadcast deployment Smaller organizations and developers

1. Jitsi Meet

Best for: Organizations looking for open-source conferencing with browser access, customizable functionality, and self-managed infrastructure.

Jitsi Meet is an open-source video conferencing application built around WebRTC technologies. It supports meetings through compatible browsers and mobile applications, making it accessible to employees and external participants without specialized conferencing equipment.

Its primary strength is combining a ready-made meeting interface with flexible server deployment and customization.

Jitsi Videobridge and SFU Architecture

One of Jitsi's distinguishing components is Jitsi Videobridge, which uses a Selective Forwarding Unit architecture.

Instead of combining all participants into a single video stream, the bridge forwards selected media streams between participants. This generally reduces server-side processing compared with full media mixing, although bandwidth consumption and participant device performance remain important.

A production deployment also requires signaling and conference coordination components, which administrators must configure as part of the complete system.

Browser Meetings and Collaboration

Jitsi Meet supports audio and video meetings, screen sharing, chat, and participant controls. Recording, streaming, and additional services can be configured through appropriate components.

For example, a development company may use Jitsi for technical discussions, allowing employees to demonstrate application changes while the IT department manages the conferencing environment. Browser access can also make it easier to invite contractors who do not use the same corporate desktop software.

Authentication and Customization

Organizations can configure authentication requirements and meeting access policies. A company may restrict meeting creation to authenticated employees while permitting authorized external guests to join existing conferences.

Jitsi also provides development tools for integrating the conferencing interface into other applications. These capabilities are relevant to IT teams that want to manage meeting access through existing systems rather than rely on a public meeting portal.

Encryption

Jitsi encrypts media traffic in transit and supports optional end-to-end encryption in compatible client configurations. However, the optional protection does not automatically apply to every collaboration feature, including text chat and polls.

Security reviews should distinguish transport encryption from optional end-to-end media protection and consider how individual meeting features are implemented.

Infrastructure and Administration

Jitsi's official self-hosting handbook provides installation and configuration instructions but does not establish one universal server size that guarantees a particular number of participants.

Capacity depends on the number of media bridges, concurrency, recording services, network throughput, and participant workloads. Organizations should begin with a representative deployment, monitor media traffic, and increase resources according to measured usage rather than rely solely on registered user counts.

Business benefit: Jitsi Meet provides a customizable conferencing environment for organizations seeking open-source software and control over deployment.

Strengths: Open-source software, browser participation, Jitsi Videobridge, screen sharing, customization, and flexible self-hosting.

Limitations: Large deployments require technical expertise. Recording, enterprise authentication, and production-scale availability may involve additional infrastructure.

2. Nextcloud Talk

Best for: Organizations that want video conferencing and messaging connected to privately managed documents.

Nextcloud Talk is a communication application integrated with the Nextcloud collaboration environment.

It connects conversations and video meetings with files stored in an organization's Nextcloud infrastructure. This can simplify communication for businesses that already use Nextcloud for document management.

Messaging and Video Meetings

Nextcloud Talk provides direct and group conversations, audio and video calls, screen sharing, and meeting controls.

Employees can discuss a project through persistent messages, organize a meeting, and continue the conversation afterward. Depending on the deployed version and supporting components, additional capabilities may include polls, breakout rooms, recording, and collaboration integrations.

The value of this approach is continuity between everyday discussions and scheduled meetings.

Integration With Nextcloud Files

Nextcloud Talk connects communication with documents stored in Nextcloud.

For example, a legal team can maintain contract drafts within an approved workspace and discuss revisions during a call without distributing uncontrolled copies through external messaging applications.

Access to the underlying files remains governed by Nextcloud permissions. This makes Talk particularly useful when a company wants communication to remain connected to an existing document environment.

High Performance Backend

Larger Nextcloud Talk deployments can use a High Performance Backend that provides additional signaling and media infrastructure.

Its SFU functionality forwards media between participants, making the architecture better suited to substantial conferencing workloads than a minimal installation. Administrators should assess expected concurrency and the performance requirements of these additional components when planning infrastructure.

Federation

Nextcloud Talk supports federated communication between compatible Nextcloud installations, enabling selected users from different organizations to communicate without maintaining all accounts on one central server.

Such connections require appropriate network accessibility, access permissions, and administrative policies. They are particularly relevant when organizations collaborate but want to maintain separate account and server environments.

Practical Application

A professional services company already uses Nextcloud for file storage and collaborative documents. By deploying Talk, the IT department adds video meetings and persistent conversations to the same environment.

Employees can review project materials, discuss changes live, and continue working with the authorized files afterward.

Business benefit: Nextcloud Talk combines video conferencing, messaging, and document collaboration in a self-managed workspace.

Strengths: Nextcloud Files integration, persistent messaging, video calls, screen sharing, federation, and optional high-performance infrastructure.

Limitations: Larger deployments require additional backend resources. The platform is most valuable when an organization also uses Nextcloud's broader collaboration environment.

3. OpenTalk

Best for: Enterprises and public institutions conducting structured meetings with moderation, voting, and corporate identity integration.

OpenTalk is a conferencing platform available through hosted services and on-premises enterprise deployment.

It emphasizes moderated meetings, structured participation, and integration with organizational infrastructure. This makes it suitable for formal discussions that require more control than an ordinary group video call.

Structured Meetings and Moderation

OpenTalk provides meeting scheduling, waiting rooms, participant controls, and moderation features.

Organizers can manage access and coordinate discussions according to the meeting's purpose. This is relevant to committees, associations, and public institutions where participant roles and meeting procedures need to be clearly defined.

The platform is designed to support organized meetings rather than simply connect cameras and microphones.

Polls and Breakout Rooms

OpenTalk supports polling and selected voting functionality, as well as breakout rooms for smaller discussions.

A public institution can use these tools to review proposals, gather participant responses, and divide a larger meeting into working groups. Specific capabilities depend on the edition and licensing, so organizations conducting formal voting should verify that the available functions meet their procedural requirements.

Whiteboards and Presentations

OpenTalk provides screen sharing and collaborative whiteboards. Participants can review documents, annotate visual materials, and discuss proposed changes.

These tools help teams work through complex proposals without requiring everyone to be physically present.

Enterprise Deployment and Identity Integration

OpenTalk Enterprise can be deployed in an organization's own data center. According to its official documentation, the enterprise product uses Docker container technology and supports distributing components across multiple systems for high availability and horizontal scaling.

OpenTalk integrates with Keycloak, allowing organizations to connect compatible identity sources, including LDAP and Microsoft Active Directory. Single Sign-On and two-factor authentication can be implemented through suitable identity configurations. The enterprise offering also supports multiple tenants, providing separate environments for different organizational units or customers.

The provider's deployment documentation has described Kubernetes support as under development. Organizations should verify the support status for the version they intend to install rather than assume that a Kubernetes deployment is covered by standard production support.

Practical Application

A public institution deploys OpenTalk Enterprise on approved infrastructure and connects authentication to its employee directory.

Meeting organizers manage attendance, conduct polls, and organize smaller discussions while maintaining the institution's established access policies.

Business benefit: OpenTalk combines structured meeting participation with enterprise identity integration and privately operated infrastructure.

Strengths: Moderation, polls, breakout rooms, corporate authentication, Docker-based deployment, and multitenancy.

Limitations: Enterprise deployment requires commercial licensing and administration. Advanced capabilities and supported orchestration methods must be verified for the selected edition.

4. BigBlueButton

Best for: Schools, universities, training providers, and organizations operating interactive virtual classrooms.

BigBlueButton is an open-source conferencing platform designed primarily for teaching and learning.

Unlike general-purpose meeting software, it provides tools organized around instructor-led lessons, participant engagement, and collaborative exercises.

As of November 2026, BigBlueButton 4.0 is the latest released major version, with version 4.0.1 published on October 29, 2026. Version 4.1 is documented as in development rather than as a released stable edition. The official release history provides the appropriate reference for checking the version status.

Virtual Classrooms and Whiteboards

BigBlueButton combines audio and video communication with presentations, screen sharing, and a multi-user whiteboard.

Instructors can annotate materials and invite students to interact with diagrams or presentations. For example, a technical trainer can display a network diagram and ask participants to identify components or suggest improvements.

The whiteboard creates a shared workspace for instruction rather than limiting participants to passive viewing.

Breakout Rooms, Polls, and Quizzes

BigBlueButton supports breakout rooms, allowing instructors to divide participants into smaller working groups.

Polls and shared notes help teachers assess understanding and collect feedback. Quizzes also provide a way to ask questions with defined answers and review participant responses.

In a professional training session, participants can examine a scenario in groups, present their findings, and complete a short quiz to check understanding.

These features make BigBlueButton more suitable for structured learning than a platform designed exclusively for ordinary business meetings.

Learning Analytics Dashboard

BigBlueButton includes a Learning Analytics Dashboard with information about attendance and participation indicators.

Supported releases provide additional visibility into activity within breakout rooms. Instructors can use these indicators to identify students who may benefit from additional guidance.

However, activity metrics should support instructional decisions rather than be treated as definitive measures of learning outcomes. A participant who speaks frequently is not necessarily learning more than someone who contributes through written answers or assignments.

Recording and LMS Integration

BigBlueButton provides recording and playback functionality, allowing students to revisit lessons or review materials after a session.

The platform can integrate with learning management systems through supported APIs and connectors. A university, for example, can connect virtual classrooms to Moodle and manage access through its existing course environment.

BigBlueButton 4.0 introduces significant changes to its conferencing infrastructure and client interface, including expanded use of LiveKit for real-time media. Organizations operating custom integrations or plugins should test compatibility with the released 4.0 series before migrating production workloads.

BigBlueButton 4.0 Server Requirements

The official BigBlueButton 4.0 installation guide recommends a clean, dedicated Ubuntu 24.04 server for production.

The published minimum recommendations include eight CPU cores with strong single-thread performance, 16 GB RAM with swap enabled, and at least 250 Mbps symmetrical network connectivity.

Recording-enabled deployments require substantially more storage than systems operating without recordings. The installation guide specifies 500 GB or more of free disk space when recordings are enabled and 50 GB when recording is disabled.

These requirements are version-specific and should not be applied to other conferencing applications.

Migrating From BigBlueButton 3.0 to 4.0

BigBlueButton 3.0 uses Ubuntu 22.04, while version 4.0 requires Ubuntu 24.04.

The official documentation states that a direct in-place upgrade from BigBlueButton 3.0 to 4.0 is not supported. Instead, administrators should prepare a clean Ubuntu 24.04 installation, deploy BigBlueButton 4.0, and migrate existing recordings.

The migration should also include testing of LMS connectors, authentication, custom plugins, recording access, and meeting workflows.

For a university running many simultaneous classes, this is an operational planning issue rather than a simple software update. Administrators should test the new environment before transferring production meetings.

Business benefit: BigBlueButton provides a purpose-built virtual classroom with interactive teaching tools, recordings, and learning analytics.

Strengths: Open-source licensing, whiteboards, breakout rooms, polls, quizzes, recordings, education-focused analytics, and LMS integration.

Limitations: The platform is primarily designed for education. Production deployment requires dedicated infrastructure, and migration from 3.0 to 4.0 requires a new server installation.

5. OpenVidu Meet

Best for: Developers and software vendors requiring embeddable video conferencing with APIs and self-managed deployment.

OpenVidu Meet is an open-source conferencing application designed for self-hosting and integration into other software.

It combines a ready-made meeting interface with developer-oriented APIs and customizable workflows, making it useful for companies adding video communication to their own services.

Browser Meetings and Collaboration

OpenVidu Meet provides video and audio communication, screen sharing, chat, and meeting controls.

Supported configurations also offer collaboration functions such as whiteboards, notes, and breakout rooms. These capabilities allow developers to integrate a complete meeting experience without building every interface component themselves.

APIs, Webhooks, and Embedding

OpenVidu Meet provides REST APIs, webhooks, and embedding options.

Developers can connect meeting creation, participant permissions, and conference events to existing applications. For example, a customer support platform can create video consultation rooms directly from customer records and control access through its own workflow.

Meeting Permissions and Recording

OpenVidu Meet supports configurable meeting roles and recording options. Recordings can be enabled for appropriate rooms, with manual or automatic triggers depending on configuration.

These capabilities can support applications where customer interactions must be documented or reviewed.

End-to-End Encryption

OpenVidu Meet supports end-to-end encryption for audio, video, chat messages, and participant names in compatible configurations.

Its official documentation states that end-to-end encryption and server-side recording cannot be enabled simultaneously for the same room.

This illustrates how encryption requirements can affect the availability of other meeting functions. Organizations that require protected content and recorded sessions should evaluate the trade-off before designing their application workflows.

Practical Application

A software company adds video consultations to its customer portal.

OpenVidu Meet supplies the conferencing application, while APIs and webhooks connect meetings with scheduling, authentication, and customer records. The company operates the conferencing environment on infrastructure it manages.

Business benefit: OpenVidu Meet enables companies to integrate self-hosted video communication into applications without developing every conferencing function from scratch.

Strengths: Embedding, REST APIs, webhooks, meeting permissions, recording, and optional E2EE.

Limitations: Deployment and integration require technical expertise. E2EE is incompatible with server-side recording in the documented room configuration.

6. Pexip Infinity

Best for: Enterprises requiring professional conferencing, distributed infrastructure, and integration with existing video equipment.

Pexip Infinity is a self-hosted conferencing platform designed for enterprise video communication and interoperability.

Its principal advantage is the ability to operate a distributed conferencing environment that connects different types of compatible endpoints.

Distributed Conferencing Infrastructure

Pexip Infinity supports deployment across data centers, private clouds, supported public cloud environments, and hybrid configurations.

Organizations can distribute conferencing nodes according to geographical locations and network requirements. This is useful for enterprises with multiple offices or regional IT infrastructure, particularly when conferencing services need to operate near groups of users.

SIP and H.323 Interoperability

Pexip supports compatible SIP and H.323 video conferencing terminals.

This allows businesses to connect professional room systems with virtual meeting environments and compatible browser participants. For example, a company using Cisco or Poly equipment can evaluate Pexip without immediately replacing every endpoint.

Compatibility still depends on equipment models, software versions, codecs, and configuration.

WebRTC and Browser Participation

Pexip supports browser-based conferencing through compatible WebRTC environments.

Remote employees and guests can join supported conferences even when other participants use professional room systems. This is valuable for organizations with established hardware investments and distributed teams.

Administration and Protocol Management

Self-Hosted Video Conferencing Architecture: P2P vs. SFU vs. MCU


The conferencing architecture affects server processing, client bandwidth, network requirements, and scalability.

Three common approaches are peer-to-peer communication, Selective Forwarding Units, and Multipoint Control Units.

Peer-to-Peer Conferencing

In a peer-to-peer conference, participants exchange media directly when network conditions allow.

This reduces the need for centralized media processing, but each participant may need to send and receive multiple streams as the group grows.

P2P is generally more practical for small meetings than large interactive conferences.

Selective Forwarding Unit

An SFU receives media streams and forwards selected streams to participants.

It generally does not need to decode and combine every video stream into a single composite image. This reduces certain server-side processing requirements, although outbound bandwidth and participant device performance remain important.

Jitsi Videobridge and LiveKit are examples of SFU-based infrastructure.

Multipoint Control Unit

An MCU receives and processes media streams and may combine participants into composite video layouts.

This can simplify media handling for compatible endpoints and support some interoperability scenarios. However, media decoding and encoding can increase server resource consumption.

P2P vs. SFU vs. MCU

Criterion P2P SFU MCU
Main principle Direct media exchange Selective forwarding Media processing and mixing

Client upload May increase with participant count Usually sends streams to an SFU Usually sends streams to an MCU
Client download Multiple peer streams Selected forwarded streams Often a composite stream
Scalability More practical for small groups Suitable for multiparty meetings Depends on processing capacity
Typical use case Individual and small group calls Browser conferencing and group meetings Media mixing and endpoint interoperability

The architecture alone does not determine conference capacity. Performance also depends on codecs, resolution, frame rates, device capabilities, server resources, and network conditions.

Insight 2: Installing a Conference Server Does Not Mean Every Media Stream Passes Through It
Organizations sometimes assume that installing conferencing software internally means all communication stays on that server.
In reality, signaling, media transport, authentication, recording, and network traversal may use different components.
A P2P application may establish direct media connections, while an SFU-based system forwards streams through designated infrastructure. Some deployments also use TURN relays or external authentication services.
A private conferencing deployment should therefore be evaluated through its complete network and data flow.
The important question is where communication is processed and which services are required, not simply where the main web interface is installed.

Self-Hosted Video Conferencing Server Requirements

Server requirements vary considerably between products.

A lightweight P2P signaling application may need relatively modest resources, while an enterprise conferencing server supporting hundreds of participants, recording, and media processing may require dedicated hardware or a distributed deployment.

There is no universal combination of CPU, RAM, and bandwidth that guarantees a particular conferencing capacity.

CPU and Memory Requirements

CPU resources are used for application services, signaling, media handling, encryption, and, where applicable, video processing or recording.

Memory requirements depend on the number of running services, participant sessions, and media workloads.

For SFU-based systems, forwarding media can reduce the need for full server-side transcoding, but CPU and memory usage still grow with concurrency and enabled functions.

Recording, transcription, AI processing, and other optional services may require separate workers or additional machines.

Bandwidth Requirements

Network capacity is particularly important for real-time conferencing because each participant generates media traffic.

In an SFU architecture, the server receives streams and distributes selected media to other participants. As more users participate, outbound server traffic can become significant even if CPU utilization remains manageable.

For example, assume a hypothetical meeting in which 20 participants each publish a video stream averaging 1 Mbps.

If every participant receives streams from the other 19 participants without bandwidth optimization, aggregate server outbound traffic would be approximately:

20 participants × 19 received streams × 1 Mbps = 380 Mbps

This is a simplified theoretical model, not a production capacity estimate. Real systems use adaptive streaming, selective subscriptions, different resolutions, and other optimizations that can substantially change bandwidth consumption.

The example nevertheless illustrates why a conferencing server with sufficient CPU and memory may still experience problems when network throughput is inadequate.

Storage Requirements

A conferencing application without recordings may require relatively modest storage. Recording-enabled deployments can generate substantially larger data volumes, especially when conferences are frequent or long.

Administrators should estimate storage based on recording duration, encoding settings, retention policies, and backup requirements.

For example, recording 100 meetings per month at an average file size of 500 MB would generate approximately 50 GB of new recordings monthly.

The actual file size depends on recording format, resolution, duration, and media content.

How to Estimate Concurrent Capacity?

Capacity planning should begin with the maximum number of participants expected to communicate simultaneously.

A company with 1,000 registered employees may require infrastructure for only 100 concurrent users. Another organization with 300 employees may need all 300 to participate in a single interactive event.

Meeting distribution also matters. Ten conferences with ten participants each may create different media and administrative workloads from one conference involving 100 participants.

A reliable sizing process considers concurrent meetings, conference size, video resolution, screen sharing, recordings, and the location of participants.

Can Self-Hosted Video Conferencing Work Without Internet Access?


Yes. Self-hosted conferencing can operate without public internet access when the platform and all required dependencies support isolated-network operation.

Some products require external registration, license validation, public authentication services, remote TURN infrastructure, or third-party integrations. A system may also support offline meetings while relying on external services for optional functions such as transcription or software updates.

LAN and Private Network Conferencing

A LAN can connect employees within one facility, while a private WAN can connect different offices. A VPN may provide access to authorized remote users, depending on security policy and network configuration.

These environments can support conferencing without exposing the server directly to the public internet.

Air-Gapped Conferencing

An air-gapped network is intentionally isolated from external networks.

To operate in this environment, conferencing software must not depend on services outside the isolation boundary for normal communication. Organizations also need approved processes for license management, software updates, certificates, and maintenance.

TrueConf Server's full licensed edition is an example of a product with documented autonomous operation in suitable isolated networks. Other platforms may be configured for restricted environments, but compatibility must be verified across every required component.

Security and Privacy in Self-Hosted Video Conferencing


Self-hosting provides greater infrastructure control, but strong security still depends on correct implementation.

A privately operated server can expose sensitive information through weak authentication, outdated software, incorrect permissions, or improperly secured administration interfaces.

Security should therefore be evaluated across the complete communication environment.

Encryption in Transit

Transport encryption protects signaling and media traffic while it moves across the network.

Organizations should verify which protocols and configurations protect meeting content, browser access, and communication between infrastructure components.

Older conferencing endpoints may impose compatibility limitations that require particular attention.

End-to-End Encryption

End-to-end encryption is designed to prevent intermediary systems from decrypting protected content.

However, E2EE may limit functions that require server-side media access, including recording, transcription, mixing, or some interoperability scenarios.

OpenVidu Meet provides a concrete example: its documentation states that E2EE and server-side recording cannot be enabled simultaneously in the same room.

Identity Management

Enterprise conferencing systems may support corporate directories, SSO, and additional authentication measures.

These capabilities simplify access management when employees join, change roles, or leave the organization. Businesses should verify integration with their actual identity infrastructure rather than assume that support for a protocol guarantees compatibility with every directory configuration.

Recording and Data Retention

Meeting recordings may contain confidential documents, personal information, and commercially sensitive discussions.

Administrators must determine who can record, where recordings are stored, how long they are retained, and who may access or delete them. An internally hosted conferencing server does not automatically guarantee that every recording or transcription component is also internally operated.

Insight 3: Self-Hosting and End-to-End Encryption Solve Different Problems
Self-hosting determines who operates and controls the communication infrastructure.
End-to-end encryption determines which systems and participants can decrypt protected meeting content.
A self-hosted conferencing server may process media internally to support recording or mixing. Conversely, an end-to-end encrypted service may protect content while relying on infrastructure operated by a third party.
Neither model automatically satisfies every security requirement.
Infrastructure control, content confidentiality, recording requirements, and administrative visibility should be evaluated separately.

How to Deploy a Self-Hosted Video Conferencing Server?


A successful conferencing deployment requires more than installing an application.

The infrastructure must support realistic media workloads, appropriate access controls, and reliable recovery procedures.

Step 1. Define Concurrent Usage

Estimate the maximum number of simultaneous participants and meetings.

For example, an organization with 2,000 registered employees may need capacity for only 150 concurrent participants, while a smaller company may regularly organize conferences involving nearly its entire workforce.

Document expected meeting sizes, video quality, screen sharing, recording, and guest participation.

Step 2. Select Infrastructure

Choose physical servers, virtual machines, private cloud resources, or customer-managed public cloud infrastructure.

Consider the operating-system requirements of the selected product, expected workload, geographical distribution, redundancy, and administrative resources.

Where vendor guidance provides minimum CPU, RAM, and bandwidth specifications, use those requirements as the initial baseline.

Step 3. Configure Networking

Prepare signaling and media connections, DNS, certificates, firewall rules, and network routing.

WebRTC deployments may require STUN or TURN services depending on topology. Administrators should verify that the conferencing media ports are accessible through intended network paths.

Step 4. Install the Platform

Follow official installation documentation for the selected release.

Depending on the product, deployment may involve Linux packages, Docker containers, virtual machines, or dedicated installation tools.

Avoid applying instructions from older software versions without checking operating-system and dependency compatibility.

For BigBlueButton 4.0, this means installing the system on a suitable Ubuntu 24.04 server instead of attempting a direct in-place upgrade from BigBlueButton 3.0. Existing installations should use a planned migration process that preserves recordings and tests integrations.

Step 5. Configure Authentication

Create administrator accounts and establish meeting access policies.

Where supported, integrate the conferencing system with the organization's identity provider. Define who can create meetings, invite guests, record conferences, and manage administrative settings.

Step 6. Configure Recording and Optional Services

Identify where recordings will be stored and how long they must be retained.

If transcription, streaming, AI processing, or integration services are required, include their infrastructure and network dependencies in the deployment.

For restricted environments, verify that these services operate within the approved boundary.

Step 7. Conduct Performance Testing

Test realistic participant numbers and meeting combinations.

Include screen sharing, multiple cameras, guest access, mobile clients, recording, and existing hardware terminals where relevant.

Monitor CPU usage, memory, bandwidth, packet loss, and connection stability. A five-person pilot meeting does not establish that a platform can handle hundreds of concurrent participants.

Step 8. Prepare Monitoring and Recovery

Configure monitoring, backups, update procedures, and documented recovery processes.

For critical environments, evaluate redundant components and test the recovery plan before production use.

Common Mistakes When Choosing Self-Hosted Video Conferencing


One common mistake is selecting a platform exclusively because the software is free to install. The organization may later discover that production operation requires additional media servers, recording components, monitoring tools, or specialist support.

Another mistake is overlooking differences between software versions. A deployment guide written for an older release may no longer describe a supported operating system or migration path. BigBlueButton's transition to Ubuntu 24.04 in version 4.0 provides a practical example of why version-specific documentation matters.

Businesses should also avoid treating a small pilot as evidence that a system can handle enterprise-scale workloads. Realistic performance testing is necessary to understand concurrent capacity, network dependencies, and the effects of recording or screen sharing.

Finally, technical teams should consider the complete operational environment rather than only the conferencing application. Authentication, media relays, storage systems, and maintenance processes can all influence availability and security.

Conclusion

Self-hosted video conferencing allows organizations to operate meetings on infrastructure they control, providing flexibility over server placement, network access, communication data, and integration with existing IT systems. Jitsi Meet, Nextcloud Talk, OpenTalk, BigBlueButton, OpenVidu Meet, Pexip Infinity, TrueConf Server, LiveKit, and MiroTalk address different needs, from open-source browser meetings and virtual classrooms to enterprise communication and programmable media infrastructure. Choosing between them requires understanding whether the organization needs a complete workplace communication platform, specialized conferencing software, or developer-oriented media services.

The main trade-off is operational responsibility. Self-hosted systems can support data sovereignty, customization, and private-network communication, but organizations must manage infrastructure, security, updates, monitoring, and recovery. Selecting the right platform requires evaluating concurrent capacity, current server specifications, network dependencies, integration requirements, and total cost of ownership. The strongest solution is the one that reliably supports the organization's communication needs within its technical, security, and operational constraints.

What are the minimum server requirements for self-hosted video conferencing?

There is no universal minimum because requirements depend on the platform and workload. For example, BigBlueButton 4.0 recommends a dedicated Ubuntu 24.04 server with eight CPU cores, 16 GB RAM, and at least 250 Mbps symmetrical bandwidth, while MiroTalk SFU lists an entry-level configuration of two vCPU and 4 GB RAM. Organizations should follow the documentation for their selected product version and validate capacity through testing.

Can self-hosted video conferencing work without internet access?

Yes, if the conferencing software and all required dependencies support isolated operation. The organization must provide internal networking, authentication, media transport, and appropriate licensing. Self-hosting alone does not guarantee that every feature works without public internet connectivity.

Is self-hosted video conferencing more secure than Zoom or Microsoft Teams?

Self-hosting provides greater infrastructure control but does not automatically guarantee stronger security. Protection depends on encryption, authentication, network configuration, software maintenance, and administrative policies. Security should be evaluated according to organizational requirements rather than hosting location alone.

What is the difference between self-hosted and on-premises video conferencing?

Self-hosted video conferencing means that an organization operates conferencing software on infrastructure it controls. On-premises conferencing specifically refers to infrastructure located within the organization's own facilities or data centers. Self-hosted software can also run on customer-managed cloud infrastructure.

Can external guests join a self-hosted video conference?

Many self-hosted platforms support external participation through browsers, mobile clients, or compatible conferencing terminals. Guest access depends on authentication policies, network configuration, and product capabilities. Isolated conferencing environments require an approved connection path for external participants.

title: Discord Drops Electron for Rust: Should You Follow?
description:
If you have ever alt-tabbed out of a game and watched Discord sit on a gigabyte of RAM, you already understand why this news landed so loudly. On November 4, 2026, Discord co-founder and CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy confirmed on X that the company is rebuilding its desktop client in Rust. Electron is going away. React Native is going away too, at least on mobile.

For users, that is a story about a lighter chat app. For developers, it is a bigger signal. One of the most visible Electron apps in the world is walking away from the framework that made web-tech desktop apps normal. That raises a fair question for the rest of us: should you do the same?

TIP

Discord is rebuilding its desktop app in Rust with the GPUI toolkit and moving mobile off React Native while sharing code through Rust. An early Windows build shown by the CTO used about 290 MB of RAM. There is no public release date yet, and most teams should optimize their Electron apps before considering a rewrite.

What Discord Actually Announced

The core facts are short. The details behind them matter more.

Detail What was reported
Who announced it Stanislav Vishnevskiy, Discord co-founder and CTO, on X, November 4, 2026
Desktop Electron is being replaced by a native client written in Rust
UI toolkit GPUI, the GPU-accelerated Rust UI framework from the team behind the Zed editor
Not chosen Tauri, which still renders the interface in the system web view
Mobile React Native is going away. Mobile keeps a native UI but shares app code with desktop through Rust
Codename Discord Phoenix, seen in the Task Manager screenshot
Early metric About 290.2 MB of RAM on Windows 11 in a screenshot
Timing Discord hopes to start user testing soon. No release date has been given

We've been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust, the holy grail was getting the whole client there. That means Electron goes away, and so does React Native, mobile keeps native UI but shares app code with desktop via Rust. We hope to get it into testing with users soon™. (And it's not Tauri, it's GPUI, so good guess everyone.) Alright, back to staring at the WoW Forever login screen.

— Stanislav (@svishnevskiy) November 4, 2026

Rust is not new at Discord. The company has used it since 2018 in infrastructure, voice technology and parts of the current client. What changed is the scope. The goal now is to bring the entire client into Rust.

Vishnevskiy described the shared core as the main prize. Mobile keeps its native interface, while state, networking and business logic move into one Rust codebase that both platforms can use. He also said the new client looks and works like the current one, which is a useful promise to hold the team to when a beta ships.

The follow-up posts added two details that got lost in the RAM headlines. Discord maintains its own patches for GPUI and wants to push useful changes upstream. The browser version is also getting a UI wrapper that can render to HTML or GPUI depending on the platform, with accessibility called out as a requirement.

What the 290MB Number Does and Does Not Prove

It is tempting to read "290 MB versus 4 GB" as a clean before and after. It is not, and the difference matters.

  • It is one screenshot from an early build. Nobody outside Discord has measured it.
  • The comparison is loose. The current app was reported at 1 to 2 GB when idle in Windows Latest testing, with spikes up to 4 GB. Those are different workloads from a freshly started test build.
  • The screenshot had two accounts signed in, according to later reporting. That makes the figure more impressive, not less.
  • Discord has not listed which features are in the build. We cannot compare like for like.
  • The same screenshot showed Chrome at about 1.57 GB across 19 processes. A single native process is a different shape of memory use, not just a smaller number.

There is also the history behind the 4 GB figure. A Discord employee said in December 2025 that the team was testing an automatic restart when memory passed 4 GB, compared with under 1 GB in normal use. A restart failsafe treats the symptom. It also admits that the problem was real.

The fair reading: the early result is promising, and the full story is not in yet.

The new Discord client using less RAM is just part of the story. Clicking around feels instant, I can't go back. Check out the boot time. https://t.co/x7ayyWBVQJ

— Stanislav (@svishnevskiy) November 5, 2026

Why Electron Became Discord's Bottleneck

Electron lets you build a desktop app with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. It does that by bundling two large pieces with every app: the Chromium browser engine and a Node.js runtime. You get one codebase for Windows, macOS and Linux, plus the web ecosystem. You also get a browser's worth of memory overhead for every app.

For a chat app that stays open all day, runs voice, video, screen sharing, overlays and thousands of messages, that overhead adds up. Discord's desktop client has been criticized for memory use for years. The criticism got louder as RAM prices rose and vendors brought back 8 GB Windows 11 configurations, which makes heavy background apps harder to defend.

Cost Why it hurts
Memory Each app carries its own Chromium and Node.js
Startup time Loading a browser engine and a large JavaScript bundle takes time
Battery Constant JavaScript and rendering work drains laptops
Disk size Installers are large because the runtime ships inside
Security surface You track Chromium and Node updates for every release

Electron also has real strengths, which is why so many products still choose it. VS Code, Slack and the ChatGPT desktop app use it, and the developer experience is excellent. The framework still works. It is simply heavy at Discord's scale.

Discord did try to trim it. An Electron 42 upgrade reportedly cut median CPU use by about 17%, but median memory use rose by around 4% at the same time. That trade-off is the reason a deeper rewrite started to look attractive.

GPUI, Tauri and Electron Compared

This is the part developers asked about first. All three options can produce a desktop app, but they draw the interface in different ways.

Tauri is written in Rust, yet it renders the UI in the operating system web view: WebView2 on Windows, WKWebView on macOS and WebKitGTK on Linux. You skip bundling Chromium, so apps are far smaller. You still write the interface with web tech, and you still depend on a web engine.

GPUI is different. It is a GPU-accelerated UI framework written in Rust and developed by the team behind the Zed editor. It draws the interface itself, without a web view or Chromium. That is closer to how a game engine renders, and it can give fast, consistent drawing. The trade-off is that you give up the web ecosystem and rebuild many things that browsers provide for free.

Electron Tauri GPUI
Language for UI JavaScript or TypeScript JavaScript or TypeScript, with a Rust backend Rust
Rendering Bundled Chromium System web view GPU drawn by the toolkit
App size Large Small Small to medium
Memory use Highest of the three Lower Lowest in principle
Web ecosystem access Full Full None
Maturity Very mature Mature Younger, smaller ecosystem
Best for Fast shipping with a web team Lean apps that still use web UI Performance critical, long running apps

Discord's choice fits its profile. It is a huge app with a big team, very long session length and a performance reputation to repair. Few projects share that profile.

The GPUI trade-off nobody mentions

GPUI renders through the GPU. At the time of writing, it did not support CPU-only rendering, according to reporting from Roboin. That is fine on a laptop with integrated graphics. On a desktop with a single dedicated GPU, the chat client now competes with the game for graphics resources.

None of that makes the choice wrong. The memory win may simply bring a different cost on some hardware, and independent testing during the beta will show whether it matters.

What This Means for Your App

1. A flagship Electron app is moving off Electron

Electron has been the default answer for cross-platform desktop apps for about a decade. A move like this leaves the framework in place, yet it changes the conversation, especially for apps that stay open all day.

2. Rust keeps moving up the stack

Rust began as a systems language for servers, tooling and infrastructure. Using it for the full client, UI included, is a statement about how far the ecosystem has come. Readers building with agents and terminal tools will recognize the pattern. If you want to see how lighter tools compare with heavier ones, read our comparison of OpenCode vs Cursor, and our guide to the OpenCode terminal UI. For the wider category, our explainer on AI coding agents covers what these tools actually do.

3. Shared code across desktop and mobile is the prize

Vishnevskiy described the goal as one core for state, networking and business logic, with platform specific UI on top. Many teams chase that and few reach it. React Native promised something similar in JavaScript. Rust gives Discord a core that also runs on servers and in the browser through WebAssembly.

4. Memory is now a product feature

With high RAM prices and cheap laptops still shipping with 8 GB, users notice apps that hog memory. Resource use has become part of how people judge quality. The same shift shows up in browser experiments, like the time GTA 5 ran in a browser tab, where engineering teams pushed hard to fit a large workload into a small footprint.

5. It resets expectations for chat and community apps

If Phoenix ships and delivers, other big Electron apps will face comparisons. WhatsApp and Teams were already named in memory tests by Windows Latest. Expect users to ask why a chat app needs a browser inside it.

Should You Rewrite Your Electron App?

For most teams, the answer is not yet, and probably not by rewriting. Discord has a dedicated engineering organization, years of runway on this project, and a product where memory use directly affects the user experience. A rewrite is expensive, risky and slow. Joel Spolsky's classic warning about full rewrites still applies: you throw away years of bug fixes while the old product stands still.

Use this decision guide.

Your situation Suggested path
Small team, web skills, need to ship now Stay on Electron and optimize it
Mostly CRUD or a dashboard, want a lean installer Evaluate Tauri
Heavy backend logic or performance critical modules Keep the Electron UI, move hot paths to Rust
App stays open all day, memory is the top complaint Profile first, then consider a staged migration
Rich text, accessibility and plugins matter out of the box Stay with a web based UI
New, performance obsessed product with Rust expertise Consider a native Rust UI such as GPUI
No Rust experience on the team Do not start a rewrite. Build skills on a small project first

Questions to Ask Before You Rewrite

  1. Is memory actually your users' top complaint? Check support tickets and reviews, not just your own opinion.
  2. Have you profiled? Most Electron memory problems come from leaks and heavy renderers, not only from the framework.
  3. Can you migrate in stages? A hybrid approach lowers risk.
  4. Does your team know Rust? The learning curve is real, and hiring is harder.
  5. What will you lose? Rich text editing, accessibility, spellcheck, input methods and extensions are all easier on the web.
  6. Do you need all three platforms at the same quality? Custom drawn UIs must handle each platform's quirks.

How to Cut Electron Memory Without a Rewrite

You can often get useful gains without replacing the framework. Start with measurement, then fix the usual suspects.

1. Measure before you change anything

Electron can report per-process usage from the main process:

const { app } = require("electron");

setInterval(() => {
  const metrics = app.getAppMetrics().map((m) => ({
    type: m.type,
    pid: m.pid,
    workingSetMB: Math.round(m.memory.workingSetSize / 1024),
  }));
  console.table(metrics);
}, 10000);

Pair this with Chrome DevTools heap snapshots in the renderer to find what is actually growing.

2. Use fewer windows and renderers

Every BrowserWindow is another renderer process. Reuse windows where you can, close hidden ones, and avoid keeping unused views alive.

3. Virtualize long lists

Rendering thousands of DOM nodes is a classic memory sink. Use virtual scrolling for message lists, logs and tables so only visible items exist in the DOM.

4. Hunt leaks

Remove event listeners, clear timers, cancel subscriptions on unmount, and watch for detached DOM nodes in heap snapshots.

5. Manage images and media

Resize images before display, avoid holding large decoded images in memory, and release video and audio resources when views close.

6. Move hot paths to Rust

You can keep your UI and still use Rust where it matters, through native Node modules. A small example with napi-rs:

use napi_derive::napi;

#[napi]
pub fn count_words(text: String) -> u32 {
    text.split_whitespace().count() as u32
}

const { countWords } = require("./native");
console.log(countWords("hello rust inside electron"));

This is the lowest risk way to get Rust performance without a full rewrite.

7. Lazy load everything you can

Load heavy modules, settings panels and rarely used features on demand, not at startup.

8. Test on low end hardware

Test on a machine with 8 GB of RAM, not just your fast laptop. If it feels heavy there, your users already know.

9. Track memory in CI

Add a smoke test that opens the app, performs common actions and fails the build if memory passes a threshold. Regressions are cheaper to catch early.

If your product is web first and you want to skip installs entirely, our guide to building a SaaS app with Puter.js shows a different route. The point is to choose the delivery model before you choose the runtime.

What to Watch Next

  • Public testing of Discord Phoenix. Independent measurements will matter more than screenshots.
  • Feature parity. Voice, video, overlays, plugins and accessibility are the hard parts.
  • Linux support. Discord has not detailed platform coverage in the announcements covered here.
  • GPU behavior during games on single-GPU systems.
  • GPUI's ecosystem. If a large product ships on it, expect more libraries, docs and contributors.
  • Third party clients and mods. A new rendering stack could change how customization works. Nothing has been announced yet.

Key Takeaways

  • Discord's CTO confirmed on November 4, 2026 that the desktop client is being rebuilt in Rust, replacing Electron.
  • The new UI uses GPUI, a GPU-accelerated Rust framework from the Zed team, not Tauri.
  • React Native is also leaving. Mobile keeps a native UI and shares app code with desktop through Rust.
  • An early Windows build showed about 290 MB of RAM. That is promising, but it is one early screenshot, not a benchmark.
  • The current Electron app is reported at 1 to 2 GB when idle, with spikes up to 4 GB.
  • There is no release date. Discord says user testing is coming soon.
  • Most teams should profile and optimize before rewriting. Rewrites are expensive and risky.
  • You can get Rust performance inside Electron with native modules, which is often the best first step.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Discord leaving Electron?

Discord has confirmed that its desktop app is being rebuilt in Rust and will no longer use Electron. Co-founder and CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy announced the change on X on November 4, 2026. The company has not announced a release date.

Why is Discord moving to Rust?

Discord wants a faster app that uses less memory and power. The current Electron client bundles a full browser engine, and reports show it can use 1 to 2 GB of RAM when idle and as much as 4 GB in extreme cases. A native Rust client aims to remove that overhead.

What is Discord Phoenix?

Discord Phoenix is the name shown in a screenshot of the early Rust based desktop client posted by Discord's CTO. The Task Manager entry showed about 290 MB of RAM on Windows 11. Discord has not confirmed that Phoenix will be the final product name.

What is GPUI?

GPUI is a GPU-accelerated user interface framework for Rust developed by the team behind the Zed code editor. It draws the interface directly without a web view or Chromium, which can improve speed and reduce memory use.

Why did Discord not choose Tauri?

Tauri is written in Rust but displays the interface in the operating system web view, so it still depends on a web engine. Discord chose GPUI, which draws the interface natively. Discord has not published a full technical explanation of the decision.

How much RAM will the new Discord use?

An early Windows 11 build showed about 290 MB in a screenshot, while signed in to two accounts. That figure comes from an early test build and is not a verified benchmark, so final memory use may differ.

Will Discord mobile apps change too?

Discord plans to drop React Native on mobile. The apps will keep a native interface and share application code with the desktop client through Rust.

Should I rewrite my Electron app in Rust?

Usually not as a first step. Profile the app, fix memory leaks, reduce renderer processes and move performance critical code to Rust modules. Consider a full rewrite only if memory or performance is the main product problem and the team has Rust expertise and time.

Conclusion

Discord's move is the clearest sign yet that the Electron default is no longer automatic. The framework still makes sense for many products, especially small teams that need to ship fast with web skills. It just has to earn its place now, and memory use is part of the argument.

If you build a desktop app, start with a profile, not a rewrite. Fix leaks, cut renderer count, lazy load the heavy parts and move the hot spots to Rust. Reach for Tauri when a smaller installer matters. Reach for GPUI only when the product, the team and the timeline all support a native UI bet.

Primary sources for this article include The Verge's report, Windows Latest on the RAM testing, Roboin's technical summary and the official GPUI site. Our contributor guide explains how to pitch a follow-up, and the editorial policy covers how we review claims like these.

This article was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by the F9XR Team before publication. The 290 MB figure comes from a screenshot and press coverage, not an independent benchmark. We will update it as Discord shares more.
