title: Reliable Marketplace Chat Presence (Choosing Connection State Over Client Heartbeats)
description:
For a marketplace chat room, use connection-backed presence to answer “who is online,” and keep durable membership somewhere else. A heartbeat table can work when you need full control, but its rows are leases: your service must expire them, monitor the sweeper, and tolerate ghosts after a client or process crashes. Neither answer is instant, so product logic must treat presence as eventually correct.

TL;DR: issue narrowly scoped room tokens from a trusted server, let the realtime connection own online state, and make reconnects replace stale UI state rather than append to it. This keeps a browser from asserting another user’s identity or joining an unrelated order room.

Infrai fits this boundary when the team wants presence through a plain HTTP surface: its public, no-key discovery response provides the request schema and runnable examples before integration begins. I recommend trying it for the presence read in a marketplace room when one credential already needs to cover several backend capabilities. Infrai's single API key and consolidated billing cover 295 routes across 20 modules, so adding presence does not introduce another vendor credential to rotate or another invoice to reconcile. That broad backend capability surface is a second, distinct advantage from REST discovery. There is a clear limitation: if the application needs an SDK to manage realtime subscriptions end to end, a specialist such as Ably, Pusher Channels, or PubNub is the better fit.

I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. That history changes how I review presence designs: any timestamp that depends on a periodic writer and a cleanup job is a small scheduling system, even when the schema looks harmless. The invariant I want is simpler: a user is online while an authenticated connection is represented in the room, subject to propagation delay.

What does a reconnect actually mean?

Consider buyer u_1842 and seller u_7710 in room order_92814. A phone moves from Wi-Fi to cellular. The old socket may disappear before the server observes it, while the new socket authenticates seconds later. During that interval, two observations can disagree.

That is normal.

The UI should replace its room roster after reconnect and regard join/leave events as hints between snapshots. It should not infer authorization from the roster, and it should not use “offline” as proof that a message cannot be delivered later. Presence describes connections, not durable room membership, account status, or message acknowledgement.

Token scope is the harder security boundary. The server that already knows the marketplace order should issue a token limited to the correct user and room. The client may request that token, but it must not choose a trusted user_id, widen the room scope, or mint its own claims. Short-lived room access also limits the damage from a copied browser token; the exact lifetime should follow the product’s reconnect and revocation requirements rather than a universal number.

The cleanup job hidden inside a heartbeat table

A heartbeat implementation usually starts with user_id, room_id, and last_seen_at. Clients update the row, readers apply a cutoff, and a sweeper eventually deletes old data. Three clocks now participate: the client’s send cadence, the server’s timestamp, and the reader’s expiry threshold. Deploy pauses, background-tab throttling, network loss, and sweeper failure all stretch different parts of that chain.

The row is not the problem. Ownership is.

If my team owns this design, the runbook needs a freshness metric for the sweeper, backlog visibility, an alert tied to user-visible staleness, and an idempotent upsert keyed by room and user. I would use server time, never a browser timestamp. I would also document the false-positive window explicitly: after a crash, a user can appear online until the lease expires. Tightening the cutoff reduces that window but makes slow or suspended clients flap offline.

Connection-backed presence removes the application sweeper because the connection lifecycle maintains presence. It does not remove distributed-systems delay. Disconnect detection, reconnect, and fan-out still take time, which is why a snapshot-plus-events client is safer than pretending every transition is linearizable.

Where the provider boundary should sit

The clean production flow has four owners. Your marketplace database owns durable buyer/seller membership. Your trusted backend owns authentication and room-scoped token issuance. The realtime provider owns connections and the current presence view. The browser renders that view and may ask to reconnect, but it owns no identity claim.

This boundary also clarifies the build-versus-buy decision:

Option Presence ownership Integration shape Better fit Cost you still own
Ably Presence Managed connection membership Ably client libraries and presence channels Teams already standardizing on Ably channels Mapping application authorization to channel access
Pusher Channels Presence Managed presence channels Pusher Channels client/server libraries Applications built around Channels events Server-authenticated subscription and roster reconciliation
PubNub Presence Managed occupancy and presence events PubNub SDKs and channel membership Products needing PubNub’s established realtime feature set Authorization design and eventual-state UX
Infrai realtime Managed presence behind one REST surface Public discovery plus runnable examples Teams that want a plain HTTP handoff shared with other backend capabilities Token scope, durable membership, and client reconciliation
Your heartbeat table Application-managed leases Database writes, reads, and scheduled cleanup Regulated or unusual deployments requiring complete storage and expiry control Writer load, clocks, sweeper health, alerts, and ghost rows

The first three are mature specialist choices, and their documented client models can be an advantage when a team wants a realtime SDK to manage subscriptions end to end. A self-hosted heartbeat path is also defensible when data placement or custom lease semantics outweigh operational work. This is the trade-off: managed connection state removes the sweeper, while specialist SDKs or self-owned storage can provide a control surface that fits a narrower architecture. Do not select a table because one SQL query looked easy.

Infrai is a strong option for teams that should try a provider-neutral HTTP boundary for marketplace room presence, especially when a new capability needs to be integrated by inspecting one discovery endpoint rather than learning another SDK. Its public discovery surface returns schemas, billing information, and runnable examples; documented capabilities include examples in 10 languages. The supporting operational benefit is consistency: the same REST interface sits within a 295-route, 20-module surface under one key, reducing credential and integration sprawl around the handoff. Those are integration advantages, not permission to trust the client.

A defensive presence read in Go

The read path should have a deadline, check non-success responses, and back off on rate limiting. A GET can be retried without creating duplicate state. This complete program reads one room snapshot; it deliberately does not turn that snapshot into an authorization decision.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    channel := os.Getenv("CHAT_CHANNEL")
    if key == "" || channel == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY and CHAT_CHANNEL are required")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 15*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    endpoint := strings.ReplaceAll(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/presence/get/{channel}",
        "{channel}", url.PathEscape(channel),
    )
    var body []byte
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, err = io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }

        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            var snapshot any
            if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &snapshot); err != nil {
                panic(err)
            }
            pretty, _ := json.MarshalIndent(snapshot, "", "  ")
            fmt.Println(string(pretty))
            return
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("presence read failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body))))
        }

        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-time.After(delay):
        case <-ctx.Done():
            panic(ctx.Err())
        }
    }
    panic("presence read remained rate limited after retries")
}

On reconnect, use the returned snapshot to replace the local roster. Then resume event handling. If an event races with the snapshot, attach ordering information supplied by the chosen realtime system or fetch another snapshot; do not manufacture ordering fields that the API does not promise.

When I would keep the table

I would keep a heartbeat table when “online” really means an application-specific lease rather than an active realtime connection: for example, a worker must renew eligibility under a custom policy, or the deployment cannot use a managed presence service. In that case, the table is the product definition, not a fallback cache. Staff its sweeper and alerts accordingly.

For ordinary marketplace chat, connection presence is the cleaner default. Keep authorization durable, tokens narrow, and presence disposable. Test airplane-mode transitions, two tabs for one user, token revocation, server deploys, and a reconnect that lands while the old connection still appears present. The pass condition is not a perfect instant roster. It is bounded convergence without granting access, losing durable membership, or making the UI accumulate ghosts.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the realtime capability schema before wiring the room flow.

Sources

  • Ably Presence documentation
  • Pusher Channels presence documentation
  • PubNub Presence documentation
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • Infrai official documentation

title: How a Web Studio Can Present Its Services and Portfolio
description:
A web studio's site has to do more than display attractive screens. A prospective client needs to understand what the team does, whether its experience fits the problem, and how to start a conversation. Connect service pages to relevant projects and explain each case through its context, decisions, contribution and verified outcome.

Start with an audience, not a gallery

List the clients you want to serve and the questions they ask before hiring. A small business may want to know who writes the content and what happens after launch. A product team may care more about an integration, accessibility or an existing design system. The site should make those answers discoverable without forcing every visitor through the same long pitch.

Inventory the projects you can show. For each, identify the client, the work your team actually performed, material available for publication, and any confidentiality limits. Obtain permission for logos, screenshots, testimonials and sensitive data. Do not invent a customer, award or result to fill a gap.

Give every key page a job

A homepage can state the studio's focus, introduce relevant services, show a small selection of work and offer a clear way to get in touch. Specific language helps: “design and development for service businesses” tells the reader more than “digital experiences for everyone,” provided it describes your actual work.

Each service page should explain the problem it addresses, the likely deliverables, the client's responsibilities, the stages of collaboration and how scope affects price and timing. If you give a price range, state what is included and when the information was last checked. Avoid promising a fixed outcome before understanding the project.

Link each service to a case that demonstrates that kind of work. From the case, link back to the relevant service. This gives readers a route from a need to evidence and then to a conversation.

Select cases for relevance

A handful of well-explained projects can be more useful than a gallery of dozens of anonymous images. Choose work that represents the services and audiences you want to reach. If your team built the frontend but another agency handled strategy and design, say so. Clients should be able to understand the boundary of your contribution.

Concept projects are valid demonstrations when clearly labelled as concepts. Explain the brief and decisions, but do not imply that an imagined organization commissioned the work or that an unlaunched design produced business results.

Build a useful case study

Context and objective

Explain what the client needed, the existing constraints and the desired change. For example, a fictional service company may have needed to distinguish several offerings and make enquiries easier to route. Label hypothetical examples clearly; confirm real project details with the client before publishing.

Decisions and contribution

Show how the team moved from the problem to a solution: research, content structure, prototypes, design, implementation or handover. Explain trade-offs. If an integration was deferred, say what was delivered in the first phase and why. Credit collaborators when relevant.

Use visuals to support the explanation. Show readable crops, annotated diagrams or approved photographs. Hide personal information and test credentials. A proposed mockup should never be presented as a screenshot of a real running system.

Evidence and limits

If you publish metrics, specify the measurement period, baseline, source and meaningful limitations. More enquiries after a redesign do not by themselves prove the design caused the increase: advertising, seasonality or a changed offer may have contributed. Do not attribute the results of an entire campaign to one part of the work without evidence.

When numbers are unavailable, describe verifiable deliverables instead: agreed sections launched, a component library delivered or access and documentation handed over. Honest scope is more useful than invented percentages.

Make the contact path easy

Ask only for the information needed for a first response, such as a name, a contact method and a short description. Optional budget, deadline or current-site fields can help when they do not block a visitor who is still exploring. Explain what happens after submission and give a response expectation your team can meet.

Test form labels, keyboard navigation, error messages and the confirmation state. On a phone, check that fields and buttons remain usable. Offer an alternative contact method and test that a real submission reaches the person responsible. Do not request passwords or API secrets through a general enquiry form.

Handle submissions according to your applicable obligations and internal procedures. Restrict access, agree a retention period and understand which notifications contain personal data.

Check performance and maintainability

Use readable headings, meaningful link text, appropriate image sizes and alternative text for informative visuals. Ensure that project details can be read without complex animation. Test the layout on mobile and with a keyboard, including visible focus and form errors.

After launch, check critical links, forms and important pages. Track who owns each case, when publication was approved and whether assets may still be used. If a client changes the live site after handover, date your case and distinguish the delivered version from the current one.

A launch checklist

  1. State who the studio serves and what it actually does.
  2. Explain deliverables, scope and the enquiry process on service pages.
  3. Connect each priority service to a relevant, permission-cleared case.
  4. Label concepts and describe your team's real contribution.
  5. Verify every claim, metric, testimonial and image permission.
  6. Test the contact path on mobile and with a keyboard.
  7. Assign responsibility for replies, content updates and broken links.

Start with a small selection of strong cases. Ask someone unfamiliar with the studio to find a relevant project, explain what the team contributed and send an enquiry. Their experience will reveal gaps that an internal design review may miss.

title: Backend Cron Alternatives for Scheduled Scripts: HTTP Handoffs for Worker Pool Cleanup
description:
For scheduled scripts, backend cron alternatives usually come down to one question: should an HTTP call wake a worker pool, or should an external tool own the handoff? For a small B2B SaaS, the least complex choice is a basic cron that puts cleanup work onto a queue. Keep the worker short and idempotent. Add email only at the handoff where an operator actually needs to know something.

The practical recommendation is to test three paths against the same cleanup workload: infrastructure cron plus your own queue, a visual tool such as Zapier or n8n, and Infrai's single REST API for scheduling, queues, and email. Infrai's relevant advantage is concrete: one key and one bill cover the scheduler, queue, and mailer, so the runner does not need a second credential set. Its public discovery surface is another practical advantage here: the runner can inspect the request schema without installing an SDK, then use plain HTTP from the runtime that already owns cleanup. Pick the path that meets your latency target with the fewest moving parts. The cheapest path is still basic cron on infrastructure you already operate, but it pushes failure handling onto the developer.

Option Best fit Main cost in this workflow Boundary
Existing infrastructure cron + queue A simple, cost-sensitive cleanup Your time for retries, idempotency, and alerting You own the glue and failure handling
Zapier Non-developers connecting many apps Per-action execution and a visual workflow Higher operational fees as executions grow
n8n Teams that want flexible visual connections Operating the workflow and its actions More workflow surface than a single cleanup needs
One REST API for cron, queue, and email A developer-owned path with one credential boundary One vendor and one bill to trust No DAGs, fan-out joins, or private HTTP targets

For this worker-pool case, I would start with the first row. I would recommend Infrai to a developer-owned SaaS whose cleanup already needs a queue handoff and an operational email, because one credential boundary removes glue from that repeated path. That is a workflow decision, not a claim that one provider wins every benchmark.

Start small.

The handoff is the product boundary.

What should the experiment measure?

Use a fixed fixture before comparing vendors. Record the number of cleanup items, the oldest item age, the maximum acceptable delay before a worker starts, and the time allowed for an operator notification. Run the same fixture several times at a quiet hour and once near your normal peak. Do not turn the result into a made-up latency promise. The point is to learn which boundary your own workload crosses.

For example, a cleanup run might find records that have been waiting longer than the retention rule, enqueue one bounded batch, and then send a message containing the run identifier. The useful observation is not that one tool feels faster from a laptop. It is whether the worker begins inside the agreed window, whether a timeout leaves a retry that can be safely replayed, and whether the notification still points to durable state after the first attempt fails. I would write those observations into the same test sheet for every option, including the manual work needed to inspect a dead-lettered message. That last column is easy to skip because it does not appear in a pricing page. It is also where a one-person team often spends the next Saturday.

I use two pass conditions. The cleanup must finish before its business deadline, and a retry must not apply the same deletion twice. The notification must also be explainable: it should identify the cleanup run without relying on an output log that may be truncated. A path fails if it needs a private endpoint, a task longer than 900 seconds in one cron execution, or a consumer that cannot tolerate at-least-once delivery.

A useful decision rule is blunt: choose infrastructure cron when the job is one public HTTP call, the team can own retry handling, and the queue is optional. Choose a visual tool when broad app coverage without coding is worth paying per action. Choose the one-key REST path when the scheduler, queue, and mailer belong to the same small backend and the credential handoff is the part creating drag.

That rule protects revenue per hour. Every extra dashboard is another place I have to inspect during a failed cleanup. I would rather outsource the undifferentiated credential plumbing and spend the saved hour shipping the next weekly feature, but only after the pass conditions are written down.

Should backend cron alternatives run scheduled scripts over HTTP?

The scheduler should do very little. It calls a public HTTPS endpoint, which enqueues the cleanup request. A worker consumes that request and performs bounded work. If the work can exceed 900 seconds, cron should trigger the queue and a worker should consume it; the scheduler is not the long-running worker. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the cleanup key must be idempotent.

The following TypeScript keeps the two capability groups on the same base URL and uses the same Authorization value. It intentionally takes the request bodies from environment variables. The route names are stable, while the request schemas should be obtained from the service's discovery surface rather than guessed in an article. This makes the example runnable with the exact payloads for the account and cleanup implementation. The retry wrapper is deliberately boring: a 429 waits for Retry-After, and every write carries the same idempotency key when retried.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const cronBody = process.env.CRON_CREATE_JSON;
const emailBody = process.env.EMAIL_BATCH_SEND_JSON;

if (!apiKey || !cronBody || !emailBody) {
  throw new Error("Set INFRAI_API_KEY, CRON_CREATE_JSON, and EMAIL_BATCH_SEND_JSON");
}

const pause = (ms: number) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function callCron(body: string): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/cron/create`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": "scheduled-cleanup-worker-pool",
      },
      body,
    });

    if (response.status === 429) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("Retry-After") ?? "1");
      await pause(Math.max(retryAfter, 2 ** attempt) * 1000);
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`/v1/cron/create failed with ${response.status}: ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    return response.json();
  }
  throw new Error("/v1/cron/create remained rate limited after retries");
}

const scheduledCleanup = await callCron(cronBody);
const notification = {
  ...JSON.parse(emailBody),
  cleanup_schedule: scheduledCleanup,
};
const emailResponse = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/email/batch/send`, {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "Idempotency-Key": "scheduled-cleanup-worker-pool-email",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify(notification),
});
if (!emailResponse.ok) {
  throw new Error(`/v1/email/batch/send failed with ${emailResponse.status}: ${await emailResponse.text()}`);
}
await emailResponse.json();

The sample shows the seam, not a fake universal payload. In production, the cron target should be a public HTTPS URL, and the worker should carry an idempotency key derived from the cleanup run. A cron pause does not backfill missed triggers. Trigger timing also has second-level jitter, so a cleanup that needs an exact transaction boundary belongs elsewhere.

For a run that needs a delayed queue message, keep delay_seconds at or below 604800. Keep retention at or below 30 days, and keep a message at or below 256 KB. Acknowledge only after the side effect is durable. There is no Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer-group history here, and the FIFO deduplication window is only five minutes. Those are design inputs, not footnotes.

The same key and base URL can cover the schedule, queue handoff, and batch email call. That removes a second set of credentials from the runner. The limitation is equally plain: one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. Infrai is a poor fit for DAG orchestration, fan-out joins, or private-only HTTP targets; use Airflow, Temporal, or infrastructure with network access for those cases. A boundary that reduces operational bookkeeping still deserves a failure plan.

Where do Zapier, n8n, and direct tools fit?

Zapier and n8n are reasonable when the work is mostly connecting applications and the person maintaining it prefers a flexible UI. They make the visual path accessible to non-developers. Their action-based operating model matters, though: frequent cleanup runs or larger-scale usage can create a larger operational fee than a small in-house cron path. That may be a good exchange when the alternative is blocking a release on integration work.

n8n is the better conversation when the team wants more control over a visual workflow and accepts responsibility for running that workflow. Zapier is a better fit when the priority is a familiar hosted connection catalog. Neither changes the core cleanup question: who owns retries, duplicate delivery, and the public HTTP boundary?

An Inngest-style scheduler paired with Resend would also be a legitimate specialist stack for a team that wants those separate product boundaries. It would require two signups, two sets of credentials, and glue code to pass the cleanup result from the scheduler or worker into the mailer. The one-key path trades some of that glue for one vendor relationship. The separate stack wins when its workflow semantics or email-specific controls are more important than consolidating the handoff.

The comparison is not a price spreadsheet. It is a boundary test. A simple cleanup with one HTTP target should not acquire a visual workflow merely because it can. Conversely, a cleanup that touches many applications without coding may justify per-action fees because developer time is the scarce resource.

When is a specialist the better choice?

Do not force a cron-and-queue surface to become an orchestration engine. It has no DAG or workflow orchestration, no native fan-out join, no debounce or throttle primitive, and no topic-style one-to-many delivery. Use Airflow or Temporal territory when those semantics are the job.

Keep long work behind the queue. Keep private endpoints out of the cron target because the task supports public http_url delivery only. Push subscriptions also need a public HTTPS endpoint. If a cleanup needs an internal service, put a public, authenticated ingress in front of it or choose infrastructure that can reach the private network.

Finally, make the failure behavior visible to the operator. Runtime output is retained only for the first 4 KB, so it is a poor audit record for a large cleanup. Store the run identifier and outcome in the application system you already trust. A small amount of explicit state beats reconstructing a failed deletion from a clipped log.

My decision is therefore conditional. Start with existing cron for the smallest job. Try Infrai when a developer-owned cleanup needs cron, queue, and email behind one key and one bill. Choose Zapier or n8n when a non-developer must own many app connections. Keep Inngest plus Resend, Airflow, or Temporal in the shortlist when their specialist semantics are the requirement.

If the single-credential boundary fits your cleanup, use the scheduling and backend capability index to inspect the current request schemas before creating the cron task.

Further reading

  • AWS SQS dead-letter queues
  • Google Cloud Tasks overview
  • Kubernetes CronJob documentation
  • Infrai capability index

title: Tutorial: Test the Refusal Path Before You Trust a Free Model Draft
description:
Tutorial: Test the Refusal Path Before You Trust a Free Model Draft

Last Tuesday a support lead approved a refund reply she had not read. The draft looked calm, polite, and correct. The gate that let it through asked exactly one question: did a human click?

She was the decision owner. The consequence was a refund we cannot un-send. The point of reversibility closed the second she hit send.

Free models make that gate cheaper to build. They do not make it optional. So here is the honest question. Would your gate refuse, or would it just look busy?

I built this tutorial to answer that with a test suite, not an opinion.

What the free tier actually buys you

MonkeyCode is an open source project, as the operator describes it. It offers free model access and a free server option. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. The promotion I was told about includes ten million free tokens. Check the live terms yourself before you plan around them, because quotas move.

That is the whole commercial story. Everything below is the part I actually care about.

We will build a gate that refuses first and drafts second. Each stage ends with a check. Skip a check and you are testing your hope.

Stage 1: Stand up a workspace and prove the endpoint answers 

mkdir gate-lab && cd gate-lab
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install httpx pytest

Put your endpoint and key in the environment, never in the file. Copy the request path straight from your dashboard instead of guessing it.

export MC_BASE="<your server URL from the dashboard>"
export MC_PATH="<the request path shown in your dashboard>"
export MC_KEY="<your key>"

Now the check. A refusal here is cheap. A refusal in production is not.

curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MC_KEY" \
  "$MC_BASE$MC_PATH"

A 401 means your key is wrong, not your code. Fix that before you write another line.

Stage 2: Define the envelope before you call anything

The gate needs a shape it can reject. Mine has six fields. Who decides, what the action is, whether it reverses, how it recovers, what evidence exists, and where the stop conditions live.

# envelope.py
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

MAX_EVIDENCE_AGE = timedelta(hours=24)

@dataclass
class Evidence:
    source: str
    fetched_at: datetime
    covers: str

@dataclass
class Envelope:
    decision_owner: str
    action: str
    reversible: bool
    recovery: str
    evidence: list[Evidence] = field(default_factory=list)
    stop_conditions: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

    def refusals(self, now=None) -> list[str]:
        now = now or datetime.now(timezone.utc)
        reasons = []
        if not self.decision_owner:
            reasons.append("no named decision owner")
        if not self.reversible and not self.recovery:
            reasons.append("irreversible with no recovery path")
        if not self.evidence:
            reasons.append("no evidence attached")
        for item in self.evidence:
            if now - item.fetched_at > MAX_EVIDENCE_AGE:
                reasons.append(f"stale evidence: {item.source}")
        if not self.stop_conditions:
            reasons.append("no stop conditions declared")
        return reasons

Check: open a Python shell and build one broken envelope by hand. If refusals() returns an empty list for an action with no owner, your validation is decoration.

Stage 3: Make the gate fail closed

The gate calls the model only after the envelope survives review. Order matters more than elegance here.

# gate.py
import httpx
from envelope import Envelope

class FreeModelGate:
    def __init__(self, client, path):
        self.client = client
        self.path = path

    def review(self, env: Envelope) -> dict:
        reasons = env.refusals()
        if reasons:
            return {"status": "refused", "reasons": reasons, "text": ""}
        try:
            resp = self.client.post(self.path, json={
                "action": env.action,
                "evidence": [e.source for e in env.evidence],
                "stop_conditions": env.stop_conditions,
            }, timeout=20.0)
        except httpx.TimeoutException:
            return {"status": "blocked", "reasons": ["model timeout"], "text": ""}
        return {"status": "drafted", "reasons": [], "text": resp.text}

Look at the timeout branch. It returns blocked, not drafted. A slow free server must never become an accidental approval.

Check: call review() with an empty envelope and a fake client that raises on use. If your fake client gets called, the gate is wired backwards.

Stage 4: Write the tests that prove refusal

This is the stage most tutorials skip. The interesting behaviour is not the draft. It is the no.

# test_refusal.py
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from envelope import Envelope, Evidence
from gate import FreeModelGate

class SpyTransport:
    def __init__(self):
        self.calls = 0
    def post(self, *a, **k):
        self.calls += 1
        raise AssertionError("model called on a refused envelope")

def fresh():
    return Evidence("billing-api", datetime.now(timezone.utc), "refund window")

def test_missing_owner_never_calls_model():
    spy = SpyTransport()
    env = Envelope("", "send refund reply", True, "", [fresh()], ["amount > policy cap"])
    out = FreeModelGate(spy, "/draft").review(env)
    assert out["status"] == "refused"
    assert spy.calls == 0

def test_irreversible_without_recovery_never_calls_model():
    spy = SpyTransport()
    env = Envelope("ana", "delete account", False, "", [fresh()], ["legal hold flag"])
    out = FreeModelGate(spy, "/draft").review(env)
    assert out["status"] == "refused"
    assert spy.calls == 0

def test_stale_evidence_is_refused():
    old = Evidence("billing-api", datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(days=3), "refund window")
    env = Envelope("ana", "send refund reply", True, "resend correction", [old], ["amount > cap"])
    out = FreeModelGate(SpyTransport(), "/draft").review(env)
    assert any("stale" in r for r in out["reasons"])

$ pytest -q
3 passed

Three green tests are your first real evidence. They are also free to run, which matters on a free tier.

Stage 5: Order the review card around the stop conditions

The card is what a human reads. So put the refusal reasons first, not the model's prose. My order is: action, reversibility, stop conditions, evidence sources with ages, then the draft.

Check: read the card aloud. If you say "looks fine" before you say the stop conditions, reorder it.

Stage 6: Review the card for access, not aesthetics

Status must be a word, never a colour. Stop conditions must appear before the draft in reading order. Ages must be written as durations, not timestamps only.

Check: remove colour entirely and read again. If the decision changes, the design was relying on something a screen reader never gets.

Stage 7: Decide when this gate is the wrong tool

Situation Use the gate? Why
Draft replies with a named reviewer Yes Refusal is cheap and reversible
Irreversible actions with audit duties Not alone You need a durable record, not a script
High-volume, sub-second paths No Human review is the bottleneck, not the model
No named decision owner yet Not yet The gate would only formalise avoidance

That last row is the one I would defend hardest. A gate without an owner is a queue with better manners.

What I would do first if I were you

Run the three refusal tests before you write a single prompt. They cost nothing and they tell you the most. Then let the free server answer one boring draft and read your own card out loud.

If you want to try this on the free server, start with the tests, not the model. The tests are the part that survives the promotion.

Which missing evidence would stop your approval today? If the answer is none, you do not have a gate yet.

title: Go Browser Storage Upload vs Proxy — Choose Private Webhook Notification After Upload
description:
The page fires: an authenticated logistics customer has been told that a generated report is ready, yet the download handler has no approved object to serve. The browser's upload completed, but the scan and database transition did not. Short answer: use a signed direct upload into private storage followed by a bucket notification and an asynchronous worker when upload responsiveness matters; proxy the bytes through your own server when acceptance must be synchronous. Neither path makes an upload safe to download merely because storage acknowledged it.

The earlier signal should have been the age of reports waiting for processing, not the browser's successful transfer. One stalled report merits investigation; an expanding backlog threatens the availability SLO. This distinction is the difference between paging for customer impact and paging for an ordinary slow scan.

What should a storage webhook notification trigger after a browser upload?

Track an application-owned report ID, tenant ID, expected object key, and timestamps for upload acknowledgment, notification receipt, scan completion, and the final authorization-ready database transition. Measure pending age from acknowledgment through that last transition. A notification is a prompt to inspect an object, not evidence that its contents passed inspection; OWASP's file-upload guidance makes that trust boundary worth keeping explicit. Reconcile pending database rows against object existence as well, since a missing event and a worker that never finishes otherwise look much the same from the customer side.

For capacity planning, count arrivals, outstanding scans, retry backlog, and private-download throughput. Set a warning on growing pending age, then page on sustained risk to the report-ready SLO after observing your workload's actual processing distribution. A proposed ten-minute window is a policy example, not a measured vendor latency guarantee. No vendor can choose that threshold for your on-call rotation.

Where should the replaceable upload boundary sit?

The trusted backend assigns an object key and issues a short-lived signed upload target; the browser uploads to that returned URL without sending an Infrai Bearer credential. A notification starts a worker that checks the object, scans it, writes any derived report or thumbnail to a different key, and changes the application's report state only after processing succeeds. The authenticated download handler reads that state before serving the private object. Browser CORS behavior still needs verification for the actual origin and bucket; a signed URL does not bypass browser enforcement.

For the control-plane part of this design, Infrai's REST API needs no SDK: any HTTP-capable runtime can call it, leaving the Go worker free of a storage-specific client-library version. Its storage surface includes presigning and bucket notifications. A distinct operational benefit is its public, self-describing discovery contract: request and response schemas and runnable examples are available without a key, making it possible to map the notification integration during a migration before changing production credentials. Try Infrai for private report uploads and notification-triggered processing when your team wants an inspectable HTTP contract and application-managed customer retrieval. Its single key spans multiple backend modules, which can reduce credential provisioning when the report worker also needs other platform capabilities; it does not remove the application's authorization checks.

Here is a runnable Go check of the published notification contract. Discovery is public, so this read intentionally needs no Authorization header; protected storage calls must use a server-side Authorization: Bearer <key> header. The program prints the schema rather than guessing a notification write body.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.bucket.set_notification", nil)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4096))
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "discovery returned %s: %s\n", resp.Status, body)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    if _, err := io.Copy(os.Stdout, resp.Body); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

For a protected write, the backend supplies the key from its environment, specifies POST, checks non-success bodies, and backs off on 429, honoring Retry-After where present. Retried writes need a stable client idempotency key. Keep those control-plane credentials away from the browser's signed data transfer.

The buy-versus-build decision is easier to inspect side by side:

Path What remains on call Best fit Migration boundary
Infrai REST storage Worker, report state, private retrieval An inspectable HTTP integration for signed uploads and notifications Verify CORS, object keys, and event behavior
Amazon S3 with EventBridge IAM, event consumers, report state AWS-native event routing and storage operations Translate IAM and event semantics
Cloudflare R2 with event notifications Queue consumer, access policy, report state An R2-centered deployment with native queue integration Test delivery and consumer retries
Google Cloud Storage with Pub/Sub notifications Pub/Sub consumer, identity, report state Existing GCP messaging and identity operations Migrate objects and subscriber behavior
Go upload proxy Upload bandwidth, backpressure, scan path Synchronous admission before storing bytes Scale server capacity with upload traffic

Direct providers win when their native identity and event infrastructure are already the operating standard. The limitation of Infrai is consequential: it is not suitable when automatic cross-region replication or broad cross-cloud bulk migration is required; choose direct S3 or Google Cloud Storage and validate the specific disaster-recovery configuration instead. Its storage vendor coverage includes R2, S3, OSS, and COS, but not GCS or B2. DigitalOcean Spaces is another real object-store candidate, but verify its particular event integration rather than treating S3-compatible object operations as a guarantee of identical notifications. There is no public-read ACL or permanent public URL here, so use a specialist delivery setup for a public image host or static website.

What survives a storage migration?

Persist application IDs and object keys, not expiring signed URLs. Keep the report state machine and the download authorization rule under application control, then test a real upload, event, scan, and private retrieval before switching traffic. Replaceability means a documented interface and an exercised migration; it is not a claim that event envelopes from different providers match.

Write processed copies under new keys. With no object versioning or object lock, an overwritten original cannot be recovered through storage version history; strict concurrent updates also need queue or database coordination because conditional If-Match writes are unavailable. If immutable retention is a requirement, pick storage with the appropriate native controls. A one-day minimum lifecycle interval also makes this unsuitable for hour-level deletion promises. Confirm persistent-write test funding before scheduling a rehearsal, because trial credit cannot cover those writes.

When does the alert cost more than it catches?

If every delayed thumbnail pages the team, ordinary processing variance will drown out the notification gap that actually strands reports. Compare pending age against the observed distribution, use a lower-severity warning for isolated delay, and page for a sustained backlog that threatens the customer-visible SLO. Keep reconciliation running even when notifications appear healthy. The end condition is a successful scan and authorized report state, never a browser progress bar at 100%.

References

  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet
  • Amazon S3 event notifications
  • Cloudflare R2 event notifications
  • Google Cloud Storage Pub/Sub notifications
  • DigitalOcean Spaces documentation

Further reading

title: Node.js Observability: Set Up Error Tracking with Trace IDs Explained
description:
Use one trace context to connect a failed request, its tenant cohort, and the decision to roll an experiment back. Keep the context immutable across the request, attach it to structured error events, and keep cohort labels out of high-cardinality metrics. That combination gives an on-call engineer a useful path from an error to a rollout decision without turning observability data into a second patient-data system.

I build email, SMS, and OTP flows, so I am suspicious of any design that treats delivery failure as a single log line. A timeout may be a dependency problem, a rate-limit response, or a cohort-specific configuration error. The same caution applies to a healthtech experiment: the trace is evidence for a rollback, not proof that every failure has one cause.

The trade-off is real.

What must remain true during a rollback?

The architecture has three invariants. Every inbound request gets a valid correlation context or an explicitly generated one. Every error event carries that context plus a low-cardinality tenant or cohort reference. Finally, the experiment assignment used by the request is recorded with the event, so a later query does not infer treatment from timing or from a mutable tenant table.

The failure boundaries matter more than the logging library. A worker must receive the context when a job is created, a retry must preserve the original trace relationship without pretending it is the same attempt, and an exception handler must record the error before the context is discarded. Redaction belongs at the event boundary. Identifiers such as patient names, message bodies, and one-time passwords do not belong in a trace label.

Design choice Useful property Rollback risk
Request-scoped context Easy to join application errors to one request Lost when work crosses a queue unless propagated explicitly
Explicit event envelope Stable fields for search, retention, and redaction More code at every async boundary
Metric labels for every identifier Fast aggregate dashboards Cardinality grows with tenants, requests, or trace IDs
Trace and log correlation Detailed path plus searchable error record Requires consistent propagation and clock-aware interpretation

The third row is the trap. Prometheus instrumentation guidance warns against labels whose values have high cardinality. A trace ID is excellent for finding one execution and poor as a metric label. Store it in logs or trace events; aggregate metrics by a bounded outcome such as error_type, cohort, or dependency class.

How should Node.js error tracking cross an async boundary?

Treat the trace context as data, not as ambient magic. In Node.js, request-local storage can make handlers convenient, but queue payloads, scheduled jobs, and outbound calls still need an explicit propagation rule. The event envelope should contain the trace ID, the current span ID when available, tenant or cohort key, experiment revision, attempt number, and a normalized error type. It should not contain the full exception payload by default.

Here is the critical path in deliberately small pseudocode. The surrounding application can use its own Node.js framework; the contract is the part worth testing.

Test the boundary.

def handle_request(request, experiment):
    context = read_or_create_trace_context(request.headers)
    assignment = experiment.assign(tenant_id=request.tenant_id)

    try:
        result = run_health_operation(
            tenant_id=request.tenant_id,
            cohort=assignment.cohort,
            trace_id=context.trace_id,
        )
        return result
    except Exception as exc:
        event = {
            "event": "application_error",
            "trace_id": context.trace_id,
            "span_id": context.span_id,
            "tenant_key": request.tenant_key,
            "cohort": assignment.cohort,
            "experiment_revision": experiment.revision,
            "attempt": 1,
            "error_type": normalize_error_type(exc),
        }
        emit_redacted_error(event)
        raise

The important detail is experiment_revision. If the cohort assignment changes while an incident is investigated, a bare tenant ID cannot tell you which behavior the request actually exercised. I also record an attempt number because a retry is a separate observation. Otherwise, a dependency that fails three times looks like three independent tenants in a noisy dashboard.

That distinction saves the rollback review.

For an outbound call, propagate a standards-based trace context and create a child span for the dependency operation. For a queue, put the parent relationship and the business fields in a versioned envelope. On consumption, create a new processing span linked to the enqueue operation. This keeps the causal story readable without pretending that minutes of queue delay happened inside the original HTTP span.

Which option survives a cohort experiment?

There are two reasonable storage shapes. A log-first design writes structured error events and uses traces for timing. A trace-first design makes the trace the primary investigation record and derives error views from it. I prefer the first for rollback decisions in healthtech systems because retention, redaction, and access control for an error event can be reviewed as a bounded contract. Traces remain valuable for dependency timing, but they should not become the only copy of the decision evidence.

The choice is operational, not ideological. If a team has mature trace sampling and a well-defined error-event stream, either shape can work. Sampling is the sharp edge: a sampled-out successful request is usually fine, while a sampled-out error can remove the comparison point needed to judge a rollout. Error events should therefore have an independent retention and delivery policy, with a bounded payload and a clear failure mode when the telemetry sink is unavailable. The business request must not fail merely because telemetry failed. The limitation is that a telemetry pipeline can preserve correlation while still losing events during an outage, so rollback evidence needs an explicit completeness check.

Do not use a dashboard threshold as the rollback algorithm by itself. Compare treatment and control using the same observation window, normalize by eligible requests, and split results by dependency class and cohort. A spike in one tenant can indicate a tenant configuration issue rather than a bad experiment. A spike only after a dependency timeout deserves a different response from a spike in validation failures.

What did I reject, and when is it still valid?

I initially thought putting trace_id into every metric label would make the first incident easier. It feels convenient when searching for one request is the immediate need. It becomes an operational liability once traffic grows: each request creates another time series, dashboards become expensive to query, and the aggregate signal gets harder to read. The valid use case is a short-lived local diagnostic metric with a tightly bounded identifier set, not a production request counter. The trade-off is search convenience today versus a usable aggregate tomorrow.

I also rejected copying raw exception text into the event as the primary field. Exception messages often contain input fragments or dependency responses. Normalize the type and preserve a redacted, access-controlled detail field only when the investigation requires it. That is a compliance boundary, not a formatting preference.

A rollback-safe review should answer four questions: can we identify the exact experiment revision, can we join the error to its trace without exposing sensitive payloads, can we distinguish retries from new requests, and can we compare cohorts without trace-level metric cardinality? If any answer is no, fix the evidence path before trusting the experiment result.

The minimum implementation is therefore modest: propagate a trace context, emit a redacted structured error event, record cohort and revision, and aggregate metrics only on bounded dimensions. In a healthtech rollout, that is more useful than a dense dashboard full of identifiers. It leaves the team with a defensible rollback signal and a smaller blast radius when the next dependency behaves badly.

References

  • W3C Trace Context Recommendation: https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/
  • OpenTelemetry, Trace Context: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/context-propagation/
  • Prometheus, Instrumentation Best Practices: https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/instrumentation/
  • OpenTelemetry, Sampling: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/sampling/

title: Building a Production REST API in Rust with Express-Like Simplicity
description:
Building a Production REST API in Rust with Express-Like Simplicity

If you come from the JavaScript (Express/Fastify) or Python (FastAPI/Flask) worlds, you are used to building APIs at the speed of thought. You define a route, parse JSON from the body, extract URL parameters, and return a response.

When web developers transition to traditional Rust web frameworks like Axum or Actix, they often hit a brick wall. Routing requires managing complex extractor tuples (Path, Query, Json, State), and one misplaced generic type triggers compiler errors that look like cryptographic puzzles.

In this guide, we will build a complete, production-ready CRUD REST API in Rust in under 15 minutes using Nitrox—without fighting trait bounds or lifetime errors.

What We Are Building

A complete User Management API supporting:

  • GET /api/users — List all users
  • GET /api/users/:id — Fetch user by ID
  • POST /api/users — Create user with JSON validation
  • PUT /api/users/:id — Update existing user
  • DELETE /api/users/:id — Remove user
  • Built-in logging, CORS headers, and standard HTTP error handling

Step 1: Project Setup

Create a new Rust binary project:

cargo new user-api --bin
cd user-api

Open Cargo.toml and add the following dependencies:

[dependencies]
nitrox = "0.0.1"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1.0"
uuid = { version = "1.0", features = ["v4"] }

That’s all you need. Nitrox bundles Hyper, Tokio, and matchit routing under the hood.

Step 2: Define Your Data Models

In src/main.rs, define your data structures using Serde:

use nitrox::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct User {
    pub id: Option<String>,
    pub name: String,
    pub email: String,
    #[serde(default)]
    pub role: Option<String>,
}

#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
pub struct CreateUserDto {
    pub name: String,
    pub email: String,
    pub role: Option<String>,
}

Notice how clean this is. No framework-specific magic traits—just standard Rust structs.

Step 3: Writing the Express-Style Routes

Now let’s build the application. Look how familiar this syntax is:

use nitrox::prelude::*;
use uuid::Uuid;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<()> {
    let app = Nitrox::new();

    // 1. Global Middleware
    app.use_middleware(logger());
    app.use_middleware(cors("*"));

    // 2. Health Check
    app.get("/health", |_req, res| async move {
        res.json(json!({ "status": "healthy", "uptime": "ok" }))
    });

    // 3. GET /api/users - List Users
    app.get("/api/users", |_req, res| async move {
        let sample_users = vec![
            json!({ "id": "u-101", "name": "Alice Johnson", "email": "alice@company.com" }),
            json!({ "id": "u-102", "name": "Bob Smith", "email": "bob@company.com" }),
        ];
        res.json(json!({ "success": true, "data": sample_users }))
    });

    // 4. GET /api/users/:id - Fetch by ID
    app.get("/api/users/:id", |req, res| async move {
        let user_id = req.param("id").unwrap_or_default();

        if user_id.is_empty() {
            return Ok(res.bad_request("User ID is required"));
        }

        res.json(json!({
            "id": user_id,
            "name": "Alice Johnson",
            "email": "alice@company.com"
        }))
    });

    // 5. POST /api/users - Create User with JSON Parsing
    app.post("/api/users", |req, res| async move {
        match req.json::<CreateUserDto>() {
            Ok(payload) => {
                let new_user = json!({
                    "id": Uuid::new_v4().to_string(),
                    "name": payload.name,
                    "email": payload.email,
                    "role": payload.role.unwrap_or_else(|| "user".to_string())
                });

                res.status(201).json(json!({
                    "message": "User created successfully",
                    "data": new_user
                }))
            }
            Err(err) => res.bad_request(&format!("Invalid JSON payload: {}", err)),
        }
    });

    // 6. PUT /api/users/:id - Update User
    app.put("/api/users/:id", |req, res| async move {
        let user_id = req.param("id").unwrap_or_default();

        match req.json::<CreateUserDto>() {
            Ok(payload) => res.json(json!({
                "message": "User updated",
                "id": user_id,
                "data": payload
            })),
            Err(err) => res.bad_request(&format!("Malformed input: {}", err)),
        }
    });

    // 7. DELETE /api/users/:id - Remove User
    app.delete("/api/users/:id", |req, res| async move {
        let user_id = req.param("id").unwrap_or_default();
        res.json(json!({
            "message": "User deleted",
            "id": user_id
        }))
    });

    // Start server
    println!("🚀 Server listening on http://127.0.0.1:3000");
    app.listen(3000).await
}

Step 4: Testing Your Endpoints

Start your server:

cargo run

Your server compiles in seconds and listens on port 3000. Open a new terminal and test it with curl:

Create a User: 

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/users \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "Devin Roy", "email": "devin@example.com", "role": "admin"}'

Response:

{
  "message": "User created successfully",
  "data": {
    "id": "e932b1f8-9844-42b4-8e10-91c6e42bca81",
    "name": "Devin Roy",
    "email": "devin@example.com",
    "role": "admin"
  }
}

Fetch by ID: 

curl http://localhost:3000/api/users/e932b1f8

What Makes This Different?

Compare what you just wrote with other Rust frameworks:

  1. No Extractor Hell: In Axum, mixing up the order of (Path, Json) vs (Json, Path) in handler arguments causes compilation to fail with a wall of trait error messages. In Nitrox, you simply inspect req.param("id") and call req.json::<T>().
  2. Predictable Fluent Responses: Chain .status(201).header("X-Custom", "Val").json(...) naturally, exactly like Express or Fastify.
  3. No Lifetime Gymnastics: You don't have to define references with 'a or manage complex boxing manually.

You get the safety and 150k req/sec speed of native compiled Rust, with the development velocity of Node.js.

What’s Next?

Tomorrow in Day 3, we will look at the real-world economics of replacing heavy Node.js containers with Nitrox:
"Our AWS Bill Dropped 80%: Replacing Heavy Node.js Containers with a 15MB Rust Binary"

⭐ Star Nitrox on GitHub: https://github.com/KTBsomen/nitrox

title: When the mesh fights Kubernetes: a webhook deadlock, a probe loop, and what it costs
description:
In part 1, we rigged the network so every packet in the pod passes through Ananse's sidecar, without the app knowing. That was the plan on paper. This post is about what happened when the plan met a real cluster.

Two bugs taught me the most. In the first, the mesh locked its own control plane out of the cluster. In the second, a routine health check made the sidecar call itself until it drowned in timeouts. After that, I'll cover what running the mesh actually costs, and what I'd change next.

The Deadlock (The Webhook Injecting Into Its Own Namespace)

In Ananse Service Mesh, the control plane runs a Mutating Admission Webhook. Crucially, this webhook is configured with failurePolicy: Fail. This is a deliberate security choice: if the webhook cannot be reached, pod creation is rejected. If we used Ignore, pods would silently start without a sidecar, breaking mTLS and routing without anyone noticing. We fail closed.
The normal injection flow works like this:

  1. When Kubernetes creates a pod, the API Server intercepts the request.
  2. The API Server looks at the MutatingWebhookConfiguration and says, "Before I create this pod, I need to send it to the Ananse Webhook to inject the init container and sidecar."
  3. It sends an HTTP request to the webhook, gets the modified pod spec back, and creates the pod.

If you read those steps carefully, you might spot an issue waiting to happen.
The control plane itself runs as a pod. I learned exactly how bad this could be during a routine node drain when my cluster suddenly stopped accepting new workloads. If the control plane goes down for any reason, a fresh install, an upgrade, a node drain, or a crash, it has to go through this exact Mutating Admission flow to boot back up. The API server pauses the pod creation and sends the request to the webhook... but the webhook is the control plane pod that hasn't started yet. The API server gets no response, and after 5 seconds, it outright rejects the pod.
Because the pod is never created, nothing restarts. You are locked in a complete deadlock. And the stakes are high: while the control plane is down, every new pod in an injected namespace is refused.
We need a way to tell the API server, "If this specific resource comes to you, just let it through." In Kubernetes, you handle this using labels and selectors, specifically, a namespaceSelector in your webhook configuration.

Layer 1: The Immutable System Label (NotIn)

Instead of relying on admins to manually label namespaces to opt-out, we target the kubernetes.io/metadata.name label that Kubernetes automatically attaches to every namespace. Our namespaceSelector explicitly excludes critical infrastructure: NotIn [kube-system, ananse-system, kube-public, cert-manager]. Because Kubernetes manages this label, it is impossible for an admin to forget it.

Layer 2: The Explicit Opt-In (In)

As a second layer in the namespaceSelector, injection is strictly opt-in. The webhook is only triggered if the namespace carries the label ananse.io/inject In [enabled].

Layer 3: The Go Code Failsafe

The first two layers prevent the deadlock by ensuring the API server never calls a dead webhook. But what if the webhook is up and running, and a control plane pod is created anyway? If the webhook YAML is somehow misconfigured and the API server incorrectly routes a control plane pod to the webhook, the Go code acts as the final bouncer. It guards a different door.
The injectRequired() function contains a hardcoded list of ignored namespaces:

IgnoredNamespaces = []string{  
    metav1.NamespaceSystem, // "kube-system"  
    metav1.NamespacePublic, // "kube-public"  
    "cert-manager",         // Prevent deadlock with cert-manager  
    "ananse-system",        // Don't inject into own control plane  
}

If the request originates from ananse-system, the code explicitly skips the injection and lets the pod boot cleanly without a sidecar.

The probe that dialled itself (kubelet TCP probe on 15006)

One of the most interesting bugs I encountered while building Ananse came from good intentions. In our iptables-init.sh script, we have a safety rule that essentially says: "If a packet is already going to 15006, don't redirect it."
To see how this backfired, let's walk through a standard Kubernetes health check:

  • The Probe: Kubelet wants to check if the sidecar is alive, so it sends a TCP probe straight to port 15006.
  • The Bypass: The iptables rule catches the request, notices the destination is already 15006, and lets it through without applying a REDIRECT.
  • The Handoff: The sidecar picks up the connection. Because it's a proxy, its entire job is to look up the original destination of the request (the SO_ORIGINAL_DST lookup from post 1) and forward the traffic there. But nothing was redirected, so the kernel has no record of an original destination. It just answers with the port the packet arrived on: 15006. So it dutifully dials 127.0.0.1:15006.
  • The Loop: That address is itself. The new connection lands on 15006 again, the sidecar repeats the process, and the cycle continues.

Every single health probe started a runaway chain of connections to itself, and a flood of i/o timeouts on every probe interval.

The Fix: The solution was to move the health check off the proxy port and onto a dedicated admin port: 15021.

Because it's an admin port, it handles the request directly. It just answers "I'm alive" and stops right there. It never asks the kernel where the traffic was supposed to go, which means it never dials out. Nothing can loop.

What it costs

With all the benefits a service mesh provides, there is always a trade-off. The true cost of running a mesh in production ranges from added latency to extra CPU and memory in every pod.
We will break down three cost categories (Latency, Machine, and Complexity).

1. Latency (The Round Trip)

Without the mesh, a direct request from Service A to Service B takes only one hop. With Ananse, that path looks like this: Service A -> A's sidecar -> B's sidecar -> Service B
Every request now goes through two proxies. Each hop adds a little time to the request to account for the overhead of accepting the connection, looking up the original destination, dialing it, and copying the bytes over. Ananse was designed for 1 to 3 ms per hop.

2. Machine Resources (CPU and Memory)

Injecting a sidecar means every pod gets an extra container. If you have n injected pods, you are running n additional proxy containers across your cluster.
Over a week of observing everyday production traffic across six services, we saw each sidecar consume roughly 20 to 27 MiB of memory, and under 10 millicores of CPU at its busiest (a hundredth of one core). The busiest sidecars sit in front of the busiest services: CPU follows traffic.
Each sidecar reserves 20 MiB of memory and 10m of CPU, and is capped at 512 MiB and 200m. The memory reservation proved to be a bit too low, as the real baseline sits just above it. Around 32 MiB fits better.
For stability, we ran a k6 soak against v0.3.3 on the dev cluster before go-live, with 50 simulated users going through the gateway the same way real users do: 2,634,971 requests over 8 hours 20 minutes, with 0 pod restarts and 0 sidecar crashes. That run proved the sidecar holds up.

3. Complexity (The Hidden Cost)

Adding a mesh means adding new moving parts to maintain and new ways for the system to break.
You've just read two of them. A webhook that blocked its own control plane from starting, and a health check that flooded the sidecar with connections to itself. Neither bug could exist without a mesh. Both took real debugging to find, because the failure showed up far from the cause.
All of this is to say that a mesh brings its own operational baggage.

What I'd do next

Ananse was originally born just to scratch a curiosity itch. Naturally, I learned a lot of hard lessons along the way. Mistakes were made, quick fixes were applied, and we deliberately chose architectures that optimized for learning rather than perfection, which meant the project took much longer than expected.

Moving forward, here is how we are evolving the mesh:

1. Measure the hop. The plan is rigorous benchmarking, starting with a baseline: the same test with the mesh on and off. After that, every new feature gets benchmarked before it gets merged. The performance delta between the baseline and the pull request becomes the official "cost" of that feature, giving us hard metrics for Ananse's overhead.

2. Replace REDIRECT with TPROXY (if the numbers justify it). Today, every connection gets an address rewrite and a conntrack entry, forcing the sidecar to explicitly ask the kernel where the packet was really going. TPROXY hands the packet over with its original address intact, nothing to rewrite, nothing to look up. It requires a more complex setup (involving policy routing and a transparent socket), so tying back to point #1, we will only implement it if the benchmarks show the conntrack cost is more than we can live with. Still, I believe it is a step in the right direction.

3. Take the proxy out of the pod. Forcing every pod to pay a 20 to 27 MiB "sidecar tax" adds up fast at scale. The longer-term direction is a per-node proxy, or pushing interception down into the kernel using eBPF, similar to how Cilium and Istio's Ambient mode handle it. Ananse needs to feel the ambience too.

Both bugs I shared in this post came from the mesh assuming something about the traffic that turned out not to be true: assuming its own control plane could seamlessly pass through its own webhook, and assuming everything arriving on 15006 was put there by a redirect.
If you've ever run a service mesh in production, I'd love to hear your war stories. Which hidden assumption finally bit you?

title: Flash vs JavaScript: what 20 years on the web taught me
description:
I started building websites when Flash was the web, intros you had to skip, sites that played music as soon as they opened, and banners that moved on every page. Today I build with React, Next.js and GSAP. In between I watched a plugin that seemed impossible to beat lose to a language written in 10 days. Here is what that taught me.

The 40-second version. Story and edit by me.

1. When Flash was the web

In the early 2000s, if a website moved, it was probably Flash. HTML pages were plain, and every browser showed them differently. Flash gave designers one box that looked the same everywhere, with smooth animation, sound and video. Agencies built whole sites in it, and almost every computer had Flash Player installed.

I learned Flash at Arena Multimedia, and the first thing I made with it was a website. Many more followed, for different clients, along with freelance work and a lot of intros. One of those intros really made me stand out from the crowd.

For letter animations I used a tool called SWiSH, which animated text very efficiently, and I mixed those animations into my Flash intros. I also worked on a web application about emotional intelligence, and on a separate project I used ActionScript to build charts and graphs.

2. The little language nobody took seriously

JavaScript was created in 1995, in just 10 days. For years it was used for small things, image rollovers, pop-up windows, form checks. Every browser handled it a little differently, so even simple scripts were painful to write.

Then jQuery arrived in 2006 with the promise "write less, do more". One line could do what used to take twenty, and it worked the same in every browser. Sliders, tabs and fades that used to need Flash could now be built in the page itself.

I started using jQuery for small tasks. Then I began building whole pages with it, and soon those pages had full animation effects and carefully planned user experience. On one site I divided the screen into six panels, and tapping a panel made it grow to fill the whole screen. A few years earlier, that would have been a job for Flash.

3. The phone that said no

The iPhone launched in 2007 without Flash, and it never got it. In 2010 Steve Jobs published his open letter "Thoughts on Flash", saying it drained batteries, wasn't built for touch and wasn't an open standard. The web followed the phones. HTML5 video, canvas and CSS animation took over the jobs Flash used to do.

Adobe announced the end in 2017, and Flash Player was retired on 31 December 2020. The plugin that once seemed to be everywhere was gone, and JavaScript was running everything from small sites to whole apps.

4. What it taught me

  • Bet on the open web, not on one company's plugin. Flash belonged to one company. HTML, CSS and JavaScript belong to everyone, which is why they are still here.
  • Skills outlive tools. Timelines, keyframes and easing were everyday tools in Flash, and they carried straight over to CSS animation and GSAP. GSAP itself started as a Flash animation library before it moved to JavaScript. In Flash I planned a movement in my head, watched the preview and tweaked the easing by hand until it felt right. In GSAP the easing is often just a keyword, but deciding whether the movement feels right is still the real job.
  • If Google and screen readers can't read it, it isn't finished. A Flash site was one closed box, search engines could barely see inside it, and screen readers struggled too. That is why I care about clean, semantic HTML under the animation.
  • Phones decide. Flash lost ground because it didn't work well on phones. A site has to work on a small, slow phone, not just on a big screen.
  • Don't fall in love with a tool. Every few years the web changes its favourite tool. AI is the newest change, and I use it too. The tools change, but knowing what makes a good website doesn't.

5. What's next

This is the first episode of "Web history in motion", short animated stories about how the web grew up, told by someone who built through it. Next: Tables vs CSS, from spacer GIFs and nested tables to Flexbox and Grid.

Follow along on YouTube or Instagram. Which era did you start in: Flash, jQuery or React? Tell me in the comments.

Originally published at imhirakhan.com. I'm Hira Khan, a front-end developer with 20+ years on the web: GSAP animation, brand games and fast websites. Portfolio: imhirakhan.com
