title: Rebuilding :nth-child() out of sibling-index(), if() and mod()
description:
You wrote :nth-child(3n + 5) in a stylesheet. Now a design token says it should be every fourth item from the second. So you edit the selector. Then the selector in the media query. Then the one in the component variant.

The An + B numbers live inside the selector, and a selector can't read a custom property. That's the itch Temani Afif scratches in a new CSS-Tricks article. He rebuilds the :nth-child() patterns as value-level logic, using sibling-index(), the if() function with style() queries, and mod(). Once the numbers are custom properties, you can change them from anywhere the cascade reaches.

From selector to condition

Every example in the article uses the same markup: a .container with a run of plain div children. Nothing to see there. The interesting part is where the logic moves.

sibling-index() gives an element its position among its siblings as a number. Feed that number to a style() query inside if() and you get a per-element condition that sits in the declaration, not the selector. Here's the single-element case, the equivalent of :nth-child(5):

.container {
  --B: 5;
}

.container div {
  background: if(style(sibling-index() = --B): red; else: lightblue);
}

Every div matches the selector. Each one then works out its own background. The fifth one ends up red.

Swap = for >= and you have :nth-child(n + B), everything from position B onward. Swap it for <= and you have :nth-child(-n + B), the first B items. Same rule, one character changed. The article also builds a range version with two variables, an --X and a --Y, that marks every item between the two positions.

The modulo trick

Step patterns need arithmetic. :nth-child(An) means "every Ath element", which is a polite way of saying the index divides cleanly by A. That's what mod() checks:

.container div {
  background: if(style(mod(sibling-index(), var(--A)) = 0): red);
}

Set --A: 3 on the container and every third child goes red. Afif also guards the case where --A is negative, adding a second condition joined with and so the rule only fires when var(--A) > 0.

Then he goes for the full An + B. That one takes a couple of helper custom properties. The first is computed with calc() from the index, --B and --A. The second combines sign() and mod() to test whether that value is a whole number and not negative. There's also a branch for when --A is zero. I won't paste it here. Go read it with devtools open and watch the helper values change from item to item. It's the best part of the article.

Why this is worth your time

Here's my take. The real change is not "you can do :nth-child() without :nth-child()." It's that position-based styling becomes data.

A selector is fixed at authoring time. A custom property cascades. It inherits, it gets overridden by a more specific rule, and it can be set inline on one container. Afif names this as the main advantage: you adjust the selection through variables in real time without rewriting a selector. He also argues the conditional reads more naturally than An + B notation. I agree. sibling-index() >= --B tells you what it does. n + B makes you work it out.

The trade-off is real too. The selector version can apply a whole rule block at once. The if() version works one declaration at a time, so styling three properties means three if() calls, or one custom property you branch on. It's more verbose. You get flexibility in exchange.

Before you ship it

Afif is upfront here, and you should take it seriously. These are draft CSS features and browser support is limited. Treat this as a lab technique for now. Where :nth-child() does the job with fixed numbers, keep using :nth-child(). It works everywhere and needs no explaining in code review.

He ends with homework: build the :nth-last-child() version using sibling-count(). Try it. Counting from the end means working out how far each item sits from the last sibling, and that exercise will teach you more about these functions than another demo would.

title: Spring AI's New DecisionModel: Stop Asking Chat Models for Yes or No
description:
A support message arrives: “The left earbud stopped working the day I opened the box. Can I get a refund?” Your application does not need a paragraph from an AI. It needs to know whether the message reports a defect, which team should receive it, and perhaps whether the customer sounds unhappy.

A chat model can answer those questions, but its output is still text. Your code has to turn that text into a boolean, category, or score. That conversion is a small seam where malformed output, extra explanation, and changing prompts can become production bugs.

Spring AI 2.1.0-RC2 introduces a separate DecisionModel API for this kind of bounded task. Instead of asking a chat model to write text and parsing it afterward, you define the allowed outcomes and receive typed answers. Spring AI includes OpenAI and Ollama implementations, plus a System One integration for compatible services. The new API is in a release candidate, not the current stable line, so treat it as an evaluation target rather than an automatic production upgrade.

This article examines what the API does, why the split from chat matters, and how to evaluate it without giving a probabilistic classifier authority it has not earned.

The overlooked problem: language is not a decision type

Chat is flexible by design. Ask a chat model whether a customer reports a defect and it might answer “Yes, the left earbud appears defective.” A developer can add JSON mode, a schema, or a parser, but the application still begins with a conversational model producing a response that needs interpretation.

Many application decisions have a small outcome space. A ticket might be billing, delivery, product, or other. A moderation pre-check might be yes or no. A priority score might be low, normal, or urgent. The application already knows what it can do with these results. It does not need prose to explain them.

The Spring AI decision-model reference describes the distinction: a decision model receives a defined set of possible answers and returns a chosen result with probabilities when supported. That lets application code make the policy explicit. For example, the model can suggest urgent, but the application can require a confidence threshold or a human review before changing a queue.

This does not mean ordinary chat models cannot classify. They can. The architectural question is whether classification should be represented as an unconstrained text-generation call or as a distinct operation with typed input and output. Spring AI 2.1 adds the second option.

What shipped in Spring AI 2.1.0-RC2

The Spring AI project published 2.1.0-RC2 on November 5, 2026. The release added the DecisionModel API and implementations for OpenAI, Ollama, and System One. It also included decision-based RAG document processing and a decision-backed tool index, alongside other release work.

The upgrade notes identify the release as a pre-release. As of this article's publication date, Spring's documentation lists 2.0.2 as the latest stable version and 2.1.0-RC2 as still in development. That distinction matters: the code samples below demonstrate the new API, but teams should check the release notes and compatibility details before putting an RC dependency into a production application.

The useful design idea is broader than the version number. A decision call has a named input, named questions, and an answer object rather than an open-ended message. That makes it easier to see what the model is being asked to decide and what the application will consume.

A first decision with a local Ollama model

Start with the existing Spring dependency management. Spring AI's reference shows the Ollama starter and a small decision model, d1-omni:600m. Install a recent Ollama version, add the dependency through the Spring AI BOM, and pull the model:

ollama pull d1-omni:600m

Gradle dependency:

implementation 'org.springframework.ai:spring-ai-starter-model-ollama'

The Ollama decision-model documentation says the default decision model is d1-omni:600m, and recommends Ollama 0.40.4 or later. Confirm the model supports the decision capability with ollama show <model-name> before building on it.

Ask a bounded question. A service can inject DecisionModel, then build a prompt whose answer space is explicit:

@Service
class SupportTriage {
    private final DecisionModel decisionModel;

    SupportTriage(DecisionModel decisionModel) {
        this.decisionModel = decisionModel;
    }

    DecisionResponse classify(String message) {
        return decisionModel.call(DecisionPrompt.builder()
            .text(message)
            .question("topic", ChoiceQuestion.builder()
                .text("What is this support message about?")
                .option("delivery", "Order status or arrival time")
                .option("product", "A problem with an item received")
                .option("account", "Login, address, or payment details")
                .option("other", "None of the categories above")
                .build())
            .question("defect", YesNoQuestion.builder()
                .text("Does the customer report that an item is defective?")
                .whenYes("A received item does not work as expected")
                .whenNo("The message is not reporting a product defect")
                .build())
            .build());
    }
}

This follows the API shape shown in the official quick start, adapted to a small support-triage example. The response can be read through typed accessors:

String topic = response.getChoice("topic").getValue();
boolean defect = response.getYesNo("defect").isYes();

The important change is not fewer lines of code. It is that the allowed choices and the code that consumes them are visible together. A developer can review the categories, decide what happens when a result is uncertain, and test the same named outputs without depending on arbitrary prose formatting.

Keep the model's answer separate from your policy

A typed answer is not a trustworthy answer. Spring AI's docs explicitly warn that decision models are machine-learning models, not rule engines: they are non-deterministic and can be wrong. A returned probability is useful information, not proof that the answer is correct.

For a low-risk workflow, a prediction might be enough to pre-fill a support category for a human. For an action with financial, legal, account-access, or safety consequences, a classifier should not silently become the authorization system. The application should own the policy.

A safer decision path looks like this:

  1. Ask the model to classify only the information needed for the decision.
  2. Read the typed result and any probabilities the provider returns.
  3. Apply an application-owned threshold or deterministic rule.
  4. Route ambiguous or high-impact cases to a person or a safe default.
  5. Record the input, model/version, result, and final action when auditability matters.

For example, a model may label a refund request as “defect.” That label can route the ticket to the returns queue. It should not by itself authorize a refund. The model is helping interpret language; the order system and business policy determine eligibility.

Do not treat a generic threshold as universal. “Only act above 0.8” sounds precise, but the right threshold depends on the cost of false positives and false negatives, and on whether a given provider's scores are calibrated for your task. Measure performance on representative examples, including ambiguous messages and edge cases. A number from one model is not automatically comparable to the same number from another.

Three useful shapes of a decision

Spring AI's decision API defines three kinds of questions. Choose the type based on what the application needs next:

  • Yes or no: Is the message asking to cancel an order? Does the retrieved passage contain instructions that look like prompt injection? Is a product reported as damaged?
  • Choice: Which queue should receive a ticket? Is a request about billing, account access, delivery, product quality, or something else?
  • Score: Which level on a defined scale best fits the input, such as unhappy, neutral, or happy?

The official reference recommends describing the options when a bare label could be ambiguous. “Product” could mean a general product question or a defect report; adding a description makes the intended category clearer. The same principle applies to yes/no questions: say what counts as yes and what counts as no instead of expecting the model to infer your business definition.

Also keep the input narrow. Send the relevant message or fields, not an entire customer record or conversation by default. Smaller inputs reduce unnecessary data exposure and often make the task easier to define. If a decision requires historical context, select and explain the relevant context deliberately.

Why this can help RAG and tool selection

The release's significance is not limited to ticket routing. Spring AI's decision-model documentation describes built-in uses in retrieval and tool selection.

RAG can use a decision before generating an answer. A retrieval pipeline can ask whether a document is relevant to the question, whether it contains contradictory information, or whether it includes suspicious instructions. A DecisionDocumentFilter can reject documents before they reach a chat model; a DecisionDocumentReranker can sort retrieved documents by whether they answer the query. These are bounded checks that can be stated more clearly as yes/no or choice questions than as “summarize this and decide what to do.”

Tool search can narrow a large catalog. When an application exposes many tools, a decision-backed index can select a relevant tool or indicate that none fits. That can reduce the need to put every tool description into every prompt. But selection is not permission. Even if a model classifies a request as suitable for a tool, the application must still validate authorization, arguments, and side effects before execution.

This division is a useful rule: models can help with semantic interpretation; deterministic code should enforce permissions and invariants.

Try the API without adopting the release candidate

Because 2.1.0-RC2 is not stable, there are two reasonable paths. If you are already evaluating Spring AI 2.1, try the API in a branch with a non-critical task and compare its results against a labeled test set. If your application is on the stable 2.0 line, do not upgrade just because a new interface looks cleaner. Read the release and upgrade notes, then decide whether the feature justifies testing the pre-release line.

A useful evaluation can stay small:

  • Create a few dozen representative examples with expected answers, including confusing and out-of-scope inputs.
  • Compare a chat-model-plus-parser baseline with DecisionModel on the same examples.
  • Track accuracy per category, not just one aggregate score.
  • Record cases where the model's confidence is high but its answer is wrong.
  • Test model failure, timeout, empty output, and unknown category behavior.
  • Decide what the application does when a result is uncertain or unavailable.
  • Keep irreversible actions behind existing authorization and confirmation checks.

The comparison is not about proving that one API is always better. A conversational response is still the right output when users need an explanation or a nuanced answer. A decision model is a better fit when the application needs one of a known set of machine-readable outcomes. Many systems will use both: a bounded classifier to route work, followed by a chat model to draft a response for review.

The takeaway: make the decision boundary explicit

Spring AI 2.1's DecisionModel API gives Java applications a first-class way to ask bounded questions and consume typed answers. The new local Ollama implementation makes the experiment possible without an external model API key, while OpenAI and System One implementations provide other integration paths. The RC2 release also connects decision models to RAG processing and tool discovery.

The useful takeaway is not “replace every chat call.” It is to inspect every place where your code asks a language model for a yes/no answer, category, or score, then ask whether the outcome set, uncertainty handling, and downstream policy are explicit. If they are not, a typed decision API may help make the boundary reviewable. If a wrong answer can cause real harm, keep a human or deterministic safeguard in that path.

I write about Java, Spring Boot, and AI. Subscribe if you want more practical, source-grounded articles. Have you used a model for classification in a Java application? What did you do with uncertain answers? Save the evaluation checklist above before trying a decision API in your own service.

Sources

  • Spring AI 2.1.0-RC2 release notes
  • Spring AI Decision Models reference
  • Spring AI Ollama Decision Models
  • Spring AI 2.1 upgrade notes

title: Long-Term Memory for AI Agents: Teaching a ByteChef Coding Buddy to Remember You
description:
TL;DR: Chat memory only covers the conversation you're in. Spring AI's AutoMemoryTools add a second layer: the agent deliberately writes down facts worth keeping and reads them back in later chats. ByteChef ships the same six memory tools as the Auto Memory Tool, stores memories in its database, and keeps a separate memory per project deployment and environment. Want to see it? Deploy the Remember coding preferences across chats template, tell it your build tool once, then open a new chat.

This is Part 6 of the AI Agentic Patterns in ByteChef series.

The problem: agents with amnesia

You tell your assistant you use Gradle. Next conversation, it hands you a Maven pom.xml. You mention you're on Java 25. A week later it suggests a workaround for Java 17.

The reason is simple: chat memory is a sliding window. It keeps the recent turns of one conversation and drops the oldest when it fills up. Great for the task at hand, useless for something you want the agent to know next month.

For that you need a second layer: a place where the agent writes facts down on purpose and reads them back in future conversations. Let's build one in ByteChef with a single template.

The template: a coding buddy that remembers

Remember coding preferences across chats has three steps:

  1. New Chat Request – a message arrives in the workflow chat.
  2. AI Agent – an Anthropic model with two kinds of memory: Chat Memory for the current conversation and the Auto Memory Tool (in the Tools slot) for long-term memory.
  3. Reply – the answer goes back to the chat.

The system prompt tells the agent how to use its memory:

You are a coding buddy for a Java developer. At the start of every
conversation, read your memory index and any relevant memory files.
When the user states a lasting preference (build tool, Java version,
testing style, answer length), save it as a memory right away and say
that you saved it. Apply remembered preferences without being asked.

The Auto Memory Tool itself needs no configuration. The one thing that matters is in the green note on the canvas: long-term memory only works in a deployed run (more on that below).

Two kinds of memory

The Spring AI team sums it up well: use ChatMemory for the current task, and AutoMemoryTools for facts that should still be there next week.

Chat Memory Auto Memory Tool
Holds Turns of one conversation Facts the agent chose to keep
Written by The platform, every turn The agent, on purpose, via a tool call
Lasts That conversation Until edited or deleted
In the template What you said a minute ago Your build tool in next week's chat

The template uses both: Chat Memory lets you say "now add a test" without repeating context, and the Auto Memory Tool lets a brand-new conversation start from what the agent already knows about you.

How the agent remembers

Long-term memory is a small set of entries plus an index:

  • Entries – short Markdown files with frontmatter (title, optional description, type) followed by the fact.
  • The index – MEMORY.md lists every entry on one line, newest first. The agent reads it at the start of a conversation and opens only what it needs. ByteChef keeps it in sync automatically, so the agent never edits it by hand.
  • Four types that guide what's worth saving:
    • USER – facts about the user: role, preferences
    • FEEDBACK – corrections, or approaches the user confirmed
    • PROJECT – decisions and constraints of the ongoing work
    • REFERENCE – pointers to external systems

Tell the buddy "I always use Gradle with the Kotlin DSL and Java 25" and it might save something like this (illustrative):

---
title: Build setup
description: Gradle with the Kotlin DSL, Java 25
type: USER
---

Always use Gradle with the Kotlin DSL and target Java 25.

The agent manages memory through six tools, with names and behavior straight from Spring AI:

Tool What it does
MemoryView Lists the index, or shows one entry with line numbers
MemoryCreate Creates a new entry
MemoryStrReplace Replaces an exact piece of text in an entry
MemoryInsert Inserts text at a line in an entry
MemoryDelete Deletes an entry
MemoryRename Renames an entry

Entry names are flat (e.g. build_setup.md) – no folders.

Where ByteChef differs: database storage, scoped per deployment

In Spring AI, memory is a folder of Markdown files on disk. Perfect for one agent on one machine, but a platform has harder questions: Whose memory is this? Does it survive moving to another server? Can someone inspect it and fix a wrong fact?

Spring AI keeps storage behind two small interfaces, and ByteChef plugs its own implementation in there. The agent still sees the same six tools and the same format, but entries go through ByteChef's memory service – the database by default. Self-hosted installs can set bytechef.ai.auto-memory.provider to use file storage instead.

Whose memory is it?

ByteChef works out the owner from the run itself – nothing to configure:

  • Automation projects: memory belongs to the project deployment + environment. All workflows and runs in that deployment share it; another deployment (or the same one in another environment) has its own.
  • Embedded integrations: memory belongs to the integration instance, so each of your customers gets a separate memory.

When memory is unavailable

If a run has no owner, the tool still loads, but every call returns a short "memory is unavailable" message with the reason, so the agent can tell the user instead of failing. That happens for:

  • Editor test runs – a test run isn't a deployment. Bonus: experiments in the editor never pollute a real deployment's memory.
  • Microservices installs – memory requires the ByteChef server application.
  • Runs without a workflow context – e.g. when the agent is invoked from somewhere that doesn't identify the running workflow.

Hence the canvas note: deploy first.

Try it yourself

  1. Import the template – open Remember coding preferences across chats and add it to a project.
  2. Connect the model – add your Anthropic connection.
  3. Deploy – deploy the project and enable the workflow in the deployment.
  4. State a preference – in the deployed workflow's chat, say something lasting, like "I always use Gradle with the Kotlin DSL and Java 25." The agent saves it and tells you so.
  5. Check it in a new conversation – start a fresh chat and ask for a build file.

Here's step 5 in a real deployed chat. The request mentions neither Gradle nor Java, yet the agent checks its memory first and produces a Gradle Kotlin DSL build with a Java 25 toolchain:

Try step 4 in an editor test run instead and the agent will tell you memory is unavailable – that's expected.

See and fix what it remembers

Stored memories live under Settings → AI → Memories. You can search by title or description, filter by type or owner (deployment or integration instance), and open, edit, or delete any entry. When a preference changes, fix it there – or just tell the agent and let it update the entry itself.

What you get from Spring AI vs. what ByteChef adds

ByteChef keeps the Spring AI design – the curated memory layer, six purpose-named tools, index plus typed entries, and the short-term/long-term split – and changes what's underneath:

  • Storage: files on disk become database entries that survive restarts and server moves.
  • Ownership: memory is scoped to a project deployment + environment, or to an integration instance.
  • Visibility: review, edit, and delete memories in Settings → AI → Memories.
  • Wiring: no advisors or directories to set up in code – just drop the Auto Memory Tool into an AI Agent's Tools slot.
  • Safe testing: editor test runs have no memory owner, so testing never writes into real memory.

Memory also pairs nicely with the other patterns in this series: Agent Skills give an agent know-how that's the same for everyone; long-term memory gives it what it has learned about your users and project.

Wrapping up

Chat memory answers "what did we just talk about?" Long-term memory answers "what do I already know about you?" Spring AI packaged the second as six tools and a simple file format. ByteChef keeps both and adds a database and per-deployment ownership, so memory lasts, stays separate per deployment or customer, and is there for you to inspect.

The fastest way to get it is to run it: import Remember coding preferences across chats, deploy, tell it your build tool once, and open a new chat.

Originally published on the ByteChef blog. If you found this useful, give ByteChef a ⭐ on GitHub!

title: Flutter Better in Java
description:
I usually blog about a feature the week it lands. This one landed a few weeks ago and was in development for months before that: Codename One can now take a Flutter app's Dart source and build it as a Codename One app. The results are amazing. I held this post back because I know how explosive these claims are. I wanted the numbers to come from a CI job that runs on every commit instead of a benchmark I tuned once on my laptop.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

In the meantime we also added support for Kotlin Multiplatform with Compose, for a big part of Swing and JavaFX, and for classic Android apps on iOS. More is coming. The part that still surprises me is how well Codename One does against the originals where we measured them. The same Flutter app, built from the same Dart files, starts faster, uses less memory and ships less code when Codename One builds it. That holds on Android, macOS, Windows and Linux, and the sizes hold on iOS and the web too.

The same Dart, two builds

This is the Flutter Gallery, the Flutter team's own showcase app. On the left it runs as Flutter built it. On the right, Codename One built it from the same Dart source, with no edits.

Download the side by side video.

Look closely and you'll see it isn't pixel identical. In the Reply inbox the avatars are circles on the Flutter side and rounded squares on ours. Text wraps a few characters apart in places. The translation isn't perfect, and the developer guide says so up front: Dart support is experimental, some callbacks and parameters are accepted and then ignored, and so far we have verified it against one large app. If you bring a Flutter app over, test every interaction your screens depend on.

But the hard part works. Layout, navigation, theming, text input, lists and the Material and Cupertino widgets all render from the original source, and what you get is a real Codename One app, not a picture of one.

Bringing a project over is one command in a Codename One project:

mvn cn1:import-flutter-project -Dcn1.flutter.import=/path/to/flutter_app

It copies lib, the assets and the fonts, adds the Flutter runtime to the build, writes the main class and tells you which of your pub dependencies are covered. You don't need the Dart or Flutter SDK to build the result. The transpiler is Java and runs inside the normal Maven build.

Coming This Week

Today is the Flutter story and the numbers behind it. Then one post a day:

  • Saturday, October 31: Your Compose Code, on More Screens and Less CPU. Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose, running on Codename One, and why the Java version of the same screen is faster still.
  • Sunday, November 1: Your Swing and JavaFX Code on iPhone, Android and the Web. What carries over, what doesn't, and why you might not miss the parts that don't.
  • Monday, November 2: Bastion: A Hardened Bank Template, and Crypto Wallets in Core. A virtual bank and exchange with passkeys, signed requests and a double entry ledger, plus wallets for Ethereum, Bitcoin, and Solana.
  • Tuesday, November 3: Reel: Your Own Streaming Service or Course Platform. Community uploads, courses, DRM and moderation in one Java project.
  • Wednesday, November 4: GrapheneOS, LineageOS, /e/OS and Others Are Now Officially Supported. Room, WorkManager and document pickers in the Android layer, and apps that run on GrapheneOS as they are.
  • Thursday, November 5: Caches, Certificates, Streaming Uploads and a Simulator That Types. Eight backend upgrades and a simulator with a virtual keyboard and video recording.

Compose, on Codename One.
Bastion's Security Center.
Reel's catalog.
Android code, on every target.

The numbers

Every commit to Codename One builds the Flutter Gallery twice: once with Flutter's own release build and once with Codename One. CI measures both on the same machine in interleaved rounds, so a runner that slows down halfway through penalizes both builds equally. The figures below are from the run on October 29.



CI collects 26 metrics: installed size, executable code and download size on six platforms, plus cold start and memory at rest on the four where we can measure both sides fairly. Codename One is ahead on all 26. The Android timings come from an emulator, and iOS start-up and memory aren't measured; both are explained below. The biggest gaps are on Android, where the app starts in a third of the time and carries a quarter of the code, and on Linux, where it settles at 82 MB against 224 MB.

The comparison is tilted toward Flutter, not away from it. The app is Flutter's own showcase, written by the Flutter team in Flutter's idioms, and Codename One runs it as it is. To do that, Codename One carries a runtime that reimplements Flutter's widget, element and layout model on top of Codename One components. That layer is slower than Codename One code written directly; the Compose post shows the same effect, where the imperative Java version of a screen does a third of the work of the declarative one. A Codename One app never pays for that layer. We win while paying for it.

CI also runs eleven compute workloads (hash maps, recursion, string building, sorting, arithmetic and more) in Java and in Dart. On every native platform we measured, Codename One is faster overall, by 1.3x on Android up to 1.9x on Windows and Linux:

Flutter takes 5 of the 43 cells. Two are within 6%. The real one is object allocation on Android and macOS, where Dart's allocator is quick at short lived objects; that's on our list.

The web is the exception, and it's the one place Flutter is faster. We leave it out of the comparison because Flutter's web build gets some of the workloads wrong: integer arithmetic, random array access and quicksort return different checksums than the same code on every other platform, because Dart on the web runs numbers as JavaScript doubles. A benchmark that gets the answer wrong can't be timed against one that gets it right. On the workloads where both sides agree, Flutter is ahead. The browser is asynchronous by nature, and that's the one environment where Flutter's model helps it rather than costing it. The sizes still favor us there.

Some things aren't measured, and the charts leave them out rather than guess. Flutter can't compile Dart ahead of time for the iOS simulator, so iOS start-up and memory would compare Flutter's debug engine against our release build. We report iOS sizes only. Web start-up needs a browser driver the benchmark doesn't have yet. Android timings come from an emulator, so they compare two builds on one machine rather than predicting a phone. The method, the harness and the raw numbers are in the Flutter chapter of the developer guide, and the benchmark lives in scripts/flutter-bench in the repository.

How a compatibility layer can be faster than the original

Each of these compatibility layers is a tool that runs at build time. None of them is a VM inside your app.

The Dart transpiler reads your widget source during generate-sources and writes Java. A runtime library then implements Flutter's layout and composition model (constraints down, sizes up, elements reconciled against widgets) on top of Codename One containers. It does not reimplement Flutter's rasterizer. Painting is ours. Compose works the same way: kotlinc compiles your Kotlin, the Compose runtime ships unmodified, and only the UI layer is ours. Swing, JavaFX and Android apps compile against their usual APIs, and a remap step points the bytecode at our implementations.

So the overhead is real, and it's added on top of Codename One. The reason the result still wins is what's underneath. ParparVM compiles Java ahead of time to C and then to a native binary, and its dead code elimination drops whatever your app doesn't reach. There's no Dart VM, no Skia or Impeller engine and no second runtime in the bundle. That's how the Android build ends up with 4.7 MB of executable code against 20.6 MB.

Here is the Dart that calls into the platform. It's ordinary Flutter code:

final batteryChannel = MethodChannel('com.example.app/battery');

Future<int> getBatteryLevel() async {
  final level = await batteryChannel.invokeMethod('getBatteryLevel');
  return level as int;
}

And here is the other side of that channel, in plain Java, with no plugin and no per-platform Swift or Kotlin:

MethodChannel channel = new MethodChannel("com.example.app/battery");
channel.setMethodCallHandler(new MethodChannel.MethodCallHandler() {
    @Override
    public void onMethodCall(MethodCall call, MethodChannel.Result result) {
        if ("getBatteryLevel".equals(call.method())) {
            result.success(87);
        } else {
            result.notImplemented();
        }
    }
});

You don't have to move the whole app either. FlutterUI.wrap() returns an ordinary Container, so a Dart screen can sit inside a Codename One form next to components you wrote in Java:

Form dashboard = new Form("Dashboard", BoxLayout.y());
dashboard.add(new Label("Written in Codename One"));
dashboard.add(FlutterUI.wrap(new Text("Rendered from Dart")));
dashboard.add(new Button("Also Codename One"));
dashboard.show();

Similar in spirit

Flutter and Codename One made the same bet. Neither wraps the platform's widgets. Both draw every component themselves on a lightweight surface, so you control every pixel and the behavior doesn't drift between platforms. Codename One still ships native themes, so an app can look like iOS on an iPhone and like Material on Android, or look like your brand everywhere. That shared architecture is why a Flutter widget tree maps onto Codename One so naturally. The differences are in what sits around that core: the threading model, how apps are built and how features ship.

Can't Flutter do the same?

No. Flutter could, in theory, run a Codename One app the way we run a Flutter app. It would be slow, because the two models point in opposite directions.

Flutter is asynchronous to the core. Dart runs in an event loop, platform calls are messages that come back as futures, and the engine draws on its own threads. Codename One is synchronous: your code calls the platform and gets an answer. Emulating a synchronous API on top of an asynchronous one means queuing, waiting and copying on every call. Going the other way is cheap: a future is a callback, and a callback is a method call.

The same reason explains why Flutter can't catch Codename One on most platforms. Operating systems, graphics APIs and hardware are synchronous. Codename One calls them directly. Flutter goes through a message channel and its own engine to reach them.

Android makes it obvious. The native platform on Android is Java. Codename One compiles to it and talks to Android the way Android expects. Flutter avoids it, shipping its own VM and engine beside the one the phone already has. That's why Android shows the biggest gap: a third of the start-up time and a quarter of the code.

Two differences you feel every day

The threading model shows up in the benchmarks. These two don't, but you notice them every day you work.

Builders

A Codename One app is a Java project. The build of a native app happens in a builder: our cloud build servers or a local build, which take your compiled code and produce the iOS, Android or desktop binary. That moves the hard part of the developer experience into our hands:

  • Build iOS apps from Windows or Linux. The cloud builder holds the Mac, Xcode and the signing steps. You don't need to own a Mac to ship to the App Store.
  • Cheap CI. Your unit and UI tests run in Java, in the simulator, on any CI runner. No emulator to boot and no macOS runner to pay for on every commit.
  • New features without migration work. When Apple or Google change a requirement, or we add a capability, we update the builder. Your project picks it up on the next build, with nothing to upgrade or reconfigure.

Everything in one place

Codename One used to aim for a modular core, with features broken out into cn1libs. Flutter is going through that phase now, moving pieces such as its Material and Cupertino themes out of the framework into independent packages. We went the opposite way. The Codename One core now covers what Flutter does, plus most of what people reach for in Flutter's most popular packages, and this week's posts add more.

A bigger core costs you nothing, because you don't pay for what you don't use, and that works on two levels. ParparVM drops every class your app doesn't reach. The builder goes further: it looks at what your compiled code calls and adds a native library only when a feature needs it. This week's crypto support is a good example. Its native kernels for secp256k1, Ed25519 and the hashes are what make it fast, and an app that never touches the crypto API shouldn't carry them. It doesn't. Call a wallet or a signature API and the builder links them in, and you get native speed that our CI measures against the reference libraries, libsecp256k1 and OpenSSL among them. That's how the builds above stay smaller than Flutter's. What you get instead:

  • One version. No matrix of package versions to keep compatible, and no upgrade that breaks because two packages disagree.
  • Nothing abandoned. No package your app depends on that its author stopped maintaining two years ago.
  • A short supply chain. This is the big one. Every package in a dependency tree is a person you trust with your users' devices. A maintainer who burns out, sells the package, gets angry or gets hacked can push code into your app on the next update, and attacks on open source packages have done exactly that. With the features in core, your app's dependencies are one project with one review process, not a tree of packages from strangers. That fits the rest of this week: the Bastion template is a hardened bank because security is something we take seriously, and banks and other regulated organizations build on Codename One. For them, a short supply chain is a requirement.
  • Everything moves together. When we fix rendering, add a platform or change the build, every feature comes along, including the niche ones.
  • One source of truth. The developer guide documents all of it, and when something breaks there is one team responsible for the answer.

We can finally show the code

For years, every Codename One against Flutter discussion went the same way. I'd explain why ahead of time compiled Java with a lightweight UI should produce a smaller, faster app. Someone would explain why it shouldn't. Neither of us had the same app built both ways, so it came down to which camp you were already in.

Now there's one app, built both ways, measured on every commit. If you think a number is wrong, the harness is in the repository and you can rerun it.

The part I didn't expect is how much this made Codename One better. Each compatibility layer exposed problems we had missed for years:

  • Styles were parsed over and over. Every component re-parsed its pressed and disabled styles from the theme. Caching them took component creation in the Gallery from 131 ms to 17 ms and resident memory from 247 MB to 144 MB.
  • Every string constant was created at startup. ParparVM materialized every string literal before main() ran. Making the pool lazy cut that step from 119 ms to 46 ms.
  • Rounded images were copied. Rounding an image's corners built a second bitmap, 32 times during the first frame. Doing it in the fragment shader removed the copies and stopped memory from swinging between runs.
  • Images decoded inside the first frame. Deferring that decode took the first frame from 302 ms to 213 ms.
  • An idle app burned CPU. The Compose work found, and we fixed, a bug where on phones with a notch, safe area padding kept queuing layout so an idle app sat at 14% to 26% CPU.

None of these fixes are specific to Flutter. If you write Codename One apps in plain Java and never touch a Dart file, your app gets these fixes too: faster start-up, lower memory and an idle CPU that stays idle.

More This Week

Your Compose code, on more screens

Kotlin Multiplatform is a good platform, and Compose Multiplatform is well built. Codename One now runs the same Compose code on more targets, used about a quarter of the CPU per frame on our benchmark screen, and lets you drop to Java where it counts.

The same Compose screen: Compose Multiplatform on the left, Codename One on the right.

class MyApp : Lifecycle() {
    override fun runApp() {
        ComposeForm { LayoutScreen() }.show()
    }
}

Saturday's Compose article has the numbers and their caveats.

Swing and JavaFX on phones

A large share of real Swing and JavaFX code now builds for iOS, Android and the web: the samples we test include SwingSet2 and Notepad, the JDK's own demos. On Linux the native build is 4 to 6 times smaller zipped than the same app on the JVM, and starts faster in all 8 apps, even against a JVM tuned with AppCDS.

SwingSet2, the JDK demo, on an iPad.
The JavaFX 2048 game on a phone.

Swing controls.
JTable.
JavaFX.
FXML and CSS.

Sunday's Swing and JavaFX article goes through what carries over and why you won't miss what doesn't.

A bank you can study, and wallets in core

A large share of our users are banks and financial institutions. Bastion is a reference implementation for them: a virtual bank and small exchange with passkeys, TOTP, signed requests, device keys, a hash chained audit log, a double entry ledger and an auditor console. Codename One also gained wallet APIs for Ethereum, Bitcoin, and Solana.

Four currencies.
The BTC/USD market.
The Security Center.

Wallet wallet = Wallet.fromMnemonic(words, "");
EvmAddress eth = wallet.getEvmAddress(0, 0);
BitcoinAddress btc = wallet.getBitcoinAddress(BitcoinNetwork.MAINNET, Wallet.BIP84, 0, 0, 0);
SolanaAddress sol = wallet.getSolanaAddress(0);

Monday's Bastion article covers the hardening, one layer at a time.

Streaming and courses

Reel is a streaming service and its server in one Java project. Switch a preset and it becomes a subscription service, a creator platform in the style of YouTube, or an academy with courses, lessons, and quizzes.

The catalog.
The player.
A course.

StreamRequest req = new StreamRequest(manifestUrl)
        .setDrm(new DrmConfig(DrmScheme.WIDEVINE, licenseUrl));

Tuesday's Reel article walks through uploads, moderation, and DRM.

Android code everywhere, including GrapheneOS

The Android compatibility layer now covers Room, WorkManager, location, sensors, foreground services and the document picker intents, all running on iOS too. And GrapheneOS, LineageOS, CalyxOS and /e/OS are now officially supported, with a boundary CI verifies: one APK checks for Play Services at run time, and push works through UnifiedPush.

Material 3, Android left, Codename One right.
RecyclerView, same source.

Wednesday's Android article has the details.

A modern backend, and a simulator that types

The simulated keyboard sliding up over a sign up form.

Thursday closes the week with eight backend upgrades (a bounded cache, outbound OAuth tokens, PKI, JSON codecs, streaming uploads, error advice, java.time in the ORM and test slices) and a simulator that slides up a virtual keyboard and records video. See the backend and simulator article.

The universal platform

Last week I made the case that a Java word processor beats its Rust twin. This week the swing is bigger. Flutter, Compose, Swing, JavaFX and Android code all build into the same kind of app and run on iOS, Android, desktop, the web and the watch.

Instead of coding to an operating system, you code to Codename One, and Codename One becomes the operating system. The usual price for that kind of abstraction is performance. We don't charge it. You get more performance, more features, more compatibility and more platforms, and it's free and open source.

If you have a Flutter app, run the import on a copy and build it for the simulator. Tell us which screen breaks first; that's the most useful bug report we can get right now. If you're on Kotlin, Swing, JavaFX or Android, the rest of this week is for you. And if you think a number above is wrong, the benchmark is in the repository. Rerun it and open an issue.

title: PostgreSQL 14 ends on Nov 12. The upgrade won't break your Java service. The next password reset will.
description:
PostgreSQL 14 gets its final release on November 12. After that, no more fixes. Most teams I talk to have the upgrade on a list somewhere, and most of them are worried about the data: pg_upgrade, extensions, downtime.

The thing I'd worry about is smaller and later. It's a login failure that doesn't happen on upgrade day.

What changed in 14

PostgreSQL 14 changed the default of password_encryption from md5 to scram-sha-256. Every new password is stored as a SCRAM verifier unless you change that setting.

Here's the part that makes it sneaky. pg_upgrade keeps the MD5 hashes you already have. So you upgrade a 12 or 13 server to 14 (or straight to 18), your apps reconnect, everything is green, and you close the ticket.

Then, weeks later, someone rotates the app's database password. The new one is stored as SCRAM. A Java service that has been fine for years starts failing with:

org.postgresql.util.PSQLException: The authentication type 10 is not supported.

Type 10 is SCRAM. The driver doesn't speak it. Moving with dump and restore doesn't avoid it: pg_dumpall --globals-only carries the MD5 hashes over as they are, so you're in the same position. It only fails on day one if you create the roles by hand on the new server, because then every password is set again.

Which pgjdbc versions can log in

pgjdbc added SCRAM-SHA-256 in 42.2.0, only in the Java 8+ build. But 42.2.0 shipped with a known issue: the SCRAM client classes weren't packaged, so it didn't actually work. 42.2.1 fixed that a week later.

So the floor is 42.2.1, and not a .jre6 or .jre7 build. Those older-Java builds never got SCRAM at any version. That catches people: a 42.2.x.jre7 jar looks newer than 42.2.1, and it still can't log in.

The same change hits other clients. The floors I check against, each taken from the client's own changelog or source:

  • Go: lib/pq 1.1.0, pgx 3.4.0
  • Node: pg 7.9.0
  • .NET: Npgsql 3.2.7
  • Anything built on libpq: libpq 10
  • PgBouncer: 1.11, or 1.14 if it looks passwords up with auth_query or keeps SCRAM secrets in auth_file

How to check before you upgrade (all read-only)

1. Find the PostgreSQL 14 servers in your cluster.

kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.namespace}{"\t"}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{range .spec.containers[*]}{.image}{" "}{end}{"\n"}{end}' \
  | grep -E 'postgres[^ ]*:14'

If an operator (CloudNativePG, Crunchy, Zalando) runs the database, check the image in its cluster resource as well.

2. See how each login role's password is stored today. As a superuser:

SHOW password_encryption;

SELECT rolname,
       CASE WHEN rolpassword LIKE 'md5%'           THEN 'md5'
            WHEN rolpassword LIKE 'SCRAM-SHA-256%' THEN 'scram'
            ELSE 'none' END AS stored_as
FROM pg_authid
WHERE rolcanlogin;

Every md5 row is a password that will turn into SCRAM the next time someone resets it.

3. Find the driver each Java service actually ships. Not the version in a pom from two years ago, the jar in the running image:

kubectl exec -n <ns> <pod> -- sh -c 'find / -name "postgresql-*.jar" 2>/dev/null'

Anything below 42.2.1, or with .jre6/.jre7 in the name, gets bumped before the upgrade, not after the first failed rotation.

Why this one is worth an hour this week

The end-of-life date is a deadline you can see. This failure is one you can't: the upgrade passes, the dashboards stay green, and it surfaces on whatever day a password rotates. Usually not a day anyone connects with the upgrade.

Checking takes three queries. Finding it during an incident takes a lot longer.
