title: Data Structures in Go[Arrays and Slices]
description:
Introduction: Why Do We Need Data Structures?

So far, we've covered the foundations of Go, including variables, data types, operators, conditional statements, loops, and functions.

These concepts give us the building blocks we need to write Go programs. However, as we begin building more practical applications, we'll encounter a new challenge such as working with large amounts of data.

Think about an application that manages users, processes transactions, stores product information, or tracks customer records.

We won't always be working with a single value at a time. We'll often need to store, organise, access, modify, and manipulate collections of related data. For example:

  • A banking application might need to store multiple customer account balances.
  • An e-commerce application might need to manage a collection of products. Storing each value in a separate variable would quickly become impractical and difficult to manage. This is where data structures come in.

Data structures are ways of organising and storing data in a program so that we can access, manage, and manipulate it efficiently.

Go provides several built-in data structures and mechanisms that help us work with collections of data.

In this module, we'll explore four important concepts:

  1. Arrays and Slices: Used to store collections of values of the same type.
  2. Maps: Used to store data as key-value pairs.
  3. Structs: Used to group related values, potentially of different types, into a single custom data type.
  4. Pointers: Used to store and work with the memory address of another value.

We'll begin with arrays, slices, and maps before moving on to structs and pointers.

Arrays and Slices in Go

In Go, arrays and slices are data structures that consist of an ordered sequence of elements. They are useful when we want to work with multiple related values, as they allow us to keep data that belongs together in a single variable and perform similar operations on multiple values at once.

Coming from a JavaScript background, I'd assume most of us are already familiar with arrays and how they work. However, Go approaches arrays and slices a little differently, so I'd still love to go over them again.

Although both are used to store multiple values of the same data type in a single variable, the major difference between them is their length.

An array has a fixed length, meaning the number of elements it can contain is determined when it is created and cannot be changed.

A slice, on the other hand, is flexible. Its length can change as we add or remove elements, making it more convenient when working with collections of data that may grow or shrink over time.

We'll explore both concepts, how to define and initialise them, how to access and manipulate their elements, and the differences between them.

Defining an Array

An array is a collection of elements of the same data type with a fixed length. The length is part of its type.

In Go, arrays are defined by specifying the size (length) of the array inside square brackets[], followed by the data type of its elements.

Syntax:

var numbers [3]int

var - Keyword used to declare a variable.
numbers - Variable name.
[3]- Length of the array (number of elements it can hold).
int - Data type of the elements stored in the array.

Important to note:

Once an array has been declared, its length cannot be changed. However, its elements can be modified, and we can also initialise an array with values.
it's important to understand that an array's length is part of its type. This is one of the major differences between arrays in Go and arrays in JavaScript.

var first [2]int
var second [3]int

Although both arrays contain integers, they have different types.

  • first has the type [2]int (an array of 2 integers).
  • second has the type [3]int (an array of 3 integers).

Because their lengths are different, their types are also different.

This means you cannot assign one array to the other or compare them directly as though they were the same type.

Important to note:

  • Array length is part of its type.
  • Arrays of different lengths are different types.
  • Arrays of the same type can be compared, provided their element type is comparable.

Declaring and Initialising Arrays

There are several ways to declare and initialise an array in Go.

1. Declaring an Array Without Specifying Initial Values

We can declare an array without providing any initial values.

var numbers [3]int

fmt.Println(numbers)

Output:

[0 0 0]

This creates an array with three integer elements and since we haven't provided any initial values, Go automatically initialises each element with the zero value of its respective data type.

For integers (int), the zero value is 0.

This behaviour also applies to other data types.

var names [3]string

fmt.Println(names)

Output: 

[  ]

For strings, the zero value is an empty string (""). When printed as part of an array, the empty strings appear as blank spaces between the brackets.
This is an important characteristic of Go. When variables are declared without explicit initial values, Go automatically assigns them their respective zero values. Arrays follow this rule element by element.

2. Initialising an Array With Explicit Values

We can also provide initial values when declaring an array.

score := [3]int{85, 90, 95}

fmt.Println(score)

Output:

[85 90 95]

Here, we are declaring and initialising an array called score with three integer values. The values are assigned in order, starting from index 0.

Index Value
0 85
1 90
2 95

The syntax consists of three main parts:

  • The array's length: [3]
  • The data type: int
  • The initial values: {85, 90, 95}

3. Specifying the Length but Providing Fewer Initial Values

Go also allows us to initialise an array with fewer values than its declared length.

numbers := [4]int{10, 20}

fmt.Println(numbers)

Output:

[10 20 0 0]

Here, we've declared an array called numbers with a length of four, but we've only provided two initial values. What happens?

  • The first element (index 0) receives 10.
  • The second element (index 1) receives 20.
  • The third element (index 2) receives the zero value, 0.
  • The fourth element (index 3) also receives the zero value, 0.

The remaining elements are automatically initialised with the zero value of their data type.Even though we provided only two initial values, the array still has a length of four which does not change because the length was already specified during declaration.

4. Allowing Go to Infer the Array Length

Go provides the ... notation for array literals when we want the compiler to determine the array's length automatically. Instead of manually specifying the number of elements, we allow Go to count the initial values and determine the length.

numbers := [...]int{10, 20, 30, 40}

fmt.Println(numbers)

Output:

[10 20 30 40]

Here, we've used ... instead of explicitly specifying the array's length.

Go counts the number of initial values and infers the array's type as [4]int.

It’s important to know that the ... notation does not mean that the array has a variable length, it simply tells the compiler to determine the array's length from the number of initial values provided. Once the array has been initialised, its length is fixed.

Go vs JavaScript: Array Initialisation

Coming from a JavaScript background, let's look at how array initialisation differs in both languages.

JavaScript:

const numbers = [10, 20];

numbers.push(30);

console.log(numbers);

Output:

[10, 20, 30]

In JavaScript, we can initialise an array with two elements and use the push() method to add another element.

The array grows from two elements to three.

Go:

numbers := [4]int{10, 20}
fmt.Println(numbers)

Output:

[10 20 0 0]

In Go, we've declared an array with a length of four, even though we've only provided two initial values.

The remaining two elements are automatically assigned their zero values.

The main difference is that Go arrays have a fixed length, whereas JavaScript arrays can grow or shrink as elements are added or removed.

To create a Go collection that can grow dynamically, we typically use slices, which we'll explore later.

Lesson Takeaway

  1. The length of an array is part of its type in Go.
  2. Go automatically assigns zero values to elements that aren't explicitly initialised.
  3. You can initialise an array with fewer values than its declared length.
  4. The ... notation allows Go to infer the array's length.
  5. Array elements can be modified, but the array's length cannot be changed.

Finding the Length of an Array Using len()

Go provides a built-in function called len() that allows us to obtain the number of elements in an array or slice. This returns the total number of elements, not the highest index.

numbers := [3]int{20, 30, 40}

fmt.Println(len(numbers))

3

Although the array's highest index is 2, its length is 3 because it contains three elements.

Go vs JavaScript: Finding Array Length

In JavaScript, we use the .length property to determine the number of elements in an array.

JavaScript:

const numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40];

console.log(numbers.length);

Output:

4

Go:

numbers := [4]int{10, 20, 30, 40}

fmt.Println(len(numbers))

Output:

4

The difference is simply how both languages provide access to the length:

  • JavaScript uses the .length property.
  • Go uses the built-in len() function.

Why is len() important?

The len() function is frequently used when working with arrays and slices, particularly when iterating through their elements using loops. It allows us to determine the number of elements we need to work with without manually counting them.

Array Assignments in Go

One of the important differences between arrays in Go and JavaScript is how they behave when assigned to another variable.

In Go, arrays are value types. This means that when we assign an array to another variable, Go copies the entire array, including all its elements.The two variables now hold separate copies of the array meaning modifying one does not affect the other.

first := [3]int{10, 20, 30}

second := first

second[0] = 90

fmt.Println(first)
fmt.Println(second)

Output:

[10 20 30]
[90 20 30]

Let's break down what's happening:

  1. We declare an array called first containing three integers.
  2. We create another variable called second and assign first to it.
  3. Go copies all the elements of first into second.
  4. We modify the element at index 0 of second, changing its value from 10 to 90.
  5. When we print both arrays, we see that first remains unchanged while second contains the modified value.

This happens because both variables hold separate copies of the array.

Go vs JavaScript: Array Assignment

JavaScript handles array assignment differently. In JavaScript, arrays are reference types. Assigning an array to another variable copies the reference to the same underlying array object, rather than creating an independent copy.

const first = [10, 20, 30];

const second = first;

second[0] = 90;

console.log(first);
console.log(second);

Output:

[90, 20, 30]
[90, 20, 30]

Notice that modifying second also affects first, This happens because both variables refer to the same array object in memory.

Go JavaScript
Arrays are value types. Arrays are reference types.
Assigning an array copies its elements. Assigning an array copies its reference.
Each variable holds an independent array copy. Both variables can refer to the same array object.
Modifying one copy does not affect the other. Modifying the shared array affects both references.

This value-copying behaviour also applies when passing arrays to functions in Go. When an array is passed as an argument to a function, the function receives a copy of the array.

This means that even if the function modifies an element, the original array outside the function remains unchanged. We'll explore this behaviour further when we get into functions and pointers.

Why Are Arrays Less Common Than Slices in Go?

Although arrays are useful in Go, they are less commonly used than slices in everyday application development. The main reason is their fixed length.
In real-world applications, the amount of data we work with can change frequently. For example:

  • The number of users in an application can increase or decrease.
  • The number of products in an online store can change.
  • The number of transactions processed by a banking application can vary.
  • The number of records returned from an API can change depending on the request.

Arrays are not particularly convenient for these situations because their length cannot be changed after declaration. Slices, on the other hand, provide more flexibility because their length can grow or shrink as needed.

So When Should We Use Arrays?

Arrays are still useful, particularly when we know the exact number of elements we need and that number is not expected to change.

For example:

  • Storing the RGB values of a colour (three integers).
  • Representing a fixed number of coordinates.
  • Working with fixed-size cryptographic keys.
  • Storing a fixed set of measurements. Takeaway
  • Use arrays when a fixed size is an intentional requirement.
  • Use slices for most collections where the number of elements may grow, shrink, or change over time.

Slices in Go

Defining Slices

A slice is a flexible, dynamically sized sequence of elements that describes a section of an underlying array. We can also think of a slice as a dynamic array because, unlike arrays, its length can grow or shrink as needed.
However, it's important to understand that a slice itself is not an underlying array. A slice is a value that describes a portion of an array that it exposes.
A slice provides access to a section of an underlying array, and multiple slices can refer to the same underlying array, this means that different slices can share the same underlying data. Changes made through one slice can affect what another slice sees if they refer to the same elements.

Slice Syntax 

collection[start:end]
  • collection: The array or slice we want to extract elements from.
  • start: The index where the slice begins. This index is inclusive.
  • end: The index where the slice stops. This index is exclusive. The start index is included in the resulting slice, while the end index is excluded. 
numbers := [5]int{10, 20, 30, 40, 50}

Now, let's create a slice called middle from this array:

middle := numbers[1:4]

fmt.Println(middle)

Output:

[20 30 40]

Our original array contains five elements so when we write:

middle := numbers[1:4]

We're extracting a section of the original array, starting at index 1 and stopping before index 4.
This means:

  • Index 1 is included (value: 20).
  • Index 2 is included (value: 30).
  • Index 3 is included (value: 40).
  • Index 4 is excluded (value: 50).

The resulting slice contains [20 30 40].

Declaring and Initialising Slices

There are several ways to declare and initialise slices in Go. Let's explore them.

1. Declaring a Slice Without Initialising It:

We can declare a slice without providing any initial values.

var numbers []int

This declares a slice of integers but unlike arrays, there is no fixed length included in the declaration.
However, there is an important distinction between declaring a slice and allowing Go to infer the length of an array. Although the declarations might look similar, they behave differently.

A newly declared slice without an initial value is a nil slice. A nil slice has:

  • Length of 0.
  • Capacity of 0.
  • No underlying array currently associated with it. We can verify this using the len() and cap() functions. 
var numbers []int

fmt.Println(numbers)
fmt.Println(len(numbers))
fmt.Println(cap(numbers))

Output:

[]
0
0

Even though the slice has no elements, we can still add elements to it using the append() function.

var numbers []int
numbers = append(numbers, 10, 20)
fmt.Println(numbers)

Output:

[10 20]

This works because append() returns a slice value containing the added elements, which we assign back to numbers. It’s also important to not that a nil slice is not the same as an array containing zero values.

var numbers [3]int

fmt.Println(numbers)

Output:

[0 0 0]

This array contains three elements, even though all three elements have the zero value of int. However:

var numbers []int

fmt.Println(numbers)

Output:

[]

This slice contains no elements. The difference is that an array has a fixed number of elements, while a nil slice has a length and capacity of zero.

2. Initialising a Slice Using a Slice Literal

Another way to create a slice is by using a slice literal. A slice literal looks similar to an array literal, except that we omit the length inside the square brackets.

numbers := []int{10, 20, 30}

fmt.Println(numbers)

Output:

[10 20 30]

This creates a slice containing three integers but lrt's notice the difference

// Array
numbers := [3]int{10, 20, 30}

// Slice
numbers := []int{10, 20, 30}

For an array, we specify the length inside the brackets while for a slice, we leave the brackets empty. The type of our slice is []int, not [3]int.
We can also initialise slices containing other data types.

String slice:

names := []string{"John", "Mary", "Peter"}

Boolean slice:

status := []bool{true, false, true}

Floating-point slice:

prices := []float64{10.5, 20.5, 30.5}

Just like arrays, all elements in a slice must have the same data type.

3. Creating a Slice Using make()

Go provides a built-in function called make() that allows us to create and initialise slices with a specified length and optional capacity.
syntax:

make([]T, length)

Where:

  • make: The built-in function used to create the slice.
  • []T: Specifies the slice's data type.
  • length: Specifies the initial number of elements in the slice. 
numbers := make([]int, 3)

fmt.Println(numbers)

Output:

[0 0 0]

This creates a slice of integers with a length of three with all three elements initially assigned the zero value of int, which is 0. We can then assign values to individual elements using their indices.

numbers := make([]int, 3)
numbers[0] = 10
numbers[1] = 20
numbers[2] = 30

fmt.Println(numbers)

Output:

[10 20 30]

The make() function is useful when we know how many elements we want to work with from the beginning, but we don't necessarily have their actual values yet.

4. Creating a Slice With a Specified Capacity

We can also provide a capacity when creating a slice using make().

syntax:

make([]T, length, capacity)
  • []T: Specifies the slice's data type.
  • length: Specifies the number of elements the slice currently contains.
  • capacity: Specifies the maximum number of elements the slice can hold before needing a larger underlying array. 
numbers := make([]int, 3, 5)
fmt.Println(numbers)
fmt.Println(len(numbers))
fmt.Println(cap(numbers))

Output:

[0 0 0]
3
5

This creates a slice of integers with Length: 3, Capacity: 5, with the slice currently containing three elements, all initialised to zero. However, its underlying array has room for five elements.

Understanding Length vs Capacity

This is an important distinction when working with slices.

Length (len) refers to the number of elements currently contained in the slice.

Capacity (cap) refers to the number of elements between the beginning of the slice and the end of its underlying array.

numbers := make([]int, 3, 4)

The slice has three elements, but its capacity is four, it's important to note that capacity does not mean the slice already contains five elements, It currently contains only three elements.
To access an element directly using its index, that index must be within the slice's current length, not merely within its capacity.

numbers[3] = 40

This would cause an index out of range panic because the slice's current length is three, and its valid indices are 0, 1, and 2. To add a fourth element, we use `append()

`go
numbers := make([]int, 3, 4)

numbers[0] = 10
numbers[1] = 20
numbers[2] = 30
numbers = append(numbers, 40)
fmt.Println(numbers)
fmt.Println(len(numbers))
fmt.Println(cap(numbers))
`

Output:

`plaintext
[10 20 30 40]
4
4

`
Notice what happened, Initially the slice had a length of 3 and capacity of 5.

  • We used append() to add another element.
  • The length increased from 3 to 4.
  • The capacity remained 5 with enough room to still grow.

This is how we can add elements to a slice without directly accessing an index outside its current length.

Shared Underlying Arrays

When you create a slice from an array, the slice does not create an independent copy of the selected elements. Instead, it refers to the relevant portion of the original array. Let's look at an example:
`go
numbers := [5]int{10, 20, 30, 40, 50}

middle := numbers[1:4]

fmt.Println(numbers) // [10 20 30 40 50]
fmt.Println(middle) // [20 30 40]
`

The original array still contains all five elements:

Index 0 1 2 3 4
Value 10 20 30 40 50

The slice middle starts at index 1 and ends before index 4. Therefore, it contains the values at indexes 1, 2 and 3: 20, 30, 40.
What happens when we modify the slice?
We can modify an element through the slice:

`go
middle[0] = 99

fmt.Println(numbers) // [10 99 30 40 50]
fmt.Println(middle) // [99 30 40]
`

Notice that changing middle[0] also changes numbers[1].

This happens because middle[0] refers to the same underlying array element as numbers[1]. The slice is not an independent copy.

Multiple Slices Can Share One Underlying Array

More than one slice can refer to different portions of the same underlying array. If those portions overlap, changes made through one slice can be visible through the other.

`go
numbers := [5]int{10, 20, 30, 40, 50}

first := numbers[0:3]
second := numbers[2:5]

fmt.Println(first) // [10 20 30]
fmt.Println(second) // [30 40 50]
`

Both slices include the element at index 2, which has the value 30, Let's modify the elements through the slices:

`go
first[1] = 28
first[2] = 29
second[2] = 45

fmt.Println(numbers) // [10 28 29 40 45]
fmt.Println(first) // [10 28 29]
fmt.Println(second) // [29 40 45]
`

  • first[1] = 28 changed numbers[1].
  • first[2] = 29 changed numbers[2], which is also visible through second[0].
  • second[2] = 45 changed numbers[4].

Even though first and second are distinct slice values, they share the same underlying array. It’s important to note that When multiple slices share an underlying array, modifying an element through one slice can affect the other slices if they refer to that same element.

You can read more about this in the official Go blog article,

Slice Length and Capacity

Every slice has two important properties:

Length (len): The length is the number of elements currently accessible through a slice. You can get it using Go's built-in len() function.

Capacity (cap): The capacity is the number of elements from the slice's starting position to the end of its underlying array. You can get it using Go's built-in cap() function.

Capacity is always greater than or equal to length.

The difference is:

  • len() tells you how many elements are currently part of the slice.
  • cap() tells you how much space is available in the underlying array from the slice's starting position.

go
numbers := make([]int, 2, 5)
fmt.Println(numbers) // [0 0]
fmt.Println(len(numbers)) // 2
fmt.Println(cap(numbers)) // 5

  • []int means we are creating a slice of integers.
  • 2 is the length.
  • 5 is the capacity.

The slice currently has two elements, both initialised to their zero value (0) and although its capacity is five, only two elements are currently accessible through the slice. We can still assign values to the existing elements

`go
numbers[0] = 10
numbers[1] = 20

fmt.Println(numbers) // [10 20]
`

Both assignments are valid because indexes 0 and 1 are within the current length of the slice.
However, this would cause a runtime panic:

javascript
numbers[2] = 30

Why?
Because the slice's length is currently 2, meaning its valid indexes are 0 and 1 and even though the capacity is 5, index 2 is not yet part of the slice's accessible elements.

Capacity does not give you permission to access elements beyond the current length.

To make the slice longer, we need to use append().

go
numbers = append(numbers, 30)
fmt.Println(numbers) // [10 20 30]
fmt.Println(len(numbers)) // 3
fmt.Println(cap(numbers)) // 5

The append() function adds an element to the slice and returns the updated slice. We assign the result back to numbers.

The length increases from 2 to 3, while the capacity remains 5 because there is still room in the underlying array.

Lesson Takeaway

  • len() tells you how many elements you can access in the slice right now.
  • cap() tells you how much room is available from the slice's starting position to the end of its underlying array.
  • You cannot access elements using an index beyond the current length, even if the capacity allows room for more elements.
  • Use append() to grow a slice.

Adding Elements to Slices with append()

We've already seen that slices can grow beyond their initial length. Go provides a built-in function called append() to add elements to a slice.

The append() function:

  • Adds one or more elements to an existing slice.
  • Returns a new slice value representing the result.
  • Does not necessarily create a new underlying array.

1. Appending a Single Element

Syntax:

go
slice = append(slice, value)

Let's look at an example:

`go
numbers := []int{10, 20, 30}

numbers = append(numbers, 40)

fmt.Println(numbers) // [10 20 30 40]
`

Here is what happens:

  1. We create a slice called numbers containing 10, 20, 30.
  2. We call append(numbers, 40) to add 40.
  3. append() returns the resulting slice.
  4. We assign the returned slice back to numbers.

Why do we assign the result back?
Because append() returns a slice value. It does not simply modify the existing slice variable in place. This is why we write:

go
numbers = append(numbers, 40)

Rather than just:

python
append(numbers, 40)

2. Appending Multiple Elements

You can append more than one element in a single operation.

`go
numbers := []int{10, 20}

numbers = append(numbers, 30, 40, 50)

fmt.Println(numbers) // [10 20 30 40 50]
`

Here, we added three elements (30, 40 and 50) in one append() operation.

3. Appending One Slice to Another

You can also append the elements of one slice to another.

To do this, Go uses the ... operator.

Example:

`go
first := []int{10, 20, 30}
second := []int{40, 50}

first = append(first, second...)

fmt.Println(first) // [10 20 30 40 50]
`

The ... operator expands the elements of second so that they can be passed as individual arguments to append().

Without ..., Go would try to append the entire second slice as one element, which would cause a type error because first is a slice of integers, not a slice of slices.

4. Does append() Always Create a New Underlying Array?

No, This is an important part of understanding how slices work, Let’s remember every slice has a length and a capacity. So when you append elements, Go checks whether the underlying array has enough remaining capacity.
There are two possible scenarios:

Scenario A: There is sufficient capacity

If the underlying array has enough capacity, Go reuses the existing array.

`go
numbers := make([]int, 2, 5)
numbers[0] = 10
numbers[1] = 20

numbers = append(numbers, 30)

fmt.Println(numbers) // [10 20 30]
fmt.Println(len(numbers)) // 3
fmt.Println(cap(numbers)) // 5
`
Initially:

  • Length = 2
  • Capacity = 5 After appending 30:
  • Length = 3
  • Capacity = 5

Since the underlying array has enough capacity, Go can reuse it without allocating a new one.

Scenario B: There is insufficient capacity

If the underlying array does not have enough capacity, Go allocates a new underlying array with sufficient capacity and copies the existing elements into it.

`go
numbers := make([]int, 2, 2)

numbers[0] = 10
numbers[1] = 20

numbers = append(numbers, 30)

fmt.Println(numbers) // [10 20 30]
fmt.Println(len(numbers)) // 3
fmt.Println(cap(numbers)) // At least 3
`

Initially:

  • Length = 2
  • Capacity = 2

When we append 30, the slice needs to grow beyond its available capacity, Go therefore allocates a new underlying array, copies the existing elements into it and adds the new element. The resulting slice now refers to the new underlying array.

Important: Go determines the new capacity internally. You should not assume that it will always double the previous capacity or grow by a particular amount.

Go vs JavaScript: append() and push()

Coming from JavaScript, you can think of Go's append() as having a similar purpose to JavaScript's .push().

Both are used to add elements to collections.

JavaScript:

`javascript
const numbers = [10, 20, 30];

numbers.push(40);

console.log(numbers); // [10, 20, 30, 40]
`

Go:

`go
numbers := []int{10, 20, 30}

numbers = append(numbers, 40)

fmt.Println(numbers) // [10 20 30 40]
`

However, there is an important difference:

JavaScript Go
Uses .push() Uses append()
.push() modifies the existing array append() returns a slice value
No need to assign the result back when using .push() You should assign the result back when using append()
JavaScript arrays grow dynamically Go slices grow dynamically, but their underlying arrays have a capacity

Lesson takeaway:
append() adds elements to a slice and returns the resulting slice. Depending on the available capacity, Go may reuse the existing underlying array or allocate a new one.

Slicing an Array or Another Slice

We've already seen how to create a slice from an array. We can also use slicing expressions to select different portions of an array or an existing slice. Let's start with an example:

`go
numbers := []int{10, 20, 30, 40, 50}

parts := numbers[1:4]

fmt.Println(parts) // [20 30 40]
`

The expression numbers[1:4] means:

  • Start at index 1 (inclusive).
  • Stop before index 4 (exclusive), therefore the resulting slice contains 20, 30, 40.

1. Omitting the Start Index

You can omit the start index to select elements from the beginning of the slice.

`go
numbers := []int{10, 20, 30, 40, 50}

parts := numbers[:3]

fmt.Println(parts) // [10 20 30]
`
This is the same as writing:

go
parts := numbers[0:3]

When the start index is omitted, Go uses 0 by default.

2. Omitting the End Index

You can also omit the end index to select elements from a particular position through to the end of the slice.

`go
numbers := []int{10, 20, 30, 40, 50}

parts := numbers[2:]

fmt.Println(parts) // [30 40 50]
`

This is equivalent to:

go
parts := numbers[2:len(numbers)]

When the end index is omitted, Go uses the length of the slice.

3. Omitting Both Indexes

You can omit both indexes:

`go
numbers := []int{10, 20, 30, 40, 50}

parts := numbers[:]

fmt.Println(parts) // [10 20 30 40 50]
`

This creates another slice describing the same elements as the original slice. It does not create an independent copy. Both slices refer to the same underlying array.

4. Creating a Slice from Another Slice

You can also create a new slice from an existing slice.

`go
numbers := []int{10, 20, 30, 40, 50}

first := numbers[1:5]
second := first[1:3]

fmt.Println(first) // [20 30 40 50]
fmt.Println(second) // [30 40]
`

Let's understand what happens here.

First:

plaintext
first := numbers[1:5]

This creates a slice containing the elements from index 1 up to, but not including, index 5 of numbers.

The result is:

[20 30 40 50]

Next:

go
second := first[1:3]

This creates another slice from first.

An important detail is that the indexes in this second slicing expression are relative to first, not the original numbers slice.

Therefore:

  • first[1] is 30.
  • first[2] is 40.

The resulting second slice is [30 40].

Both slices still refer to portions of the same underlying array.

5. Valid Slice Indexes

When using a two-index slice expression, the indexes must satisfy certain rules:

  • The start index must not be negative.
  • The end index must not exceed the length of the collection.
  • The start index must not be greater than the end index.

For example:

`go
numbers := []int{10, 20, 30, 40, 50}

parts := numbers[1:4] // Valid
`
But these would cause runtime panics:

python
numbers[-1:3] // Negative start index
numbers[1:6] // End index exceeds length
numbers[4:2] // Start index is greater than end index

Remember that the end index is exclusive.

Removing Elements from a Slice

Go does not have a built-in remove() function for slices.

However, a common technique is to combine slicing and append() to remove an element.

Let's say we have this slice:

go
numbers := []int{10, 20, 30, 40, 50}

We want to remove the element at index 2, which is 30.

We can do this:

`go
i := 2

numbers = append(numbers[:i], numbers[i+1:]...)

fmt.Println(numbers) // [10 20 40 50]
`

Let's break down what happens.
Step 1: Declare the index to remove

plaintext
i := 2

We declare i and assign it the value 2.

This is the index of the element we want to remove.

Step 2: Select the elements before the index

python
numbers[:i]

Since i is 2, this becomes:

python
numbers[:2]

It selects the elements from the beginning up to, but not including, index 2.

The result is:

[10 20]

Notice that the element at index 2 (30) is excluded.

Step 3: Select the elements after the index

python
numbers[i+1:]

Since i is 2, this becomes:

python
numbers[3:]

It selects the elements starting from index 3 through to the end.

The result is:

[40 50]

Step 4: Combine both portions using append()

go
numbers = append(numbers[:i], numbers[i+1:]...)

This is where everything comes together.

  • numbers[:i] gives us the elements before the element we want to remove: [10 20].
  • numbers[i+1:] gives us the elements after the element we want to remove: [40 50].
  • ... expands the second slice into individual elements.
  • append() adds those elements to the first portion.
  • We assign the resulting slice back to numbers.

The final result is:

[10 20 40 50]

The element 30 is no longer part of the resulting slice.

What Does the ... Operator Do Here?

Remember that append() can accept multiple individual values:

go
numbers = append(numbers, 40, 50)

But when we want to append the elements of another slice, we use ...:

go
numbers = append(numbers, anotherSlice...)

The ... operator expands the slice into individual arguments.

Without it, Go would attempt to append the entire slice as a single value, which would cause a type error when working with a []int.

JavaScript vs Go: Removing Elements

In JavaScript, you can use the .splice() method to remove elements from an array.

JavaScript:

`javascript
const numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50];

numbers.splice(2, 1);

console.log(numbers); // [10, 20, 40, 50]
`

The .splice() method takes:

  • The index where removal should begin.
  • The number of elements to remove.

In Go, we use slicing and append():

Go:

`go
numbers := []int{10, 20, 30, 40, 50}

i := 2
numbers = append(numbers[:i], numbers[i+1:]...)

fmt.Println(numbers) // [10 20 40 50]
`

The difference is that JavaScript provides .splice() as a built-in array method, while Go's approach is more explicit.

In Go, we describe the elements before and after the position we want to remove, then combine them using append().

Lesson takeaway:
Slicing allows you to select portions of arrays and slices. By combining slicing with append(), you can also remove elements from a slice.

Copying Slices

Before we discuss copying slices, let's revisit something we've already learnt. When you create a slice from an array, the slice provides a view into the array's data. Similarly, assigning one slice variable to another does not copy the underlying elements. It copies the slice value (descriptor).

`go
first := []int{10, 20, 30}

second := first

second[0] = 99

fmt.Println(first) // [99 20 30]
fmt.Println(second) // [99 20 30]
`

Why does this happen?

When we write:

pascal
second := first

Go copies the slice descriptor, not the underlying elements, Meaning both first and second still refer to the same underlying array.

Therefore, modifying an element through second also affects what we see through first.

Using copy() to Create Independent Slices

If we want two slices whose elements can be modified independently, we can use Go's built-in copy() function.

The copy() function copies elements from a source slice into a destination slice.

However, the destination must have sufficient length if we want to copy all the source elements.

Example:

`go
first := []int{10, 20, 30}

second := make([]int, len(first))

copy(second, first)

second[0] = 99

fmt.Println(first) // [10 20 30]
fmt.Println(second) // [99 20 30]
`

Let's understand what happens:

Step 1: Create the original slice

go
first := []int{10, 20, 30}

This creates our source slice.

Step 2: Create a destination slice

go
second := make([]int, len(first))

We create another slice with the same length as first.

Since first has three elements, second also has a length of three.

At this point, second contains three zero values:

[0 0 0]

Step 3: Copy the elements

plaintext
copy(second, first)

This copies the elements from first into second.

Now both slices contain:

[10 20 30]

However, they have separate underlying arrays.

Step 4: Modify the destination

python
second[0] = 99

This changes only the first element of second.

When we print both slices:

go
fmt.Println(first) // [10 20 30]
fmt.Println(second) // [99 20 30]

The original slice remains unchanged because second has its own underlying array.

How Many Elements Does copy() Copy?

The number of elements copied depends on the lengths of the source and destination slices.

The copy() function copies the minimum of the two lengths.

In other words:

Number of elements copied = min(len(destination), len(source))

`go
source := []int{10, 20, 30, 40}

destination := make([]int, 2)

n := copy(destination, source)

fmt.Println(destination) // [10 20]
fmt.Println(n) // 2
`

Here:

  • The source has a length of 4.
  • The destination has a length of 2.
  • Only two elements are copied.
  • copy() returns 2, representing the number of elements copied.

The remaining source elements (30 and 40) are not copied because the destination only has room for two elements within its current length. copy() does not automatically grow the destination slice. Its length determines how many elements can be copied into it.

Lesson Takeaway

  • Assigning one slice to another copies the slice descriptor, not the underlying elements.
  • Two slices assigned this way can share the same underlying array.
  • Use copy() when you need independent element storage.
  • The number of elements copied is the smaller of the source and destination lengths.
  • copy() returns the number of elements successfully copied.

Nil Slices vs Empty Slices

In Go, a nil slice and an empty slice can look similar when printed, but they are not the same. Let's look at both declarations.

1. Declaring a Nil Slice

`go
var first []int

fmt.Println(first) // []
fmt.Println(len(first)) // 0
fmt.Println(cap(first)) // 0
fmt.Println(first == nil) // true
`

When we declare a slice using var without initialising it, Go creates a nil slice.

A nil slice:

  • Has a length of zero.
  • Has a capacity of zero.
  • Does not currently reference an underlying array.
  • Is equal to nil.

2. Declaring an Empty Slice

`go
second := []int{}

fmt.Println(second) // []
fmt.Println(len(second)) // 0
fmt.Println(cap(second)) // 0
fmt.Println(second == nil) // false
`

Here, we use an empty slice literal.

Although the slice contains no elements, it is initialised and is not nil.

An empty slice:

  • Has a length of zero.
  • Has a capacity of zero.
  • Is not equal to nil.

3. Comparing Nil and Empty Slices

Let's put both declarations together:

`go
var first []int

second := []int{}

fmt.Println(first) // []
fmt.Println(second) // []

fmt.Println(first == nil) // true
fmt.Println(second == nil) // false
`

Both slices print as [], and both have a length of zero.

However, the difference is that the first is nil, while the second is an initialised empty slice.

4. Can You Append to Both?

Yes!

Both nil slices and empty slices can be used with append().

Example:

`go
var first []int
second := []int{}

first = append(first, 10)
second = append(second, 20)

fmt.Println(first) // [10]
fmt.Println(second) // [20]
`

Go automatically handles the underlying storage when elements are appended.

Why Does the Difference Matter?

The distinction between nil and empty slices can matter in a few situations:

Checking whether a slice has been initialised

You can compare a slice to nil to determine whether it is nil.

Returning data from functions

A function might return a nil slice when there is no result, while another might return an initialised empty slice. These are different values even though both contain zero elements.

Encoding data into formats such as JSON

The distinction can affect the output.

For example:

`go
var first []int
second := []int{}

firstJSON, _ := json.Marshal(first)
secondJSON, _ := json.Marshal(second)

fmt.Println(string(firstJSON)) // null
fmt.Println(string(secondJSON)) // []
`

A nil slice is encoded as null, while an empty slice is encoded as an empty array ([]). This can matter when building APIs because clients may treat null and [] differently.

Can You Compare Slices Directly?

Go does not allow you to compare two slices directly using == to check whether their elements are equal.

For example:

`go
first := []int{10, 20, 30}
second := []int{10, 20, 30}

// fmt.Println(first == second) // Compile-time error
`

You can, however, compare a slice to nil:

go
fmt.Println(first == nil) // false

If you need to check whether two slices contain the same elements, you need to compare their elements or use an appropriate equality function.

General Lesson Takeaway: Arrays and Slices

Arrays and slices are both used to store collections of elements of the same data type in Go. However, they behave differently.

Arrays

  • Arrays have a fixed length.
  • Their length is part of their type.
  • Arrays store elements of the same data type.
  • Arrays are value types, meaning assigning an array to another variable copies its elements.
  • Their elements can be accessed and modified using indexes.
  • Use arrays when you need a collection with a fixed, known size.

Slices

  • Slices are flexible and can grow or shrink.
  • Slices are built on top of underlying arrays.
  • Multiple slices can share the same underlying array.
  • Assigning one slice to another copies the slice descriptor, not the underlying elements.
  • Use append() to add elements.
  • Use copy() when you need to copy elements into independent storage.
  • Use slicing expressions to select portions of arrays and slices.
  • Use len() to get the current number of elements.
  • Use cap() to get the available capacity.
  • A nil slice and an empty slice both have a length of zero, but they are not the same.

Important Go Functions and Operations

Function / Operation Purpose
len() Returns the number of elements in an array or slice.
cap() Returns the capacity of a slice or array.
append() Adds elements to a slice and returns the resulting slice.
copy() Copies elements from one slice into another.
make() Creates and initialises a slice with a specified length and optional capacity.
numbers[start:end] Creates a slice from a selected range of elements.

Arrays vs Slices: Quick Comparison

Feature Arrays Slices
Size Fixed Flexible
Length Part of the type Can change
Assignment Copies elements Copies slice descriptor
Underlying array The array itself Refers to an underlying array
Adding elements Cannot grow Uses append()
Length and capacity len() len() and cap()
Common use Fixed-size collections Everyday collections and application data

Think of an array as a fixed size container, A slice is a flexible view into an underlying array. You can create slices from arrays or other slices, append elements, copy elements into independent storage, and select different portions using slicing expressions.

title: Keep AI-suggested loading skeletons matched to real content height
description:
Agents love inventing skeleton screens. Ask for a loading state and you get a neat gray card with three lines… that is half the height of the real content. When data arrives, the layout jumps. CLS goes up. Reviewers shrug because “at least there is a skeleton.”

I’ve started treating height match as a hard constraint, not a nice-to-have. If the skeleton doesn’t reserve roughly the same vertical space as the loaded UI, send it back.

Why height mismatch slips through

AI drafts tend to:

  • Copy a generic “3 lines + avatar” pattern from training data
  • Ignore the real card’s padding, media block, or multi-row meta
  • Use fixed h-4 bars that look pretty in isolation and wrong in the page
  • Forget mobile denser layouts vs desktop taller cards

The PR still “has a loading state,” so it merges. Users feel the jump every time.

What I ask for instead

Paste the real component (or a Storybook story) and constrain the skeleton to geometry, not vibes:

Add a loading skeleton for `ProductCard`.

Constraints:
- Match the loaded card’s outer height ±8px at the default Storybook viewport
- Preserve the same grid/flex structure (media block + title row + price row)
- Use the same padding tokens / gap as the loaded card
- No new skeleton library — reuse our existing `Skeleton` primitive
- Show both states side-by-side in Storybook (`Loading` + `Loaded`) so the jump is obvious in review

If you can’t match height without inventing fake content, stop and explain why.

The ±8px line matters. Without a number, agents will claim “close enough” while the page still shifts a full media block.

Quick review checks

Reject / send back

  • Skeleton shorter than the loaded card by a media block or more
  • Different padding or gap than the real component
  • A brand-new shimmer library when the repo already has one
  • Skeleton only in one breakpoint while the card grows on desktop

Accept

  • Same outer box model as the loaded UI
  • Structural placeholders (media / title / meta) that mirror real rows
  • Story that toggles loading ↔ loaded without a visible jump
  • Token reuse — no one-off gray hexes

Tiny habit

Next time an agent drops a pretty skeleton into a PR, open the Storybook pair and watch the toggle. If the page jumps, don’t debate aesthetics — paste the height constraint and ask again. A skeleton that doesn’t hold space is just a prettier spinner.

title: Large File Browser Direct Upload with Multipart Presigned Parts (S3-Compatible)
description:
For a large file browser direct upload, use multipart upload with presigned parts, and make completion or abort an explicit application operation. That choice keeps retries bounded to one part instead of restarting a video or document, but it also means your service owns the upload state and cleanup path.

My production rule is simple: the browser never decides that an upload is complete. The server creates the session, records it, signs each part, verifies the returned part metadata, and completes only after every expected part has succeeded. A canceled session gets an abort request, even if the user has already closed the tab.

Short version: completion and abort belong to your application.

How should a large file browser direct upload use multipart parts?

The workflow has four stages. First, a trusted server creates a multipart session for the target bucket and object key. It returns an upload ID and a part plan. Second, the browser asks the server for a presigned URL for each part and uploads those byte ranges directly to storage. Third, the browser reports each successful part, including its ETag or equivalent checksum, to the server. Finally, the server calls complete with the ordered part list.

That ordering matters for SLOs. A 20 GB upload split into 64 MB parts can retry one failed request; a single PUT retries all 20 GB. The trade-off is bookkeeping: your database needs an upload row, expected part count, received part metadata, owner, object key, and an expiry policy. Listing objects by prefix cannot reconstruct that state reliably. I keep that row even after completion for audit and support, because a later object listing tells me what exists, not which browser session produced it, which parts were retried, or who should be allowed to cancel it.

The failure path is part of the design, not a janitorial task. If the user cancels, a part fails permanently, or an upload session exceeds your application deadline, issue an abort and mark the row closed. Lifecycle policies are day-based, so they are too coarse for quick cleanup of abandoned multipart fragments.

Here is the shape of a small Go service client. It shows the two control-plane calls that define the contract; the browser-side PUT uses the presigned URL returned by the presign operation, while the service keeps the URL and storage credentials away from the page. I've kept the example intentionally narrow so it does not become a vendor endpoint catalog.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type createRequest struct {
    Key      string `json:"key"`
    PartSize int64  `json:"part_size"`
}

type createResponse struct {
    UploadID string `json:"upload_id"`
}

func call(method, path string, body any) (*http.Response, error) {
    payload, err := json.Marshal(body)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    req, err := http.NewRequest(method, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"+path, bytes.NewReader(payload))
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    return http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
}

func readJSON(resp *http.Response, dst any) error {
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        data, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        return fmt.Errorf("storage request %s: %s", resp.Status, string(data))
    }
    return json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(dst)
}

func create(bucket, key string) (string, error) {
    // Equivalent check for the documented route: curl -X POST https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/multipart/create/{bucket}
    resp, err := call(http.MethodPost, "/storage/multipart/create/"+bucket, createRequest{
        Key: key, PartSize: 64 * 1024 * 1024,
    })
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    var out createResponse
    if err := readJSON(resp, &out); err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    return out.UploadID, nil
}

func main() {
    uploadID, err := create("media", "videos/example.mp4")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println("created", uploadID, "at", time.Now().UTC())
}

In the omitted browser loop, the service signs each part, the browser makes an explicit PUT to that returned URL, and the service completes the session with the ordered successful parts (POST /v1/storage/multipart/complete/{upload_id}). On cancellation, invoke the documented abort operation by name. Do not substitute REST-shaped paths such as /multipart/jobs.

Retries need two guardrails. Back off on HTTP 429 and honor Retry-After; a tight loop turns a transient limit into an outage. Also make create and complete idempotent with a client-supplied idempotency key, so a tab refresh cannot create duplicate sessions or finalize the same object twice. Store the idempotency key with the upload row and make completion conditional on the recorded part set. A 429 is a scheduling signal, not permission to hammer the endpoint; exponential delays such as 1s, 2s, and 4s are a reasonable starting point, though I'm not sure your workload's best cap without observing its rate-limit headers.

Keep it boring.

How should this compare with S3-compatible alternatives?

Multipart semantics are familiar across S3-compatible services, but operational edges differ. A buy-vs-build review should weigh the storage contract, browser policy, cleanup tooling, and the on-call surface together.

Option Strength Catch for this workflow Choose it when
Amazon S3 Mature multipart APIs, lifecycle controls, and ecosystem tooling More service configuration and IAM policy surface to operate You need the broadest AWS integration and already run there
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible API with Cloudflare-adjacent delivery options Account and egress choices still require Cloudflare-specific operational knowledge Your delivery path is already centered on Cloudflare
Backblaze B2 Straightforward object storage and published pricing Check region, lifecycle, and S3-compatibility details against your required controls You want a focused storage product and can own the integration
Infrai storage One plain REST API and one credential can cover storage alongside other backend capabilities; swapping the provider behind that capability does not require rewriting your application contract No public-read ACL, object versioning, object lock, cross-region replication, or hourly lifecycle expiry; browser CORS configuration is not self-service You value a consistent multi-capability control plane and can enforce visibility and retention in your own service

Infrai's useful advantage here is interface stability, not a claim that it replaces every storage product. Its REST surface is self-describing and can be called without installing an SDK, so a platform team can keep one integration boundary while changing the vendor behind a capability. That only helps if your application already has the missing policy layers: private access, CORS handling, concurrency coordination, and an upload ledger.

The catch is important. Infrai is not suitable for a static website that needs a permanently public object URL, for WORM retention, or for strict cross-region disaster recovery without an external replication design. Stick with S3 when AWS-native controls are the requirement; choose another provider when its compliance or replication model is the actual constraint.

The preventative path: state, SLOs, and cleanup

Define an upload SLO separately from the object-store SLO. For example, measure time from session creation to completion, the percentage of sessions aborted within your cleanup target, and the rate of part retries. A green storage dashboard does not prove that abandoned browser sessions are being closed.

The database row should move through explicit states such as created, uploading, completing, completed, and aborted. A worker can scan rows past the application deadline and issue abort, while a unique constraint on (owner, object_key, active) prevents two active sessions from racing. Since there is no If-Match conditional write, use that database coordination or a queue when concurrent writers must be mutually exclusive.

Keep the object private and return an application-authorized download URL or proxy response. Public ACLs and permanent direct links are outside this pattern. Also remember that metadata is not server-searchable; if you need content type, tenant, or retention queries, persist those fields in your own database rather than depending on a prefix listing.

This advice does not fit every file. For small objects, a single authenticated PUT is easier to reason about and cheaper to test. For a workload requiring immutable financial records, add an external WORM-capable system. For a browser flow where you cannot configure CORS, direct upload will stop at the browser boundary until that policy is provided by the surrounding platform.

References

  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.bucket.create
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/API/API_CreateMultipartUpload.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/multipart-objects/
  • https://www.backblaze.com/docs/cloud-storage-s3-compatible-api
  • https://www.backblaze.com/cloud-storage/pricing
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7231

title: Figma MCP design system prep for AI agents
description:
Figma now lets coding agents write straight to the canvas, and on October 29 it explained how its own editing model learns to do the same. Both posts say agents work "using your components and variables." Neither says what your files need to look like for that to be true.

This article argues that the gap is where teams lose the benefit. The agent follows the rules you write down and the structure you actually built, not the system in your head. It is for design leads and product managers who are about to let an agent touch a production library.

The announcement skips the part you have to do

In March, Figma opened the canvas to agents. Its launch post says the use_figma tool works with your components and variables, and that auto layout, components and variables are the structures agents operate on. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot and others can connect.

The same post gives no guidance on preparing a file. It points to the help center and developer docs for the rest. Figma's MCP server FAQ fills in some practical limits. You need a Full seat to write outside your drafts. Fonts must be uploaded to your Figma account. Components must be published before Code Connect mappings can be completed. And the output "is beta quality and may need manual review and cleanup."

That last line matters most. Figma is telling you the agent is a fast first pass, not a finished one. How much cleanup you face depends on inputs you control.

On October 29, Figma's VP of engineering described the model behind the agent in How we're training a Figma-fluent editing model. The post is candid about one thing worth repeating. Post-training improves the model's part of a larger system that also includes canvas context, design system context and tools. Two of those three are your files. A better model does not rescue a messy library.

What goes wrong when you just point an agent at a library

Bitovi ran the agent against real components and wrote up the result in Figma just opened the canvas to agents. The good news first. From an existing Button, the agent produced a component set with correct variants, styles and clean layer names.

The agent "doesn't pick up on a linked design system unless you tell it to. Every time." It used plain frames for some components while using real library components for others. Left to defaults, it hardcoded colors, spacing and type. Bitovi's summary is the line I would put on a wall: the agent optimizes for the literal goal you gave it, not the implicit standards in your head.

Hardcoded values are not a model flaw you wait out. A designer who never opened the variables panel produces the same output. The agent is a very literal junior, so every gap in your system gets reproduced, quickly.

Treat one test with care. Bitovi's piece is one team's experience, and output varies between runs. The pattern is useful. No one has published a failure rate.

Five file problems that make agents guess

Practitioner guides, such as the Figma file best practices in the camoa dev guides and a uxdesign.cc practical guide, agree on the problems. They are blog advice, not Figma documentation, so read them as heuristics. I rank them by cost.

Hardcoded fills and spacing. If a button's fill is a hex value instead of a variable, the agent has nothing to bind to and copies the hex. Bind every fill, stroke, radius and gap to a variable first. This single fix removes the failure Bitovi saw most clearly.

Primitives and semantic tokens matter here. A variable named blue-500 tells the agent a color. A variable named action-primary tells it a purpose. Agents choose by purpose when you ask for "a primary action", so semantic names carry the instruction.

Generic layer names come next. "Frame 234" and "Group 1" give the agent no hint about what a thing is, and the code it produces inherits the vagueness. Name layers the way an engineer would name a component, and match component and property names to your code (a "Style" property in Figma against a "variant" prop in code is enough to break mapping).

Then structure. Agents read auto layout as intent. If a card has fixed positions instead of padding, gap and direction, the agent cannot tell what should grow and what should wrap. Guides also warn against nesting auto layout very deeply, though I have not seen a measured threshold, so treat any specific number as folklore.

Finally, missing descriptions. Guides report that component descriptions reach the agent as context. A two-line note on a star rating component, saying what its states mean and when not to use it, costs nothing and is read every time.

Why rules matter more than a better prompt

Figma's answer to inconsistency is skills, which are markdown files that spell out workflow steps, sequencing and conventions. The foundational /figma-use skill teaches the agent how the tool works, and teams can add their own. Figma says skills make output more predictable because the same prompt can yield different results from a non-deterministic model.

Read that as a statement about where your effort belongs. A prompt lives for one request. A skill lives for every request after it. Bitovi's suggested directives show the right grain. Check for a linked design system before generating anything, and use variables for color and spacing.

This is the logic behind approval UX for agents. You cannot review every action at agent speed, so judgment moves into rules written in advance.

My first skill would be short. Name the library to use and require the agent to load it before drawing anything. State that every color, space and radius comes from a variable, and that a missing token should be reported, not invented. Say which components to use for buttons, inputs and cards, and that plain frames are never acceptable as stand-ins. Describe the naming pattern for new layers. End with what to report: any value the agent could not bind, and any component it had to build.

An agent that lists its own exceptions turns cleanup from a hunt into a checklist.

Where the model gains help, and where they do not

Figma's own numbers show real progress. Typical tasks are about 20% faster than in beta. Against expert designers in head-to-head testing, the new agent beats or matches the previous production agent 62% of the time. User ratings are 33% higher and users undo the agent's work 60% less often.

Those are Figma's internal results, measured on its own tasks, and the post itself says one evaluation is only one input among many. They show the model improving. They do not show your library behaving.

The post also names errors that remain, such as overlapping icons and text and clipped arrows. These are visual faults that structure alone will not prevent. They are why Figma's agent takes a screenshot of its own output and iterates on mismatches, and why you should still look at what it makes.

A better model helps everyone equally. An agent-ready file helps only you, and it makes each model upgrade mean less cleanup.

A one-week plan for a production library

Do this on a duplicate of your library, as Figma recommends, never on the live file.

On day one, audit variables. Find every fill, stroke, radius and spacing value in your core components that is not bound to a variable. Start with the 20 most used components.

On day two, rename. Replace generic layer names in those components, and align component and property names with the code names your engineers use.

On day three, check auto layout in your cards, forms and navigation. Every container should express direction, gap and padding rather than fixed positions.

On day four, add descriptions to components that have states or usage rules. Keep each to two or three lines.

On day five, write your first skill using the template above and run five fixed prompts against the duplicate, such as a settings page, a card variant, a form with errors, an empty state and a mobile screen. Record how many values were hardcoded and how many components were faked with frames. Run the same five after any change to the skill.

That count is your metric. If you already test your system visually, the method in AI agent visual regression testing for design systems pairs well with it, since it catches the clipped and overlapping output Figma admits still happens.

If the first week shows twenty hardcoded values, you have learned something real about your library, and you learned it before the agent shipped the same flaws into a product. That is the point. The agent is a mirror, and it is more honest than a design review.
