title: Beyond a Successful Update: Validating Workspace Continuity and Local Data Persistence in Tables
description:
An engineering investigation into application lifecycle reliability, DynamoDB connectivity, and persistent local development environments.

Introduction

A software update is generally considered successful when the new version installs correctly and the application launches without errors. However, for stateful desktop development tools, this is only one dimension of reliability.

The more important question is whether users can resume their existing workflows without losing context, configuration, or access to the data they depend on.

This becomes particularly relevant for database management applications, where a single working session may involve multiple AWS connections, active DynamoDB tables, saved query configurations, and containerized development services.

I investigated these concerns using Tables by ServerlessCreed, a desktop application for managing Amazon DynamoDB.

The investigation followed an application upgrade from v3.3.37 to v3.3.42, with additional verification of local database persistence through a controlled Docker container restart.

The objective was to examine how different layers of application and database state behave across lifecycle transitions, and to understand what constitutes meaningful evidence of reliability.

1. Why Application Updates Are a State Management Problem

An application update is not simply a replacement of executable files.

Desktop applications frequently maintain state outside their installation directories, including user preferences, cached workspace information, connection profiles, and locally persisted configuration.

A database management application introduces an additional layer of complexity because the interface interacts with data stored in external systems.

To evaluate update behavior accurately, I separated the environment into three distinct layers.

Application and Workspace State

This includes open table tabs, query drafts, saved queries, and user preferences.

These elements preserve the context of an active working session. Their disappearance may not affect the underlying database, but it can still significantly disrupt developer productivity.

Connection and Authentication State

AWS connection profiles represent the application's ability to access a configured cloud environment.

A profile remaining visible after an update does not necessarily prove that authentication and authorization continue to work.

A functional database request provides stronger evidence of connection continuity.

Database and Storage State

DynamoDB data stored in AWS exists independently of the desktop application's installation.

DynamoDB Local introduces a different persistence model because its database files depend on the configured local storage environment.

Consequently, verifying that a desktop application opens successfully cannot establish that local database records remain durable.

This separation became the foundation of the investigation.

2. Establishing a Reproducible Pre-Update Baseline

The initial environment used Tables v3.3.37 on Windows, connected to an AWS environment in the ap-south-1 Region.

The application was configured to receive updates through Microsoft Store, with automatic downloads enabled.

Before upgrading, I documented the existing workspace and selected recognizable state markers that could be examined later.

Two DynamoDB tables were open:

  • TC-W8-Sandbox
  • SportsEquipment

The TC-W8-Sandbox table also served as the reference environment for query-state verification.

Within the query interface, I entered the test value:

UI-TEST-001

I retained this value in the filter field, navigated between tables, and restarted the application.

The value remained available after navigation and restart, establishing that this particular query-interface state could persist under normal application lifecycle operations.

This baseline was important because persistence claims require knowledge of what existed before the operation being evaluated.

Without a recorded initial state, a post-update observation cannot reliably establish whether data was retained, recreated, or absent from the beginning.

Figure 1 — Application version and update configuration

Figure 2 — Pre-update DynamoDB workspace

3. Evaluating the Application Upgrade

The application subsequently moved from v3.3.37 to v3.3.42 through its Microsoft Store update channel.

After the update, I navigated to:

Settings → Preferences & Lifecycle → Updates

The interface reported version 3.3.42, confirming the updated application build.

Rather than treating the version change as the end of the test, I returned to the previously configured workspace to examine its operational state.

The existing table tabs remained accessible, and the query configuration was still available.

I also located the saved query PLAT-Update-Test, associated with TC-W8-Sandbox, through the application's command palette.

This provided evidence that the tested workspace context remained usable after the version transition.

Functional Verification of AWS Connectivity

Connection continuity required a separate check.

The existing AWS connection was available after the update, but I did not rely solely on the presence of its profile in the interface.

I executed a DynamoDB Scan operation against the test table.

The request completed successfully.

From a technical perspective, this established that the application could still communicate with DynamoDB and perform the tested read operation using the configured connection.

It did not establish unrestricted access to every DynamoDB API operation, nor was such a claim necessary.

The relevant finding was that the existing AWS workflow remained functional following the application upgrade.

Figure 3 — Updated application build

The application reported the newer version while retaining the Microsoft Store update channel.

Figure 4 — Workspace continuity after the update

The previously configured workspace remained accessible, and an authorized database read completed successfully.

4. Investigating the Local Development Runtime

The next part of the investigation focused on the local development environment.

Tables provides access to DynamoDB Local and related development services, allowing database workflows to be exercised against a local endpoint.

The DynamoDB Local endpoint was configured as:

http://localhost:8000

The AppSync Simulator endpoint was configured as:

http://127.0.0.1:8080/graphql

These services introduce dependencies that exist outside the desktop application's own process.

Distinguishing Runtime Availability from Application Failure

During testing, Tables displayed a warning indicating that Docker Desktop was installed but not running.

At that point, the local services were unavailable.

This observation highlighted an important diagnostic distinction.

A desktop application may be functioning correctly while an external runtime dependency is stopped.

After starting Docker Desktop, I was able to bring DynamoDB Local online and access the local development environment.

The application's service-health indicators made it possible to distinguish between the state of Tables itself and the state of the services it manages or connects to.

This distinction is particularly valuable during upgrade investigations because environmental failures can otherwise be incorrectly attributed to application changes.

Figure 5 — Local development environment

5. Understanding Persistence in Containerized Databases

The most technically significant part of the local development investigation involved database persistence.

Containerized services introduce an important separation between the lifecycle of a running process and the lifecycle of its stored data.

Stopping a container terminates its running process, but it does not inherently delete the container's writable filesystem or attached persistent storage.

Removing or recreating a container introduces different considerations, particularly when database files are not stored in a durable location.

For DynamoDB Local, the effective persistence behavior depends on how the database process is configured and where its database files are written.

Inspecting the Storage Configuration

The Local Development interface identified the storage mode as:

Persistent

The DynamoDB Local runtime configuration also exposed the following values:

InMemory: false
Database path: /home/dynamodblocal/data
SharedDb: true

These details provided useful information about the configured database runtime.

InMemory: false indicated that DynamoDB Local was not configured to operate exclusively as an in-memory database.

The database path identified the location used for its local storage.

SharedDb: true indicated that the runtime was configured to use a shared database file rather than separate files for different credential and Region combinations.

However, configuration values alone do not prove data durability.

To validate persistence behavior, I needed a known record that could be examined before and after a controlled service restart.

6. Building a Controlled Persistence Test

I created a dedicated DynamoDB Local table named:

PLAT-Local-Test

The table used a String partition key:

PK

I then inserted a record with the following key:

{
  "PK": "PLAT-TEST-001"
}

The table was created specifically in DynamoDB Local, keeping this experiment separate from the AWS-hosted DynamoDB tables.

After insertion, the local table was active and the record was available through the application's data interface.

This established a concrete persistence fixture: a known table containing a known item.

Restarting the Existing Container

With the test record established, I stopped the DynamoDB Local container through Docker Desktop.

I then started the same container again without deleting or recreating it.

This was an intentional constraint.

The purpose was to investigate whether database state survived a routine service restart, not whether data would survive container removal, volume replacement, or a fresh environment installation.

Once the service returned to its running state, I reopened the local table in Tables and inspected its contents.

The table remained accessible, and the record identified by PLAT-TEST-001 was still present.

This demonstrated that the configured DynamoDB Local environment retained the tested record across the container stop/start lifecycle.

Interpreting the Result Correctly

The observation supports a specific conclusion: the existing DynamoDB Local container retained the test data through a controlled restart.

It does not independently establish durability across container deletion, storage-volume removal, or application reinstallation.

It also does not retroactively prove that local records created before the v3.3.37-to-v3.3.42 upgrade survived that update, because an equivalent pre-upgrade local data fixture had not been established.

Maintaining this distinction is essential to technically defensible reliability testing.

7. What the Investigation Revealed About Reliability Boundaries

The combined observations revealed several important aspects of desktop application reliability.

Workspace Persistence Is Not Database Persistence

The retention of query drafts, saved queries, and open tabs demonstrates continuity at the application-workspace level.

The retention of a DynamoDB Local record demonstrates continuity at the database-storage level.

These are related user expectations, but they involve different components and failure modes.

Connection Visibility Is Not Connection Functionality

An existing AWS profile may remain visible even when its credentials are invalid or the underlying permissions have changed.

Executing an actual DynamoDB request provides a more meaningful operational check than inspecting the interface alone.

Service Restart Is Not Storage Reinitialization

A Docker container restart and a database reset are fundamentally different operations.

Testing them interchangeably can produce misleading conclusions about data durability.

Recovery Requires Its Own Test Design

The successful version transition and container restart provide evidence about normal lifecycle behavior.

Interrupted updates, rollback operations, and application reinstallation introduce different risks.

Evaluating those scenarios responsibly requires an approved recovery procedure, a controlled environment, and a reliable baseline from which to restore application and database state.

These scenarios should be treated as separate engineering investigations rather than assumed consequences of a successful upgrade.

8. Designing Stronger Lifecycle Verification

This exercise also helped clarify how I would design a more comprehensive persistence investigation.

A stronger upgrade test would establish a complete state fixture before the application version changes.

That fixture would include known local database records, saved query definitions, active workspace tabs, connection configuration, and selected application preferences.

Each element would have an identifiable expected state.

Following the update, the verification would compare those elements against the original baseline.

For local databases, record-level comparison would provide stronger evidence than simply confirming that a table exists.

For application state, both persistence and functional usability would matter.

For example, a saved query appearing in a list is useful evidence, but successfully reopening and executing it would provide additional confidence.

Similarly, a local database service displaying a healthy status is not equivalent to verifying that its expected records remain accessible.

The central principle is to make every reliability claim traceable to a specific observation.

Conclusion

The reliability of a desktop database tool cannot be evaluated solely by whether a new application version launches successfully.

It must also be considered in terms of the developer workflows that continue afterward.

During this investigation of Tables by ServerlessCreed, the upgrade from v3.3.37 to v3.3.42 retained the tested workspace context, including open table tabs, query state, and usable AWS connectivity.

A separate Docker lifecycle experiment demonstrated that a known DynamoDB Local record remained available after restarting the existing database container.

Together, these observations reinforced an important engineering principle:

Application continuity, connection functionality, and database durability are separate reliability properties that require independent verification.

Understanding those boundaries makes upgrade investigations more precise, prevents unsupported data-loss conclusions, and provides a stronger foundation for evaluating future application lifecycle changes.

For QA engineers working with database development tools, the goal is not simply to confirm that software still runs. It is to establish, through reproducible evidence, which parts of a developer's working environment remain dependable as the software evolves.

Application: Tables by ServerlessCreed

Versions evaluated: 3.3.37 → 3.3.42

Technologies: Amazon DynamoDB, DynamoDB Local, Docker Desktop, Microsoft Store, AWS

Application download: https://tables.serverlesscreed.com/downloads

title: Mastering Next.js File-Based Routing (App Router)
description:
Hello folks, as promised, back with the blog of Next.js file-based routing.

Next.js has one of the most elegant routing systems in the React ecosystem: file-system based routing. Instead of manually declaring routes in a configuration file, the structure of your folders and files is the routing structure. This blog focuses exclusively on the modern App Router (app/ directory) and covers every major routing convention in detail.

Introduction – File-Based Routing & App Router vs Pages Router

Traditionally, you often write something like:

router.get('/blog/:slug', handler)

Next.js flips this model. You create a folder named blog, put a file inside it, and the route appears automatically.

There are two routing systems in Next.js:

  • Pages Router (pages/ directory) – the original system (still fully supported).
  • App Router (app/ directory) – introduced in Next.js 13, built on React Server Components, nested layouts, streaming, and more powerful conventions.

This guide uses the App Router, which is the recommended approach for all new projects.

Core Mental Model

Three rules govern almost everything:

  1. Folders = Route Segments

    Every folder inside app/ becomes a route segment in the URL.

  2. page.tsx (or page.jsx) makes a route public

    A folder without a page.tsx is not a public route. It can still contain nested layouts, components, or other files.

  3. Special files create UI and behavior

    • layout.tsx → shared UI that wraps the segment and all children (can be global or nested)
    • loading.tsx → loading UI
    • error.tsx → error boundary
    • not-found.tsx → 404 UI (can be global or nested)

Folders + Files = URLs

With these rules in mind, let’s explore each routing pattern.

1. Static Routes + Nested Static Routes

Folder structure

app/
├── page.tsx                        → /
├── about/
│   └── page.tsx                    → /about
├── blog/
│   └── page.tsx                    → /blog
└── dashboard/
    ├── page.tsx                    → /dashboard
    ├── analytics/
    │   └── page.tsx                → /dashboard/analytics
    └── settings/
        ├── page.tsx                → /dashboard/settings
        └── profile/
            └── page.tsx            → /dashboard/settings/profile

Static routes are the simplest form: the folder name becomes the exact URL segment. Nesting folders creates nested URLs. Each level can optionally have its own layout.tsx that only wraps that segment and its children.

Key technical notes

  • The root app/page.tsx is required for the homepage (/).
  • A folder without page.tsx is invisible to the router (great for colocation).
  • Layouts nest automatically: root layout → dashboard layout → settings layout.

2. Dynamic Routes (Single Segment)

Folder structure

app/
└── blog/
    ├── page.tsx                    → /blog
    └── [slug]/
        └── page.tsx                → /blog/:slug

A dynamic segment is created by wrapping the folder name in square brackets: [slug]. The value of slug is extracted from the URL and passed to your page.

Accessing the parameter (server component)

// app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx
export default async function Page({
  params,
}: {
  params: Promise<{ slug: string }>;
}) {
  const { slug } = await params;
  return <h1>Blog Post: {slug}</h1>;
}

Key technical notes

  • In recent Next.js versions, params is a Promise — you must await it.
  • Client Components can use the useParams() hook from next/navigation.
  • Use generateStaticParams() to pre-render known dynamic paths at build time (covered later).

3. Multiple Dynamic Route Segments

Folder structure

app/
└── shop/
    └── [category]/
        └── [productId]/
            └── page.tsx            → /shop/:category/:productId

You can stack as many dynamic segments as you need. Each [param] is independent and appears in the params object.

Example

URL params
/shop/electronics/iphone-15 { category: "electronics", productId: "iphone-15" }
/shop/clothing/nike-air { category: "clothing", productId: "nike-air" } 
export default async function Page({
  params,
}: {
  params: Promise<{ category: string; productId: string }>;
}) {
  const { category, productId } = await params;
  // fetch product data using both values
}

You can freely mix static and dynamic segments (e.g. /shop/[category]/reviews/[reviewId]).

4. Catch-All Routes

Folder structure

app/
└── docs/
    └── [...slug]/
        └── page.tsx                → /docs/*  (one or more segments)

The [...slug] syntax (ellipsis inside brackets) captures one or more segments as an array. This is introduced because when we don't know about the depth of level in multiple dynamic routes then this is the best option to choose.

URL params.slug
/docs/getting-started ['getting-started']
/docs/api/auth ['api', 'auth']
/docs/a/b/c/d ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']

Important: A regular catch-all does not match the parent path /docs. That would 404 unless you also have a docs/page.tsx.

export default async function Page({
  params,
}: {
  params: Promise<{ slug: string[] }>;
}) {
  const { slug } = await params;
  return <div>Path: {slug.join(' / ')}</div>;
}

5. Optional Catch-All Routes

Folder structure

app/
└── docs/
    └── [[...slug]]/
        └── page.tsx                → /docs  AND  /docs/*

Double square brackets [[...slug]] make the catch-all optional. It now also matches the route with zero additional segments means it solves the problem of catch-all-routes also.

URL params.slug
/docs undefined
/docs/getting-started ['getting-started']
/docs/api/auth ['api', 'auth']

This pattern is extremely useful for documentation sites, knowledge bases, or any UI that needs a root view plus arbitrary depth.

Always handle the undefined case in your component.

Important: Don't ever use both the catch all routes and optional catch all routes together not under the same folder. Either use first one or the second one; but not together under same folder.

export default async function Page({
  params,
}: {
  params: Promise<{ slug?: string[] }>;
}) {
  const { slug } = await params;
  return <div>Path: {slug ? slug.join('/') : '(no slug — matched /page itself)'}</div>;
}

6. Route Groups (+ Private Folders)

Folder structure

app/
├── (marketing)/
│   ├── page.tsx                    → /
│   ├── about/
│   │   └── page.tsx                → /about
│   ├── pricing/
│   │   └── page.tsx                → /pricing
│   └── layout.tsx                  // marketing layout only
├── (shop)/
│   ├── products/
│   │   └── page.tsx                → /products
│   ├── cart/
│   │   └── page.tsx                → /cart
│   └── layout.tsx                  // shop layout only
├── (dashboard)/
│   ├── layout.tsx                  // dashboard layout
│   └── settings/
│       └── page.tsx                → /settings
└── layout.tsx                      // root layout

Route groups are created by wrapping a folder name in parentheses: (marketing). The parentheses and the name inside them never appear in the URL. They exist purely for organization and for applying different layouts to different sets of routes. If we don't want to show the folder structure in the route/URL itself, then we will use this.

Common use cases

  • Separate marketing pages from authenticated dashboard pages
  • Apply different root layouts
  • Organize by team or feature without polluting the URL

Private folders (related convention)

Prefix any folder with an underscore (_components, _lib, _utils). These folders and everything inside them are completely ignored by the router — perfect for colocation.

Important rules

  • Two different route groups cannot resolve to the same URL path (build-time error).
  • Navigating between routes that use different root layouts triggers a full page load.

Practical Tips

Mixing conventions

You can combine everything freely:

app/
└── (shop)/
    └── [category]/
        └── [...slug]/
            └── page.tsx

generateStaticParams

For dynamic and catch-all routes you often want static generation:

// app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx
export async function generateStaticParams() {
  const posts = await getAllPosts();
  return posts.map((post) => ({ slug: post.slug }));
}

Layouts interaction

  • Layouts wrap their children and persist across navigations within the same segment.
  • A layout inside a route group only applies to routes inside that group.
  • Root layout is required (unless you intentionally create multiple root layouts via route groups).

Common pitfalls

  • Forgetting that a folder needs a page.tsx to be public.
  • Conflicting paths between two route groups.
  • Not awaiting params in newer Next.js versions.
  • Expecting a regular catch-all [...slug] to match the parent path.
  • Putting business logic or shared components directly in route folders instead of using private folders or a top-level components/ directory.

Conclusion & Further Reading

File-based routing in the App Router is both powerful and surprisingly simple once the core mental model clicks: folders define segments, page.tsx makes them public, and special naming conventions ([], [...], [[...]], ()) give you dynamic behavior and organization.

Master these patterns and you can model almost any URL structure cleanly while keeping your project organized and performant.

Official documentation

  • Defining Routes
  • Dynamic Route Segments
  • Route Groups
  • Project Structure

Happy routing!

title: Use real superscript markup when you control the page
description:
The raised 2 in x² is a different Unicode character from the plain 2 in x2. That makes it convenient in a plain-text message. It also means a search for the exact string x2 does not necessarily find it.

When I write HTML, I prefer markup where the text represents an exponent or an index:

<p>The area is x<sup>2</sup>.</p>
<p>The molecule is H<sub>2</sub>O.</p>

The browser can position the numbers while the source keeps ordinary digits. For longer equations, use the notation your document or platform already supports. Decorative Unicode has gaps in its alphabet, and font coverage can differ between devices.

If a chat box takes plain text, it can be useful to copy a raised digit. For example, type 2 into a Unicode superscript tool and place the resulting ² after a normal x. The same idea works for the lower digit in H₂O. Check the result in the app where you will paste it.

Disclosure: I work on the Small Text Studio superscript generator, which shows supported and unchanged characters. You can use it to inspect the output before copying a character.

title: Refunded or disputed, but the customer still has access? Your Stripe webhook only listens for the purchase
description:
A lot of paywalls handle exactly one Stripe event. checkout.session.completed arrives, the handler sets paid = true, and that's the end of it. Nothing in the code ever sets it back.

So a refund goes out, or a customer's bank opens a dispute, or a subscription ends, and the database still says paid. The app keeps the door open for someone who's no longer paying. This post covers the events that should take access away, how to tie them back to the right user, and the edge cases worth deciding on up front. Every claim links to the doc it comes from (see Sources at the end).

How to tell if access is one-way

  1. Open the webhook endpoint in the Stripe Dashboard and look at the events it's subscribed to. If the list is only checkout or payment-success events, Stripe never tells the app about refunds or disputes.
  2. Refund a test-mode purchase, then reload the app as that test user. If the paid content is still there, access only ever goes one direction.
  3. Search the handler for charge.refunded, charge.dispute.created and customer.subscription.deleted. If none of them appear, nothing revokes access.

The events that should take access away

From Stripe's list of event types:

  • charge.refunded: "Occurs whenever a charge is refunded, including partial refunds."
  • charge.dispute.created: "Occurs whenever a customer disputes a charge with their bank."
  • charge.dispute.closed: "Occurs when a dispute is closed and the dispute status changes to lost, warning_closed, or won." This is the one to use for giving access back after a dispute is won.
  • refund.failed: "Occurs whenever a refund has failed." Stripe's refund docs say that in that case "you need to arrange an alternative way to provide your customer with a refund."

For subscriptions, Stripe's cancellation docs describe customer.subscription.deleted as "Sent when a subscription is canceled. The cancellation can result from a direct call to delete the subscription or when a subscription with cancel_at_period_end: true reaches the end of its billing period."

Setting cancel_at_period_end doesn't end anything yet. The same docs say customer.subscription.updated is "Sent for any subscription update, including when cancel_at_period_end is set to true." The customer has paid through the end of the period, so keep access until the deleted event arrives.

Each of these has to be added to the endpoint's event list, in the Dashboard or through enabled_events on the endpoint. Stripe only sends the events an endpoint is subscribed to. Stripe's refund docs also recommend that you "verify webhook signatures" for these events, which matters because the same handler that revokes access also grants it.

Map the event back to the user

Refund and dispute events carry a Charge or a Dispute, not the Checkout Session that granted access. Both point back to the payment:

  • On the Charge object, payment_intent is the "ID of the PaymentIntent associated with this charge."
  • On the Dispute object, payment_intent is the "ID of the PaymentIntent that’s disputed," and charge is the "ID of the charge that’s disputed."

The Checkout Session object has a payment_intent field too. So at fulfillment time, store the session's payment_intent next to the user. Revoking then becomes a single lookup.

// Inside a verified webhook handler (signature already checked on the raw body)
switch (event.type) {
  case 'checkout.session.completed': {
    const s = event.data.object;
    await grantAccess(s.client_reference_id, { paymentIntent: s.payment_intent });
    break;
  }
  case 'charge.refunded': {
    const charge = event.data.object;
    // refunded is true only for a full refund; decide what a partial refund means
    if (charge.refunded) await revokeByPaymentIntent(charge.payment_intent, 'refunded');
    break;
  }
  case 'charge.dispute.created':
    await revokeByPaymentIntent(event.data.object.payment_intent, 'disputed');
    break;
  case 'charge.dispute.closed':
    if (event.data.object.status === 'won') {
      await restoreByPaymentIntent(event.data.object.payment_intent);
    }
    break;
  case 'customer.subscription.deleted':
    await revokeBySubscription(event.data.object.id, 'canceled');
    break;
}
return new Response('ok', { status: 200 });

Decide the edge cases before they happen

Partial refunds. charge.refunded fires for those too. On the Charge, refunded means "Whether the charge has been fully refunded. If the charge is only partially refunded, this attribute will still be false," and amount_refunded holds the refunded amount. Pick a rule, such as revoking only on a full refund, and write it down.

Inquiries. Stripe's dispute docs explain that "Some card networks initiate a preliminary phase before creating a formal dispute," which Stripe calls an inquiry, and that in the API an inquiry's status "is prepended with warning," as in warning_needs_response. The same page notes the bank often asks "because the cardholder doesn’t recognize the transaction description." To avoid cutting off a customer over a confusing statement line, revoke on formal dispute statuses and leave warning_ statuses alone.

Disputes that are won. When charge.dispute.closed arrives with status won, restore access, as in the switch above.

Things that make revocation fail quietly

  • Access granted by the success page. If /success unlocks access on its own, a webhook can't keep it revoked. Grant from the webhook and have the page only read the database.
  • Duplicate deliveries. The same event can arrive more than once, so revoke and restore should be safe to run twice.
  • An endpoint Stripe can't reach. Then neither grants nor revokes arrive at all.

Clean up the customers who already kept access

Stripe's refund docs point to a Dashboard view of refunded payments. To catch disputes as well, page through charges with the API and check refunded and disputed ("Whether the charge has been disputed") on each one. Revoke each match with the same function the webhook now calls.

Checklist

  • [ ] The endpoint subscribes to charge.refunded, charge.dispute.created, charge.dispute.closed and customer.subscription.deleted
  • [ ] Fulfillment stores the Checkout Session's payment_intent with the user
  • [ ] Revoke runs only for a full refund, or a written rule covers partial ones
  • [ ] warning_ inquiry statuses are handled on purpose
  • [ ] cancel_at_period_end keeps access until customer.subscription.deleted
  • [ ] A won dispute restores access
  • [ ] Past refunds and disputes have been cleaned up

None of this helps if Stripe can't reach the endpoint in the first place. WebhookProof's free checker sends 3 harmless test requests to a webhook URL you own and reports whether Stripe can reach it and whether unsigned requests are rejected. The full guide, with the revoke logic and a cleanup approach, is here: Refunded or disputed Stripe payment still has access?

WebhookProof is an independent tool, not affiliated with Stripe, Inc. Quotes are from the linked documentation as read on 2026-11-04.

Sources

  • Stripe API, Types of events (charge.refunded, charge.dispute.created, charge.dispute.closed, refund.failed): https://docs.stripe.com/api/events/types
  • Stripe, Refund and cancel payments (alternative refund when refund.failed, verify webhook signatures, Dashboard view of refunded payments): https://docs.stripe.com/refunds
  • Stripe, Cancel subscriptions (customer.subscription.deleted, customer.subscription.updated when cancel_at_period_end is set): https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/cancel

title: Your chart library doesn't need a dark mode
description:
A Recharts chart can follow your page's dark mode with no theme state and no re-render: it names CSS variables, and the page declares them. This article shows the container that declares them, the trap that catches the hand-written version, and what still needs a line of your own.

The examples here are screenshots; they run live in the original article.

The problem

A chart library takes its colours as strings — stroke="#0ea5e9" — so nothing your page does to its own theme reaches the chart. Your cards turn dark and the chart keeps its light-mode lines, black axis labels and a white tooltip. The fixes land one bug at a time: axis labels in one project, tooltips in another, labels, series and tooltips in a third, all in the last three months. Recharts itself discussed a theming API through most of 2026 and is shipping one in its 3.11 pre-releases, marked experimental.

The usual fixes each cost something:

  • Pick the colour in React: stroke={theme === 'dark' ? '#38bdf8' : '#0ea5e9'}. Every chart reads the theme, so every chart re-renders on a switch, and a server render has to guess the theme.
  • Variables in a global stylesheet. This is the right mechanism, and it works until a section of the page has a theme of its own. More on that below.

The chart names variables, the container declares them 

import { ChartContainer } from '@box-kite/react/components/chart';
import { Line, LineChart, ResponsiveContainer } from 'recharts';

const months = [
  { month: 'Jan', revenue: 12, cost: 8 },
  { month: 'Feb', revenue: 18, cost: 9 },
];

export function Revenue() {
  return (
    <ChartContainer series={['revenue', 'cost']} height={30}>
      <ResponsiveContainer width="100%" height="100%">
        <LineChart data={months}>
          <Line dataKey="revenue" stroke="var(--color-revenue)" />
          <Line dataKey="cost" stroke="var(--color-cost)" />
        </LineChart>
      </ResponsiveContainer>
    </ChartContainer>
  );
}

ChartContainer is a Box that declares a numbered palette, --chart-1 to --chart-6, with a lighter twin of each under the dark theme. It also declares one --color-<series> per name, pointing at the palette in order. The chart names no colour at all, so its dark mode is the page's.

What a switch costs. We put a render counter in the chart component and flipped the page from light to dark: every line changed colour, and the chart rendered zero more times. The theme is a class on an ancestor, and the browser re-resolves the variables. React is not involved.

The rest of the chart

The palette covers the series. The grid, the axis labels and the tooltip are yours, and they work the same way: declare a variable on the container with vars, give it a dark value under theme, and name it in the chart.

import Box from '@box-kite/react';
import { ChartContainer } from '@box-kite/react/components/chart';
import { Area, AreaChart, CartesianGrid, ResponsiveContainer, Tooltip, XAxis, YAxis } from 'recharts';
import type { TooltipContentProps } from 'recharts';

const months = [
  { month: 'Jan', revenue: 12, cost: 8 },
  { month: 'Feb', revenue: 18, cost: 9 },
  { month: 'Mar', revenue: 15, cost: 11 },
  { month: 'Apr', revenue: 22, cost: 12 },
  { month: 'May', revenue: 26, cost: 13 },
  { month: 'Jun', revenue: 31, cost: 15 },
];

function ChartTooltip({ active, payload, label }: TooltipContentProps) {
  if (!active || !payload?.length) return null;

  return (
    <Box
      p={2}
      b={1}
      borderRadius={2}
      fontSize={12}
      bgColor="white"
      color="slate-900"
      borderColor="slate-200"
      theme={{ dark: { bgColor: 'slate-900', color: 'slate-100', borderColor: 'slate-700' } }}
    >
      <Box fontWeight={600}>{label}</Box>
      {payload.map((entry) => (
        <Box key={String(entry.dataKey)}>
          {entry.name}: {entry.value}
        </Box>
      ))}
    </Box>
  );
}

export function SalesChart() {
  return (
    <ChartContainer
      series={['revenue', 'cost']}
      vars={{ 'chart-grid': 'slate-200', 'chart-label': 'slate-500' }}
      theme={{ dark: { vars: { 'chart-grid': 'slate-800', 'chart-label': 'slate-400' } } }}
      height={60}
    >
      <ResponsiveContainer width="100%" height="100%">
        <AreaChart data={months}>
          <CartesianGrid stroke="var(--chart-grid)" strokeDasharray="3 3" vertical={false} />
          <XAxis dataKey="month" stroke="var(--chart-label)" fontSize={12} />
          <YAxis stroke="var(--chart-label)" fontSize={12} width={32} />
          <Tooltip content={ChartTooltip} />
          <Area dataKey="revenue" stroke="var(--color-revenue)" fill="var(--color-revenue)" fillOpacity={0.15} />
          <Area dataKey="cost" stroke="var(--color-cost)" fill="var(--color-cost)" fillOpacity={0.15} />
        </AreaChart>
      </ResponsiveContainer>
    </ChartContainer>
  );
}

The tooltip is the one part that needs a component. Recharts' default tooltip writes background-color: rgb(255, 255, 255) as an inline style, and we measured it staying white under a dark theme. A tooltip drawn as a Box takes theme like anything else on the page.

The trap in the hand-written version

The hand-written version is a stylesheet like this one:

:root {
  --chart-1: #0284c7;
  --color-revenue: var(--chart-1);
}
.dark {
  --chart-1: #7dd3fc;
}

When the dark class is on <html>, it works. Put it on a section instead (a dark sidebar, a dark card, a preview), and the revenue line stays the light-mode blue. A custom property is resolved where it is declared and inherited as a finished value: --color-revenue became #0284c7 on :root, and redeclaring --chart-1 further down never reaches it. In our probe the dark section's --chart-1 read #7dd3fc while the line's stroke read rgb(2, 132, 199), a light-mode blue.

ChartContainer declares --color-<series> on itself, below whatever theme is around it, so the alias resolves inside the section that chose the theme. Each theme rule is scoped to the subtree that declared it, so a light chart inside a dark page works the same way.

Colours of your own

A list of series takes the palette in order. A record names each series' paint, as anything fill takes, including a colour with an opacity:

import { ChartContainer } from '@box-kite/react/components/chart';
import { Bar, BarChart, ResponsiveContainer, XAxis } from 'recharts';

const weeks = [
  { week: 'W1', completed: 4, started: 3 },
  { week: 'W2', completed: 6, started: 2 },
  { week: 'W3', completed: 5, started: 4 },
  { week: 'W4', completed: 8, started: 2 },
];

export function Goals() {
  return (
    <ChartContainer
      series={{ completed: 'violet-600', started: 'violet-600/35' }}
      theme={{ dark: { vars: { 'color-completed': 'violet-400', 'color-started': 'violet-400/35' } } }}
      height={50}
    >
      <ResponsiveContainer width="100%" height="100%">
        <BarChart data={weeks}>
          <XAxis dataKey="week" stroke="currentColor" fontSize={12} />
          <Bar dataKey="completed" stackId="goals" fill="var(--color-completed)" />
          <Bar dataKey="started" stackId="goals" fill="var(--color-started)" />
        </BarChart>
      </ResponsiveContainer>
    </ChartContainer>
  );
}

A named paint is the same in both themes, so the dark value is a theme override, and we measured it winning. A paint the palette does not have ('tael-500') declares nothing. In development it warns, with the nearest token: Did you mean "teal-500"?

The honest limits

  • Every series still names its variable. Recharts takes one string per <Line> or <Area>, so var(--color-revenue) is written once per series. A variable nobody declared paints nothing: our grid disappeared until --chart-grid existed.
  • A canvas chart cannot read a variable. ctx.fillStyle = 'var(--chart-1)' is ignored (we checked), so a chart that draws on a canvas needs the resolved colour from getComputedStyle and a redraw on every theme change. This approach is for SVG charts.
  • The palette has six slots, and a seventh series wraps round to the first colour.
  • Theme rules need @scope: Chrome 118, Safari 17.4, Firefox 128 and later. Below that, the light values show.
  • Recharts' own themes are coming. Its experimental provider takes a theme object per chart. Its CSS-variable example uses the same --chart-1 names, declared by hand in a stylesheet. The container is that stylesheet as a prop.

Try it

  • Charts: the container, and the small charts that need no library at all.
  • Dark mode without the flash: the theme the chart follows.
  • npm install @box-kite/react recharts, and wrap one chart in <ChartContainer>.

Originally published on box-kite.dev. Box Kite is open source under MIT — if it is useful to you, a star on GitHub helps other people find it. Install it with npm install @box-kite/react.

title: 0.85ms writes: I re-ran Firenook's 40x claim on a 4-core VM
description:
0.85ms writes: I re-ran Firenook's 40x claim on a 4-core VM

Firenook claims its Rust Firebase emulators write 40x faster than Google's official ones: 5.1 ms median against 208.2 ms. I installed it, ran 300 writes, 100 reads, and 20 queries against it on a 4-vCPU VM — and then audited their benchmark data, because a 40x claim deserves a second look. My median write was 0.85 ms. The claim holds up, but not for the reason the headline suggests.

What I ran

Firenook 0.2.1, installed with npm install firenook (73 MB of node_modules, a 75 MB single Rust binary inside). Node 24.22.1, a 4-vCPU VM with 8 GB of RAM. A minimal project: firebase.json with Firestore, Auth, and Storage emulators, rules wide open. No functions, no listeners, no SDK — plain Firestore REST calls over loopback, sequential, one at a time. That is a lighter workload than theirs, and the difference matters: their numbers come from two hours of a real app's traffic with listeners and a Firestore-triggered function attached to every write.

single-doc writes:       n=300  median=0.85ms  p95=1.39ms  p99=1.77ms  max=4.90ms
single-doc reads:        n=100  median=0.34ms  p95=0.71ms  p99=4.36ms  max=4.36ms
orderBy n DESC limit 20: n=20   median=0.77ms  p95=1.18ms  max=1.18ms

Every write was a fresh document with three fields, acknowledged by the server before I timed the next one. The read-back check passed on all 300 documents, and every orderBy query returned exactly 20 documents in the right order. The write path is sub-millisecond at this scale — faster than Firenook's own published 5.1 ms, which makes sense: their 5.1 ms includes a triggered function and listener delivery on every write; mine includes neither.

The restart number matched theirs exactly

The claim I could check most precisely was the restart. Their docs say restarting with data kept takes 0.59–0.60 s, against 30.8 s for the official emulator. I loaded 2,000 documents (2.11 s, 947 docs/s), stopped the suite, and restarted with --keep-data:

cold start (empty store):  ready in 0.85s, tree RSS 99.8 MiB
loaded 2000 docs in 2.11s (947 docs/s); RSS after load 114.7 MiB
.firenook on disk: 2,169 KiB
stop: 0.16s, exit code 0
CLEAN restart with 2000 docs kept: ready in 0.59s
bulk docs after clean restart: 2000 (expected 2000)

0.59 s, all 2,000 documents present with correct values, clean stop. One wrinkle worth reporting: --keep-data refuses to run with --only firestore — it needs the firestore, auth, and storage services together, because the state receipt covers all three. I hit that error, added the other two emulators to firebase.json, and it worked. Also worth noting: my first "restart" measurement was bogus — the old process was still holding port 8080 and answered in 0.03 s. I killed it, re-ran clean, and got the 0.59 s above. If a benchmark number looks too good, check whether the thing you think you restarted actually restarted.

I audited their benchmark file, not just their blog post

Firenook publishes its benchmark methodology and the raw frozen data in the repo (docs/benchmarks.md, benchmarks/020-paired-acceptance.json). I checked the doc's headline numbers against the JSON:

write commit, median/p99:   official 208.2 / 279.8 ms, firenook 5.1 / 50.6 ms, n=5280
listener delivery:          official 209 / 258 ms,    firenook 11 / 60 ms,   n=60000
memory peak (PSS):          official 22.57 GiB,        firenook 2.11 GiB
resumed start, 3 runs:      firenook 0.59 / 0.59 / 0.59 s; official 30.8 / 31.7 / 30.67 s
stop with data saved:       firenook 0.05–0.26 s;      official 54–58 s (export)

Every figure in the doc matches the frozen JSON. The methodology is also unusually candid for a vendor benchmark: it names the host (Ryzen 5 3600, 64 GiB, NVMe), the workload (211,205 documents, 33,352 storage objects, 6.7 GB), the sample counts, and — the part I liked — where Firenook loses. Storage downloads were slower on Firenook (2.30 ms vs 2.12 ms median), and the doc says so. A benchmark page that prints its own loss is more credible than one that doesn't.

What I could not check

I did not run the official emulator side by side. This VM has no Java, 8 GB of RAM, and the official stack peaked at 22.57 GiB of emulator memory alone on their 64 GiB host — it would not have fit here. So the 208.2 ms official-emulator number is theirs, not mine. What I verified is the Firenook side of the comparison at my scale, plus the internal consistency of their published data. That is a weaker claim than a full A/B, and it is the honest one.

The other thing to keep in perspective: 40x is a ratio, and ratios flatter the faster side when the baseline is slow. The official emulator's 208 ms median write is the real story — it is a Java process that keeps everything in heap and only persists on export. Firenook being a native binary with data on disk explains most of the gap; the interesting number is not 40x but the absolute one: sub-millisecond writes and a 0.59-second restart with your data intact. On my VM, both of those reproduced.

Sources: firenook.dev; firenook-dev/firenook on GitHub (Apache-2.0, 64 stars, created 2026-09-09); docs/benchmarks.md and benchmarks/020-paired-acceptance.json in that repo. All latency, memory, and restart numbers above are from my own runs on 2026-11-06, firenook 0.2.1; the official-emulator figures are Firenook's published numbers, verified against their frozen benchmark JSON, not measured by me.

title: Show HN: Agentic Identity Broker, OAuth Delegation for AI Agents
description:
Hi HN, I’m Jan. I am co-author of the Agentic Identity Broker (AIB), an MIT-licensed OAuth2 broker in the Zalando Incubator, that lets a user give an AI agent scoped, revocable access to MCP services.

The broker solves three major challenges that are especially relevant in corporate environments: (A) Enable users to delegate workloads to agents without providing the agents all the user’s tokens. (B) Connect fragmented identity and authorization systems. (C) Centralize tool approvals and audit logging.

We built AIB to fill an infrastructure gap in our own agent platform. At this moment in time, IETF working groups are still finalizing standards for agent identity, and vendors are still turning the necessary infrastructure into off-the-shelf products. We needed that infrastructure today.

How it works: the user consents once per agent and service. The broker stores the third-party tokens encrypted. At request time a gateway (e.g. Agentgateway) does RFC 8693 token exchange. Agents never see user tokens and MCP servers only implement tools and don’t need to care about all the OAuth 2.1 plumbing.

AIB is v0.1 and runs in production, bringing together hundreds of our agents with dozens of internal and external MCP servers.

To try it locally: clone the repo, run "just compose-up-detached".

The current features focus on on-behalf-of (OBO) use cases, where human actors delegate to agents. Next we are looking to also support headless agents, where agents are invoked by machines. Intent-based authorization is yet another package on our roadmap. If you’ve built either, or have feedback on the UI/UX, I’d like to hear from you!

title: Building a MapleStory-style game UI in Unity UI Toolkit
description:
Play Sakura Shrine in your browser · Cascade Lite (free): https://u3d.as/45jX · Cascade Pro: https://u3d.as/45jT

Sakura Shrine is a small 2D side-scroller I built to see whether Unity's UI Toolkit can carry a whole game interface: a HUD, scroll windows, an inventory, a shop, skills, a quest, character select, and a level-up moment that feels like a reward. It's a showcase for Cascade, my tween library for UI Toolkit (arrow keys, Z to attack, F1 for help).

Sakura Shrine is built with Cascade and is coming as a sample for it.

The style: an Edo shrine, not a computer window

I wanted the classic 2D MMO feel without copying anyone's art, so every window is a hand scroll: an indigo title band with a thin gold rule, washi paper, small gold corner brackets. Buttons are vermilion lacquer tags. The "+" on a stat is a tiny red seal. Labels are Japanese with English underneath. I designed every screen in Figma first, from components, and only then rebuilt them in UI Toolkit.

How much of it is Cascade

Almost everything that moves on screen is a Cascade tween: 104 Animate() chains, about 260 verbs. There is no Unity Animator, no USS transitions and no hand-written per-frame animation. Two things aren't Cascade: where the characters stand (that's the physics, which has to follow held keys every frame), and the drawings themselves.

Windows unroll from the title band down. Seals stamp in with a bounce and a tiny shake:

public static TweenSequence Stamp(VisualElement e, float from = 1.35f) =>
    e.Animate().ScaleTo(1f, 0.28f).From(from).Spring(SpringPreset.Bouncy)
     .Then().NudgeX(2f, 0.04f).Then().NudgeX(-2f, 0.04f).Then().NudgeX(0f, 0.04f);

One tween for the whole time of day

Press T and the shrine moves from morning to dusk to night. That's one Value tween. Every part of the scene reads the same number: the sky tint, the sun shafts, the lanterns, the fireflies and the moon.

_labelHost.Animate().Value(0f, 1f, 1.8f, v => Apply(Mathf.Lerp(from, to, v) % 3f)).Ease(Ease.InOutCubic);

Going from night back to morning continues forward through a dawn instead of rewinding through dusk.

The samurai: drawings by AI, motion by Cascade

UI Toolkit has no sprite animator, so the character is two layers. The drawings are 88 frames (idle, walk, jump, attack, dash, climb, cheer). Cascade decides which frame shows: a looping Value tween steps the frame index.

_el.Animate().Value(0f, _frames.Length, _frames.Length / (fps * rate), Show).Ease(Ease.Linear).Loop(LoopMode.Restart);

On top of the frames, Cascade adds the take-off stretch, the landing squash, the lunge, the dash lean, the hurt flash and the blink while you're invulnerable.

The frames took a few tries:

  1. A cut-out puppet (head, body, scarf, sword arm) from one illustration. The legs were one piece, so walking was a slide.
  2. Local video generation on my laptop. Green smears, colour blobs, 5 to 20 minutes per try. I deleted it.
  3. fal.ai, pay per clip (about $7 for the whole set): an image model redrew the samurai side-on, then an image-to-video model animated each move. A tracking shot gave a walk that stays centred; using the pose as the last frame too made the idle loop seamless.
  4. The backdrop bled into the clothes. A light grey background leaked into the cream hakama. A chroma-green backdrop with an exact key fixed it.
  5. The video model refused the hurt clips (the prompt described being hit). Getting hurt is a Cascade flash and recoil instead, and it reads better anyway.

Try it

Play Sakura Shrine in your browser. Cascade has a free Lite tier and a Pro tier on the Unity Asset Store:

  • Lite (free): https://u3d.as/45jX
  • Pro: https://u3d.as/45jT
  • Docs: https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/

The music and ambience were generated with ElevenLabs on fal; the sound effects are Kenney's (CC0). Fonts are OFL (Shippori Mincho, Zen Old Mincho, Yuji Syuku, Dela Gothic One).

title: AWS launches support for amortization of EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML
description:
AWS Data Exports for Cost and Usage Report (CUR) 2.0 and AWS Cost Explorer now amortize the upfront fee for Amazon EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML across the duration of each reservation. You can see the amortized cost of each instance launched into a Capacity Block and the amortized cost of unused capacity, so you can attribute your upfront fee to the workloads that used it and identify capacity that went unused.

Previously, a Capacity Block's upfront fee appeared as a single charge on the purchase date, making it difficult to see how that cost was spread across usage over the reservation. Now the amortized cost appears alongside your instance usage, so you can allocate GPU costs to the teams, projects, and applications that ran on the reserved capacity. You can also see what share of your reservation went unused and plan future Capacity Block purchases. In CUR 2.0, the amortized costs appear in the reservation_amortized_upfront_fee_for_billing_period, reservation_effective_cost columns, and reservation_net_effective_cost shows the amortized cost after discounts. In Cost Explorer, select the amortized cost view to see Capacity Block costs allocated for the reservation.

 Amortization for Capacity Blocks is available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions except the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions. To learn more, see the CUR 2.0 data dictionary and exploring your data using Cost Explorer.

title: Your Brain Was Not Designed for a Never-Ending Election
description:
What political uncertainty, algorithmic amplification, and nonstop news exposure do to our attention and emotional regulation.

The phone is in your hand before your feet touch the floor. It is the morning of November 4, and the screen has been busy overnight. One headline declares a winner. Another asks what happens next in a race nobody has called. Notifications stack up like unopened mail. One friend is posting confetti; another has written a paragraph that begins, "I genuinely cannot believe." A commentator is already explaining the consequences of decisions that have not yet been made.

You lock the screen, decide to make coffee, and unlock it again before the kettle is warm.

Wanting to know what happened is reasonable. But somewhere between the first check and the fifth, the purpose of checking quietly changes. The first look informs. The later ones are often less about learning than about quieting an uncertainty that refuses to settle.

The election may have an official ending. The information cycle does not.

Part 1 of this series examined how economic uncertainty occupies mental bandwidth before any loss arrives. This essay follows that thread into political uncertainty and an information environment that almost never goes quiet.

The Brain on an Unresolved Question

In a 2013 review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience, Dan Grupe and Jack Nitschke described anxiety as the anticipatory changes in feeling, thinking, and behavior that arise when a possible future threat is uncertain. Uncertainty is costly, they argued, because it undermines preparation.

Their Uncertainty and Anticipation Model of Anxiety identifies five processes that, when exaggerated, characterize clinical anxiety. Two are especially relevant here: heightened vigilance toward threat, and heightened reactivity to uncertainty itself, where not knowing becomes distressing in its own right.

The model describes clinical anxiety, and the authors stress that the same circuitry serves adaptive purposes. A voter refreshing results is not displaying a disorder, but the vocabulary is useful. A ballot count is exactly the kind of unresolved, consequential, largely uncontrollable question that anticipatory vigilance is built to monitor. Scanning feels like doing something. Often, it is the only thing available to do.

When the Coverage Becomes the Stressor

The most cited evidence that media exposure carries a psychological cost comes from crisis research. After the 2013 Boston Marathon bombings, E. Alison Holman, Dana Rose Garfin, and Roxane Cohen Silver surveyed a representative national sample of 4,675 U.S. adults two to four weeks after the attack. Adjusting for pre-bombing mental health and prior trauma exposure, they found that people reporting six or more daily hours of bombing-related media in the first week reported higher acute stress than people who had been at or near the event.

The study was cross-sectional and cannot establish that media caused the stress. And an election is not a terrorist attack; the finding offers a cautious signal about repeated exposure, not an equivalence.

There is also a complication. In a three-year longitudinal study (2019), Rebecca Thompson and colleagues found that the relationship runs in both directions: distress after one collective trauma predicted heavier media consumption around a later one, which in turn predicted more distress. Anxious people seek more news; more news can sustain anxiety.

Political news has been studied more directly. Brett Ford, Matthew Feinberg, and colleagues (2023) combined daily diary studies with experiments using political news clips. Daily politics reliably evoked negative emotions, which tracked with worse psychological and physical well-being, yet also predicted greater motivation to volunteer, donate, or protest. Participants who dampened those emotions through distraction or reappraisal felt better and were less motivated to act.

Political distress is not simply a malfunction. It is partly the fuel of participation.

The Feed Meets the Anxious Brain

Imagine two posts from accounts you follow: a plain update on certified results, and an emotionally charged prediction about what happens next. A chronological feed shows them in the order they were posted. A ranked feed weighs many signals, often including predicted engagement: how likely you are to click, reply, share, or linger. If the model expects the charged post to hold your attention, it can rise above the plain one, even if it arrived later. Objectives differ across platforms and change over time, so no single description fits every system.

Does emotional content travel further? Analyzing more than 560,000 tweets on polarizing issues, William Brady and colleagues reported in 2017 that each additional moral-emotional word was associated with roughly a 20 percent increase in retweets, mostly within like-minded networks. The size of that effect has been debated (Burton et al., 2021), and a 2025 preregistered meta-analysis by Brady's group, pooling 27 studies, put it closer to 12 percent per word. But retweets are human choices. More sharing is not proof that an algorithm amplified anything.

Direct tests of ranking are more mixed. A 2025 audit by Smitha Milli and colleagues found that, compared with a chronological feed of the same accounts, Twitter's engagement-based algorithm amplified emotionally charged, out-group hostile political content, the kind users said made them feel worse about the other side. Yet when Andrew Guess and colleagues, working with Meta, moved consenting Facebook and Instagram users to chronological feeds for three months during the 2020 election, time on the platforms fell substantially while polarization, political knowledge, and other key attitudes did not measurably change. In these studies, ranking changed what people saw and how long they stayed more clearly than it changed what they believed.

Emotions themselves can spread, modestly. In the 2014 Facebook "emotional contagion" study, Adam Kramer, Jamie Guillory, and Jeffrey Hancock reduced positive or negative posts in 689,003 users' feeds for a week; those shown fewer positive posts wrote slightly fewer positive words, and vice versa. The effects were tiny, the measure was word choice rather than felt emotion, and the journal issued an Editorial Expression of Concern about consent. My interpretation, not a finding, is that a feed's emotional texture may make anger look more universal than it is.

So the answer is conditional. When a system rewards engagement and a person is searching for certainty, the two can plausibly feed each other: uncertainty drives checking, checking produces engagement signals, and those signals can favor whatever is most arousing. The evidence supports pieces of that loop, not a complete causal chain.

The Developer's Paradox

Many DEV.to readers sit on both sides of this screen: we build notification pipelines and ranking services, then pick up phones running them.

We have become extraordinarily sophisticated at engineering information delivery without becoming equally sophisticated at protecting the attention that receives it.

This is not a story of villains. Engagement is often a reasonable proxy for relevance. The tension is that the easiest metrics to measure are not always what users would choose on reflection, the very gap Milli's team documented.

A few evidence-informed starting points:

Batch rather than drip. In a two-week field experiment with 237 smartphone users in India, Nicholas Fitz and colleagues found that delivering notifications three times a day lowered self-reported stress and inattention and lifted mood, though it also raised fear of missing out. Switching notifications off entirely raised anxiety without improving attention.
Rank by stated preferences, not only behavior. In Milli's analysis, ranking by what users said they valued reduced angry and hostile content, though it risked reinforcing existing views.
Make ranking legible and optional. A plain-language "why am I seeing this" and an easy chronological mode give people control. Their mental-health effects are unestablished; frame them as respect for agency, not therapy.

The Election Ends. The Uncertainty Changes Shape.

Back to November 4. Even when a race is called, its question gives way to new ones. Which policies will change? What happens to prices and jobs? How much of the commentary is evidence, and how much is forecasting dressed as fact?

Vigilance tries to resolve uncertainty by gathering information. But here lies the quiet mismatch at the center of the morning:

Much post-election uncertainty is not informational. It is temporal.

The answers depend on decisions not yet made and events not yet arrived. They will come on the schedule of legislatures, courts, and economies, not push alerts. Checking again cannot make them arrive sooner; it can only make the waiting louder.

None of this argues for looking away; Ford's research ties political discomfort to the willingness to act. Nor is any party or group of voters uniquely susceptible. These processes are human, not partisan. Responsibility is shared. Individuals choose when to check. Newsrooms choose how often to alert and how clearly to separate reporting from speculation. Platforms choose what their systems optimize for. Only the last two operate at scale.

The distinction worth protecting is between attention that serves understanding and attention that has become reflex. One informs a vote, a conversation, a decision. The other mostly keeps the question open.

Democracy asks citizens to pay attention. The attention economy asks them never to stop. Between those two demands lies a design problem, and many people reading this are equipped to work on it.

So the question for you: if you could change one default in the products you build, so that a person searching for certainty would be better served rather than merely more engaged, what would it be?

This is Part 2 of America Under Pressure: The Psychology of Uncertainty. Part 1 examined economic insecurity and anticipatory stress. Part 3 turns to the financial and emotional pressures of the holiday season.

References

Grupe, D. W., & Nitschke, J. B. (2013). Uncertainty and anticipation in anxiety: An integrated neurobiological and psychological perspective. Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 14(7), 488–501. https://doi.org/10.1038/nrn3524

Holman, E. A., Garfin, D. R., & Silver, R. C. (2014). Media's role in broadcasting acute stress following the Boston Marathon bombings. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 111(1), 93–98. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1316265110

Thompson, R. R., Jones, N. M., Holman, E. A., & Silver, R. C. (2019). Media exposure to mass violence events can fuel a cycle of distress. Science Advances, 5(4), eaav3502. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aav3502

Ford, B. Q., Feinberg, M., Lassetter, B., Thai, S., & Gatchpazian, A. (2023). The political is personal: The costs of daily politics. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 125(1), 1–28. https://doi.org/10.1037/pspa0000335

Brady, W. J., Wills, J. A., Jost, J. T., Tucker, J. A., & Van Bavel, J. J. (2017). Emotion shapes the diffusion of moralized content in social networks. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 114(28), 7313–7318. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1618923114

Burton, J. W., Cruz, N., & Hahn, U. (2021). Reconsidering evidence of moral contagion in online social networks. Nature Human Behaviour, 5(12), 1629–1635. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-021-01133-5

Brady, W. J., Rathje, S., Globig, L., & Van Bavel, J. J. (2025). Estimating the effect size of moral contagion in online networks: A pre-registered replication and meta-analysis. PNAS Nexus. https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgaf327

Milli, S., Carroll, M., Wang, Y., Pandey, S., Zhao, S., & Dragan, A. D. (2025). Engagement, user satisfaction, and the amplification of divisive content on social media. PNAS Nexus, 4(3), pgaf062. https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgaf062

title: Next.js 15 is a one-line upgrade. The breaking changes are in every file that reads a cookie.
description:
Upgrading to Next.js 15 is one line:

- "next": "14.2.15"
+ "next": "15.0.3"

The work is in the files that line affects. Three changes cause most of it.

1. Request APIs are async

cookies(), headers() and draftMode() now return promises.

  import { cookies } from "next/headers";

  export default async function Page() {
-   const theme = cookies().get("theme");
+   const theme = (await cookies()).get("theme");
    ...
  }

Next.js keeps a temporary synchronous fallback that logs a warning, which is kind for the upgrade and unkind for finding the problem: the code keeps working, and the warning sits in your logs.

In route params, the same applies: params and searchParams in pages and layouts are promises too.

2. fetch() isn't cached by default

In 14, fetch() in a server component was cached unless you opted out. In 15 it isn't cached unless you opt in:

await fetch(url, { cache: "force-cache" });

Nothing breaks. Some pages that were fast because of a cache you never meant to rely on get slower.

3. GET route handlers aren't cached

Same idea for app/**/route.ts: a GET handler is dynamic by default now. Add export const dynamic = "force-static" where you really wanted it cached.

Finding every affected file

The official codemod handles most of change 1:

npx @next/codemod@canary upgrade latest

Then search for what's left, because codemods miss dynamic patterns and helper functions:

grep -rnE "cookies\(\)|headers\(\)|draftMode\(\)" app src
grep -rn "fetch(" app src | grep -v "cache:"

And run your build and tests before you call it done. next build catches type errors from the async change if your project is typed.

This "the release notes say what changed, but not where it hits your code" step is the part Versyka automates: it reads the release notes against your repository, rewrites the affected calls and runs your checks before and after.

Have you moved to Next.js 15 yet? What broke first?
