title: Spring Data JPA Transactions and Queries
description:
The last but not least part of my series of articles on Spring Data JPA guide, employing best practices to help you keep the code base clean and avoid common mistakes.

This guide was initially written based on observations from a huge legacy project, and to promote good practices, I collected all the problems, systematized them, and shared them with my former colleagues. The guide is updated and completely rewritten to utilize the latest features of Spring Data JPA.

Other articles in the series:

  • Spring Data JPA Best Practices: Entity Design Guide
  • Spring Data JPA Best Practices: Repositories Design Guide

Some of the examples may seem obvious, but they’re not. It’s only from your experienced perspective. They’re real examples from the production code base.

Keep in mind that this series of articles explains the latest version of Spring Data JPA, so there may be nuances that I’ll highlight differently.

Table of contents

  • 1 Manual and automatic transaction management
    • 1.1 Using EntityManager to manage transactions
    • 1.2 Using TransactionTemplate
    • 1.3 Using @Transactional annotation
  • 2. Manual Querying
    • 2.1 Query vs TypedQuery
    • 2.2 Native Queries
    • 2.3 The Criteria API
    • 2.4 Passing parameters into queries
    • 2.5 Calling stored procedures
  • 3 Projection data with EntityManager
    • 3.1 Mapping entity to DTO with mapping libraries
    • 3.2 Mapping using a constructor
    • 3.3 Mapping with Tuple and Object Array
  • At the end

1 Manual and automatic transaction management

Imagine you need custom logic to work with your database, such as managing transactions, but Spring Data JPA repositories are insufficient for you. So what could you do? Spring Data JPA offers various approaches to achieve this.

1.1 Using EntityManager to manage transactions

You can use the JPA EntityManager together with EntityTransaction to manage transactions in Spring manually, as it provides low-level access to the persistence context and database operations, but managing transactions yourself quickly becomes error-prone and requires a lot of careful attention.

There is one more catch: you cannot use the injected EntityManager to start a transaction directly. In a typical Spring setup, that EntityManager is a container-managed proxy, and Spring expects you to use its own transaction management mechanisms instead.

Creating your own EntityManager from an EntityManagerFactory and using JPA’s EntityTransaction API is technically possible, but it bypasses Spring’s transaction infrastructure and is generally discouraged except in very special cases.

Let’s examine a small code example that utilizes the entity manager to manage transactions.

try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
    EntityTransaction tx = em.getTransaction();
    try {
        tx.begin();
        em.persist(new MyEntity());
        tx.commit();
    } catch (Exception e) {
        if (tx.isActive()) tx.rollback();
        throw e;
    }
}

Ouch! There is a lot of code. You should always use the entity manager factory to create an instance of the manager. Be careful, as it should be closed at the end of the logic. Additionally, ensure that commits and rollbacks are placed. That looks like a burden with different ways to shoot yourself in the foot.

I couldn’t recommend this approach to managing transactions, but real life has plenty of nuances, and for some reason, you may have to use it. Actually, I used it before (spoiler: it was a legacy project), as I had complex low-level logic to manage database transactions.

1.2 Using TransactionTemplate

Manual transaction management with an entity manager is a headache, but Spring @Transactional annotation too magical? There is a solution in the middle, it’s a TransactionTemplate.

This approach gives you the best of both worlds: you get programmatic control over exactly where a transaction starts and ends, but you let Spring handle commits, rollbacks, and closings of the entity manager.

The beauty here is that, unlike the manual approach, you can use the injected EntityManager. Because the transaction template interacts directly with Spring’s PlatformTransactionManager, it correctly binds the transaction to the current thread, allowing the standard container-managed proxy to function exactly as intended.

Look at this! The explicit try-catch-finally block is gone, along with the closing entity manager.

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class CustomTransactionService {

    private final PlatformTransactionManager txManager;
    private final EntityManager em;

    public void saveSafely() {
        TransactionTemplate tmplt = new TransactionTemplate(txManager);

        tmplt.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
            em.persist(new MyEntity()); 
            // No manual commit needed; it happens automatically on exit.
        });
    }
}

If your code inside the lambda throws a RuntimeException, the template automatically marks the transaction for rollback. If you need to roll it back based on a specific condition without throwing an exception, you can simply call status.setRollbackOnly().

This is the preferred way to write “custom” transaction logic in the Spring ecosystem. It keeps your code clean, concise, and integrated with the container’s lifecycle.

1.3 Using @Transactional annotation

Now we arrive at the most common approach. Why write code to manage transactions when you can just declare them with some Spring magic? This is the declarative style, and it is likely what I’ve seen in many Spring applications.

Instead of injecting managers or creating templates, you simply annotate your method (or class) with @Transactional. Spring’s AOP infrastructure takes over, wrapping your bean in a proxy that handles the begin, commit, and rollback logic for you.

It looks so simple, you focus entirely on business logic, and the container handles the atomicity.

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class UserService {

    private final UserRepository userRepository;

    @Transactional
    public void createUser(String name) {
        userRepository.save(new User(name));
        // If an unchecked exception (RuntimeException) is thrown here, 
        // the transaction rolls back automatically.
    }
}

However, there are many nuances. I’ll briefly explain some of them. However, the subject actually warrants a dedicated article.

Since it relies on Spring proxies, the interception only happens when the method is called from outside the bean. If you call a transactional method from another method within the same class (self-invocation), the proxy is bypassed, and no transaction is started.

@Service
public class TicketService {

    // 1. External caller invokes this method (Proxy intercepts here)
    public void bookBatch() {
        // 2. Inside the class, "this" refers to the raw Target object, not the Proxy.
        // 3. PROBLEM: Calling a @Transactional method from within the same class.
        // The Proxy is completely bypassed. No new transaction is started.
        reserveSeat(); 
    }

    @Transactional
    public void reserveSeat() {
        // Logic that EXPECTS a transaction, but won't get one 
        // if called from bookBatch().
        repo.save(new Ticket());
    }
}

In this scenario, if you call bookBatch() from a Controller, Spring intercepts that first call, but when bookBatch() calls reserveSeat(), it is a direct Java method call inside the instance. Spring’s proxy wrapper is sitting outside, unaware that reserveSeat() is running, so the spring transaction annotation is ignored.

What else? Spring Proxies cannot intercept private methods. If you do so, Spring will silently ignore your annotation without errors or warnings, which could lead to significant problems and make your app unreliable. The best way to mark this annotation is for public methods only.

One common bug in Spring transaction management is that transactions are always rolled back in the event of any exceptions. But it’s not, Spring only rolls back for RuntimeException (unchecked) with its child and Error. It does not rollback for checked exceptions (like IOException or your custom BusinessException if it extends from Exception).

Best practices here? Tell Spring what to rollback or extend your exceptions from RuntimeException and you’ll sleep well.

Using spring transactional annotation is a better approach than using an entity manager to manage transactions, as it eliminates the need for boilerplate code. However, you have to spend time learning all the nuances of using this annotation. Your education is a foundation for a better future for your applications.

2. Manual Querying

Repositories are fantastic, and they could close 90% of your work. But for the last 10 percent, you’ve to write some queries in a less abstract way. For example, you need a complex report, a specific join, or a database-specific function that Spring Data’s method naming convention just can’t handle. You could use mentioned before EntityManager.

One important note: EntityManager is a good way to query, but many tasks can be resolved with JPA repositories, as it provides a way to write native queries, and you don’t need to write boilerplate code as above. If your project has a convention for using an entity manager or other reasons, use it. Otherwise, give it a try to write queries with Spring Data JPA repositories.

2.1 Query vs TypedQuery

When you create a query in JPA, you have two choices. You can use the raw Query interface, or the generic TypedQuery. The raw Query interface returns Object or List<?>. It tells the compiler, “Trust me, I know what I’m doing.” This forces you to manually cast the result, which is a code smell and a potential runtime crash waiting to happen.

Just look at this example. There is casting data without verification, which could lead to different runtime problems; it’s better to avoid it.

public User getUserViaSimpleQuery(Long id) {
    // Returns a raw Query. We have to cast (User) manually.
    Query query = entityManager.createQuery(
        "SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.id = :id"
    );
    query.setParameter("id", id);
    return (User) query.getSingleResult();
}

Always prefer TypedQuery. It carries the type information with it, allowing you to delete those unchecked casts and let the compiler help you.

public User getUserViaTypedQuery(Long id) {
    // Pass the class type! Now we get TypedQuery<User>
    TypedQuery<User> query = entityManager.createQuery(
        "SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.id = :id", User.class
    );
    query.setParameter("id", id);
    return query.getSingleResult();
}

2.2 Native Queries

Sometimes JPQL isn’t enough. You need to use database-specific features (like CONNECT BY in Oracle or specific window functions). This is a place where createNativeQuery should be used. But there is a problem.

If you are fetching a whole Entity, you can still map it. But if you are fetching a single column (scalar value), things get messy. In legacy code, I saw that developers were assuming that if a database column is a number, Java would return a Long.

public Long getActiveVersionId() {
    Query query = entityManager.createNativeQuery(
        "select id from utl_rep_version_cfg where rownum = 1"
    );
    // DANGER: In Oracle, this returns BigDecimal. 
    // Casting (Long) throws ClassCastException!
    return (Long) query.getSingleResult(); 
}

If you run this against Oracle, your app will throw exceptions. The JDBC driver often maps numbers to BigDecimal or BigInteger, and you cannot cast an object of type BigDecimal directly to Long.

When dealing with native queries and scalars, treat the result as a generic Number. It may seem verbose, but this approach is safer than the previous one. Use it or not; it’s only your choice. However, I suggest learning a bit about JDBC data mapping, especially for your DBMS. For Oracle, you can refer to this documentation.

public Long getActiveVersionId() {
    Query query = entityManager.createNativeQuery(
        "select id from utl_rep_version_cfg where rownum = 1"
    );
    Object result = query.getSingleResult();
    // Safely convert whatever number the DB driver returns
    return result != null ? ((Number) result).longValue() : null;
}

2.3 The Criteria API

If TypedQuery is safe, the Criteria API adds more type safety. It allows you to build queries programmatically, protecting you from typical problems. However, I must admit that I dislike the criteria code because it is overly wordy. It’s hard to read. It looks like you are writing an abstract syntax tree instead of SQL. However, it is the only safe way to build dynamic queries where filters change at runtime.

Unfortunately, I have seen this a lot. One of the common security bugs is passing parameters with string concatenation. This approach leads to problems because user input is not sanitized properly and becomes part of the raw SQL query. To solve this, you could use named parameters and pass them safely, or you could also utilize the criteria API for this purpose.

The following example is not complex and highlights only the SQL injection issue. In the real world, developers often use a criteria API to build custom filters depending on user input.

// BAD: Concatenation logic that creates a wide-open security hole
public boolean login(String username, String password) {

    // DANGER: We are pasting user input directly into the query string.
    String hql = "SELECT count(u) FROM User u " + 
                 "WHERE u.username = '" + username + "'" + 
                 "AND u.password = '" + password + "'";

    Long count = (Long) entityManager.createQuery(hql).getSingleResult();
    return count > 0;
}

Let’s take a look at the alternative criteria: Yes, this is a lot of code, but we’ve introduced simple logic. If the password is missing, it shouldn’t be used in the WHERE clause. When using simple queries, string concatenation is required, which can lead to security issues. Here, you’re avoiding this, bringing more flexibility, but overall, it adds complexity to your codebase.

public boolean loginSafe(String username, String password) {
    CriteriaBuilder cb = entityManager.getCriteriaBuilder();
    CriteriaQuery<Long> cq = cb.createQuery(Long.class);
    Root<User> user = cq.from(User.class);

    // 1. We want to count users
    cq.select(cb.count(user));

    // 2. Build predicates dynamically
    List<Predicate> predicates = new ArrayList<>();
    predicates.add(cb.equal(user.get("username"), username));

    // Example of dynamic logic: simple IF statement, no string mess
    if (password != null) {
        predicates.add(cb.equal(user.get("password"), password));
    }

    cq.where(predicates.toArray(new Predicate[0]));

    // 3. Execute safely
    return entityManager.createQuery(cq).getSingleResult() > 0;
}

As I mentioned earlier, I don’t like this approach because it’s too wordy, contains a lot of code, and adds complexity. However, on the other hand, you could use string concatenation. It’s not pure evil. With a proper approach, there wouldn’t be a problem, but it’s a slippery road you’ve to avoid.

2.4 Passing parameters into queries

We have discussed how to write the queries, and in the example code, I used named parameters to pass parameters safely. This may seem trivial, but in a large codebase, differences in passing parameters can cause significant issues. There are generally two ways to pass parameters: positional (?) and named (:id). If you value your sanity and the time of your colleagues, you should have a strong preference for this approach. For me, it’s named parameters.

Positional parameters are a relic. They depend entirely on the order of arguments. If a developer comes along six months later and adds a new condition in the middle of your WHERE clause, the parameter indexes shift, and your code breaks – often silently or with confusing data errors.

Look at this fragile code. You need to mentally prepare to update and verify the passed parameters and their indexes. To me, it’s not as cool as it seems, as it leads to problems. If you could avoid problems from the start, it’s better to avoid them.

TypedQuery<User> q = em.createQuery(
    "SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.id = ?1 AND u.status = ?2",
    User.class
);

q.setParameter(1, id);
q.setParameter(2, Status.ACTIVE);

//and with native query
Query q = em.createNativeQuery(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ? AND status = ?",
    User.class
);
q.setParameter(1, id);
q.setParameter(2, "ACTIVE");

After seeing this example, I hope you find named parameters more effective, as they provide a clearer way to keep your code clean and maintainable. Just look at this example. This is kind of self-documented code. The parameter names tell us what they are, and we don’t need to concern ourselves with indexes for now.

TypedQuery<User> q = em.createQuery(
    "SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.id = :id AND u.status = :status",
    User.class
);

q.setParameter("id", id);
q.setParameter("status", Status.ACTIVE);

2.5 Calling stored procedures

You can also call stored procedures via the EntityManager.

The usual pattern is:

  1. Create a StoredProcedureQuery by specifying the procedure name
  2. Register all parameters with registerStoredProcedureParameter
  3. Set the parameter values

In many codebases, these last two steps differ – registering a parameter, setting it, and then registering the next one. This makes the code jump back and forth between two ideas (declaring parameters and providing values). I find it clearer to first register all parameters and only then set their values, but this is mostly a matter of preference.

public void execute(Long userId) {
    StoredProcedureQuery spq =
        em.createStoredProcedureQuery("pkg_base_computing.recalc");

    spq.registerStoredProcedureParameter("p_user_id",   Long.class, ParameterMode.IN);
    spq.setParameter("p_user_id", userId);

    spq.registerStoredProcedureParameter("p_result_id", Long.class, ParameterMode.OUT);

    spq.execute();
}

For better readability, first register all parameters and then assign their values.

It’s a small stylistic change, but it slightly improves readability and maintainability, because with a quick glance, you can see which parameters the procedure uses.

public void execute(Long userId) {
    StoredProcedureQuery spq =
            em.createStoredProcedureQuery("pkg_base_computing.recalc");

    spq.registerStoredProcedureParameter("p_user_id",   Long.class, ParameterMode.IN);
    spq.registerStoredProcedureParameter("p_result_id", Long.class, ParameterMode.OUT);

    spq.setParameter("p_user_id", userId);

    spq.execute();
}

3 Projection data with EntityManager

In the previous article about Spring Data JPA repositories, we discussed how to project data into DTOs or Interfaces. However, when using EntityManager, you must handle projections manually. You generally have three options: mapping an entity after fetching it, selecting directly into a DTO, or dealing with raw data.

3.1 Mapping entity to DTO with mapping libraries

The easiest way to get a DTO is to fetch the Entity and map it. Libraries like MapStruct or ModelMapper make your code cleaner and more readable (probably).

public UserDto getUserDtoViaMap(Long id) {
    // 1. Fetches the WHOLE entity (all columns)
    User user = entityManager.find(User.class, id);

    // 2. Maps it in memory
    UserDto userDto = new UserDto();
    modelMapper.map(user, userDto);
    return userDto;
}

This is functionally correct. Mapping libraries use some magic to generate the mapping logic, and while they might introduce a tiny bit of CPU overhead (especially reflection-based ones like ModelMapper), they generally make your work easier.

3.2 Mapping using a constructor

If you use JPQL, you can construct the DTO directly inside the query. This query is faster because the database only sends the columns you asked for. However, there is one major problem: you must specify the full path to the DTO.

Why is this a problem? If you rename your DTO class or move it to a different package, the string in your query won’t update automatically. The compiler misses this problem, and it will only appear as a RuntimeException when the code is executed. IntelliJ IDEA is smart enough to catch this and highlight it, but only if you analyze your entire codebase or open the specific file. If you miss the IDE warning, you are shipping a bug.

Here is a small example of using constructor expressions:

public UserDto getUserDtoViaQuery(Long id) {
    // Note: You must use the fully qualified class name!
    TypedQuery<UserDto> query = entityManager.createQuery(
        "SELECT new com.app.dto.UserDto(u.username, u.email) " +
        "FROM User u WHERE u.id = :id",
        UserDto.class
    );
    query.setParameter("id", id);
    return query.getSingleResult();
}

3.3 Mapping with Tuple and Object Array

When you are forced to use Native SQL, you can’t use the new Class(...) syntax. This leaves you with a choice: the raw Object array or strictly typed Tuples.

Actually, it’s insane, it’s scary as hell, but I see this often. Let me introduce – using object arrays for data mapping. You get an array of generic objects, and you have to know which index corresponds to which column and what type it is. If something changes in the database or you modify the indexes, an exception occurs.

// BAD: Object[] projection (Hard to read, error-prone)
public List<UserDto> getActiveUsersBad() {
    List<Object[]> results = entityManager.createNativeQuery(
        "SELECT id, username, is_active FROM users WHERE is_active = 1"
    ).getResultList();

    List<UserDto> dtos = new ArrayList<>();

    for (Object[] row : results) {
        // MAGIC NUMBERS! What is row[1]? What is row[2]?
        // You have to manually cast everything.
        Long id = row[0] != null ? ((Number) row[0]).longValue() : null;
        String username = (String) row[1];
        Boolean active = (Boolean) row[2]; // Hope this isn't a BigDecimal in Oracle!

        dtos.add(new UserDto(id, username, active));
    }
    return dtos;
}

The better way is to use Tuple interface. It allows you to access results by alias (name) rather than index. It is cleaner, safer, and self-documenting.

// BETTER: Tuple projection with aliases
public List<UserDto> getActiveUsersSafe() {
    // 1. Note the aliases (AS id, AS username)
    List<Tuple> tuples = entityManager.createNativeQuery(
        "SELECT u.id AS id, u.username AS username, u.is_active AS active " +
        "FROM users u WHERE u.is_active = 1",
        Tuple.class
    ).getResultList();

    List<UserDto> dtos = new ArrayList<>();

    for (Tuple t : tuples) {
        // 2. Fetch by name and type. No casting needed.
        Long id = t.get("id", Long.class);
        String username = t.get("username", String.class);
        Boolean active = t.get("active", Boolean.class);

        dtos.add(new UserDto(id, username, active));
    }
    return dtos;
}

Using Tuple makes your intent clear. You are telling the next developer exactly what columns you expect, and you don’t care what order they are in.

At the end

That was a tough series of articles. I’m pleased to say that I’ve finally adopted my biggest guide and published it in three separate articles. I’ve more ideas for upcoming articles, and if you enjoy my articles, please connect with me on LinkedIn to stay informed about new content.

If you missed the previous articles, here they are:

  • Spring Data JPA Best Practices: Entity Design Guide
  • Spring Data JPA Best Practices: Repositories Design Guide

This post is part of my Spring Data JPA guide. Read next: Spring Data JPA: Batch Insert Performance Tuning.

title: Ask the agent for a Playwright assertion, not another manual QA checklist
description:
After a UI PR, agents (and humans) love dumping a fresh “manual QA checklist” into the description: click here, hover there, check mobile, verify empty state. Those bullets rot by the next sprint. Nobody re-runs them. Regressions still ship.

I’ve started asking for something sharper: one Playwright assertion (or whatever E2E runner the repo already uses) that fails without the fix and passes with it. Same interaction. Same locator style. No new checklist theater.

What “one assertion” means here

  • Cover the changed flow only — one interaction, not the whole suite
  • Reuse existing test helpers / page objects / fixtures
  • Fail without the fix; pass with it (prove it once locally or in CI)
  • Match the locator strategy already in the folder (getByRole, data-testid, whatever neighbors use)
  • Land in the same PR as the UI change

If the agent can’t point at an existing helper, that’s a signal the flow isn’t tested yet — still better than a checklist you’ll never open again.

Prompt shape that gets a real assert 

Add one Playwright assertion for the checkout zip-before-city fix.

Constraints:
- Extend `e2e/checkout.spec.ts` (or the nearest existing file)
- Reuse helpers from `e2e/helpers/checkout.ts` — do not invent a second page object
- One interaction: blur city with empty zip → expect the existing error copy
- No new test runner, no `page.waitForTimeout`, no screenshot-only checks
- Show the failing assertion output before the fix, then the green run after

If you need a new framework or a second suite, stop and explain why.

The “failing output first” line matters. Agents will happily invent a green path that never exercised the bug. A red run without the fix is the receipt.

What I reject in review

Reject / send back

  • “Please manually verify…” as the only QA section
  • A brand-new test runner “because Playwright is cleaner” when Cypress (or the reverse) already owns CI
  • Flaky waitForTimeout / sleep-based waits
  • Screenshot diffs with no assert on the behavior you fixed
  • A 40-step checklist pasted from a template

Accept

  • One focused spec touching the changed flow
  • Locators matching neighbors in the same folder
  • Assertion on the user-visible outcome (error text, button state, URL)
  • Helper reuse instead of a parallel abstraction

Why this beats another checklist

Manual QA bullets feel thorough in the PR. They also:

  • Drift from the product the week after merge
  • Don’t fail CI when someone reintroduces the bug
  • Hide whether the agent actually understood the interaction

An assertion is boring and durable. The checklist is theater that ages into noise.

Tiny habit

Next time an agent (or a teammate) offers a manual QA list for a UI fix, paste the constraints above and ask for one Playwright assertion instead. If the draft invents a second framework or leans on sleep waits, stop — narrow the prompt and try again. The regression you care about usually fits in one expect.

What Is a QR Menu? A Guide for Restaurants
description:
A QR menu is a restaurant menu that guests open on their own phone by scanning a QR code at the table, counter or door. The code holds a web address; the phone's camera reads it and opens the menu in the browser, with no app to install. Some QR menus only show dishes and prices; others also let guests order, call a waiter or pay from the same page.

How a QR menu works for the guest

  1. The guest points the phone camera at the code printed on the table card, sticker or stand.
  2. The phone shows the address the code contains; one tap opens it in the browser.
  3. The menu loads as a normal web page: sections, dishes, prices and, where the restaurant adds them, photos and allergen information.
  4. Depending on the restaurant, the guest either orders from a server as usual or places the order from the same page.

Two kinds of QR menu

View-only and ordering QR menus

View-only QR menu Ordering QR menu
What the guest can do Read the menu Read the menu and send an order
How the order reaches the kitchen A server takes it It arrives on a screen or printer in the kitchen, with the table number
Codes needed One code for the whole room is enough One code per table, so orders carry the right table
Staff change None Someone watches incoming orders during service

Many restaurants start with a view-only menu and turn ordering on later. A QR menu can also be a PDF file rather than a web page; the difference, and why it matters on a phone, is covered separately.

Read QR code menu vs PDF menu for the comparison.

What a QR menu does well

  • Changes are immediate: a new price or a sold-out dish is visible to the next guest without reprinting.
  • Guests can read it in their own language when the menu offers more than one.
  • Allergen and dietary information can sit next to each dish, and guests can filter by it.
  • Photos help guests understand unfamiliar dishes.
  • A busy room keeps moving: guests can browse while they wait for a server.

Where it falls short

  • Not every guest has a phone with them, a working camera or a data connection — keep a printed menu available.
  • Some guests simply prefer paper; a QR menu works best as an option, not a requirement.
  • A code that is damaged, badly placed or printed too small will not scan in a dim room.
  • Codes can be tampered with: check table cards and stickers when you reset tables.

What to get right before switching

  • A menu address that will not change for as long as the codes are printed.
  • Complete allergen information. In the European Union, allergen information must be made available for non-prepacked food, which includes dishes served in restaurants.
  • Readable on a small screen without zooming, and quick to load on mobile data.
  • A short web address printed next to the code for anyone whose camera cannot read it.
  • Someone responsible for keeping prices and availability current.

For the practical steps, see how to create a QR code menu.

A QR menu with Thmenu

Thmenu gives each table its own QR code. The menu opens in the language of the guest's phone — the interface is available in 31 languages — and guests can filter dishes by allergen and diet. A dish can be marked unavailable during service so it cannot be ordered. Ordering from the table is a separate switch: it starts off for a new restaurant, and the restaurant turns it on in Settings when it is ready.

See how the Thmenu QR menu works.

Sources

  • Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 on the provision of food information to consumers — Article 44 (non-prepacked food)

Originally published at thmenu.com/en/blog/what-is-a-qr-menu.

title: 🏗️ 1. WebGL2 GLSL 핵심 문법과 개념 정리
description:
WebGL 보일러플레이트(HTML/JS)는 이미 구성되어 있다는 가정 하에, 셰이더 코드(vert.glsl, frag.glsl) 자체에서 알아야 하는 문법과 개념만 다룹니다. 기준 버전은 WebGL2에서 사용하는 GLSL ES 3.00(#version 300 es)입니다.

1. 셰이더 파이프라인 기본 구조

GPU 파이프라인에서 버텍스 셰이더는 정점 단위로, 프래그먼트 셰이더는 픽셀 단위로 동시에 실행됩니다. 버텍스 셰이더가 out으로 내보낸 값은 래스터화 과정에서 보간되어 프래그먼트 셰이더의 in으로 들어옵니다.

vert.glsl (버텍스 셰이더) 

#version 300 es
// [필수 개념 1: in / out]
// in: 보일러플레이트(JS)에서 버퍼로 넘겨준 데이터를 받는 키워드 (구버전의 attribute)
in vec2 a_position;

// [필수 개념 2: varying 대체]
// 버텍스 셰이더에서 프래그먼트 셰이더로 데이터를 넘길 때 out을 사용합니다.
out vec2 v_uv;

void main() {
    // [필수 개념 3: gl_Position]
    // 버텍스 셰이더는 반드시 이 내장 변수에 좌표를 할당해야 합니다.
    // a_position은 보통 -1.0 ~ 1.0 범위입니다.
    gl_Position = vec4(a_position, 0.0, 1.0);

    // [필수 개념 4: 벡터 연산과 스위즐링(Swizzling)]
    // -1~1 범위를 0~1 범위로 변환하여 프래그먼트 셰이더로 넘깁니다.
    // xy, xyz 등 원하는 축을 뽑아내는 문법을 스위즐링이라고 합니다.
    v_uv = a_position * 0.5 + 0.5;
}

frag.glsl (프래그먼트 셰이더) 

#version 300 es
// [필수 개념 5: 정밀도 설정]
// WebGL은 모바일 환경을 고려해 정밀도를 명시적으로 지정해야 합니다.
precision highp float;

// [필수 개념 6: uniform]
// JS에서 프레임마다 셰이더 전체에 동일하게 전달하는 전역 값입니다.
uniform float u_time;
uniform vec2 u_resolution;

// 버텍스 셰이더에서 넘어온 데이터를 받습니다. (구버전의 varying)
in vec2 v_uv;

// [필수 개념 7: out 변수]
// GLSL ES 3.00부터는 gl_FragColor 대신 직접 out 변수를 선언합니다.
out vec4 fragColor;

void main() {
    // 1. 종횡비(Aspect Ratio) 보정
    vec2 uv = v_uv;
    uv.x *= u_resolution.x / u_resolution.y;

    // 2. 중심점 계산
    vec2 center = vec2(u_resolution.x / u_resolution.y * 0.5, 0.5);

    // [필수 개념 8: 내장 수학 함수]
    // distance(A, B): 두 점 사이의 거리
    float dist = distance(uv, center);

    // sin()은 -1.0 ~ 1.0을 반환하므로 * 0.5 + 0.5로 0.0 ~ 1.0 범위로 정규화합니다.
    float wave = sin(dist * 15.0 - u_time * 3.0) * 0.5 + 0.5;

    // [필수 개념 9: vec3 색상 표현]
    // RGB 각 채널을 0.0(어둠) ~ 1.0(밝음) 실수로 표현합니다.
    vec3 color1 = vec3(0.1, 0.5, 1.0);
    vec3 color2 = vec3(1.0, 0.2, 0.4);

    // mix(A, B, t): t가 0.0이면 A, 1.0이면 B, 중간값이면 보간된 색을 반환합니다.
    vec3 finalColor = mix(color1, color2, wave);

    // [필수 개념 10: 최종 출력]
    // vec4(R, G, B, Alpha) 형태로 출력합니다.
    fragColor = vec4(finalColor, 1.0);
}

2. 데이터 타입

  • float: 소수 타입입니다. GLSL에서는 정수 리터럴을 거의 사용하지 않으며, 1이 아니라 1.0처럼 소수점을 명시해야 타입 불일치 에러를 피할 수 있습니다.
  • int, uint: 정수 타입입니다. 반복문 인덱스나 비트 연산에 사용되며, float과 자동 형변환되지 않으므로 float(i)처럼 명시적 캐스팅이 필요합니다.
  • bool: 논리 타입입니다. if 조건이나 step() 같은 함수의 반환과 호환됩니다.
  • vec2, vec3, vec4: float 여러 개를 묶은 벡터 타입입니다. 위치, 색상, UV 좌표 등에 사용됩니다.
  • mat2, mat3, mat4: 행렬 타입입니다. 이동, 회전, 투영 변환에 사용됩니다.
  • sampler2D: 텍스처 유닛을 참조하는 핸들 타입입니다. 변수 자체에 데이터가 들어있지 않고, texture() 함수와 함께 사용합니다.

3. 변수 한정자 (Qualifier)

  • in: 외부(JS 또는 이전 스테이지)로부터 데이터를 받는 한정자입니다.
  • out: 다음 스테이지(프래그먼트 셰이더 또는 프레임버퍼)로 데이터를 내보내는 한정자입니다.
  • uniform: JS에서 셰이더 전체에 동일하게 전달하는 전역 변수입니다. 정점/픽셀마다 값이 바뀌지 않습니다.
  • const: 컴파일 타임 상수입니다. 반복문의 상한값처럼 GPU가 미리 알아야 하는 값에 사용됩니다.
  • flat: 보간 없이 값을 전달하는 한정자입니다. 보통 정수형 out/in 변수에 필수로 붙여야 합니다(정수는 보간이 정의되지 않기 때문입니다).

4. 자주 쓰는 내장 함수

함수 설명
mix(a, b, t) 선형 보간. 색상이나 값을 부드럽게 섞을 때 가장 많이 사용됩니다.
clamp(x, min, max) x를 min~max 범위로 제한합니다.
smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x) 부드러운 S자 보간. 마스킹이나 경계를 부드럽게 처리할 때 사용됩니다.
step(edge, x) x가 edge보다 작으면 0.0, 크거나 같으면 1.0을 반환하는 계단 함수입니다.
length(v) 벡터의 길이(크기)를 반환합니다.
distance(a, b) 두 점 사이의 거리를 반환합니다.
normalize(v) 벡터를 길이 1인 단위 벡터로 변환합니다.
dot(a, b) 내적입니다. 두 벡터의 방향 유사도나 조명 계산에 사용됩니다.
cross(a, b) 외적입니다. 법선 벡터 계산 등에 사용됩니다.
reflect(I, N), refract(I, N, eta) 반사/굴절 벡터 계산에 사용됩니다.
pow(x, y), exp(x), log(x) 지수/로그 연산입니다.
floor(x), ceil(x), fract(x) 내림, 올림, 소수부 추출입니다. 그리드 패턴이나 반복 패턴을 만들 때 자주 사용됩니다.
mod(x, y) 나머지 연산입니다. 반복(타일링) 패턴에 사용됩니다.
abs(x), sin(x), cos(x) 절댓값, 삼각함수입니다.

GLSL ES에는 Perlin/Simplex 노이즈 같은 노이즈 함수가 내장되어 있지 않습니다. 노이즈가 필요한 경우 해시 함수 기반의 커스텀 구현을 셰이더 코드에 직접 포함시켜야 합니다.

5. 스위즐링 (Swizzling)

벡터 컴포넌트를 자유롭게 조합해서 추출하는 문법입니다.

vec3 v = vec3(1.0, 2.0, 3.0);

v.x;     // 1.0 (위치 표기: xyzw)
v.r;     // 1.0 (색상 표기: rgba, 의미는 동일)
v.xy;    // vec2(1.0, 2.0)
v.xyy;   // vec3(1.0, 2.0, 2.0) — 임의 조합 및 중복 가능
v.xy = vec2(5.0, 6.0); // 일부 컴포넌트만 대입(write-swizzle)도 가능

6. 텍스처 샘플링

GLSL ES 3.00부터 텍스처를 읽는 함수는 texture()로 통일되었습니다. 구버전의 texture2D()는 사용하지 않습니다.

uniform sampler2D u_texture;
in vec2 v_uv;
out vec4 fragColor;

void main() {
    vec4 texColor = texture(u_texture, v_uv);
    fragColor = texColor;
}

7. 분기와 반복문

if/else, for, while을 모두 사용할 수 있지만, GPU는 SIMD 방식으로 픽셀을 묶어서 처리하기 때문에 분기 비용이 CPU보다 큽니다. 같은 그룹 내 픽셀들이 다른 분기를 타면 양쪽 분기를 모두 계산하고 결과만 선택하는 방식으로 동작할 수 있습니다.

for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
    // const 또는 컴파일 타임에 알 수 있는 상한값을 권장합니다.
}

가능하면 if/else 대신 step(), mix(), smoothstep() 같은 함수로 분기를 대체하는 것이 일반적인 최적화 패턴입니다.

8. 배열과 구조체 

// 배열
float values[4] = float[4](0.1, 0.3, 0.6, 1.0);

// 구조체
struct Light {
    vec3 position;
    vec3 color;
};

Light light;
light.position = vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0);

9. 사용자 정의 함수와 매개변수 한정자

함수 매개변수에는 in(기본값, 읽기 전용), out(함수 내부에서 값을 채워 반환), inout(읽고 쓰기 모두 가능) 한정자를 붙일 수 있습니다.

float square(in float x) {
    return x * x;
}

void getMinMax(in float a, in float b, out float minV, out float maxV) {
    minV = min(a, b);
    maxV = max(a, b);
}

10. discard와 알파 클리핑

프래그먼트 셰이더 내에서 특정 픽셀의 출력을 완전히 버릴 때 사용합니다.

void main() {
    float alpha = texture(u_texture, v_uv).a;
    if (alpha < 0.1) {
        discard;
    }
    fragColor = vec4(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, alpha);
}

11. 정밀도(precision) 한정자

lowp, mediump, highp 세 단계가 있으며, 프래그먼트 셰이더는 기본 정밀도가 정의되어 있지 않아 precision 지시어를 직접 선언해야 컴파일 에러를 피할 수 있습니다. 버텍스 셰이더는 highp가 기본값으로 잡혀 있는 경우가 많지만, 명시적으로 선언하는 것이 안전합니다.

precision highp float;
precision highp int;

모바일 GPU에서는 mediump만 사용해도 충분한 경우가 많고, 성능 최적화 시 정밀도를 낮추는 것도 고려 대상이 됩니다.

12. Multiple Render Targets와 layout(location = ...)

여러 개의 out 변수를 동시에 다른 프레임버퍼 어태치먼트로 출력할 때는 layout(location = N)으로 인덱스를 명시합니다.

layout(location = 0) out vec4 fragColor;
layout(location = 1) out vec4 fragNormal;

같은 방식으로 버텍스 셰이더의 in 변수에도 layout(location = 0) in vec2 a_position;처럼 attribute 위치를 명시적으로 고정할 수 있습니다.

13. 자주 쓰는 내장 변수

  • gl_Position (버텍스 셰이더, 필수): 클립 공간 좌표입니다.
  • gl_PointSize (버텍스 셰이더): gl.POINTS로 그릴 때 점의 픽셀 크기를 지정합니다.
  • gl_FragCoord (프래그먼트 셰이더): 현재 픽셀의 화면 좌표(xy)와 깊이(z)를 담고 있습니다. u_resolution을 넘기지 않고 화면 좌표 기반 효과를 만들 때 사용됩니다.
  • gl_FragDepth (프래그먼트 셰이더): 깊이 값을 직접 덮어쓸 때 사용합니다.

14. 참고: 구버전(GLSL ES 1.00) 문법과의 차이

GLSL ES 1.00 (WebGL1) GLSL ES 3.00 (WebGL2)
attribute in (버텍스 셰이더)
varying 버텍스: out / 프래그먼트: in
texture2D(), textureCube() texture()
gl_FragColor 직접 선언한 out vec4 변수
버전 지시어 없음 또는 #version 100 #version 300 es

기존 WebGL1 예제 코드를 참고할 때는 이 표를 기준으로 치환하면 대부분 호환됩니다.

title: Playwright page.pdf(): missing backgrounds, a 0.7 pt header and @page sizes, each measured
description:
I wanted page.pdf() to produce a report with a page-number footer, a coloured banner and A4 pages. Four things behaved differently from what I expected, so I measured each one. I read the PDFs back with pdf.js, which gives text size, position, fill colours and page size, so nothing below was judged by eye.

The short version:

  • Without printBackground: true the background colour is dropped. White text on it stays, on a white page.
  • A header or footer template without a font-size is drawn at about 0.7 pt. The text is in the PDF and nobody can read it.
  • A CSS @page { size } is ignored unless preferCSSPageSize: true, but its orientation is not. A landscape @page turned my format: 'A4' into a landscape page.
  • break-inside: avoid stops cards from splitting across pages. A <thead> repeats on every page, a plain <tr> header does not.

Setup

Playwright 1.63.0 (Chromium 153.0.8010.12), pdfjs-dist 6.5.438, Node v24.22.2, Linux, 2026-11-06. All pages come from page.setContent(), so no network is involved.

npm i playwright@1.63.0 pdfjs-dist

First a helper that reads a PDF back: page size, text items with font size and y position, and the fill colours the page uses.

// inspect.mjs
import { getDocument, OPS } from 'pdfjs-dist/legacy/build/pdf.mjs';

// Per page: size in pt, text items with font size and y, and the fill colours used.
export async function inspect(buf) {
  const doc = await getDocument({ data: new Uint8Array(buf) }).promise;
  const pages = [];
  for (let n = 1; n <= doc.numPages; n++) {
    const page = await doc.getPage(n);
    const [x0, y0, x1, y1] = page.view;
    const items = (await page.getTextContent()).items
      .filter((t) => t.str.trim())
      .map((t) => ({ str: t.str.trim(), size: +t.transform[0].toFixed(1), y: Math.round(t.transform[5]) }));
    const ops = await page.getOperatorList();
    const fills = new Set();
    ops.fnArray.forEach((fn, k) => {
      if (fn === OPS.setFillRGBColor) fills.add(ops.argsArray[k][0]);
    });
    pages.push({
      size: `${Math.round(x1 - x0)}x${Math.round(y1 - y0)}`,
      text: items.map((i) => i.str).join(' '),
      items,
      fills: [...fills],
    });
  }
  return pages;
}

Then one script that runs every experiment. I will go through the output section by section.

// run.mjs
import { chromium } from 'playwright';
import { inspect } from './inspect.mjs';

const browser = await chromium.launch();
const page = await browser.newPage();
console.log('chromium', browser.version());

// 1. Backgrounds
await page.setContent(`<style>.bar{background:#c00;color:#fff;padding:8px}</style>
  <div class="bar">Banner</div><p>Body</p>`);
for (const printBackground of [false, true]) {
  const [p] = await inspect(await page.pdf({ printBackground }));
  console.log('printBackground', printBackground, '-> fills', p.fills.join(' '));
}

// 2. Header and footer
await page.setContent('<p>Body text</p>');
const m = { top: '20mm', bottom: '20mm' };
const cases = {
  'no size, margins': { headerTemplate: '<div>MYHEADER</div>', margin: m },
  'no size, no margin': { headerTemplate: '<div>MYHEADER</div>' },
  'font-size 9px, margins': { headerTemplate: '<div style="font-size:9px">MYHEADER</div>', margin: m },
  'footer with page numbers': {
    headerTemplate: '<div></div>',
    footerTemplate: '<div style="font-size:9px">Page <span class="pageNumber"></span> of <span class="totalPages"></span></div>',
    margin: m,
  },
};
for (const [name, opts] of Object.entries(cases)) {
  const [p] = await inspect(await page.pdf({ displayHeaderFooter: true, footerTemplate: '<div></div>', ...opts }));
  console.log(name.padEnd(25), p.items.map((i) => `${i.str} (${i.size}pt, y=${i.y})`).join(' | '));
}

// 3. Page size
for (const css of ['size:A4 portrait', 'size:A4 landscape', 'size:A5', 'size:100mm 150mm']) {
  await page.setContent(`<style>@page{${css}}</style><p>Hi</p>`);
  const size = async (o) => (await inspect(await page.pdf(o)))[0].size;
  console.log(css.padEnd(18), 'default', await size({}), '| preferCSSPageSize', await size({ preferCSSPageSize: true }), '| format A4', await size({ format: 'A4' }));
}

// 4. Page breaks
const card = (i) => `<div class="card"><b>Card ${i}</b><br>line a ${i}<br>line b ${i}<br>line c ${i}</div>`;
const cards = Array.from({ length: 30 }, (_, i) => card(i + 1)).join('');
for (const [name, extra] of [['plain', ''], ['break-inside: avoid', '.card{break-inside:avoid}']]) {
  await page.setContent(`<style>body{font:14px sans-serif}.card{border:1px solid #333;margin:0 0 10px;padding:6px;line-height:20px}${extra}</style>${cards}`);
  const pages = await inspect(await page.pdf({ margin: { top: '20mm', bottom: '20mm' } }));
  const seen = {};
  pages.forEach((p, i) => { for (const [, id] of p.text.matchAll(/(?:Card |line [abc] )(\d+)/g)) (seen[id] ??= new Set()).add(i + 1); });
  const split = Object.keys(seen).filter((id) => seen[id].size > 1);
  console.log(name.padEnd(20), `${pages.length} pages, split cards: [${split}]`);
}
const rows = Array.from({ length: 70 }, (_, i) => `<tr><td>row ${i + 1}</td><td>x</td></tr>`).join('');
for (const [name, head] of [['thead', '<thead><tr><th>HEADCELL</th></tr></thead>'], ['plain tr', '<tr><th>HEADCELL</th></tr>']]) {
  await page.setContent(`<table>${head}<tbody>${rows}</tbody></table>`);
  const pages = await inspect(await page.pdf());
  const on = pages.flatMap((p, i) => (p.text.includes('HEADCELL') ? [i + 1] : []));
  console.log(name.padEnd(20), `${pages.length} pages, HEADCELL on pages [${on}]`);
}
await page.setContent('<style>.s{break-after:page}</style><div class="s">One</div><div class="s">Two</div><div class="s">Three</div>');
console.log('break-after last     ', (await inspect(await page.pdf())).length, 'pages for 3 sections');

await browser.close();

Output of that run:

chromium 153.0.8010.12
printBackground false -> fills #ffffff #ababab #000000
printBackground true -> fills #cc0000 #ffffff #000000
no size, margins          Body text (12pt, y=719) | MY H E A D E R (0.7pt, y=776)
no size, no margin        Body text (12pt, y=776) | MY H E A D E R (0.7pt, y=776)
font-size 9px, margins    Body text (12pt, y=719) | MYHEADER (6.7pt, y=770)
footer with page numbers  Body text (12pt, y=719) | Page 1 of 1 (6.7pt, y=17)
size:A4 portrait   default 612x792 | preferCSSPageSize 595x842 | format A4 596x843
size:A4 landscape  default 792x612 | preferCSSPageSize 842x595 | format A4 843x596
size:A5            default 612x792 | preferCSSPageSize 420x595 | format A4 596x843
size:100mm 150mm   default 612x792 | preferCSSPageSize 283x425 | format A4 596x843
plain                4 pages, split cards: [9,26]
break-inside: avoid  4 pages, split cards: []
thead                2 pages, HEADCELL on pages [1,2]
plain tr             2 pages, HEADCELL on pages [1]
break-after last      3 pages for 3 sections

Backgrounds are off by default

The banner in the fixture has background:#c00 and color:#fff. With the default options the PDF contains no #cc0000 fill. The text is still white. The result is white text on white paper. With printBackground: true the red fill appears. The option docs list printBackground as defaulting to false, so this is documented, just easy to miss when your screen preview looks fine.

The default run also lists a grey fill, #ababab, that I did not track down. It is not the banner.

A header template without font-size is 0.7 pt

I passed <div>MYHEADER</div> as headerTemplate. The header is in the PDF, but pdf.js reports it at 0.7 pt, and the letters come out spaced (MY H E A D E R). With font-size:9px on the div it is 6.7 pt, which is 9 px converted to points. That is the only difference between the two cases.

The second finding is about margins. With no top margin, the header and the first line of the body are both at y=776 on a 792 pt page. They overlap. With margin: { top: '20mm' } the body moves down to y=719 and the header has its own space.

The docs say that script tags in templates are not evaluated and page styles are not visible inside them. They do not mention the font size, so set it inline in every template. The page-number classes from the same docs work once the size is set: the footer with page numbers row shows Page 1 of 1 at 6.7 pt, near the bottom edge (y=17).

@page size: dimensions ignored, orientation not

Four @page rules, each rendered three ways:

  • Default options: the page is always Letter, 612x792 pt. For A4 landscape it is 792x612, so the orientation arrived and the size did not.
  • preferCSSPageSize: true: the page matches the CSS (595x842 for A4, 283x425 for 100x150 mm).
  • format: 'A4': 596x843 for portrait rules, and 843x596 for landscape ones. The @page rule changed the orientation of a page whose size I set in code.

The docs say that preferCSSPageSize gives the CSS size priority over width, height and format. They do not say that orientation still passes through when it is off. The script only tries A4 in both orientations, A5 and 100x150 mm portrait, so I do not know how every size keyword behaves. If your stylesheet is shared between screen and print, either set preferCSSPageSize: true and let CSS own the size, or keep size out of @page and use only margins there.

Page breaks

30 cards of four lines each, 20 mm top and bottom margins:

  • Plain: 4 pages, and cards 9 and 26 are cut in two.
  • .card { break-inside: avoid }: still 4 pages, no card is split.

A table with 70 rows: with <thead> the header text is on pages 1 and 2, with a normal <tr> of <th> cells it is only on page 1. If a report has long tables, <thead> is all it takes.

I also tried break-after: page on every section, including the last one, because I remembered it leaving a blank page at the end. With three sections I got three pages. I could not reproduce a blank trailing page in this Chromium version. I did not try break-before on a nested element or a table row.

Limits

  • This is one Chromium build and one Playwright version. Run the script on yours before relying on a number.
  • pdf.js tells me what is in the file, not how it looks. "Unreadable" for the 0.7 pt header is a conclusion from the size, I did not rasterise the page.
  • I did not test web fonts, right-to-left text or CJK. Font embedding is a separate problem.

Written with AI assistance. Every code sample was run on 2026-11-06 with Playwright 1.63.0 (Chromium 153.0.8010.12) and pdfjs-dist 6.5.438; the output above is from that run.

title: Native dependencies are the part of your Java stack nobody owns
description:
Most Java services I've looked at have at least one dependency that isn't really Java. It usually arrives as a wrapper: a JNI binding or a ProcessBuilder call around Ghostscript, a headless browser, ImageMagick or libvips. The Java side looks tidy, with a Maven coordinate and a sensible API. The part doing the actual work is a .so file or a binary on the PATH, and nobody on the team thinks of it as theirs.

That's fine right up until it isn't. In my experience it stops being fine at one of three moments, and none of them are when you'd choose.

The base image changes

Someone moves the service to a slimmer container image to cut startup time or image size. Alpine is the classic choice, and Alpine uses musl instead of glibc. A native library built against glibc either refuses to load or loads and then behaves strangely, and the error you get is an UnsatisfiedLinkError that tells you almost nothing about why.

The Java code didn't change and the JVM didn't care, but the binary underneath did.

The CPU architecture changes

A few years ago this was rare. Now half the developers on a team are on Apple Silicon laptops, and the cloud bill keeps nudging people toward ARM instances like AWS Graviton. The JDK has run on ARM for a long time, so pure Java code moves across without anyone noticing. A native dependency needs an ARM build to exist, to be packaged, and to be the same version as the x86 one you tested against. Sometimes all three are true. Often one isn't, and you find out in CI or, worse, on the first deploy.

Someone publishes a CVE

In September 2023, libwebp had a heap buffer overflow (CVE-2023-4863) that was being exploited in the wild. It was patched in Chrome quickly. It was patched much more slowly in everything else that had quietly bundled libwebp, which turned out to be a lot of things, including a lot of server-side image pipelines.

If your image handling goes through a native library, patching means knowing that library is there, knowing which version you shipped, and rebuilding whatever image or package contains it. If it's a Java library, patching is a version bump in your build file, and your existing dependency scanning probably flagged it already.

There's also a difference in how bad the bug is. A malformed file that triggers an out-of-bounds read in C is a potential remote code execution. The same malformed file in Java hits a bounds check and throws an exception. That's still a bug, and a crafted file can still cause a denial of service, but it's a much smaller category of bad day.

The licensing question nobody asked

Ghostscript is AGPL unless you buy a commercial license. That's a perfectly reasonable model, and Artifex is entitled to it, but I've seen it turn up in a dependency audit long after the service shipped, at which point the conversation involves lawyers instead of developers! Native tools tend to be pulled in by someone who needed it working by Friday, and license review doesn't always follow binaries the way it follows Maven dependencies.

What pure Java costs you

I'd be misrepresenting things if I said pure Java is free because it isn't!

Somebody has to implement the format. The PDF specification is enormous, image formats are full of vendor quirks, and a native library that's been hammered on for twenty years has handled edge cases a newer implementation may not have met yet.

Performance can also lag for some workloads, particularly where the native code leans on hand-tuned SIMD.

The JDK itself doesn't help as much as you'd hope. ImageIO dates back to Java 1.4, picked up TIFF support in Java 9, and still has no built-in support for WebP, AVIF or HEIC. It also has habits that waste an afternoon, like ImageIO.read returning null when it can't find a reader instead of throwing, or rejecting CMYK JPEGs that every other tool opens without complaint. So "just use the JDK" often isn't an option, and you end up choosing between a native wrapper and a third-party Java library anyway.

How to decide

Before adding a native dependency, I'd want answers to a few things. Who updates it when a CVE lands, and how would we find out? Does it have builds for every OS, libc and CPU architecture we run on, including developer laptops? What happens to the JVM if it segfaults? (The answer is that the whole process dies and leaves an hs_err_pid file behind, which is a worse failure mode than an exception you can catch.) What's the license, and has anyone outside engineering looked at it?

If those answers are all good, a native library will be the right call. Plenty of them are excellent. But the questions usually get asked after the first incident rather than before the first commit.

Disclosure: I work at a company that builds pure Java libraries for PDF and image processing, so I'm not neutral on this. The tradeoffs above apply regardless of whose library you use.

title: Designing Recoverable Inquiry Forms: Labels, Errors, and State Boundaries
description:
This technical design exercise adapts Designing Home Care Inquiry Forms People Can Finish, published by Robert, CTO of Primetime Home Health Services. It is shared through Jeremy Nwokorie’s account; his health informatics and public health background is relevant context for information design, not a claim that this example is deployed.

PTHHS’s current contact page is call-first. The form below is a hypothetical implementation sketch, not an existing PTHHS feature, a reported defect, or a completed test. It handles an ordinary inquiry about nonmedical personal assistance, not clinical intake or service eligibility.

Define the state contract before the component

For a proposed short inquiry, imagine a required callback number, an optional preferred name, and an optional general topic. The office must review the purpose and proposed fields before release. Avoid a broad “Tell us everything” field that invites private records.

Separate three concerns in the design:

  • Input state: the permitted answers entered during this process.
  • Validation state: which answers need correction under the agreed rules.
  • Submission state: whether the server accepted the inquiry, rejected a field, or returned an uncertain result.

A validation failure should update the relevant error state without resetting unrelated permitted answers. A network failure is not proof of successful submission. Avoid success language until the receiving system confirms acceptance.

Connect the label, hint, and error

This illustrative fragment shows the relationships for one missing-value error. It is not a complete form or production-ready validation system:

<div role="alert">
  <p>Please correct this answer:</p>
  <a href="#callback">Phone number for a return call</a>
</div>

<label for="callback">Phone number for a return call (required)</label>
<p id="callback-hint">Use a phone format supported by this service.</p>
<input id="callback" name="callback" type="tel" required
       aria-invalid="true"
       aria-describedby="callback-hint callback-error">
<p id="callback-error">
  Enter the phone number you want us to use for a return call.
</p>

The example deliberately contains no real phone number. Replace the generic hint with the actual reviewed format instructions. When the error is resolved, remove the obsolete error state and update the description references. Test whether following the summary link puts keyboard and assistive-technology users in the expected place; markup alone does not establish correct focus or announcement behavior.

Visible labels must survive typing. See W3C’s instructions and labeling tutorials. Its notification guidance explains summaries and field associations. Do not rely on a red border to communicate a correction.

Agree on browser and server behavior

If the server supports punctuation variations, the browser should accept them too. Do not silently reinterpret an ambiguous number. A tel input does not establish number ownership or replace server-side validation. Keep syntax checks separate from decisions about service availability or eligibility.

W3C’s validation tutorial distinguishes browser checks from the server checks still needed. Document the supported formats once, then test both paths against the same synthetic cases.

Bound recovery to the supported process

Preserving an answer during a correction does not automatically justify cross-session storage. Decide the lifetime of each value before choosing persistence mechanisms. Do not add indefinite browser storage simply to make Back work. Do not send entered names, numbers, or free text to analytics or error reports.

W3C’s redundant-entry explanation distinguishes entry within a process from storage between sessions. Test Back, return, reload, and any documented expiry behavior. Describe actual retention behavior instead of promising recovery the implementation cannot provide.

Use a journey-based acceptance matrix

These are proposed checks using synthetic values, not results from a deployed PTHHS form:

Scenario Expected evidence
Submit without callback Specific field error; unrelated permitted answers retained
Correct that field Obsolete error removed; other answers unchanged
Try supported punctuation Browser and server agree on each documented case
Follow summary by keyboard Correct control is reachable; no trap or lost position
Use intended screen reader/browser pairs Label, hint, and current error make sense together
Narrow viewport or larger text Correction controls remain readable and reachable
Interrupt, return, or expire Retention and clearing match the documented policy

Record the environment, input case, expected result, observed result, and retest after a fix. Automated checks do not replace the complete interaction or review by the staff who answer inquiries.

Sources and limits

The original company article includes the full operational context and source notes, researched November 5, 2026. This adaptation was prepared with AI assistance and reviewed for source accuracy and company scope. It makes no measured conversion or workload claim, accessibility or security certification, or clinical, eligibility, or regulatory assessment. Any actual service arrangement must be confirmed with the office.

title: Building a Regional Digital Health Platform in Bangladesh: Next.js 16, Supabase, and Offline-First PWA
description:
Access to reliable, affordable healthcare remains one of the most critical challenges in developing nations. While capital cities often attract telemedicine startups and digital health investments, regional districts and tier-2 cities are frequently left navigating fragmented, pen-and-paper systems.

Patients in district headquarters like Feni Sadar (Bangladesh) regularly struggle with:

  1. Finding verified, BMDC-registered specialist doctors and their updated chamber visiting hours.
  2. Unpredictable, out-of-pocket diagnostic lab expenses.
  3. Lack of transparent emergency ambulance contacts during critical golden hours.

To bridge this gap, we engineered and launched Health Club Feni—a modern, full-stack digital healthcare directory and membership network designed specifically for the local ecosystem.

(Note: Despite the name, Health Club is strictly a medical care directory and membership platform, not an athletic fitness gym).

In this article, I want to break down the architectural choices, engineering constraints, performance optimizations, and search engine strategies we used to build this platform for real-world patients and healthcare providers.

🛠️ The Tech Stack

When designing for regional users who often browse on budget Android smartphones and fluctuating 3G/4G connections, every millisecond and kilobyte counts.

  • Framework: Next.js 16 (App Router) with React 19
  • Rendering Architecture: React Server Components (RSC) first, with strict client boundary isolation
  • Database & Auth: Supabase (PostgreSQL) paired with Prisma ORM
  • Styling: Tailwind CSS v4 + Radix UI / shadcn accessible primitives
  • Offline & Service Worker: Modern PWA caching via Serwist
  • Form State & Validation: React Hook Form + Zod
  • SEO / AEO Engine: Generative Engine Optimization (GEO), Schema.org MedicalWebPage & Physician entity graphs, IndexNow integration

🏛️ Core Architectural Challenges & Solutions

1. High Performance via Pure React Server Components (RSC)

Rather than loading heavy client-side JavaScript bundles, over 85% of Health Club's public pages are rendered as pure Server Components.

When a patient visits the Feni Specialist Doctor Directory or the Diagnostic Tests & Investigations Catalog, the server delivers pre-rendered semantic HTML with zero hydration overhead:

// Server Component: Instant database query with zero client JS bundle bloat
import prisma from "@/lib/prisma";
import { DoctorCard } from "@/components/doctors/DoctorCard";

interface Props {
  searchParams: Promise<{ department?: string; location?: string }>;
}

export default async function ConsultantsPage({ searchParams }: Props) {
  const { department, location } = await searchParams;

  const doctors = await prisma.doctor.findMany({
    where: {
      status: "ACTIVE",
      ...(department && { department }),
      ...(location && { location }),
    },
    include: { partner: true },
    orderBy: { priorityOrder: "asc" },
  });

  return (
    <section className="max-w-7xl mx-auto px-4 py-8">
      <h1 className="text-3xl font-extrabold text-slate-900">
        Specialist Doctor Roster in Feni Sadar
      </h1>
      <div className="grid grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3 gap-6 mt-6">
        {doctors.map((doctor) => (
          <DoctorCard key={doctor.id} doctor={doctor} />
        ))}
      </div>
    </section>
  );
}

This guarantees near-perfect Google Core Web Vitals (LCP < 1.1s, CLS = 0) even on constrained mobile hardware.

2. Solving Diagnostic Affordability: The 10–30% Member Discount Network

In Bangladesh, high out-of-pocket medical expenditure pushes millions into financial vulnerability. Diagnostic investigations (blood work, ultrasound, digital X-rays, CT scans) often constitute the largest initial bill.

Health Club built a formal offline-to-online network with verified Partner Hospitals and Diagnostic Centers in Feni Sadar. Through the platform's Digital Membership Card, registered patients receive an official 10% to 30% discount on laboratory and radiology investigations simply by presenting their verified digital member ID at partner reception desks.

+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                 Health Club Membership Flow                 |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
   1. Patient Registers Online (Free/Nominal Annual Sub)
                          │
                          ▼
   2. Instant Dynamic QR & Member ID Card Issued (PWA-cached)
                          │
                          ▼
   3. Patient visits Contracted Diagnostic Partner in Feni Sadar
                          │
                          ▼
   4. Partner Scans/Verifies ID ──> 10-30% Instant Discount Applied

Architectural rule: To maintain contract compliance and integrity, discounts are communicated as percentage benefits (10-30% Member Discount) while providing transparent market reference ranges rather than misleading fixed prices.

3. Emergency Triage: 24/7 Helplines & Symptom Navigator

Regional patients frequently hesitate during medical emergencies, unsure whether a symptom warrants immediate hospitalization or a scheduled specialist visit.

We built two key safety nets:

  1. 24/7 Feni Ambulance & Emergency Helplines: A verified, community-updated directory of oxygen suppliers, blood donor networks, and ambulance hotlines with direct one-tap mobile dialing.
  2. Clinical Symptom Triage Navigator: A lightweight clinical decision-tree based on WHO and DGHS emergency protocols, identifying critical "Red Flag" symptoms (e.g., crushing chest pain, sudden unilateral weakness, acute breathlessness) and redirecting users to the nearest emergency ward before booking standard outpatient appointments.

4. Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) & Machine-Readable Knowledge Bases

With users increasingly finding medical information through AI answer engines (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude) alongside traditional Google search, we integrated state-of-the-art GEO (Generative Engine Optimization):

  • Entity Disambiguation: Every doctor, partner clinic, and test is enriched with Schema.org JSON-LD (@type: Physician, Hospital, MedicalWebPage).
  • Standardized Machine Knowledge Bases: We publish machine-readable markdown files at /llms.txt and /llms-full.txt directly mapping all verified doctors, test guidelines, and partner facilities for LLM web crawlers (GPTBot, PerplexityBot, ClaudeBot).
  • Bilingual Intent Handling: In Bangladesh, queries alternate between conversational Bengali and English/Banglish keywords (e.g., "Feni doctor serial", "CT scan price in Feni"). Every entity satisfies both intents simultaneously.

📈 Key Engineering Takeaways

  1. Keep Client Boundaries Minimal: In Next.js App Router, resisting the temptation to slap "use client" on top-level pages dramatically cuts bundle size and eliminates client-side hydration waterfalls.
  2. Design for Low-Bandwidth Reality: Heavy single-page apps (SPAs) with 500KB+ vendor bundles fail real-world users in district towns. Pure RSC + responsive WebP/AVIF images deliver real accessibility.
  3. Structured Data is the Future of Local Search: Deep schema graphs and clear entity definitions allow both Googlebot and modern LLM answer engines to cite local services with high accuracy.

🔗 Project Links & Resources

If you are interested in exploring the live platform or inspecting the UI/UX architecture:

  • 🌐 Official Website: healthclubfeni.com
  • 👨‍⚕️ Doctor Serial Directory: Specialist Doctors in Feni
  • 🏥 Diagnostic Centers: Partner Hospital & Clinic Network
  • 🔬 Diagnostic Test Pricing Guide: Test Directory & Prep Rules
  • 🚑 Emergency Support: 24/7 Feni Ambulance Directory
  • 💳 Digital Membership: Health Club Member Card

All medical information on the platform is reviewed by the **Health Club Editorial Team* in accordance with established clinical guidelines.*

title: React: un presupuesto de foco para interfaces rápidas
description:
La accesibilidad y el rendimiento suelen revisarse en tickets distintos. En una interfaz real, sin embargo, el usuario los vive juntos: pulsa un botón, aparece un estado de carga, el foco cambia (o se pierde) y la pantalla vuelve a pintar. Si esa secuencia no está diseñada, una mejora visual puede sentirse como un fallo.

Este patrón es especialmente útil en formularios de registro, verificación y pruebas de email. Incluso cuando alguien busca tempmailso para validar un flujo, la experiencia no debería depender de adivinar donde quedó el cursor.

El foco también tiene un presupuesto

Llamo “presupuesto de foco” a una regla simple: cada interacción debe mover el foco solo cuando existe una razón clara. Por ejemplo:

  • Si el usuario abre un diálogo, el foco entra al diálogo y vuelve al control que lo abrió al cerrarlo.
  • Si un formulario falla, el foco puede ir al primer error solo después de que el usuario intentó enviarlo.
  • Si una operación tarda, el foco permanece donde estaba mientras el estado de carga se anuncia.

El error común es enfocar siempre el primer elemento que cambia. Eso parece servicial, pero interrumpe a quien está usando teclado o lector de pantalla. También puede generar scroll inesperado y más trabajo de composición en pantallas pequeñas.

Una buena referencia para un flujo parecido es este feedback de email que respeta el foco. La idea no es añadir más movimiento, sino hacer que cada movimiento tenga sentido.

Medir antes de mover

Antes de añadir focus(), escribo la secuencia en tres estados: idle, loading y result. Después respondo estas preguntas:

  1. ¿Qué control conserva el foco durante la espera?
  2. ¿Qué texto comunica el resultado y con qué urgencia?
  3. ¿Qué ocurre si la respuesta llega dos veces o llega tarde?

El tercer punto suele olvidarse. Un estado antiguo puede devolver el foco a un botón que ya no representa la acción actual. No hace falta una instrumentación enorme: una marca de tiempo, el nombre del estado y una prueba con teclado ya muestran bastante.

Si el flujo tiene errores de validación, conviene revisar también estos errores inline sin saltos. Un mensaje debajo del campo es más estable que insertar un bloque encima y empujar toda la pantalla.

Un patrón pequeño en React

El componente no necesita controlar todo el documento. Un ref para el mensaje y un efecto ligado al resultado suele ser suficiente:

import { useEffect, useRef, useState } from "react";

export function VerifyButton() {
  const [status, setStatus] = useState("idle");
  const messageRef = useRef(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (status === "success" || status === "error") {
      messageRef.current?.focus();
    }
  }, [status]);

  async function handleVerify() {
    setStatus("loading");
    try {
      await verifyEmail();
      setStatus("success");
    } catch {
      setStatus("error");
    }
  }

  return (
    <section aria-busy={status === "loading"}>
      <button onClick={handleVerify} disabled={status === "loading"}>
        Verificar
      </button>
      <p ref={messageRef} tabIndex={-1} role="status">
        {status === "loading" && "Comprobando…"}
        {status === "success" && "Listo, revisa tu bandeja."}
        {status === "error" && "No se pudo comprobar. Inténtalo de nuevo."}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}

En una aplicación completa, verifyEmail debe recibir un identificador de operación para ignorar respuestas viejas. El ejemplo se concentra en la relación entre estado, foco y mensaje. tabIndex={-1} permite enfocar el párrafo sin añadirlo al orden normal de tabulación.

Hay una pequeña trampa: mover el foco en cada cambio de estado también puede ser molesto. Por eso el mensaje solo se enfoca en estados finales, no durante loading. La intención es clara y la carga no roba control.

CSS que no roba estabilidad

El foco visible necesita diseño, no solo una regla genérica. Un contorno consistente ayuda a localizarlo sin cambiar las dimensiones del control:

button:focus-visible,
[tabindex="-1"]:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #145cff;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

.feedback {
  min-height: 1.5rem;
}

Reservar espacio para el feedback evita que el formulario salte cuando aparece el texto. También es preferible cambiar color u opacidad con cuidado: un estado no debe comunicarse solo con color, y una transición larga puede hacer que el resultado se sienta lento aunque el servidor ya respondio.

Si incluyes un enlace contextual como temp mail mail, mantenlo subordinado a la explicación y no lo repitas en cada sección. El enlace sirve al lector cuando necesita probar un flujo; no reemplaza el contenido.

Checklist de revisión

  • Navega todo el flujo con Tab, Shift+Tab y Enter.
  • Comprueba que el foco tiene un indicador visible en tema claro y oscuro.
  • Verifica que el botón no cambia de tamaño al pasar a carga.
  • Usa un lector de pantalla para confirmar el mensaje de resultado.
  • Simula una respuesta lenta y otra fuera de orden.
  • Revisa que el foco no salte al principio del documento sin motivo.
  • Prueba una etiqueta de búsqueda como “tempail mail” solo como entrada de usuario, no como nombre de una función.

La revisión final debe incluir móvil. Un foco bien colocado en escritorio puede quedar oculto por el teclado virtual o por un scroll automático en una pantalla estrecha.

Preguntas rápidas

¿Siempre debo enfocar el mensaje de éxito?

No. Si el usuario sigue trabajando en el formulario, un role="status" puede anunciar el resultado sin desplazar el foco. Enfócalo cuando el resultado sea el siguiente paso importante o cuando la persona necesite conocerlo antes de continuar.

¿El rendimiento exige quitar las transiciones?

Tampoco. Usa transiciones cortas, respeta prefers-reduced-motion y evita animar propiedades que cambian el layout. El objetivo es que el estado sea perceptible y predecible.

¿Qué métrica debo mirar?

Empieza con una medida sencilla: tiempo desde la acción hasta el primer feedback visible, junto con errores de interacción y pérdida de foco observada en pruebas. No conviertas una cifra en objetivo si empeora la comprensión.

La interfaz pulida no es la que hace más cosas automáticamente. Es la que comunica el estado correcto, conserva la orientación de la persona y deja que React trabaje con una cantidad razonable de cambios.
