title: Cloudflare Publishes a Wire Service for Critical Vulnerabilities
description:
TL;DR

  • Zero Wire is a public vulnerability intelligence feed inside Cloudflare Radar that publishes short briefings on critical vulnerabilities in Internet-facing software; one briefing can cover several related CVEs when grouping them clarifies the response.
  • Cloudflare announced it on 3 November 2026, with each briefing covering what happened, who should investigate, what to do now and where the evidence sits.
  • The homepage sorts briefings into "Needs attention" and "Reference", and each card carries a status plus a last-checked date; a briefing in Reference can still concern an organisation with unfinished remediation.
  • Evidence links point at CVE records, research and CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog, and the network charts count requests matching WAF managed rules. Cloudflare says these counts measure attempts seen by its rules; evidence from an organisation's systems is required to determine compromise.
  • Each briefing offers a pre-compiled prompt that asks an AI agent connected by your team to perform a read-only assessment of your environment.
  • Where a WAF rule exists, the card reports its availability and sends you to review your configuration; the link opens the relevant configuration for review; rule activation requires a separate configuration action.
  • The format stops at the edge of your estate: asset identity, ownership, installed version and control state stay with your team, and those four fields decide whether a briefing becomes an answer.

Capture of the Cloudflare post "Introducing Zero Wire, a hub for investigating critical Internet vulnerabilities", taken 3 November 2026 from blog.cloudflare.com/zero-wire.

Cloudflare published Introducing Zero Wire, a hub for investigating critical Internet vulnerabilities, on 3 November 2026. The product is small and specific: a public feed inside Cloudflare Radar that publishes briefings on critical issues in Internet-facing software and can cover several related CVEs together when that makes the response clearer, written so that a security lead can read it in the time it takes to finish a coffee and an engineer can follow the same page down to the technical guidance. The framing in the post is a wire service, and that framing carries the design.

A curated feed for exposed software

The choice of scope reads as deliberate. Zero Wire focuses on critical CVEs in web applications, the runtimes and libraries they depend on, and services exposed to the internet. It is a curated set of significant issues, with vendor advisory and vulnerability-database coverage left where it already exists. Cloudflare describes the feed as public and says that issues can be included independently of WAF rule availability.

Netics editorial visual: the fields a Zero Wire briefing carries, and the date that tells a returning reader what changed.

A briefing carries five fields and one date

Open a card and the structure is the same every time. The overview explains what happened, why it deserves attention and which teams should investigate. "What to do now" gives a short list of next steps, which can mean identifying affected deployments, checking versions with a hosting provider, applying vendor updates, reviewing suspicious activity or holding compensating controls in place. The evidence section links outward. The Cloudflare section says what the vendor's own controls cover. The update chronology records new advisories and changes to guidance.

Two fields do the quiet work

The homepage places issues requiring active assessment or action under “Needs attention” and keeps briefings under “Reference” when guidance has stabilised; the last-checked date says when the underlying evidence was last reviewed. Cloudflare is explicit that the two categories answer different questions, and that a briefing in Reference can still matter to an organisation that has not finished remediation. That sentence is the honest part of the design: a Reference label describes the state of public guidance, and a patched estate is a fact about your own systems.

Cloudflare figure, 3 November 2026: the Zero Wire homepage, with briefings grouped into "Needs attention" and "Reference". Source: radar.cloudflare.com/security/zero-wire.

The php2shell entry shows where traffic evidence stops

The most useful briefing in the launch set is probably the one on php2shell, the two PHP runtime vulnerabilities that landed in October 2026. The card explains that the flaws sit in the runtime itself, which matters for anyone running WordPress or Magento on a platform they did not build: updating a plugin or an application bundle leaves the interpreter untouched. The briefing names the system owners who should care and links the PHP project's own security guidance for affected versions.

The evidence section on that page includes a chart of HTTP requests matching Cloudflare's WAF managed rules for php2shell over time. Read it as a measure of attacker interest. Cloudflare's own note is explicit: a matched request is an attempt in flight, and the count tracks how much attention a vulnerability is attracting. The number of compromised systems requires separate evidence. The corollary is stated too, in the general briefing text. Determining whether a particular organisation was compromised requires evidence from that organisation's systems, and exploitation elsewhere remains possible when Cloudflare's network records no attempts.

That paragraph is the reason this feed is worth reading. Most vulnerability dashboards place the internet's activity and a specific company's exposure on the same plane. A chart of blocked requests is telemetry about the traffic Cloudflare saw, and the only party that can turn it into a statement about your estate is the party holding the asset list.

Cloudflare figure, 3 November 2026: requests matching WAF managed rules for php2shell, offered as a measure of attacker focus. Source: radar.cloudflare.com/security/zero-wire.

Status and last-checked describe the evidence, and the reader supplies the asset

Start with the four fields an operator must supply, and the format becomes clearer. Your own records must identify which of your hosts runs the affected runtime, who approves an out-of-band update, whether that host answers the internet at all, and whether the rule that would mitigate the issue is actually switched on. Those four answers live in an inventory, a rota and a change record.

Consider a hypothetical case. A Casablanca logistics company runs its customer portal on a managed PHP platform and a small intranet on an old interpreter image that nobody has touched since the migration. The php2shell briefing applies to both: the hosting provider's patch process covers the portal, and the company owns remediation of the intranet image. An asset register that records the interpreter version distinguishes them.

Netics editorial visual: the four facts about a specific estate that a public briefing cannot know.

The pre-compiled prompt produces questions for your estate

Each briefing ships with a prompt intended for an AI agent, asking for a read-only assessment of deployed software, relevant vendor fixes, exposure and compensating controls, with per-asset evidence, explicit unknowns and next actions. Cloudflare defines the scope carefully: the prompt asks the AI agent connected by your team to perform a read-only assessment. It structures the conversation your team has with its own tooling.

That is a reasonable shape for the job, and the wording that matters is "unknowns". Confident answers about an estate nobody has inventoried amount to plausible fiction. An assessment that lists its unknowns gives an operator concrete questions to pursue.

The same logic applies to the update chronology, which records new advisories and revisions to the response guidance. A team that read a briefing on the first day and returns a week later needs to know what moved, and the chronology with the last-checked date answers that question without a full re-read.

Cloudflare figure, 3 November 2026: the update chronology that records new advisories and changes to guidance on a single briefing. Source: radar.cloudflare.com/security/zero-wire.

WAF coverage carries a review step

Where a CVE can be addressed with a WAF rule, the briefing reports that a rule exists and what configuring it requires, with links that take paid and free plans to the relevant dashboard. The next step printed on the card is a review step: check your configuration to determine whether you are protected. A link opens the relevant configuration for review; rule activation requires a separate configuration action.

Cloudflare's own caveat is the one to keep: a WAF mitigation provides a compensating control for covered traffic, and actions already performed at the origin remain in effect after requests are blocked. If an attacker reached the interpreter before the rule was deployed, the rule changes nothing about what already happened. A WAF mitigation provides a response window. Following the vendor's remediation guidance fixes the vulnerable software, and the feed is clear about the role it offers.

Cloudflare figure, 3 November 2026: the coverage block that reports whether a WAF rule exists for an issue and what configuration it needs. Source: radar.cloudflare.com/security/zero-wire.

What an operator attaches to the card

The briefing format is worth adopting internally even for a team that never opens Radar. Four fields turn a public card into a decision: the asset, the owner, the version read from the host, and the state of the compensating control. Two of those are inventory work, one is a change-management habit, and one is a configuration check performed in the dashboard. Monitoring adds the fifth, which is the evidence that something tried the door — the sort of alerting that belongs in infrastructure monitoring with plain-language alerts and should reach operators as events occur.

The habit that makes the format pay off is smaller than a programme. When a briefing arrives, write the four answers next to the card, including the ones you cannot answer. The unknowns become the backlog, and the next disclosure finds a shorter list.

Netics editorial visual: five steps that convert a public briefing into a recorded answer for one estate.

Originally published on the Netics blog.

title: Capacity Reservation Resource Groups now support Amazon EC2 Capacity Blocks and interruptible Capacity Reservations in AWS GovCloud (US) Regions
description:
Starting today, you can add Amazon EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML and interruptible Capacity Reservations to Capacity Reservation Resource Groups in AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. Amazon EC2 offers different reservation offerings such as On-Demand Capacity Reservations (ODCRs), interruptible Capacity Reservations, and Capacity Blocks for ML. Previously, a Capacity Reservation Resource Group could only include ODCRs. Now you can add any type of Capacity Reservation to a Capacity Reservation Resource Group, making it easier to launch EC2 instances across your entire portfolio of reserved capacity.

To use this feature, create a Capacity Reservation Resource Group, add any Capacity Reservation to it, and then target the group in your launch request. When using EC2 Fleet and EC2 Auto Scaling groups, you can also specify your prioritization preferences across reservation types, and configure automatic fall back to EC2 On-Demand capacity when there is no capacity remaining across your reservations.

There are no additional charges for using this feature. With the addition of AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, this feature is now available in all AWS Regions where Capacity Blocks for ML and interruptible ODCRs are supported, excluding China Regions. To get started, see Capacity Reservation Resource Groups and the Capacity Reservations user guide.

title: A Dropdown With z-index: 9999 That Still Hides Behind the Page
description:
Here is a bug that many front-end teams run into sooner or later.

You click a menu in the header. It opens, but only its top edge shows. The rest is hidden behind the hero banner below the header.

So you do what everyone does. You give the dropdown z-index: 9999. Nothing changes. You try 99999. Still nothing.

The number was never the problem. The problem is where the number lives.

Think of z-index as a version number

MDN has a helpful way to picture this:

To figure out the rendering order of stacked elements along the z-axis, think of each index value as a "version number" of sorts, where child elements represent minor version numbers underneath their parent's major version number.

Here is what that means in practice.

Say the header is version 0 and the hero banner is version 1. The dropdown sits inside the header. So its full number is not 9999. It is 0.9999.

And 0.9999 is still smaller than 1. The hero wins.

The box that holds those "minor" numbers is called a stacking context. MDN says:

"Each stacking context is self-contained. After an element's contents are stacked, the entire element is considered as a single unit in the stacking order of its parent stacking context."

In short: a child can never climb above its stacking context. It can only move up or down inside it.

Bug 1: The sticky header

Here is that page, cut down to the parts that matter.

<header class="site-header">
  <nav>
    <div class="nav-item">
      Products
      <div class="dropdown">...</div>
    </div>
  </nav>
</header>

<section class="hero">...</section>

.site-header {
  background: white;
  position: sticky;
  top: 0;
}

.nav-item {
  position: relative;
}

.dropdown {
  position: absolute;
  top: 100%;
  left: 0;
  z-index: 9999;
}

.hero {
  position: relative;
  z-index: 1; /* added earlier for a background effect */
}

Two things are going on.

First, position: sticky makes the header a stacking context on its own. MDN's list of triggers includes "Element with a position value fixed or sticky." So the dropdown's 9999 only counts inside the header.

Second, the header itself has no z-index. In the parent's stack, it sits at the same level as z-index: 0. The hero has z-index: 1. So the whole header, dropdown and all, paints under the hero.

We checked this in Chrome 156 with document.elementFromPoint(). A point inside the lower part of the dropdown returned the hero, not the dropdown.

The fix

Raise the header, not the dropdown.

.site-header {
  background: white;
  position: sticky;
  top: 0;
  z-index: 10; /* the fix */
}

Now the header is version 10 and the hero is version 1. The dropdown comes along with its parent. The same elementFromPoint() check now returned the dropdown.

The dropdown can go back to a small number too. z-index: 1 is plenty inside the header.

Bug 2: The fade-in that never ends

This one is sneakier, because the page looks the same before and after the bug.

.panel {
  animation: fade-in 0.3s forwards;
}

@keyframes fade-in {
  from { opacity: 0; }
  to   { opacity: 1; }
}

The panel holds a menu with position: absolute and z-index: 1. Below the panel is a position: relative box with no z-index. The menu opens and hides behind that box.

Why? opacity below 1 makes a stacking context. That part is well known. But the animation ends at opacity: 1, so it should be fine, right?

Not quite. MDN's list also includes an "Element that has had stacking context-creating properties (such as opacity) animated using @keyframes, with animation-fill-mode set to forwards."

So forwards keeps the stacking context alive after the animation ends. The panel stays a closed box, and the positioned box after it paints on top.

The fix

Here the end value of the animation, opacity: 1, is the same as the normal value. So forwards does nothing useful. Drop it.

.panel {
  animation: fade-in 0.3s;
}

In our Chrome 156 test, this one change let the menu show above the box below it.

If you really do need forwards, give the panel a z-index and position: relative so you control where its box sits.

Other things that quietly create a stacking context

These are the ones we run into most. The full list is on MDN.

  • a relatively or absolutely positioned box that also sets a number for z-index
  • any position: fixed or position: sticky box, even when it has no z-index
  • opacity below 1, such as 0.99
  • any non-none transform, filter, backdrop-filter, clip-path or mask
  • isolation: isolate
  • will-change that names one of those properties
  • a child of a flex or grid layout that sets a number for z-index, even without position

The last one surprises people. A flex or grid child with z-index: 1 can trap a menu just like a transform can.

Stop the next one before it starts

The fixes above work. But on a big team the same bug keeps coming back. Someone adds z-index: 1 to a section, and a menu somewhere else breaks.

Two habits help a lot.

1. Keep a small z-index scale

Put every layer your app uses in one place.

:root {
  --z-base: 0;
  --z-raised: 1;
  --z-header: 100;
  --z-overlay: 200;
  --z-modal: 300;
  --z-toast: 400;
}

.site-header { z-index: var(--z-header); }
.hero        { z-index: var(--z-base); }

Now nobody types 9999. They pick a named layer. And when two layers clash, you fix it in one file.

This is common in design systems, and it works best for top-level page parts. Inside a component, small local numbers like 1 and 2 are fine, because they stay inside that component's stacking context anyway.

2. Seal off sections that use z-index inside

If a section needs z-index for its own inner layout, wrap it with isolation: isolate.

.hero {
  isolation: isolate;
}

isolation: isolate is on MDN's list of stacking context triggers. It makes the section a closed box without moving it. The z-index values inside it can no longer fight with the header or with menus from other parts of the page.

When a menu has to beat everything

Some things, like a modal, must appear above the whole page no matter what. For those, the top layer is a better tool than any z-index.

Elements opened with the Popover API or with dialog.showModal() go into the browser's top layer. That layer sits above the normal page, so no ancestor can trap them. See the MDN links below for how each one works.

We tested both bugs in Chrome 156 only, so please check your layout in Firefox and Safari too.

Quick checklist when z-index "does nothing"

  1. Find the element that is hidden and the element that covers it.
  2. Walk up from the hidden one. Look for the first ancestor that makes a stacking context (use the list above).
  3. Compare that ancestor with the covering element, not the dropdown.
  4. Raise the ancestor, or remove the property that made the context.

Further reading

  • Stacking context (MDN): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_positioned_layout/Stacking_context
  • The z-index property (MDN): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/z-index
  • The isolation property (MDN): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/isolation
  • The animation-fill-mode property (MDN): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/animation-fill-mode
  • Popover API (MDN): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Popover_API
  • CSS 2 spec, Elaborate description of stacking contexts: https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/zindex.html

title: Figma: 'line-height: auto' não se traduz sozinho no Browser
description:
Se você já exportou um design do Figma e o espaçamento entre linhas "quebrou" não ficou perfeito como o seu perfeccionismo de pixel perfect queria no navegador, a explicação é pra você acalmar o seu suricato mental que reclama toda vez que isso acontece.

Vamos salvar 5 minutos do seu dia? Ok.

TL;DR

Contexto auto / normal
Figma Métricas intrínsecas da fonte (engine própria)
Navegador Métricas intrínsecas da fonte (engine do browser)
Resultado Pode divergir em 1–3px

Aos designers: defina valores explícitos. Seu dev agradece.

Agora falando mais sério, o problema:

No Figma, o campo de Line Height vem com a opção Auto selecionada por padrão. Parece inofensivo, até gentil! Mas esse "Auto" não é igual ao normal do CSS. Daí quando você é chato, aqueles pixels incomodam bastante.

O Auto do Figma usa as métricas verticais intrínsecas da fonte (hhea/OS/2 no .ttf/.otf), definidas pelo designer tipográfico. Cada fonte tem um valor diferente: uma pode ter ~1.2× o font-size, outra ~1.4×.

Vamos pegar a fonte Montserrat por exemplo. Com size 16px, o leading dela é 20px. Aliás, leading é o termo correto para essa parte técnica da tipografia.

No navegador, o line-height: normal (que é o default) também usa métricas da fonte, mas cada engine de texto resolve de forma ligeiramente diferente. Resultado: o que você vê no Figma não é pixel-perfect no Chrome, Firefox ou Safari. E se você, como eu, tem o hábito de usar um reset para line-height: 1, também vai quebrar.

Tá, mas e aí, como descobrir o leading real no Figma

O Figma não exibe o valor numérico do Auto. Mas dá pra puxar de um jeito muito simples que me fez sentir besta de tão óbvio:

  1. Crie um texto de uma linha só na fonte e tamanho desejado.
  2. Deixe o Line Height em Auto.
  3. Olhe a altura da camada de texto no painel de propriedades — esse é o leading em px. O height. Simples assim.

Na prática

O projeto com consistência entre design e código:

  • Defina um line-height fixo (em px ou em unidade relativa) no Figma. Ex.: 1.5 ou 24px pra fonte de 16px.
  • Evite depender do Auto se o dev vai reproduzir o layout manualmente... Ou se a sua IA não é treinada para pensar no leading.

Espero ter resolvido uma coceira de perfeccionismo por aí.

title: Cómo reencuadrar un vídeo a 9:16 con ffmpeg y diferencia de fotogramas
description:
Los editores de vídeo suelen vender el reencuadre automático como seguimiento de sujetos con IA. Para el caso más habitual, una persona que se mueve delante de un fondo que no cambia, basta un método mucho más simple: comparar cada fotograma con el anterior y ver dónde ha cambiado la imagen. La herramienta de reencuadre de la aplicación de escritorio osFoundry funciona así, en Rust y ffmpeg. Abajo está el mismo método en unas 60 líneas de Python, aplicado a un clip de 7.5 segundos en 1920×1080 con tres planos. Da los mismos recortes que la aplicación, al píxel.

1. Reducir el vídeo a fotogramas grises de 64×36

No hace falta mirar los fotogramas a tamaño completo para encontrar qué se ha movido. ffmpeg puede entregar el vídeo como bytes en bruto, cuatro fotogramas por segundo, reducido a 64×36 y convertido a un byte de gris por píxel:

import math, re, subprocess, sys

FFMPEG, SRC = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
W, H, FPS = 64, 36, 4

raw = subprocess.run(
    [FFMPEG, "-loglevel", "error", "-i", SRC,
     "-vf", f"fps={FPS},scale={W}:{H}", "-pix_fmt", "gray", "-f", "rawvideo", "-"],
    capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
frames = [raw[i:i + W * H] for i in range(0, len(raw) - W * H + 1, W * H)]

Cada fotograma ocupa 2304 bytes. El clip de 7.5 segundos da 30 fotogramas y por tanto 29 pares que comparar. Al reducir el tamaño también se promedia casi todo el grano, y eso importa en el paso siguiente.

2. Encontrar el centro de lo que cambió

Para cada par de fotogramas, se calcula la diferencia de cada celda, se ignoran las diferencias pequeñas y se obtiene el centro de masa del resto, ponderado por cuánto cambió cada celda:

def centroid(prev, curr, floor=12):
    total = sx = sy = 0
    for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(prev, curr)):
        d = abs(b - a)
        if d < floor:
            continue
        total += d
        sx += d * (i % W)
        sy += d * (i // W)
    if total < W * H * 0.5:
        return None
    return sx / total / W, sy / total / H

samples = [centroid(a, b) for a, b in zip(frames, frames[1:])]

Las dos constantes son lo que lo hace utilizable. El umbral de ruido de 12 (sobre 255) descarta los cambios que vienen del sensor y de la compresión. En este clip, con el umbral en 12 cuentan como cambiadas una media de 381 de las 2304 celdas. Con el umbral en 1 son 1855, casi todo el fotograma, y el centro se desplaza hacia la mitad de la imagen: la primera muestra cae en 0.44 del ancho en lugar de 0.40.

La segunda comprobación devuelve None cuando el cambio total es mínimo. Si nada se movió, el "centro del cambio" es el centro del ruido, y seguirlo hace que el encuadre se desplace sin motivo. None significa "mantén la posición anterior".

3. Limitar la velocidad del encuadre

Un centroide sin filtrar da un salto cada vez que entra una segunda persona en el plano. Limitar el paso al 5% del fotograma por muestra evita que el encuadre pegue latigazos:

def smooth(samples, step=0.05):
    cur = next((s for s in samples if s), (0.5, 0.5))
    out = []
    for s in samples:
        if s:
            cur = tuple(min(1, max(0, c + max(-step, min(step, t - c))))
                        for c, t in zip(cur, s))
        out.append(cur)
    return out

track = smooth(samples)

Parte de la primera observación real, así que un clip que empieza con una imagen fija no entra con un paneo desde el centro.

4. Encontrar los cortes con la puntuación de escena de ffmpeg

El filtro select de ffmpeg asigna a cada fotograma una puntuación de escena entre 0 y 1, y showinfo imprime los fotogramas que la superan. Las marcas de tiempo salen por stderr, no por stdout:

log = subprocess.run(
    [FFMPEG, "-hide_banner", "-i", SRC,
     "-filter_complex", "select='gt(scene,0.35)',showinfo", "-f", "null", "-"],
    capture_output=True, text=True).stderr
cuts = [round(float(t) * 1000) for t in re.findall(r"pts_time:([\d.]+)", log)]

En este clip encuentra cortes en 1767 ms y 4733 ms. Si se imprime la puntuación de cada fotograma (select='gte(scene,0)',metadata=print), se ve lo ancho que es el margen: los dos cortes puntúan 0.616 y 0.432, y ningún otro de los 225 fotogramas pasa de 0.068.

5. Un recorte por plano

Por último, se promedia la trayectoria dentro de cada plano y se coloca una ventana 9:16 alrededor de ese punto. 1080 × 9/16 es 607.5; el ancho se redondea hacia abajo a 606 porque H.264 necesita dimensiones pares.

duration = len(frames) * 1000 // FPS
per = duration / len(track)
bounds = [0] + [c for c in cuts if 0 < c < duration] + [duration]
cw = int(1080 * 9 / 16) // 2 * 2
for start, end in zip(bounds, bounds[1:]):
    a = int(start // per)
    part = track[a:max(a + 1, math.ceil(end / per))]
    bx = sum(p[0] for p in part) / len(part)
    x = min(max(round(1920 * bx - cw / 2), 0), 1920 - cw)
    print(f"{start / 1000:.2f}-{end / 1000:.2f}s  crop={cw}:1080:{x}:0")

0.00-1.77s  crop=606:1080:369:0
1.77-4.73s  crop=606:1080:668:0
4.73-7.50s  crop=606:1080:932:0

Son los mismos tres recortes que produjo la aplicación para este clip. El script entero tardó 3.5 segundos en este Mac, la mayor parte en el bucle de Python puro.

Los cortes importan más de lo que parece. Promediado sobre todo el clip, el sujeto queda en x = 707, a solo 50 píxeles de un recorte centrado simple (657), porque camina por la izquierda en un plano y por la derecha en otro. Solo por planos tiene sentido el promedio.

Volver a unir los planos

Los recortes se convierten en un único filter_complex: se recorta cada plano en el tiempo, se le aplica su crop y se unen las partes. Esta es la forma que construye la aplicación:

[0:v]trim=start=0.000:end=1.767,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,crop=606:1080:369:0[v0];
[0:v]trim=start=1.767:end=4.733,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,crop=606:1080:668:0[v1];
[0:v]trim=start=4.733:end=7.500,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,crop=606:1080:932:0[v2];
[v0][v1][v2]concat=n=3:v=1:a=0[out]

(Quita los saltos de línea al pasarlo a -filter_complex.) La salida es de 606×1080 y dura lo mismo que la entrada.

El Rust de la aplicación explica por qué no anima el recorte dentro de un plano, aunque ffmpeg podría hacerlo:

/// 🔴 Per scene, not per frame. ffmpeg can animate a crop, but a crop that moves continuously is
/// a pan the editor never asked for; cutting between fixed framings is what an editor would
/// actually do, and it is also what stays honest when the tracking is wrong — a bad framing
/// lasts one scene rather than smearing across the whole clip.
pub fn reframe_segments(
    cuts: &[i64],
    duration_ms: i64,
    track: &[(f64, f64)],
    width: u32,
    height: u32,
    target: f64,
) -> Vec<ReframeSegment> {

Dónde falla la diferencia de fotogramas

El método encuentra lo que se mueve, no a quién le importa. Funciona cuando el sujeto es lo principal que se mueve y la cámara está quieta. Falla cuando:

  • la cámara hace un paneo, así que cambian todas las celdas y el centro cae cerca del medio;
  • el fondo está cargado, como el tráfico o una multitud;
  • dos personas se mueven en lados opuestos y el promedio queda entre ellas.

Los reflejos son un caso más suave. En el primer plano de este clip, el reflejo de la mujer en una ventana también se mueve, pero queda cerca de ella, así que el encuadre la sigue encontrando. Un detector de caras o de personas resuelve mejor los casos difíciles, a costa de un modelo. La respuesta de la aplicación para esos casos es un ajuste manual: el usuario arrastra un punto sobre el sujeto y se omite el análisis.

La aplicación de escritorio usada aquí es gratuita en la página de descarga de osFoundry.

title: dx-styles 1.5.0: half the build time, and a benchmark you can rerun
description:
dx-styles 1.5.0 is out. It requires wyw-in-js 2.7.1, and that is where the speed comes from. On a generated design-system scene with 1,308 recipe variants, going from dx-styles 1.4.1 on wyw-in-js 2.4.4 to 1.5.0 on 2.7.1 takes a warm production build from 1.34 s to 0.68 s (−49%). With all styles in one module, it goes from 1.79 s to 0.78 s (−56%).

On wyw-in-js 2.7.1, dx-styles 1.4.1 and 1.5.0 build byte-identical bundles in the same time. If you already updated your bundler integration, you have had this speed for a while; 1.5.0 makes 2.7.1 the minimum.

In July I promised a build-time benchmark with numbers you can rerun rather than take on faith. It ships with this release: dx-styles/benchmarks. It builds the same scene with dx-styles, eight other libraries and plain CSS Modules, and the results include the cases where dx-styles does not win.

Where the speed comes from

dx-styles is a set of processors on top of wyw-in-js, the engine that also runs Linaria. A build evaluates your style declarations, writes the CSS and leaves class names in the JavaScript, and most of that time is spent in the engine.

Two releases did most of the work, and the two layouts of the scene respond to them differently.

wyw-in-js 2.5 made parsing cheaper on large projects: the parser hands its AST over without a JSON round trip, and parse results are shared between files. When the styles are spread over 41 modules, this is the bigger step, from 1.35 s to 0.91 s.

wyw-in-js 2.6 stopped several passes from doing their work once per styled declaration. CSS extraction used to copy the rules collected so far for every processor in a file, so its cost grew with the square of the number of styles; now the rules are merged in place, and the Stylis plugin chain is built once per file. The check of whether processor tags are referenced walked the whole program once per tag and now walks it once. With all styles in one module, this step is the larger one, from 1.34 s to 0.78 s, as you would expect from a cost that grew with the number of styles per file.

wyw-in-js 2.4 takes off 6 to 8%. 2.7 fixes an exponential loop check on deep module graphs, which does not show on this scene because its graph is shallow. The release also picks up the correctness fixes of wyw-in-js 2.5 to 2.7, and the changelog lists the ones that reach dx-styles builds.

Build time by wyw-in-js release

dx-styles wyw-in-js Per-component modules, s One styles module, s
1.3.0 2.3.0 1.43 1.94
1.3.0 2.4.4 1.35 1.78
1.3.0 2.5.1 0.91 1.34
1.3.0 2.6.0 0.68 0.78
1.3.0 2.7.1 0.68 0.78
1.4.1 2.4.4 1.34 1.79
1.4.1 2.7.1 0.68 0.78
1.5.0 2.7.1 0.68 0.78

The series uses dx-styles 1.3.0, the one release whose range accepts every wyw-in-js from 2.3.0 to 2.7.1; the last three rows are the actual upgrade path. Each number is the median of 7 warm builds. The entries alternate forward and backward in every round, so a slow minute on the machine hits all of them alike. Every step except the one from 2.6.0 to 2.7.1 is outside the noise, since the ranges of the runs do not overlap, and each dx-styles release builds a byte-identical bundle on every wyw-in-js release it was built with.

The same scene in other libraries

Library Warm build, s Total gzip, KB First paint, ms
styled-components 6.6.0 0.16 97.2 208
Emotion 11.14 0.17 93.5 212
Panda 2.4.0 0.21 89.2 188
next-yak 9.10.3 0.30 96.3 168
vanilla-extract 1.21.3 0.56 94.9 160
CSS Modules (no library) 0.66 102.9 156
dx-styles 1.5.0 0.68 99.4 162
Linaria 8.3.0 1.86 105.3 160
StyleX 0.19.1 2.06 89.5 168
Compiled 2.0.0 5.93 88.7 168

styled-components and Emotion build fastest because they do no CSS work at build time. Their styles travel in the JavaScript and are injected at runtime, which is also why they paint about 45 to 50 ms later than dx-styles. Of the libraries that extract CSS at build time, dx-styles builds in about the time of plain CSS Modules, which have no CSS-in-JS layer at all; the 0.02 s between them is noise.

Linaria runs on the same engine, wyw-in-js 2.7.1, and here it builds in 1.86 s because of how this port models tokens. Every style module interpolates tokens from a shared JS object, so the engine evaluates that object for each of the 41 modules. dx-styles declares its tokens once, as a contract that its processors resolve without evaluating anything. Written with static CSS variables instead, the same Linaria scene builds in 0.38 s, faster than dx-styles, so the dx-styles layer (typed token contracts and recipes) costs about 0.3 s on top of the engine on this scene.

The output of every library is also checked in a browser by comparing 22 computed properties of all 3,642 elements with the dx-styles render. All of them match except Compiled 2.0.0. With its default class hash, two different declarations, color: var(--tk-color-danger600) and color: var(--tk-color-info800), get the same atomic class, and 5 elements are painted the wrong color. Hash collisions are a known issue of the default hash. The opt-in collisionResistantHash option fixes this one with the same build time and 1.4 KB more gzip.

Where dx-styles does not win

  • Panda (0.21 s), next-yak (0.30 s), vanilla-extract (0.56 s) and Linaria with static CSS variables (0.38 s) build faster than dx-styles (0.68 s), and plain CSS Modules (0.66 s) build in the same time.
  • dx-styles ships 99.4 KB gzip in total, more than every other lane here except Linaria and plain CSS Modules. Its CSS is 382 KB raw against 314 KB for vanilla-extract, which hashes its token variable names. dx-styles keeps them readable (--tk-color-accent600) because they are the theming contract.
  • Its first paint (162 ms) is level with CSS Modules, vanilla-extract and Linaria at 156 to 160 ms.

How it was measured

The scene is generated from one description: 104 design tokens, 45 structural slots and 34 recipe families (buttons, tabs, badges, alerts, inputs, menu items and more) with 1,308 variants. It renders as an issue-tracker screen plus a gallery of every variant, 3,642 elements in all, with the styles in 41 modules. Each library has its own generator, which writes the scene with that library's token layer and API and builds it through its documented Vite integration.

  • Machine: Apple M3 Max (16 cores, 64 GB), macOS 26.6.2, Node 24.4.1, Vite 8.3.5, React 19.3.1; Chromium 156 for first paint.
  • Every library is its own project with exact pins and a lockfile. The whole wyw-in-js stack is pinned through npm overrides, and npm ls checks that each pinned package is installed once.
  • All projects are installed in one session. The harness then waits 90 s for the file-system indexing that a fresh install triggers, does a warm-up build of each, and runs 7 rounds. A round builds every project cold and then warm, in alternating order, and starts only when the machine is quiet. The tables give the median of the warm builds. Cold builds are at most about 0.1 s slower (Panda's includes its codegen); RESULTS.md has them, with the minimums.
  • First paint is measured in headless Chromium on a fast machine with no throttling, so a difference of a few milliseconds means nothing; only the gap of the runtime libraries holds.
  • It is one machine and one scene, and the scene is large and regular on purpose, which is not how every app looks. Build times are comparable only within one run.

To rerun it:

git clone https://github.com/dx-styles/benchmarks
cd benchmarks
npm ci
npx playwright install chromium
npm run bench

A full run takes about an hour. If a library is set up unfairly, or a scenario you care about is missing, open a pull request.

Upgrading 

npm install dx-styles@^1.5.0
npm install -D @wyw-in-js/vite@2.7.1

With Next.js, update @wyw-in-js/nextjs to 2.7.1 instead; with another bundler, update its wyw-in-js integration. Update the integration together with dx-styles: the build runs the transform that the integration installs, and dx-styles 1.5.0 needs wyw-in-js 2.7.1 or newer.

Anton Evzhakov maintains Linaria and is the author of wyw-in-js, the zero-runtime engine behind Linaria and MUI's Pigment CSS. He builds dx-styles.

title: TTF to WOFF2 in the tab when the brand font is still a desktop file
description:
Brand just dropped a .ttf (or .otf) in Slack. Design opened it on macOS and it looks perfect. Marketing wants it on the landing page by Friday. The web does not want a raw TrueType file sitting in /public/fonts.

I used to either ship the TTF "for now", bounce it through Font Squirrel, or ask design to export WOFF2 from a desktop app I don't have installed. That path works for a brand refresh. It's painful when the file already exists and you just need a web-safe package before a deploy.

What the web actually wants

Browsers can load TTF. That doesn't mean you should ship it as the primary format.

A boring but complete handoff usually includes:

  • WOFF2 — the format you put in @font-face first (smaller, modern browsers)
  • Optional WOFF — legacy fallback if you still care about very old clients
  • Optional subset — Latin / brand glyphs only, not the full multilingual dump from the foundry
  • A license note — so the next person doesn't assume every desktop font is free to host

You don't need five formats. You need the format your CSS actually references — and it should come from the same master file so metrics stay consistent.

What goes wrong with the usual shortcuts

Ship the TTF raw in /public/fonts — works in Chrome until someone audits payload size, or a license check asks how you redistributed the desktop file. Also often larger than WOFF2 for the same glyphs.

Font Squirrel / "webfont generator" upload sites — easy when the font is free. Awkward when the mark is a licensed brand face and you just put it in a stranger's converter bucket.

Desktop converters / Glyphs / FontLab export — correct for a foundry pipeline; overkill when you're on a locked laptop and the only ask is "make this loadable on the marketing site."

Ask design for "the web font package" — right for a rebrand; slow when they already handed you the TTF and assumed frontend would package it.

Copy-paste @font-face from an old project that still lists truetype first — you'll keep serving the heavy file forever because nobody revisits font CSS until Lighthouse yells.

What I actually need from the convert step

For frontend / DX use, the checklist is boring:

  1. WOFF2 out — not just "a smaller TTF"
  2. Same family metrics — no mystery tracking changes after convert
  3. No upload — brand font stays in the tab (Offline litmus still applies)
  4. Predictable name — BrandSans-Regular.woff2, not download (3).woff2
  5. Optional subset note — know whether you converted the full face or trimmed glyphs

If the tool can't do those five, I'm back to fonttools / woff2_compress in a one-off script.

A tab that fits the handoff

When the brand font is still a desktop .ttf / .otf and I just need WOFF2 before a deploy, I've used Uwarp's TTF → WOFF2 tool — drop the file, grab WOFF2 in the browser. Worth trying when the alternative is another desktop install or an upload converter you can't audit.

For a recurring pipeline (every brand refresh, every white-label tenant), script it: fonttools ttLib / pyftsubset, Google's woff2 CLI, or a tiny CI job that emits the files your @font-face lists. The tab is for the one-offs that shouldn't block a PR.

Wire the files you actually ship

A few rules that stopped me from collecting orphan fonts in /public:

  • Commit WOFF2 (and maybe WOFF), not the raw TTF — keep the master desktop file in the design / brand repo if needed, not in the public web root
  • @font-face with font-display and a real fallback stack — don't leave font-family: BrandSans without a system fallback
  • Name by family + weight (BrandSans-700.woff2), never final_font_v2.ttf
  • Document license + source in the README so the next person doesn't "just host whatever Slack sent"

Font packaging is packaging, not design. Treat it like that and the folder stays boring.

Tiny habit

Next time a repo needs a web font and you already have a clean TTF from brand, don't reopen Font Squirrel and don't upload the licensed face. Convert in a local-ish tab (or a one-liner CLI), drop the WOFF2 next to your CSS, verify @font-face loads, ship.

Fewer blocked deploys. Fewer mystery .ttf files in /public/fonts. Same brand face — just the format the browser and the network tab actually want.

title: Shey Light Dey House? How I Built an ESP32 Power Monitor for My Home
description:
Originally published on my blog.

Imagine you’re at work, and you are deciding on whether to charge your devices before you leave office or to charge them when you get home, but then you wonder, "omo shey light dey house?". Well, I often find myself in situations where I want to know if I currently have light, when they took the light, or how long I've had light. So, I built a system that tells me exactly that.

The Idea

To solve this issue, I thought of building a simple device that communicates with my web server to notify me when I have power or not. The device works by sending a beat —an HTTP request every 30 seconds to my server. The device is plugged into a socket that only gets power from NEPA (the grid), not from the inverter.

With this socket setup, I only receive beat requests whenever there is direct power supply from NEPA since the device is off otherwise. So all I have to do to determine if I have power at home is to check on the server side, when I last received a beat from the device. If the database says that the last beat was received more than 90 seconds ago, I can assume that there is no power at home.

System Architecture

An ESP32-C3 dev module is programmed to send a request every 30 seconds to a small VPS running a Rust (Axum) backend service and an SQLite database.

When the server receives a request, it records it in the SQLite database. A simple dashboard built, with no extra libraries like React, displays analytics that answer my opening questions: whether power is ON/OFF, how long it has been ON/OFF, and how many hours of power there's been today and this week. The dashboard polls the server every 30 seconds and the server queries the SQLite database to get the relevant data.

The ESP32 Device

How does the ESP32 device work?

The ESP32-C3 is powered by a USB cable which is connected to a socket that only works when NEPA is available.

When NEPA is available, the ESP32 turns on and begins sending beat requests to the server every 30 seconds.

The ESP32 is attached to a 3D printed sleeve that slides over a USB-C phone charger. I used a spare phone charger I had lying around.

What is a beat request made of?

Each beat is a small JSON POST to /beat. Here is a sample request below:

POST /beat HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>

{"device_id": "homev1", "boot_id": 2435, "reset_reason": "power_on", "uptime_ms": 4120}

A beat request is made of 4 fields:

  1. device_id: This lets the server tell devices apart, so one server could be used to monitor multiple devices.
  2. boot_id: This is randomly generated every time the ESP32 powers on. It lets the server detect a reboot of the ESP32, which usually means they took the light and brought it back.
  3. reset_reason: This contains the reason why the ESP32 rebooted. The ESP32 could reboot either due to power outage, or due to random system crashes. A reset_reason of power_on or brownout is most likely because of a power outage, while a reset_reason of watchdog or panic means the ESP32 board crashed and there might not have been a power outage. See Espressif's full list of reset reasons.
  4. uptime_ms: When the ESP32 boots up, it spends some time setting up the Wi-Fi connection before the first beat request is sent. This tracks how long the ESP32 has been on. The server subtracts uptime_ms from the current time to find the actual time when the power came back.

A beat request also contains an "Authorization" header carrying an API key, so only my device can send beats.

The boot_id and reset_reason are set once when the board boots:

const char* getReasonForReset() {
    esp_reset_reason_t reason = esp_reset_reason();

    switch (reason) {
        // ...
        case esp_reset_reason_t::ESP_RST_PANIC:
            return "panic";
        case esp_reset_reason_t::ESP_RST_INT_WDT:
        case esp_reset_reason_t::ESP_RST_TASK_WDT:
        case esp_reset_reason_t::ESP_RST_WDT:
            return "watchdog";
        default:
            return "unknown";
    }
}
void setup() {
    // ...
    // Connect to Wi-Fi network
    setupWifi();

    boot_id = esp_random();
    reset_reason = getReasonForReset();
}

The Web Server

The backend code that handles all requests and communicates with the SQLite database is written in Rust. SQLx and Axum were the main libraries used for database communication and request handling respectively.

How is a beat request stored in the database?

The server doesn't store beats. It stores power periods. A power period represents a continuous stretch of power, i.e., a period (duration) in which there is light.

CREATE TABLE power_periods (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  device_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  boot_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  reset_reason TEXT NULL,
  started_at TEXT NOT NULL,
  last_seen_at TEXT NOT NULL
);

The started_at column represents when the power came on, i.e., the time they brought light, and last_seen_at is the time the latest beat for that period was received.

When a beat request arrives, the Rust backend code first checks if the boot_id of that beat is the same as the boot_id in the last updated power period for that device_id.

  • If the boot_ids are the same, then we update the last_seen_at column of the last updated power period to the current time.
  • If the boot_ids are different or there are no power periods yet, we insert a new power period row into the database. The started_at column of the new row is the current time minus uptime_ms. A change in the boot_id usually means that there was an outage.

This method of using each beat to update or insert a new power period instead of storing each beat is advantageous because it dramatically reduces the growth rate of the database.

How does it know there is no light?

Say the server receives a beat from the ESP32 device at 12:10 AM, and then receives no new beat from that device within a 90-second window. We can assume the ESP32 is not receiving any power, and therefore there is no light. This isn't 100% certain: if the Wi-Fi the ESP32 is connected to goes down, the beats stop too.

Using the absence of a regular signal to detect a problem is the same idea as a dead man's switch.

Dashboard

The dashboard shows if there is currently light, how long there has been light or how long there has been no light. It was written using plain HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript.

The dashboard refreshes every 30 seconds. The timeline chart shown in the dashboard is drawn as an SVG by hand, without a chart library.

Improvements and Future Ideas

  1. High and low voltage alerts: Add a voltmeter to the ESP32 device and then send alerts to the users on the dashboard in the case of a low voltage or high voltage situation.
  2. Telling power sources apart: Modify the device to be able to distinguish between various power sources (inverter, NEPA, generator) based on variation in frequency of the power source. My guess is that each power source has a unique frequency variation. For instance, a generator's frequency might fluctuate a lot while that of an inverter might be very stable.
  3. Predicting power: Add a prediction mechanism that can predict if you'll have power and at what time.
  4. More homes: The device_id already lets one server track several devices. With devices in various homes, the dashboard could become a live map of which areas have light.

Conclusion

Now, when I'm away from home wondering whether there's light, I don't have to call anyone. I just open the dashboard.

The only thing I actually paid for was the ESP32-C3 (₦9,000) from Nerdshed. Everything else I already had: a spare charger, a USB-C cable, my VPS, and my domain I use for other projects.

The full code, firmware and server, is on GitHub. If you build your own, or have ideas for any of the improvements above, I'd love to hear about it.

title: How much does a Solana smart contract audit cost? Numbers by project size
description:
Audit pricing is mostly effort: how many security engineers, for how many days. By the method used in our free audit cost calculator ($1,600-2,800 per engineer-day, Anchor unless noted, fix review included, no rush), indicative costs look like this.

Project Code in scope Engineer-days Indicative cost
Token vesting (simple) 500 lines 3.5 $5,500-10,000
Staking (standard) 1,500 lines 7.5 $12,000-21,000
Lending, 2 programs, oracle (DeFi) 3,000 lines 23 $37,000-64,500
Perps DEX, native Rust, 3 programs 6,000 lines 56.5 $90,500-158,000

Audit next to the build

For a tiny program the audit can cost more than the build (a vesting program with a basic interface is about $3,000-5,500 to build), because an audit day costs several times a freelancer day. For a large lending protocol the audit is roughly 44-50% of the build cost.

What drives the price

  • Code size in scope, excluding tests and generated code.
  • Complexity: custom math, token flows, CPIs, oracles and upgrade logic.
  • Number of programs and integrations.
  • Timeline: rush audits cost more and often find less.
  • Deliverables: fix review, public report, design review.

These are indicative figures, not quotes. Full guide with FAQ and the calculator: https://orivions.com/blog/solana-smart-contract-audit-cost
Checklists to prepare before the audit: https://github.com/JakeMalarczyk/solana-security-checklists

title: How a Gallery-Style Shopify Store Can Sell Stock and Take Custom Enquiries
description:
Public interface screenshot from NM Art & Design.

NM Art & Design brings sculpture, ceramics, textiles, lighting and collectible furniture together in a gallery-like catalogue. ESH Gruppa designed the experience. The public site lets visitors browse by work or artist, and the Ignith Lamp page shows how an enquiry can begin without leaving the work behind. This is a design case study followed by a proposed Shopify implementation. Design case study · Live product page

Design decisions

Give the artwork the strongest visual signal. Black, warm greys and a pale canvas make room for the objects’ materials. A warm accent identifies important actions. The live enquiry page uses it on both Enquire and Send. Large uppercase titles, thin arrows and plus signs leave the photography room to breathe. The desktop catalogue shows three columns, while the artist directory shows four and has a separate alphabet index.

Support two buying paths. A priced, purchasable piece can go to the bag. A piece that needs a quote can say Price upon request and open an enquiry drawer. On the Ignith Lamp page that drawer keeps the title, artist, thumbnail and pricing status in view. Name, email, country and a short message give the seller enough context to follow up. The site is doing more than collecting an email address: it carries the visitor’s selection into the next step.

Give professional buyers a place to assemble a room. Save to Project and Download PDF sit under the main action. The design case explores named projects, shareable selections, documents and invoice-based payment. Public pages show the save and download entry points. Logged-in permissions and payment behaviour were not tested for this article. Artists, exhibition archives and product pages also offer routes back into the catalogue rather than treating each item as an isolated listing.

Six Shopify modules

Module What the case shows Data and implementation Front-end and acceptance check
Gallery grid and menu Spacious desktop grids and a compact menu Start with an Online Store 2.0 theme. Define canvas, text and accent variables and adapt the theme menu drawer. Use CSS Grid and test narrower viewports. A long title, portrait image and price status should all remain legible. Check keyboard focus when the menu opens and closes.
Artist index and exhibition archive Alphabet navigation, material labels and related works Define artist and exhibition metaobjects, and reference the artist from the product. Enable metaobject web pages if artists need their own URLs. Render artist information from the reference. For related works, maintain explicit references or build a supported lookup. A product-to-artist reference does not automatically create a reverse list.
Buy and enquire A priced buy path and a drawer for quote-led work Store the transaction mode on the product or variant. Keep size, finish, year and edition in separate fields. Read the current variant in the buy-button area. Verify quick add and alternate sales paths too. Include the selected variant and product URL in the enquiry instead of assuming the form knows them.
Filters and selected chips Availability, category, artist, material, edition and price Configure filters in Search & Discovery. Keep made-to-order separate from inventory availability, using a supported field type. Use theme facets for the desktop panel and mobile drawer. Test selecting, removing and clearing filters, including a combination with no results.
Product and project PDFs A way to share specifications with a client Read the same structured data used on the product page. Use print styles for a save-to-PDF workflow or a server-side exporter for a downloadable file. Check size, finish, variant, quantity and whether prices should appear. Keep quotations as snapshots, separate from a current specification sheet.
PRO projects and invoice-led payment Named selections, a shareable project and a payment workflow Start with the project data and its permissions. Evaluate a wishlist app against the actual sharing requirements or build a dedicated module. Use Draft Orders for reviewed quotes and assess native B2B terms separately. Test owner, read-only recipient and unauthorised visitor. Basic, Grow, Advanced and Plus have native B2B features, with plan-specific differences. Manual payment leaves an order pending until payment is received and recorded.

Metaobject web pages · Storefront filters · B2B plan features · Draft-order payments

Three checks before launch

Images. Identify which image actually determines Largest Contentful Paint. Prioritise that image and give the browser responsive sizes. Defer images outside the initial viewport and load lightbox assets when needed. Check the request waterfall on mobile rather than loading every slide at the same priority. Shopify theme performance

Enquiries. In a test submission, confirm that the seller receives the right product, variant and destination. Record a GA4 generate_lead event only after a successful submission and where consent allows. Keep qualified enquiries, quotations and completed sales as distinct steps. GA4 recommended events

Specifications. Render material, dimensions, colour, year and edition as readable text. Keep the product page, PDFs and any applicable Product JSON-LD aligned. Avoid publishing a price for an offer that does not exist. Change one measurement in a preview theme and see whether all intended outputs follow it. Google product structured data

Start with one real piece customers can buy, one they need to enquire about and one that belongs in the archive. If the three paths work from the catalogue through to the seller’s next action, the team has a concrete basis for deciding how much of the professional workspace to build.

title: ai-ui.fscss: shell, messages, prompt, and stream — without a UI kit runtime
description:
ai-ui.fscss is a presentation layer for AI product surfaces in the FSCSS ecosystem: tokens, layout, and chrome only. No models, no streaming clients, no backend.

Your app still owns data, events, and model I/O. This module owns how the shell, messages, prompt bar, and related pieces look and sit on the page — and it compiles to plain CSS.

What it covers

Surface Role
Shell App grid: sidebar + main + room for the prompt
Messages User / assistant rows, bubbles, avatars
Prompt Textarea + send control
Stream Caret on partial assistant text
Thinking Processing dots
Citations Source chips under answers
Artifacts Code / JSON / doc cards
Workflow Step nodes and edges
Usage Token and metric cards

Same contract as other FSCSS modules: import registers @define helpers, you call them with host selectors, markup uses those class names, design tokens flow through CSS variables.

Install mindset

You need FSCSS 1.2.6+ (CLI, browser runtime, IDE, or the Python wrapper - same language).

Registry-style import:

@import((*) from ai-ui)

Or selective, when you only want part of the surface:

@import((
  ai-root,
  ai-theme-research,
  ai-shell,
  ai-messages,
  ai-message,
  ai-message-assistant,
  ai-bubble,
  ai-citations,
  ai-citation,
  ai-stream
) from ai-ui)

In the browser IDE, package automation can scaffold demos with something like libon ai-ui / libck ai-ui to enable the pack in your workspace.

Tokens and themes

Start from a root once:

@ai-root()                 /* :root */
/* or @ai-root(root.my-scope) for a scoped tree */

Themes override token values on that root:

Helper Character
@ai-theme-minimal() Quiet, near-monochrome
@ai-theme-copilot() Blues / greens, product-chat feel
@ai-theme-research() Slate + cyan, citation-heavy
@ai-theme-support() Calm support-desk green
@ai-theme-dashboard() Stronger accent for ops / agent boards

Composition presets apply root + theme in one call:

@ai-compose-copilot()
/* same idea as @ai-root() + @ai-theme-copilot() */

Also available: @ai-compose-minimal(), @ai-compose-research(), @ai-compose-support(), @ai-compose-dashboard().

You still call shell / message / prompt helpers for structure. Presets only set the token layer.

Typical tokens you will override locally:

  • Surfaces: --ai-bg, --ai-surface, --ai-card
  • Brand: --ai-accent, --ai-accent-2
  • Roles: --ai-user, --ai-assistant
  • Type: --ai-text, --ai-text-muted
  • Layout: --ai-sidebar-w, --ai-prompt-h, --ai-msg-max 
.ai-shell {
  --ai-accent: #a78bfa;
  --ai-sidebar-w: 240px;
}

Minimal copilot shell

Structure helpers take the host selector:

@import((*) from ai-ui)

@ai-compose-copilot()

@ai-shell(.ai-shell)
@ai-sidebar(.ai-sidebar)
@ai-main(.ai-main)
@ai-messages(.ai-messages)
@ai-message(.ai-message)
@ai-message-user(.ai-message-user)
@ai-message-assistant(.ai-message-assistant)
@ai-bubble(.ai-bubble)
@ai-avatar(.ai-avatar)
@ai-prompt(.ai-prompt)
@ai-prompt-box(.ai-prompt-box)
@ai-prompt-send(.ai-prompt-send)

Markup shape:

<div class="ai-shell">
  <aside class="ai-sidebar">/* threads, nav */</aside>
  <main class="ai-main">
    <div class="ai-messages">
      <div class="ai-message ai-message-user">
        <div class="ai-avatar">U</div>
        <div class="ai-bubble">Track order 12389</div>
      </div>
      <div class="ai-message ai-message-assistant">
        <div class="ai-avatar">AI</div>
        <div class="ai-bubble">Out for delivery…</div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <form class="ai-prompt" onsubmit="return false">
      <textarea class="ai-prompt-box" placeholder="Ask…" rows="1"></textarea>
      <button class="ai-prompt-send" type="submit" aria-label="Send">↑</button>
    </form>
  </main>
</div>

User rows align one way; assistant rows the other. Bubbles and avatars are separate pieces so you can swap markup without fighting the layout grid.

Stream, thinking, citations, artifacts

When the answer is still arriving:

@ai-stream(.ai-stream)
@ai-thinking(.ai-thinking)

<div class="ai-bubble ai-stream">Partial answer…</div>
<div class="ai-thinking">
  <span class="ai-dot"></span>
  <span class="ai-dot"></span>
  <span class="ai-dot"></span>
  Thinking…
</div>

Citations under an answer:

@ai-citations(.ai-citations)
@ai-citation(.ai-citation)

<div class="ai-citations">
  <a class="ai-citation" href="#"><span class="ai-cite-num">1</span> source.api</a>
</div>

Artifact card (code / JSON / doc):

@ai-artifacts(.ai-artifacts)
@ai-artifact-header(.ai-artifact-header)
@ai-artifact-body(.ai-artifact-body)

<div class="ai-artifacts">
  <div class="ai-artifact-header">
    <span>status.json</span>
    <span>JSON</span>
  </div>
  <div class="ai-artifact-body">{ /* … */ }</div>
</div>

Workflow strip for agent steps:

@ai-workflow(.ai-workflow)
@ai-node(.ai-node)
@ai-edge(.ai-edge)

Usage / stats for an ops board:

@ai-usage(.ai-usage)
@ai-stat(.ai-stat)

<div class="ai-usage">
  <div class="ai-stat">
    <span class="ai-stat-label">Tokens today</span>
    <span class="ai-stat-value">48.2k</span>
    <span class="ai-stat-delta up">+12%</span>
  </div>
</div>

Tool chips (search / generate / etc.):

@ai-tools(.ai-tools)
@ai-tool-chip(.ai-tool-chip)

Utilities when you need a plain card or divider in the same token system: @ai-card, @ai-divider, @ai-scroll-fade.

Compose with others

ai-ui does not draw charts. For an ops dashboard you combine modules:

  • ai-ui — shell, message column, prompt, workflow, usage chrome
  • st-core@v2 — pure CSS charts from arrays and custom properties
  • circle-progress — rings for quotas or completion
  • overlapui — avatar stacks in a sidebar or header

Import both (or all) and keep selectors in their own namespaces. Example depth pattern:

@import((*) from ai-ui)
@import((*) from st-core@v2)

@ai-compose-dashboard()
@st-root()
/* chart fill / line helpers on a card inside .ai-main */

That is the same idea as a product screen: one token story for the AI chrome, another for the chart series, no shared class collisions by design.

What this is not

  • Not a chat backend
  • Not a streaming protocol
  • Not a replacement for accessibility work in your markup (labels, live regions, focus order stay your job)

It is the CSS layer so you are not rewriting the same shell for every AI experiment.

Mental model

  1. Register — @import from ai-ui
  2. Theme — @ai-compose-* or @ai-root + @ai-theme-*
  3. Structure — @ai-shell, @ai-messages, @ai-prompt, … with your selectors
  4. Markup — class names that match those selectors
  5. Ship — compile with CLI / IDE / Python wrapper, or prototype with the browser runtime

Selective imports keep the emitted CSS small when you only need research citations or a dashboard strip.

If you are building copilots, research assistants, support bots, or agent ops boards and you already like FSCSS modules, ai-ui.fscss is the matching piece for the conversation chrome: detailed enough to look intentional, light enough that the framework and the model stay outside the stylesheet.

Source and full helper list live in the ai-ui.fscss repo
try a compose preset first, then add stream, citations, and artifacts only where the product actually needs them.

title: One screen in our app has eight empty states, and four of them are the same emptiness for four different reasons
description:
The screen in Nakodo that shows a brand its conversations with creators has five views: Needs you, In progress, Introduced, Closed, All. It is behind the login, so you cannot look at it, which you can confirm in one line:

$ curl -sI https://nakodo.app/campaigns/x/outreach | head -2
HTTP/2 307
location: /login?next=%2Fcampaigns%2Fx%2Foutreach

What I can show you is the code, and the thing worth showing is not the table. It is the eight different ways this one screen says "there is nothing here", because that turned out to be where most of the thinking went.

Five views over eight states

A conversation has one of eight statuses, and they live in the schema with a comment each:

export const OUTREACH_STATUSES = [
  "drafting",   // the first email is being written
  "review",     // waiting for the brand to approve the first email
  "queued",     // approved; goes out at nextActionAt
  "contacted",  // sent, no reply yet
  "talking",    // the creator replied and Nakodo answered
  "needs_you",  // the creator asked something only the brand can answer
  "handed_off", // the creator is interested and was introduced to the brand
  "closed",
] as const;

The views are a separate list, in src/lib/outreach/labels.ts, and they are deliberately not one view per status:

export const THREAD_VIEWS = [
  { key: "attention", label: "Needs you", statuses: ["needs_you", "review"] },
  { key: "active", label: "In progress", statuses: ["drafting", "queued", "contacted", "talking"] },
  { key: "introduced", label: "Introduced", statuses: ["handed_off"] },
  { key: "closed", label: "Closed", statuses: ["closed"] },
  { key: "all", label: "All", statuses: null },
] as const satisfies readonly { key: string; label: string; statuses: readonly OutreachStatus[] | null }[];

Eight statuses, four buckets, one catch-all with statuses: null. The grouping is by who the next move belongs to, not by what happened: Needs you is the two states where the brand has to do something, In progress is the four where Nakodo does, Introduced and Closed are the two where nobody does.

Count the statuses in those four lists and you get eight, each one exactly once. That is a partition, it is load bearing, and nothing enforces it. Add a ninth status tomorrow and it appears in All, in none of the other four views, and no test fails. The fix is a type-level one: a check that the union of the four statuses arrays is OutreachStatus, which TypeScript can express and which I have not written. That is the first of two findings in this post.

The screen opens on the view with work in it 

const attention = inView("attention").length;
const requested = THREAD_VIEWS.find((v) => v.key === sp.view)?.key;
const view: ThreadView = requested ?? (attention > 0 ? "attention" : "all");

No stored preference, no "last view" cookie. If the URL asks for a view, you get it; otherwise the screen opens on Needs you when something needs you, and All when nothing does. An unknown ?view= in the URL falls through the same ??, because requested comes from a lookup in the list rather than from the query string, so a typo or a stale link is not an error, it is just the default.

The tab bar shows the count of every view next to its label, and the one that needs the brand gets a mark beside it:

<nav className="..." aria-label="Conversations by state">
  {THREAD_VIEWS.map((v) => (
    <Link key={v.key} href={href({ view: v.key })} aria-current={view === v.key ? "page" : undefined} scroll={false} ...>
      {v.key === "attention" && attention > 0 && <AttentionMark label="Waiting on you" />}
      {v.label}
      <span className="text-xs tabular-nums opacity-80">{inView(v.key).length}</span>
    </Link>
  ))}
</nav>

scroll={false} because switching view should not jump the page to the top, aria-current="page" because the selected tab is a link to the page you are on, and the counts are tabular-nums so they do not shuffle the labels sideways as they change.

One more line in that area is the sort:

const shown = view === "active" ? scheduledFirst(inView(view)) : inView(view);

Only In progress is reordered, and the comment says why: "In progress leads with the emails waiting to go out, soonest first: the rest of that view is already out of the brand's hands." Four of the five views are a list of things to read. One of them is a timetable.

The list gets key={view}, which remounts it on every view change, with one line of explanation:

<ThreadList
  // A new view starts again at the first page, with nothing selected.
  key={view}

Using key to throw client state away is one of the few React tricks I reach for without hesitating. The alternative is an effect that watches view and resets three pieces of state, and that effect will be wrong the day a fourth piece is added.

Four ways to have no conversations

Here is the first empty state, which is not one empty state:

<EmptyState illustration={<AlcyEnvelope size="m" className="illo-loop" />} title="No conversations yet.">
  {!automatic
    ? `Select ${w.many} on the ${w.Many} tab and choose Contact. Nakodo writes the first email and takes it from there.`
    : !hasOffer
      ? "Save your proposal first. Nakodo then starts writing to the best fits, and the first emails appear here."
      : !startsConversations(campaign)
        ? "Nakodo starts writing to the best fits once the campaign's emails are running."
        : "Nakodo writes to the best fits as they're found. The first emails appear here within a few minutes."}
</EmptyState>

Same heading, four different bodies, in a deliberate order: what you must do, then what you must do first, then what is switched off, then nothing is wrong and it is coming.

The reason this is four sentences and not one is that "No conversations yet" has four completely different meanings in this product, and three of them are actionable. A brand that chose manual sending is waiting for itself. A brand with no proposal saved has blocked the thing it is waiting for. A paused campaign is not going to produce anything, ever, until it is resumed. And a brand that has done everything right is correctly looking at an empty screen for a couple of minutes.

A single generic sentence there, which is what the first version had, is the app knowing exactly why nothing is happening and refusing to say.

Four more, one per view

Once there are conversations but the current view has none, each view says what would be in it:

View Heading Body
Needs you Nothing needs you right now. First emails to approve and replies Nakodo can't answer show up here.
In progress Nothing in progress right now. First emails being written or waiting to go out, and conversations Nakodo is carrying on, show up here.
Introduced No introductions yet. When a creator says yes, Nakodo introduces you by email, and they're listed here.
Closed Nothing closed yet. When a creator says no, doesn't reply after the follow-ups, or you stop a conversation, it's listed here.

Every one of those bodies is a definition of the view. An empty view is the only moment a reader will ever read the definition of that view, because a view with rows in it explains itself. So the empty state is not an apology, it is documentation that appears exactly when it is useful and never when it is not.

There is no fifth row in that table, and there is a comment saying why:

) : shown.length === 0 ? (
  // All is never empty once there are conversations, so only the other views get here.

Which is true, and is an invariant expressed in a comment rather than in code, and is the second finding: if that ever stops being true the screen renders the Closed empty state for the All view, because the chain of ternaries ends with closed as the fallback. A switch over the four keys with no default would have made that impossible, the same way the rest of the repo does it.

The mascot changes with the state too: an envelope that loops while something is being written, a perched bird when nothing needs you, a ring for introductions, a sleeping bird for closed. There are twelve poses of the mascot in src/components/illo and twenty EmptyState call sites in the app; the one with no illustration at all is the error boundary, which was its own post, because a mascot next to a failure is the app being pleased with itself while the customer is not.

What it adds up to

Eight states, five views, eight empty strings of prose, and two findings worth fixing: a partition that nothing checks, and a ternary chain whose fallback is a lie waiting to happen.

The ratio is the thing I keep noticing. The table in this screen is a few dozen lines. The explanation of what it means when the table has nothing in it is more than that, and it is the part people actually read, because every single user sees the empty version of this screen before they ever see a full one. How it works is the public version of the same sentences, written for somebody who has not signed up yet.
