title: Our getting-started checklist stores no progress, and three of its five steps are asking about different campaigns
description:
Nakodo has one screen behind the login that a new account lands on, and at the bottom of it, until it is no longer true, there is a checklist: start a campaign, review and launch, wait while Nakodo finds creators, approve the first emails. A progress bar, a tick, one hint under whichever step is next.

It is 118 lines in src/app/(app)/campaigns/checklist.tsx, it is used in exactly one place, and there is no table behind it. No onboarding_steps rows, no completed_at columns, no dismiss button, nothing to migrate when a step changes. It is derived from the campaign rows the page has already loaded for other reasons.

This post is that design, what it costs, and the bug writing it up found.

Progress as a projection

The component takes a list of campaign summaries. Each one carries what the list page already selects anyway:

type CampaignSummary = {
  id: string;
  kind: CampaignKind;
  status: string;
  launchedAt: Date | null;
  hasOffer: boolean;
  autoSend: boolean;
  conversations: number;
  contacted: number;
};

Every step's done is an expression over that:

const launched = campaigns.some((c) => c.launchedAt);
const steps: Step[] = [
  { label: "Start a campaign", done: true, ... },
  { label: "Review and launch", done: launched, ... },
  ...,
  {
    label: `Wait while Nakodo finds ${many}`,
    done: campaigns.some((c) => c.conversations > 0),
    ...
  },
];

"Start a campaign" is done: true as a literal, which looks like a joke and is not: the component only renders when there is at least one campaign, so by the time anybody sees the list, that step is finished. It is on the list because a checklist whose first item is already ticked is a checklist you believe. Starting at zero of four makes a reader feel behind before they have read it.

The two conditional steps are the ones that make this worth writing about.

Save your proposal only exists for a campaign that was launched without one:

...(launched && !campaigns.some((c) => c.hasOffer)
  ? [{ label: "Save your proposal", done: false, href: `${base}/outreach/proposal`, hint: "..." }]
  : []),

Normally the proposal is part of the review page you see before launching, so the step would be a lie: it was done as part of step two. It appears only for the people for whom it is a real outstanding task.

Approve the first emails only exists if the account has not turned on automatic sending:

if (!latest.autoSend) {
  steps.push({ label: "Approve the first emails", done: false, href: `${base}/outreach?view=attention`, hint: "..." });
}

So the list is four steps, or five, and {done} of {steps.length} done counts whichever list you got. A denominator that moves is usually a sign of a bug. Here it is the point: the checklist is a description of your remaining work, not a fixed curriculum, and an account that will never see an approval queue should not be told it has a step it cannot do.

One hint, on the step that is next 

const next = steps.findIndex((s) => !s.done);
if (next < 0) return null;

next is the first unfinished step. It gets a ring instead of a dashed circle, a highlighted row, and it is the only step whose hint is rendered. Finished steps get a tick and line-through. Steps after it are dashed circles with nothing under them.

Four hints exist in the file and at most one is on screen. That was a deliberate trade: the first version showed every hint, and a five item list with a sentence under each item is not a checklist, it is a page of documentation with ticks on it. The reader has exactly one next action, so exactly one sentence is relevant.

The state is also announced, because a tick and a ring are nothing to a screen reader:

<span className="sr-only">{s.done ? " (done)" : current ? " (next)" : ""}</span>

The whole row is a Link, so the target is the full width of the card rather than the label, and the circle with the tick in it is aria-hidden because the text next to it now says the same thing.

Two ways to disappear 

const latest = campaigns[0];
if (!latest || campaigns.some((c) => c.contacted > 0)) return null;

and

if (next < 0) return null;

The first is the interesting one. Once any campaign has contacted anybody, the checklist is gone, whether or not its steps are finished. Somebody whose campaign is already emailing creators does not need to be told to approve the first emails: the product is working, and a getting-started panel on a working account is noise with a progress bar on it.

That is also what makes the no-storage design safe. contacted only ever goes up, so the checklist cannot come back from the dead and ask you to start again. There is no dismiss button because there is nothing to dismiss: the condition that shows it stops being true by itself.

The cost is real, though, and it is worth naming: because nothing is stored, a step cannot be skipped. If you deliberately never want a proposal, there is no "not for me". Your only way out of that step is doing it, or contacting somebody, which removes the whole panel. For a four item list shown to brand new accounts I will take that trade. For a longer one I would not.

The bug this post found

Look again at the subjects of those expressions.

const latest = campaigns[0];                                  // the newest campaign
const launched = campaigns.some((c) => c.launchedAt);          // any campaign
...!campaigns.some((c) => c.hasOffer)                          // any campaign
done: campaigns.some((c) => c.conversations > 0)               // any campaign
if (!latest.autoSend)                                          // the newest campaign
const base = `/campaigns/${latest.id}`;                        // every link

Three of the five steps ask "do any of your campaigns have this", two ask about the newest one, and every link in the list points at the newest one.

For one campaign, which is the whole audience this panel was written for, those are the same question. For two they are not. Start a second campaign while the first one is running and the checklist says "Review and launch" is done, because the first one was launched, with a link to the new one's brief page. The proposal step vanishes because the old campaign has a proposal. The waiting step is already ticked because the old campaign has conversations.

It is not a crash and it is not visible to most accounts, because the panel disappears as soon as the first campaign contacts anybody, and a first campaign usually gets there before a second one is created. That is exactly the kind of bug that lives for months.

The fix is to pick one subject and say so in the type. Either the checklist is about one campaign, in which case it takes a campaign and not a list, or it is about the account, in which case latest.autoSend and the hrefs need to be account-level questions too. I think it is the first: this panel is "get your first campaign going", so it should take latest and nothing else, and the three some calls become reads of one object.

One file, 118 lines, no migration either way. Nakodo describes the same journey in prose on how it works, which is the version everybody sees before they sign in, and which has the advantage of not having to know which campaign you mean.

title: Five notes tour the big card on our homepage, and two of the four places a note can sit have never rendered
description:
Scroll down the Nakodo homepage to the big bordered card with a creator on it, called Open Rate Lab. Leave the pointer alone. After about a second the card starts explaining itself: a small dark note opens beside one of its lines, waits three seconds, closes, and the next one opens somewhere else. Five notes, then it stops and gets out of the way.

That is 249 lines in src/app/(marketing)/showcase.tsx, and this post is what is in them. The card is the one place on the site where we show the product instead of describing it, so the thing pointing at its parts had to be the least annoying version of a guided tour I could build.

The notes are part of the card, not tooltips

The first decision is the one that drove the rest. Every note is a span inside the card's own layout, absolutely positioned against the thing it describes. It is not a tooltip in a portal.

The comment at the top of the file says why:

// The notes are part of the page rather than tooltips in a portal: a tooltip
// is positioned by script against a fixed layer, so while a note is open and
// the page scrolls it is dragged back into place a frame late and visibly
// judders. A note that sits in the plate's own flow scrolls with it exactly.

A tour that starts when you scroll to something is guaranteed to be open while you are still scrolling. A portal tooltip handles that by recomputing its position on every scroll event, which is always a frame behind the thing it is pointing at. A note inside the card has nothing to recompute: it moves because the card moves.

The price is that the note cannot escape its container, so there is a table of four positions, each one a set of Tailwind classes for where the note sits, which way it travels as it opens, and where its little rotated-square arrow points:

const SIDES = {
  top: {
    note: "bottom-full left-0 pb-2 sm:left-1/2 sm:-translate-x-1/2",
    arrow: "bottom-0 left-4 -translate-x-1/2 translate-y-1/2 sm:left-1/2",
    shut: "translate-y-1",
  },
  bottom: { ... },
  left: { ... },
  right: { ... },
} as const;

Each entry has a phone shape and then an sm: shape, because there is no room to centre a note over a word on a phone, and no room at all beside a label: a left note drops underneath on a narrow screen and only moves to the side at sm.

Four positions. The homepage uses two of them: three notes are top (the default) and two are left. bottom and right have never rendered on the live site. I am leaving them, because the first time a note needs to point up at something they are the half hour I do not spend, but they are untested code and worth saying out loud.

Four timers, and what each one is waiting for 

const STEP_MS = 3000;
const FADE_MS = 150;
const START_MS = { scrolled: 1300, mounted: 700 };

START_MS has two values because the card has an entry animation. Its bars grow in with animation: grow-x 0.7s and a 70ms stagger per bar, so a tour that starts at once points at a chart that is still drawing itself. 1300ms is that animation plus a beat. The 700ms case is for a reader who loaded the page already looking at the card, where the bars never animated at all.

Which one you get is decided once, on mount, by asking where the card is:

const box = el.getBoundingClientRect();
if (box.top < window.innerHeight * 0.75 && box.bottom > 0) {
  start(START_MS.mounted);
  return () => window.clearTimeout(timer);
}
const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
  ([entry]) => {
    if (!entry.isIntersecting) return;
    observer.disconnect();
    start(START_MS.scrolled);
  },
  { threshold: 0.25 },
);

The observer disconnects itself on the first intersection, so the tour runs once per page load and scrolling back up does not restart it. FADE_MS is the odd one out: it is not a tour timing at all, it is how long a note takes to fade, and the tour needs to know because of the step counter, which I will come back to.

Two rules so the tour never talks to an empty screen

A three second timer is a promise that the reader is looking. Two things break that promise, and each one has a rule.

The pointer. The whole card has onPointerEnter and onPointerLeave, and while the pointer is inside it the step timer does not run:

useEffect(() => {
  if (!running || held || !inView) return;
  const timer = window.setTimeout(() => setCurrent((c) => c + 1), STEP_MS);
  return () => window.clearTimeout(timer);
}, [current, running, held, inView]);

Reaching for a note is the clearest signal in the whole interaction that the reader is reading, so hovering holds the tour where it is.

The viewport. On a phone the card is taller than the screen, so the note the tour wants to open next can be below the fold. Each step watches itself and tells the tour:

const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
  ([entry]) => setInView(entry.isIntersecting),
  { threshold: 1 },
);

threshold: 1 means fully visible, not partly, and inView is in that effect's guard above. A step that is off screen opens its note and then waits there until you scroll to it, rather than counting down three seconds at a reader who cannot see it.

Then two ways to say stop:

const onKey = (e: KeyboardEvent) => e.key === "Escape" && end();
const onPointerDown = (e: PointerEvent) => {
  if (e.pointerType !== "mouse") return;
  if (!ref.current?.contains(e.target as Node)) end();
};

Escape ends the tour, and so does a mouse click anywhere outside the card. pointerType !== "mouse" is the interesting half: on a phone, a touch outside the card is nearly always the start of a scroll, and ending the tour because somebody scrolled is exactly the wrong reading of that gesture. Ending means jumping to count, not skipping one step, because somebody who clicks away has said no to the whole thing.

The step counter outlasts the tour by one fade

While the tour is guiding, each note carries 3/5 and a Next button. Afterwards the notes stay, and open on hover, without either. That is one piece of state:

useEffect(() => {
  if (current < count) return;
  const timer = window.setTimeout(() => setGuiding(false), FADE_MS);
  return () => window.clearTimeout(timer);
}, [current, count]);

If guiding flipped the moment the last note closed, the last note would lose a line of content and visibly shrink while fading out. Waiting FADE_MS means the reader never sees that. This is the kind of detail nobody will ever thank you for, which is also why it is the kind of thing worth writing down: the whole fix is a 150ms timeout and knowing what it is for.

It is all in the server HTML

The note is in the DOM whether it is open or not. Open is three classes:

open
  ? "pointer-events-auto translate-none opacity-100 duration-200 ease-out"
  : cn("opacity-0 duration-150 ease-in", place.shut)

So it fades both ways, and the text is readable by assistive software at any point through aria-describedby, not just during its three seconds. You can check that without running any of our JavaScript:

curl -s https://nakodo.app/ | grep -o 'role="tooltip"' | wc -l   # 5
curl -s https://nakodo.app/ | grep -o 'aria-describedby' | wc -l # 5

Five of each, and 498 characters of note text, in 596,325 bytes of HTML. They are the only five on the site: no other page in our 76 has a role="tooltip" in it.

The ids are React's, from useId, and they look like _R_9irilfebrb_. They are per render and they match, which is the whole point of the hook.

The bug this post found

Writing the "it is all in the server HTML" part, I went looking for how a keyboard user gets at the notes. The answer is aria-describedby and nothing else. The step is a button, so Tab reaches it, but open is showing || (tour.done && hovered) and hovered is only ever set by onPointerEnter and by a click. Focus does not open the note. There is even an onBlur that clears hovered, which means I had thought about focus and then only handled the leaving half of it.

So that is the open work: onFocus should set hovered the way onPointerEnter does, and the tour should probably hold while a step is focused, for the same reason it holds while a step is hovered. Five lines, and the tour on nakodo.app will do the right thing for somebody who never touches the mouse.

title: The blog wall that hummed at 50 Hz
description:
Much like my past life as a sound engineer, my current work is a delicate mix of UX, design, and code. And just like accidentally creating a 50Hz ground loop hum with 10kW of bass behind it, mixing these three up usually results in a very loud, very public, less enjoyable UX.

The blog on idunworks.com used to be a tidy grid of cards. Same size, same corners, same polite little "Read more". It looked like every other blog. So I wrote the brief for its replacement in one line:

"There should be NO sweet cards, only splashy brutalist, uneven ones, served at a random pace."

This is the story of that sentence, two follow-ups, and the night the wall started to vibrate. It's about what happens when design tasks pile up on top of code that has to measure things, and the one rule that would have saved us an evening.

Task one: no sweet cards

The first version came out nicely rude. Cards in different sizes, tilted a few degrees this way and that, loud colours, heavy type. Even the link got bored of saying the same thing: "Read more" became ten different labels, from "Dive in" to "Feed your brain" to "Click for mo'" to "Down the rabbit hole". It is not for every corporate eye with a stick up their ass. It is me. Oh is your ass "profanity"? I must have misunderstood something.

"Random" needed a small cheat. If the page picks a card's look by rolling dice, the server rolls one number and the browser rolls another. The page then redraws itself the moment it loads. So every card's look is worked out from the post's own address. It looks random to you and stays identical for the server and the browser. Random enough, and repeatable.

Task two: break the grid

Uneven cards in a grid leave holes. A short card next to a tall one leaves a gap under the short one, and the wall looks like a mouth missing teeth. So a small script started packing the cards: measure each one, give it exactly the height it needs, and let later cards slide up into the gaps.

Then I looked at it again. It still wasn't what I wanted.

"I need to have a negative margin left/right for some cards, so they stick out of their parent sideways."

So cards in the outer columns got permission to hang over the edge of the wall. To do that, the script has to know which cards ended up on an edge, and it can only know that after it has packed them.

And then, of course, even more offset where there is room, in big screens. So a design is not just a design but needs to be checked, rechecked, recoded, repeated for all screens. 20 years ago, we had problems with different browsers interpreting CSS differently. We still have the same problem but from screens having different sizes and resolutions.

It is like the famous 3 times winner of Tour de France, Greg LeMond said: "It never gets easier, you just go faster".

More overhang on wide screens. Kept clear of the window edge, so nothing leaks off the page. Fine. Shipped. It looked great.

The night it vibrated

A couple of weeks later, after an unrelated deploy, the blog cards started flickering. "Probably 50hz", by my estimate. We opened the page and saw nothing. A tidy, uneven, perfectly still wall.

The catch, which took longer to find than it should have: "now scroll, I got it after scrolling."

The wall loads lazily. You get one screenful, and more cards arrive as you scroll. The first screen was fine. It was the cards that came later that started fighting.

Here's the fight in one card's view of it:

  1. I'm in the last column, so I'm an edge card. I get to stick out. I get wider.
  2. Wider means my text wraps differently. I get shorter.
  3. Shorter means the packing changes. Now I fit somewhere else, one column in.
  4. I'm not on the edge any more, so I don't get to stick out. I get narrower.
  5. Narrower means taller. Taller means I'm back in the last column. Go to 1.

Every step was correct. Every rule did exactly what it was told. Together they made a loop, and the browser ran it every frame. When we counted, a card on the live site changed its mind about 700 times a second. That's not a flicker, that's a hum. And you can hear the hiss of your computer's fans revving up like they're partying. Ouch.

Quick checks never caught it, because quick checks look at the first screen. Nobody scrolls in a quick check. That is what testers are for: they do the stuff a dev would never do because for a dev, when the logic is sound, leave it. Testers' job is to try to break that logic. Kudos to you!

The fix: you get two changes of heart

The fix is almost embarrassingly small. Each card may change its "I'm on the edge" status twice. After that it keeps whatever it has. The count only starts over when something real happens from outside: the window changes width, or new cards load.

We tested it the honest way. With the limit, the count dropped to zero. Then we took the limit out again just to be sure, and the hum came straight back. Put it back. Zero. It has been still ever since, on the live site too.

What happened, and how else it could be done

The problem: a layout rule (stick out if you're on the edge) changed the very thing it depended on (where you are), so the script and the cards argued forever. The fix: a limit on how often a card may change sides, reset only by outside events.

There are other ways out, and they trade differently:

  • Ours, the limit: a few lines, no design change. The cost is that once in a while a card may keep an overhang it no longer strictly deserves. Nobody will ever notice.
  • Shift the card instead of widening it. If the overhang only moves the card sideways, without making it wider, the text never rewraps and the loop can't start. The cost: the card pulls away from its neighbour on the inner side, so the wall gets gaps where it should touch.
  • Measure once, then stop measuring. Pack the wall, decide the edges, apply the overhang and don't look again until the window changes. No loop by design. The cost: a card that grows from its overhang can now bump into the card below, so you need extra spacing to be safe.
  • Let the browser do it. Native masonry layouts in CSS are on their way, and then there's no script at all to argue with. The cost: not every browser has them yet, so for now you still need the script as a backup.

The rule of thumb I'm keeping: any code that measures something and then changes what it measured is a loop, whether you meant it or not. Give it a way to stop. And when you test a page that loads more as you scroll, scroll.

Each design task was small. "Uneven." "Stick out." "A bit more where there's room." The code said yes to every one. That's the risk: it never tells you which yes was one too many.

The wall is on idunworks.com/blog. Scroll all the way down. It holds still now. Promise!

Originally published at idunworks.com.

title: The error messages a Rust rewrite got subtly wrong: what a black-box probe found in uutils coreutils
description:
When you rewrite a command-line tool, the happy path is the easy part. Output for valid input gets compared early and often. Error messages are where rewrites quietly drift: a different wording, a missing file name, a raw (os error 20) instead of the sentence a script or a person expects.

I have been running behave against uutils coreutils, the Rust rewrite of GNU coreutils. behave probes a CLI as a black box (flags from --help, stdin, files, odd inputs), records what the reference tool does, and replays the same cases against the rewrite. I record from GNU 9.12, the release uutils targets.

One probe case added in v0.1.7 is simply "a regular file passed with a trailing slash" (f/). It turned out to be a good bug finder, because every utility has to turn ENOTDIR into a message, and each one does it a little differently.

What it found

All of these were reported upstream with a fix PR and a test:

  • cp f/ dest printed Not a directory (os error 20); GNU says cannot stat 'f/': Not a directory (#15691, #15692)
  • shred dir said Not a file; GNU says failed to open for writing: Is a directory (#15630, #15631)
  • mv missing/ g reported the wrong reason for the source (#15704, #15705)
  • ln f/ link blamed the link instead of the source (#15713, #15714)
  • mv a missing/b printed only the OS error, no cannot move 'a' to ... (#15721, #15722)
  • mv -T f d left the source out of cannot overwrite directory (#15724, #15725)
  • paste open and read errors without the file name (#15642)
  • sort -c dir exited 0 with no message at all (#15615, fixed in #15616, merged)

And one that is not about messages: mv -n z z fails with 'z' and 'z' are the same file, while GNU skips the move and exits 0, because it never runs the same-file check when it would not replace the target anyway (#15824, #15825).

Why these slip through

None of these are hard to fix. Most patches are a few lines plus a test. They slip through because a rewrite's own test suite tends to assert what the authors thought of, and nobody thinks of cp f/ dest. A black-box recording of the original tool asserts everything it actually does, including the boring corners.

Two lessons from the review rounds:

  1. Match the reference release. GNU 9.7 and 9.12 differ in small ways (quoting in tail -v headers), so recording from an old GNU produces false positives.
  2. Exact OS error text differs between platforms. Tests that compare full strerror text need to be Unix-only, while the context part (cannot move 'a' to 'b') can be checked everywhere.

Try it 

brew install emirmrkaljevic/tap/behave
# or: go install github.com/emirmrkaljevic/behave/cmd/behave@latest
behave probe cp                                        # record the reference (GNU cp)
behave diff behave-cp --impl ./target/release/cp --skip-tag meta   # replay against your rewrite

As of 6 Nov 2026 the same approach has led to 30 upstream bug reports and 37 fix PRs in uutils, 21 of them merged. The cases above are the error-message slice of that work.

If you are porting a CLI to Rust or Go, I would love to hear which cases behave misses.

title: We honour reduced motion in JavaScript and ignore it in CSS, and the three elements that prove it are all on the homepage
description:
Two greps, one against the repository and one against the live stylesheet.

# in the source
grep -rc 'reducedMotion\|prefers-reduced-motion' components | grep -v ':0'
# components/FrothCameo.tsx:1
# components/HostController.tsx:1
# components/PlayerLobby.tsx:1
# components/lab/EffectsLab.tsx:1
# components/vfx/ParticleCanvas.tsx:1
# components/player/PlayerShell.tsx:1

# in what the browser actually gets
curl -s https://pub-trivia.app/_next/static/chunks/2ox5qqp3hzrjs.css | grep -c 'prefers-reduced-motion'
# 0

Six implementations, all of them JavaScript, none of them CSS. That split is defensible for most of this site, because almost nothing here animates in CSS. It stops being defensible on exactly one page, and this is a post about finding the three elements where it matters.

What the stylesheet contains

Two stylesheets now, 107,598 bytes together. Their entire animation surface:

@keyframes        4      enter, exit, pulse, spin
animation:        2      var(--animate-spin), var(--animate-pulse)
prefers-reduced-motion   0
forced-colors            0
@media print             0

Four keyframes, two of which (enter and exit) come from the animation plugin and are driven by the popover and dialog primitives rather than by a page. The other two are Tailwind's spin and pulse.

Now count how many elements across all 79 public pages use them. I fetched every URL in the sitemap and grepped the markup:

animate-spin     0 occurrences, 0 pages
animate-pulse    3 occurrences, 1 page

The spinner keyframe ships to all 79 pages and no public page uses it. It is on the sign-in form and the dashboard, which are behind a session and not in the sitemap, so the keyframe rides along with the stylesheet for pages that will never reference it. That is a rounding error in bytes and it is worth knowing which of your keyframes are decoration on the delivery side.

The pulse is the interesting one, and all three of its uses are on the homepage:

<p class="animate-pulse ...">Waiting for the first team at The Red Lion</p>
<p class="animate-pulse ...">Waiting for the first question…</p>
<span class="h-2 w-2 animate-pulse rounded-full bg-muted-foreground/50"></span>

Those are inside the two demos on the page: a big-screen view waiting for teams, a phone waiting for the quiz to start, and the little dot next to "Waiting for the others". A pulse is the correct idiom for "nothing is wrong, something is coming". It is also a two-second infinite opacity animation, three of them at once, in the part of the page a visitor looks at longest.

And there is no prefers-reduced-motion rule anywhere in the stylesheet, so those three pulse for everybody, whatever their operating system says.

The fix is three lines, and I will take it:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .animate-pulse { animation: none; }
}

There is a small piece of history here. This project did have exactly one prefers-reduced-motion block in CSS, for about two hours on 4 November, inside 41 lines that arrived with a landing-page experiment and left with it. The rule covered a marquee that no longer exists. The gap it was accidentally covering is the one above.

Where the JavaScript side does work

The five non-canvas implementations are all the same line, wrapping a subtree:

<LazyMotion features={domAnimation}>
    <MotionConfig reducedMotion="user">
        {/* ... */}

reducedMotion="user" is framer-motion's own handling: it reads the media query and, when the preference is set, skips transform and layout animations while keeping opacity ones, on the reasoning that a fade is not what makes people ill. The sixth implementation is the particle canvas, which reads the query itself on every call and simply refuses to spawn anything.

The five wrappers are on the mascot cameo, the player shell, the host controller, the player lobby and the effects lab. Trace that onto the homepage and you get an uneven answer:

Homepage subtree Motion provider Honours the preference
The two mascot cameos FrothCameo Yes
The phone demos PlayerShell Yes
The big-screen demo HostDemo No
The three pulses CSS No

HostDemo opens a LazyMotion and never opens a MotionConfig:

import { LazyMotion, domAnimation, useInView } from 'framer-motion'
// ...
<LazyMotion features={domAnimation}>

So the leaderboard rows still slide, the podium still rises and the stage still transitions for a visitor who has asked their machine for less of that. Nothing in the code says this was decided; the components that got a MotionConfig are the ones that were written after the mascot, and the host demo was written before. That is what an undocumented default looks like six weeks later.

The structural fix is obvious once it is in a table: put MotionConfig at the top of the tree instead of at five leaves. reducedMotion="user" is the behaviour you want everywhere, so it belongs in the root layout, and then no new component has to remember.

Two things that will trip up an audit of this

One: three files import the light proxy under the heavy name.

// components/AppDemo.tsx
import { LazyMotion, domAnimation, m as motion, useInView } from "framer-motion"

m is the version with no features bundled in, which is the whole point of pairing it with LazyMotion. Aliasing it to motion keeps the JSX reading as <motion.div> and makes a grep for motion\. report four files when only one of them is actually the eager import. That one is the footer wordmark:

// components/FooterWordmark.tsx
import { motion, useScroll, useTransform } from "framer-motion"

Which is why 76 of our 79 pages ship an animation library: a decorative, aria-hidden, desktop-only wordmark that fades in behind the footer to five per cent opacity. The three pages that do not ship it are the legal pages, which use a compact footer. I have written about that trade before and it is still the right call to measure rather than guess, but the alias is a reminder that an import census has to read the import, not the call site.

Two: the m invariant is enforced by a comment.

/**
 * Uses `m` rather than `motion`, so whatever renders a mascot must sit inside a
 * <LazyMotion> (PlayerGame and the lab already do).
 */

That is the top of the shared mascot parts file. Render a mascot outside a provider and you get a runtime failure, in production, in a component tree that type-checks perfectly. Nine files open a LazyMotion to satisfy that rule (a tenth file matches a grep for it, and that tenth is this comment), and on the homepage they nest two deep, because the demo wrapper opens one and the player shell inside it opens another. Nesting is harmless and the duplication is the symptom: a requirement that every call site must satisfy, with no way to state it in the type system, becomes a requirement every call site satisfies redundantly.

A provider at the root would fix this one too, which is the same conclusion as the section above, arrived at from the other end.

Check it yourself

All of this is observable from outside:

# three pulses, all on one page, none of them stopped by CSS
curl -s https://pub-trivia.app/ | grep -o 'animate-pulse' | wc -l        # 3
curl -s https://pub-trivia.app/faq | grep -o 'animate-pulse' | wc -l     # 0

# the stylesheets, and what is not in them
curl -s https://pub-trivia.app/ | grep -o '/_next/static/chunks/[a-z0-9]*\.css' | sort -u

Then the part a grep cannot show you. Turn on reduced motion in your operating system (macOS: Accessibility, Display, Reduce motion. Windows: Accessibility, Visual effects, Animation effects. GNOME: Accessibility, Reduce animation) and open the homepage.

The pint stops bobbing and stops blinking. The phone demo still advances but stops springing. The big screen keeps every one of its transitions. And all three "Waiting" lines keep pulsing, on a two-second loop, forever.

Two of those four behaviours are correct. I would rather publish the table than the half of it that looks good.

title: A tiny CSS sprite-sheet preview with a reduced-motion fallback
description:
An animation can look good frame by frame and still feel too fast or uneven in context. A small browser preview makes it easier to compare the loop at its intended size before adding it to a game.

This example assumes you already have a transparent PNG with six equal 64 × 64 frames in one horizontal row (a 384 × 64 image). Replace sprite.png with your own sheet. It doesn't generate or rearrange frames.

<div class="character" role="img" aria-label="Animated character preview"></div>

.character {
  width: 64px;
  height: 64px;
  background-image: url("sprite.png");
  background-repeat: no-repeat;
  background-size: 384px 64px;
  animation: walk 600ms steps(6) infinite;
}

@keyframes walk {
  to { background-position: -384px 0; }
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .character { animation: none; background-position: 0 0; }
}

The six steps show each frame for one sixth of the 600 ms loop, or 100 ms per frame. The end position is one frame past the last image: the animation restarts there, avoiding a duplicate last frame. Change both the duration and frame count to match your sheet; don't use this exact offset for a vertical sheet or differently sized cells. The reduced-motion rule freezes the first frame; choose a meaningful still frame for your own character.

Three checks before using the loop

  1. Alignment: compare the feet against a stationary line. If the character jumps around, inspect the source frames and their shared canvas/pivot; CSS can't fix inconsistent alignment automatically.
  2. Timing: change 600 ms to 900 ms and compare. Evenly spaced cells are a useful starting point, not a substitute for hand-tuned holds on a landing or anticipation frame.
  3. Actual game size: view the sprite over a representative background. For deliberate pixel art, try image-rendering: pixelated when scaling by whole-number multiples; omit that rule for styles that need smooth edges.

References: MDN on CSS steps() and prefers-reduced-motion.

Disclosure: This tutorial was generated by an AI assistant for the MotifDeck team. MotifDeck is our AI game art workspace; its motion preview lets users inspect extracted frames and choose their sequence and timing. The CSS example works independently with a compatible sprite sheet.

title: AWS Glue Data Catalog now supports catalog-vended credentials with Apache Iceberg REST catalog federation
description:
AWS Glue Data Catalog now supports external catalog's vended credentials in Apache Iceberg REST catalog federation. You can now read external Iceberg tables from Amazon Athena, Amazon EMR, Amazon Redshift, and AWS Glue using coarse-grained table grants in your external Iceberg catalog.

Glue Data Catalog already federates to external Iceberg REST catalogs through an AWS IAM role that you configure with access to your Amazon S3 buckets. This enhancement in Glue Data Catalog provides another way to connect to an external Iceberg catalog and read only the tables that the external catalog authorizes. It uses temporary security credentials that are scoped to the Amazon S3 storage prefix and vended by your external Iceberg catalog. AWS Lake Formation manages access control when you query an external table using any AWS analytics engine, letting you restrict access further down to specific rows and columns and share external Iceberg tables across AWS accounts.

This feature is available through the AWS Lake Formation Management Console, AWS CLI, and the AWS Glue and Lake Formation SDKs. This feature is available in all commercial AWS Regions where Glue and Lake Formation are supported. To learn more, visit the documentation.

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.22

We've released version 6.22 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Transcript separation for chat

You can now configure Google Cloud CCaaS to deliver a separate transcript file for each participant segment in a chat, instead of one combined transcript per session. Under Settings > Chat > Chat Transcript, select Per Segment in Transcript Separation to generate individual transcript files for each agent, virtual agent, or supervisor who joins the chat—helpful for identifying which participant handled each part of a transferred or escalated conversation. Your consumers still receive a single, full-chat transcript regardless of this setting.

For more information, see Chat transcripts and chat history.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Campaign-based scheduled callbacks

Agents can now schedule a callback during an outbound campaign call. The callback belongs to the campaign, not to an individual agent, and the dialer calls the consumer back in the time slot they chose. Administrators set slot length, capacity, booking window, and expiry for each campaign, and supervisors can track upcoming, completed, and expired callbacks from the campaign list.

For more information, see Campaign management.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where direct access point (DAP) greeting messages played twice when a call was deflected to an internal phone number due to queue overcapacity.

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata for top-level menu paths and selected menus was incorrectly displayed in English instead of the user's configured language.

  • Fixed an issue where a failed Salesforce lookup was incorrectly treated as having no matches, which resulted in the creation of duplicate records.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound transfer restrictions remained in force even after being hidden in the administrator interface, causing queues to become silently unreachable for transfers.

  • Fixed an issue where hold music continued to play throughout a call recording after a warm transfer was completed.

  • Fixed an issue where outbound virtual agent audio was prematurely truncated during multi-message turns.

  • Fixed an issue where the Real-time Monitoring Queues report didn't accurately count skill-matched agents for skills-based queues, often displaying zero available agents despite their availability.

  • Fixed an issue where calls deflected to an external phone number after entering a queue were incorrectly recorded as abandoned by the customer.

  • Fixed an issue where the credit card tokenizer was missing from the SmartActions menu during outbound callback calls.

  • Fixed an issue where mandatory call dispositions were discarded if an agent's voice connection dropped but their session remained active.

  • Fixed an issue where the text resize menu in the chat widget wasn't scrollable at 400% browser zoom, which prevented users from accessing all available text size options.

  • Fixed an issue where the system incorrectly prevented saving automatic call redirection settings when the target was a virtual agent-operated queue.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate call records were created for a single inbound call, causing incorrect wait times to appear in the real-time queue view.

  • Fixed an issue where empty data attributes caused an error in the agent interface during call connections.

  • Fixed an issue where the Transfer Restrictions destination picker provided no feedback when a queue was ineligible, making it indistinguishable from a typo or search error.

  • Fixed an issue where incoming calls were rejected with a SIP 603 error due to high database latency and connection timeouts.

  • Fixed an issue where the documentation for the Apps API and call session metadata schema didn't define the top-level parentId and finishReason fields.

  • Fixed an issue where certain inbound call failures were incorrectly reported as a busy signal.

  • Fixed an issue where the event processor service crashed during scaling or rebalancing of the system.

  • Fixed an issue where the conversation ID was missing from chat events during active sessions.

  • Fixed an issue where report exports didn't download or remained stuck in a processing state indefinitely.

  • Fixed an issue where agents could transfer calls to queues that were already closed if their transfer list was loaded while the queue was still open.

  • Fixed an issue where queued chats were assigned to agents after the end-user had become unresponsive without being prompted to check in.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls cold-transferred to an over-capacity queue generated duplicate reporting records and incorrect queue wait times if the callback leg failed.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls deflected to voicemail during after-hours played three separate audio prompts sequentially.

  • Fixed an issue where a single call was simultaneously assigned to two different agents if the pickup coincided with the cascade timer expiry.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls weren't projected to agents in a breakthrough-enabled status if another call was already waiting in their queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a gray empty area appeared below the chat container in the agent adapter when the iframe width was narrower than 449px.

  • Fixed an issue where several Kubernetes and Google Cloud service accounts were granted overly broad permissions, which could have allowed for unauthorized privilege escalation.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's status sequence was recorded in the incorrect order following a brief connection loss during an active chat.

  • Fixed an issue where selecting a contact during a native campaign call didn't automatically open the corresponding record in the CRM.

  • Fixed an issue where AI-generated Smart Disposition suggestions were inconsistently displayed for outbound calls during the wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where call recordings became distorted or garbled when multiple holds were placed during a call.

  • Fixed an issue where audio uploads were accepted based on the file extension rather than the actual file content, which caused call disconnections when incompatible formats were played.

  • Fixed an issue where the call duration timer in the external call adapter didn't match the In-call status timer in the agent desktop for inbound calls.

  • Fixed an issue where the sentiment score was incorrectly displayed in the call adapter for calls escalated from a virtual agent, even when the Sentiment Analysis setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate reporting rows were generated for call and wrap-up durations due to concurrent system events.

  • Fixed an issue where agents couldn't sign in or refresh their status if their account was linked to a deleted or unknown status.

  • Fixed an issue where the Manager API documentation for agent activity logs omitted 17 chat routing and activity values, leading to incomplete reporting data for customers.

  • Fixed an issue where IVR custom callback numbers for certain international regions, including Norway and Denmark, were incorrectly dialed with a +1 prefix.

  • Fixed an issue where metadata for calls deflected between virtual agent assignment and connection wasn't exported to the Cloud Storage bucket.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent to human chat escalations experienced delays of up to 300 seconds during agent assignment.

  • Fixed an issue where the Answer button didn't appear for dial-by-extension calls when other calls were already waiting in an agent's queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a supervisor's name didn't appear in the chat widget when joining a conversation using the monitor then barge workflow.

  • Fixed an issue where ending a chat session in one browser tab didn't automatically close the chat widget in other open tabs.

Bug ID Description

Fixed

Bug ID Description
568535165 Skip main_task_wait_time and nio_task_wait_time metrics for the first 12 Prometheus scrapes during Message Processor startup warmup.
573602919 Fix generated OpenAPI specs' servers[] to carry the Apigee envgroup hostname instead of the backend target host.
562964081 The sgpUserIntentMatchingMode verdict-log field is now always present, including on dry-run policy records, and shows the mode used for the evaluation, including when sgpUserIntentMatching isn't set (CONSTRAINTS_AND_INTENT, or INTENT_ONLY when no policies match the tool call).
524115876 Fix an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests.
572025634 Responses with a compressed text/event-stream body to a proxy with an EventFlow now skip EventFlow processing and pass through intact instead of returning a corrupted body.
549078690 If no SGP policy is attributed for a denial, a customer sees the generic fallback message. This fix short-circuits to show the rationale instead when no matched policy has a configured denial message.
492041991 VerifyAPIKey and VerifyAccessToken now set the apiproduct.operation.llmTokenQuota.* flow variables only from the LLM operation(s) that matched the request; they are no longer set from unmatched LLM operations or for requests that match no LLM operation.
567244615 Semantic Governance now evaluates LLM requests it previously skipped, such as OpenAI requests whose message content is an array of parts, which can produce new denials and judge-model usage. It considers every system message rather than only the last, and a non-streaming OpenAI or an Ollama tool call whose arguments are not valid JSON is now an evaluation error.
567244615 Semantic Governance no longer evaluates a request or response with a field it cannot read when a tool call is involved. It records verdict ERROR naming the field, with status MODEL_ERROR. The inline SemanticGovernance policy instead raises GovernedLLMResponseParseError or GovernedLLMProviderDetectionFailed (HTTP 500), in DRY_RUN too unless continueOnError is true. It also reads every text part of a Gemini system instruction and Gemini tool parameters given as parametersJsonSchema, and no longer loses the rest of a Claude or Gemini request when one field has an unexpected shape.
560272924 Added continuous-scan bidirectional gRPC streaming support for the SanitizeModelResponse policy over Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams, preserving native LLM provider SSE JSON envelopes and event framing.
555332621 Model Armor policies now honor HTTPClient.managementplane.skip.proxy: with it set, Model Armor callouts bypass the forward proxy like other googleapis traffic. Streaming (ContinuousScan) Model Armor traffic uses the forward proxy.
158204922 VerifyJWT now rejects a JWT whose header contains "b64":false, with fault steps.jwt.InvalidToken, as RFC 7797 section 7 requires. Previously, such a token could be accepted if KnownHeaders listed b64, IgnoreCriticalHeaders was true, or the header had no crit.
158204922 GenerateJWS supports RFC 7797 unencoded payloads. GenerateJWS now raises MissingPayload, InvalidPayload or FailedToResolveVariable for payload errors, where it previously raised GenerationFailed. KnownHeaders and CriticalHeaders in the JWS and JWT policies accept names separated by whitespace, such as one per line. A b64 header supplied through AdditionalHeaders is now rejected, with steps.jws.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWS and steps.jwt.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWT. A proxy that set b64 through an AdditionalHeaders variable produced an RFC 7797 JWS before this change, and must move to UnencodedPayload, with DetachContent for the detached form.
158204922 VerifyJWS verifies RFC 7797 unencoded-payload JWS (b64:false), attached or detached. b64 in crit no longer needs a KnownHeaders entry. VerifyJWS rejects b64:false unless crit lists b64, with the new fault steps.jws.UnencodedPayloadNotCritical; IgnoreCriticalHeaders does not change that. DecodeJWS reports the raw payload of such a JWS.
559228730 ext_proc: ImmediateResponse now carries any Content-Type (raw body bytes + preserved Content-Type); replies too large to buffer use StreamedImmediateResponse.
544751120 Semantic Governance Policies marked as dry run are now evaluated and logged without blocking the request. Each dry-run policy adds a second judge evaluation per tool-calling response, whose tokens are billed. Dry-run verdicts are written to the semantic-governance-policy log as separate records flagged sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation=true; queries that count verdicts should add sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation != true to exclude them.
554114419 Fixed: an AssignMessage/HTTPModifier/RaiseFault policy that creates a new request (createNew="true") in an HTTP/2 flow can now set the :path and :authority pseudo-headers instead of failing with an invalid-header error.
567812025 FILESYSTEM persistence mode makes the synchronizer skip Cassandra entirely (no connections, reads, writes, or datastore health probes).
559009293 Fixed elevated OAuth latency and Cassandra read load for AppGroup apps, including access token verification and token and authorization-code generation, by caching AppGroup lookups in the message processor runtime, matching Developer behavior.
568860869 Fixed RegularExpressionProtection patterns of the form "...." whose middle section contains regular expression syntax (for example, ".?Exception in thread." or "(?i).<script.>.*") being matched as literal text instead of as regular expressions. Such patterns now raise steps.regexprotection.ThreatDetected for all matching input.
564945600 Enhance VerifyAPIKey policy to better handle leading spaces.
502231886 Fixed the default source templates for SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse so a policy that omits the source element extracts content correctly when IgnoreUnresolvedVariables is false.
562964081 Semantic Governance now honors the sgpUserIntentMatching AuthzExtension metadata key (ENABLED or DISABLED) to toggle user-intent matching in policy evaluation; DISABLED evaluates against constraints only.
565004219 Fixed Semantic Governance Policy skipping evaluation for Anthropic requests that send system as a content-block array (the form ADK and LiteLlm emit). Affected agents are now evaluated, which may produce new denials and new judge-model usage on the consumer project.
527517087 SGP policy logs written to your project now identify their originating region. resource.type changes from "global" to "generic_node" and the region appears in resource.labels.location. Anything selecting these entries by resource.type="global" must be updated -- including log-based metrics, sinks, exclusion filters and alerts, which stop matching silently rather than erroring.
575439485 JavaCallout policies that run remotely (per-contract offload) can now pass every value type allowed by the GCP-2025-023 setVariable restriction between policies (collections, maps, arrays, primitive wrappers including Character, Date, BigDecimal, UUID, java.time, atomics, JDK enums, Optional), with their types preserved, instead of failing with steps.remotepolicy.NonSerializableVariable.
575439485 Remotely executed (per-contract offload) JavaCallout policies with continueOnError="true" now continue the flow when the callout faults, instead of returning HTTP 500.
567244901 In enforce mode, Semantic Governance now blocks a tool call when the governance check cannot be completed, instead of letting it through.
573622417 Fixed an issue where istio-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
571679067 removes old version of ApigeeTelemetry CRD.
571378258 The Apigee Redis container is now built from the Valkey engine (BSD-3-Clause, Linux Foundation) at version 8.1.10. Wire protocol is unchanged (RESP2) and the redis-server/redis-cli binary names are preserved.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Single-user quota limits

Gemini Enterprise administrators can configure single-user quota limits on the Usage & Spending > Usage page in the Google Cloud console to prevent an individual user from using all of an edition's shared subscription quota pool. You can enable a single-user quota limit and set a quota multiplier for each edition and location across the Gemini Enterprise Standard, Gemini Enterprise Plus, and Gemini Enterprise Standard Emerging Market editions.

This feature is generally available (GA). For more information, see:

  • Single-user quota limits
  • Configure a single-user quota limit
  • Configure pay-as-you-go usage above quota

Announcement

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Argon becomes the default model for AlphaEvolve on October 26, 2026

On October 26, 2026, Gemini 4 Argon will replace Gemini 3.8 Flash as the default model for new AlphaEvolve experiments. AlphaEvolve uses the default model when you don't specify a model in the models field of generationSettings.

From that date, new experiments that use the default model are billed at Gemini 4 Argon token prices instead of Gemini 3.8 Flash token prices. To keep using Gemini 3.8 Flash, specify gemini-3.8-flash in the models field.

Experiments created before October 26, 2026 keep the model recorded in their configuration.

For more information, see Default model.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Advanced reporting dashboards prerelease notes 6.24

Here are the pre-release notes for updates to the advanced reporting dashboards and other reporting in CCAI Platform. When we release these updates, we expect the new capabilities to be as shown here.

Important: The next version of the advanced reporting dashboards could be greater than 6.24.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where call and chat type names were cut off in the Dashboard Reports selector on wide-screen displays.

  • Fixed an issue where the Individual Call History and Individual Chat History reports, run for all agents, left out calls and chats that were never assigned to an agent (for example, abandoned, deflected, or expired calls) when only one agent or no agents had activity in the selected period. The All Call History and All Chat History files are now always included.

  • Fixed an issue where the Interactions Detail by Agent report omitted outbound calls placed without a queue when generated for all agents.

  • Fixed an issue where the Real-time Queue Monitoring and Campaign dashboards incorrectly displayed English queue names for French and Spanish interactions.

  • Fixed an issue where "wrap-up" and "hold" metrics in advanced reporting were displayed with inconsistent and inaccurate French Canadian (fr_CA) translations.

  • Fixed an issue where Spanish chat queues incorrectly displayed English names in Real-time Queue Monitoring and advanced reporting dashboards.

  • Fixed an issue where call disposition fields appeared blank on dashboards when viewing date ranges between 46 and 365 days.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware 1.34.1000-gke.111 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade clusters. Google Distributed Cloud 1.34.1000-gke.111 runs on Kubernetes v1.34.7-gke.200.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for use with GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.34.1000-gke.111:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed an issue where updating or upgrading a cluster to an advanced cluster failed to join control plane nodes if the cluster's certificate authorities (CAs) were previously rotated. For more information, see Control plane nodes fail to join during an update or upgrade to an advanced cluster after CA rotation.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal 1.34.1000-gke.111 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade clusters. Google Distributed Cloud for bare metal 1.34.1000-gke.111 runs on Kubernetes v1.34.7-gke.200.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for installations or upgrades with the GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

Feature

The following features were introduced in 1.34.1000-gke.111:

  • Fixed an issue in clusters using bundled BGP load balancing where control plane upgrades or configuration updates could cause up to 20 seconds of API server connection failures while a control plane node restarted. After the fix, failover to a healthy control plane node completes in approximately 4 seconds.
  • Fixed an issue where the NodePool controller prematurely updated Status.ManagedFields on partial reconciliation failures, causing removed taints and labels to remain stranded on affected nodes.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.34.1000-gke.111:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed BareMetalMachine conditions during maintenance mode transitions.
  • Fixed an issue where updating control plane configurations caused multiple API servers to restart simultaneously, leading to transient control plane unavailability.

This note is missing a fix included in 1.34.1000-gke.111. See entry for October 26, 2026.

Google SecOps

Feature

Bulk case selection

In the enhanced Investigation Management experience, you can select up to 50 cases at a time in the case queue to perform bulk operations:

  • Range selection: Hold Shift while clicking to select a range of cases.
  • Select all: Click the header checkbox to select up to 50 loaded cases; this action automatically scrolls your view back to the top of the list. Consolidated Settings and Navigation

The Consolidated Settings and Navigation feature is now in public preview. It replaces the separate SIEM Settings and SOAR Settings menus with a single Settings menu, grouped into Administration, Access Management, Investigation, Detection and Data Management, and updates the navigation menu. Each settings page is shown only to users with the correct permissions. Cloud IAM, Viewer and Editor users can now view certain SOAR settings pages in read-only mode. Note that the Google SecOps documentation has been updated to reflect the new navigational changes imposed by the unified Settings menu. For more information, see Navigate the Google SecOps platform.

Looker

Announcement

Looker 26.22 will roll out to Looker (original) instances on the following schedule:

  • Expected Looker (original) deployment start: Monday, October 26, 2026
  • Expected Looker (original) final deployment and download available: Monday, November 9, 2026

The Looker 26.22 rollout for Looker (Google Cloud core) will be announced separately.

Looker 26.22 is expected to include the following changes, features, and fixes.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where table column options menus and search boxes appeared behind drill dialogs, which prevented users from interacting with them. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where configuring a LookML model could trigger unnecessary derived table rebuilds. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the Show filters option was displayed on dashboard tiles that failed to load data in view mode. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where drilling into results that were filtered by string dimensions that contained backslashes returned zero rows. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where pivoted queries in SQL Runner could fail to render or re-pivot unexpectedly. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the View (Expanded / Full Screen) option appeared in the tile action menu on embedded dashboards in view mode. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where custom visualization tiles were truncated in dashboard PDF exports when the Expand tables to show all rows option was enabled. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

Table row group subtotals are now displayed only for sum and count measures. For other measure types (such as averages and count distinct) and table calculations, subtotals are now left blank rather than displaying an inaccurate summed value.

Fixed

The System Activity query_metrics Explore now records connection acquisition time (acquire_connection) for queries that are canceled while waiting in the connection pool.

Fixed

Conversational Analytics DELETE endpoints now return HTTP 404 Not Found instead of HTTP 204 No Content when you attempt to delete nonexistent resources.

Fixed

The System Activity query_metrics Explore has been updated to accurately record model initialization time for models that are loaded from cache.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where adding a new series to a categorical chart, such as adding a new pivot value, could cause category bars to appear ungrouped. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed in the TypeScript and JavaScript SDKs where calling methods that have only optional parameters without passing an empty object could result in compilation or runtime errors. This feature now performs as expected.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.26

We've released version 6.26 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Scheduled callback for IVR overcapacity

Scheduled callback is now available as an overcapacity deflection option for IVR queues. When a queue is over capacity, callers can choose to schedule a callback. Google Cloud CCaaS then hands the call to your configured virtual agent, which books the callback through the Callback call API. Administrators choose the virtual agent, an optional greeting, and the data parameters to pass at the global or queue level. Reporting shows whether each caller submitted a callback or left without one.

Administrators: You can configure scheduled callback for overcapacity deflection globally at Settings > Call > Overcapacity Deflection, or per queue at Settings > Queue > IVR (Interactive Voice Response) > Edit / View > [QUEUE] > Overcapacity Deflection > Configure.

For more information, see Overcapacity deflection per-queue and Callback call API.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Salesforce: PKCE and refresh token rotation support

You can now connect Google Cloud CCaaS to Salesforce apps that require Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) and refresh token rotation. Salesforce turns both settings on automatically for newly created connected apps and external client apps. Google Cloud CCaaS uses PKCE when authorizing Salesforce administrator and agent connections. It also saves replacement refresh tokens returned by Salesforce, keeping connections working across subsequent token refreshes. Salesforce apps that don't use these settings keep working as before. This update adds no new configuration steps in Google Cloud CCaaS.

For more information, see Salesforce integration guide.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Branded caller ID label was truncated in the Outbound Number selector when the agent application language was set to French Canadian.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls experienced significant delays in connecting after being assigned to an agent.

  • Fixed an issue where whisper announcements played more than once and the call panel was slow to load in the agent desktop.

  • Fixed an issue where Salesforce case creation was delayed until the end of a call for inbound callers without a matching contact record.

  • Fixed an issue where callbacks to Norwegian, Danish, and Swedish landline numbers were incorrectly dialed with a +1 prefix, causing the calls to fail.

  • Fixed an issue where merged call recordings incorrectly reported only the duration of the first segment in the Calls API.

  • Salesforce account linking now completes only in the browser that started it. An authorization link opened in another browser or an incognito window is refused and can't be reused afterwards, and an administrator's Link New User action must be finished by the same signed-in administrator. Android and iOS agent apps link as before. This behavior is off by default and can be enabled per instance.

  • Fixed an issue that affected call connection stability during active calls for instances using Agent Assist.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent callback calls incorrectly required manual acceptance even when queues were configured for Auto-Answer.

  • Fixed an issue where Telnyx and Twilio virtual agent calls remained stuck in a connected state for an extended period if the carrier didn't send a terminal status callback.

  • Fixed an issue where SMS replies to auto-dismissed chats were incorrectly recorded as an agent timeout instead of an end-user timeout.

  • Fixed an issue where the Unanswered Transferred Call Expiration setting wasn't enforced for calls parked in an overcapacity deflection state.

  • Fixed an issue that affected connection stability and prevented calls from being accurately recorded as end-user hangups when callers hung up while waiting in a queue.

  • Fixed an issue where the external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) new call event payload was missing the queue service level field.

  • Fixed an issue where callers were disconnected when an agent finished their wrap-up following a queue transfer to a virtual agent.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls escalated from a virtual agent to a human agent reported inaccurate call-level queue and wait durations in reporting and data exports.

  • Fixed an issue where unrecorded voicemails incorrectly created Salesforce cases even when the Create CRM records for abandoned calls setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where activating a new language in the CCaaS portal caused the Languages & Messages page to crash or display an infinite loading spinner.

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata files were duplicated across different day folders in external storage when re-uploads occurred after midnight.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls became permanently stuck in a queued status without reaching a terminal state.

  • Fixed an issue where active agents were incorrectly signed out due to inactivity because the system didn't recognize activity outside the embedded call panel.

  • Fixed an issue where a permanent loading spinner appeared in the agent desktop top bar for instances with the email channel disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound keypad (DTMF) entries didn't reach the virtual agent during periods of stream instability or reconnection.

  • Fixed an issue where the external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) new call event payload was missing required parameters.

Cloud DNS

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, CNAME chasing behavior will change so that Cloud DNS follows CNAME chains between public and private zones. If your private zones or response policies have overlapping domain names with public CNAME targets, queries might resolve to unintended internal IP addresses or return resolution errors.

The following table outlines the current and updated behaviors.

Source of CNAME answer Current behavior (until January 5, 2027) New behavior (starting January 5, 2027)
Cloud DNS public zone Subsequent queries search only public DNS zones and internal DNS. Private zones, forwarding zones, and response policies are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order: response policies, private zones, forwarding or peering zones, internal DNS, and public zones.
Cloud DNS private zone Subsequent queries search only authorized private zones. Public DNS zones are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in authorized private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.
Cloud DNS response policy zone Cloud DNS systems don't perform queries for CNAME answers received from response policy local data rules. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in response policies or private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.

Review your CNAME chasing needs before January 5, 2027. Test your DNS query paths using dig or nslookup to identify CNAME chasing scenarios.

  • Look for private-to-public CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from response policies or private zones that don't match any response policy or record in a private zone. Previously, these queries resulted in a NXDOMAIN answer but after January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a record in a public zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses.
  • Look for public-to-private CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from public zones that don't match any record in a public zone. Previously, these CNAME chasing scenarios would have resulted in a NXDOMAIN response. After January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a response policy or record in a private zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses if the private zone doesn't have the record.
  • For CNAME chasing scenarios under your control: As best practice, configure matching time-to-live (TTL) values for all records in the CNAME chain.

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, Cloud DNS will disable full responses to DNS queries of type ANY (QTYPE=ANY) in public authoritative zones. Instead, a single resource record will return for ANY queries, chosen from the existing resource record sets that match the query.

Standard traffic from web browsers, applications, and API traffic query specific record types directly and are therefore unaffected with no action required.

However, certain legacy scripts, automated health checkers, debugging commands (for example, dig example.com ANY), or custom third-party monitoring systems that explicitly query ANY records will receive the first available record instead of a full zone inventory. You must complete the following configuration updates before January 5, 2027:

  • Identify legacy queries: Review internal tools, deployment scripts, or third-party DNS monitoring configurations for commands or API calls that request the ANY record type. Cloud DNS logs in Cloud Logging can be helpful with this.
  • Transition to specific queries: Update the tools to query the specific, individual record types they require (for example, querying for A, AAAA, MX, or TXT records separately).
  • Retrieve full zone records: If you use ANY queries to retrieve all records in a zone, use the Cloud DNS REST API (resourceRecordSets.list), the gcloud CLI (gcloud dns record-sets list), or the Google Cloud Console instead.

Risks associated with not making these changes include the following:

  • False monitoring alarms: Automated uptime or DNS monitoring tools checking ANY responses may misinterpret the new response as a system failure and trigger false alerts.
  • Broken automation pipelines: Internal deployment or CI/CD scripts that rely on parsing a full zone dump with an ANY query will fail to retrieve the expected data payload and may crash.
  • Disrupted IT diagnostics: Network administrators running manual legacy troubleshooting commands will no longer see a quick summary of all domain records, which could delay active network incident diagnostics.

title: October 28, 2026
description:
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Announcement

The following AlloyDB AI and vector search features and improvements are generally available (GA):

  • The alloydb_scann extension supports four-level tree (4LT) ScaNN vector indexes on PostgreSQL 17 and later, providing support for tables with up to 10 billion vector rows. For more information, see Four-level ScaNN tree indexes.

  • 4LT ScaNN vector indexes support automatic index maintenance. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and Maintain vector indexes automatically.

  • You can enable streaming functionality for ScaNN vector indexes by setting the scann.satisfy_limit parameter to relaxed_order. When enabled, the vector scan continues searching through additional leaf partitions until it finds enough results to satisfy the LIMIT clause of your query, improving recall on filtered searches. Additionally, you can enable this feature for parallel process scans by setting the scann.enable_parallel_satisfy_limit database flag to on. For more information, see ScaNN index reference and Best practices for tuning ScaNN indexes.

  • Vector assist simplifies the deployment and management of your AlloyDB vector workloads by helping you set up production-ready vector search capabilities, including embedding generation, query optimization, and index creation for vector types such as Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW). For more information, see Vector assist overview.

  • For AlloyDB for PostgreSQL instances running PostgreSQL 17 and later, the maximum supported value for num_leaves when building ScaNN vector indexes is increased from 30,000,000 to 104,857,600. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and ScaNN index reference.

  • You can use the external_search_fdw extension to connect to external search clusters and query their data directly from your database using the following search sources:

    • Elasticsearch

    • Solr

    • OpenSearch

  • AlloyDB supports the rum extension for high-performance full-text search operations on PostgreSQL 17 and earlier. The rum extension extends standard GIN indexes by storing positional information directly in the index, letting you perform faster phrase searches and relevance ranking without accessing the table data. For more information, see Create and manage a RUM index.

Fixed

AlloyDB provides more accurate memory usage estimation and prevents out-of-memory (OOM) errors when you build a ScaNN four-level tree index. This feature is in Preview. This update improves the stability of index builds by enforcing memory limits and improving memory estimation under constrained conditions.

Feature

Identity and Access Management (IAM) group authentication is generally available (GA) for new and existing AlloyDB clusters running PostgreSQL 15 and later. With IAM group authentication, you can manage database roles and privileges at the group level across primary instances and read pool instances, including first-time sign-ins directly to read pool instances. You can also preserve individual and IAM group user configurations when you migrate from a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL backup.

For more information, see IAM database authentication overview and Manage IAM authentication.

Security

In response to GCP-2026-071, Google is updating AlloyDB managed components. The fix to the certificate store is shipped in a new maintenance version that AlloyDB applies during scheduled maintenance, so you don't need to manually update AlloyDB managed instances. You can also apply the fix by performing self-service maintenance.

Depending on how you connect to AlloyDB, take the following actions:

  • If you use the AlloyDB Auth Proxy, then upgrade it to v1.17.2 or later. If you run the standalone proxy binary, then also update the host's certificate authority (CA) certificates.

  • If you use the AlloyDB Language Connectors, then update the language runtime and operating system CA certificates (for example, Go 1.26.10 or 1.27.3 or later).

Application Integration

Security

A Deserialization of Untrusted Data vulnerability was discovered in the SubWorkflow task in Application Integration versions prior to September 11, 2026. For more information, see the GCP-2026-074 security bulletin.

Feature

Application Integration agent skills

Application Integration agent skills are available in the public google/skills repository: application-integration-basics, application-integration-authoring, and application-integration-troubleshooting. AI coding agents that use these skills can help you set up Application Integration; build, publish, and run integrations through the REST API; and troubleshoot failed runs. For more information, see Application Integration agent skills and Build an integration with an AI agent.

Bigtable

Feature

You can configure Bigtable tables with microsecond timestamp granularity to capture and store high-frequency data. By supporting microsecond precision for cell timestamps, Bigtable helps you prevent data loss from write collisions in workloads with high event rates. This feature is generally available (GA) for instances in the Enterprise Plus edition. For more information, see Data type enforcement in Bigtable.
