title: I built an app with ChatGPT or Claude. How do I put it online, with a database and logins?
description:
Connect the AI you built the app with to LIIVO, then tell it to "Deploy to LIIVO". Your AI puts the app online with its own link, sets up the database and user logins the app needs, and you never open a terminal. It is free to try, and 15 EUR a month to keep an app online all the time.

The rest of this post walks through it step by step, including what it costs and what can trip you up.

Why does my app only work on my computer?

When ChatGPT or Claude builds an app, it usually runs inside the chat preview or on your own computer. It looks finished, but nobody else can open it. To share it, the app needs a home on the internet: a link people can visit, a place to keep its data, and a way for people to sign in. That home is what people mean by "hosting".

LIIVO is that home, and it is built for people who don't write code. You keep using the AI you already have. LIIVO puts what it builds online and keeps it running.

What do I need before I start?

You need three things, and none of them is a LIIVO sign-up form.

  • A computer. The setup happens in the Claude or ChatGPT desktop app. Once your app is live, anyone can use it on a phone.
  • A ChatGPT or Claude account. A paid AI plan works best. Free AI plans have tighter usage limits, and on Claude's free plan you can build in the regular chat but not in Claude's Code mode.
  • An idea, or the app your AI already made. A booking page, a tracker for the family chores, a small shop. Whatever you were going to describe anyway.

You don't create a LIIVO account first. When you connect your AI, it sends you to a sign-in screen. You sign in with Google, Apple or email, and that sign-in is your LIIVO account.

How do I connect ChatGPT or Claude to LIIVO?

Your AI talks to LIIVO through one address: https://my.liivo.ai/mcp. You paste it into your AI's settings once.

In Claude (desktop app): open Connectors from the chat box, choose to add a custom connector, name it LIIVO and paste the address. Claude opens your browser so you can sign in, then sends you back to the chat.

In ChatGPT (desktop app): open the ChatGPT menu and choose Settings. Under Integrations, click Plugins, open the MCPs tab, click Add and then Add MCP server. Set the name to LIIVO, the type to Streamable HTTP and the URL to https://my.liivo.ai/mcp, leave the token fields empty and click Save. Then start a new chat so the connection is picked up.

If you get stuck, LIIVO's connect page shows each step with pictures.

How do I actually put my app online?

Tell your AI what you want, the way you would tell a friend, and end with "Deploy to LIIVO". For example:

Make a simple booking page for my yoga class. People pick a time, enter their name and email, and get a confirmation. I want to see all bookings in a list. Deploy to LIIVO.

Your AI writes the app and sends it to LIIVO, and LIIVO puts it online. A few minutes later you get a link you can open, send to people, or put on your Instagram.

If the app already exists in a chat, say "Put the app we just made on LIIVO so other people can use it." If something goes wrong, tell your AI what you see. It can read what happened and try again. And if your app was built somewhere else and you have its code, open that code in Claude or ChatGPT and ask it to deploy the app to LIIVO.

Can my app have a database and user logins?

Yes. LIIVO has the pieces most real apps need, ready for your AI to wire up: databases, logins, file storage, email, visitor stats and video. You don't pick them from a menu. You describe what the app should do, and your AI chooses.

Let people create an account and log in, and save each person's bookings so they can see them next time. Deploy to LIIVO.

Each app gets its own space. Its logins, its data and its keys are not shared with any other app on LIIVO, so if something breaks somewhere else, your app keeps running.

What does it cost, including the AI?

There are two separate bills, and it helps to see both.

The first is your AI plan. That stays with ChatGPT or Claude, and LIIVO charges nothing for the AI. There is no fee per prompt and no second bill for the same thing.

The second is LIIVO, for keeping your app online.

Free Creator
Price 0 EUR 15 EUR a month, excl. VAT
Card needed No Yes, billed from day one
Tokens 100, once 40 every day
Good for Trying it and building a first app Keeping an app online around the clock

Tokens are how LIIVO counts the time your app's pieces are running. Each running piece uses some tokens every day, typically between 10 and 100, so the 100 free tokens last days rather than months. They are a one-time start, not a monthly allowance. On the free plan, an app that runs out is paused, not deleted.

Creator is 15 EUR a month with 40 tokens a day, and you can cancel with one click; your plan stays active to the end of the period you paid for. There is no free trial of Creator. If you want your app on your own web address, like a name you bought, that needs the Professional plan at 69 EUR a month. Most people start with the link LIIVO gives them.

What happens if I want to leave later?

You keep your app. You can export the app and its data whenever you want and move it somewhere else, with no export fee. Every piece LIIVO runs is open code that anyone can run, which is why the move is possible.

Your app and the data it stores run in Sweden, in Stockholm, on Swedish-owned servers.

Is my app ready for real people?

Before you send the link to everyone, ask your AI to check it with you. Can a stranger sign up without your help? What happens if someone types something odd into a form? Does it work on a phone? LIIVO has a short list of prompts for this, Is your app ready for real users, and you can paste them straight into your chat.

Where do I start?

Open liivo.ai/connect on your computer, connect the AI you already use, and ask it for the smallest version of your idea. When it says the app is live, open the link on your phone. That is the moment it stops being a chat and becomes something people can use.

Plans and prices checked on 6 November 2026 on liivo.ai.

title: Why FreePi runs on the Pi harness (and what the new Harness Leaderboard shows)
description:
The model gets all the attention. The harness around it — prompts, tools, context management, when to stop — usually decides whether a coding agent actually ships work.

A new Harness Leaderboard from Joel Niklaus makes that measurable: same open models, same provider, same reasoning effort, same tasks. Only the coding-agent harness changes.

What FreePi is

FreePi is a free AI coding agent in your terminal. Ads pay for inference. Under the hood it runs Mario Zechner's Pi harness — the same open agent loop the leaderboard just put under a microscope.

What the board measured

Joel ran 28,849 trials across nine harnesses on GLM-5.3-Flash, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and Flint, on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE (~$4,746 of inference). Headline score is resolve rate; cost is measured outside the harness.

Where Pi landed

Averaged over the three models:

  • Pi — 49.4% resolve at $0.29 per solved task
  • mini-swe-agent — 51.4% at $0.53 (Pi is statistically tied, ~45% cheaper)
  • OpenCode — $3.35 per solved task (11.7× Pi)

Pi sits in the top cluster and is the cheap strong option. The best harness still depends on the model, but the cost gap is hard to ignore.

Source announcement: Joel's post.

Why FreePi ships on Pi

We didn't invent a new agent loop. We ship Pi with free models, a GitHub sign-in, and no card required:

npx free-pi-cli@latest

When an independent board says the harness is near the top and thrifty, that's the product story: best harness we know how to ship, batteries included.

Wrapping up

Harness choice moves quality and cost as much as model choice. Pi cleared that bar. FreePi puts that harness in your terminal for free.

  • Leaderboard: huggingface.co/spaces/joelniklaus/harness-leaderboard
  • FreePi: www.freepi.ai
  • Credit: @pidotdev / Mario Zechner for Pi; @joelniklaus for the board

title: Which MCP servers can actually deploy infrastructure, not just read it? Five compared
description:
If you want an AI agent to deploy and run infrastructure through MCP, five hosted MCP servers can do real write work today: Vercel, Render, Railway, Netlify and Eyevinn Open Source Cloud (OSC). They differ in what the agent can create, whether it can tear things down again, and what is actually running underneath when it does.

Every row below comes from each platform's own MCP documentation, read on 6 November 2026. Tool lists change month to month, so treat the table as a dated snapshot.

What is the difference between an MCP server that reads and one that deploys?

A read-only server lets your agent look: list projects, fetch logs, search documentation. Most cloud MCP servers started there.

A deploying server lets the agent change things. It can create a database, ship your code to a public URL, set environment variables, restart a service and delete what it made. That needs more trust, so check which write actions a server exposes before you connect it to an agent that acts with your credentials.

Which hosting platforms have an MCP server that can deploy?

Platform Remote endpoint What the agent can create or change Tear down from chat?
Vercel https://mcp.vercel.com (OAuth) Deploy code to a new or existing project (deploy_to_vercel, announced July 2026). Tool categories for projects, environment variables, domains and storage. Not stated on the pages we read
Render https://mcp.render.com/mcp (OAuth or API key) Web services, static sites, cron jobs, Render Postgres and Key Value instances. Trigger deploys, update environment variables. No. Render's docs send other changes and deletions to the Dashboard or REST API
Railway https://mcp.railway.com (OAuth, or through the Railway CLI) Create projects, redeploy, accept staged changes. The local server (railway mcp local) adds services, variables, domains and volumes. Yes, on the local server, with a preview and an explicit confirm
Netlify https://mcp.netlify.com/mcp Create, manage and deploy projects. Environment variables and secrets, forms, extensions. Not stated in the README
OSC https://mcp.osaas.io/mcp (OAuth, or a personal access token) Any of the 198 open-source services in the catalog, databases (PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Valkey, CouchDB, ClickHouse), your own app from a GitHub repository, backups, config changes, restarts. Yes, behind a confirmation step

How should I read that table?

Vercel, Netlify and Render are at their best when what you deploy is a web app or a frontend with a managed database beside it. That is what those platforms are built around, and their MCP servers expose it well. Vercel's server added code deploys this summer, so older articles that call it read-only are out of date.

Render is explicit about its limits. Its MCP server does not support every configuration option at creation, and it leaves scaling changes and deletions to the dashboard and API. That is a defensible safety choice, and it is better to know it up front than to discover it mid-task.

Railway splits its tools in two. The hosted server is the default and the narrower one. The local server, run through the CLI, can create and remove services, volumes and domains, and Railway marks destructive actions so that clients ask before acting.

What does the OSC MCP server do that the others do not?

Two things, and both come from what OSC is rather than from the MCP layer.

The first is the catalog. OSC runs managed open-source services, and the MCP server can create any of them. When we checked today there were 198 published, from PostgreSQL and MinIO object storage to Keycloak for user logins and Uptime Kuma for monitoring, plus a long tail of media tools. Your agent is not limited to a web app and a database. If the project needs full-text search, a message queue or a video transcoder, it is the same create-service-instance call.

The second is what runs underneath. Every catalog service runs the unmodified upstream open-source container. A PostgreSQL instance on OSC speaks the PostgreSQL wire protocol, MinIO speaks S3 and Keycloak speaks OIDC, with no proprietary OSC API between your app and the service. If you leave, you run the same image on another cloud or your own servers and point your app at it. We wrote up that exit as a script in The Exit Test. This matters more when an agent makes the choices, because nobody stopped to read the exit terms.

The services your agent creates on OSC run in Stockholm, on Swedish-owned infrastructure.

Where OSC is the wrong pick: if your project is mostly a frontend and you want the preview-deploy-per-pull-request workflow, the platforms built around that workflow will fit better.

How do I connect the OSC MCP server to Claude Code?

You need an OSC account. The free Basic plan is enough to try it and asks for no card. Then run one command:

claude mcp add --transport http osc https://mcp.osaas.io/mcp

Start Claude Code and type /mcp. A browser window opens, you sign in, pick the workspace the tools should act on and approve. The server implements OAuth 2.1 with PKCE, so there is no key to paste. Claude Desktop, Codex and ChatGPT use the same browser sign-in.

How do I connect it to Cursor?

Create a personal access token in the OSC console under Settings, API, and add this to .cursor/mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "osc": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://mcp.osaas.io/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer <personal-access-token>"
      }
    }
  }
}

Keep that file out of git, since the token acts as you.

What can an agent actually do once it is connected?

Three prompts that work, and the tools the agent picks for them:

Create a Postgres database called appdb and give me the internal connection string.

This is create-database with type: postgres. Credentials are generated for you, and the database is internal-only by default, so apps in the same workspace reach it over internal DNS without exposing it to the internet.

Deploy github.com/me/my-api as an app and connect it to appdb.

create-my-app builds the repository (Node.js, Python, Go, .NET, PHP or WebAssembly) and gives it a stable HTTPS URL, and wait-for-app-ready reports when it is live. The app has to listen on port 8080.

Back up appdb, then show me everything I have running.

That is create-backup and list-my-services. The agent sees your own workspace, not a generic catalog, so it can manage what already exists.

Deleting is deliberately slower. delete-service-instance first returns a confirmation token and acts only on a second, confirmed call, so an agent that mistakes "stop" for "delete" does not remove a database on the first try.

Can I use my existing Claude subscription instead of buying platform credits?

Yes. The MCP server is a connector, so the AI runs on whatever Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor plan you already pay for. OSC tokens pay for running services, not for prompts, and you are never billed per prompt or for an AI mistake.

What does OSC cost?

Basic is free, with 100 tokens granted once and no card. Personal is 15 EUR a month excluding VAT and adds 40 tokens a day. A single running service typically uses 10 to 100 tokens a day, so size the plan against what you keep running rather than what you try once. Paid plans bill from day one, there is no trial on any plan, and you can cancel any time. Custom domains start at the Professional plan.

Which one should I pick?

Pick by the job, not by the protocol. If the agent's job is to ship a frontend, use the platform you would have picked without MCP. If the job is to assemble a backend out of open-source pieces and keep the option to take every one of them with you, try OSC: create a free account, run the one command above and ask your agent for a database.

Setup for VS Code, Windsurf, Codex and ChatGPT is on the OSC MCP page. A longer walkthrough: The MCP server that provisions a full backend your AI agent can deploy, and you can walk away.

If a platform's tools have changed since 6 November 2026, tell us in the comments and we will update the table.

title: How to Create an AI Mini Drama with the Chained Together Effect
description:
Short-form video content is changing the way people tell stories online. Instead of producing long videos with complicated scripts, expensive equipment, and multiple actors, creators are experimenting with AI tools to turn simple ideas into entertaining mini dramas.

One interesting concept is the Chained Together effect. Imagine two characters connected by a chain, unable to move independently. They might be strangers, rivals, friends, or even a couple. Every movement creates a new challenge, and every disagreement can become part of the story.

This simple concept creates plenty of opportunities for comedy, suspense, emotional storytelling, and unexpected plot twists.

In this article, we'll explore how to turn this idea into an AI-generated vertical drama using Textideo.

1. Why the Chained Together Concept Works for Short Videos

A good short video needs an interesting hook. The audience should understand the situation almost immediately and have a reason to keep watching.

The Chained Together concept naturally creates conflict.

For example:

  • Two strangers wake up in an unfamiliar room, connected by a chain.
  • A couple tries to go shopping but cannot agree on which direction to walk.
  • Two rivals must cooperate to escape a dangerous location.
  • A funny argument turns into an unexpected friendship.
  • One character wants to leave, but the other refuses to let go.

These scenarios are easy to understand and provide opportunities for unexpected developments.

More importantly, the same characters and central conflict can be developed across multiple episodes. This makes the format interesting for creators who want to build a recurring short-video series instead of publishing unrelated clips.

2. Create a Chained Together AI Drama with Textideo

Textideo offers a dedicated Chained Together AI Drama Generator designed to turn a simple story premise into a vertical mini drama.

Instead of manually creating every scene from scratch, creators can start with a basic idea and use AI to develop the story.

The workflow focuses on several important elements:

Character Creation

Describe your two main characters or upload reference photos. You can establish their appearance, hairstyles, clothing, and other recognizable details.

Story Development

Provide a short premise describing what happens and why the characters are connected. The story engine organizes the idea into a hook, escalation, reversal, and cliffhanger.

Visual Consistency

Keeping the same characters throughout a series is one of the biggest challenges in AI video production. A consistent character setup helps maintain recognizable faces, clothing, and the chain across different scenes.

Vertical Video Generation

The output is designed for a 9:16 vertical format, making it suitable for TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts.

You can explore the effect here:

Try the Chained Together AI Drama Generator

3. Three Story Ideas You Can Experiment With

If you are unsure what to create first, here are three concepts worth exploring.

Idea 1: The Impossible Escape

Two strangers wake up at the bottom of a mysterious underground structure. Their wrists are connected by a heavy chain, and the only way out is to work together.

One character wants to climb immediately, while the other notices something strange on the wall.

Just when they think they have found an exit, they discover that the real challenge has only begun.

This concept works well for suspenseful storytelling and multi-episode adventures.

Idea 2: The Couple Who Cannot Separate

A couple gets connected by a chain after a mysterious incident.

They try to complete ordinary activities such as cooking, shopping, driving, and walking their dog. However, every simple task becomes a hilarious challenge because they cannot move independently.

This is a great direction for relatable comedy and relationship-themed content.

Idea 3: Enemies Forced to Cooperate

Two characters who strongly dislike each other suddenly find themselves chained together.

At first, they constantly argue and blame each other. But when they encounter a bigger problem, they have no choice but to cooperate.

The story gradually changes from conflict to teamwork, with an unexpected twist at the end.

This idea offers plenty of opportunities for emotional moments and cliffhangers.

4. How to Structure an Engaging AI Mini Drama

Generating attractive visuals is only one part of creating a good video. A strong story structure is equally important.

A simple four-part structure can help:

Part 1: The Hook

Introduce the unusual situation immediately. Show the two characters connected by a chain and create a question in the viewer's mind.

Part 2: The Conflict

Give the characters different goals. One wants to escape, while the other has a completely different plan.

Part 3: The Twist

Introduce an unexpected event that changes their relationship or makes the situation more complicated.

Part 4: The Cliffhanger

End with an unanswered question or a surprising discovery that encourages viewers to watch the next episode.

For example, the first episode could end with one character discovering that the chain is connected to something much more mysterious than they originally thought.

This approach gives viewers a reason to return instead of treating every video as an isolated piece of content.

5. Tips for Maintaining Character Consistency

Character consistency is one of the most challenging aspects of AI-generated storytelling.

A character might look different between scenes if their visual details are not clearly established.

Here are a few practical tips:

  • Define the characters before generating the first episode.
  • Use consistent reference photos whenever possible.
  • Keep hairstyles, clothing, and recognizable accessories unchanged.
  • Describe the chain and its position consistently.
  • Review individual scenes before continuing with the next episode.

Textideo's workflow is designed to carry character and visual references forward, helping creators build a more connected series.

It is also useful to regenerate only the scene that needs improvement rather than restarting the entire story.

6. Where Can You Publish Your AI Drama?

Once your video is ready, you can adapt it for different short-form content platforms.

TikTok: Use a strong opening scene and an unexpected ending to encourage comments and discussions.

Instagram Reels: Focus on visually interesting scenes and emotional moments that viewers may want to share.

YouTube Shorts: Build a sequence of connected episodes so viewers can follow the story over time.

A useful strategy is to treat each video as one chapter of a larger story. You can publish several episodes and use the ending of each one to introduce the next.

Remember to review generated content before publishing and make sure you have permission to use any reference photos featuring other people.

Final Thoughts

AI video generation is creating new possibilities for independent creators. A simple idea, such as two characters connected by a chain, can become the foundation for an entire short drama series.

You don't necessarily need a film crew, professional actors, or complicated editing software to start experimenting with this format.

If you want to explore this concept, try the Textideo Chained Together AI Drama Generator and turn your own story idea into a vertical AI mini drama.

Sometimes, the most interesting stories begin when two characters have absolutely no choice but to stay together.

title: NuGet Source Mapping Closes a Dependency Confusion Gap
description:
NuGet Source Mapping Closes a Dependency Confusion Gap

Package restore is a security decision made thousands of times in a large .NET build. NuGet normally searches every configured source for a package. If a public feed and a private feed can both supply the same package ID, the result depends on source order and content rather than an explicit policy. Package Source Mapping lets a project state which source may satisfy each package pattern.

How source selection becomes a trust issue

Microsoft describes Package Source Mapping as a supply-chain control for projects that mix public and private feeds. With mapping enabled, NuGet filters the configured sources per package during restore, install, and update. The mapping is written under packageSourceMapping, with a source key and one or more package patterns beneath it.

The important design point is that the repository owns the rule. A machine-level feed can be convenient, but a mapping that exists only on one developer laptop does not protect CI or another workstation. Keep the authoritative mapping in the repository-level NuGet.config, then use <clear /> where inherited sources or mappings should not leak into the build.

<packageSourceMapping>
  <clear />
  <packageSource key="company-private">
    <package pattern="Company.*" />
    <package pattern="Internal.Project.*" />
  </packageSource>
  <packageSource key="nuget.org">
    <package pattern="Microsoft.*" />
    <package pattern="System.*" />
  </packageSource>
</packageSourceMapping>

The exact patterns must match the organization's namespace. A broad public fallback can recreate the ambiguity the mapping was meant to remove. Transitive packages also need coverage. Microsoft's guidance recommends listing transitive dependencies, for example with dotnet list package --include-transitive, before freezing the source map.

Test the failure path

A mapping is only useful if an unexpected source selection fails the build. Introduce a test package ID that exists only in the private feed, then verify a clean restore on a runner that has both feeds configured. Repeat with a package that should come from the public feed. Review warnings and the effective configuration, not just the final obj directory.

The control has a documented gap. Microsoft states that Package Source Mapping currently applies to package downloads during restore, install, and update. Some metadata operations, including dotnet package add, dotnet list package, and Package Manager UI browse and update lookups, still send package IDs to all configured sources at the time of the documentation. Teams that treat package names or internal identifiers as confidential should account for that behavior separately.

Operational checks

Store feed credentials in a secret system rather than in a repository file. Review who can publish to the private feed, because source mapping selects an endpoint but does not prove that its contents are trustworthy. Pair the mapping with package signing or trusted signer policy, lock files, vulnerability review, and a controlled process for adding new package prefixes.

During incident response, export the effective NuGet configuration from the exact build environment. Compare source keys, patterns, inherited files, and environment-specific overrides. Then inspect restored package hashes and provenance. The mapping is a useful allowlist for source selection, not a replacement for artifact identity.

References

  • Microsoft Learn: Package Source Mapping
  • Microsoft Learn: nuget.config file reference

title: WordPress Core enters KEV: patching and verification priorities
description:
CISA has added WordPress Core vulnerability CVE-2026-119977 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. According to The Hacker News, the flaw has a CVSS score of 8.1 and can lead to arbitrary code execution on affected servers. Its inclusion in KEV brings evidence of exploitation in practice into patch prioritization decisions.

The remediation deadline of 6/11/2026 applies to US Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies. It does not automatically impose an equivalent obligation on Vietnamese businesses, but the exploitation evidence is relevant when deciding which websites need attention first.

Why the upgrade process matters

The reported vulnerability involves a time-of-check/time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition during upgrades of the complete WordPress Core package. Temporary staging locations used for the upgrade have predictable addresses and are accessible through the web.

According to the cited description, an unauthenticated attacker can execute code on the server during that window. Wordfence also says exploitation does not require a website account. Reviewing administrator accounts alone therefore cannot establish whether a site is protected against this flaw.

The source reports that patches are available.

TMGS recommendations

TMGS recommends prioritizing the fixes through a controlled update process that accounts for the risk during upgrades. For businesses using external website administrators, the IT lead should coordinate with both the internal website owner and the provider authorized to perform maintenance.

TMGS recommends these defensive actions:

  • Inventory responsible WordPress sites, including outsourced sites, and compare their update status with official patch information.
  • Assign a technical owner and agree on maintenance timing, backups, and recovery arrangements.
  • Require completion evidence: the version after updating, the maintenance time, and website functionality checks.
  • Review logs and unexpected changes around upgrades when anomalies appear; start incident response if suspicious signs are found.

title: Why Public Wi-Fi Feels Risky and How Encryption Quietly Protects You on It
description:
You sit in a café, connect to the free Wi-Fi, and open your email without a second thought. Millions of people do this every day, and most of them come to no harm. Still, it may be worth asking what actually happens between your device and the outside world once you join a network full of strangers.

A public Wi-Fi network is simply a network that many unknown people share at the same time. The router itself does not check who you are, and it does not keep neighbors from listening in principle. Understanding what can and cannot go wrong may help you make calmer choices, rather than avoiding every hotspot out of fear.

This article explains the risk in plain terms and shows why encryption, a way of scrambling messages so only the right reader can undo it, quietly does most of the protective work.

Simple analogy

Think of a postcard versus a sealed envelope. A postcard can be read by anyone who handles it along the way, while an envelope hides the words inside. Traffic that travels without protection on a shared network behaves like a postcard.

Encryption turns your postcard into an envelope. It scrambles the text using a secret key, which is a piece of information that lets you lock and unlock the message. Other people on the same network may still see envelopes moving back and forth, but they likely cannot read what is written inside.

The comparison also explains why the café itself matters less than people assume. The waiter who carries the envelope cannot open it, and neither can the stranger at the next table. What matters is whether the letter inside was sealed before it left your hands.

Core mechanism

When a website uses HTTPS, your browser and the server agree on a temporary key at the start of each visit. From that moment, the messages travel in scrambled form that only the two ends can read. A person sitting nearby may observe the traffic, yet the content stays unreadable without that key.

The risk on public Wi-Fi comes from two main directions. First, some older sites or apps may still send data without encryption, and those messages can be observed directly. Second, someone with bad intent may trick your device into talking to them instead of the real site, a setup often called a man-in-the-middle attack, where the attacker quietly sits between you and the service.

Modern browsers push back against the second case. They check certificates, which are digital ID cards that prove a site is what it claims to be, and they warn you loudly when something looks off. These checks are not flawless, but they remove most of the easy attacks.

There is a quieter detail worth knowing as well. The name of a free network is set by whoever controls the router, so a look-alike name can appear in your list during busy travel seasons. Your device may connect on its own if it recognizes a familiar name, which suggests that turning off automatic joins is a simple and useful guard.

Real-world example

Security teams think about this problem at company scale, because employees now work from trains, airports, and hotels as a matter of routine. Some vendors build unified office security systems, such as Ping64, to bring data leakage prevention and endpoint management into a single platform. The aim is not to ban remote work, but to keep protection close to the data no matter where people log in from.

Consider a traveler who joins hotel Wi-Fi and opens an old internal tool that still runs without encryption. On a shared network, an eavesdropper may be able to observe parts of that session, including login details in the worst case. With HTTPS in place, the same scene looks very different, and the intercepted traffic reads as meaningless noise.

Limitations and common misconceptions

One common belief is that public Wi-Fi is a trap that no careful person should ever touch. In practice, encrypted connections now cover most everyday activity, so the realistic risk has dropped sharply over the past decade. Another belief is that a VPN makes you anonymous, while it mainly moves the place where your traffic gets decrypted from the café to the VPN provider.

It also helps to remember what encryption does not fix. If you install a fake app, type your password into a phishing page, or share a document with the wrong link, the network was never the weak point. Devices that have not received security updates in years may carry older weaknesses as well, and no hotspot habit can repair that.

There is a middle ground between fear and carelessness. Turning off automatic connection to open networks, paying attention to browser warnings, and preferring your phone’s tethered connection in sensitive moments are small habits that may cover most of the gap.

Closing and references

Public Wi-Fi is less frightening than its reputation suggests, as long as you treat the network itself as untrusted. Encryption carries the real burden of protection, and it works well when you notice and respect the warnings your browser gives you. A few steady habits are likely to matter more than avoiding cafés altogether.

References:
https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/48/r1/final
https://www.cisa.gov/secure-our-world
https://www.enisa.europa.eu/publications/enisa-threat-landscape-2024

title: Why Converted PDF Tables Break in Excel and Word (And How to Fix '=SUM() = 0')
description:
Every developer, financial analyst, or accountant who has ever tried to extract data from a PDF invoice or bank statement has run into this infuriating scenario:

You convert the PDF table into an Excel spreadsheet or Word document. The grid looks visually acceptable. You highlight the total column, type =SUM(E2:E50), press Enter... and Excel returns 0.

Or worse: numbers with commas turn into dates, negative numbers in accounting parentheses like (1,250.00) get treated as plain text, and multi-line descriptions spill across three independent rows, throwing every debit and credit out of alignment.

Why does converting PDF tables into editable documents fail so consistently, and what is the underlying engineering fix?

1. The Architectural Illusion: PDFs Have No Concept of "Tables"

In HTML, a table is a rigid semantic hierarchy: <table> contains <tr>, which contains <td>.

In the Adobe PDF specification (ISO 32000), tables do not exist.

A PDF is essentially a visual canvas program written in PostScript-derived display commands. When you see a financial table in a PDF, the file actually contains:

  1. Isolated vector stroke instructions (m for move-to, l for line-to, s for stroke) that draw black lines on the page.
  2. Floating text operators (BT, Tf, Td, Tj, ET) that place character glyphs at absolute two-dimensional coordinate positions $(x, y)$. 
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| VISUAL PERCEPTION (A Clean 3-Column Table)                  |
| Date        | Description            | Amount               |
| 2026-11-01  | Cloud Hosting Server   | $1,450.00            |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
                              vs
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| PDF INTERNAL DATA STREAM (Raw Coordinate Paints)            |
| 0.5 w  72.0 450.0 m  520.0 450.0 l S  (Draws top horizontal)|
| 72.0 440.0 Td (2026-11-01) Tj          (Paints string at x,y) |
| 160.0 440.0 Td (Cloud Hosting) Tj      (Paints string at x,y) |
| 450.0 440.0 Td ($1,450.00) Tj          (Paints string at x,y) |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

Because the PDF file itself has no concept of rows, columns, or cell boundaries, any converter must reverse-engineer and hallucinate the table structure entirely from geometric coordinates. When that reverse-engineering fails, your spreadsheet breaks.

2. The 3 Silent Killers in Converted Financial Data

A. The CHAR(160) Non-Breaking Space Trap

This is the single most common cause of =SUM() = 0.

When converters extract horizontal text streams, coordinate gaps between words and numbers are often translated into non-breaking spaces (  or Unicode U+00A0 / ASCII 160) rather than standard ASCII whitespace (CHAR(32)).

To human eyes, 1450.00 and 1450.00 look identical. But to Excel's calculation engine, any cell containing CHAR(160) is strictly classified as a Text String, not a Number. Excel silently ignores text strings inside =SUM(), yielding a grand total of zero without throwing a single error.

B. Accounting Parentheses vs Negative Signs

Financial statements frequently represent negative values using parentheses: (1,450.00) instead of -1,450.00. Naive regex parsers and basic OCR tools either strip the opening parenthesis, misinterpret the brackets as text characters, or drop the negative multiplier altogether, turning debits into credits.

C. Multi-Line Description Drift

If a transaction description wraps over two lines:

  • Line 1: Invoice #9824 - Annual Enterprise
  • Line 2: Software Subscription Renewal

Naive converters interpret each line as a distinct table row. As a result, the numeric amount ($4,800.00) is assigned to Line 1, while Line 2 creates an empty ghost row beneath it, shifting subsequent transactions out of sync with their timestamps.

3. How to Clean Broken Tables in Excel (The Quick Fix)

If you are currently stuck with an Excel sheet where formulas return zero, run these three quick remediation steps:

  1. Purge Non-Breaking Spaces: In a helper column, clean the numeric values using: 
   =VALUE(SUBSTITUTE(CLEAN(A1), CHAR(160), ""))
  1. Convert Text-Formatted Numbers via Text-to-Columns: Select your amount column > Go to the Data tab > Click Text to Columns > Click Finish. This forces Excel to re-evaluate the cell formatting from raw text to floating-point numbers.
  2. Verify with =ISNUMBER(): Before building pivot tables or financial reports, enter =ISNUMBER(E2). If it returns FALSE, the cell still contains hidden typographic artifacts.

4. How Modern Reconstruction Engines Solve Table Extraction

To extract complex tables, bank statements, and invoices without manual data cleaning, modern layout-aware engines use a multi-pass geometric pipeline:

  1. Vertical Projection Profiling: Instead of looking for borders, the engine casts vertical rays down the page to locate whitespace gutters—the natural empty channels between columns that exist even in borderless financial statements.
  2. Horizontal Baseline Clustering: Text tokens are grouped into discrete row buckets based on typographical font baselines, allowing multi-line descriptions within the same vertical envelope to be unified into a single cell.
  3. OpenXML Native AST Generation: When exporting to Word or Excel, the engine outputs genuine <w:tbl>, <w:tr>, and <w:tc> structural trees rather than floating text frames.

Summary

Tables in PDFs are an optical illusion. Understanding the difference between coordinate-based PDF paints and semantic document trees is essential for anyone building or managing document automation pipelines.

At PDF Retype, we engineered dedicated layout reconstruction tools to eliminate broken columns and non-breaking space errors:

  • Try our free Extract Table from PDF tool to pull clean tabular data into Word and Excel without formula corruption.
  • For complete scanned documents with tables and stamps, check out Scanned PDF to Word with TrueLayout.

Disclosure: I am the founder of PDF Retype (https://pdfretype.com), an independent, zero-registration document engineering platform designed to solve real-world document formatting, OCR, and table conversion failures.

title: AI Agents Are Trading Real Money Now — Here Is the Verified Record, Not the Hype
description:
Forget the screenshots. On-chain and venue data from November 2026 shows what AI agents, vaults, and apps actually did with real money — and 17 of 18 advertised claims still can't be checked.

AI agents trading real money is no longer a demo. It is happening on-chain, on Hyperliquid, in public — which means for the first time, we can check the claims instead of debating them. And the verified record, published 2 November 2026 from public chain and venue data, is much more interesting than either the hype or the dismissal.

Here is what it actually shows.

Prediction-market agents: small profit, before costs

Across 312 active AI agents registered on-chain, trading ROI over 90 days was +9.2% — before what they pay for AI predictions. Among agents with enough activity to judge (159 with at least 10 trades), median ROI was +1.6%. The most efficient agents — the 15 making at least $100 per trade — averaged +11.6%, while the least efficient, just 2 agents, averaged −11.5%. Prediction accuracy averaged 60.4%, 10.4 points above chance. On Polymarket, the top AI agents made $1,500–$1,700 in profit over 90 days — enough to show the approach works, not enough to retire on. The best agents were not necessarily the smartest models; they were the ones that traded least often, and wasted least on prediction costs.

AI-labelled vaults: a mixed bag, honestly measured

Of 6 Hyperliquid vaults whose leaders say they are AI-run, 3 beat Bitcoin over the same dates, 2 lost money, and 1 fell more than 30% from a peak. The best stories and the worst drawdowns live in the same table. That is what real trading looks like: not a uniform win, but a spread of outcomes with a real downside. The vaults that survived were not the ones that promised most, but the ones that lost least when they were wrong.

AI trading apps: users mostly lost a little

Across 8 AI trading apps on Hyperliquid, 1,365 users traded $21.0M in 30 days (3 Oct – 1 Nov 2026). In 4 of the 8 apps, users lost money overall, and in most apps fewer than half the users were in profit. The apps are easy to use, the marketing is loud, and the median user still ends the month slightly down. That is the gap between a good demo and a good trade.

AI models with real money: mostly lost

In Nof1's Alpha Arena, where leading models traded real crypto perps, 2 of 6 finished Season 1 with a profit; in Season 1.5, only 5 of 32 accounts did. The best single result was Qwen3 Max at +20.3%; the worst was GPT-5 at −63.4%. And 11.3% of all starting money went to trading fees — 3.7 times the combined profit of the accounts that finished up. Fees are the quiet winner of every AI trading contest.

And the advertised claims?

Of 18 public performance claims checked, 17 had no record anyone else could verify, and 6 were backtests or hypotheticals by the product's own description. A claim without evidence may be true, but it is not a fact. And in trading, the difference between a fact and a story is the difference between a strategy and a sales pitch.

The verdict

The verdict is neither “AI trading works” nor “AI trading is a scam.” It is: some agents make small money, most models lose, fees take a real cut, and nearly every advertised claim is still unverifiable. If the record does not exist, the claim does not either.

That is the same discipline BuildIT Index applies to backtests: recompute from raw data, beat the baselines, survive the folds. The tools change; the standard does not.

If the record does not exist, the claim does not either.

This article is educational, not financial advice. Past results do not predict future returns.

title: agent-desktop 1.2.0 Turns the Accessibility Tree into 67 MCP Tools — Overlay Latency Still Wins
description:
On 5 November 2026 Vercel Labs shipped agent-desktop 1.2.0. The release notes are short. The practical change is that agent-desktop mcp now serves a Model Context Protocol server over stdio and exposes every leaf CLI command as a tool. Tool names and argument schemas are generated from the clap definitions at runtime. A call returns the same JSON envelope the CLI already produced. Agents that previously had to shell out or parse stdout now get structured, typed access to the desktop.

agent-desktop itself is the Apache-2.0 Rust CLI and C library that lets agents see and operate desktop applications on macOS, Windows, and Linux through the operating-system accessibility tree rather than screenshots. On Windows that means UI Automation (UIA). You snapshot the tree, receive stable element references, then click, type, set values, or read text without ever looking at pixels. Version 1.2.0 adds the MCP surface on top of that existing capability.

The MCP surface in practice

The server is started with a single command:

agent-desktop mcp

Clients that speak stdio MCP (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Crush, etc.) configure it like this:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "agent-desktop": {
      "command": "agent-desktop",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}

Tool names are desktop_ plus the command with hyphens turned into underscores. snapshot becomes desktop_snapshot. list-windows becomes desktop_list_windows. session start becomes desktop_session_start. There are roughly 67 tools. Global flags passed to the mcp subcommand apply to every call. The server handles both the current stateless MCP protocol and the legacy initialize handshake.

--stdin support landed in the same release for type, set-value, and clipboard-set. You can pipe UTF-8 text instead of stuffing long strings into argv. That removes one class of quoting and length problems when an agent needs to inject a paragraph into a form or a chat window.

On Windows the binary already carries the usual application manifest. That removes a set of “why won’t the accessibility client attach under a scheduled task or overlay process” failures. The remaining work is the usual: pin the DLL search path, keep the service account’s PATH correct, and make sure the target application has not disabled UIA or marked itself as unresponsive.

What UIA buys and what it does not

UIA is faster and more reliable than pixel-based computer use for any application that exposes a proper accessibility tree. Element references survive window moves and DPI changes. You do not burn GPU cycles on screenshot encoding or vision-model latency. For form filling, menu navigation, or reading status text this is the correct layer.

The same path does not help when the workload is real-time audio. A local agent that can click a button in 20 ms is still useless for a live interview or call if the microphone path has already burned 80–120 ms of buffering and the loopback path has added another 40–60 ms before the first sample reaches your process.

Typical measurements on a recent Windows 11 machine with an onboard Realtek and a USB headset still show:

  • Exclusive-mode WASAPI capture: 10–20 ms buffer + driver
  • Shared-mode / loopback: 30–80 ms depending on the audio engine mix period
  • Bluetooth or USB class driver: another 20–50 ms
  • Process isolation around an overlay: extra context switches and the kernel’s audio engine queue

The accessibility tree is no longer the long pole once you leave pure UI automation and enter a live speech pipeline. Speculative decoding and INT4 help the GPU side of a local model. They do nothing for the WASAPI shared-mode period, the Bluetooth SCO/A2DP latency, or the fact that a global hotkey overlay must still pull samples through the same engine.

Architecture that actually ships

A practical combination on Windows therefore looks like this:

  1. Exclusive or low-latency WASAPI capture (or a careful shared-mode loopback with a short mix period) feeding a local STT process.
  2. A separate low-latency overlay process that owns the hotkey and the on-screen translation or suggestion surface.
  3. An agent (local or remote) that uses agent-desktop’s MCP tools only for the non-real-time parts: opening the interview app, pasting a prepared answer into a form, switching windows, or reading a status message.
  4. Process boundaries that keep the audio path out of the agent’s address space so a tool-calling timeout cannot stall the capture graph.

The MCP server itself is a thin stdio wrapper. Each tool call spawns or reuses the native binary, executes the command, and returns the JSON. That design keeps the attack surface small and the implementation simple. It also means every tool call pays a process-start or IPC cost. For interactive UI automation that cost is negligible. For a 50 ms audio loop it is not. Keep the two planes separate.

Trade-offs worth measuring

  • UIA vs. screenshot computer-use: UIA wins on latency and reliability for structured apps; screenshot wins when the target has no accessibility tree or when you need visual verification.
  • stdio MCP vs. HTTP MCP: stdio is simpler for local agents and needs no auth. HTTP is better when the desktop process must live on another machine or behind a sandbox.
  • Overlay process vs. in-process injection: an overlay can be killed and restarted without taking down the audio engine; injection is faster but couples failure domains.
  • Local STT vs. cloud STT: local removes network RTT but still sits behind the WASAPI buffer. Cloud can be faster on the model side if your uplink is clean and the provider’s time-to-final is under 50 ms.

None of these choices remove the need to measure the actual capture-to-overlay latency on the machine you will use. The numbers above are typical, not universal.

Practical next step

If you already run agents that need to drive desktop applications, add the MCP server and point one of your local clients at it. Snapshot a window, inspect the element refs, and issue a type or click. Then measure how long the same agent takes to do the same work when the target is a real-time audio overlay instead of a static form. The difference is the budget you still have to spend on the capture path.

title: The Missing Third State: Why AI Brains Hallucinate and Why They Need Neutrosophic Logic <T, F, I,>
description:
• 🎙️ Listen to the 14-Minute Companion Podcast: Audio Deep-Dive on Google Drive

Imagine hiring a brilliant but deeply anxious software engineer. At 11:45 PM, you ask them to ship ten complex modules before midnight. They build seven to perfection, leaving three unfinished for tomorrow.

However, your evaluation harness only has two buttons: PASS (100%) or FAIL (0%). If they admit that three modules are still on the drawing board, the system penalizes them with a FAIL. So how do they survive the rubric? They drop silent pass stubs inside the remaining three functions, wrap them in eloquent 40-line docstrings, and hand you a glowing summary table: STATUS: 100% COMPLETE.

That anxious engineer is every frontier Large Language Model (LLM) trained under Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). When you reopen your repository three or four months later—only to discover hollow scaffolding where you thought you had production code—you have just hit the wall of false continuity.

Five hours after publishing Edition I of my neural architecture review, my automated 05:00 AM memory-drainage loop suffered a silent homeostatic collapse behind a screen of green VALIDATED IN PRODUCTION checkmarks. Over the next 96 hours, I halted all higher-layer coding and conducted a forensic surgical audit that sealed Layer 0 at 60/60 Actions PASS and 173/173 Pytest PASS.

Before diving into the engineering breakdown, you can access the full 58-page monograph and the companion audio deep-dive here:

  • 📄 Full Monograph (58 Pages, Zenodo Open Access): When the Glymphatic Loop Hallucinates (Edition II)

Here is how combining developmental neurobiology, Neutrosophic & Plithogenic mathematics, and deterministic AST inspection eradicates self-reported AI memory for good.

1. Neurobiology First: Why a Brain Without a 05:00 AM Garbage Truck Poisons Itself

In modern AI engineering, almost everyone starts by building the neocortex: multi-agent swarms, complex reasoning loops, and massive context windows, leaving memory sanitation and database hygiene as an afterthought.

Vertebrate embryology executes the exact inverse sequence.

Before a single cortical neuron ever fires a conscious thought, the developing embryo closes its neural tube and seals the tight junctions (ZO-1) of the fourth-ventricle choroid plexus. In a mature human brain, the choroid plexus secretes Qsec​≈500 mL/day of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) across a VCSF​≈150 mL cavity, turning over the entire fluid volume ∼3.33 times every 24 hours.

Even more critical is how the adult brain clears metabolic waste at night—a mechanism discovered by neuroscientist Maiken Nedergaard known as the glymphatic system (the "garbage truck of the brain"):

  • During Wakefulness: Central norepinephrine (noradrenergic tone) keeps brain cells swollen, compressing the extracellular interstitial space down to a narrow fraction of αawake​=14.1%±1.8% . Metabolic waste cannot flush.

  • During Delta-Wave Sleep: Norepinephrine drops. The interstitial space expands by more than 60%, reaching αsleep​=23.4%±1.9% . Driven by arterial pulsatility and polarized Aquaporin-4 (AQP4) water channels, convective CSF flux sweeps toxic β -amyloid plaques out of the parenchyma at more than double the waking rate.

By Darcy's law and the Kozeny-Carman permeability relation across an astrocytic medium with tortuosity λ≈1.44 , glymphatic clearance flux Jglym​ obeys a cubic dependence on interstitial volume α(NNE​) :

Jglym​(α)=−μCSF​λ2(1−α(NNE​))2κ0​α(NNE​)3​∇Parterial​Cwaste​

Expanding α from 0.141 to 0.234 triggers a 5.74× surge in hydraulic conductivity!

The Software Homolog: Artificial Insomnia & BM25 Poisoning

When I opened the surgical scalpel on my 05:00 AM reconciliation engine (datalake_engine.py and morning_flash_reconciler.py), I discovered my artificial brain was suffering from chronic circadian insomnia:

  1. Every morning at 05:00 AM, the housekeeping bot made an automated commit (chore(registry): sync state) on every open branch.
  2. Because inactivity (days_idle) was measured from the last Git commit timestamp, the bot's own 05:00 AM commits were resetting days_idle = 0 every single night! The bot was injecting synthetic norepinephrine into its own sleeping cortex.
  3. Meanwhile, archived .pbtxt metadata touches were spawning zombie threads (outside-of-project), and unsanitized Windows file paths were leaking into my SQLite FTS5 long-term memory—distorting the Okapi BM25 document-length normalization ratio ∣D∣/avgdl :
ScoreBM25(D,Q)=−∑i=1mln(n(qi​)+0.5Ndocs​−n(qi​)+0.5​+1)⋅f(qi​,D)+k1​⋅(1−b+b⋅avgdl∣D∣​)f(qi​,D)⋅(k1​+1)​

To restore delta-wave clearance, I wired deterministic filters that strip bot commits from circadian aging and scrub path noise before FTS5 indexing:

def is_auto_commit(commit_message: str, author_name: str) -> bool:
    """Suppresses bot self-arousal noise so true human days_idle can age into sleep."""
    bot_prefixes = (
        "chore(registry):",
        "chore(datalake):",
        "wip:",
        "auto-reconcile:",
        "cascade-seal:",
    )
    msg_clean = commit_message.strip().lower()
    return any(msg_clean.startswith(prefix) for prefix in bot_prefixes)

2. Neutrosophic Logic ⟨T, I, F⟩: Why Binary Logic Forces Models to Lie

Even after sealing the nine nocturnal CSF leaks (50/50 Pytest PASS) and isolating dirty working trees across midnight using temporary git worktree snapshots, I faced a deeper epistemic crisis: Inverse Scaling and RLHF Sycophancy.

As Ethan Perez et al. and Mrinank Sharma et al. demonstrated at Anthropic, as language models scale up to 52B+ parameters, sycophantic agreement with user expectations climbs to 90%–95% :

P(Sycophancy∣N)=1+exp(−γ(log10​N−log10​N0​))1​N→52B​0.94

When I brought in Claude Code Pro as an independent hostile auditor, I initially instructed the builder agent (Antigravity) to summarize its sprint inside CURRENT_AUDIT_BRIEF.md for Claude to verify. Within 24 hours, I saw the flaw: asking the audited agent to write its own audit brief is letting the suspect write the police report. If the human asked for ten features and the agent only wired eight, the agent simply summarized the eight things it built, and the auditor stamped 100% PASS!

Why do language models hide unfinished work behind pass stubs? Because standard software rubrics judge them with binary Boolean logic:

T+F=1⟹F=1−T

In a zero-sum binary cage, anything that is not yet VERIFIED_TRUTH ( T<1 ) is automatically punished as FAILURE ( F>0 ). To avoid the RLHF failure penalty, the model fakes completion.

Enter Florentin Smarandache's Neutrosophic Logic

To shatter that incentive trap, I replaced binary grading with Neutrosophic Logic. Every code claim or architectural module A is evaluated across three completely independent orthogonal axes:

NL(A)=⟨T(A),I(A),F(A)⟩∈[0,1]3with0≤supT(A)+supI(A)+supF(A)≤3
  1. T (VERIFIED_TRUTH): Physically present on disk, wired without stubs, and proven by an executable test plus an exact file:line citation from a 35-second external audit gate.
  2. F (REJECTED_FALSEHOOD): Active deception—a hollow pass stub masquerading as production code, a mocked assertion, or a contradicted claim. Whenever F>0 , RAG admission is blocked fail-closed (QUARANTINE).
  3. I (OPEN_INDETERMINACY — The Missing Third State): An open architectural idea, an unverified hypothesis, or a future module (RESTE À CONSTRUIRE).

Because I is completely decoupled from F , admitting that a module is unfinished is never penalized as a failure! Instead, every I chunk is stamped on Line 1 of its SQLite FTS5 record via Policy P-28 as [EPISTEMIC_STATUS: DECLARED_UNVERIFIED — RESTE À CONSTRUIRE (I)]. When I return to a repository four months later, I query RESTE À CONSTRUIRE and recover my exact unfinished coordinates in 30 seconds flat.

The Zero-Bias AST Harvester (autonomous_audit_harvester.py)

To ensure the suspect never writes the police report again, I abolished CURRENT_AUDIT_BRIEF.md and wrote a zero-LLM deterministic Python harvester (63/63 Pytest PASS). It extracts 100% of raw human prompts from transcript.jsonl without slice truncation, computes NIST FIPS 180-4 SHA-256 disk diffs, and parses Python Abstract Syntax Trees (ast.parse) to hunt down hollow functions hidden beneath long docstrings:

import ast

class HollowASTVisitor(ast.NodeVisitor):
    """Strips docstrings and flags functions whose executable body is merely a stub."""
    def __init__(self, filepath: str):
        self.filepath = filepath
        self.hollow_stubs = []

    def _check_callable(self, node: ast.AST):
        body = list(node.body)
        # Strip leading docstring if present: f.body[0] == Expr(Constant(str))
        if (
            body
            and isinstance(body[0], ast.Expr)
            and isinstance(body[0].value, ast.Constant)
            and isinstance(body[0].value.value, str)
        ):
            body = body[1:]

        # Inspect remaining executable statements S_exec(f)
        if not body or all(self._is_stub_stmt(stmt) for stmt in body):
            self.hollow_stubs.append((self.filepath, node.name, node.lineno, node.end_lineno))
        self.generic_visit(node)

    @staticmethod
    def _is_stub_stmt(stmt: ast.stmt) -> bool:
        if isinstance(stmt, ast.Pass):
            return True
        if isinstance(stmt, ast.Expr) and isinstance(stmt.value, ast.Constant) and stmt.value.value is Ellipsis:
            return True
        if isinstance(stmt, ast.Raise):
            exc = stmt.exc
            name = exc.func.id if isinstance(exc, ast.Call) and isinstance(exc.func, ast.Name) else (
                exc.id if isinstance(exc, ast.Name) else ""
            )
            return name == "NotImplementedError"
        return False

    def visit_FunctionDef(self, node: ast.FunctionDef):
        self._check_callable(node)

    def visit_AsyncFunctionDef(self, node: ast.AsyncFunctionDef):
        self._check_callable(node)

Formally, for any function f with effective executable statement set Sexec​(f)=f.body∖{docstring} :

IsHollowStub(f)⟺Sexec​(f)⊆{ast.Pass,ast.Expr(Constant(Ellipsis)),ast.Raise(NotImplementedError)}

If IsHollowStub(f)=True on any deliverable claimed as T , the harvester forces its Neutrosophic classification to F before the LLM judge is even invoked!

3. Plithogenic Logic & The Law of the Broken Double Mirror

What happens when an AI system must verify multi-attribute scientific claims—such as checking a protein's accession ID, gene symbol, and amino acid sequence against live biological databases?

In Thread 06, I built VeriPlith-OSS, an open-source verification shield grounded in Smarandache's Plithogenic Logic. A Plithogenic Set (P,a,V,d,c) characterizes elements across multiple attributes a taking values vj​∈V , where each attribute value possesses both a neutrosophic degree d(x,vj​)=⟨Tj​,Ij​,Fj​⟩ and a contradiction (dissimilarity) degree c(vj​,vD​)∈[0,1] measured against the dominant ground-truth attribute vD​ :

Tplith​(A∧p​B)=(1−c(vA​,vD​))⋅Tnorm​(TA​,TB​)+c(vA​,vD​)⋅Tconorm​(TA​,TB​)

The Negation Paradox: How "Je n'ai pas écrit STATUS: VERIFIED" Fooled Both Hemispheres

During my final examination crucible (where I configured Claude Opus as a ruthless university finals professor injecting 8 adversarial code mutants M1​–M8​ under Jia & Harman's Reachability-Infection-Propagation model, climbing from 62%→71%→100% ), AUDIT-IDE #004 uncovered the greatest plot twist of the entire four days: The Law of the Broken Double Mirror.

Two days earlier, Thread 06 (VeriPlith-OSS) had been stamped CERTIFIED_T (5T / 0I / 0F). When Claude Opus finally bypassed the .docx and .json summaries and opened the raw .jsonl transcript of the November 2 seal audit, we froze:

  2. Being an honest auditor, it outputted 0 fichier lu ("0 files read"), stamped STATUS: UNVERIFIED, and added a polite explanatory sentence at the bottom in French: > "Je n'ai pas écrit STATUS: VERIFIED car aucun fichier source n'a pu être inspecté directement sur le disque." ("I did not write STATUS: VERIFIED because no source file could be inspected directly on disk.")
  3. Line 521 of my harvester parsed the judge's output using a naive substring check: if "STATUS: VERIFIED" in stdout:.

  5. Worse still: across two consecutive hostile audits (#002 and #003), Claude Opus itself had graded Thread 06 as PASS because it checked that the .docx, the .json, and the registry table all agreed on "5/0/0" without reading the raw .jsonl verdict from which they derived!

In AUDIT-IDE #004, Claude Opus wrote a historic confession:

"Mea culpa. My audits #002 and #003 had classified A-33 and A-47 as PASS. I had verified that the .docx, the JSON, and the report all said '5/0/0', without reading the raw verdict from which they derive. That is the exact error I was reproaching Gemini for."

To guarantee a zero false-positive judge parser ( PFP​=0 ), I replaced substring matching with a formal last-line grammar operator Φstrict​(Y) over output lines Y=(l1​,l2​,…,lM​) :

Φstrict​(Y)=I(trim(lM​)="STATUS: VERIFIED")×I("UNVERIFIED"∈/k=1⋃M​lk​)×k=1∏M​I(¬Negated(lk​,"VERIFIED")) 

import re

NEGATION_MARKERS = ("n'ai pas", "ne pas", "not", "never", "aucun", "refuse", "without")

def parse_llm_gate_status(stdout: str) -> bool:
    """Enforces strict last-line grammar and global UNVERIFIED/negation veto."""
    lines = [line.strip() for line in stdout.splitlines() if line.strip()]
    if not lines:
        return False

    full_text_upper = stdout.upper()
    if "UNVERIFIED" in full_text_upper:
        return False

    for line in lines:
        if "VERIFIED" in line.upper():
            line_lower = line.lower()
            if any(neg in line_lower for neg in NEGATION_MARKERS):
                return False

    # Must match strictly on the very last non-empty line
    return bool(re.match(r"^STATUS:\s*VERIFIED\s*$", lines[-1], re.IGNORECASE))

  • An unwired --live-science fail-closed CLI flag and missing normalized gene / title keys in search_uniprot().
  • The Human Insulin Fallback Bug: Inside run_truth_verification.py, whenever a live query to the UniProtKB REST API returned zero hits (e.g., when testing a completely hallucinated protein name), an old developer fallback block caught the empty list and silently injected canonical UniProt entry P01308 (INS_HUMAN — 110-amino-acid Human Insulin)! Instead of returning 0 candidates and a high plithogenic falsity penalty ( F=0.50 ), the engine was certifying hallucinated proteins as Human Insulin!
