title: Product photo to video with AI: from 1–10 shop photos to 5-second clips that keep the label (real outputs inside)
description:
Most product pages on Shopify or Etsy still have only photos. A 5-second clip of the product spinning, splashing or being worn shows the back, the scale and the finish better than another still, and you no longer need a shoot to make one. This post walks through how we turn product photos into short clips in RefVid: what kind of AI model keeps the label intact, which photos to give it, which shots to make first, and how to write the prompt. Every image below is a frame from a real output, next to the photos it came from. The full guide, with every template and the current prices, is on our product photo to video page.


A frame from a 5-second clip made from one side-view photo of AERO 1, an invented running shoe, on Kling 4. Prompt: "the shoe on a wet rock by a mountain stream at sunrise, the camera moving slowly along it". Not edited.

Image-to-video vs reference-to-video

There are two ways to turn a product photo into a video, and the difference decides whether your label survives.

  • Image-to-video animates the photo itself as the first frame. Once the camera moves away from that frame, the model has to invent the product, so it drifts: the logo warps, the stitching changes, the colour shifts.
  • Reference-to-video treats your photos as a description of the product and builds every frame around it. The shape and label hold through the whole clip, and a second and third clip match the first, which matters when a listing or an ad set needs several videos of one item.


One of the three AERO 1 photos behind the next two clips: a plain background, even light, the label readable.



Two scenes from the same three photos, the same shoe in both (Kling 3.0 Omni in RefVid).

RefVid is reference-to-video: you save the product once from its photos, and every clip in any scene starts from that saved product.

Step 1: give it the right photos

One sharp photo is enough to start: your main product-page angle, on a plain background, with the label readable and the colours accurate. If that is all you have, RefVid can draw three more angles from it with the same shape, colours and label text, so the video model sees more than one side.

With three to five photos the result gets steadier: add a side, the back and a close-up of the label. You can save 1 to 10 photos per product. If the photos are already on your shop page, paste the product link instead of uploading; RefVid reads the photos from Shopify stores, Amazon listings and shop pages that describe the product in structured data.

Leave out photos with price stickers, props that are not part of the product, or phone-screenshot clutter. A screenshot of a listing brings the status bar and the app's buttons into the video, so crop it first:


Adding a photo in the studio. When a photo has a phone screenshot's shape, the studio offers Crop; the model sees the cropped photo.

Step 2: make the clips that sell first

Start with the clips that sell, not the ones that impress. A turntable spin shows the back on a product page. An unboxing shows what arrives. Someone holding the product and talking works as a TikTok or Reels ad. A lifestyle shot on a shelf or a desk shows scale and use.

Each of these exists in RefVid as a template that opens the studio with the shots, length and shape already written, so your photos are all you add. A few of the 27 product templates:

Template What you get Length and shape
360 turntable Your product spins slowly through a full turn on a white studio turntable 5 s, square 1:1
Unboxing Hands open a kraft box, lift the product out, turn the label to the camera, with paper sounds 10 s, vertical 9:16
Water splash The product drops into clear water in slow motion and settles upright 5 s, vertical 9:16
Perfume reveal Mist and one puff of spray in warm backlight, then light through the glass onto the label 5 s, vertical 9:16
Jewelry on hand A hand wearing your ring or bracelet turns slowly in warm window light 5 s, square 1:1
Tech reveal A line of light traces your device in the dark, then the camera arcs around it 5 s, wide 16:9

Three of them, each with a reference photo and a frame from its real example clip. The products are AI-made samples; the prompts are the templates' own, word for word, with {1} where your product's name goes.

360 turntable: AERO 1, from 3 photos.

{1} on a round white turntable in a photo studio, rotating slowly through a full 360 degrees, light grey seamless background, soft even studio light, locked-off camera, sharp focus on every detail.



Every side faces the camera once as it turns, so photograph the front, both sides and the back at the same height; the back is the side a listing rarely shows, so include it, above all if it carries a label. 5 seconds, square, silent, on Kling 3.0 Omni: the cheapest of the three to make, and the template RefVid's paying customers make most. 360 turntable template.

Perfume reveal: NOIR 07, from 3 photos.

{1} stands on glossy black glass wrapped in slowly drifting soft mist; a single fine puff of perfume spray bursts from the top and catches a warm golden backlight, then the mist clears and a beam of light passes through the glass, ending on the label sharp and centred. Low-key, luxurious, slow push-in.



Shoot the bottle straight on with the label square to the lens and no glare: the clip ends on that label. 5 seconds, 9:16, with sound, on Kling 4. Perfume reveal template.

Jewelry on hand: HALO, from 4 photos.

Close-up: a woman's hand with a soft natural manicure, wearing {1}, rests on cream silk and turns slowly toward the camera, {1} catching small sparkles in warm window light. Shallow depth of field, gentle slow push-in, elegant and natural.



No hand model needed. Show the piece from the angle a wearer sees, plus the band and the setting; a photo of it on a finger helps the size look right. 5 seconds, square, with sound. Jewelry on hand template.

Step 3: let the photos describe the product, the prompt describe the rest

The prompt should cover the place, one motion, the camera move, the light and the last frame. Use the product's saved name instead of describing it again: a second description in words competes with the photos and is the most common reason a label changes. Two prompts that work:

AERO 1 slowly rotates on a round white plinth in a minimal studio, static camera at shoe height, soft key light, sharp focus

A hand lifts AERO 1 out of a kraft box on a wooden table and turns it toward the camera, soft daylight


Made from the three AERO 1 photos with a prompt close to the first one. Short, concrete prompts beat long lists of adjectives.

Pick the shape for where it goes

Square 1:1 for product pages, vertical 9:16 for TikTok, Reels and Shorts, wide 16:9 for your own site. Clips run 3 to 30 seconds on Kling 4 (up to 15 on Kling 3.0 Omni), can have sound, and one clip can hold up to three subjects, such as the product and the person holding it.



The same prompt and the same three photos, made vertical for social and square for a product page.

If the clip is going into paid placements rather than a product page, it is built in three beats: something that stops the eye, the product doing the one thing you sell, and a last frame on the label. We wrote that up in making a video ad of your own product from photos, with three ad formats from the same photos to test against each other.

Check every clip before it goes live

Watch each clip at full size. The label and logo should read the same as on the real item; small print is the part most likely to change, so keep the takes where it holds. Check the colours against the photo, and never show features or accessories the product does not have.

What it costs

New accounts start with free credits and no card: they cover a first 5-second clip on Kling 3.0 Omni (Vidu Q2 in some regions), and every clip, free or paid, has no watermark and may be used commercially. After that, clips are priced in credits by the second. A 5-second silent clip on Kling 3.0 Omni, such as the 360 turntable, is 155 credits; the same 5 seconds on Kling 4 at 720p, with sound, is 290. Here is what each way of paying buys, from the RefVid pricing page:

How you pay Price 5-second Kling 3.0 Omni clips, like the turntable 5-second Kling 4 clips
One video, no plan $2.99 up to 5 s, $4.99 up to 10 s, $6.99 up to 15 s 1 1
Credit pack, one time $9.90 for 1,500 credits (also $19.90 for 3,200, $49.90 for 8,500) 9 5
Basic plan $10 a month, or $96 a year, for 2,000 credits a month 12 a month 6 a month

Credits never expire: unused plan credits roll over and pack credits stay. Failed videos give their credits back, and unused pack credits are refunded in full within 14 days.

The full product photo to video guide lists all the templates with their lengths and shapes, and answers the questions shop owners ask us most, like whether one photo is enough and how to get a 360-degree spin.

— Louis Chi, RefVid

title: Menyiapkan pertanyaan integrasi dari lapisan antarmuka Orkvex
description:
Materi teknologi Orkvex menyebut beberapa pilihan antarmuka. Sebelum membahas implementasi, saya akan menyusun kebutuhan aplikasi yang ingin dipenuhi.

Berikut format pembacaan yang saya gunakan.

Tentukan satu pekerjaan

Contoh umum: aplikasi perlu menampilkan informasi yang tetap dapat dipahami setelah koneksi terputus dan tersambung kembali.

Dari skenario ini, muncul pertanyaan tentang waktu data, urutan pembaruan, dan cara memperoleh kembali kondisi yang relevan.

Contoh tersebut bukan deskripsi perilaku antarmuka platform.

Cari kontrak perilaku

Saya ingin menemukan definisi respons, arti status, kondisi kesalahan, dan batas penggunaan.

Dokumentasi juga perlu dibaca untuk mengetahui apakah suatu operasi aman diulang. Jawabannya tidak boleh ditebak dari nama metode atau contoh singkat.

Catat asumsi yang belum terjawab

Jika suatu detail belum dijelaskan, saya menuliskannya sebagai pertanyaan implementasi.

Cara ini menjaga rancangan awal tetap dapat ditinjau. Kita tahu bagian mana yang berasal dari sumber dan bagian mana yang membutuhkan klarifikasi.

title: Don't write like a robot: llms.txt for AI agents
description:
This morning I asked Claude to grill me about my blog. My idea was that most of my readers are now AI agents, so my posts should be written for them. Its first question was what that claim rested on. Fair.

We ended up somewhere I didn't expect. I didn't rewrite a single post. The prose stays for people, and the agents get a frame around it: AI agents named in robots.txt, a generated llms.txt, and a Markdown copy of every post.

Then I fact-checked it, and part of it is a cheap bet rather than a sure thing. I couldn't find anyone who confirms that agents read llms.txt, and the one study on this (GEO) says quotes, numbers and cited sources matter most.

The full post covers the Hugo recipe, tested on Hugo 0.152.2, what the evidence does and doesn't say, and a prompt you can paste into your own coding agent to audit your blog.

Read the full post, with the recipe and the audit prompt: https://digitaldias.com/blog/2026-11-06-robots-txt-llms-txt-ai-agents/

title: Crypto AI Vaults: 3 of 6 Beat Bitcoin, 1 Fell 30% — What That Actually Proves
description:
The most checkable corner of AI trading is Hyperliquid vaults — public numbers, no screenshots. The results split the hype cleanly in two.

Crypto is where AI trading claims can actually be checked, because Hyperliquid vaults publish their numbers on-chain. No screenshots, no self-reported PnL — just public data. So what does the checkable corner of AI trading actually show?

As of the 2 November 2026 verified check: of 6 Hyperliquid vaults whose leaders say they are AI-run, 3 beat Bitcoin over the same dates, 2 lost money, and 1 fell more than 30% from a peak. Among the vaults passing strict safety and drawdown gates, results ranged from +26.5% (with a −24.2% max drawdown) to −0.1% (with a −10.8% drawdown) — and the top-ranked vault overall, not AI-labelled, returned +24.1% with an −11.9% drawdown while trailing Bitcoin by 4.2 points over the same period.

First, “AI-run” predicts nothing

The label is the operator’s claim, not a performance category. AI-labelled vaults appear across the entire distribution — top, middle, and bottom. If a label predicted returns, the spread would be narrow. It is not. The label tells you what the operator says about their process. It tells you nothing about whether that process works.

Second, beating Bitcoin is the right benchmark — and most don’t

Holding Bitcoin costs nothing, needs no skill, and takes no drawdown decisions. Any vault that trails it over the same dates charged you complexity, fees (typically a 10% profit share for the leader), and drawdown risk for less than doing nothing. Several vaults in the data did exactly that.

Third, drawdown is the story the return hides

A vault up 26.5% that fell 24.2% from a peak is a different proposition from a vault up 8% that fell 3%. The first can wipe out a depositor who arrived at the wrong time; the second is boring in the best way. Rankings by return alone are how people buy the top of a drawdown.

How to evaluate any vault in two minutes

(1) Return vs Bitcoin over the same dates. (2) Max drawdown from peak. (3) Leader’s profit share and stake. (4) How long it has been live (a month of numbers is an anecdote, not a record). (5) Whether deposits are open and what happens in a drawdown — who bears it, you or the leader?

The checkable corner of AI trading does not vindicate the hype or confirm the dismissal. It shows variance: some AI-labelled vaults beat the benchmark, some lose, one fell hard. That variance is the honest answer to “do AI vaults work?” — sometimes, for some operators, with drawdowns that demand respect. Anyone selling you a simpler answer is selling you something else.

BuildIT Index applies the same standard to backtests: recompute from raw data, beat baselines, check folds, count trials, model costs. A vault that cannot survive those checks on its own history is a bet on luck, not skill.

If the label predicted returns, the table would not look like this.

This article is educational, not financial advice. Past results do not predict future returns.

title: From Backtest to Funded Account: The Validation Checklist Prop Traders Need Before Paying
description:
Challenge fees are $200–$1,000+ per attempt, and ~90% of attempts fail. This checklist — run before you pay, not after — is the cheapest money in prop trading.

A prop challenge fee is $200–$1,000+ per attempt, depending on account size. About 90% of attempts fail. That means the average trader pays several fees before ever seeing a funded account — or never does. The cheapest money in prop trading is the validation you run before you pay, not after.

Here is the checklist, in order. Skip a step and you are paying to discover what that step would have told you.

1. Recompute from raw predictions

If your strategy's numbers come from a claimed-accuracy column, a vendor's screenshot, or a backtest you cannot reproduce from raw data, stop. Recompute accuracy from the raw predictions yourself. If the recomputed number is much lower than the claimed one, you just saved a challenge fee.

2. Beat the dumb baselines

Always-bullish and no-change, on the same data. If your model cannot beat both, it adds nothing — it is riding the base rate of up-moves. On a bare CSV with no price history, those two baselines are the honest ones.

3. Check walk-forward folds, not the average

A single overall accuracy hides decay. Demand fold-by-fold results, earliest to latest. A model decaying from 80% to 56% across folds is a dying edge with a flattering average — and it will die faster under challenge pressure.

4. Count the trials and correct for them

How many configurations did you try before this one? If the answer is “hundreds” and no multiple-testing correction was applied, the headline number is partly luck. Apply a Bonferroni-style correction, or at least discount the result honestly.

5. Model costs and slippage

Backtest with realistic spread, slippage, commissions, and taxes. A strategy whose edge survives only at zero friction does not survive.

6. Backtest against the firm's exact rules

Daily drawdown from intraday peaks (5% at FTMO), total drawdown (10%), profit target (10% phase 1, 5% phase 2), minimum trading days. Run the strategy through those constraints historically. If it breaches the daily cap in backtest, it will breach it live — with a fee attached.

7. Size for the worst streak, not the average

Set risk per trade at 0.5–1%, so a normal four-loss streak stays inside the daily cap. Then set a personal daily stop below the firm's cap (stop at 3% down, not 5%).

8. Forward-test on paper first

Two to four weeks of live paper trading under the same rules. Backtesting tells you if a strategy could have worked; forward testing tells you if it actually functions — with real data flow, real fills, and real psychology.

9. Only then, pay

One challenge, sized to the account you can afford to lose the fee on, with the validated strategy and the validated risk parameters.

Most traders do this list backwards: pay first, discover the failures with money. The traders who pass are usually the ones who did the boring work first. Validation is not the opposite of ambition. It is the cheapest form of it.

BuildIT Index runs steps 1–5 mechanically on any prediction file: recompute accuracy, beat baselines, check folds, count trials, model costs, return a verdict with an exit code.

Validation is not the opposite of ambition. It is the cheapest form of it.

This article is educational, not financial advice. Past results do not predict future returns.

title: The instrumentation pattern: an agent you cannot see is an agent you cannot operate
description:
§ 01 · The blind spot

Most agents are instrumented the way a web service is: log the errors, watch latency, alert on a crash. That catches the failures that announce themselves. The failures that hurt most in production do the opposite. They are confident, well formed, and wrong. The agent that silently misrouted tickets after a model swap threw no error and kept its latency flat the entire time it was getting worse. The agent that double charged customers logged a clean retry. The agent that followed a hidden instruction made one more ordinary looking API call. None of these tripped a guard built for crashes, because none of them was a crash.

This week a cloud platform shipped agent observability as a primitive and, with it, a score for how instrumented your agent is. The market has decided that observability is a measurable property of an agent. The instrumentation pattern is how you earn that score: decide, up front, what an agent must emit so that you can debug it, operate it, and account for it.

§ 02 · Three streams, three questions

A production agent emits three distinct streams. They are not the same data at different verbosity. They answer three different questions, for three different people, at three different times.

◆ Decision traces answer "why did it do that," for the engineer, during a debug.

◆ Behavioral metrics answer "is it still doing the right thing," for the operator, continuously.

◆ The action log answers "what did it actually do, and on whose authority," for the auditor, after the fact.

Miss any one and you go blind to a whole class of failure. Most teams ship the first as raw logs, approximate the second with latency and cost, and never build the third. The pattern is to build all three deliberately.

── Stream one: decision traces ──

§ 03 · Stream one: decision traces

A decision trace is the record of a single agent run as a causal chain: the input it received, the context it assembled, each tool it called with the arguments it passed and the result it got back, the intermediate reasoning that led from one step to the next, and the action it finally took. The unit is the run, and the trace is hierarchical, because in any multi step or multi agent system one run spawns others and you need to follow the call down and back.

The question it answers is "why did it do that," and you only ask that question when something has already gone wrong. So the test of a good trace is reconstruction: can an engineer who was not there replay the decision from the trace alone, without rerunning the agent. If reproducing a bad decision requires running the agent again and hoping it misbehaves the same way, your trace is too thin. Capture the inputs and tool results verbatim, not a summary of them, because the summary throws away the one detail the bug turns on.

The cost is volume, so sample in the healthy case and capture in full on anything that escalated, errored, or crossed a confidence threshold. You want every trace you will actually need, and you will need the ones around the failures.

── Stream two: behavioral metrics ──

§ 04 · Stream two: behavioral metrics

Behavioral metrics are the aggregate shape of what the agent does, over time. Not latency and cost, those are operational metrics and they stay green during the failures that matter. Behavioral metrics measure the decisions: the distribution of outputs across categories, the escalation rate, the retry rate, the rate at which a human overturns the agent in the approval queue, the task success rate where you can measure it, and the share of runs that hit each tool.

The question they answer is "is it still doing the right thing," asked continuously, by whoever is on call. The power of this stream is that it catches the silent regression. When a model changes under the agent, the code is untouched and no error fires, but the distribution of decisions moves, and a moving distribution is an alarm. The triage agent's collapse would have been a Saturday morning alert instead of a four day incident if one number, the share of tickets routed to urgent, had been on a dashboard with a band around it.

Set baselines and alert on deviation, not on absolute thresholds. You rarely know the right absolute value. You always know that a sharp move from last week's value is worth a human look. The overturn rate in your approval queue deserves special attention: a rising overturn rate means the agent and the humans are drifting apart, and that is an early warning that the agent is degrading before any customer feels it.

── Stream three: the action log ──

§ 05 · Stream three: the action log

The action log is the durable, append only record of every consequential, externally visible thing the agent did: every message sent, record changed, transaction posted, job kicked off. Each entry carries what the action was, when it happened, which agent and version took it, on whose behalf, and under what authority, the same fields the identity note argued every action must carry. It is append only because its job is to be trustworthy after the fact, and a log you can edit is not evidence.

The question it answers is "what did it actually do, and on whose authority," asked by an auditor, a compliance team, or you on the worst day, after something has already happened. This is the stream teams skip, because on a good day it does nothing. It exists for the bad day. When an agent does something it should not have, the action log is the difference between "we can show exactly what happened, to whom, and stop it" and "we think it was one of our agents, we are reconstructing." Governance, the line this week's data drew between agents that scale and the majority that get rolled back, lives or dies on this stream.

── How they work together ──

§ 06 · Why you need all three

The three streams cover the three time horizons of operating an agent, and each is blind where the others see.

Behavioral metrics tell you something is wrong, now, in aggregate. They do not tell you why. Decision traces tell you why this specific run went wrong, but only once you know to look, and you know to look because a metric moved. The action log tells you what reached the outside world and who answers for it, which neither of the others is built to prove and an auditor will not accept on the strength of a debug trace. Detection, diagnosis, accountability. Three questions, three streams, no substitutions.

A useful way to see the dependency: the metric is the smoke alarm, the trace is the fire investigator, the action log is the insurance claim. You do not get to pick one.

── The file ──

§ 07 · The OBSERVABILITY.md

Create an OBSERVABILITY.md in the agent repository. It records, for decision traces, what is captured, the sampling rule, and the retention period. For behavioral metrics, the list of metrics, the baseline for each, and the alert band. For the action log, which actions are logged, the fields each entry carries, where it is stored append only, and who can read it. It names the dashboards, the alert targets, and the owner.

This is the document that answers, in one place, the question the platforms now score and buyers now ask: can you see your agent. An agent without it is not unobservable by accident. It is unobservable by omission, and that omission is invisible right up until the day you need to see, and cannot.

── End of pattern ──

◆ Three streams, three questions. Decision traces for why, behavioral metrics for whether it is still right, the action log for what it did and on whose authority. Miss one and you go blind to a class of failure.

◆ Operational health (latency, cost, errors) stays green during the failures that matter. Behavioral metrics, the distribution of decisions over time, are what catch the silent regression.

◆ The action log does nothing on a good day and is the only thing that helps on the worst one. Append only, or it is not evidence.

ORBIRESEARCH

Originally published on the OrbiResearch Lab. We build production AI agents at orbiresearch.com.

title: Your AI Is Only as Reliable as Its Data: Designing an AI-Ready Data Architecture
description:
An AI model can be powerful, your infrastructure can scale, and your application can have a clean architecture.

But if the model receives outdated records, incomplete documents, inconsistent features, or data the user isn't authorized to access, the system can still produce unreliable results.

This is one of the reasons enterprise AI projects often struggle after the proof of concept.

The bottleneck isn't always model performance. It's the data architecture surrounding the model.

Traditional analytics platforms are designed to help people understand data through dashboards and reports. AI systems have a different requirement: they need data that is fresh, trusted, contextual, traceable, and permissioned at the moment of inference.

At SotaTek, we approach AI-ready data architecture as a foundation for production AI, connecting enterprise sources, data pipelines, governance, AI serving, and feedback into one operating system.

Let's look at how to design that foundation.

1. An AI-Ready Data Platform Is Different From an Analytics Stack

A traditional analytics architecture typically moves data from operational systems into a warehouse, transforms it, and makes it available to BI tools.

An AI application consumes data differently.

It may need structured customer records, PDF contracts, product images, transaction events, support tickets, or IoT sensor data in the same workflow.

The data also needs to carry enough context for a machine to interpret it correctly.

Consider the difference:

Dimension Traditional analytics AI-ready data architecture
Main consumer Analysts and dashboards Models, agents, applications
Data types Mostly structured tables Tables, documents, images, audio, events
Freshness Daily or hourly batches Use-case-dependent, from batch to near real time
Metadata Documentation for people Machine-readable metadata
Quality Periodic audits Automated pipeline checks
Access control Table and report level Row, column, and document level
Lineage Useful for reporting Needed to trace model outputs
Feedback Limited Corrections and outcomes return to the data layer

There are four questions an AI-ready platform should answer for every dataset:

  • Fresh: Is the information current enough for this workflow?
  • Trusted: Is it reliable, and can its origin be traced?
  • Contextual: Does it include the schema, definitions, and ownership needed to interpret it?
  • Permissioned: Can this user access it, including when the AI retrieves it?

A dataset doesn't need to be perfect before AI can use it. It needs to meet the requirements of the workflow it supports.

2. The Six Layers of an AI-Ready Data Architecture

There is no single universal layer model. The following six-layer architecture is a practical way to understand how data moves from enterprise systems into AI applications.

+--------------------------------------+
|  6. Consumption & Feedback           |
|  Model APIs | Agents | Apps | BI      |
+--------------------------------------+
                    |
+--------------------------------------+
|  5. AI Serving                       |
|  Feature Store | Embeddings | RAG     |
+--------------------------------------+
                    |
+--------------------------------------+
|  4. Governance & Metadata            |
|  Catalog | Lineage | Policies        |
+--------------------------------------+
                    |
+--------------------------------------+
|  3. Storage & Processing             |
|  Warehouse | Lakehouse | Object Store|
+--------------------------------------+
                    |
+--------------------------------------+
|  2. Ingestion & Integration          |
|  Batch ELT | CDC | Event Streaming   |
+--------------------------------------+
                    |
+--------------------------------------+
|  1. Source Systems                   |
|  ERP | CRM | Apps | IoT | Documents   |
+--------------------------------------+

Each layer solves a different engineering problem.

Layer 1: Source Systems

This is where enterprise data originates.

Typical sources include:

  • ERP and CRM platforms
  • Transactional databases
  • Internal applications
  • IoT devices and sensors
  • Documents, PDFs, and emails
  • Images, audio, and video
  • Logs and event streams

The first task is not to ingest everything.

Identify which sources are required for the target AI workflow, who owns them, and what access restrictions apply.

Layer 2: Ingestion and Integration

This layer moves data from source systems into the platform.

The ingestion strategy should match the freshness requirement.

Pattern Suitable use case
Batch ELT Historical reporting and periodic model training
Change Data Capture (CDC) Synchronizing operational database changes
Event streaming Workflows that must react to events quickly

For example, a customer support assistant may only need policy documents refreshed every few hours.

A fraud detection system may need transaction events within seconds.

Streaming every dataset is not automatically better. It introduces infrastructure, monitoring, and operational complexity. Use it when the workflow actually needs low-latency updates.

A simplified CDC flow:

Operational Database
        |
        v
  Change Log / CDC
        |
        v
   Ingestion Service
        |
        v
    Data Platform
        |
        v
   Downstream Consumers

The ingestion layer should also detect schema changes and prevent unexpected source modifications from silently breaking downstream consumers.

Layer 3: Storage and Processing

AI workloads often need both structured and unstructured data.

A lakehouse is one possible architecture for managing these data types within a governed platform.

A common organization pattern is the medallion architecture:

Bronze
  |
  | Raw source data
  v
Silver
  |
  | Cleaned and conformed data
  v
Gold
  |
  | Business-ready datasets
  v
AI / Analytics Consumers
  • Bronze: Preserve raw source data.
  • Silver: Clean, validate, deduplicate, and standardize.
  • Gold: Prepare data for specific business and AI workloads.

Keeping the raw layer matters. When transformation logic changes, teams may need to rebuild features, reprocess records, or re-embed documents.

For storage, open table formats such as Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, and Apache Hudi can help support different processing engines without tying the entire architecture to one proprietary format.

The important decision is to choose storage based on workload requirements, not simply because a particular technology is popular.

Layer 4: Governance and Metadata

Governance should not be a document created after the data pipeline is finished.

It should be part of the data path.

This layer manages:

  • Data catalog and ownership
  • Schema definitions
  • Data lineage
  • Data contracts
  • Quality expectations
  • Access policies
  • Sensitive-data classification
  • Data observability

A data contract makes expectations between producers and consumers explicit.

For example:

dataset: customer_profile

owner: customer-platform

schema:
  customer_id:
    type: string
    required: true

  email:
    type: string
    required: false
    classification: personal_data

  updated_at:
    type: timestamp
    required: true

quality:
  unique_key: customer_id
  freshness_sla: 15m
  null_threshold:
    customer_id: 0

This is an illustrative contract, not a framework-specific configuration.

If an upstream service changes a field or stops sending required values, validation should detect the issue before it reaches model training or inference.

Lineage is equally important.

When an AI system produces an answer or prediction, teams should be able to trace the relevant data sources and transformations behind it.

Layer 5: AI Serving

This is where data becomes usable by AI models.

The serving architecture differs depending on the workload.

For traditional machine learning, a feature store can help maintain consistency between training and inference features.

For generative AI, the architecture may include document parsing, chunking, embeddings, vector indexes, and retrieval services.

A simplified RAG ingestion and query flow:

Document Sources
      |
      v
Parsing & Extraction
      |
      v
Chunking + Metadata
      |
      v
Embedding Generation
      |
      v
Vector Index
      |
      v
User Query
      |
      v
Retrieval + Filtering
      |
      v
Relevant Context
      |
      v
LLM

The vector database is only one component of this architecture.

It does not automatically solve document quality, metadata, freshness, authorization, or source traceability.

Those responsibilities need to be handled across the data and serving layers.

Layer 6: Consumption and Feedback

The final layer delivers data and AI capabilities to applications, agents, APIs, and users.

But the flow should not stop when a model returns a response.

Capture relevant outcomes:

  • What data was retrieved?
  • Which model and prompt versions were used?
  • Was the result accepted or corrected?
  • Did the user complete the intended workflow?
  • Did a human reviewer override the output?

Human corrections and confirmed business outcomes can become valuable inputs for evaluation and future improvements.

This creates a feedback loop:

Data Sources
     |
     v
AI Processing
     |
     v
Model Output
     |
     v
User / Business Workflow
     |
     v
Feedback & Evaluation
     |
     v
Updated Data / Features
     |
     +----------> AI Processing

3. Permission-Aware Retrieval Is a Security Requirement

One of the easiest mistakes in enterprise RAG is treating retrieval as a search problem only.

Imagine an organization with three departments:

  • Finance
  • Human Resources
  • Engineering

All three departments share one document platform, but they do not have permission to access the same documents.

A naive retrieval system may search across the entire index and send the top matching chunks to the LLM.

Even if the model is instructed not to reveal confidential information, the unauthorized information has already entered its context.

The correct approach is to enforce permissions during retrieval.

A simplified example:

def retrieve_context(query, user):
    filters = {
        "tenant_id": user.tenant_id,
        "allowed_roles": {
            "$in": user.roles
        }
    }

    documents = vector_store.search(
        query=query,
        filters=filters,
        top_k=8,
    )

    return documents

This example illustrates the filtering concept. Actual implementations must enforce authorization in a trusted server-side layer, use the identity and policy model of the organization, and account for document-level permissions and permission changes.

The principle is straightforward:

Access control must follow the data into the retrieval layer.

A RAG system should never become an alternative route around the permissions already enforced by enterprise applications.

4. Choose the Architecture Pattern Based on the Actual Constraint

Warehouse, lakehouse, data mesh, and data fabric are not interchangeable labels for the same platform.

Each addresses a different architectural constraint.

Pattern Best suited for Main trade-off
Cloud data warehouse Structured, BI-heavy workloads Less flexible for unstructured data
Lakehouse Mixed data, ML, and analytics Requires disciplined data engineering
Data mesh Multiple domains with distributed ownership Higher coordination complexity
Data fabric Data spread across systems and clouds Depends heavily on metadata quality

A practical starting rule:

  • If your first AI use case mainly uses structured tables owned by one team, a warehouse plus a vector index may be sufficient.
  • If PDFs, support tickets, images, and tables all matter, consider a lakehouse.
  • If domain ownership is slowing down delivery, introduce data products and mesh-style ownership.
  • If data must remain distributed across multiple systems, a fabric-style metadata and integration layer may help.

These patterns can coexist. An enterprise might use a lakehouse for storage, domain ownership for data products, and a fabric-style catalog for discovery.

The goal is not to adopt every architecture pattern. It is to solve the constraint that is currently blocking the AI use case.

5. Build a Thin Slice Before Building an Enterprise-Wide Platform

Trying to make every dataset AI-ready before launching the first use case is an expensive mistake.

Start with one workflow and build only the data foundation it needs.

A practical implementation sequence:

Step 1: Pick one use case and define readiness

Identify the workflow, business owner, required data, freshness target, quality threshold, and access requirements.

Step 2: Inventory and score the data

List the sources, owners, formats, quality issues, and sensitivity levels.

Evaluate each source against four dimensions:

  • Freshness
  • Trustworthiness
  • Context
  • Permissions

The output should be a prioritized gap list, not a company-wide data-cleanup project.

Step 3: Build a thin platform slice

Set up ingestion for the selected sources, a bronze-to-gold transformation path, a catalog entry, lineage, and automated data tests.

Avoid implementing layers that the first use case does not need.

Step 4: Add AI serving and evaluate

Create features or embeddings, implement permission-aware retrieval where required, and test against a representative evaluation dataset.

Use real data from the selected workflow rather than relying exclusively on small synthetic samples.

Step 5: Operate and expand

Monitor freshness, quality, drift, and cost. Capture user corrections and business outcomes.

Once the first workflow is reliable, reuse the same foundation for the next use case.

6. Common Engineering Mistakes

Several architecture decisions can create problems that only become visible after deployment.

Buying the platform before defining the use case

Technology selection should follow data requirements, latency, governance, and operational constraints.

Treating the vector database as the entire architecture

A vector index cannot fix incorrect source records, missing metadata, or broken access policies.

Cleaning every dataset before starting

Enterprise-wide data cleanup delays value. Start with the sources required by the first workflow and expand incrementally.

Ignoring unstructured data

Contracts, manuals, emails, images, and support tickets may contain important context that isn't represented in relational tables.

Leaving datasets without an owner

Every important dataset needs someone accountable for quality, freshness, and access.

Treating governance as a final approval gate

If governance happens only after development, teams may create unmanaged data copies to avoid delays. Put quality checks, classification, and access enforcement into the pipeline itself.

Final Thoughts

An AI-ready data architecture is not simply a bigger data warehouse or a vector database connected to an LLM.

It is a platform that delivers fresh, trusted, contextual, and permissioned data to AI systems, with governance and traceability built into the data flow.

The six layers provide a practical foundation:

Sources → Ingestion → Storage → Governance → AI Serving → Consumption & Feedback

Start with one workflow. Identify its data requirements. Build a thin slice. Measure its reliability. Then expand the architecture based on what the next use case actually needs.

At SotaTek, we approach this foundation as part of production AI engineering, connecting data readiness, architecture design, AI integration, and MLOps rather than treating data preparation as a separate preliminary task.

For a deeper breakdown of the six architectural layers, design principles, and five-step implementation plan, read our AI-Ready Data Architecture guide.

title: The Daily Drawdown Trap: Why One Bad Morning Ends Your Prop Challenge
description:
You can be net profitable for two weeks and still fail a prop challenge. Not because your strategy broke. Because one bad morning breached the daily cap — and the challenge does not care about your two good weeks.

The rule most traders misunderstand

FTMO's daily drawdown limit is 5%, calculated from the highest equity point of the day. That “highest equity point” clause is the trap: intraday peaks count against you. If your account peaks 3% up in the morning and then falls 5% from that peak, you have breached the daily limit even though you are only 2% down on the day. Many traders learn this clause only when it eliminates them.

The math that makes it inevitable at normal risk sizes

Risk 2.5% per trade and two consecutive losses end your challenge. Risk 2% and three losers in a row does it. With typical win rates of 45–55%, losing streaks of two, three, and four are not rare events — they are routine occurrences across any meaningful sample of trades. Data from prop-firm analyses puts daily-drawdown breaches behind roughly 70–79% of all evaluation failures. The challenge is not filtering for bad traders. It is filtering for traders whose position sizing cannot survive their own normal losing streaks.

What passers actually do

They risk 0.5–1% per trade — even when the rules allow two or three times that. At 1% risk, a four-loss streak costs 4% and stays inside the daily cap. At 0.5%, it costs 2%. The difference between passing and failing is rarely strategy quality. It is whether a normal bad morning is survivable.

How to survive it (before you pay)

Backtest against the exact rules — daily cap from intraday peaks, total cap, profit target, minimum days — not just for profit.

Size positions so that your worst normal losing streak (not your average streak, your worst) stays inside the daily cap.

Set a personal daily stop below the firm's cap — stop trading at 3% down, not 5%. The buffer is the difference between a bad day and a failed challenge.

Validate the strategy first: recompute from raw predictions, beat the baselines, check walk-forward folds. A strategy that cannot survive its own rules on paper will not survive them with a fee attached.

The daily drawdown trap is not unfair. It is the product: firms sell evaluations, and the evaluation is designed to filter. Knowing the filter exists — and sizing for it — is the entire game. Most traders pay to discover it. You just read it for free.

BuildIT Index runs that validation mechanically: recompute accuracy, beat baselines, check walk-forward folds, model costs, count trials, return a verdict with an exit code. The same standard applies to prop challenge strategies.

Most traders pay to discover the filter. You just read it for free.

title: AI Automation Cost: Why $0.12 Per Run Can Become $12,000 at Scale
description:
Originally published on Soluma AI.

One of our workflows cost about $0.12 per prospect across a 500 run test. That is either trivial or a $12,000 decision, depending entirely on the multiplier behind it.

One of the most useful lessons we learned about AI cost started with a number that looked almost too small to care about: $0.12. That was roughly what one of our AI workflows was costing to research a prospect. Twelve cents. For a workflow doing real research, that sounded perfectly reasonable, and at small volume it was.

Then we did the obvious calculation we probably should all do much earlier when building AI systems. What happens at 100,000 runs? The answer is $12,000. Suddenly, a fraction of a dollar is no longer a technical detail. It is an operating decision.

That led us to look much more carefully at what the $0.12 actually contained. The workflow was not making one simple AI request. It was carrying out six separate buyer searches, processing the findings and performing a final analysis. The interesting question was never which AI model is cheapest. It was what one completed piece of work actually costs, where that money goes, and how much can be removed before the work gets worse.

How much does AI automation actually cost per run?

There is no universally good AI automation cost per run. The useful number is the cost of producing one acceptable completed job, including model usage, tool calls, search or retrieval, external APIs, retries and other resources required by the workflow. A $0.12 workflow may be economical at 500 runs and material at 100,000. The cost only makes sense when it is viewed alongside volume, quality and the commercial value of the output.

Quick takeaways

  1. 1Tiny unit costs become real budgets at volume: $0.12 per run becomes $12,000 across 100,000 runs.
  2. 2Model price is only part of the cost. Search, retrieval, tools, retries and workflow design create a cost floor that changing models does not remove.
  3. 3Cheaper output is not automatically better economics. If saving a few cents reduces research quality, the cheaper workflow may create less business value.
  4. 4Measure before you optimise. Establish a quality baseline, calculate the full cost per acceptable job, then change one part of the workflow at a time.

The $0.12 problem: tiny number, real money

Here is what the same workflow looks like at different volumes. Nothing changed technically between the first row and the last. Only the multiplier changed.

RUNS COST AT $0.12 PER RUN
100 $12
500 $60
1,000 $120
10,000 $1,200
50,000 $6,000
100,000 $12,000

This is one of the easiest things to miss while prototyping. During development you might test ten rows, twenty, fifty, so a workflow can feel almost free. Then someone adds a Run All button, and that button changes the economics completely. If 100,000 eligible records sit behind it, a twelve cent workflow has turned one click into roughly $12,000 of authorised usage.

The question is not whether $0.12 is cheap. It is how many times you are about to spend $0.12.

Model cost and workflow cost are not the same thing

A common way to estimate AI cost is to read the model pricing page: input tokens cost X, output tokens cost Y, multiply and you have your number. That works for a single model request. It becomes incomplete once the model sits inside a larger workflow.

  • web searches and retrieval
  • external APIs and database operations
  • multiple model calls and reasoning steps
  • validation calls and secondary models
  • retries and failed attempts

OpenAI, for example, currently prices its web search tool at $10 per 1,000 calls, or $0.01 per search call, with search content tokens additionally billed at the selected model rates. That mattered in our workflow. Each prospect required six buyer searches, so six search calls alone contributed six cents before any analysis. That is half of a $0.12 run in tool call fees.

This is what we mean by a structural cost floor. If the workflow genuinely requires those six searches, switching to a cheaper analysis model does not make that six cent layer disappear.

Our 500 run test changed what we wanted to optimise

Before scaling further we ran the workflow across approximately 500 prospects, roughly $60 in operating cost. We were not testing cost alone. We wanted to know whether the searches produced useful evidence, whether the buyer questions were realistic, whether the final analysis retained the right context, whether outputs were consistent enough to use downstream, and where failures happened.

If we had optimised for price before establishing a quality baseline, we would have had no reliable way to tell whether a cheaper version was still doing the same job. We did test cheaper configurations. The cost went down and so did the quality. That told us some of the spend was not waste. It was buying information the workflow needed.

Cost per run can still hide the real number

Even after calculating cost per run, there is another level worth measuring: cost per acceptable completed job. Suppose a workflow costs $0.12 every time it starts. If only 90 percent of outputs meet the acceptance standard, you did not pay twelve cents for every usable result. You paid more.

Cost per acceptable completed job = total workflow cost divided by accepted outputs.

ACCEPTANCE RATE EFFECTIVE COST PER ACCEPTED RESULT
100% $0.120
95% $0.126
90% $0.133
80% $0.150

This is why an apparently cheaper configuration can lose its advantage quickly if it creates more failures, retries or unusable outputs. The business is not buying API calls. It is buying completed work.

The cheapest model does not necessarily create the cheapest system

Model choice obviously matters, and current model line ups reflect that trade off between frontier capability, balanced cost and high volume workloads. But a cheaper model only saves money on the work that model is responsible for. It does not reduce search calls, external API fees, duplicate retrieval, unnecessary workflow stages, poor retry logic, or calls that should never have happened.

OPTIMISATION LAYER WHAT YOU CHANGE TYPICAL EXAMPLES
Model optimisation How expensive each model operation is Smaller model, lower reasoning effort, shorter output, prompt caching
Architecture optimisation How much work the system performs Fewer calls, reused results, conditional research, deterministic processing, controlled retries

Both matter, but the second becomes increasingly important as volume rises. If your system performs eight paid actions where four would produce the same result, changing models treats the symptom while the workflow keeps doing unnecessary work.

The better question: what is the lowest cost that preserves the job?

There is a dangerous version of AI optimisation that looks excellent on a spreadsheet. Version A costs $0.12. Version B costs $0.08. Success. Except Version B misses more evidence, produces weaker classifications, requires more human checking or sends poorer output into the next stage. The four cent saving is real. So is the quality loss.

For prospect research that influences who a business contacts and what it says to them, four cents is an absurd place to compromise when the downstream opportunity is worth hundreds or thousands of dollars. A better target is the lowest cost at which the workflow still performs its job to the required standard.

What we are optimising next

Our approximately $0.12 figure is the baseline, not the finish line. The working target we are testing towards is around $0.08 per run while maintaining the same output quality. That is not a market benchmark. Another workflow could reasonably cost $0.01, $0.40 or $4 depending on what it does.

VOLUME $0.12 PER RUN $0.08 PER RUN POTENTIAL SAVING
500 $60 $40 $20
10,000 $1,200 $800 $400
50,000 $6,000 $4,000 $2,000
100,000 $12,000 $8,000 $4,000

At 500 runs the difference is $20 and easy to dismiss. At 100,000 runs the exact same engineering improvement is worth $4,000. That is why we test small but design with the larger volume in mind.

Where should you look for AI cost savings first?

1. Establish the quality baseline

Take a representative sample and run the version you currently trust. Define what a good output means before changing anything. Accuracy alone may not be enough. Depending on the task you may also care about evidence quality, completeness, consistency, format compliance, latency or human review time.

2. Break the run into cost components

Do not leave yourself with one number called AI cost. Separate model input, model output, tool calls, retrieval and search, external APIs, retries, failures and infrastructure. Now you know what is actually worth optimising.

3. Find the structural floor

Ask which costs remain even if you changed the model tomorrow. In our case, six paid buyer searches immediately exposed a meaningful part of the floor, which changes where engineering effort should go.

4. Remove duplicated work before reducing intelligence

Could a result already collected in step two be reused in step five? Is static context being repeatedly sent? Could deterministic code handle filtering, joining, ranking, deduplication or validation instead of another model call? Current OpenAI guidance recommends bounded programmatic processing for predictable operations rather than forcing every intermediate step through a model.

5. Use cheaper models where the task genuinely allows it

Classification does not need the same model as final synthesis, and extraction does not need the same reasoning level as strategic analysis. Current guidance recommends evaluating model tiers and reasoning levels against representative tasks. The key word is evaluating. Do not downgrade and assume equivalence. Test it.

6. Make prompts leaner, not merely shorter

A shorter prompt only helps if it still contains the instructions that affect the result. Remove repeated instructions, irrelevant tools and unnecessary examples, while retaining guidance that corrects measured quality gaps. The goal is not prompt minimalism. It is removing instructions that are not earning their cost.

7. Use caching where repeated context makes it worthwhile

If large parts of the prompt stay identical across runs, prompt caching can reduce the cost of reprocessing the same input. Measure actual cache hits. A feature being available does not mean your workflow is structured to benefit from it.

8. Consider batch processing where the workload fits

For asynchronous work that does not need an immediate response, the OpenAI Batch API currently offers a 50 percent discount within a 24 hour completion window. That can be meaningful at volume, though tool heavy workflows should be tested for compatibility rather than moved wholesale.

9. Control retries and stopping conditions

Retries are useful when something genuinely failed. They are expensive when nobody told the system when to stop. Define what counts as success, recoverable failure, permanent failure and stop. This matters even more when the workflow can run without anyone watching.

What the Run All button really means

A button labelled Run All Empty Rows looks operational. Financially it is closer to: authorise every eligible row to consume the resources required to finish. Two hundred rows at $0.12 is about $24. Ten thousand is about $1,200. One hundred thousand is about $12,000.

This is not an argument against automation. It is an argument for attaching economics to automation. Before enabling large autonomous queues, a production system should know how many records are eligible, the expected cost per record, the likely failure rate, the maximum acceptable spend and how execution can be stopped.

Four numbers we now want before scaling an AI workflow

  1. 1Cost per acceptable completed job, not just the model request or the tokens.
  2. 2Structural cost floor, meaning the costs inherent in the current architecture.
  3. 3Expected volume, because a unit cost without volume is almost meaningless.
  4. 4Value of the output, because cost must be judged against the value created.

A four cent saving on an internal classification task could matter enormously across millions of runs. A four cent saving on high value B2B research may matter far less than preserving the quality of the research.

What people often misunderstand about AI cost optimisation

The biggest misunderstanding is treating optimisation as a race towards the cheapest possible model. Sometimes the model is the problem and sometimes it is not. The useful question is which part of this workflow is expensive without improving the final result. That could be a model, a redundant search, duplicated context, excessive reasoning, a needless intermediate summary, poor retry logic or a human review step caused by unreliable output upstream.

Removing useful intelligence is cost cutting. Removing unnecessary work is optimisation. They are not the same thing.

When cost optimisation may not be worth doing yet

If a workflow runs 200 times per year and costs a few dollars in total, spending days redesigning it to save two cents per run is poor economics. Likewise, if a workflow is still changing dramatically, premature cost engineering may optimise architecture that disappears next week. Prove the job works, measure it, understand the cost, then optimise what survives.

High volume repeatable workflows are different. At 100,000 runs, a one cent reduction is worth $1,000 and a four cent reduction is worth $4,000. Now the engineering conversation changes.

Questions to ask before scaling an AI workflow

  • What does one acceptable completed job cost?
  • Which part of that cost comes from models, and which from tools, search, APIs or retrieval?
  • What is the unavoidable cost floor?
  • What percentage of runs produce acceptable outputs, and what happens when something fails?
  • Can the workflow retry indefinitely?
  • Is repeated information being fetched or processed more than once?
  • Could simpler steps use cheaper models or deterministic code?
  • How much quality can change before the optimisation stops being worthwhile?
  • What is the expected monthly or annual volume, and what is a successful output worth commercially?

If those answers are unknown, Run All is still partly a guess.

How should businesses think about value, not just API price?

An AI workflow is economically useful when the value of the work it produces comfortably exceeds the cost of producing and operating it. Model pricing makes it easy to become obsessed with decimal places. If high quality research costs twelve cents and materially improves a high value sales process, twelve cents may be excellent economics. If a workflow performs a low value task ten million times, twelve cents may be completely unacceptable.

The lesson from twelve cents

The important thing we learned was not that our workflow costs $0.12. That number will change. Models change, pricing changes and the architecture will change. The more useful lesson is how we now think about scaling: we test before we multiply, we establish what good output looks like, we measure where the money is actually going, then we optimise the system without quietly removing the things that made it useful.

An AI demo only has to work. A production AI system has to work repeatedly, economically and at the quality the business actually needs. That is how we approach the systems we build with clients at Soluma: start with the business problem, test the workflow under real conditions, measure the economics, then improve the architecture before volume magnifies every unnecessary decision.

Frequently asked questions

What is a good cost per run for AI automation?

There is no universal good cost per run. A useful target depends on task complexity, volume, success rate and the value of the finished output. The correct comparison is between cost and business value, not between your workflow and an arbitrary industry average.

How do I calculate the real cost of an AI workflow?

Add model token costs, tool and search fees, external APIs, retrieval, retries, failed runs and other operating resources, then divide total spend by the number of acceptable completed outputs. This gives a more useful figure than model cost alone.

Are web search calls charged separately from model tokens?

Yes, for OpenAI's current web search tool. OpenAI lists web search at $10 per 1,000 calls, with search content tokens additionally billed at the selected model rates.

Is using a cheaper AI model always the best way to reduce cost?

No. A cheaper model helps only if it maintains the required quality and reliability. Workflow architecture, duplicate calls, unnecessary retrieval, retries and excessive context can sometimes offer better savings without weakening the result.

When should I start optimising AI costs?

Start measuring costs during testing, but make major optimisation decisions after you have a reliable quality baseline. Otherwise you risk reducing cost without knowing whether you also reduced the value of the output.

How do I stop an AI automation from creating a surprise bill?

Set clear run limits, budget thresholds, stopping conditions, retry limits and cost monitoring before allowing large autonomous queues. Forecast expected spend by multiplying eligible volume by measured cost per acceptable completed task.

What is the difference between cost per run and cost per completed task?

Cost per run measures one execution attempt. Cost per completed task measures what you actually spent to obtain a usable result after accounting for failures, rejected outputs and retries. For business decisions, the second number is usually more useful.

This article first appeared on soluma.ai.

Talk to Soluma AI
