title: ChatGPT Can’t Backtest: Why “AI” Trading Bots With 10-Year Backtests Are Fiction
description:
A bot that needs live ChatGPT calls cannot have a 2019 backtest — ChatGPT didn't exist. That single fact exposes most “AI EAs” on the market.

Here is a fact that eliminates most “AI trading bots” on the market in one sentence: a bot whose decisions require live calls to a language model cannot be backtested — because the model did not exist for most of the backtest window.

ChatGPT launched in 2022. A product showing you a flawless 2019 backtest for its “ChatGPT-powered” bot is showing you fiction — or, more charitably, a conventional strategy with AI branding. Real AI decisions require live API connectivity, cost money per call, and take seconds per decision (roughly 3–7 seconds end to end in published breakdowns). You cannot retroactively generate historical decisions from a model that did not exist, and you cannot backtest a system whose response times and model versions change underneath you. GPT-5 thinks differently from GPT-4. A backtest run on one is not evidence about the other.

The five red flags that expose fake AI EAs

Perfect long backtests. Five to ten years of flawless “AI-optimised” results. If the AI did not exist for those years, the backtest is not AI. Period.

No live record. No public wallet, no vault, no exchange-verified account. Only screenshots — which can be cropped from a cherry-picked window.

Hidden recovery systems. “Our AI intelligently scales positions for optimal recovery” is usually a martingale system doubling down on losses, described in softer words.

Annualised short windows. A good fortnight dressed as a triple-digit APR. Always ask: over what window, in what market, net of what fees?

No losing months shown. Every real trading record has losing months. A record without them is a curated exhibit, not a record.

How to validate a real AI trading system, then?

Forward testing. Since backtesting is impossible for genuine LLM-driven bots, the only honest validation is: demo for at least 30 days, then small live capital, with every trade logged and every cost counted. If a vendor refuses forward testing and offers only a backtest, that refusal is the answer.

The broader lesson applies to every trading claim, AI or not: recompute from raw data, beat the baselines, demand the trial count, check the folds. A claim that cannot survive those checks is marketing, whatever technology word is printed on it.

BuildIT Index applies that standard to any prediction file: recompute accuracy, beat baselines, check folds, count trials, return a verdict with an exit code.

If a vendor refuses forward testing and offers only a backtest, that refusal is the answer.

This article is educational, not financial advice. Past results do not predict future returns.

title: Building a Medical Investigation AI on an OpenAI-Compatible API
description:
November 6, 2026 | 8 min read

Most medical AI demos are a chat box with a medical prompt.

You send a symptom. You get a paragraph. It can look impressive in a screenshot. Then you try to use it on a real case and discover the hard parts: the record is fragmented, the values have dates, the medications interact, the evidence needs a source, and the model has no idea what it does not know.

Premedice is a medical investigation AI. The product is built around a different unit of work: the whole case, not the single question.

This post is a technical look at how that works, and how to call the API from your own stack.

THE PROBLEM WITH A SINGLE PROMPT

A standard medical RAG pipeline retrieves a few passages and asks a model to answer. That is useful for general questions. It is not enough for an investigation.

An investigation needs four things a single retrieval call usually lacks.

Temporal context. A potassium of 5.3 means something different if it was 4.1 last month. A medication started nine days ago matters. A lab trend matters. A snapshot does not.

Tool access. The answer may depend on a drug label, an interaction database, a clinical trial, or a guideline. Retrieval alone does not check those sources.

A citation trail. A high-stakes claim without a source is a hypothesis. The user needs to inspect the basis, not just read the conclusion.

Explicit uncertainty. A good investigation names the gaps. What is missing? Which value conflicts? Which symptom has no explanation yet?

That is the design brief for a medical investigation AI.

WHAT "MEDICAL INVESTIGATION AI" MEANS

Medical investigation AI is software that takes a health question and investigates it across the full available record, rather than generating an answer from a single prompt.

It collects the history, labs, medications, documents, and symptoms. It correlates changes over time. It verifies claims against literature and drug sources. It states what is missing. Then it returns a structured brief for a human to review.

Premedice is built for that job. It is not a diagnosis engine. It is an investigation layer that sits between the record and the clinician.

THE ARCHITECTURE, IN PRACTICAL TERMS

Premedice exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. If you already use the OpenAI SDK, you change the base URL, the API key, and the model name. The rest of your client code stays the same.

Base URL: https://api.premedice.com/v1

Model: Premedice/Premed-4

Context window: 128K tokens

Max output: 16K tokens

Streaming: OpenAI SSE

Tools: eight medical tools are preloaded on every request. PubMed, OpenFDA, RxNorm, DailyMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, Semantic Scholar, Europe PMC, and create_file.

The tools are always on. That is a deliberate product decision. A medical investigation should not require the caller to remember which database to attach. The model should be able to check the label, the interaction, the trial, and the literature as part of the investigation.

The response includes the answer and its sources. The exact shape is the normal chat completion shape, so existing streaming, retries, and logging code should carry over.

WHAT A GOOD RESPONSE SHOULD CONTAIN

A medical investigation AI should return more than a paragraph. A useful brief has five parts.

The signals. The values or findings that changed and deserve attention.

The evidence. The source value, trend, guideline, label, or paper behind each signal. The reader should be able to check it.

The correlations. The medication, condition, or history that may explain the signal. Correlation is not causation, and the brief should say so.

The gaps. The missing history, the conflicting value, the symptom that has no explanation yet.

The boundary. A clear statement that the output is decision support, not a diagnosis, and that urgent symptoms need urgent care.

If your medical AI output does not have those five parts, it is probably a chat response, not an investigation.

DESIGN LESSONS

Three lessons shaped the product.

Preload the tools. A medical investigation should not fail because the caller did not attach the right database. The tools are part of the investigation environment, not an optional plugin.

Make citations first-class. A citation is not a footnote added after the fact. It is part of the answer. If a high-stakes claim cannot be tied to a source, the claim should be marked as uncertain.

Keep the uncertainty visible. Models are good at sounding complete. A medical investigation AI has to be good at sounding incomplete when the evidence is incomplete. That is a product behavior, not just a prompt.

The model matters too, but it is not the whole product. Premedice 4 scored 84.6 percent on an internal MedQA replication. That is an exam-style benchmark, not a clinical validation or an outcome study. It has not been peer-reviewed. It is a signal about reasoning, not proof of accuracy in a real patient.

Benchmarks are a floor, not a finish line.

WHAT TO BUILD WITH IT

The API is useful anywhere a developer needs a cited medical investigation rather than a generic answer.

Patient education tools that explain labs in plain language and show the source.

Clinical preparation tools that assemble a pre-visit brief from a record.

Research prototypes that need to correlate labs, medications, and literature.

Caregiver tools that help someone organize a family member's records and questions.

Second-opinion workflows that review the whole case against the evidence.

The API is not a diagnosis engine. It is not a telehealth service. It is not an emergency service. It is a reasoning and evidence layer that a human should review.


SAFETY AND PRIVACY FOR DEVELOPERS

If you are building in health, the non-negotiables are not optional.

Use a lawful basis for processing. Do not send identifiable data without consent or another valid legal basis.

Keep API keys server-side. A pm_live key is a secret. Do not ship it in a client bundle.

Log carefully. Do not store full patient records in application logs or error trackers.

Respect the boundary. Do not present the output as a diagnosis. Do not use it for emergency triage.

Check the data flow. Premedice is designed around GDPR-native, EU-resident data handling, with AES-256 at rest and TLS 1.3 in transit. User data is not used for model training. The API is a developer surface, but your application still needs its own privacy review.

For a clinical deployment, a clinic still needs a data protection impact assessment, a retention policy, a clinical safety review, and a clear escalation path.

PRICING AND ACCESS

API keys are generated in the Premedice dashboard. Billing uses the same per-token rates as the in-app chat and is debited from the account's token balance.

The app itself has a free tier. Pro is 5.99 EUR per month, and Advanced is 20 EUR per month. The API is the developer path for teams that want to integrate the investigation into their own product.

GETTING STARTED

Read the API docs at api.premedice.com/docs.

Create a key in the Premedice dashboard.

Point your OpenAI SDK at https://api.premedice.com/v1.

Use the model name Premedice/Premed-4.

Send a synthetic case first. Check the citations. Check the uncertainty. Then decide whether the output is good enough for your workflow.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

  • Medical investigation AI is a whole-record, tool-using, cited workflow. It is not a single-prompt chatbot.
  • Premedice exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint with a 128K context window and eight preloaded medical tools.
  • Citations and explicit uncertainty are product requirements, not prompt decoration.
  • Premedice 4's 84.6 percent MedQA replication is an internal, non-peer-reviewed benchmark, not clinical validation.
  • The API is decision support. A human remains accountable.


FAQ

Is the API OpenAI-compatible?
Yes. Use the base URL https://api.premedice.com/v1, your Premedice key, and the model Premedice/Premed-4.

Which tools are preloaded?
PubMed, OpenFDA, RxNorm, DailyMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, Semantic Scholar, Europe PMC, and create_file. They are on by default.

Does the API diagnose patients?
No. It is decision support. It does not diagnose, prescribe, or replace a clinician.

Is patient data used for training?
No. Premedice states that user data is not used for model training.

Where are the docs?
https://api.premedice.com/docs

SOURCES

Premedice 4 model page.
https://premedice.com/models/premedice-4/

Premedice API documentation.
https://api.premedice.com/docs

Jin D, et al. What Disease Does This Patient Have? A Large-Scale Open Domain Question Answering Dataset from Medical Exams. arXiv:2009.13081.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.13081

World Health Organization. Patient safety.
https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/patient-safety

COVER IMAGE

Ready to use: https://premedice.com/og-home.jpg (1200 x 630)
Alt text: Premedice medical investigation AI product preview with a cited answer interface.

Custom cover direction: a terminal window beside a lab report, with three values highlighted and a source list on the right. No stock photos, no robot hands, no blue-purple gradient.

title: Sell the same key twice, or take money and deliver nothing: the bug every key store must make impossible
description:
A digital-goods store can fail in exactly two ways that really matter:

  1. It sells the same license key to two people. One of them gets an "already redeemed" error, a refund request and a chargeback.
  2. It takes someone's money and assigns no key at all. That's worse.

At Increddy, a storefront for game and software keys, preventing both is the whole job. Here's the problem as a puzzle. Try solving it before you scroll.

The puzzle

  • A customer pays. Your backend receives order.placed.
  • Your payment provider sends payment.captured.
  • Either event can arrive more than once, because providers retry by design.
  • They don't always arrive in the order you expect.
  • Each order must end up with exactly one key. Not zero. Not two.

What's your design?

The answer most people reach first

"Reserve a key when order.placed fires."

It works in every test you'll write. Then one busy weekend a webhook retries, the handler runs twice, and a customer gets two keys. Or the event never shows up, and they get nothing.

Retries aren't an edge case. They're the normal case. A system that only works when every webhook arrives exactly once works in staging and breaks in production.

The second answer (still wrong)

"Fine, check whether the order already has a key before reserving one."

if (!order.hasKey) {
  assignKey(order)   // two handlers can both get here
}

This is the bug that gets past code review. Two handlers can both run the check, both see "no key", and both write. Check-then-write has a race right in the gap between the check and the write.

What we actually built

One: make the write itself idempotent. Idempotency lives at the data layer, not in an if statement. A second attempt to reserve a key for an order that already has one is a no-op, however many handlers race to do it.

Two: two independent triggers. order.placed is the primary path. payment.captured is a fully independent safety net. Since the write is idempotent, both can fire, both can retry, and the result is still exactly one key.

Three: a sweep for whatever slips through. Some cases fall through both triggers, like a captured payment where no order event ever fires. So a job runs every 15 minutes, finds payments captured more than 5 minutes ago with no key assigned, and fixes them.

That job isn't a patch. Every event-driven system has a tail of cases that need a sweep, not a trigger. It's cheaper to build that in on day one than to find out you need it from a support ticket.

The decision that surprises everyone

There's one more piece, and it runs against every inventory instinct you have: Increddy lets customers buy products that are sold out.

It's on purpose, and why it's the right call for a key store is in the full write-up on our blog.

The rule to steal

Make the state transition idempotent ("this order has a key"), not the event that triggers it. Treat reconciliation as part of the design, not a fix after the first incident.

Want the whole picture? The key engine was one module in a full backend rebuild under a live storefront. Read the Increddy case study on kryeo.com →

We're Kryeo. We build order-fulfillment logic like this as part of our Medusa development work.

title: Building Better Social Media Content with AI: Exploring ViralMeme.ai
description:
Memes are more than just funny pictures on the internet. They have become an important part of online communication, social media marketing, and digital content creation. A simple image, short video, or humorous caption can quickly spread across communities and become a recognizable internet trend.

For developers, creators, and digital marketers, one interesting challenge is finding a way to combine AI technology with internet culture. How can we discover trending memes, understand why they become popular, and use AI to create our own versions?

In this article, we'll explore how AI-powered meme discovery and generation tools can make this process easier, using ViralMeme.ai as an example.

1. Understanding the Evolution of Internet Memes

Internet memes evolve constantly. Some begin with a popular social media video, while others come from gaming communities, celebrity moments, movies, or everyday situations.

The interesting thing about memes is how quickly people adapt them. One original image can inspire thousands of variations, each with a different caption, character, or humorous situation.

For content creators, keeping up with these trends can be time-consuming. You need to discover new formats, understand their original context, and decide whether they are still relevant.

This is where meme discovery platforms become useful.

ViralMeme.ai is a platform designed to help users explore popular internet memes, understand their meanings and origins, and find creative ways to remake them.

2. Discover Trending Memes with ViralMeme.ai

Instead of spending hours browsing different social media platforms, creators can use a dedicated meme discovery page to explore popular formats.

ViralMeme.ai provides a collection of trending and established memes, with individual explanations covering:

  • What each meme means.
  • Where the original trend came from.
  • How people use the meme online.
  • Whether the trend is currently rising, peaking, or declining.

This information is useful because understanding the context behind a meme is just as important as creating the content itself.

You can explore the collection here:

Explore Popular Memes on ViralMeme.ai

For developers and marketers, this kind of organized information can also provide inspiration for content research, trend analysis, and creative experiments.

3. From Meme Templates to AI-Generated Content

One of the most interesting developments in AI content creation is the ability to transform ordinary photos into creative visual content.

Traditional meme generators mainly focus on adding text to existing images. AI-powered tools take this concept further by allowing users to experiment with different visual transformations.

ViralMeme.ai offers several creative options.

Meme Caption Editor

Users can choose a meme format, customize the text, preview the result, and download a finished image. The caption editor is free and does not require an account.

AI Image Generation

For supported templates, users can upload their own photos and generate new meme-inspired images.

AI Video Generation

Some templates also support short AI-generated videos, making it possible to experiment with more dynamic content for social media.

Not every meme supports AI generation, and the available outputs and credit requirements depend on the selected template.

You can explore these features through the ViralMeme.ai Meme Maker.

4. A Practical AI Meme Creation Workflow

For developers and creators who want to experiment with AI-powered content, here is a simple workflow:

Step 1: Research a Trend

Start by exploring popular memes and identifying formats that match your audience.

Step 2: Understand the Context

Read about the meme's origin and meaning. This helps avoid using a popular format incorrectly.

Step 3: Choose a Creative Template

Find a suitable meme template based on the type of content you want to create.

Step 4: Customize Your Content

Add your own captions, upload a photo, or experiment with an available AI image or video generator.

Step 5: Review and Share

Check the final result, make any necessary adjustments, and download your content for your preferred social media platform.

This workflow can help reduce the time spent searching for inspiration and make content experimentation more accessible.

5. Why AI Meme Generators Are Interesting for Developers

AI meme generation is an interesting example of how artificial intelligence can be applied to everyday creative activities.

It combines several areas of technology:

  • Image processing and visual transformation.
  • Generative AI models.
  • Template-based content creation.
  • User-friendly editing interfaces.
  • Trend discovery and content organization.

From a product development perspective, combining these capabilities creates a more complete creative experience than offering a simple image generator alone.

It also demonstrates how specialized AI applications can make advanced technology accessible to users who do not have professional design or video editing skills.

6. Final Thoughts

AI is changing the way people discover, create, and share digital content. Meme creation is a simple but interesting example of this transformation.

By combining meme discovery, contextual information, customizable templates, and AI-powered image and video generation, creators have more opportunities to experiment with internet culture.

If you enjoy exploring internet trends or want to experiment with AI-generated social media content, take a look at ViralMeme.ai.

It is a useful starting point for discovering popular memes and turning creative ideas into shareable content.

title: Bind an abstract edit to the current source before comparing wording
description:
A candidate may be a reasonable edit of yesterday's paragraph and still be unsuitable for the paragraph the author has selected today. In an academic editing workflow, preserve that distinction before asking whether the new wording is better.

We are the RigorMed team. The following complete, standard-library Python example was run locally. All text is fictional teaching material. This is a small source-binding demonstration, not a public product API, a manuscript-editing model or a clinical research run.

The input and the decision

The current source is one identified segment: “We evaluated 72 records from a retrospective study.” The candidate carries both its proposed wording and the exact source text it was prepared against. The positive case uses the current sentence. The stale case carries a different source sentence with 68 records.

The function below answers only one question: does this candidate refer to the current segment and carry the exact current source? It does not decide whether the proposed scientific wording is correct.

import json


def bind_candidate(current, candidate):
    key = candidate['segment_id']
    return key in current and current[key] == candidate['source_text']


current = {'seg_0001': 'We evaluated 72 records from a retrospective study.'}
candidate = {
    'segment_id': 'seg_0001',
    'source_text': current['seg_0001'],
    'edited_text': 'A retrospective study evaluated 72 records.',
}
stale = dict(candidate, source_text='We evaluated 68 records from a retrospective study.')
print(json.dumps({
    'current_source_matches': bind_candidate(current, candidate),
    'stale_source_matches': bind_candidate(current, stale),
    'semantic_review_performed': False,
}, indent=2))

The actual output was:

{
  "current_source_matches": true,
  "stale_source_matches": false,
  "semantic_review_performed": false
}

Use the result to route review

The false stale-source result is a reason to stop applying that candidate and regenerate or review it against the current paragraph. Do not silently replace its stored source with the new sentence and keep the old edit: that would conceal the mismatch rather than resolve it.

The true result only establishes the source association. The edited sentence must still be compared with its source. For example, record counts, sample counts and repeated measurements have different meanings; matching a segment identifier does not establish any of those facts.

An integration can present four existing pieces together: the current source, the proposed edit, the stated change reason and unresolved author checks. Keep the source untouched and let the author accept or reject the candidate after reviewing the actual change. An identifier or a text match is not a quality score.

What the larger local precheck demonstrated

In a separate self-written fictional biomedical paragraph, we prepared one candidate that retained 126 adults and one deliberately incorrect candidate that changed 126 to 162. Our existing local academic-text precheck returned REVIEW_REQUIRED for the first, with no blockers and one semantic-review item. The changed-number counterexample returned BLOCKED with two blockers and no edited-text preview.

Those results belong to that separate precheck, not to the small function above. They show how a source-bound handoff and deterministic checks can provide useful review material while still retaining unresolved semantic work. Neither a matching source nor a rule result authorizes submission or establishes scientific validity.

For a real handoff, use text the author is authorized to process, retain the selected segment and editing goal, and ask for changes and unresolved checks alongside the draft. Do not infer missing study facts from a request to improve language.

For an existing academic-text task, the RigorMed research entry is https://rigormed.com/en?utm_source=dev&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=d54_noon_edit_focus . Model use follows displayed credit terms. This article reports the local examples above; it does not claim a new production run, an external Skill integration or measured time savings.

title: Open source AI shorts generators: the repos worth running in 2026
description:
Most open source AI shorts generators fall into two families: faceless stock-footage pipelines and long-video clippers. Here are five on GitHub with the facts I checked today, what each one does and doesn't do, and where they fall down for code content.

Full disclosure first: I build ReelMint, a closed-source video studio for developers making vertical Shorts, so I have a stake here. This post is for someone who typed "open source ai shorts generator" into a search box and wants to know which repos are real, what they need to run, and whether any of them fit technical content. Stars, licences and last-commit dates below come from the GitHub API on 3 November 2026. Feature details come from each repo's README on the same day. I did not install or benchmark any of them, so I describe what they claim to do, not how well they do it.

What an open source AI shorts generator does (and doesn't)

The category splits into two families, and mixing them up is the most common mistake in search results.

  • Topic to video (faceless pipelines). You give a topic. An LLM writes a script, a TTS engine reads it, stock footage is matched to the sentences, captions are burned in, and an MP4 comes out.
  • Long video to clips. You give a podcast or a YouTube URL. Whisper transcribes it, an LLM picks highlight moments, and the tool crops them to 9:16.

What both families leave to you: editing a finished result, keeping a consistent brand look across videos, and judging whether the content is any good. Most also leave the publishing step half-built, and that last point matters more than it looks (see the YouTube policy section below).

The repos worth running (verified)

All figures below were read from https://api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<repo> on 3 November 2026. Star counts move daily, so treat them as a snapshot.

MoneyPrinterTurbo (harry0703/MoneyPrinterTurbo): MIT, Python, about 137,900 stars, last push 2 Nov 2026. It takes a topic or keyword and generates the script, matches stock footage, adds voiceover, subtitles and background music, and renders an HD video. The README lists a web UI and an API, Docker support (docker compose -f docker-compose.release.yml up, UI on port 8501), and LLM options including OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini and DeepSeek. Edge TTS needs no key; other voice providers need their own. The README says the minimum is 4 CPU cores and 4 GB RAM with no GPU. It lists publishing to TikTok, Instagram and YouTube Shorts as a feature but gives no setup details, so check that part yourself before relying on it.

OpenShorts (mutonby/openshorts): MIT, Python, about 7,400 stars, last push 2 Nov 2026. This is the long-video family: it detects moments, reframes with face tracking, adds subtitles and can dub. It also has an AI actor tool and a title and thumbnail tool. Self-hosting is docker compose up --build, then you enter keys in Settings. The README names Gemini as required for the AI features, fal.ai for the AI actor shorts, ElevenLabs for voice and dubbing, and Upload-Post for social posting (TikTok, Reels, YouTube Shorts). It ships an MCP server, at localhost:8000/mcp when self-hosted. There is also a hosted version; the README lists a free plan of 20 minutes a month with a watermark and paid plans from $12 a month.

ShortGPT (RayVentura/ShortGPT): MIT, Python, about 8,100 stars, last push 10 Feb 2025. The repo describes itself as an experimental framework for YouTube Shorts and TikTok channel automation, covering script, voiceover, footage, captions and rendering. I am not calling it abandoned. I am reporting that the last push was in February 2025, and that the README says documentation is still coming. The README does not list required keys, though it names OpenAI, ElevenLabs and Pexels as technologies used.

AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator (SamurAIGPT/AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator): MIT, Python, about 5,700 stars, last push 3 Nov 2026. It is a long-video clipper pitched as an open source alternative to Opus Clip. Give it a YouTube URL and it uses Whisper, an LLM for highlights, and automatic cropping to produce ranked 9:16 clips. API mode needs a MUAPI_API_KEY; local mode needs an OpenAI or Gemini key plus ffmpeg. The README does not mention uploading to YouTube. It also promotes a hosted per-clip API from the same ecosystem.

MoneyPrinterV2 (FujiwaraChoki/MoneyPrinterV2): AGPL-3.0, Python, about 32,300 stars, last push 15 Sep 2026. It bundles several automations, including a scheduled YouTube Shorts automator, a Twitter bot and affiliate tooling, configured through config.json and requiring Python 3.12. The AGPL licence matters if you plan to run a modified version as a service. I could not confirm the upload credentials it needs from the README.

Comparison list

  • MoneyPrinterTurbo: topic to video, MIT, key for an LLM (Edge TTS free), stock footage, active as of 2 Nov 2026.
  • OpenShorts: long video to clips plus extras, MIT, Gemini required, optional fal.ai, ElevenLabs and Upload-Post keys, has an MCP server, active as of 2 Nov 2026.
  • ShortGPT: topic to video framework, MIT, last push Feb 2025, documentation incomplete.
  • AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator: long video to clips, MIT, one API key (MuAPI, or OpenAI/Gemini in local mode), no upload described.
  • MoneyPrinterV2: multi-automation toolkit, AGPL-3.0, config-file driven, last push 15 Sep 2026.

I also looked for n8n and Make templates that wrap these steps. I did not verify any specific template well enough to list it, so I left them out rather than guess.

Automating YouTube Shorts: what YouTube's policy actually says

Developers asking about "youtube shorts automation" usually worry about getting a channel flagged. The relevant text is YouTube's channel monetization policies page, support.google.com/youtube/answer/1311392, which I read on 3 November 2026. A July 2025 update on that page renamed the policy from "repetitious content" to "inauthentic content".

What I took from it, in my own words. Automation and AI are not banned. The page says that if you use automated tools or templates, the final product still has to show your creative vision and give viewers educational or entertainment value. The things it names as a problem are content that looks made from a template, and AI content made with generic or unoriginal templates that gives the impression of mass production. Channels whose videos are interchangeable are described as not eligible to monetize. Note the scope: this is about eligibility for the YouTube Partner Program. Content that breaks the Community Guidelines is a separate matter and can be removed. I found no numeric threshold, such as a maximum number of uploads per day, and I won't invent one.

The practical reading for a pipeline: a script written by an LLM from a bare keyword, stock clips, a default voice and the same layout on every video is the pattern the page describes. A video built from your own repo, your own terminal output and your own explanation is not interchangeable with the next channel's. That is a judgement about the content, which no repo can make for you.

Where open-source pipelines fall down for technical content

The topic-to-video family matches stock footage to sentences. Ask it for a video about a Postgres index and you get b-roll of servers and someone typing, not the query plan. There is no step where a real code snippet, a terminal session or a chart is rendered as the visual. The long-video family has the opposite problem: it needs a long recording to exist already, and it crops talking heads, not syntax-highlighted code that must stay legible at 9:16.

Three more gaps show up for developers specifically. First, editing: when scene four has the wrong variable name, you re-run the pipeline or open the MP4 in a separate editor. Second, consistency: nothing carries a code theme, font or colour palette from one video to the next. Third, accuracy: an LLM writing narration over stock footage has nothing checking that the code on screen is the code being described, because no code is on screen. Our own take on the editing problem is in editable AI Shorts generators, and the content side is in YouTube Shorts for developers.

Where ReelMint fits (and that it isn't open source)

ReelMint is not open source. It is a hosted product; you cannot read or self-host the code. What it is: a Remotion-based render pipeline where every generated scene is editable in a visual editor, with code cards, terminal cards and chart animations as scene types. It is driven by an MCP server that Claude Desktop, Claude Code and Cursor can connect to, with 130+ MCP tools. It is BYOK, meaning you bring your own OpenAI, Anthropic, ElevenLabs and similar keys, and there is a free tier. It publishes to YouTube Shorts. Instagram Reels publishing is pending Meta App Review, so I am not counting it.

On time, the only number I will stand behind: on the MCP path, a 60 to 90 second reel took me 45 to 60 minutes elapsed, of which 10 to 20 minutes were hands-on. That is one person, the person who built it, so a newcomer will be slower.

When ReelMint is not the right pick

  • You need to read or modify the source, or run everything offline on your own hardware. Use MoneyPrinterTurbo or OpenShorts.
  • You have a long recording and want clips from it. Use OpenShorts or AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator. That is not what we do.
  • You want zero-cost faceless channel output from a keyword and do not care about technical accuracy. A stock-footage pipeline is closer to that job.
  • You need a proof or equation animation. That is Manim territory, not ours.

Is there a free open source AI shorts generator?

Yes. MoneyPrinterTurbo, OpenShorts, ShortGPT and AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator are all MIT licensed per the GitHub API on 3 November 2026, and MoneyPrinterV2 is AGPL-3.0. Free to use does not mean free to run: most need at least one LLM key, and some need voice, video or posting keys, billed by those providers.

Can I automate YouTube Shorts with an API?

Partly. OpenShorts documents a REST API and an MCP server, and MoneyPrinterTurbo documents API docs at port 8080 in its Docker setup. Both can generate clips programmatically. Uploading is a separate step handled by YouTube's own APIs or a service like Upload-Post, which OpenShorts uses. I did not test any of these end to end, so verify the upload path before building on it.

Will YouTube penalise auto-generated Shorts?

YouTube's policy page does not ban automation or AI. It says the final video still has to show your creative vision and have educational or entertainment value, and it describes template-made, mass-produced, interchangeable content as ineligible for monetization. It reads as a monetization policy, not a ban on uploading. I found no stated upload-volume threshold.

If your content is technical, the easier route to non-interchangeable videos is to put real code and real output on screen. You can try that with the code explainer Shorts maker on the free tier.

Originally published on reelmint.io.

title: Expand seed keywords into hundreds of Google and YouTube autocomplete ideas, grouped by intent
description:
Autocomplete is the cheapest keyword research there is: it shows what people actually type, in their own words, ranked by how often Google sees them. The manual version is typing "coffee maker a", "coffee maker b" and so on into a search box and copying what drops down. The scripted version runs every letter, digit and question word against Google and YouTube, for each market you sell in, and hands you a deduplicated list.

This post turns a few seeds into a content plan grouped by intent, then compares the autocomplete scrapers on the Apify Store using the prices their Store pages listed at the time of writing.

Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built the Google Autocomplete Scraper. It's a paid tool (prices below). Check each Store page before you buy: prices change.

How the expansion works

For each seed, source (Google Search, YouTube) and market (country and language), the tool asks autocomplete for the seed plus every modifier in expansions:

  • alphabet: seed + a to z and 0 to 9, 36 queries.
  • questions: how, what, why, which, can and other question words + seed, in English, Spanish, French, German, Portuguese or Italian, following the market's language.
  • prepositions: for, with, without, near, vs, or and similar words, which is where comparison and use-case phrases come from.

Each unique phrase is one row: keyword, seed, source, country, language, the modifier and query that produced it, its position in the suggestion box, and intents (question, commercial, local, comparison) tagged by word rules. A phrase that repeats in the same source and market is dropped and not charged. depth: 2 expands the results once more for long-tail phrases.

Seeds to a content plan 

pip install apify-client

import csv
import os
from collections import defaultdict

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
run = client.actor("aurelix/google-autocomplete-scraper").call(
    run_input={
        "keywords": ["coffee maker", "espresso machine"],
        "sources": ["google", "youtube"],
        "expansions": ["alphabet", "questions", "prepositions"],
        "countries": ["us", "ca"],
        "languages": ["en"],
        "maxResults": 2000,
    }
)
rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

groups = defaultdict(dict)
for r in rows:
    for intent in r["intents"] or ["other"]:
        best = groups[intent].get(r["keyword"])
        if best is None or r["position"] < best["position"]:
            groups[intent][r["keyword"]] = r

with open("content_plan.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["intent", "keyword", "seed", "sources", "best_position"])
    for intent, kws in sorted(groups.items()):
        for kw, r in sorted(kws.items(), key=lambda x: x[1]["position"]):
            srcs = sorted({x["source"] for x in rows if x["keyword"] == kw})
            w.writerow([intent, kw, r["seed"], "+".join(srcs), r["position"]])

for intent, kws in sorted(groups.items()):
    print(f"{intent}: {len(kws)} keywords")

How to read the groups:

  • question: one FAQ entry or one article each. "how coffee maker works" is a headline as it stands.
  • comparison: "espresso machine vs ..." phrases are buyer's guides and comparison pages.
  • commercial: best, cheap, price, deal, review phrases are close to purchase; product and category pages.
  • local: "near me", "nearby" and "open now" phrases mean a store finder or a local landing page.
  • Found on Google and YouTube (sources = google+youtube): a topic worth both a written page and a video.

For a second language, add it to languages (for example ["en", "fr"] with "countries": ["ca"]): the question and preposition modifiers switch to that language, so French Canadian searchers get French modifiers, not English ones.

Autocomplete scrapers on the Apify Store compared

Prices per 1,000 keywords from each Store page at the time of writing:

Aurelix Google Autocomplete Scraper automation-lab/google-autocomplete-scraper memo23/google-suggest-scraper
Free plan $0.45 $1.00 $0.50
Bronze $0.35 $0.90 $0.50
Gold $0.35 $0.65 $0.50
Start fee per run $0.0005 $0.005 ($0.00375 on Gold) $0.005
YouTube autocomplete yes no (Google only) no (Google only)
A to Z modifiers yes yes yes
Question and preposition modifiers 6 languages English question words English question words
Several countries and languages in one run yes no (one each) yes
Intent tags yes not stated not stated
Duplicates dropped and not charged yes not stated not stated

Where each wins: automation-lab has the most users of the three and the longest track record. memo23 is close on price on the free plan. The Aurelix tool is the cheapest of the three on every plan, and the only one of the three that reads YouTube autocomplete, uses question and preposition modifiers in six languages and tags each phrase by intent.

Limits

  • No search volume, CPC or difficulty. Autocomplete gives phrases and their order only. To compare how much interest a few shortlisted phrases get, and how it moves over time and by region, use Google Trends on the shortlist.
  • At most 10 suggestions per query, so a seed yields at most about 60 queries' worth per source and market at depth 1.
  • Suggestions are personalised by location and change over time; the country setting localises them, but they can differ slightly from what a signed-in user sees.
  • Intent tags come from word rules, not a model, so rare phrasings can be missed or mis-tagged.
  • At most 20 country and language combinations per run, and depth at most 2.
  • Google can throttle datacenter IPs; the run then stops early with the keywords collected so far.

Cost

At the time of writing the Store page lists $0.45 per 1,000 keywords on Apify's free plan and $0.35 per 1,000 on paid plans, plus $0.0005 per run. Only unique keywords are charged, and a seed with no suggestions of its own is not expanded, so a typo costs only the start fee. Apify's free plan includes $5 of credit a month, about 11,000 keywords.

  • Google Trends Scraper on the Apify Store
  • automation-lab/google-autocomplete-scraper, memo23/google-suggest-scraper

title: Motion Canvas vs Remotion: which one should you build video with?
description:
Generator functions and signals on one side, React components and frames on the other. A head-to-head on the axes that decide it, with the same small scene sketched in both.

Motion Canvas vs Remotion is a question that comes up when you want to write video as code and have narrowed it to two TypeScript options. Full disclosure: I build ReelMint, which is built on Remotion, so I have a stake. I checked both projects' repositories, docs and licenses on November 3, 2026, and I mark below what I did not run myself. Short version: Motion Canvas is an animation tool with its own timeline model and editor, Remotion is React rendered frame by frame to video. They overlap less than the search results suggest.

What each one is

Motion Canvas is, in its own docs' words, a tool for building animations in code. You write scenes as generator functions and the animation plays as you yield instructions. It works with TypeScript or JavaScript, the guide recommends TypeScript, and the quickstart scaffolds a project with npm init @motion-canvas@latest. Its GitHub repository is MIT licensed.

Remotion is a framework for making video with React. A video is a component that reads the current frame and returns markup, and Remotion renders it by stepping through frames and encoding the result. Anything the browser can draw is available: HTML, CSS, SVG, canvas, npm packages.

Mental model: generator functions and signals versus components and frames

In Motion Canvas you describe a sequence of events. You add nodes to the view, hold references to them with createRef, and yield* tweens one after another. To run things at once you wrap them in all(). Values that change over time live in signals created with createSignal, and a text node can take a function so the label updates whenever the signal does. The scene reads like a script: do this, then this, then these two together.

In Remotion nothing persists between frames. Each frame is a pure function of useCurrentFrame(), and you express motion as math on the frame number, usually with interpolate() or spring(). There is no sequence of events to write; there is a picture for every frame number. If you know React this is familiar. If you think in timelines, the Motion Canvas model will feel closer to how you plan an explainer.

The practical consequence: sequencing (A, then B, then A and C together) is easy in Motion Canvas and takes deliberate offsets in Remotion, where you place Sequence components or compute frame ranges. Layout, data-driven UI and reusing existing React components go the other way.

A worked example: a counter ticks up and a bar grows over 3 seconds

Motion Canvas first. This is a sketch built from the patterns on the official docs pages (generators, createRef, createSignal, all, tweening a signal). I did not run it, and import paths have changed between major versions, so check the current docs before pasting:

import { makeScene2D, Rect, Txt } from "@motion-canvas/2d";
import { all, createRef, createSignal } from "@motion-canvas/core";

export default makeScene2D(function* (view) {
  const count = createSignal(0);
  const bar = createRef<Rect>();

  view.add(
    <>
      <Txt fill="white" fontSize={120} text={() => Math.round(count()).toString()} />
      <Rect ref={bar} y={160} height={40} width={0} fill="#3b82f6" />
    </>,
  );

  yield* all(count(100, 3), bar().width(600, 3));
});

The same scene in Remotion, also unrun. It is a 90-frame composition at 30 fps, and extrapolateRight: "clamp" is the option shown in the interpolate() docs for holding the end value:

import { AbsoluteFill, interpolate, useCurrentFrame } from "remotion";

export const CounterBar = () => {
  const frame = useCurrentFrame();
  const opts = { extrapolateRight: "clamp" } as const;
  const count = interpolate(frame, [0, 90], [0, 100], opts);
  const width = interpolate(frame, [0, 90], [0, 600], opts);
  return (
    <AbsoluteFill style={{ background: "#0b0b0f", alignItems: "center", justifyContent: "center" }}>
      <div style={{ color: "white", fontSize: 120 }}>{Math.round(count)}</div>
      <div style={{ marginTop: 40, height: 40, width, background: "#3b82f6" }} />
    </AbsoluteFill>
  );
};

// <Composition id="CounterBar" component={CounterBar} width={1920} height={1080} fps={30} durationInFrames={90} />

Look at the shapes. The Motion Canvas version states intent: count to 100 and grow the bar to 600 wide, both over 3 seconds, together. The Remotion version states a mapping: for every frame between 0 and 90, here is the number and the width. Remotion is longer here, but the pattern does not change when the bar becomes a chart, the number becomes a styled code block, or the scene becomes a phone-shaped layout.

Editor and preview

Both ship an editor. Motion Canvas runs its editor at localhost:9000 after npm run serve; it previews the animation and updates when you save a file. Remotion Studio opens with npx remotion studio, lives in the @remotion/cli package, and is described in the docs as allowing fast editing and playback of compositions. I did not benchmark either for hot-reload speed, so I won't rank them. The difference I can state from the docs is the unit being edited: Motion Canvas edits an animation timeline, Remotion Studio plays compositions that are React components.

Output and rendering

This is the clearest difference in output. In the Motion Canvas rendering docs, clicking RENDER saves each frame as an image to the project's output folder, as PNG, JPEG or WebP, and the page suggests converting frames to video with a tool like ffmpeg or importing the sequence into a video editor. The page does not describe a built-in video export, so check the current docs and release notes in case that has changed.

Remotion renders video directly. npx remotion render <composition-id> <output-location> uses the H.264 encoder by default, and --codec accepts h264, h265, av1, vp8, vp9, prores and audio-only codecs such as mp3, aac and wav. Audio follows the same split. In Motion Canvas you import an audio file in project.ts, set the audio property in makeProject, and shift it with audioOffset (seconds); the docs page does not say how audio is exported. In Remotion you place the file in public/ and add an audio component with staticFile(), trimming and volume are props, and the audio ends up in the rendered file.

If your end product is an MP4 for YouTube Shorts, Remotion has fewer steps between code and finished file. If your end product is a frame sequence you will composite elsewhere, Motion Canvas is already there.

Licensing

Motion Canvas: the GitHub API reports an MIT license on the repository (checked November 3, 2026). Remotion is source-available with a two-tier license. The LICENSE.md in the Remotion repository says you are eligible to use it for free if you are an individual, a for-profit organization with up to 3 employees, a non-profit or not-for-profit organization, or evaluating it without yet using it commercially. Larger for-profit organizations need a company license. The file also says the license will change slightly in Remotion 5.0. Read the current terms on Remotion's license page before committing a team. I'm not a lawyer and this is a pointer, not advice.

Maintenance and community

Numbers from the GitHub API and web checks on November 3, 2026:

  • Motion Canvas (motion-canvas/motion-canvas): 19,662 stars, 177 open issues, not archived, MIT. Latest commit July 2, 2026 (a docs domain update). Latest GitHub release: v3.17.2, published December 14, 2024. motioncanvas.io returned HTTP 200.
  • Remotion (remotion-dev/remotion): 70,298 stars, 191 open issues, not archived. Latest commit November 3, 2026. Latest release: v4.0.540, published November 2, 2026.

Note that GitHub's open-issue count includes pull requests, so treat both figures as rough. I am not drawing a conclusion from the dates; they are what a reader can check themselves. If you plan to build a lot on either, read the recent commits and release notes.

Is Motion Canvas still maintained?

As of November 3, 2026, the motion-canvas/motion-canvas repository is not archived, motioncanvas.io responds, the most recent commit was on July 2, 2026, and the latest GitHub release is v3.17.2 from December 14, 2024. Those are the facts I could verify. Check the repository's recent activity yourself for the current picture.

Is Motion Canvas free for commercial use?

The repository carries the MIT license according to the GitHub API, and MIT permits commercial use with the license notice kept. Read the LICENSE file in the version you install, and note that this covers the code, not any fonts, audio or footage you put in a project.

Can I use Motion Canvas with React?

Motion Canvas scenes are written in TSX, so the syntax looks like React, but they are not React components. Scenes are generator functions that build nodes like Txt and Rect, and they render to a canvas, not the DOM. I did not find a documented way to drop an arbitrary React component into a scene, so if you need your existing React components in the video, Remotion is the direct route.

Motion Canvas alternatives if it's not for you

  • Remotion, if you want React components, layout work and a direct MP4 render.
  • Manim, if the content is math or geometry. See our Manim alternatives roundup, and our Remotion vs Manim comparison for the Manim side in detail, including Motion Canvas vs Manim.
  • Tools built on Remotion, if you want a pipeline rather than a framework. A Claude Code workflow is covered in our Claude Code and Remotion post.

Which should you pick?

  • You think in sequences and want an animation-first timeline: Motion Canvas.
  • You think in React components and layout: Remotion.
  • You need a finished MP4 with audio from one command: Remotion. A frame sequence you finish elsewhere is fine: Motion Canvas.
  • You are a for-profit company above 3 employees: read Remotion's company license terms first. Motion Canvas is MIT.
  • You want an LLM to write the scenes: see below.

On agent-friendliness, I have no measurement of which one a model writes correctly more often, and I won't invent one. What I can point to is documentation: Remotion's docs include a section on prompting videos with coding agents and a set of Agent Skills installed with npx skills add remotion-dev/skills, as I confirmed in the Remotion vs Manim post on October 31, 2026. I did not look for an equivalent for Motion Canvas on November 3. Whichever you pick, run the code and look at the frames; generated animation code often needs a pass. Generator-based tweens and signals are also a smaller, newer API surface, and the import-path changes between versions are a place an agent can go wrong.

Where ReelMint fits

ReelMint is built on Remotion. It adds a visual editor for every generated scene and an MCP server at https://studio.reelmint.io/api/mcp that Claude Desktop, Claude Code and Cursor can drive (130+ MCP tools; see /mcp). You bring your own provider keys (BYOK), there is a free tier, and it publishes to YouTube Shorts. Instagram Reels publishing is pending Meta App Review, so I won't promise it. Its strengths are code cards, terminal cards and chart animations for developer Shorts.

It is not the right pick for math or academic animation. There are no equation-morphing primitives. For that, use Manim. And if you want frame-level control of an animation as code, with an animation-first timeline, Motion Canvas or Remotion directly will serve you better than a higher-level tool. For a typical 60 to 90 second reel through the MCP path I measured 45 to 60 minutes elapsed, of which 10 to 20 minutes is hands-on; that is one measurement by the person who built it.

title: Remotion alternatives: what to use instead, depending on why you're leaving
description:
People search for a Remotion alternative for four different reasons, and the right answer changes with each one. Here are the real options, with repo facts and license terms checked on 3 November 2026.

Disclosure first: I build ReelMint, and ReelMint is built on Remotion. Our render pipeline is Remotion underneath, so I am not selling you a way out of it. What I can offer is a map of why people look for a Remotion alternative and what exists for each reason, including the cases where the honest answer is a different tool, or Remotion itself.

Everything with a date below was checked on 3 November 2026 against the live repository, license page or pricing page. Where I could not check something, I say so. For the Python and math side of this question, I won't repeat myself: see Remotion vs Manim and the Manim alternatives roundup.

Why people look for a Remotion alternative

Four reasons cover nearly every case I have seen, and they point to different tools:

  • License. Remotion is free for some users and paid for others, and a company that grows past the free tier needs a plan.
  • No React. Remotion videos are React components. If your team writes Python, Go or plain TypeScript, that is a tax on every video.
  • Need a GUI. You want to drag a clip, fix a typo in a title and re-export, without opening a code editor.
  • Need an agent or an API. You want Claude Code, Cursor or a backend job to produce videos, ideally without owning a render farm.

Speed and render cost sometimes make a fifth reason. I have not benchmarked any of these tools against each other, so I won't rank them on it. Measure on your own hardware with your own scene.

Is Remotion free for commercial use?

Often yes, not always. As of 3 November 2026, the LICENSE.md in the Remotion repository says you are eligible for the free license if you are "an individual", "a for-profit organization with up to 3 employees", "a non-profit or not-for-profit organization", or "evaluating whether Remotion is a good fit, and are not yet using it in a commercial way". It adds that "a company license is required for for-profit organizations of a certain size".

Remotion's own pricing page, read the same day, words it as "individuals and companies up to three people" for free, and a Company License for "collaborations and companies of 4+ people". It lists two paid tracks: Remotion for Creators at $25 per month per seat, and Remotion for Automators at $0.01 per render with a $100 per month minimum. The LICENSE.md also says the license will change slightly in Remotion 5.0. Read the current terms at remotion.dev/docs/license before you commit a team. I am not a lawyer, and this is a pointer, not advice.

Remotion alternatives by reason

If the problem is the license: a Remotion open source alternative

Two code-first tools are MIT licensed. Motion Canvas is a TypeScript animation tool with a browser editor for previewing and syncing to audio. We compared Motion Canvas with Remotion head-to-head. On 3 November 2026 the motion-canvas/motion-canvas repository showed 19.6k stars, an MIT license, was not archived, and its latest commit was 2 July 2026. Revideo describes itself as a rendering engine for creating videos in code, with a headless render API and a React player for previews. Its repository (now at midrender/revideo) showed 4.2k stars, an MIT license, and a latest commit on 15 July 2026.

Both use a generator-function style: you write scenes as TypeScript that yields animations in order, instead of React components keyed to a frame number. That is a different mental model, not a drop-in replacement. Porting a large Remotion project means rewriting it, so this route suits new projects more than migrations. Commit dates are not a health report. Check each project's open issues before building a business on it.

A different way to read the license problem: for a lot of teams, paying is fine. Remotion's terms exist to fund the project, and the paid tracks above are priced per seat or per render. Compare that against the engineering cost of switching before you assume free is cheaper.

What is the best Remotion alternative that doesn't need React?

It depends on what you are making. For TypeScript without React, Motion Canvas and Revideo are the closest code-first options. For a declarative, no-code-framework approach, Editly assembles a video from a JSON5 spec or a small JavaScript API on top of ffmpeg. Its repository showed 5.6k stars, an MIT license and a latest commit on 12 May 2025, so it is stable rather than fast-moving. For Python and math content, Manim, covered in the posts linked above.

If you want no framework at all, scripting ffmpeg directly is always available. It handles cuts, overlays, subtitles and concatenation well, and it gets painful the moment you want animated layout, because ffmpeg has no layout engine.

If you need a GUI: timeline editors and template APIs

Code-first tools make a poor fit when a non-developer must edit the result. There are two honest families. The first is template-based video APIs such as JSON2Video and Creatomate: you design a template, then fill it with data over an API. JSON2Video's pricing page listed, on 3 November 2026, a $49.95 one-time pack of 7,200 credits described as up to 120 minutes of rendered video, and a free entry tier of 600 credits. Creatomate listed a monthly Essential plan with 2,000 credits and a 50-credit trial. I did not read the full fine print of either, so confirm what a credit buys for your resolution before you budget.

The second family is After Effects with Lottie export. Lottie is a playback format for vector animation, not a general video renderer, so it fits UI motion and small loops, not a 60-second narrated explainer. The airbnb/lottie-web player showed 32.3k stars and an MIT license on 3 November 2026. Theatre.js (Apache-2.0, 12.8k stars) is a motion design editor for the web rather than a video encoder, and its latest commit was 14 August 2024, so treat it as a tool for animating in the browser, not an off-the-shelf video pipeline.

If you need an agent or an API: keep Remotion, change who drives it

Here the answer is often not to leave Remotion at all. Remotion's docs have a page on prompting videos with coding agents, naming Claude Code, Codex, Kimi Code and OpenCode, with an install step of npx remotion skills add. A coding agent can write Remotion compositions today.

What an agent loop still lacks is a persistent project: scenes you can read back, patch one at a time, preview and re-render without regenerating the whole file. That is the gap ReelMint fills. It keeps Remotion rendering underneath, exposes 130+ MCP tools at https://studio.reelmint.io/api/mcp that Claude Desktop, Claude Code and Cursor can drive, and keeps every generated scene editable in a visual editor. It runs on your own provider keys (BYOK) and has a free tier. If you want the wiring, see connecting Claude Code to a video pipeline and what MCP video generation is.

Comparison list: language, license, last commit, output

All figures from GitHub's API and each project's own pages on 3 November 2026. "Last commit" is the repository's most recent push date.

  • Remotion: TypeScript and React. Source-available with a company license above the free tier (terms above). 70.3k stars, latest commit 3 Nov 2026. Output: video and images, any dimensions.
  • Motion Canvas: TypeScript, generator scenes. MIT. 19.6k stars, latest commit 2 Jul 2026. Output: video through its editor and render pipeline.
  • Revideo: TypeScript, generator scenes, headless render API. MIT. 4.2k stars, latest commit 15 Jul 2026.
  • Editly: JSON5 or JavaScript on ffmpeg. MIT. 5.6k stars, latest commit 12 May 2025. Output: video or GIF at any dimensions, including 9:16.
  • Manim Community: Python. MIT. 42.2k stars, latest commit 2 Nov 2026. Output: landscape by default, math-focused.
  • Theatre.js: TypeScript, in-browser editor. Apache-2.0. 12.8k stars, latest commit 14 Aug 2024. A motion editor, not a video encoder.
  • JSON2Video and Creatomate: hosted template APIs, usage-priced, closed source.
  • ReelMint: MCP server and visual editor on a Remotion render pipeline. Free tier, BYOK. YouTube Shorts publishing is available; Instagram Reels publishing is pending Meta App Review.

Which Remotion alternative is right for you?

  • License is the blocker and you write TypeScript: try Motion Canvas or Revideo on a small project before committing.
  • You do not want React and you assemble clips: Editly, or ffmpeg directly.
  • Non-developers need to edit the output: a template API, or a tool with a visual editor.
  • You want vector UI motion rather than video: Lottie.
  • You want an AI agent to produce vertical Shorts you can still edit: ReelMint, or Remotion plus a coding agent if you are happy owning the React project.
  • Your content is math: Manim, per the posts linked at the top.

Can an AI agent drive Remotion?

Yes. Remotion documents the workflow itself, and I covered a hands-on version in Claude Code and Remotion for motion graphics. The limit is not whether the agent can write the code but whether the result stays maintainable: a one-shot generated composition is hard to patch scene by scene. A persistent, tool-driven project helps there, which is the job of an MCP server rather than a prompt.

When Remotion is still the right call

Stay on Remotion if you already write React, your team is within the free license or happy with the paid one, and you want full frame-level control. It has the largest community of the code-first tools above by star count, and its latest commit was the day I wrote this. Nothing on the alternatives list gives you its component model and web ecosystem together. And if you only want a finished Short, with no code ownership, ReelMint is the wrong pick for some people: a template API or an editor-first tool will get a non-technical user there with less setup. Our fit is developers who want an agent in the loop and an editable result. Start from the code explainer Shorts maker or the pricing page and judge for yourself.

Originally published on reelmint.io.

title: PostgreSQL 14 stops on November 12: test your old dumps first
description:
On 12 November 2026, PostgreSQL 14 gets its final release. After that date, no more fixes, not even for a security flaw. One week later, PostgreSQL 19 is due to ship as a final release.

Prepare your upgrade before support ends. Before you pick 18 or 19, ask yourself a simple question. Do your dumps restore on the new version?

TL;DR: I backed up the real schema of one of my projects on PostgreSQL 14. Then I restored it on 18 and on 19 RC1. The data comes through unchanged. But without the roles, application privileges disappear, and psql still reports success. And when my 14 server had standard_conforming_strings set to off, 19 left a table empty. Test your restores on the target version, and take your dumps with its pg_dump.

Versions and source status: snapshot as of October 31, 2026. Check the latest fixes before deploying.

This article is for developers and teams running PostgreSQL 14 in production. It also helps if you keep PostgreSQL 14 dumps in an archive. No deep PostgreSQL knowledge needed.

The key lab result is simple: data can come back while permissions are lost. psql can even return 0. Check errors, data and permissions together.

The calendar: 14 stops, 19 arrives

PostgreSQL supports each major version for five years. The major version is the first number: 14, 18 or 19. Minor versions, like 14.24, only bring fixes.

Version 14 came out on 30 September 2021. The official table sets its final release on 12 November 2026. After that, a flaw found in 14 will not be fixed.

Version 18 is the current stable release, at 18.6. It is supported until 14 November 2030. Version 19 has been a release candidate since 15 October. Its final release is planned for 19 November, unless a problem delays it.

To move from one major version to another, you need a dump and a restore, or the pg_upgrade tool. The documentation explains why. The internal data format can change between two major versions.

A physical backup copies exactly those internal files. It gives you back a 14, not an 18. To change versions from a backup, you need a dump.

My test: a real schema, three PostgreSQL versions

PostgreSQL is in the stack of every one of my freelance projects. So before writing about this date, I wanted to test it for real.

I took the schema of one of my projects: 11 databases, one per service, and 129 SQL migrations. That makes 58 tables, triggers, functions and 72 RLS policies. I described them in my article on tenant isolation.

I added a few made-up rows, with no real data at all. Some of them hold traps: backslashes (the \ character), apostrophes, emoji and JSON.

Then I exported each database with pg_dump 14.24, in two formats:

  • the plain format, an SQL script you replay with psql;
  • the custom format, a binary file you read back with pg_restore.

I restored each dump on PostgreSQL 18.6 and on 19 RC1, with the tools of each version. Everything ran in Docker, with the official images.

To compare, I computed a fingerprint per table: the row count and a hash of the content. I also counted indexes, constraints, policies and privileges. Same fingerprint, same data.

Good news: the data comes through unchanged

With the default settings, my 14 dumps restore on 18 and on 19. All 58 tables keep the same fingerprint as the source.

Indexes, triggers, functions and RLS policies are there too. That holds for both formats and both versions.

But I had recreated the roles on the target server before restoring. Without them, the result is very different.

The data comes back, the privileges do not, and psql says success. Three restores of my 14 schema on 18 and 19. Without the roles, 393 privileges disappear. With an old setting, 19 leaves a table empty.

Trap 1: your dump does not contain your roles

A role is a PostgreSQL account. Your services connect with it, and table privileges are granted to these roles.

pg_dump exports a single database. Roles belong to the whole server, so they are not in the dump. The documentation points to pg_dumpall to export them.

My schema grants privileges to 24 application roles. I restored the dumps on a fresh server, without those roles. psql printed this kind of line 126 times:

ERROR:  role "app_identity_app" does not exist

All the data is there. But three things changed, on 18 as on 19:

  • The 393 table privileges granted to the application roles are gone.
  • 5 of the 72 RLS policies no longer exist. They targeted a specific role, so creating them failed.
  • In custom format, two functions restricted to my application roles became executable by any role again.

The last point is the sneakiest. In a custom dump, revoking the public privilege and granting the role's privilege travel in the same command. When the grant fails, the revoke is rolled back with it.

And psql? On a single database, it printed 35 errors, then returned exit code 0, the success code. A CI job reading that code would show green. pg_restore returns 1.

The fix takes two steps. Export the roles separately, then recreate them on the target server before the databases:

# On the source: roles and tablespaces, including password hashes.
pg_dumpall -U postgres --globals-only > globals.sql

# On the target: review duplicate CREATE ROLE statements first.
psql -X -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U postgres -f globals.reviewed.sql

In my trial, one error came from the postgres role already present on the new server. Prepare a copy named globals.reviewed.sql before a strict restore. Check existing roles. Remove only reviewed duplicate CREATE ROLE statements. Keep the intended attributes and memberships. Any other error must stop the restore.

This file holds the password hashes of your roles. Store it like a secret.

Also add -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 to psql, or --exit-on-error to pg_restore. The first error then stops the restore, with a failure exit code.

Trap 2: an old setting that 19 refuses

standard_conforming_strings decides how PostgreSQL reads a backslash in a string. With on, a backslash is a normal character. With off, it escapes the next character.

The default has been on since PostgreSQL 9.1. But if your server has it off, every dump records it in its first lines:

SET standard_conforming_strings = off;

The PostgreSQL 19 release notes are clear. This setting is now forced to on. A dump made by an older pg_dump, on a server set to off, will not load properly.

I wanted to see what "not properly" means. I switched my 14 server to off, then dumped three databases again. On 18, everything restores without an error. On 19, the restore prints these errors at the start, then carries on:

ERROR:  non-standard string literals are not supported
ERROR:  unrecognized configuration parameter "escape_string_warning"

Further down, one of my tables stays empty. It has a CHECK constraint that validates emails with a regular expression:

CHECK (email ~* '^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$')

On a server set to off, pg_dump writes the backslashes of this constraint twice. Version 19 now reads those two backslashes as two characters. The regular expression changes meaning, and my test emails no longer pass. Loading the whole table fails.

With the --inserts option of pg_dump, it gets worse. Rows are written as INSERT statements, and every backslash comes back doubled in your data. No error reports it:

on 14: Le fichier est dans C:\Partage\Docs
on 19: Le fichier est dans C:\\Partage\\Docs

Here again, psql returned exit code 0.

I tested two fixes, and both work. If your 14 server is still running, take the dump with the pg_dump of 19. It writes SET standard_conforming_strings = on, and the restore is clean.

If all you have left is the file, restore it on an 18 first. Then take a new dump from that 18, with the pg_dump of 19. My values came back intact.

To find out whether your dumps are affected, one line is enough:

# plain format
grep -m1 standard_conforming_strings base.sql

# custom format
pg_restore -f - base.dump | grep -m1 standard_conforming_strings

Take your dumps with the pg_dump of the target version

In the other direction, everything went fine. The pg_dump of 18 and of 19 read my 14 server without a single warning. Their dumps restored without an error, with the same fingerprints.

It is also the official advice. For a major upgrade, use pg_dump and pg_dumpall from the new version. With Docker, you do not even need to install them:

docker run --rm -e PGPASSWORD postgres:18.6 \
  pg_dump -h old-server -U postgres -Fc -d my_db > my_db.dump

Plan the rollback before you migrate

I also tested the reverse path. The pg_restore of 14 refuses a custom dump made by the pg_dump of 18 or 19:

pg_restore: error: unsupported version (1.16) in file header

And the pg_dump of 14 refuses to read a 19 server:

pg_dump: error: aborting because of server version mismatch

The documentation confirms it. Nothing guarantees that a dump loads into an older major version. So keep the old server and its tools as long as a rollback is still possible. Keep a dump made with those tools too.

The checklist

A backup counts if it restores on the version where you will use it.

  • [ ] List your PostgreSQL 14 servers and their migration date
  • [ ] Run SHOW standard_conforming_strings; on each one
  • [ ] Look for that line in the dumps you keep in your archive
  • [ ] Export the roles with pg_dumpall --globals-only, and store the file like a secret
  • [ ] Restore a real dump on the target version, in a throwaway container
  • [ ] Add -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 to psql and --exit-on-error to pg_restore
  • [ ] Compare rows, privileges and RLS policies before and after
  • [ ] Take the migration dumps with the pg_dump of the target version
  • [ ] Keep the old server and its tools until a rollback is no longer possible

What to remember

In my article on backups, I wrote that a backup never restored is only a hope. A major upgrade adds a question: restored on which version?

In my test, with the default settings, the data from 14 came through unchanged. What broke came from the side: roles missing from the dump, and an old server setting. And psql returned the success code in both cases.

You need to migrate a PostgreSQL 14 and want to test your restores before 12 November? Let's talk.

Sources: PostgreSQL, versioning policy · PostgreSQL 19 RC 1, announcement of 15 October 2026 · PostgreSQL 19 release notes · PostgreSQL, upgrading a cluster · pg_dump · pg_dumpall · pg_restore · psql, exit status · standard_conforming_strings · Official postgres Docker images
