title: Why Functional Testing Isn't Enough for Web Application Security
description:
A web application can pass every functional test and still contain serious security vulnerabilities.

The login page works. The contact form submits successfully. The API returns the expected response. The deployment pipeline is green.

Everything looks fine.

But what happens when someone changes a request parameter, accesses another user's resource, or submits input the application wasn't designed to handle?

These scenarios highlight an important distinction between functional testing and security testing.

Functional testing verifies whether an application behaves as expected. Web application vulnerability assessment examines how the application behaves when its security assumptions are challenged.

Let's explore why both are necessary and how development teams can approach vulnerability assessment more effectively.

1. Functional correctness does not guarantee security

Consider a simple API endpoint:

GET /api/orders/1042
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

A functional test might verify that an authenticated user can retrieve order 1042.

If the API returns the expected data, the test passes.

But what if the user changes the request to:

GET /api/orders/1043
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

If order 1043 belongs to another customer, the application must enforce object-level authorization.

Otherwise, a user may access data they should not be able to see.

This is an example of a broken object-level authorization vulnerability.

The application may work perfectly from a functional perspective while failing to protect sensitive information.

This is why security testing needs to examine more than expected user behavior.

2. What does a web application vulnerability assessment cover?

A vulnerability assessment identifies and evaluates security weaknesses in an application.

The exact scope depends on the architecture, business requirements, and sensitivity of the data involved.

Common assessment areas include:

Area Typical security concerns
Authentication Weak login protection, account recovery issues
Authorization Unauthorized access to functions or data
Input handling SQL injection, cross-site scripting
Session management Insecure cookies, session handling weaknesses
File uploads Unsafe file processing and validation
APIs Missing authorization, excessive data exposure
Configuration Exposed debug features, insecure settings

These categories are not independent.

For example, a weakness in session management may interact with an authorization flaw, increasing the potential impact.

A useful assessment therefore considers both individual vulnerabilities and how application components interact.

3. Automated scanning is useful, but it has limits

Automated vulnerability scanners can help identify common security weaknesses.

They are particularly useful for repeatable checks, broad endpoint coverage, and detecting known patterns.

For example, a scanner may flag missing security headers, outdated components, or certain input validation weaknesses.

However, automated scanning cannot reliably understand every application's business rules.

Consider an expense approval system.

An employee can submit a reimbursement request, and a manager can approve it.

A security issue may exist if employees can approve their own requests by manipulating an API call.

Detecting this requires understanding the intended business workflow and authorization rules.

An automated scanner may not have enough context to identify the problem.

This is where manual security testing becomes valuable.

A balanced assessment often combines automated checks with targeted manual verification.

4. API security deserves particular attention

Modern web applications frequently depend on APIs.

A single frontend may communicate with several backend services, including authentication systems, payment providers, and internal business applications.

As a result, API security has become a central part of application security.

Consider an endpoint:

PATCH /api/users/204/profile
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

{
  "displayName": "Example User"
}

The backend should verify that the authenticated user is authorized to modify the requested profile.

It should also validate the accepted fields and prevent unauthorized changes to protected properties.

Important API security considerations include:

  • Object-level and function-level authorization
  • Input validation
  • Authentication and token handling
  • Rate limiting where appropriate
  • Sensitive data exposure
  • Secure configuration
  • Logging and monitoring

The OWASP API Security Top 10 provides a useful framework for identifying common API security risks.

However, a checklist alone is not sufficient. Testing must reflect the application's actual data flows and permission model.

5. When should vulnerability assessments happen?

A common mistake is treating security testing as a one-time activity immediately before launch.

While pre-release testing is important, vulnerabilities can also be introduced after deployment.

For example, a team may add a new API endpoint, modify user permissions, or integrate an external service.

Each change can affect the application's security posture.

There are several useful assessment points throughout the development lifecycle.

Before production release

Assess critical application functions, authentication, authorization, and data handling before exposing the system to real users.

After significant changes

Reassess affected components when introducing new functionality, changing access controls, or modifying integrations.

During ongoing operations

Schedule assessments based on the application's risk level, exposure, and rate of change.

After major vulnerability disclosures

When a serious vulnerability is reported in a framework, library, or runtime used by the application, investigate exposure and apply the relevant remediation.

The goal is to make security verification part of the application lifecycle rather than an isolated event.

6. Integrating security testing into CI/CD

Not every security test needs to be performed manually.

Development teams can automate several security checks within their pipelines.

A simplified workflow might look like this:

Code Commit
    |
    v
Static Analysis / SAST
    |
    v
Dependency Scanning
    |
    v
Build & Deploy to Test Environment
    |
    v
Automated DAST
    |
    v
Manual Security Review (Risk-Based)
    |
    v
Production Release

Static Application Security Testing (SAST) examines source code or related artifacts for potential security issues.

Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) examines a running application.

Dependency scanning helps identify known vulnerabilities in third-party components.

These approaches complement one another, but none guarantees complete coverage.

For applications with complex business logic or sensitive workflows, manual assessment remains important.

7. Finding vulnerabilities is only the beginning

A vulnerability assessment produces findings, but those findings do not automatically make an application more secure.

The next step is remediation.

A practical process usually includes:

  1. Validation: Confirm whether a finding represents a real security issue.
  2. Prioritization: Evaluate severity, exploitability, exposure, and business impact.
  3. Remediation: Fix the underlying weakness.
  4. Retesting: Verify that the issue has been resolved.
  5. Regression testing: Confirm that the fix has not broken expected functionality.

Severity scores can support prioritization, but they should not be the only factor.

A moderate-severity issue affecting a critical business workflow may require urgent attention.

Similarly, an issue in an internet-facing system may deserve different treatment from the same issue in a tightly restricted environment.

8. Choosing a vulnerability assessment approach

The appropriate assessment depends on the application.

A public marketing website, a customer portal, and a financial transaction platform have different threat models.

Before selecting an assessment method, engineering teams should clarify:

  • Which applications, APIs, and environments are in scope?
  • What sensitive data does the system handle?
  • Which user roles and permission levels exist?
  • What testing methods are permitted?
  • Who will implement and verify fixes?
  • How will findings be prioritized and documented?

These questions help ensure the assessment produces actionable results rather than just a long list of scanner alerts.

For teams looking for a more detailed overview, SotaTek Japan has published a Japanese-language guide covering web application vulnerability assessment, common testing categories, assessment methods, costs, and implementation steps.

Further reading: Web Application Vulnerability Assessment: Testing Areas, Costs, and Process — SotaTek Japan

The guide also discusses how assessment findings can be connected to remediation and follow-up verification.

Final thoughts

A web application that functions correctly is not necessarily secure.

Functional tests verify expected behavior, while vulnerability assessments examine potential weaknesses in authentication, authorization, input handling, APIs, and other security-sensitive components.

Automated scanners can provide valuable coverage, but manual testing is often needed to evaluate business logic and complex access-control scenarios.

Most importantly, security assessment should not end with a report.

The real value comes from identifying risks, fixing the underlying issues, and verifying that the application is safer afterward.

Suggested tags: #security #webdev #testing #devops

title: Romanian Address Format: The Rules and a React Form
description:
TL;DR

The Romanian address format starts with the street line (type, name, number, then bl., sc., et. and ap. for block, staircase, floor and apartment), adds the sector in Bucharest, and ends with the 6-digit postal code, the locality and, in domestic use, the county as jud. Cluj. The first two digits of the postal code identify the county, so a form can flag a code from the wrong one. In React, build it as a county select, a locality search that ignores diacritics, street and number, an optional block row and a numeric postal code.

Search for an address form React example and you get a US layout: street, city, state, ZIP. Ship that to customers in Romania and they have nowhere to put the block, the staircase or the Bucharest sector, so the courier calls to ask. This tutorial covers the Romanian address format part by part, checked against the Universal Postal Union's sheet for Romania, with English labels and Romanian data. Then it builds the form in React on Address Input, a component from Wingo UI, the library we build, so we are not neutral.

What is the Romanian address format?

A Romanian address runs from the most specific line to the broadest: the street line with the building details, the sector in Bucharest, then the postal code and the locality. The UPU addressing sheet for Romania (dated October 2007) gives four rules:

  1. The street type comes before the name: Str. (strada), Bd. (bulevardul), Calea, Aleea, Șos. (șoseaua).
  2. The number usually ends the street line.
  3. Building details can go at the end of the same line: block, staircase, floor, apartment.
  4. In Bucharest, the sector can sit on its own line between the street and the locality.

The 6-digit postal code goes to the left of the locality. Here is a Romania address format example from the sheet for an apartment in Bucharest, and one for an office in Craiova:

ASTRA
Drumul Taberei nr. 35, bl. F5, sc. 2, parter, ap. 23
Sector 6
061357 BUCHAREST
ROMANIA

SC PASAJ SA
Str. Bariera Valcii, nr. 215
200716 CRAIOVA
ROMANIA

The sheet writes Valcii for Vâlcii, which matters for search later. Both stop at the locality, since the postal code implies the county. In domestic mail, invoices and courier forms, people add the county (județ) after the locality as jud. Cluj, which also tells apart villages that share a name. Here is the Romanian postal address format as form fields, with English labels:

Form label Romanian Written as
County județ jud. Cluj
Sector sector (București only) Sector 6
City or village municipiu, oraș, comună, sat Cluj-Napoca, sat Vâlcele
Street stradă, bulevard, calea, aleea Str. Memorandumului
No. număr nr. 28
Block bloc bl. A2
Entrance scară sc. 1
Floor etaj et. 3, or parter for the ground floor
Apt. apartament ap. 12
Postal code cod poștal 400114

The labels are Address Input's English defaults. We label the scară "Entrance" because each staircase of a block has its own door, which is what a courier looks for.

How do you write a Bucharest or village address?

In Bucharest the sector takes the place of the county, and in the countryside a village usually needs its commune as well. București is a municipality with the rank of a county, split into six sectors. Written on one line, as a courier form or an invoice prints it, a Bucharest address ends with "Sector 6, 061357 București" and has no jud. part.

Villages add a level. Counties contain municipalities (municipii), towns (orașe) and communes (comune), and a commune groups several villages (sate). The National Institute of Statistics keeps the official list as SIRUTA, a register on those three levels that it publishes as a CSV on data.gov.ro. A village address names the village and usually its commune, as in "sat Vâlcele, com. Feleacu, jud. Cluj": Feleacu is a commune of five villages, one of them Vâlcele. In many rural communities there are no street names at all.

RoAddress, the value type, has no commune field. Keep the village in locality and its SIRUTA code in localityId: the register links every village to its commune, so you can print the commune when a courier needs it.

How do Romanian postal codes relate to counties?

The first two digits of a Romanian postal code identify the county, or the sector in Bucharest. Romania moved to 6-digit codes on May 1, 2003, and the UPU sheet reads them as a postal region, a district of that region (or a sector in Bucharest), then the delivery area. Per Wikipedia's article on postal codes in Romania, cities of more than 50,000 people get a code per street or small group of addresses, a smaller town has one code for the whole town, and village codes have a 7 as their third digit, like Feleacu's 407270. Poșta Română's postal code search finds the full code for an address.

Here is the Romanian counties list with the ISO 3166-2:RO code (the letters on license plates) and the postal prefix. Address Input stores the county as this code, and the prefixes match its RO_POSTAL_PREFIXES:

County Code Postal prefix
Alba AB 51
Arad AR 31
Argeș AG 11
Bacău BC 60
Bihor BH 41
Bistrița-Năsăud BN 42
Botoșani BT 71
Brașov BV 50
Brăila BR 81
București B 01 to 06 (Sector 1 to 6)
Buzău BZ 12
Caraș-Severin CS 32
Călărași CL 91
Cluj CJ 40
Constanța CT 90
Covasna CV 52
Dâmbovița DB 13
Dolj DJ 20
Galați GL 80
Giurgiu GR 08
Gorj GJ 21
Harghita HR 53
Hunedoara HD 33
Ialomița IL 92
Iași IS 70
Ilfov IF 07
Maramureș MM 43
Mehedinți MH 22
Mureș MS 54
Neamț NT 61
Olt OT 23
Prahova PH 10

That gives a cheap check. If someone picks Iași and types a code that starts with 40, one of the two is wrong: postalCodeMatchesCounty("400114", "IS") returns false. In Bucharest a chosen sector narrows it to one prefix, so postalCodeMatchesCounty("061357", "B", "6") is true and the same code with sector "3" is false.

Address Input shows a mismatch as an amber warning under the postal code once the field loses focus, and the form stays valid. We chose a warning on purpose: the check only knows prefixes, and a person who knows their own code should never be stuck at checkout.

How do I build a Romanian address form in React?

Split it into a county select, a locality search, street and number, an optional block row and a six-digit postal code, then validate on submit and again on the server. Address Input ships those parts. It is a Pro component, so sign in once with npx wingo-ui@latest login on a Pro account, then run npx wingo-ui@latest add address-input. The CLI adds what it builds on, including ro-locations, text-match, the select and the combobox. The component renders the county, the locality, street and number, a collapsed row for block, staircase, floor and apartment, the postal code and a details field for the intercom or a landmark. Its labels follow the locale (the locale prop, then the provider, then the page language): English, or Romanian for ro.

A checkout step that validates on submit and saves through the Server Action shown further down:

// app/checkout/shipping-step.tsx
"use client";

import { useState } from "react";
import {
  AddressInput,
  EMPTY_RO_ADDRESS,
  validateRoAddress,
  type AddressErrors,
  type RoAddress,
} from "@/components/ui/address-input";
import { Button } from "@/components/ui/button";
import { saveShipping } from "./actions";

export function ShippingStep({ onDone }: { onDone: () => void }) {
  const [address, setAddress] = useState<RoAddress>(EMPTY_RO_ADDRESS);
  const [errors, setErrors] = useState<AddressErrors>();

  return (
    <form
      noValidate
      className="flex flex-col gap-4"
      onSubmit={async (event) => {
        event.preventDefault();
        // the submit already made AddressInput show every error
        if (!validateRoAddress(address).valid) return;
        const result = await saveShipping(address);
        if (result.ok) onDone();
        else setErrors(result.errors);
      }}
    >
      <AddressInput
        label="Delivery address"
        value={address}
        errors={errors}
        onValueChange={(next) => {
          setAddress(next);
          setErrors(undefined);
        }}
        showSummary
      />
      <Button type="submit">Continue to payment</Button>
    </form>
  );
}

showSummary prints formatRoAddress under the form, the way the courier will read it: Str. Memorandumului 28, bl. A2, sc. 1, et. 3, ap. 12, 400114 Cluj-Napoca, jud. Cluj.

The parts a hand-rolled form usually misses:

  • Phones. The county and locality lists open as bottom sheets below 768px, the postal code takes six digits with the numeric keypad, and Enter moves to the next part.
  • Autofill. The county uses address-level1, the locality address-level2, the street address-line1 and the code postal-code, so a saved browser address fills the parts.
  • Paste. "Str. Memorandumului nr. 28, bl. A2" pasted into the street fills the street, number and block.
  • County changes. Picking București swaps the locality for a sector select. Changing the county clears the locality and a postal code from another county, and keeps the street and number.

Live demo: Address Input. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Clear the postal code, type six digits that start with 70, the prefix of Iași, and press Tab: the county is Cluj, so a warning appears while the readout still says valid. Then pick București as the county to get the sector select). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Address Input docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add address-input

How do I search localities without diacritics?

Fold both strings before you compare them: lowercase, decompose with NFD and drop the combining marks. "Iași".includes("iasi") is false, and folded, both sides read iasi. Ș and ț with a comma below only arrived in Unicode 3.0 in 1999, and older encodings had only the cedilla forms ş and ţ, which still turn up in imported data. Both decompose to a base letter plus a combining mark, so NFD folding treats Ștefănești, Ştefăneşti and stefanesti as one name.

text-match does that folding, ranks matches (exact, prefix, word prefix, inside a word) and returns the ranges to highlight, in about 200 lines with no dependencies. ro-locations builds its searchLocations on it, and Address Input's locality combobox filters with it.

Live demo: Romanian locations. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Type iasi, manastur or sector 3 without diacritics: each finds its place, with the matched letters highlighted). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Romanian locations docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add ro-locations

Folding does not cover abbreviations or old spellings. People type "Tg. Mureș" for Târgu Mureș, and records from before the 1993 spelling rule write î inside words (Tîrgu). filterByText takes keywords next to the label, so aliases handle both:

// lib/locality-search.ts
import { filterByText } from "@/lib/text-match";

// county is the plate code ("CJ"), the code Address Input stores and passes to loadLocalities
export type Locality = { id: string; name: string; county: string; commune?: string };

// how people also write a name: "Tg. Mures", and "Tirgu" from before the 1993 spelling rule
function aliases(name: string) {
  return [name.replace(/^Târgu /, "Tg. "), name.replace(/(?<=\p{L})â(?=\p{L})/gu, "î")];
}

export function searchLocalities(list: readonly Locality[], county: string, query: string) {
  return filterByText(
    list.filter((locality) => locality.county === county),
    query,
    (locality) => [locality.name, ...aliases(locality.name)],
    { limit: 20 },
  );
}

Now "tg mures" and "tirgu mures" both find Târgu Mureș, ranked a little below a direct hit on the name.

How do I load every village from SIRUTA?

Serve the SIRUTA list from your own route and give Address Input a loadLocalities function that queries it. Without one, the component searches a built-in list of 332 cities, towns and large communes and accepts any other locality as typed, with a quiet note under the field. text-match has no "use client" directive, so the same search runs in a route handler:

// app/api/localities/route.ts
import type { NextRequest } from "next/server";
import { LOCALITIES } from "@/data/localities"; // built from the SIRUTA CSV
import { searchLocalities } from "@/lib/locality-search";

export function GET(request: NextRequest) {
  const params = request.nextUrl.searchParams;
  const results = searchLocalities(LOCALITIES, params.get("county") ?? "", params.get("q") ?? "");
  return Response.json(
    results.map(({ item }) => ({
      value: item.id,
      label: item.name,
      // tells apart villages with the same name
      description: item.commune && `com. ${item.commune}`,
    })),
  );
}

<AddressInput
  label="Delivery address"
  loadLocalities={async (county, query, { signal }) => {
    const params = new URLSearchParams({ county, q: query });
    const response = await fetch(`/api/localities?${params}`, { signal });
    return response.ok ? response.json() : [];
  }}
/>

The value you return becomes localityId, so the SIRUTA code is saved with the address.

How do I validate the address on the server?

Check it again in the Server Action, with a zod 4 schema (npm install zod) in a file that has no "use client". Copied component code has a trap here: address-input.tsx starts with "use client", so on the server every export is a client reference. Calling validateRoAddress or formatRoAddress in a Server Component or a Server Action throws "Attempted to call formatRoAddress() from the server but formatRoAddress is on the client". Type imports are fine, and ro-locations has no directive, so the schema can use its county lookup:

// lib/ro-address-schema.ts
import { z } from "zod";
import { getCounty } from "@/lib/ro-locations";

const text = z.string().trim();

export const roAddressSchema = z
  .object({
    county: text.refine((code) => Boolean(getCounty(code)), { error: "Choose a county from the list" }),
    locality: text,
    localityId: text.optional(),
    sector: z.enum(["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]).optional(),
    street: text.min(1, { error: "Enter the street" }),
    number: text.min(1, { error: "Enter the number" }),
    building: text.optional(),
    entrance: text.optional(),
    floor: text.optional(),
    apartment: text.optional(),
    postalCode: z.union([z.literal(""), z.string().regex(/^\d{6}$/, { error: "A postal code has 6 digits" })]).optional(),
    details: text.optional(),
  })
  // bucharest has sectors where other counties have localities
  .refine((a) => a.county.toUpperCase() !== "B" || Boolean(a.sector), { error: "Choose a sector", path: ["sector"] })
  .refine((a) => a.county.toUpperCase() === "B" || a.locality.length > 0, {
    error: "Enter the city or village",
    path: ["locality"],
  });

// app/checkout/actions.ts
"use server";

import type { AddressErrors } from "@/components/ui/address-input";
import { roAddressSchema } from "@/lib/ro-address-schema";

export async function saveShipping(input: unknown): Promise<{ ok: true } | { ok: false; errors: AddressErrors }> {
  const parsed = roAddressSchema.safeParse(input);
  if (!parsed.success) {
    // the first message per field, the shape of AddressInput's errors prop
    const errors: AddressErrors = {};
    for (const issue of parsed.error.issues) errors[issue.path[0] as keyof AddressErrors] ??= issue.message;
    return { ok: false, errors };
  }
  // save parsed.data with the order
  return { ok: true };
}

Errors from the action land on the matching part through the errors prop and win over the component's own. To format an address on the server for an order email, move formatRoAddress and its helpers into a module without the directive. You own the source.

What should I build next?

Try the postal code check in the demo above, then add the form to your checkout with npx wingo-ui@latest add address-input. Address Input and ro-locations are part of Wingo UI Pro ($8 a month, $80 a year or $150 once as of October 2026), and text-match is free. If the same checkout takes company details, Romanian CUI validation covers tax IDs and the IBAN validation guide covers bank accounts, while React form components explains the label, hint and error anatomy every part of this form shares. More step-by-step React builds live in the Build it category.

Components in this post

  • Address Input (Pro): A Romanian address form: county, locality search, street, number, block and apartment, postal code checked against the county. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add address-input
  • Romanian locations (Pro): Romania's counties, cities and neighbourhoods with coordinates, diacritic-free search, distances and within-radius lists. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add ro-locations
  • Text match (Free): Search that ignores case and diacritics, ranks the best matches first and returns the ranges to highlight. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add text-match

FAQ

How do you write an address in Romania?

Write the street type, name and number first (Str. Memorandumului 28), then the block, staircase, floor and apartment on the same line (bl. A2, sc. 1, et. 3, ap. 12). The next line holds the 6-digit postal code and the locality (400114 Cluj-Napoca), followed in domestic use by the county as jud. Cluj, and in Bucharest a Sector line goes above the postal code. Mail from abroad ends with ROMANIA on its own line.

How many digits does a Romanian postal code have?

Six. Six-digit codes replaced the four-digit ones on May 1, 2003. The first two digits identify the county, and in Bucharest they identify the sector, from 01 for Sector 1 to 06 for Sector 6.

What do bl., sc., et. and ap. mean in a Romanian address?

They abbreviate bloc (the apartment building), scară (the staircase, which has its own entrance), etaj (the floor) and apartament (the apartment). The ground floor is written parter.

How many counties does Romania have?

Romania has 41 counties (județe) plus the municipality of Bucharest, which is divided into six sectors. Their ISO 3166-2:RO codes, such as RO-CJ for Cluj and RO-B for Bucharest, use the same letters as Romanian license plates.

Should a Romanian address form require diacritics?

No. Accept what people type and match it without diacritics: the UPU's own sample addresses for Romania are written without them, and older data uses the cedilla forms ş and ţ. Store the official spelling from your locality list once the person picks a match.

Are Address Input and the Romanian locations data free?

Address Input and ro-locations are part of Wingo UI Pro. text-match, the diacritic-insensitive search both of them use, is free and installs with npx wingo-ui@latest add text-match.

This article was originally published on the Wingo UI blog: Romanian Address Format: The Rules and a React Form. The original has the live, interactive demos and is kept up to date.

title: A component foundation still in use eight months later
description:
I shipped a component foundation from scratch: layout primitives, theme, color palette, interactive documentation. Eight months later, other teams are extending it, and other developers have written its tests.

What matters to me is that others use it without me. Here are the choices that helped.

A semantic palette, not a list of colors. A component doesn't say "use this green", it says "use the action color". Changing the theme then happens in one place.

A typed palette. If roles are typed, you can't use a role that doesn't exist: the editor refuses it before you even run the app.

// generic example
const palette = {
  text: { primary: "#1a1c1b", muted: "#5a5f5c" },
  action: { default: "#0b7a5b" },
} as const;

type TextTone = keyof typeof palette.text; // "primary" | "muted"

Contrast fixed in the palette itself. Light grey text on a white background looks nice and is unreadable. Fix the contrast once, in the palette, and it's fixed everywhere. For body text, the target is a ratio of 4.5 to 1.

Interactive documentation. A component you can't try without running the application won't get reused. The documentation shows each component in each of its states, and doubles as a visual check.

What I aim for with a foundation: a developer on another team can use it without asking me anything.

Amine Affif, full-stack developer in Paris. amineaffif.com

title: Java: When Life Gives You Problems, Build a ProblemFactory
description:
We've already explored PHP's questionable decisions, JavaScript's complicated relationship with logic, Python's ability to produce confidently incorrect results, and C#'s enterprise-grade surprises.

Now it's Java's turn.

Java is different.

Java is serious.

Java is strongly typed, object-oriented, carefully specified, and famously obsessed with backward compatibility.

This is a language that makes you declare what things are before you're allowed to do anything with them.

Surely, then, Java should be relatively free of surprises?

Well.

Let's talk about that.

1. String Concatenation: Apparently, + Needed a Performance Review

Let's start with something that every Java developer has written thousands of times.

String message = "Hello, " + name + "!";

Perfectly reasonable.

Now consider:

System.out.println("Total: " + 1 + 2);

Output:

Total: 12

But:

System.out.println(1 + 2 + " total");

Output:

3 total

Same numbers. Same operator. Different arithmetic.

Because Java evaluates these expressions from left to right, and once a string enters the expression, + becomes string concatenation.

Fine. We can live with that.

But Java has another surprise waiting.

Meet StringBuilder

Java strings are immutable.

Once created, a String cannot be modified.

So what happens when you repeatedly append characters?

String result = "";

for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
    result += i;
}

Conceptually, each iteration creates a new string containing the accumulated result plus the new value.

As the string grows, increasingly large amounts of data may need to be deal with by the jvm.

That's potentially a lot of unnecessary work.

Java developers have traditionally solved this problem with StringBuilder.

StringBuilder result = new StringBuilder();

for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
    result.append(i);
}

String finalResult = result.toString();

One mutable buffer, rather than repeatedly rebuilding an immutable string.

Much better for this kind of workload.

For years, the conventional advice was simple:

Use + for simple concatenation. Use StringBuilder when you're building strings in loops.

But Java being Java, it couldn't leave things quite that straightforward.

Plot Twist: The Compiler Was Already Helping

Before Java 9, the Java compiler typically translated ordinary string concatenation expressions into StringBuilder operations behind the scenes.

So this:

String message = "Hello, " + name + "!";

Wasn't necessarily doing the naive string-building work you might imagine.

Then Java 9 introduced a new concatenation mechanism using invokedynamic.

This allowed the runtime to select and optimize string-concatenation strategies more flexibly, without requiring the compiler to generate an explicit StringBuilder sequence.

So now we've got:

  • Strings that can't be changed.
  • A mutable class specifically for building strings.
  • A compiler that historically generated that class automatically.
  • A newer mechanism that can optimize concatenation differently.
  • Performance characteristics that depend on the expression, loop structure, compiler, and runtime.

Congratulations. We've turned joining two strings into a discussion about bytecode generation.

To be fair, modern Java handles ordinary + concatenation quite well.

The real performance concern remains repeated accumulation into a growing string, particularly in loops. An explicit StringBuilder is still a sensible choice there.

The lesson: Java's simple syntax can hide considerable compiler and runtime sophistication. And performance advice from 2005 doesn't always survive contact with modern JVMs.

2. Two Integers Are Equal. Until They Aren't.

Here's one of Java's most entertaining party tricks.

Integer a = 127;
Integer b = 127;

System.out.println(a == b);

Output:

true

Okay.

Now:

Integer a = 128;
Integer b = 128;

System.out.println(a == b);

On a typical JVM configuration:

false

Wait. What?

Two integers containing the same number can compare equal or unequal depending on the number.

The trick is that Integer isn't the same thing as int.

int is a primitive value.

Integer is an object wrapper around an integer value.

And for objects, == checks reference identity, not numerical equality.

But Java caches certain Integer objects.

Specifically, Integer.valueOf() is guaranteed to cache values from -128 through 127.

Autoboxing uses this mechanism.

So when you write:

Integer a = 127;
Integer b = 127;

Both variables normally refer to the same cached object.

But outside the guaranteed range, Java is allowed to create separate objects.

Hence the surprising result for 128.

There's one more complication: implementations are permitted to cache additional values, so 128 isn't guaranteed to produce false everywhere.

Which makes relying on this behavior an even worse idea.

The correct comparison:

System.out.println(a.equals(b));

Or compare the underlying primitive values when appropriate.

The lesson: In Java, == can mean numerical equality or object identity depending on the types involved. And integer caching makes that distinction particularly easy to overlook.

3. Arrays.asList() Gives You a List. Terms and Conditions Apply.

Here's a perfectly ordinary bit of Java:

String[] names = {"Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"};

List<String> list = Arrays.asList(names);

You now have a list.

And lists are mutable collections, right?

Let's add someone.

list.add("Dave");

Result:

java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException

Excuse me?

We created a list.

We tried to add an item.

And Java objected.

Here's the explanation.

Arrays.asList() returns a fixed-size list backed by the original array.

It isn't a regular, independently resizable ArrayList.

You can replace existing elements:

list.set(0, "Zoe");

That works.

But you can't change the list's size.

No adding.

No removing.

And here's the really interesting part:

System.out.println(names[0]);

Output:

Zoe

Changing the list changed the original array!

Because they're backed by the same storage.

The reverse is true too. Change an element in the array, and the list reflects that change.

So Arrays.asList() gives you something that:

  • Looks like a normal list.
  • Lets you replace elements.
  • Refuses to grow or shrink.
  • Shares its underlying data with the original array.

Java also offers List.of(), which creates an unmodifiable list.

And new ArrayList<>(...), which creates a separate, resizable list.

Three ways to obtain something called a list, with three different sets of rules.

The fix when you want an independent, resizable list:

List<String> list =
    new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(names));

The lesson: In Java, knowing that something implements List doesn't tell you everything about what operations it supports.

Sometimes the interface makes a promise that the implementation politely declines to fulfill.

4. Removing an Integer Can Remove the Wrong Integer

This one is genuinely nasty.

Suppose you have a list of numbers:

List<Integer> numbers =
    new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 20, 55));

Now you want to remove the number 1.

numbers.remove(1);

What happens?

The list becomes:

[1, 55]

You can kind of guess this one.

Our friend List has two overloaded remove() methods.

One removes an element by index.

The other removes an element by value.

Conceptually:

remove(int index)
remove(Object value)

And when you pass the literal integer 1, Java selects the overload accepting a primitive int.

So:

numbers.remove(1);

Means:

"Remove the element at index 1."

Not:

"Remove the integer whose value is 1."

If you actually want to remove the value 1:

numbers.remove(Integer.valueOf(1));

Now Java selects the object-based overload.

Same method name.

Same apparent kind of argument.

Completely different operation.

And because both operations are perfectly valid, the compiler has absolutely nothing to complain about.

The lesson: Method overloading, autoboxing, and collection APIs can combine into a surprisingly effective footgun.

Sometimes Java's type system is so helpful it confidently does the wrong thing you explicitly asked it to do.

5. Two Decimal Numbers Can Be Equal but Not Equal

For our final example, let's involve money.

Java provides BigDecimal for decimal arithmetic where precision matters.

Unlike ordinary binary floating-point numbers, BigDecimal can represent decimal values exactly.

Very useful for financial applications.

Now consider:

BigDecimal a = new BigDecimal("2.0");
BigDecimal b = new BigDecimal("2.00");

System.out.println(a.equals(b));

Output:

false

Seriously?

Two dollars is not equal to two dollars?

Now try:

System.out.println(a.compareTo(b) == 0);

Output:

true

So the numbers compare as equal.

But equals() says they're different.

Why?

Because BigDecimal stores both an unscaled numerical value and a scale.

2.0 and 2.00 represent the same numerical value, but they have different scales.

And BigDecimal.equals() considers scale part of equality.

compareTo() compares their numerical values instead.

That's actually defensible. Scale can matter for certain decimal calculations.

But it creates a wonderfully awkward consequence.

Consider:

Set<BigDecimal> hashSet = new HashSet<>();

hashSet.add(new BigDecimal("2.0"));
hashSet.add(new BigDecimal("2.00"));

System.out.println(hashSet.size());

Output:

2

Now:

Set<BigDecimal> treeSet = new TreeSet<>();

treeSet.add(new BigDecimal("2.0"));
treeSet.add(new BigDecimal("2.00"));

System.out.println(treeSet.size());

Output:

1

Two sets. Same values. Different answers about how many distinct elements exist.

Why?

HashSet uses equals() and hashCode() to determine uniqueness.

TreeSet uses ordering comparisons, which for BigDecimal normally means compareTo().

And BigDecimal explicitly defines those operations differently.

So Java gives you two completely legitimate definitions of uniqueness for the same numerical values.

Imagine discovering that while reconciling financial records.

The lesson: Equality, numerical comparison, and collection uniqueness aren't necessarily interchangeable. With BigDecimal, choosing the wrong one can produce very real business problems.

Java Is Predictable. You Just Need to Predict the Right Things.

Here's what makes Java interesting.

Unlike JavaScript, Java generally doesn't let values wander casually between unrelated types.

Unlike PHP, it doesn't enthusiastically reinterpret everything based on context.

And unlike Python, it tends to insist that you explain exactly what you're trying to do.

Java is explicit.

Java is disciplined.

Java is designed to make large programs easier to reason about.

And yet...

An integer can be identical to another integer until you increase it by one.

A list can refuse to let you add anything.

Removing a number can remove a completely different number.

Two decimal values can be equal according to one method and unequal according to another.

And joining strings can involve compiler transformations, runtime call sites, and an optimization discussion that lasts longer than the code itself.

None of this is random.

There are carefully documented reasons for every behavior.

But that doesn't make the surprises any less entertaining.

In fact, it makes them more interesting.

Java is a language where even the weirdness comes with a specification.

But Wait. Which Java Are We Talking About?

There's one more twist.

We've spent this article discussing Java, the programming language.

But Java is also commonly used to describe an entire development platform.

And that platform has a rather complicated family tree.

For starters, there's the JVM: the Java Virtual Machine.

The thing that executes Java bytecode.

Except there isn't just one implementation of the JVM.

There's HotSpot, the familiar JVM used by most OpenJDK distributions.

There's Eclipse OpenJ9, a separate JVM implementation with different approaches to memory management, startup performance, and garbage collection.

Then there's GraalVM, which builds on HotSpot while offering advanced compilation technology and Native Image, a way to compile Java applications into native executables that don't require a JVM at runtime.

And that's before we get into the different JDK distributions.

Oracle JDK.

Eclipse Temurin.

Amazon Corretto.

Azul Zulu.

Microsoft's Build of OpenJDK.

Those are distributions rather than entirely separate JVM implementations, but their packaging, support, licensing, and release policies can differ.

And then there's the small matter of the languages.

Because the Java Virtual Machine doesn't actually require you to write Java.

You can use Kotlin.

Scala.

Clojure.

And plenty of others.

So now we have one language, multiple JVM implementations, multiple JDK distributions, multiple languages targeting the JVM, and an alternative compilation model that can eliminate the need for a running JVM altogether.

Remember Java's original promise?

Write once, run anywhere.

Turns out the more interesting question is:

Run where, on which JVM, from which vendor, using which language?

And that's a rabbit hole worthy of its own article.

Coming next: the Java ecosystem, where the language is only the beginning of the confusion.

title: Top 10 PostgreSQL Production Outages & SRE Incident Troubleshooting Runbooks
description:
Top 10 PostgreSQL Production Outages & SRE Incident Troubleshooting Runbooks

Introduction

PostgreSQL is one of the most widely adopted open-source relational database systems, powering applications ranging from startups and SaaS platforms to large-scale enterprise infrastructure.

However, running PostgreSQL in production introduces challenges that go beyond writing SQL queries and designing database schemas.

A sudden database outage can cause application downtime, failed transactions, delayed background jobs, broken APIs, and even data loss. Sometimes, the database remains technically available but becomes so slow that applications experience timeouts and users cannot complete their operations.

For Site Reliability Engineers (SREs), Database Administrators (DBAs), and backend engineers, understanding how to identify, troubleshoot, and recover from PostgreSQL incidents is essential.

🚀 Keep Learning with DevsCampus

Technology evolves continuously, and staying updated with practical engineering knowledge is essential for every developer.

At DevsCampus, we publish technical articles, engineering tutorials, and learning resources covering PostgreSQL, Database Engineering, DevOps, Cloud Computing, System Design, Artificial Intelligence, and emerging technologies.

Whether you are a student preparing for a software engineering career or an experienced developer looking to strengthen your technical skills, DevsCampus helps you explore concepts, understand real-world engineering challenges, and keep up with the latest technology trends.

Explore these resources to continue learning:

  • PostgreSQL Engineering Articles – Explore PostgreSQL architecture, implementation, and production best practices.
  • SQL Learning Hub – Learn SQL, database design, indexing, query optimization, and production database engineering.

Visit DevsCampus.com to read more technical articles, explore practical tutorials, and stay updated with the latest developments in technology.

Now, let's explore the 10 most common PostgreSQL production outages, their root causes, and practical SRE troubleshooting runbooks that engineers can use to investigate and resolve real-world incidents.

Whether you manage PostgreSQL on Kubernetes, AWS RDS, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, or self-hosted Linux servers, these runbooks will help you respond to production incidents systematically.

1. PostgreSQL Connection Pool Exhaustion

Incident Scenario

Your application suddenly starts returning errors:

FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved
for non-replication superuser connections

Your API response times increase, background workers stop processing jobs, and new application connections fail.

Root Cause

PostgreSQL has a configured maximum number of concurrent connections.

The following configuration controls the connection limit:

SHOW max_connections;

Common causes include:

  • Application connection leaks.
  • Too many application instances.
  • Incorrect connection pool configuration.
  • Long-running transactions.
  • Background workers opening excessive connections.
  • Missing connection pooling.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Check active connections

SELECT
    state,
    COUNT(*)
FROM pg_stat_activity
GROUP BY state;

Step 2: Identify applications consuming connections

SELECT
    application_name,
    client_addr,
    state,
    COUNT(*) AS connections
FROM pg_stat_activity
GROUP BY application_name, client_addr, state
ORDER BY connections DESC;

Step 3: Identify long-running connections

SELECT
    pid,
    usename,
    application_name,
    state,
    now() - query_start AS duration,
    query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state <> 'idle'
ORDER BY duration DESC;

Step 4: Terminate confirmed problematic sessions

SELECT pg_terminate_backend(12345);

Replace 12345 with the actual process ID after verifying that terminating the session is safe.

Recovery Strategy

  • Configure connection pooling using PgBouncer.
  • Set appropriate application pool limits.
  • Implement connection timeouts.
  • Close unused connections.
  • Investigate connection leaks.
  • Monitor active connections against max_connections.

Production Prevention: Establish connection budgets across all application instances rather than allowing every service to independently consume the entire database connection limit.

Related Reading: Explore PostgreSQL engineering resources on DevsCampus to learn more about PostgreSQL architecture, connection management, and production database operations.

2. PostgreSQL High CPU Utilization

Incident Scenario

The PostgreSQL server suddenly reaches 95–100% CPU utilization.

Applications become slow, API requests time out, and database queries take significantly longer than usual.

Root Cause

High CPU utilization can result from:

  • Missing database indexes.
  • Expensive JOIN operations.
  • Inefficient SQL queries.
  • Large sequential scans.
  • Excessive concurrent queries.
  • Poor query execution plans.
  • Incorrect database statistics.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Identify expensive queries

SELECT
    pid,
    now() - query_start AS duration,
    state,
    query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'active'
ORDER BY duration DESC;

Step 2: Identify frequently executed expensive queries

If pg_stat_statements is enabled:

SELECT
    query,
    calls,
    total_exec_time,
    mean_exec_time,
    rows
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;

Step 3: Analyze the execution plan

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 1001;

Remember that EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query. Exercise caution with expensive queries and statements that modify data.

Step 4: Check server CPU usage

top

Or:

htop

Recovery Strategy

  • Identify and optimize expensive queries.
  • Add appropriate indexes.
  • Update database statistics using ANALYZE.
  • Reduce unnecessary query concurrency.
  • Review execution plans.
  • Consider read replicas for read-heavy workloads.

Production Prevention: Monitor query execution time, CPU utilization, and database workload continuously.

Related Reading: Learn how production database schemas influence query performance and scalability in Production Database Design on DevsCampus.

3. PostgreSQL Disk Space Exhaustion

Incident Scenario

Your application starts reporting database write failures:

ERROR: could not extend file
No space left on device

Insert and update operations begin failing. PostgreSQL may also experience problems writing WAL files or temporary query files.

Root Cause

Common causes include:

  • Rapid database growth.
  • Unbounded application logs.
  • Large temporary files.
  • WAL accumulation.
  • Failed replication slots retaining WAL.
  • Missing WAL archiving cleanup.
  • Large database indexes.
  • Long-running transactions preventing cleanup.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Check available disk space

df -h

Step 2: Identify large directories

sudo du -sh /var/lib/postgresql/*

Adjust the PostgreSQL data directory according to your installation.

Step 3: Check database sizes

SELECT
    datname,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_database_size(datname)) AS size
FROM pg_database
ORDER BY pg_database_size(datname) DESC;

Step 4: Check WAL directory size

sudo du -sh /var/lib/postgresql/*/pg_wal

Step 5: Check replication slots

SELECT
    slot_name,
    active,
    restart_lsn,
    pg_wal_lsn_diff(
        pg_current_wal_lsn(),
        restart_lsn
    ) AS retained_wal_bytes
FROM pg_replication_slots;

Recovery Strategy

  • Expand the underlying storage volume.
  • Investigate inactive replication slots.
  • Correct WAL archiving failures.
  • Review temporary file generation.
  • Remove only confirmed obsolete files through supported PostgreSQL maintenance procedures.
  • Implement database growth alerts.

Critical Warning: Never manually delete files from PostgreSQL's pg_wal directory. Doing so can cause database corruption or prevent PostgreSQL from starting.

Production Prevention: Configure disk usage alerts at 70%, 80%, and 90% capacity.

4. PostgreSQL Replication Lag

Incident Scenario

Your production application uses PostgreSQL primary-replica architecture.

The primary database processes writes successfully, but read replicas return outdated data.

Users update their profiles but continue seeing old information.

Root Cause

Replication lag can occur because of:

  • Network latency.
  • High write throughput.
  • Slow replica storage.
  • Long-running queries on replicas.
  • Replication conflicts.
  • Insufficient replica resources.
  • WAL receiver or replay delays.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Check replication status on the primary

SELECT
    application_name,
    client_addr,
    state,
    sync_state,
    write_lag,
    flush_lag,
    replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;

Step 2: Check replication status on the replica

SELECT
    pg_is_in_recovery(),
    pg_last_wal_receive_lsn(),
    pg_last_wal_replay_lsn();

Step 3: Calculate replay delay

SELECT
    now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp()
    AS replication_delay;

This timestamp-based calculation is most meaningful when the primary is actively committing transactions.

Recovery Strategy

  • Investigate network connectivity.
  • Increase replica compute and storage capacity where necessary.
  • Optimize queries running on replicas.
  • Investigate WAL receiver and replay activity.
  • Review replication configuration.
  • Temporarily route consistency-sensitive reads to the primary.

Production Prevention: Monitor replication lag and establish thresholds that trigger alerts before application consistency is affected.

5. PostgreSQL Deadlocks

Incident Scenario

Your application starts reporting transaction failures:

ERROR: deadlock detected
DETAIL: Process 1234 waits for ShareLock on transaction 5678

Multiple transactions are waiting for resources held by each other.

Root Cause

A deadlock occurs when two or more transactions wait indefinitely for locks held by one another.

Example:

Transaction A:

BEGIN;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 100
WHERE id = 1;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance + 100
WHERE id = 2;

COMMIT;

Transaction B:

BEGIN;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 50
WHERE id = 2;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance + 50
WHERE id = 1;

COMMIT;

Both transactions acquire locks in different orders, potentially creating a deadlock.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Inspect database locks

SELECT
    locktype,
    relation::regclass,
    mode,
    granted,
    pid
FROM pg_locks
ORDER BY pid;

Step 2: Identify blocked queries

SELECT
    pid,
    pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocking_pids,
    query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;

Step 3: Inspect PostgreSQL logs

Look for:

ERROR: deadlock detected

Recovery Strategy

  • Acquire database locks in a consistent order.
  • Keep transactions short.
  • Avoid unnecessary operations inside transactions.
  • Implement application-level transaction retries.
  • Review transaction isolation requirements.

Production Prevention: Enable appropriate deadlock logging and monitor deadlock frequency.

6. PostgreSQL Slow Queries and Query Timeouts

Incident Scenario

Your application starts experiencing intermittent API failures:

ERROR: canceling statement due to statement timeout

Some database queries take several seconds or even minutes to complete.

Root Cause

Common reasons include:

  • Missing indexes.
  • Inefficient joins.
  • Large table scans.
  • Outdated database statistics.
  • Lock contention.
  • Excessive sorting.
  • Poor pagination strategies.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Find long-running queries

SELECT
    pid,
    now() - query_start AS execution_time,
    wait_event_type,
    wait_event,
    query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'active'
ORDER BY execution_time DESC;

Step 2: Analyze query execution

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'PENDING';

Step 3: Check table statistics

SELECT
    relname,
    n_live_tup,
    n_dead_tup,
    last_analyze,
    last_autoanalyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables;

Step 4: Review timeout configuration

SHOW statement_timeout;
SHOW lock_timeout;
SHOW idle_in_transaction_session_timeout;

Recovery Strategy

  • Optimize problematic SQL.
  • Add appropriate indexes.
  • Review JOIN conditions.
  • Update statistics.
  • Investigate lock waits.
  • Apply sensible timeout limits.

Production Prevention: Use pg_stat_statements to identify queries with high total execution time and monitor query latency percentiles.

Related Reading: Learn more about production schema design, indexing considerations, and query scalability in Production Database Design – DevsCampus.

7. PostgreSQL Database Crash or Unexpected Restart

Incident Scenario

Your production application suddenly loses database connectivity.

Monitoring reports:

Connection refused

The PostgreSQL service is no longer accepting connections.

Root Cause

Possible causes include:

  • Operating system out-of-memory termination.
  • Hardware failures.
  • Storage problems.
  • PostgreSQL process crashes.
  • Invalid configuration changes.
  • Container or Kubernetes restarts.
  • Host-level resource exhaustion.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Check PostgreSQL service status

sudo systemctl status postgresql

Step 2: Inspect recent PostgreSQL logs

sudo journalctl -u postgresql \
    --since "30 minutes ago"

Depending on the distribution, PostgreSQL logs may also be available under:

/var/log/postgresql/

Step 3: Check memory utilization

free -h

Step 4: Check kernel OOM events

dmesg -T | grep -i -E 'oom|killed process'

Step 5: Check storage health

df -h

Recovery Strategy

  • Identify the actual crash reason before restarting repeatedly.
  • Verify storage availability.
  • Check memory and CPU pressure.
  • Review PostgreSQL recovery logs.
  • Restore service after confirming the underlying issue is resolved.
  • Validate application connectivity and transaction processing.

Production Prevention: Implement database health checks, infrastructure monitoring, automated backups, and tested recovery procedures.

8. PostgreSQL VACUUM Problems and Table Bloat

Incident Scenario

Your database size keeps increasing even though application data is not growing significantly.

Queries become slower, indexes grow larger, and disk utilization increases.

Root Cause

PostgreSQL uses MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) to manage concurrent transactions.

Updates and deletes create obsolete row versions that must eventually be cleaned up by VACUUM.

Table bloat can increase when:

  • Autovacuum is disabled or incorrectly configured.
  • Long-running transactions prevent cleanup.
  • High update/delete workloads generate dead tuples.
  • Autovacuum cannot keep up with table modifications.
  • Replication slots or standby feedback retain old row versions.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Identify tables with dead tuples

SELECT
    relname,
    n_live_tup,
    n_dead_tup,
    last_vacuum,
    last_autovacuum
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC
LIMIT 10;

Step 2: Inspect autovacuum configuration

SHOW autovacuum;
SHOW autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor;
SHOW autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor;

Step 3: Identify long-running transactions

SELECT
    pid,
    usename,
    state,
    now() - xact_start AS transaction_duration,
    query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY transaction_duration DESC;

Recovery Strategy

  • Investigate long-running transactions.
  • Ensure autovacuum is enabled.
  • Tune autovacuum for large and frequently updated tables.
  • Run targeted VACUUM operations where appropriate. 
VACUUM (ANALYZE) orders;

For severe table bloat, evaluate specialized maintenance approaches such as pg_repack, accounting for locking, disk-space, and operational requirements.

Production Prevention: Monitor dead tuples, autovacuum activity, transaction age, and table growth.

Related Reading: PostgreSQL maintenance is essential for preventing table bloat and keeping query performance stable. Explore Database Maintenance on DevsCampus to understand VACUUM, ANALYZE, index maintenance, and database statistics in greater detail.

9. PostgreSQL WAL Growth and Checkpoint Problems

Incident Scenario

Your database experiences increased disk utilization and write latency.

PostgreSQL logs contain messages related to checkpoints:

checkpoint starting: time
checkpoint complete

The WAL directory continues growing, and storage consumption becomes a concern.

Root Cause

Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) is essential for PostgreSQL durability and crash recovery.

WAL growth can result from:

  • High transaction volume.
  • Inactive replication slots.
  • WAL archiving failures.
  • Replication lag.
  • Long-running backups.
  • Incorrect WAL retention configuration.

Frequent checkpoints can also increase I/O pressure.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Check WAL configuration

SHOW wal_level;
SHOW max_wal_size;
SHOW min_wal_size;
SHOW checkpoint_timeout;
SHOW checkpoint_completion_target;

Step 2: Check replication slot retention

SELECT
    slot_name,
    active,
    restart_lsn,
    wal_status
FROM pg_replication_slots;

Step 3: Check archiver statistics

SELECT
    archived_count,
    failed_count,
    last_archived_wal,
    last_failed_wal,
    last_failed_time
FROM pg_stat_archiver;

Step 4: Review PostgreSQL logs

Search for:

checkpoints are occurring too frequently

Recovery Strategy

  • Fix WAL archiving failures.
  • Investigate inactive replication slots.
  • Tune checkpoint settings based on workload.
  • Ensure storage capacity is sufficient.
  • Review replication and backup configurations.

Production Prevention: Monitor WAL generation rate, retained WAL, checkpoint frequency, and archiving failures.

Important: Never delete WAL files manually to free disk space.

10. PostgreSQL Backup and Recovery Failure

Incident Scenario

A production database becomes corrupted or unavailable.

The SRE team attempts to restore the latest backup but discovers that the backup is incomplete, outdated, or unusable.

This is one of the most serious production incidents because it directly affects business continuity and data recovery.

Root Cause

Common reasons include:

  • Backup jobs silently failing.
  • Incorrect backup retention policies.
  • Missing WAL archives.
  • Unverified backup integrity.
  • Incomplete restore procedures.
  • Missing encryption keys.
  • Backups stored in the same failure domain as the database.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Check backup availability

For pg_dump backups:

ls -lh /backup/postgres/

Step 2: Create a logical backup

pg_dump -Fc -U postgres \
    -d production_db \
    -f production_db.dump

Step 3: Validate the dump archive

pg_restore -l production_db.dump

This checks whether the archive can be listed, but it does not prove that a complete restore will succeed.

Step 4: Restore into a separate database

createdb -U postgres recovery_test

pg_restore -U postgres \
    -d recovery_test \
    production_db.dump

Step 5: Validate restored data

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM important_table;

Compare the results against expected records and application-level consistency checks.

Recovery Strategy

  • Maintain automated database backups.
  • Use continuous WAL archiving for point-in-time recovery (PITR).
  • Store backups in a separate failure domain.
  • Define Recovery Point Objective (RPO) and Recovery Time Objective (RTO).
  • Perform regular restore drills.
  • Document disaster recovery procedures.

Production Prevention: A backup should never be considered reliable until a successful restore has been tested.

PostgreSQL SRE Incident Response: A Practical Framework

Knowing individual PostgreSQL failures is important, but production reliability requires a consistent incident response process.

SRE teams should follow a structured approach whenever a database outage occurs.

Step 1: Detect

Use monitoring and alerting tools to identify incidents before customers report them.

Monitor:

  • Database availability.
  • Active connections.
  • CPU utilization.
  • Memory utilization.
  • Disk utilization.
  • Query latency.
  • Replication lag.
  • WAL growth.
  • Deadlocks.
  • Database errors.

Step 2: Triage

Determine the impact and severity.

Ask:

  • Is the database completely unavailable?
  • Are writes failing or only reads?
  • Are all applications affected?
  • Is the problem isolated to one database or replica?
  • Is data integrity at risk?

Avoid making configuration changes before understanding the incident.

Step 3: Mitigate

Prioritize restoring critical application functionality.

Examples:

  • Terminate confirmed problematic sessions.
  • Route consistency-sensitive reads to the primary.
  • Scale infrastructure resources.
  • Reduce non-critical database workloads.
  • Restore available service capacity.

Always evaluate the impact of each mitigation action.

Step 4: Recover

After resolving the immediate issue:

  • Verify database health.
  • Validate application connectivity.
  • Test read and write operations.
  • Confirm replication health.
  • Check for data consistency issues.
  • Monitor the system for recurring failures.

Step 5: Conduct a Blameless Postmortem

Every major production incident should produce a postmortem.

A useful postmortem includes:

Section Description
Incident Summary What happened?
Timeline When did the incident begin and end?
Impact Which services and customers were affected?
Root Cause What technical condition caused the failure?
Detection How was the incident identified?
Resolution What actions restored service?
Prevention What engineering improvements are required?
Action Items Who owns each improvement and its deadline?

The goal is not to blame an engineer. The goal is to improve the system so the same failure is less likely to happen again.

Essential PostgreSQL Production Monitoring Metrics

A production-ready PostgreSQL environment should continuously monitor the following metrics.

Metric Why It Matters
Active Connections Detect connection exhaustion
CPU Utilization Identify expensive database workloads
Memory Utilization Detect memory pressure
Disk Utilization Prevent storage exhaustion
Query Execution Time Identify slow SQL
Replication Lag Detect replica synchronization problems
Deadlocks Identify transaction conflicts
Dead Tuples Detect vacuum-related issues
WAL Generation Monitor write workload and WAL growth
Checkpoint Frequency Identify excessive checkpoint activity
Transaction Age Detect long-running transactions
Backup Status Ensure recoverability

Recommended PostgreSQL Monitoring Tools

1. Prometheus and Grafana

Use Prometheus with PostgreSQL Exporter to collect database metrics and Grafana to build operational dashboards.

2. pg_stat_statements

A PostgreSQL extension that provides statistics about SQL query execution.

3. PgBouncer

A lightweight connection pooler that helps manage database connection overhead.

4. pgBadger

A PostgreSQL log analyzer that helps identify slow queries and database workload patterns.

5. Patroni

A high-availability solution for managing PostgreSQL clusters with automated failover capabilities.

Learn More: Production Database Monitoring

Monitoring is one of the most important responsibilities of an SRE team. Identifying performance degradation before it becomes a production outage requires more than checking whether a database is online.

Explore Production Database Monitoring on DevsCampus to understand:

  • Database latency and p99 query performance.
  • Active and available database connections.
  • Replication lag monitoring.
  • Cache and buffer hit ratios.
  • Lock waits and deadlock detection.
  • Table and index bloat monitoring.
  • Production database alerting strategies.

This learning resource complements the troubleshooting runbooks covered in this article.

PostgreSQL Production Readiness Checklist

Before deploying PostgreSQL into production, validate the following:

Availability

  • [ ] Configure appropriate connection pooling.
  • [ ] Implement database health checks.
  • [ ] Configure replication where required.
  • [ ] Define failover procedures.

Performance

  • [ ] Enable pg_stat_statements.
  • [ ] Monitor slow queries.
  • [ ] Review index usage.
  • [ ] Configure autovacuum appropriately.

Storage

  • [ ] Configure disk utilization alerts.
  • [ ] Monitor WAL growth.
  • [ ] Monitor replication slots.
  • [ ] Review backup retention policies.

Security

  • [ ] Use strong authentication.
  • [ ] Apply least-privilege database permissions.
  • [ ] Enable encrypted connections.
  • [ ] Store database credentials securely.
  • [ ] Audit privileged database access.

Disaster Recovery

  • [ ] Automate backups.
  • [ ] Configure point-in-time recovery where required.
  • [ ] Define RPO and RTO.
  • [ ] Perform regular restore tests.
  • [ ] Document disaster recovery runbooks.

Conclusion

PostgreSQL production outages are not always caused by database crashes. Many incidents originate from connection exhaustion, inefficient queries, storage pressure, replication lag, transaction conflicts, or inadequate backup strategies.

For SREs and database engineers, the ability to identify symptoms, investigate root causes, and execute safe recovery procedures is critical.

The ten incident scenarios covered in this guide provide a practical starting point for building reliable PostgreSQL operations.

However, production reliability is not achieved by troubleshooting incidents alone. It requires continuous monitoring, capacity planning, automation, tested disaster recovery procedures, and a culture of learning from failures.

Remember: A production-ready database is not simply one that runs without errors. It is one that can detect failures, recover safely, and maintain data integrity when things go wrong.

  2. Production Database Design – Understand database schema design, scalability, and production-ready architecture.

  3. Database Maintenance – Learn about VACUUM, ANALYZE, index maintenance, and database performance.

  4. Production Database Monitoring – Understand monitoring metrics, replication lag, query latency, and database observability.
