title: Understanding Goroutines and OS Threads in Go: Scheduling and Runtime Interactions Explained
description:
Introduction

Go’s concurrency model is a double-edged sword: its simplicity in spawning goroutines abstracts away the complexity of OS threads, but this abstraction often obscures critical runtime interactions. At the heart of this model lies the Go scheduler, a cooperative, preemptive system that multiplexes thousands of goroutines onto a handful of OS threads. This decoupling, managed by runtime abstractions like Ps (processors) and Ms (worker threads), enables lightweight concurrency but introduces subtle failure modes. For instance, a goroutine making a blocking syscall doesn’t just stall—it triggers a P handoff, where the scheduler reassigns the P to another M, ensuring other goroutines continue executing. This mechanism, while efficient, is often misunderstood, leading to deadlocks or goroutine leaks when developers misjudge blocking behavior or channel semantics.

The challenge deepens when considering GOMAXPROCS, the environment variable that caps the number of OS threads the Go runtime can use. This constraint, while optimizing resource usage, creates a bottleneck: if all threads are blocked (e.g., by syscalls), the scheduler’s ability to maintain concurrency collapses. Similarly, work stealing, a dynamic load-balancing mechanism, is not a silver bullet. Idle Ps steal goroutines from busy Ps, but this process is non-deterministic and depends on runtime heuristics, making it a common source of unfair scheduling if not understood properly. These edge cases—where abstraction meets reality—are where most developers stumble.

To bridge this gap, a step-through visualizer maps goroutine scheduling onto a timeline, treating each OS thread as a lane. This tool demystifies interactions like unbuffered vs buffered channels, where blocking behavior differs based on sender/receiver synchronization. For example, an unbuffered channel blocks both sender and receiver until both are ready, while a buffered channel only blocks the sender if the buffer is full. Such nuances are invisible in code but become obvious when visualized step by step. The tool also highlights deadlock scenarios, such as the “all goroutines are asleep” state, which arises from circular dependencies or unhandled blocking. By checking each scenario against a runnable Go program, the visualizer ensures accuracy, though it simplifies details like work stealing order and async preemption timing for clarity.

Without such insights, developers risk inefficient code, runtime errors, and debugging nightmares. For instance, a goroutine leak from an unreceived send is not just a memory issue—it’s a symptom of mismanaged concurrency. Similarly, assuming goroutine preemption is instantaneous (it’s not; it occurs at safe points like function calls) can lead to resource exhaustion. As Go’s popularity grows in concurrent and networked applications, understanding these mechanisms isn’t optional—it’s essential for writing performant, reliable, and maintainable code. The visualizer isn’t just a tool; it’s a lens into the runtime’s black box, turning abstract concepts into observable, actionable knowledge.

Goroutines vs. OS Threads: A Comparative Analysis

At the heart of Go’s concurrency model lies a fundamental distinction between goroutines and OS threads. Goroutines are lightweight, user-space threads managed entirely by the Go runtime, while OS threads are kernel-level entities managed by the operating system. This abstraction allows Go to multiplex thousands of goroutines onto a smaller set of OS threads, drastically reducing the overhead of context switching and memory consumption. The visualizer tool illustrates this by mapping goroutines onto OS thread lanes, revealing how the scheduler dynamically assigns work.

Creation and Management Mechanisms

Goroutines are created via the go keyword, which spawns a new coroutine with a minimal stack (starting at 2KB). The Go runtime manages these stacks dynamically, expanding or shrinking them as needed. In contrast, OS threads are created by the operating system, incurring significant overhead (e.g., stack allocation, kernel scheduling). The Go scheduler abstracts this complexity by multiplexing goroutines onto a fixed pool of OS threads, controlled by GOMAXPROCS. This pool is represented as Ps (processors), each bound to an OS thread (M). When a goroutine blocks (e.g., on a syscall), its P is handed off to another M, ensuring the OS thread remains utilized. This handoff mechanism is critical for maintaining concurrency, as demonstrated in the visualizer’s syscall scenario.

Scheduling and Context Switching

The Go scheduler employs a cooperative, preemptive model. Goroutines yield control at specific safe points (e.g., function calls, channel operations), allowing the scheduler to preempt them if they exceed their time slice. However, preemption is not instantaneous; it relies on runtime heuristics, which the visualizer simplifies for clarity. OS threads, on the other hand, are preempted by the kernel, which incurs higher latency. The scheduler’s work-stealing mechanism balances load by redistributing goroutines from busy Ps to idle ones. This dynamic process is non-deterministic, introducing the risk of unfair scheduling if certain goroutines dominate resources. The visualizer highlights this by showing goroutines migrating between Ps, but it abstracts the exact timing of work stealing for simplicity.

Blocking Behavior and Deadlocks

Blocking operations (e.g., syscalls, channel sends/receives) expose the interaction between goroutines and OS threads. When a goroutine blocks on a syscall, its P is handed off to another M, but the OS thread executing the syscall remains blocked. This can lead to resource exhaustion if GOMAXPROCS is too low and all threads are blocked. Channel operations introduce additional complexity: unbuffered channels block both sender and receiver until both are ready, while buffered channels block the sender only if the buffer is full. The visualizer’s deadlock scenarios (e.g., “all goroutines are asleep”) demonstrate how improper channel usage or circular dependencies can halt execution. These failures occur when goroutines are stuck in blocking states with no mechanism to unblock them.

Edge Cases and Failure Modes

Goroutine leaks often arise from unreceived sends, where a goroutine sends data on a channel that no receiver reads. This creates a dangling goroutine, consuming resources indefinitely. The visualizer explicitly shows these leaks, emphasizing the importance of proper channel management. Another edge case is simultaneous work stealing and preemption, where a goroutine is preempted while its P is being stolen. While rare, this scenario can lead to inefficient load distribution if not handled correctly. The visualizer simplifies preemption timing, but in reality, the runtime must ensure preemption occurs at safe points to avoid corruption.

Practical Insights and Decision Rules

  • If you observe high latency in a Go application, use the visualizer to check for goroutine blocking or unfair scheduling. Adjust GOMAXPROCS to match CPU cores, but avoid setting it too high, as this increases context-switching overhead.
  • If deadlocks occur, inspect channel operations for circular dependencies or unbuffered channels without receivers. Buffered channels can mitigate blocking but introduce buffer overflow risks.
  • If goroutine leaks are suspected, audit channel sends to ensure every send has a corresponding receiver. Tools like go tool pprof can identify leaking goroutines.

By understanding these mechanisms and leveraging the visualizer, developers can diagnose and resolve concurrency issues more effectively. The tool’s simplification of work stealing and preemption timing provides a clear, actionable view of scheduler behavior, bridging the gap between theory and practice.

Scheduling Dynamics: How Goroutines and Threads Interact

The Go scheduler operates as a cooperative, preemptive system, multiplexing thousands of goroutines onto a smaller set of OS threads. This abstraction reduces context-switching overhead and memory consumption, but it introduces complexities in how goroutines and threads interact. The visualizer tool maps these interactions onto a timeline, treating OS threads as lanes and goroutines as steps. Here’s how the mechanics break down:

1. Goroutine Scheduling Across Ps and Ms

Goroutines are scheduled onto Ps (processors), which are then assigned to Ms (worker threads). The number of Ms is capped by GOMAXPROCS, limiting the maximum number of OS threads. When a goroutine blocks (e.g., on a syscall), its P is handed off to another M, ensuring other goroutines continue executing. This handoff mechanism is critical for maintaining concurrency, but it introduces a risk: if all Ms are blocked, the program stalls. For example, if GOMAXPROCS=2 and both threads are blocked on syscalls, no goroutines can run until the OS unblocks a thread.

2. Multiplexing and Context Switching

The Go runtime multiplexes goroutines onto OS threads by context switching at safe points (e.g., function calls, channel operations). Unlike OS threads, goroutines are lightweight, starting with a 2KB stack that dynamically resizes. However, context switching is not free. Each switch involves updating the scheduler’s internal state, and frequent switches can degrade performance. The visualizer highlights this by showing goroutines jumping between OS thread lanes, revealing potential bottlenecks when goroutines are rescheduled too often.

3. Blocking Syscalls and P Handoff

When a goroutine makes a blocking syscall, its associated P is handed off to another M. This prevents the P from becoming idle, but the OS thread executing the syscall remains blocked. If GOMAXPROCS is too low, multiple blocking syscalls can exhaust available threads, stalling execution. For instance, in a scenario with GOMAXPROCS=4 and 5 concurrent blocking syscalls, one goroutine will be forced to wait until a thread becomes available. The visualizer demonstrates this by showing a goroutine’s lane freezing while its P moves to another lane.

4. Channel Operations and Deadlocks

Channels introduce blocking behavior that can lead to deadlocks. Unbuffered channels block both sender and receiver until both are ready, while buffered channels block the sender only if the buffer is full. A common deadlock scenario is the “all goroutines are asleep” state, where goroutines are stuck in blocking states due to circular dependencies. For example, if goroutine A sends to an unbuffered channel and goroutine B receives but never starts, both goroutines block indefinitely. The visualizer steps through these scenarios, showing how goroutines freeze in place, highlighting the causal chain of blocking operations.

5. Work Stealing and Load Balancing

The Go scheduler uses work stealing to balance load across Ps. When a P becomes idle, it steals goroutines from busy Ps. However, work stealing is non-deterministic, introducing the risk of unfair scheduling. For example, if a P consistently steals from the same busy P, some goroutines may be starved of CPU time. The visualizer simplifies work stealing order for clarity, but in reality, the mechanism depends on runtime heuristics. To mitigate unfair scheduling, developers should monitor goroutine latency and adjust GOMAXPROCS to match CPU cores.

6. Goroutine Leaks and Lifecycle Management

Goroutine leaks occur when a goroutine is launched but never terminates, often due to unreceived sends on channels. For example, if a goroutine sends to a channel but no receiver exists, the goroutine blocks indefinitely, consuming resources. The visualizer flags such leaks by showing dangling goroutines that never complete. To prevent leaks, developers should audit channel sends to ensure every send has a receiver and use tools like go tool pprof to identify orphaned goroutines.

Practical Insights and Decision Dominance

  • If you observe high latency in goroutine execution, use the visualizer to check for blocking syscalls or unfair scheduling. Adjust GOMAXPROCS to match CPU cores to reduce thread contention.
  • If deadlocks occur, inspect channel operations for circular dependencies or unbuffered channels without receivers. Buffered channels can mitigate blocking but introduce buffer overflow risks.
  • If goroutine leaks are suspected, audit channel sends to ensure every send has a receiver. Use go tool pprof to identify and eliminate orphaned goroutines.

By visualizing these interactions, developers can diagnose inefficiencies and edge cases, ensuring their Go applications are performant, reliable, and maintainable.

Case Studies: Real-World Scenarios and Visualizer Walkthroughs

To demystify the intricate dance between goroutines and OS threads in Go, we’ll dissect six real-world scenarios using the step-through visualizer. Each case is grounded in the analytical model of Go’s scheduling mechanisms, exposing causal chains and edge cases that developers often overlook.

1. Goroutine Multiplexing Across Ps and Ms: The Role of GOMAXPROCS

When GOMAXPROCS is set to 4, the visualizer shows four OS thread lanes (Ms) with goroutines multiplexed onto them via Ps. The causal chain is clear: GOMAXPROCS caps the number of Ms, and each P is assigned to an M. If all Ms are busy, new goroutines queue, even if CPUs are idle. This bottleneck arises because Ps cannot run without Ms, and the runtime doesn’t create additional Ms beyond GOMAXPROCS. Practical insight: Set GOMAXPROCS to match CPU cores to avoid underutilization, but beware of excessive context switching if goroutines outnumber cores.

2. Blocking Syscall and P Handoff: Keeping Concurrency Alive

A goroutine executing a blocking syscall (e.g., disk I/O) triggers a P handoff. The visualizer shows the blocked goroutine’s P moving to another M, allowing other goroutines to run. The mechanism is critical: Ps are decoupled from Ms, ensuring that a blocked syscall doesn’t stall the entire program. However, if all Ms are blocked (e.g., GOMAXPROCS=2 with 3 blocking syscalls), execution stalls. Edge case: Work stealing doesn’t occur during handoff, so load imbalance persists until the syscall completes. Rule: If blocking syscalls dominate, increase GOMAXPROCS, but monitor for thread exhaustion.

3. Unbuffered vs Buffered Channels: Blocking Behavior Decoded

Unbuffered channels block both sender and receiver until both are ready. The visualizer highlights this deadlock when a sender has no receiver. Buffered channels block only when full, but introduce buffer overflow risks. Causal logic: Unbuffered channels enforce synchronization, while buffered channels trade off latency for throughput. Practical insight: Use buffered channels for decoupled producers/consumers, but audit buffer sizes to prevent resource leaks. Edge case: A full buffer with no receiver leads to indefinite blocking, mimicking an unbuffered channel deadlock.

4. Goroutine Leak from Unreceived Sends: The Silent Resource Drain

A goroutine sending to a channel without a receiver leaks indefinitely. The visualizer shows the goroutine stuck in a send state, consuming stack and heap resources. Mechanism: The runtime doesn’t terminate goroutines blocked on sends, assuming a receiver will eventually appear. Practical insight: Always pair sends with receivers, and use go tool pprof to detect leaks. Edge case: Buffered channels mask leaks temporarily, but overflow still occurs if sends exceed buffer capacity.

5. “All Goroutines Are Asleep” Deadlock: Step-by-Step Breakdown

This deadlock occurs when all goroutines are blocked, often due to circular dependencies in channel operations. The visualizer shows all lanes idle, with goroutines stuck in send/receive states. Causal chain: No goroutine can proceed without another’s action, creating a stalemate. Practical insight: Inspect channel dependencies for cycles, and use buffered channels to break deadlocks. Edge case: Work stealing doesn’t resolve deadlocks, as no P has runnable goroutines.

6. Work Stealing and Unfair Scheduling: Dynamic Load Balancing Gone Wrong

Idle Ps steal goroutines from busy Ps, but this non-deterministic process risks unfair scheduling. The visualizer shows goroutines migrating between Ps, but some Ps remain underutilized. Mechanism: Work stealing prioritizes local queues, leading to starvation if a P’s queue is consistently empty. Practical insight: Adjust GOMAXPROCS to match CPU cores to minimize stealing overhead. Edge case: Simultaneous stealing and preemption can cause inefficient load distribution, as goroutines bounce between Ps. Rule: If latency spikes, check for unfair scheduling and redistribute work manually if necessary.

Each scenario underscores the importance of understanding Go’s scheduling abstractions. The visualizer bridges the gap between theory and practice, exposing mechanisms that are otherwise invisible. By analyzing these cases, developers can avoid common pitfalls and write code that leverages Go’s concurrency model effectively.

Conclusion and Best Practices

Understanding the intricate dance between goroutines and OS threads in Go is not just academic—it’s a practical necessity for writing efficient, scalable, and reliable code. The visual step-through tool for the Go scheduler demystifies this complexity by mapping goroutine scheduling onto a timeline, treating OS threads as lanes. This visualization bridges the gap between theory and practice, exposing otherwise invisible scheduling mechanisms. Here’s what you need to take away and apply:

Key Takeaways

  • Goroutine Multiplexing and GOMAXPROCS: Goroutines are multiplexed onto a fixed pool of OS threads (Ms), limited by GOMAXPROCS. If all Ms are busy, goroutines queue even if CPU cores are idle. Mechanism: Ps (processors) cannot run without Ms, leading to underutilization if GOMAXPROCS is too low. Rule: Set GOMAXPROCS to match CPU cores to avoid underutilization.
  • Blocking Syscalls and P Handoff: When a goroutine blocks on a syscall, its P is handed off to another M, ensuring concurrency. However, the OS thread remains blocked, risking thread exhaustion if GOMAXPROCS is too low. Mechanism: Blocking syscalls decouple Ps from Ms, but excessive blocking exhausts Ms. Rule: Increase GOMAXPROCS if blocking syscalls dominate your workload.
  • Channel Operations and Deadlocks: Unbuffered channels enforce synchronization but risk deadlocks if not paired with receivers. Buffered channels trade latency for throughput but introduce buffer overflow risks. Mechanism: Deadlocks arise from circular dependencies or unhandled blocking. Rule: Use buffered channels for decoupled producers/consumers, but audit buffer sizes to prevent overflow.
  • Goroutine Leaks: Unreceived sends on channels lead to indefinite blocking, consuming resources. Mechanism: The runtime doesn’t terminate blocked goroutines, assuming eventual receivers. Rule: Pair every send with a receiver. Use go tool pprof to detect leaks.
  • Work Stealing and Unfair Scheduling: Idle Ps steal goroutines from busy Ps, but this is non-deterministic, risking starvation. Mechanism: Local queue prioritization in work stealing can lead to inefficient load distribution. Rule: Adjust GOMAXPROCS to match CPU cores and monitor for unfair scheduling if latency spikes.

Practical Best Practices

Armed with these insights, here’s how to leverage the Go scheduler effectively:

  • Match GOMAXPROCS to CPU Cores: This ensures optimal utilization of OS threads without excessive context switching. Edge Case: If goroutines exceed cores, frequent context switches degrade performance.
  • Audit Channel Usage: Inspect channel operations for circular dependencies or unbuffered channels without receivers. Mechanism: Deadlocks occur when all goroutines are stuck in blocking states.
  • Profile for Leaks and Inefficiencies: Use go tool pprof to identify orphaned goroutines and inefficient scheduling. Mechanism: Leaks and unfair scheduling manifest as resource exhaustion and high latency.
  • Explore the Visualizer: The tool simplifies work stealing and preemption timing, making it easier to diagnose concurrency issues. Insight: Visualizing scheduling dynamics exposes patterns that logs or static analysis might miss.

Final Thoughts

The Go scheduler is a powerful abstraction, but its complexity demands a deep understanding to avoid pitfalls like deadlocks, leaks, and resource exhaustion. The visualizer is not just a learning tool—it’s a diagnostic instrument for real-world scenarios. By mastering these mechanisms and applying the best practices outlined above, you’ll write Go code that’s not only performant but also resilient and maintainable. Explore the visualizer further, experiment with edge cases, and share your findings—the Go community thrives on collective understanding.

What scheduler behavior would you want to see visualized next? The tool is free, open for suggestions, and ready to evolve.

title: What a tiny Django ticket taught me about open source
description:
Hi, I'm Stephen, a Djangonaut contributing to Django core. This was my second ticket, and it looked tiny: a one-line capitalization bug in makemessages. It turned into a lesson in code review, minimal diffs, and a lot of git 😂.

Here is the story.

The bug: a helpful message that gives wrong advice

Django's makemessages command extracts translatable strings into .po files, one folder per locale. If you pass a locale that doesn't exist, it tries to help by suggesting a valid one.

Here is what happened when you typed a script-based locale like Simplified Chinese:

$ python manage.py makemessages --locale zh-hans
invalid locale zh-hans, did you mean zh_HAns?

zh-hans is invalid because Django expects an underscore. But the suggestion, zh_HAns, is also invalid. The correct locale is zh_Hans.

The bug was reported on the Django forum and filed as ticket #36642.

Why it happened

Locales come in several shapes:

Locale Parts
de language
pt_BR language + region (2 letters)
en_001 language + numeric region
zh_Hans language + script (4 letters)
nl_NL-x-informal language + region + private use

The suggestion code split the input into a language and "everything after the separator", then assumed that part was a country code and uppercased its first two characters:

territory = (
    locale_parts["territory"][:2].upper()
    + locale_parts["territory"][2:]
)

That is right for pl_pl → pl_PL. For hans it gives HA + ns, which is HAns. The code was written for one locale shape and silently applied to all of them.

One constraint shaped everything: any fix had to leave validation alone. en_001 was valid before, and a fix that broke it would trade one bug for another.

Test first

Django's workflow is to write the test, watch it fail, then fix. My regression test copied the structure of the neighbouring test_invalid_locale_lower_country:

def test_invalid_locale_mixed_case_script(self):
    out = StringIO()
    management.call_command(
        "makemessages", locale=["zh-hans"], stdout=out, verbosity=1
    )
    self.assertIn("invalid locale zh-hans, did you mean zh_Hans?", out.getvalue())
    self.assertNotIn("processing locale zh-hans", out.getvalue())
    self.assertIs(Path("locale/zh-hans/LC_MESSAGES/django.po").exists(), False)

Before the fix, it failed exactly as the ticket described:

AssertionError: 'invalid locale zh-hans, did you mean zh_Hans?' not found in
'invalid locale zh-hans, did you mean zh_HAns?\n'

[Add your failing-test screenshot here]

The fix, three versions

Version 1: the first PR

My first PR looked locales up in Django's LANG_INFO dictionary. It fixed zh-hans, but en_001 stopped being recognized as valid. The reviewer, Jacob Walls, caught that regression. I left is_valid_locale() alone and changed only how the suggestion is formatted.

Version 2: format each subtag by type 

def format_subtag(m):
    subtag = m.group()
    if len(subtag) == 4:  # script, e.g. Hans
        return subtag.title()
    if len(subtag) == 2:  # region, e.g. CN
        return subtag.upper()
    return subtag

territory = re.sub(r"[a-zA-Z]+", format_subtag, territory) + x + private

Private-use parts like -x-informal were split off first with partition("-x-") so they stayed untouched.

Review: "Why special-case length 4?"

Jacob pointed out that another Chinese locale, zh-yue, has a three-letter subtag. A rule built on "scripts are 4 letters" was a guess. Only the 2-letter case needs upper(), so the helper and re.sub could go.

Version 3: the simple rule

Jacob suggested a simpler approach that handles only the 2-letter case. I made the change:

# Two-letter subtags are region codes (e.g. GB), which
# are uppercased. Others, such as scripts (e.g. Hans),
# are title-cased.
if len(territory) == 2:
    territory = territory.upper()
else:
    territory = territory.title()
proposed_locale = f"{language}_{territory}" + x + private
Input Suggestion
zh-hans zh_Hans
pl_pl pl_PL
en-001 en_001
nl-nl-x-informal nl_NL-x-informal

He also suggested .title() over slicing, and asked for a comment explaining why 2-letter strings are special. Both made the code easier for the next reader.

What I chose not to solve

zh_hans_cn still suggests zh_Hans_cn, which is invalid. Fixing it means deciding which subtag is a script, a region, or a variant, and without a length rule, that is guessing. Jacob said that coming back with "I explored it, but it's too error-prone" would also move the PR forward. Knowing when to stop was part of the fix.

The messy middle

The code took an afternoon. The git around it took longer 😂.

  • Old base: my branch was built on old code, so the diff against main listed hundreds of files. I backed it up with git branch backup, ran git reset --hard upstream/main, and re-applied only my changes by hand.
  • A file I overwrote: test_extraction.py had been replaced with an older copy, which reverted unrelated tests and triggered flake8 errors on lines I never touched. git diff revealed it.
  • Push rejected as "stale info": --force-with-lease had no record of the remote branch. git ls-remote --heads origin showed what was actually there.
  • Wrong remote: I once pointed upstream at my own fork instead of django/django.
  • A push that never landed: GitHub looked unchanged. Comparing git log with git log origin/<branch> showed the push had not gone through.
  • The PR bot: it failed my PR on an "Incomplete Checklist" because the boxes had lost their - [x] syntax when I copied the description.

Lessons for first-time contributors

  1. Keep diffs minimal. Reviewers notice whitespace and cosmetic changes.
  2. Verify, don't assume. Check git diff --stat, git log and the remote after every big step.
  3. Back up before destructive commands.
  4. Specific test names beat docstrings.
  5. Reviewers can give you a way out.
  6. Expect the workflow to take longer than the code.
  7. A small ticket is the best way to learn the whole process.

Thank you to Jacob Walls and Tim Schilling for the patient reviews.

Links

  • Trac ticket: https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/36642
  • Pull request: https://github.com/django/django/pull/19984
  • Django contributing guide: https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/dev/internals/contributing/

title: What Happens When Your Team Adds Azure to AWS and GCP
description:
It usually starts with one reason.

A new enterprise client requires Azure. Or the company gets acquired by a Microsoft shop. Or the data team wants Azure OpenAI Service. Or legal requires a specific Azure region for data residency. Whatever the trigger — it's never "let's add Azure because we wanted three clouds."

But the result is always the same: you now have a third cloud, and the operational complexity doesn't just add — it multiplies.

I've seen this happen at multiple companies — teams that had a reasonably clean AWS + GCP setup suddenly find themselves managing three credential models, three consoles, three billing dashboards, and databases spread across providers that have no awareness of each other.

Here's what actually happens, and what you can do about it.

The Azure Credential Model Is Different

AWS uses IAM roles and access keys. GCP uses service accounts with JSON key files. Azure uses something called service principals — identities registered in Azure Active Directory (now called Microsoft Entra ID) with roles assigned at the subscription or resource group level.

If your team already has muscle memory for aws configure and GCP service account JSON files, Azure will feel unfamiliar at first.

A minimal setup for database management looks like this:

# Create a service principal with Reader role on a resource group
az ad sp create-for-rbac \
  --name "1datacloud-reader" \
  --role Reader \
  --scopes /subscriptions/<subscription-id>/resourceGroups/<rg-name>

This gives you a clientId, clientSecret, tenantId, and subscriptionId — four values you'll need to authenticate against Azure APIs.

Compared to a GCP service account (one JSON file) or AWS IAM (access key + secret), it's more moving parts. And it's completely separate from the mental model your team already uses for the other two clouds.

The Azure Database Landscape

Before you can manage Azure databases, you need to know what Azure calls them.

Azure SQL Database — Microsoft's managed relational service. Similar to AWS RDS for SQL Server, but Azure-native. Good performance, tight Active Directory integration, T-SQL.

Azure Database for PostgreSQL — Flexible Server — Managed PostgreSQL. This is the one that matters most if your team is already on PostgreSQL on RDS or Cloud SQL. Flexible Server is the current generation (the old Single Server was deprecated in 2025).

Azure Database for MySQL — Flexible Server — Same generation shift. If you're migrating from RDS MySQL, this is the target.

Azure Cosmos DB — A globally distributed, multi-model NoSQL database. Supports multiple APIs: SQL (document), MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table. If your team uses DynamoDB on AWS, Cosmos DB is the Azure equivalent in terms of positioning.

Azure SQL Managed Instance — A deployment option that gives you a full SQL Server engine (including SQL Server Agent, cross-database queries, linked servers) rather than the PaaS-scoped Azure SQL Database. Useful for migrations from on-prem SQL Server.

Azure Synapse Analytics — Azure's answer to BigQuery and Redshift. Distributed SQL at scale, integrated with Azure Data Lake.

That's six different service types, each with its own API surface, pricing model, and management interface — before you've written a single query.

What Breaks First

1. Nobody knows what's running

With AWS and GCP, at least your team knows which console to open. With Azure added, there are now resources in Resource Manager that the DevOps team created, resources in the old Classic deployment model that nobody touches, and resources across multiple subscriptions that were set up at different times for different reasons.

Azure has resource groups as an organizing layer, but if your team didn't enforce naming conventions and resource group discipline from day one, you'll spend a lot of time clicking around the portal to understand what exists.

2. Schema awareness disappears

When a new database gets spun up on Azure — say, a PostgreSQL Flexible Server for a new product — it often happens outside the normal provisioning process. Someone clicks through the portal. It doesn't get added to the inventory spreadsheet. The team doesn't know its schema until someone asks "where does this data live?"

This is the same problem that exists on AWS and GCP, but Azure makes it worse because it's the new unknown. Your AWS and GCP databases are at least in the mental model of the team. The Azure ones aren't yet.

3. Credential rotation gets complicated

Now you have three sets of credentials to rotate on a schedule:

  • AWS: IAM access keys (or instance profiles if you're doing this right)
  • GCP: service account JSON keys
  • Azure: service principal secrets (which have an expiry date and will stop working when they expire)

Azure service principal secrets expire — the default is 1 year. If you don't have rotation automation in place, you'll get a failed deployment or a broken integration six months from now, traced back to an expired credential nobody remembered to rotate.

4. Monitoring is fragmented

Azure Monitor is its own ecosystem, completely separate from CloudWatch and Cloud Monitoring (GCP). Each provider has its own metrics, its own alerting primitives, its own cost of learning. Teams that didn't have unified observability before will feel this most acutely.

The Multi-Cloud Inventory Problem, Revisited

If you were managing AWS and GCP and already felt like you lacked a complete picture of your databases, adding Azure makes that problem structurally harder.

Every provider has native tooling that shows you that provider's resources only. No cross-cloud view exists unless you build it or use a tool designed for this.

With three providers, the options are:

  • Three console tabs always open
  • A custom aggregation script that you maintain (and that breaks when any provider updates its API)
  • A unified tool that connects to all three and maintains the view automatically

What Good Multi-Cloud Database Management Looks Like

The goal isn't to eliminate Azure's complexity — that complexity reflects real engineering tradeoffs. The goal is to not re-solve the same "where are my databases?" problem every time you add a provider.

A good multi-cloud database management setup:

  1. Connects to each provider once using that provider's native credential model (IAM for AWS, service account for GCP, service principal for Azure)
  2. Auto-discovers all instances across accounts, subscriptions, and projects — without you clicking through consoles
  3. Maintains schema metadata so you know not just that an instance exists, but what tables and columns are inside it
  4. Requires no agents or infrastructure changes — purely API-based, read-only by default

This is what 1DataCloud does. AWS, GCP, and MongoDB Atlas are fully supported today. Azure support is in active development — SQL Database, Cosmos DB, and PostgreSQL Flexible Server are coming. If you want to be notified when Azure goes live, sign up for the free tier and you'll get early access.

Practical Steps for Your Next 30 Days

If your team just added Azure (or is about to), here's a pragmatic checklist to avoid the worst outcomes:

Week 1 — Inventory what exists:

  • List all Azure subscriptions your organization has
  • List all resource groups with "sql", "db", "postgres", "mysql", "cosmos" in the name
  • For each: note engine type, region, size, who owns it

Week 2 — Tighten credential hygiene:

  • Create service principals with Reader role (not Contributor) for monitoring/inventory access
  • Set explicit expiry reminders for all Azure service principal secrets
  • Document where the credentials are stored (Key Vault, secrets manager, etc.)

Week 3 — Connect schema metadata:

  • For each database with real production data: connect and document the top-level schema (database names, table count)
  • Flag any instances that are publicly accessible (Azure portal → Networking → Public access)

Week 4 — Unify the view:

  • Either add Azure to your existing inventory tool, or start using a tool that handles all three providers together
  • Set a calendar reminder to verify the inventory is still accurate in 90 days

The Bigger Picture

Adding Azure isn't a mistake — for many teams it's the right call. Enterprise integrations, Microsoft ecosystem dependencies, data residency requirements, specific services like Azure OpenAI — these are real reasons.

But adding a cloud provider without a plan for managing what you deploy there is how you end up with databases nobody tracks, credentials that expire in production, and schema documentation that's six months out of date.

The teams that handle multi-cloud well aren't the ones that avoided complexity. They're the ones that decided early on how they were going to keep a complete picture of what they have.

Is your team running Azure alongside AWS or GCP? What's been the hardest part to manage? I'm particularly curious about organizations that migrated workloads TO Azure from another cloud — the other direction is less common.

Abd Alrhman Alloush is the Founder & CEO of 1DataCloud — a unified dashboard for managing and querying databases across AWS, GCP, and MongoDB Atlas, with Azure support in development.

title: Show an "update ready" banner in your Flutter app (OTA updates)
description:
When you ship over-the-air (OTA) updates to a Flutter app, the update downloads in the background and runs at the next launch. By default users see nothing, which is usually what you want.

But sometimes you do want to tell them, for example: "New update downloaded. Restart the app to apply it."

OverPush doesn't draw any UI itself. It sends events, and your app shows them in its own design. Here's a small banner you can drop into any app.

The events

OverPush.events is a stream. The ones you'll care about:

  • OverPushPatchFound: a new update exists
  • OverPushDownloading: download progress (percent, progress)
  • OverPushPatchReady: downloaded, will run at next launch
  • OverPushFailed: something went wrong; nothing changed on the device

The banner 

import 'dart:async';
import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:overpush/overpush.dart';

class UpdateBanner extends StatefulWidget {
  const UpdateBanner({super.key});

  @override
  State<UpdateBanner> createState() => _UpdateBannerState();
}

class _UpdateBannerState extends State<UpdateBanner> {
  StreamSubscription<OverPushEvent>? _subscription;
  Timer? _hideTimer;
  String? _message;

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    _subscription = OverPush.events.listen(_onEvent);
  }

  void _onEvent(OverPushEvent event) {
    _hideTimer?.cancel();
    switch (event) {
      case OverPushPatchFound():
        _show('New update found…');
      case OverPushDownloading(:final percent):
        _show(percent == null ? 'Downloading update…' : 'Downloading update · $percent%');
      case OverPushPatchReady():
        _show('Update downloaded. Restart the app to apply it.');
        _hideTimer = Timer(const Duration(seconds: 6), () => _show(null));
      case OverPushFailed():
        _show(null); // nothing changed; stay quiet
      default:
        break;
    }
  }

  void _show(String? message) {
    if (mounted) setState(() => _message = message);
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _subscription?.cancel();
    _hideTimer?.cancel();
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final message = _message;
    return Positioned(
      left: 16,
      right: 16,
      bottom: MediaQuery.paddingOf(context).bottom + 24,
      child: IgnorePointer(
        child: AnimatedSwitcher(
          duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 250),
          child: message == null
              ? const SizedBox.shrink()
              : Material(
                  key: const ValueKey('update-banner'),
                  color: const Color(0xFF1F2430),
                  borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(12),
                  elevation: 6,
                  child: Padding(
                    padding: const EdgeInsets.all(14),
                    child: Text(
                      message,
                      style: const TextStyle(color: Colors.white, fontWeight: FontWeight.w600),
                    ),
                  ),
                ),
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

Put it above your app 

MaterialApp(
  builder: (context, child) => Stack(
    children: [child!, const UpdateBanner()],
  ),
  home: const HomePage(),
);

That's it. It's your own widget, so restyle it however you like: a snackbar, a dialog with a "Restart now" button, or a small dot in the settings screen.

Try it

  • Getting started: https://docs.overpush.in/getting-started.html
  • Full banner with a progress bar: https://docs.overpush.in/update-ui.html
  • https://overpush.in (free for 5,000 patch installs a month)

title: Database Schema Drift: Why Your Docs Are Always Wrong
description:
Somewhere in your company there's a schema diagram. Maybe it's an ERD in Confluence, a .sql file someone exported two migrations ago, or a wiki page titled "Database Structure" that hasn't been opened since the person who wrote it left. It was accurate once. It almost certainly isn't now.

This is schema drift: the gap between what your documentation says a database looks like and what it actually looks like. Every team has it. Almost nobody tracks it, because tracking it manually means someone re-documenting the schema by hand every time a column gets added, a table gets renamed, or a migration quietly ships without an announcement.

TL;DR

Schema documentation goes stale the moment a migration ships, because nothing in a normal deploy workflow touches the wiki. 1DataCloud sidesteps that by reading schema — tables, columns, types, relationships — directly from the connected database each time it syncs, across AWS, GCP, MongoDB Atlas, and on-prem MySQL/PostgreSQL/MariaDB. Try it free →

Why Schema Docs Go Stale the Moment They're Written

Migrations don't update the wiki. A column gets added in a migration file, the PR merges, the deploy goes out — and the ERD nobody opens stays exactly as it was. Nothing in that workflow touches documentation, because documentation isn't part of the deploy.

Tribal knowledge fills the gap, badly. When the docs are wrong, people stop trusting them and start asking around instead. "Does users still have that legacy_status column?" becomes a Slack message to whoever's been around longest, not a doc lookup.

Nobody owns keeping it current. Schema documentation is everyone's responsibility in theory and nobody's job in practice. It gets written once, usually during onboarding or an audit, and then drifts for months or years.

The bigger the team, the worse it gets. A two-person startup can mostly keep a schema in their heads. A team running a dozen services against a shared database, or a company with instances scattered across AWS, GCP, and MongoDB Atlas, can't — and that's exactly when stale docs start costing real time.

What Actually Fixes This

The fix isn't "document better" — better documentation still goes stale the next time someone ships a migration. The fix is not relying on a written document at all for the one thing that changes constantly: what the schema actually is right now.

That's the problem 1DataCloud's schema mapping solves. When you connect a database — AWS RDS or Aurora, GCP Cloud SQL or Spanner, MongoDB Atlas, or an on-premise MySQL, PostgreSQL, or MariaDB instance — the Unified Dashboard reads the real table names, column names, data types, and relationships directly from the database itself. Not from a doc someone wrote. From the schema as it exists.

How this stays accurate

To be precise about the mechanism: this isn't a live change-detection system watching for schema edits and alerting you when something changes. It's simpler than that — each time a database is synced, what you see reflects what's actually in the database at that moment, because it was just read from the source instead of pulled from a document. Re-sync, and you're looking at the current structure, not whatever was true when someone last updated a wiki page.

Why this matters for natural-language querying specifically

Schema accuracy isn't just a documentation nicety — it's the difference between a natural-language query tool that works and one that quietly gives wrong answers. Query1AI turns a plain-English question into SQL using the schema metadata the Unified Dashboard has mapped. If that schema map were based on a six-month-old doc, a column rename or a dropped table would mean Query1AI either fails outright or — worse — generates a query against a structure that no longer matches reality.

Because it works from schema read directly off the connected database, a question like "how many orders shipped last week" gets translated against the tables and columns that exist today, not the ones that existed when someone last wrote things down.

Where This Shows Up in Practice

Onboarding a new engineer. Instead of a stale ERD and a round of "ask Dave," a new hire opens the dashboard and sees the actual current schema for every connected database — tables, columns, types, relationships.

Debugging a query that used to work. When a column gets renamed or a table gets dropped, the documentation doesn't know. The dashboard does, because it reads the schema fresh rather than relying on anything written down.

Handing a database off between teams. Transferring ownership usually means transferring tribal knowledge along with it. A schema that's mapped directly from the source doesn't depend on whoever's leaving remembering to write it all down first.

Reviewing what's actually in a database before an audit. Instead of trusting a document that might be a year old, the current table and column structure is what's shown — because it's read from the database, not transcribed from someone's notes.

What This Isn't

Worth being precise here: this is schema mapping, not schema monitoring. It doesn't watch your database in real time, diff versions against each other, or alert you the moment a migration runs. It reads the current structure when a database is connected or re-synced. If you need a system that flags every schema change the instant it happens, that's a different kind of tool — what 1DataCloud gives you is confidence that what you're looking at, whenever you look, is real.

Summary

Schema documentation is wrong the moment it's written, because nothing in a normal deploy process updates it. The alternative isn't a better doc — it's not needing one for structural facts at all. Reading schema directly from the database, on every sync, means what you see is what's actually there, and it's also what powers accurate natural-language querying through Query1AI.

title: Cloud Storage vs Physical Hard Drives: Which One Is Safer for You?
description:
Cloud storage and physical hard drives both keep your files safe — but in very different ways. Hard drives are fast, cheap, and fully in your control, while the cloud keeps your files backed up and reachable from anywhere. The safest setup is both: follow the 3-2-1 rule, with three copies of your files, on two different kinds of storage, and one copy off-site.

Read the full post on GridDigest: https://griddigest.blogspot.com/2026/11/cloud-storage-vs-physical-hard-drives.html

title: Understanding AI: The Fundamentals Finally Make Sense When You See How They Connect
description:
Artificial Intelligence can feel complicated when you encounter terms like tokens, embeddings, attention, transformers, fine-tuning, RAG, and AI agents.

But these concepts are not isolated technologies. They are building blocks that solve specific problems, one after another.

The easiest way to understand modern AI is to follow the journey of how a computer goes from processing ordinary text to understanding context, generating responses, retrieving information, and eventually taking action.

Let's break it down.

1. Tokens: Teaching Computers to Read Text

You want a computer to understand text. The problem is that computers fundamentally process numerical representations, not words the way humans do.

So, how do you make text readable to a machine?

You use tokens.

A tokenizer breaks text into smaller pieces called tokens. These can be whole words, parts of words, or even individual characters.

For example, "Unbelievable" might be split into:

  • Un
  • believ
  • able

Each token is assigned a numerical ID.

Now the computer has a numerical representation of the text it needs to process.

But there is a problem. Those numbers are simply identifiers. They don't inherently communicate meaning.

The token for "dog" could be 4521, while "puppy" could be 9873. Nothing about those numbers tells the computer that the two words are related.

2. Embeddings: Giving Numbers Meaning

This is where embeddings come in.

Instead of representing each token with a single numerical ID, embeddings transform tokens into vectors: lists of numbers that capture aspects of their meaning and relationships.

Words with similar meanings tend to have similar vector representations.

For example:

  • Dog and puppy are semantically related.
  • King and queen have a meaningful relationship.
  • Dog and Paris are generally unrelated.

These relationships can be represented geometrically in a high-dimensional space.

Now the computer has more than numerical labels. It has numerical representations that carry semantic information.

But another problem emerges.

A word can have different meanings depending on the sentence in which it appears.

Consider the word "bank":

  • I deposited money at the bank.
  • We sat beside the river bank.

The word is identical, but the meaning is different.

Embeddings alone do not fully resolve this contextual ambiguity.

3. Attention: Understanding Context

This is where attention mechanisms become important.

Attention allows a model to examine relationships between tokens and determine which other tokens are relevant when interpreting a particular token.

Consider:

"The man deposited money at the bank."

The model can use the surrounding words, particularly "deposited" and "money", to understand the intended meaning of "bank".

In the sentence:

"The fisherman sat beside the bank."

The surrounding context points towards a riverbank.

The model is no longer treating every word as an isolated piece of information. It can consider how words relate to one another.

This mechanism is central to the Transformer architecture, which powers most modern large language models.

But having the architecture does not automatically mean the model knows anything useful.

Where does its knowledge come from?

4. Training: Learning Patterns from Data

This is where training comes in.

A language model is exposed to enormous amounts of text and learns through an objective that, in its simplest form, involves predicting the next token.

For example:

"The capital of France is..."

The model learns to assign probabilities to possible next tokens, with "Paris" being a highly likely continuation.

Whenever its predictions differ from the training target, the model's parameters are adjusted through an optimization process called gradient descent, using backpropagation to calculate how those parameters should change.

These parameters are commonly called weights.

After processing vast amounts of training data, the model learns patterns involving language, grammar, information, relationships, and problem-solving.

However, a model trained primarily to predict the next token is not automatically a helpful conversational assistant.

Ask it a question, and it might simply continue generating text rather than answering in the way you expect.

How do we change that?

5. Fine-Tuning: Turning a Language Model into an Assistant

This is where fine-tuning comes in.

The model undergoes additional training using carefully prepared examples that demonstrate desirable behaviours.

For example:

  • User asks a question.
  • Assistant provides a useful answer.
  • User requests an explanation.
  • Assistant explains step by step.
  • User provides an instruction.
  • Assistant follows the instruction.

Instruction fine-tuning helps the model learn how to respond to requests rather than simply continue arbitrary text.

Other alignment techniques, including preference optimization and reinforcement learning, can further improve how the model responds.

The result is a model that behaves much more like an assistant.

But there is still another consideration.

How predictable or creative should its responses be?

6. Temperature: Controlling Randomness in Responses

This is where temperature comes in.

Temperature influences how the model samples from the probability distribution of possible next tokens.

A lower temperature generally makes the model more predictable, favouring higher-probability choices.

A higher temperature makes less likely alternatives more competitive, increasing variation and randomness.

Think about the practical applications:

  • Code generation: Lower temperature can help produce more consistent outputs.
  • Factual explanations: Lower temperature can improve predictability, although it does not guarantee accuracy.
  • Brainstorming: Higher temperature can encourage more varied ideas.
  • Creative writing: Higher temperature can introduce more stylistic diversity.

Temperature does not make a model more intelligent. It changes how it selects its responses.

Now imagine giving the model a 500-page company policy document and asking it a question about page 400.

Or imagine having a conversation that runs for hours.

Why might the model fail to remember information from earlier in the conversation?

7. Context Window: The Model's Working Space

This is where the context window comes in.

A context window defines how much information a model can process at once.

It can include:

  • Your current message.
  • Previous conversation messages.
  • System instructions.
  • Retrieved documents.
  • Tool outputs.

If the information exceeds the available context, some content may need to be removed, truncated, or summarized.

This is why even powerful models can struggle with very long conversations or large documents.

The context window is not the same as permanent memory. It is the information available to the model during a particular processing operation.

Now consider another problem.

You ask an AI assistant about your company's internal HR policies, but those documents were never included in its training data.

How can it answer accurately?

Sometimes it cannot. Worse, it may generate an answer that sounds convincing but is completely incorrect.

8. Hallucinations: When AI Sounds Confident but Is Wrong

This behaviour is commonly called hallucination.

A language model generates responses based on learned patterns and the information available in its context.

It does not automatically verify every statement against an authoritative source.

For example, ask it about an internal company policy it has never seen. It might generate a plausible answer based on general knowledge, even though that answer has nothing to do with your actual company policy.

It is not necessarily deliberately misleading you.

It is generating a likely response without sufficient grounding.

So, how do we connect language models to information they were not trained on?

9. RAG: Giving AI Access to External Knowledge

This is where Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) comes in.

Instead of expecting the model to remember everything, you build a system that retrieves relevant information before the model generates its response.

A simplified RAG workflow looks like this:

  1. Documents are collected from sources such as SharePoint, databases, PDFs, and internal systems.
  2. Documents are divided into smaller chunks.
  3. The chunks are converted into embeddings.
  4. The embeddings are stored in a vector database or another retrieval system.
  5. When a user asks a question, the system searches for relevant content.
  6. The retrieved content is added to the model's context.
  7. The model generates an answer using that information.

Think of it as an open-book examination rather than a memory test.

For example, an employee asks:

"What is our company's maternity leave policy?"

Instead of guessing, the system retrieves the relevant section from the actual HR policy and provides an answer based on it.

RAG improves grounding, but it does not guarantee correctness. Retrieval quality, document freshness, permissions, and answer verification still matter.

But there is another limitation.

The model can retrieve information and generate responses, but can it actually do something?

Can it query a database, check a server, send an email, or create a support ticket?

Not without additional capabilities.

10. Tools and Function Calling: Giving AI the Ability to Act

This is where tool calling comes in.

You give the model access to predefined tools that allow it to interact with external systems.

For example:

  • A database query tool.
  • An email-sending tool.
  • A ticket creation API.
  • A weather API.
  • A payment status verification API.
  • A SharePoint document search tool.

The model can determine when a tool is needed, generate the required arguments, and request its execution.

The application executes the tool, returns the result, and the model uses that result to decide what to do next.

For example:

User: "Check whether payment transaction TXN123 was successful."

The AI could:

  1. Identify that it needs payment information.
  2. Call the payment verification API.
  3. Receive the transaction status.
  4. Interpret the response.
  5. Tell the user whether the payment succeeded.

Notice the distinction: the model does not magically access your payment system. Your application provides the integration and controls what the model is allowed to do.

And this brings us to one of the most talked-about concepts in AI today.

11. AI Agents: Bringing Everything Together

An AI agent combines a language model with tools, instructions, context, and a process for taking actions towards a goal.

Unlike a traditional chatbot that primarily responds to messages, an agent can work through a sequence of steps.

Imagine an AI agent responsible for handling customer support requests.

A customer reports a failed payment.

The agent could:

  1. Understand the customer's request.
  2. Retrieve the customer's relevant information.
  3. Check the payment transaction through an API.
  4. Investigate the transaction status.
  5. Determine whether escalation is necessary.
  6. Create a support ticket.
  7. Notify the customer.
  8. Record the outcome.

It can use the results of one action to determine its next action.

That is the difference between simply generating a response and completing a task.

Of course, agents still need guardrails, permissions, monitoring, and human approval for sensitive operations. More autonomy does not automatically mean better outcomes.

The Bigger Picture: How Everything Connects

Look at the progression:

Concept The problem it solves
Tokens Converts text into processable units
Embeddings Represents semantic meaning numerically
Attention Helps interpret relationships and context
Training Learns patterns from data
Fine-tuning Adapts the model to desired behaviours
Temperature Controls randomness in generation
Context window Defines the information available at once
Hallucination Describes unsupported or incorrect generation
RAG Retrieves external knowledge to ground responses
Tool calling Connects the model to external capabilities
AI agents Orchestrates reasoning and actions towards goals

The important thing to understand is that these concepts are not competing technologies. They solve different problems and often work together.

You do not need to understand every mathematical detail before building useful AI solutions.

But you should understand what each component does, why it exists, and when to use it.

Because building AI applications is not simply about connecting an API to ChatGPT or prompting a model to generate something.

It is about understanding the entire system around the model: data, retrieval, context, integrations, permissions, orchestration, and execution.

The real opportunity in AI engineering is not just building systems that can talk. It is building systems that can understand business problems, access the right information, make informed decisions, and safely get work done.

title: Syncing Inventory Across Multiple Shopify Locations Without Overselling
description:
Syncing Inventory Across Multiple Shopify Locations Without Overselling

The moment a product sells across more than one location or channel, inventory sync stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the thing standing between you and an oversold order you have to apologize for.

⚡ The Actual Race Condition

Two orders for the last unit arriving within milliseconds of each other, from two different channels, is the scenario that breaks naive sync logic. Whichever system checks available inventory a moment too late sells a unit that's already gone.

🔒 The Reservation Pattern That Fixes It

Inventory needs to be reserved at the moment of checkout initiation, not just decremented after payment succeeds — a short-lived hold that releases automatically if checkout isn't completed within a few minutes. This closes the race window that a simple decrement-on-sale approach leaves open.

📊 Buffer Stock Is a Pragmatic Backstop

Even with good reservation logic, keeping a small safety buffer (2-3 units reported as unavailable before true zero) absorbs sync-delay edge cases across third-party channels that don't support real-time reservation at all, like some marketplace integrations.

Originally published on the KLYX blog.

title: I wanted backups on a VPS I rent, not another Dropbox subscription
description:
Most people need a backup. The usual choices feel bad: a monthly fee to keep files on someone else's computers, "pro" backup software with schedules that are easy to set up wrong, or a USB drive you forget until the day you need it.

I wanted something in the middle — a small always-on computer I rent (a VPS), almost no setup, and defaults that back up the folders I'd miss. That's OpenBackup.

What you get

  • Automatic backups of Documents, Pictures, Videos, Music, Desktop (and folders you add)
  • Only changed pieces of files are uploaded, so daily runs stay light
  • History — restore yesterday's version, or last week's
  • A dashboard in the browser to see devices and download a file or folder as a ZIP
  • An optional desktop app if you prefer buttons over a terminal
  • Optional encryption, so even the server can't read the files (you keep a recovery code)
  • Agents for Windows, macOS and Linux

It does not try to clone your whole OS install. It backs up your files. System folders, trash, caches, node_modules, build output and huge VM images are skipped on purpose.

Android is not ready yet.

Install in four steps

1. Put the server on a VPS (Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04 is easiest):

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/foisalislambd/openbackup/main/scripts/install-server.sh | sudo sh

It prints a web address like http://YOUR_IP:18200 plus a sign-in email and password. Open that, sign in, change the password. Prefer reading the script first if you don't like piping to sh — it's in the repo at scripts/install-server.sh.

2. Create a connection code in the dashboard under Devices. It looks like ABCD-EFGH-JKLM, works once, expires in 24 hours.

3. Connect each computer

  • Windows: download the desktop installer from Releases
  • Mac / Linux: 
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/foisalislambd/openbackup/main/scripts/install-agent.sh | sh
openbackup connect --server http://YOUR_IP:18200 --code ABCD-EFGH-JKLM

Use HTTPS for real use — the install-server docs cover that.

4. Check

openbackup status
openbackup doctor

Then restore one file while nothing is broken, so you know how when you need it.

Everyday commands (optional)

The background service keeps working without you. Handy when you want control:

openbackup backup
openbackup folders
openbackup folders add ~/Projects
openbackup pause --for 2h
openbackup find "tax return"
openbackup restore --path Documents/report.docx --to .

Encryption 

openbackup encrypt

You'll get a recovery code. Write it down somewhere safe that is not only on that same computer. Lose the code and those encrypted backups can't be opened. There is no "reset password" on the server side — that's the point.

Status and license

Server, agent, dashboard and desktop app work end to end. Current release is v0.2.9. Until 1.0, treat minor versions as able to change the wire protocol — upgrade the server before the agents. MIT. Repo: github.com/foisalislambd/openbackup.

Disk on the VPS matters more than CPU. The README's tip is that many people run this on a roughly €4–6/month plan. prices change; pick a plan with enough disk for your photos and video.

If you try it, I'd like to hear where the defaults were wrong for your machine, and whether the connection-code flow felt clear. Issues and discussions are open on GitHub.

— foisal

title: How a Daily Silver Benchmark Is Computed (And Why Unit Conversion Is the Hard Part)
description:
A daily metal "rate" looks like one number on a page. Under the hood it is a small data pipeline, and in my experience most of the bugs are not in the fetch step. They are in the units.

This is a purely methodological note. I am not quoting any live prices, tax rates or dealer margins here, because those change and are exactly the parts people copy-paste without checking.

Start from one fixing, not from a scraped list

The cleanest design is to pick a single authoritative wholesale fixing for a defined fineness, in a defined unit, for a defined trading day. Everything else on the page is derived from that one value.

If you instead scrape several "silver price today" widgets and average them, you have silently mixed:

  • different fineness assumptions,
  • different units (per gram vs per 10 grams vs per kilogram),
  • wholesale versus retail quotes,
  • and different as-of dates.

You cannot reconcile those after the fact. Pick one input, document it, and derive.

The conversion table is the real schema

Once the base is fixed, the derived numbers are arithmetic. A useful mental model is to treat every published figure as a row with four columns: unit, fineness, quote type, as-of date.

For a base expressed per kilogram of 999 fine metal:

Published unit Divisor from the base
per 100 grams 10
per 10 grams 100
per gram 1000
per tola 1000 / grams-per-tola

Two traps worth writing tests for:

  1. Fineness is a multiplier, not a new source. 925 and 999 describe the metal content of an object, not a different market price. Applying the fineness fraction to a number that is already retail-quoted double counts it.
  2. Making charges are not part of the metal. A jewellery bill contains a craftsmanship component that resale usually does not return. If you fold that into a "price per gram" and then compare it with a wholesale fixing, the comparison is meaningless.

So the invariant to assert in code is boring but effective: per_kg == per_g * 1000 == per_10g * 100, and every derived row must carry the same as-of date as its source.

Why a retail quote never equals the benchmark

Readers often treat the difference as an error. It is not. A retail quote can legitimately include a dealer premium, a making charge, applicable tax, and a buyback policy that prices the same object differently on the way out. A benchmark is a reference for the metal content, not a price you can transact at.

That distinction belongs in the UI, not in a footnote. The most useful thing a price page can show is the basis of each number it prints: what unit, what fineness, what quote type, what date.

Data quality problems that actually bite

  • Trading day vs calendar day. A fixing published on Monday may be Friday's session after a holiday. Store both the publication date and the reference date.
  • AM vs PM sessions. Some sources publish more than one fixing per day. If you pick one, record which one; if you switch, you have silently changed the series.
  • Time zones. "Today" in the source's locale is not "today" for the reader. Normalise to a single zone before generating slugs or filenames.
  • Caching and staleness. A cached HTML widget can look perfectly valid and be a day old. Persist the fetched timestamp next to the value, and refuse to render if it is older than your threshold.
  • Anti-bot responses. A 403 is not a missing price. Treat "blocked" as a distinct state from "no data", because retrying a blocked fetch with a different parser will not help.
  • Silent unit changes upstream. If a source switches from per-kilogram to per-10-grams, an unconverted pipeline will happily publish a number 100× too small. Assert plausible ranges.

A small validation checklist

  • One documented base source, one fineness, one unit, one as-of date.
  • Derived values recomputed from the base, never re-scraped.
  • Unit-consistency assertions in the build step.
  • Explicit separation of benchmark, spot-derived conversion, and retail quote.
  • Reference date displayed next to every table, not just in the page footer.
  • A visible "no current data" state instead of a stale number.

None of this is glamorous, but it is the difference between a page that survives an audit and one that quietly publishes the wrong number for weeks.

Wrapping up

If you maintain any kind of daily price or rate page, the highest-value work is almost never adding another source. It is making the units, the fineness and the as-of date impossible to misunderstand — for the reader and for your own future self.

General methodology notes, not financial, tax or purchase advice. Rules and costs change; verify against primary source documents before relying on any figure.

Further reading

If you want to see these ideas applied to a live data page, the data methodology page for India's daily silver benchmark documents the base source, reference dates and unit conversions, and the per-gram, 10-gram and 1kg explainer shows the arithmetic without any live rate assumptions.

title: I got tired of pasting API keys into every coding agent, so I built a local router
description:
You open Cursor and paste an OpenAI key. Then Claude Code wants Anthropic. OpenCode wants something else. Switch models for a week and you're editing three config files and hoping you didn't leave a key in a screenshot.

I wanted one address on my own machine that every OpenAI-compatible client could talk to, with the provider keys staying on disk. That's WowRouter.

What it actually is

WowRouter is a local AI router. It listens only on this computer:

What Address
Web panel http://127.0.0.1:8787
OpenAI-compatible API http://127.0.0.1:8787/v1

You add provider keys in the panel, turn models on, create a router key (shown once, starts with sk-airoute-), and point Cursor or any OpenAI client at that base URL with the router key.

A public model id looks like openai/gpt-4o-mini. You can also set the model to auto (or auto/cheap, auto/fast, auto/coding) and let the router pick among the chat models you turned on. Named combos use ids like fallback/daily and fall through when a model fails.

Provider keys are encrypted with a local secret. Router keys are stored as hashes — the panel cannot show a router key again after you leave the create screen. The server rejects a listen address that isn't loopback (127.0.0.1, localhost, or ::1).

Install

Node.js 20 or newer:

npm install -g wowrouter
wowrouter

npm install -g airoute is the same program. Desktop builds for Windows, macOS and Linux are attached to each GitHub release. Docker works too, still bound to this computer:

docker run -d --name wowrouter \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8787:8787 \
  -v wowrouter:/data \
  foisalislambd/wowrouter:latest

First setup

  1. Open the panel.
  2. Providers — save an API key (GitHub Enterprise Copilot uses Sign in with GitHub; Copilot Web asks for a bearer token). Rows marked Unsupported have no stable API.
  3. Turn on the models you want. A model that is off is not offered to clients.
  4. API keys — create a router key.
  5. In Cursor (or any OpenAI client): base URL http://127.0.0.1:8787/v1, API key = that router key.

Chat calls need three things at once: a saved provider key, the model switched on, and a router key on the request. Password / OIDC on the panel are off by default. Leave them off on your own computer. Turn one on before you publish the port (for example from Docker on a VPS).

Some providers ship with an empty model list. Load models on that provider's page fills it from the provider.

What's in the panel

Overview, Providers, Routing (auto presets and named fallbacks), API keys, Playground, Activity (each gateway call with request/response), Clients (copy-paste setup plus a confirmed one-click writer for Claude Code, OpenCode and Codex), Usage (calls by model, 14-day chart, estimated cost), Memory (optional notes prepended to chat), and Settings.

Closing the browser tab does not stop the router.

Stack and license

Go server and SQLite, React panel, native desktop wrapper, npm CLI that launches the server. MIT. Current release is v1.5.5. Repo: github.com/foisalislambd/wowrouter.

Honest limits

  • It's young. The repo started in October 2026. I'm one person.
  • Some providers are marked Unsupported. Decision models use POST /v1/systemone, not chat completions.
  • If you expose the port past loopback without a panel password or OIDC, that's on you — the README is clear about locking it first.
  • I have not counted how many providers the catalog currently lists; open the Providers page after install rather than trusting a number from a blog post.

If you try it and something breaks, open an issue on the repo. If your setup is "three agents, five keys, one laptop", I'd like to know whether one local endpoint actually helped.

— foisal

title: Test your prompts like code: a Node.js prompt test sheet for AI students
description:
Most students learning generative AI write a prompt, try it twice and move on. Developers test. Here is a weekend project that turns prompt testing into code: a tiny Node.js script that runs one prompt over a list of test inputs and checks each answer against simple rules.

It doesn't depend on any one AI provider. You plug in whichever API you have access to.

What you will build

  • cases.json: 10 test inputs, each with rules the answer must pass
  • test.mjs: sends each input with your prompt, checks the rules, prints a pass/fail table

Step 1: the test cases 

[
  { "input": "Library closes at 6 pm on Saturday from next week.",
    "mustInclude": ["6 pm", "Saturday"], "maxWords": 25 },
  { "input": "Fee deadline for semester 5 is extended to 20 November.",
    "mustInclude": ["20 November"], "maxWords": 25 }
]

The prompt's job here: summarise a college notice in one short sentence without losing dates and times. Write at least 10 cases, including awkward ones (two dates, Hindi-English mixed text, an empty notice).

Step 2: the checker 

// test.mjs  (Node 18+; .mjs so import and top-level await work)
import fs from "node:fs";

const PROMPT = "Summarise this college notice in one sentence. Keep every date and time exactly as written.";
const cases = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync("cases.json", "utf8"));

async function ask(text) {
  // Replace with your provider's API call. It must return the model's reply as a string.
  throw new Error("connect your AI API here");
}

function check(answer, c) {
  const problems = [];
  for (const word of c.mustInclude || []) {
    if (!answer.includes(word)) problems.push(`missing "${word}"`);
  }
  const words = answer.trim().split(/\s+/).length;
  if (c.maxWords && words > c.maxWords) problems.push(`${words} words`);
  return problems;
}

let passed = 0;
for (const c of cases) {
  const answer = await ask(`${PROMPT}\n\nNotice: ${c.input}`);
  const problems = check(answer, c);
  if (problems.length === 0) passed++;
  console.log(problems.length ? "FAIL" : "PASS", "|", c.input.slice(0, 40), "|", problems.join(", "));
}
console.log(`${passed}/${cases.length} passed`);

Keep your API key in an environment variable, never in the file, and never commit it to GitHub.

Step 3: improve the prompt, not the tests

Run it, look at the failures, change one thing in PROMPT, run again. Write down each change and the new score. After three or four rounds you will have a short, honest record like "v1 7/10, v2 9/10 (added 'keep dates exactly')". That record is a far better interview story than "I know ChatGPT".

Ideas to extend it

  • Run each case 3 times, because AI answers vary.
  • Add a mustNotInclude rule to catch made-up details.
  • Save results to a CSV and compare two models.

I put this together for students at Dzimark Training in Mohali, where the AI programmes cover prompt engineering, AI agents and AI-powered full-stack work. If you are in the Tricity and want the structured version, the course outline is on the Dzimark Training AI programmes page.
