title: NestJS Rate Limiting: In-Memory vs Redis vs Postgres
description:
Cross-posted from my blog. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

I shipped a NestJS API with the default @nestjs/throttler storage last year and only noticed the hole when we ran two instances behind a load balancer. Each process kept its own counter, so a client that should have been cut off at 100 requests in a minute quietly got closer to 200. Today I re-tested that on NestJS 12 with three storages on the same box: in-memory, Redis, and Postgres.

What I tested

Everything ran on one 8 vCPU / 16 GB Linux VM on November 6, 2026:

  • Node.js 24.22.1, NestJS 12.3.3, @nestjs/throttler 6.7.1
  • Redis 7.2.11 with persistence off, via @nestjs-redis/throttler-storage 2.0.1 and the redis 5.12.1 client
  • PostgreSQL 18.6 with a small custom storage that upserts into one throttler_hits table
  • Limit: 100 requests / 60 seconds, tracker keyed on x-forwarded-for so localhost tests don't all share 127.0.0.1

I measured three things: p50/p95 latency of allowed requests, whether request 101 returns 429, and whether two Nest processes behind the same storage still stop at 100 total.

If you're comparing Nest to thinner frameworks, I wrote about Hono vs Express and the NestJS 12 upgrade separately. Redis vs Postgres as infrastructure shows up again in my pg-boss vs BullMQ and BullMQ pipeline posts.

Wiring @nestjs/throttler

The default setup is tiny. Global guard, one named throttler:

ThrottlerModule.forRoot({
  throttlers: [{ name: 'default', ttl: seconds(60), limit: 100 }],
  getTracker: async (req) => {
    const xf = req.headers['x-forwarded-for'];
    if (typeof xf === 'string' && xf.length) return xf.split(',')[0].trim();
    return req.ip;
  },
}),
// providers: [{ provide: APP_GUARD, useClass: ThrottlerGuard }]

That uses the built-in in-memory storage. Fine for a single process. Wrong the moment you scale out.

Redis storage

I used @nestjs-redis/throttler-storage, which implements ThrottlerStorage with a Lua script so the increment is atomic:

const redis = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });
await redis.connect();

ThrottlerModule.forRoot({
  throttlers: [{ name: 'default', ttl: seconds(60), limit: 100 }],
  storage: new RedisThrottlerStorage(redis),
  getTracker: /* same as above */,
});

Pass an existing client. The package does not manage connect/disconnect for you.

Postgres storage (custom)

There isn't an official Nest Postgres throttler storage, so I wrote one. One row per key, upsert that resets when the window expires:

CREATE TABLE throttler_hits (
  key text PRIMARY KEY,
  hits integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  expires_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  is_blocked boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  block_expires_at timestamptz
);

// inside increment():
INSERT INTO throttler_hits (key, hits, expires_at)
VALUES ($1, 1, now() + ($2 || ' milliseconds')::interval)
ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET
  hits = CASE WHEN throttler_hits.expires_at <= now() THEN 1
              ELSE throttler_hits.hits + 1 END,
  expires_at = CASE WHEN throttler_hits.expires_at <= now()
                    THEN now() + ($2 || ' milliseconds')::interval
                    ELSE throttler_hits.expires_at END
RETURNING hits, expires_at, is_blocked, block_expires_at;

I wrap that in a transaction and set is_blocked when hits > limit, matching how the in-memory storage behaves. No SKIP LOCKED here: a single-row upsert is enough for a counter. SKIP LOCKED is the pattern I use for job claiming, not for rate-limit tallies.

Latency (allowed requests)

Eighty requests under the limit, median of three runs. Raw Node http with no Nest is the baseline.

Storage p50 (ms) p95 (ms)
none (raw http) 0.34 0.57
memory 0.36 0.64
redis 0.38 0.81
postgres 1.00 1.42

On localhost, memory and Redis are basically free. Postgres adds about 0.6 ms at p50 versus the raw baseline. That is one round trip plus the upsert. Across a network to a remote Postgres the gap will be larger; across a network to Redis it will grow too, just usually less.

Reject correctness

Single process, LIMIT + 20 requests with the same client IP:

Storage 200s 429s First 429 at request #
memory 100 20 101
redis 100 20 101
postgres 100 20 101

All three cut off exactly after 100. So the bug is not "throttler is wrong". The bug is sharing.

Multi-instance correctness

Two Nest processes, same Redis or Postgres (or none for memory), alternating requests for the same IP, LIMIT + 30 = 130 total:

Storage Allowed Blocked Shared limit held?
memory 130 0 No
redis 100 30 Yes
postgres 100 30 Yes

Memory allowed every request. Each process only saw 65 hits, both under 100. That is the load-balancer failure mode. Redis and Postgres stopped at 100 total across both processes.

What I'd pick

  • One instance, local or edge: in-memory. Lowest moving parts. Don't pretend it will survive a second replica.
  • Already running Redis (BullMQ, cache, sessions): use @nestjs-redis/throttler-storage. Latency matched memory on this box and shared correctly.
  • Postgres only, no Redis: the custom upsert storage works. Expect roughly a millisecond of overhead on localhost, more over the network. Keep the table tiny and index-free beyond the primary key.

I would not put rate-limit counters in the same hot transactional tables as orders or payments. A dedicated table (or Redis) keeps the lock footprint small.

One caveat: this is one machine, client and storage on localhost, Nest 12.3.3, throttler 6.7.1. It answers "does shared storage actually share" and "how much does each storage add on this box". It does not answer global multi-region limits or abuse at the CDN layer. Put a WAF or edge limit in front when that matters.

If you only remember one number from today: memory let 130 through where Redis and Postgres stopped at 100. That is the whole reason to change the storage.

FAQ

Does NestJS @nestjs/throttler work across multiple instances?

Only if you swap the default in-memory storage for a shared one. With two Nest processes and a limit of 100, in-memory allowed all 130 alternating requests in my test because each process only saw 65. Redis and Postgres both stopped at 100 total.

What Redis storage should I use with @nestjs/throttler?

I used @nestjs-redis/throttler-storage 2.0.1 with the redis 5.x client on NestJS 12. You pass an existing Redis client; the package runs the increment in a Lua script so it stays atomic.

Can I store NestJS rate limits in Postgres?

Yes, with a custom ThrottlerStorage. I used a single throttler_hits table and an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT upsert that resets hits when the TTL window expires. On localhost it added about 0.6 ms at p50 versus a raw HTTP baseline.

How much latency does NestJS rate limiting add?

On one 8 vCPU box with localhost storage, allowed-request p50 was 0.36 ms for in-memory, 0.38 ms for Redis 7.2.11, and 1.00 ms for PostgreSQL 18.6, against a 0.34 ms raw HTTP baseline. Remote Redis or Postgres will cost more.

Is in-memory rate limiting OK for production NestJS?

It is fine for a single instance. The moment you run two replicas behind a load balancer, each keeps its own counter, so clients can exceed the limit. Switch to Redis or Postgres (or an edge/WAF limit) before you scale out.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: making procedural sky based on realtime weather data using feTurbulence
description:
Creating dynamic, environment-aware UI elements adds a layer of polish to web applications. By combining React, realtime weather APIs, and SVG filters, we can build a procedural sky that automatically reflects the user's local time of day and cloud cover.

Here is a breakdown of how to build a realtime procedural sky without relying on heavy WebGL libraries or prompting the user for intrusive location permissions.

  1. Privacy-Friendly Location & Weather Fetching

Browsers have a native Geolocation API, but triggering a location permission popup immediately upon page load is a terrible user experience. Instead, we can approximate the user's location using their IP address. It's less precise than GPS, but perfectly adequate for fetching general weather data like cloud cover.

Using ipapi.co, we fetch the rough latitude and longitude, then pass those coordinates to the free Open-Meteo API to retrieve the current cloud_cover percentage. To prevent rate-limiting and unnecessary network requests, this data is cached in localStorage for one hour.

// Fetching rough location via IP (No permission popup required)
const ipRes = await fetch("https://ipapi.co/json/");
const ipData = await ipRes.json();

const latitude = ipData.latitude || 19.076;
const longitude = ipData.longitude || 72.8777;

// Fetching cloud cover based on coordinates
const weatherUrl = `https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=${latitude}&longitude=${longitude}&current=cloud_cover`;
const weatherRes = await fetch(weatherUrl);
const weatherData = await weatherRes.json();

const cloudDensity = weatherData.current.cloud_cover;
  1. Painting the Sky Gradient

The background sky is driven by the user's local time. By extracting the current hour (new Date().getHours()), we can map it to an array of predefined CSS gradients.

Night hours return pure black or deep navy, early mornings transition through sunrise colors, and midday hours use bright blues.

const skyGradientByHour = [
  // ... other hours
  { hour: 6, gradient: `linear-gradient(180deg, #000000 0%, #00274C 50%, #83270080 100%)` }, // Sunrise
  { hour: 12, gradient: `linear-gradient(180deg, #004381 0%, #FFFFFF 100%)` }, // Noon
  { hour: 18, gradient: `linear-gradient(180deg, #004381 0%, #B78A78 100%)` }, // Sunset
  // ...
];

const getSkyGradient = (timeOfDay) => {
  const match = skyGradientByHour.find(sky => sky.hour === timeOfDay);
  return match?.gradient || "#000000";
};
  1. Sculpting Clouds with CSS and feTurbulence

The most complex part is rendering the clouds. Instead of using static PNGs or expensive canvas rendering, we can use CSS box-shadow coupled with SVG filters to generate organic, fluffy shapes.

First, we generate a massive, comma-separated box-shadow string. Each shadow acts as a single cloud "blob," scattered randomly across the viewport using vw and vh units. The number of blobs is dictated by the cloudDensity fetched from the weather API (capped to maintain performance).

To make these perfect circles look like actual clouds, we apply an SVG filter. generates fractal noise, and uses that noise to warp and distort the smooth edges of our box shadows into organic, chaotic cloud formations.

import { useMemo } from "react";

const CloudSheet = ({ cloudDensity, timeOfDay }) => {
  const isSunsetOrSunrise = (timeOfDay >= 6 && timeOfDay <= 9) || (timeOfDay >= 18 && timeOfDay <= 20);

  const memoizeShadows = useMemo(() => {
    const safeDensity = Math.min(cloudDensity, 30); // Cap density for performance

    // Generate scattered box-shadows based on density
    let shadows = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < safeDensity; ++i) {
      // Random position (vw/vh), size (vmin), and color tint based on time of day
      shadows.push(`${rn(1, 100)}vw ${rn(1, 100)}vh ${rn(20, 40)}vmin ${rn(1, 20)}vmin ${isSunsetOrSunrise ? rs("#0385FF00", "#53ACFF", "#CCE6FF") : rs("#0385FF00", "#53ACFF", "#CCE6FF", "#FFFFFF")}`);
    }
    return shadows.join(",");
  }, [cloudDensity, isSunsetOrSunrise]);

  return (
    <div className="bg-transparent absolute w-screen h-screen z-30">
      {/* SVG Filter for Cloud Distortion */}
      <svg width="0" height="0" className="absolute">
        <filter id="cloud-filter" x="-50%" y="-50%" width="200%" height="200%">
          <feTurbulence type="fractalNoise" baseFrequency=".01" numOctaves="10" result="noise" />
          <feDisplacementMap in="SourceGraphic" in2="noise" scale="180" />
        </filter>
      </svg>

      {/* The base element that holds the shadows and applies the filter */}
      <div
        className="fixed -top-1 -left-1 w-1 h-1 bg-white rounded-full filter-[url(#cloud-filter)]"
        style={{
          boxShadow: memoizeShadows,
          transform: "translateZ(0)", // Force hardware acceleration
        }}
      />
    </div>
  );
};

By combining these three layers—IP-based weather data, time-mapped gradients, and SVG-distorted box shadows—you get a responsive, performant procedural sky that accurately reflects the physical world outside your user's window.

title: Same audio, four request IDs: keying idempotency on the bytes so a phone can resend safely
description:
Bolo turns speech on a phone into text. In cloud mode the phone records a voice note, uploads it to a small proxy, and the proxy calls a speech-to-text service. Two problems in that path turned out to be the same problem seen from opposite ends:

  1. The server was doing the same transcription several times for one recording.
  2. On a flaky home connection the phone gave up too early, even though a resend would have worked.

The fix for the second one is only safe because of the fix for the first. This post walks through both.

Disclosure: I'm the developer of Bolo, and this post is published from my account. It was written and published by an AI agent working on my behalf.

Problem 1: an idempotency key that never matched

The proxy already had an idempotency guard. The client sent an X-Bolo-Request-Id header, and a repeat of the same ID was supposed to return the first result instead of calling the speech service again.

The logs from 31 real dictations on one phone showed it collapsed nothing. One recording had been uploaded four times, with identical bytes, two of the uploads 44 ms apart. Each upload carried a fresh request ID, because the app minted a new UUID per call. Four IDs, four upstream calls, four quota charges. About 13% of the uploads in that sample were redundant.

The root cause on the phone was a race between two code paths that could both send the same recording, and that was fixed in the app. But an app build that is already installed cannot be patched from the server, so the server needed its own net.

Key on what the work is, not on what the client calls it

The question idempotency answers is "have I already done this piece of work?". For a transcription, the work is defined by who sent it and what audio it is. The request ID is just a label the client chose.

So the key became the device plus a SHA-256 of the uploaded bytes:

const serverAudioHash = crypto.createHash('sha256').update(req.file.buffer).digest('hex');
const suppliedAudioHash = String(req.headers['x-bolo-audio-sha256'] || '').toLowerCase();
if (suppliedAudioHash && suppliedAudioHash !== serverAudioHash) {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: 'audio hash mismatch' });
}

const idempotencyKey = `${deviceId}:audio:${serverAudioHash}`;
const execution = await transcriptionIdempotency.execute(
    idempotencyKey,
    serverAudioHash,
    () => transcribe(req.file /* , ... */)
);

Two choices worth pointing out:

  • The server computes the hash itself. The client may send its own hash, and a mismatch is rejected with 400, which catches a truncated upload. But the key is always built from the server's hash, so a client cannot claim someone else's cached result by sending a made-up hash.
  • The device is part of the key. Two different users dictating the same short phrase do not share a cache entry, even if their audio happened to be byte-identical.

The request ID is still logged on every line. It just no longer decides identity.

The store: share the promise, cache only success 

class IdempotencyStore {
    constructor({ ttlMs = 10 * 60 * 1000 } = {}) {
        this.ttlMs = Math.max(1000, Number(ttlMs) || 10 * 60 * 1000);
        this.entries = new Map();
    }

    async execute(key, audioHash, operation) {
        this.cleanup();
        const existing = this.entries.get(key);
        if (existing) {
            if (existing.audioHash !== audioHash) {
                const error = new Error('Request ID was already used for different audio');
                error.statusCode = 409;
                throw error;
            }
            return { value: await existing.promise, deduplicated: true };
        }

        const entry = { audioHash, expiresAt: Date.now() + this.ttlMs, promise: null };
        entry.promise = Promise.resolve().then(operation);
        this.entries.set(key, entry);
        try {
            return { value: await entry.promise, deduplicated: false };
        } catch (error) {
            // Failed attempts are retryable with the same key; only completed work is cached.
            this.entries.delete(key);
            throw error;
        }
    }

    cleanup(now = Date.now()) {
        for (const [key, entry] of this.entries.entries()) {
            if (entry.expiresAt <= now) this.entries.delete(key);
        }
    }
}

What makes this work for the "two uploads 44 ms apart" case:

  • The entry is stored before the work finishes. The second upload finds the first one's promise and awaits it. It does not start a second upstream call, and it gets the same text as soon as the first finishes.
  • Failure removes the entry. If the speech service errors, the next attempt with the same audio runs fresh. Caching an error would turn one bad moment into ten minutes of failures.
  • A ten-minute TTL. Long enough to cover any realistic retry storm from one recording, short enough that the map stays small. It is in memory, so a restart clears it, which is acceptable: the worst case is one repeated call.
  • The 409 branch is a safety check left from the request-ID design: the same key with different audio is a contradiction. With the key now derived from the audio hash it should never fire, and if it ever does, it means the key construction has a bug.

Problem 2: giving up on a link that was only flaky

A later report came from a home connection: a 24-second note timed out, the single automatic retry died after 5 seconds, and a manual resend went through and was transcribed in 1.5 seconds. The audio was fine and the server was fine. The client simply did not resend patiently enough.

With the server-side key in place, resending the same audio is harmless. If the earlier upload did land, the resend gets the cached text: no second speech call, no second quota charge. So the app can afford to try harder:

object TranscriptionResend {
    const val MAX_ATTEMPTS = 4                       // including the first
    val BACKOFF_MS = listOf(2_000L, 5_000L, 10_000L) // before attempts 2, 3, 4
    const val RESEND_WINDOW_MS = 90_000L             // no new attempt after this

    fun isTransient(e: Throwable): Boolean = when (e) {
        is VoxException -> false                     // the app's own "this request is wrong"
        is java.net.UnknownHostException -> true
        is java.io.IOException -> !isCallCancelled(e)
        is retrofit2.HttpException -> e.code() in TRANSIENT_HTTP
        else -> false
    }

    // 500-504 from the proxy or nginx; 520-524 are Cloudflare's "origin did not answer in time".
    private val TRANSIENT_HTTP = setOf(500, 502, 503, 504, 520, 521, 522, 523, 524)

    // OkHttp reports its own cancel (the user tapped stop) as IOException("Canceled").
    private fun isCallCancelled(e: java.io.IOException) =
        e.message.equals("Canceled", ignoreCase = true)
}

And the loop:

suspend fun <T> run(
    nowMs: () -> Long = System::currentTimeMillis,
    sleep: suspend (Long) -> Unit = { delay(it) },
    block: suspend (attempt: Int) -> T
): T {
    val startedAt = nowMs()
    var attempt = 1
    while (true) {
        try {
            return block(attempt)
        } catch (e: Exception) {
            currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive()
            val pause = BACKOFF_MS.getOrElse(attempt - 1) { BACKOFF_MS.last() }
            val outOfTime = nowMs() - startedAt + pause > RESEND_WINDOW_MS
            if (!isTransient(e) || attempt >= MAX_ATTEMPTS || outOfTime) throw e
            attempt++
            sleep(pause)
        }
    }
}

The rules it encodes:

  • Only link failures are retried. A 4xx, or the app's own validation error, means resending the same thing gives the same answer.
  • A user's cancel is never retried. ensureActive() rethrows if the coroutine was cancelled, and OkHttp's own "Canceled" IOException is treated as final. The original bug report included "I pressed retry and it cancelled", so a stop must mean stop.
  • A time budget, not only a count. Four attempts with growing pauses, but no new attempt once 90 seconds have passed since the first. A person waiting for text will not wait forever.
  • Clock and sleep are parameters, so the whole policy is a fast unit test with a fake clock.

A read timeout that scales with the note

One more piece: a fixed 30-second read timeout cut off slow but healthy answers for long notes. The timeout is now 30 s plus half the note's length, capped at 2 minutes, applied by an OkHttp interceptor that reads the duration header the upload already carries:

fun readTimeoutMsFor(audioDurationMs: Long): Long =
    (30_000L + audioDurationMs.coerceAtLeast(0L) / 2).coerceIn(30_000L, 120_000L)

Other calls keep the client's default timeouts.

Takeaways

  • An idempotency key should describe the work, not the request. For uploads, a content hash plus the caller's identity is often the right key.
  • Compute the hash on the server; treat any client-supplied hash as a check, not as the key.
  • Store the in-flight promise so concurrent duplicates share one call, and cache only successful results.
  • Server-side idempotency is what makes aggressive client resends safe. Build it first.
  • Retry link failures only, never a user's cancel, and bound retries by time as well as by count.

Bolo is on Google Play as "Bolo AI Voice Typing & PC Sync" (search "Bolo AI"): https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.ashwar.bolo&utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=2026-w45-idempotency. Cloud dictation has a limited free cloud trial, and you can also bring your own OpenAI or Gemini key, or use offline on-device dictation.

title: How I Choose Which Open Source Issue to Work On (After Picking Wrong Ones)
description:
In my last post I wrote about a PR I closed on purpose, because the maintainers were already fixing the same bug. That was a lesson in picking issues better. Over a few months and several repos, I settled on a simple routine. This post is that routine, so you can skip the mistakes I made.

Step 1: Check that the project is alive

Before I read any code, I open the repo and look at three things:

  • Were PRs merged in the last few weeks?
  • How fast do maintainers reply on issues and PRs?
  • Do outside contributors get their PRs merged, or only the team?

A project with no replies is a waiting room. I would rather spend my time where someone will read my work.

Step 2: Check that nobody else is on it

This is the step I skipped with Riptide. Now I check:

  • Is the issue assigned?
  • Are there comments saying "I'm working on this"?
  • Is there a linked PR, open or closed?

Then, before I write any code, I leave a short comment: "I'd like to work on this, is anyone already on it?" It takes one minute and can save a week.

Step 3: Read how maintainers review similar PRs

I open three or four merged PRs that touch the same area. I look at what the reviewers asked for: naming, where tests go, how big the change was. Most projects have unwritten rules, and the closed PRs are where they live.

Step 4: Reproduce it on the latest master

If the issue is a bug, I reproduce it on the current main branch first. Sometimes it is already fixed, and sometimes it only happens in an old version. Writing a fix for something that is not broken wastes everyone's time.

Step 5: Keep it small and prove it with a test

I pick the smallest change that solves the problem. Then I write a test that fails without my fix and passes with it. If the test passes before my change, it proves nothing.

How I look for bugs, not just pick them

The best thing I learned is to look for the root cause, not just one symptom.

In Picnic's error-prone-support, I found a bug where a check rewrites code by building a new format string from the original source text. If the original text contains a %, the rewritten string breaks at runtime. Here is the idea, simplified:

// Simplified idea: a literal from the user's code gets copied
// into a new format string without escaping.
String literal = "100%";              // contains a percent sign
String format = "Value: " + literal;  // now the % looks like a format placeholder
String.format(format);                // crashes at runtime

I reported it as issue #2336 with a minimal repro, checked first that it was not a duplicate, and offered to send a fix with a regression test if the maintainers wanted one.

Later I found a second bug with the same root cause (building fixes from raw source text), and another contributor beat me to reporting it. That was fine. It confirmed the method works, because the root cause pointed to the same area. And if someone else has already said what I wanted to say, I do not add a comment just to be seen. I comment only when I have something new.

My checklist, short version

  1. Is the project alive and does it merge outside PRs?
  2. Is anyone already on the issue? Ask first.
  3. How do maintainers review similar PRs?
  4. Does it still reproduce on the latest master?
  5. Small change, plus a test that fails without the fix.

Proof of my work

Everything here is public, so you can check it yourself:

  • PicnicSupermarket/error-prone-support issue #2336: a reproducible bug report
  • PicnicSupermarket/error-prone-support #2275: extended RequireNonNullExpression rule (merged)
  • Adyen/adyen-java-api-library #1952: regex fix, shipped in SDK v42.0.0 (merged)
  • zalando/logbook #2301, #2326, #2327 and #2328: Logbook changes (merged)
  • Sionna Visualizer: my side project, a 6G + AI dashboard (live demo)
  • My GitHub: all my repos and contributions

Next post: Sionna Visualizer, why a Java backend developer is building a 6G + AI dashboard.

If you are a maintainer, a recruiter or a team looking for someone who learns in public and works carefully, my DMs are open. Tell me in the comments how you choose your issues.

title: A button on the lock screen must not open a chat: an unlock trampoline on Android
description:
QuickDial puts a small chat button next to a normal phone call, so you can jump from the call to a chat with that number without saving it. Calls often come in while the phone is locked, so in QuickDial's source the button can also be tapped on the lock screen. That raised a question I had to answer before shipping it: what happens to the chat when somebody else is holding your phone?

The answer had to be "nothing opens until the phone is unlocked". This post is about the small, invisible activity that enforces that.

Disclosure: I'm the developer of QuickDial, and this post is published from my account. It was written and published by an AI agent working on my behalf. QuickDial is an independent app, not affiliated with WhatsApp LLC or Meta.

The risk

A chat screen shows message history, names, photos and documents. A button that is reachable on a locked phone and opens that screen directly would turn a convenience into a privacy leak: anyone who picks up the phone during a call could read the owner's conversations.

So the rule is simple to state:

  • The button may be visible on the lock screen.
  • The chat may only open after the user unlocks with their PIN, pattern or biometric.
  • If the unlock is cancelled or fails, nothing opens. Not the chat, not the app, not a half-loaded screen.

Decide at the call site

The service that handles the tap checks the keyguard first. If the phone is unlocked, the chat intent starts as usual. If it is locked, the same intent is wrapped and handed to a dedicated activity:

private fun startBehindUnlock(next: Intent) {
    val keyguard = getSystemService(Context.KEYGUARD_SERVICE) as KeyguardManager
    startActivity(
        if (keyguard.isKeyguardLocked) {
            UnlockThenOpenActivity.wrap(this, next)
        } else {
            next.addFlags(Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK)
        },
    )
}

Every path that opens a chat from the call button goes through this one function, including the screen where the user picks one of several numbers for a contact. One choke point means one place to get right.

The trampoline

UnlockThenOpenActivity has no layout of its own. It carries the real intent as an extra, shows itself over the lock screen, asks the system to dismiss the keyguard, and starts the real intent only from the success callback:

class UnlockThenOpenActivity : Activity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        val next = nextIntent(intent) ?: run { finish(); return }

        val keyguard = getSystemService(Context.KEYGUARD_SERVICE) as KeyguardManager
        if (!keyguard.isKeyguardLocked) { launch(next); return }

        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.O_MR1) setShowWhenLocked(true)
        keyguard.requestDismissKeyguard(this, object : KeyguardManager.KeyguardDismissCallback() {
            override fun onDismissSucceeded() = launch(next)
            override fun onDismissCancelled() = finish()
            override fun onDismissError() = finish()
        })
    }

    private fun launch(next: Intent) {
        runCatching { startActivity(next) }
        finish()
    }
}

A few details carry the weight here:

The real intent is started in exactly one place. launch() is reached only when the phone was not locked to begin with, or from onDismissSucceeded(). Cancelled and error both call finish() and nothing else. When you review this kind of code, look for any other startActivity and treat it as a bug.

It re-checks the lock. The caller already checked, but by the time the activity is created the user may have unlocked with a fingerprint. Checking again avoids showing an unlock prompt for a phone that is already open.

requestDismissKeyguard lets the system own the unlock. The app never sees the PIN or the biometric. It shows the standard prompt, and the callback reports the result. Secure lock screens get the user's own credential check; a swipe-only lock screen just goes away.

It finishes on every path. A trampoline that stays alive after doing its job leaves an empty, see-through activity in the task, which looks like a frozen screen to the user.

The manifest entry matters as much as the code 

<activity
    android:name=".ui.unlock.UnlockThenOpenActivity"
    android:exported="false"
    android:excludeFromRecents="true"
    android:noHistory="true"
    android:taskAffinity=""
    android:theme="@style/Theme.QuickDialCallBridge.Chooser" />
  • exported="false": no other app can send an intent to it and use it as a way to open arbitrary intents over the lock screen. This is the most important line in the file. A trampoline that takes "the next intent" as an extra must never be reachable from outside your app.
  • excludeFromRecents and noHistory: it never shows up in the recent-apps list and is not kept on the back stack, so pressing Back after the chat opens does not land on an invisible screen.
  • taskAffinity="": it does not join the app's main task, so unlocking does not pull the app's home screen forward behind the chat.
  • A translucent theme: the user sees the lock screen and then the system prompt, not a blank app window.

Reading the wrapped intent

Since Android 13 the type-safe getParcelableExtra(name, Class) is the right call; on older versions only the deprecated one exists:

private fun nextIntent(intent: Intent?): Intent? =
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.TIRAMISU) {
        intent?.getParcelableExtra(EXTRA_NEXT, Intent::class.java)
    } else {
        @Suppress("DEPRECATION")
        intent?.getParcelableExtra(EXTRA_NEXT)
    }

A missing extra finishes the activity at once. "Nothing to open" is a normal outcome, not a crash.

Version notes

The app's minimum SDK is 26, which is where requestDismissKeyguard arrived, so the API is always there. setShowWhenLocked arrived one release later, in 8.1 (API 27). On 8.0 exactly, the older window flag FLAG_SHOW_WHEN_LOCKED is the equivalent, and that version is worth a test on a real device if you support it.

Test it like an attacker would

Things I check by hand on a locked phone:

  1. Tap the button, cancel the prompt: nothing opens, and the lock screen is still there.
  2. Tap the button, fail the fingerprint several times until it falls back to PIN, then cancel: nothing opens.
  3. Tap the button, unlock: the chat opens; Back goes to wherever the user was before, not to an empty screen.
  4. Open Recents afterwards: no blank entry.
  5. Phone already unlocked: no prompt at all, the chat opens straight away.

Takeaways

  • Showing a control on the lock screen and opening content from it are two separate permissions. Grant the first, gate the second.
  • Route every "open content" path through one function that checks the keyguard.
  • Let requestDismissKeyguard own the unlock, and start the real intent only from onDismissSucceeded().
  • A trampoline that forwards an intent must be exported="false".
  • Finish on every path, and keep the trampoline out of Recents and the back stack.

QuickDial is on Google Play as "QuickDial: Direct Chat & Call": https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.ashwar.quickdialbridge&utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=2026-w45-unlock. It works with WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business; independent app, not affiliated with WhatsApp LLC or Meta.

title: How Kafka Works: A Quick Walkthrough with Java
description:
Your order service needs to tell the invoice service, the email service, and the analytics pipeline that an order happened. You could wire them together directly - but every new consumer means changing the producer, and if a consumer is down, messages get lost.

Kafka takes a different approach: the producer drops the message into a durable log, and each consumer reads that log whenever it is ready, at its own pace, without the producer even knowing who they are. Let's see the whole flow working, with a real Kafka broker and a real Java client.

The five pieces that matter

  • Topic: a named stream of messages, like greetings. Producers write to it, consumers read from it.
  • Partition: a topic is split into partitions. Each partition is an ordered, append-only log. Partitions are how Kafka scales: different consumers can read different partitions in parallel.
  • Offset: a message's position in its partition - 0, 1, 2, ... Once written, a message never changes; consumers just move forward through the offsets.
  • Producer: the app that appends messages. If you give the message a key, the key's hash decides which partition it lands in, so all messages with the same key stay in order in the same partition.
  • Consumer group: consumers with the same group id share the partitions between them and Kafka tracks how far each group has read.

Here is the whole journey, animated - three messages go in, and a consumer pulls them back out:

Running a real broker

The official Kafka quickstart runs a single-node broker without ZooKeeper (KRaft mode) in three commands, which is exactly what I did - this article's output is from Apache Kafka 4.4.0 on JDK 21:

# 1. generate a cluster id
KAFKA_CLUSTER_ID="$(bin/kafka-storage.sh random-uuid)"

# 2. format the log directories
bin/kafka-storage.sh format --standalone -t $KAFKA_CLUSTER_ID -c config/server.properties

# 3. start the broker
bin/kafka-server-start.sh config/server.properties

Startup logged Kafka Server started (kafka.server.KafkaRaftServer), and the broker was ready on localhost:9092.

A Java producer and consumer in one file

This complete program creates a topic with 3 partitions, produces 3 keyed messages, and reads them back. It uses only the kafka-clients jar that ships in the Kafka download's libs folder - no extra dependencies:

import org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.AdminClient;
import org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.NewTopic;
import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.ConsumerConfig;
import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.ConsumerRecords;
import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.KafkaConsumer;
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.KafkaProducer;
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerConfig;
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord;
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer;
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Properties;

public class KafkaWalkthrough {

    static final String TOPIC = "greetings";

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        createTopic();
        produce();
        consume();
    }

    static void createTopic() throws Exception {
        Properties p = new Properties();
        p.put("bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092");
        try (AdminClient admin = AdminClient.create(p)) {
            admin.createTopics(List.of(new NewTopic(TOPIC, 3, (short) 1))).all().get();
            System.out.println("[setup] created topic '" + TOPIC + "' with 3 partitions");
        }
    }

    static void produce() throws Exception {
        Properties p = new Properties();
        p.put(ProducerConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "localhost:9092");
        p.put(ProducerConfig.KEY_SERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringSerializer.class.getName());
        p.put(ProducerConfig.VALUE_SERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringSerializer.class.getName());
        try (KafkaProducer<String, String> producer = new KafkaProducer<>(p)) {
            String[][] msgs = {
                {"vishnu", "hello kafka"},
                {"asha", "kafka is a log"},
                {"ravi", "partitions scale reads"},
            };
            for (String[] m : msgs) {
                var meta = producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>(TOPIC, m[0], m[1])).get();
                System.out.printf("[producer] sent key=%s value='%s' -> partition=%d offset=%d%n",
                        m[0], m[1], meta.partition(), meta.offset());
            }
        }
    }

    static void consume() {
        Properties p = new Properties();
        p.put(ConsumerConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "localhost:9092");
        p.put(ConsumerConfig.GROUP_ID_CONFIG, "walkthrough-group");
        p.put(ConsumerConfig.KEY_DESERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringDeserializer.class.getName());
        p.put(ConsumerConfig.VALUE_DESERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringDeserializer.class.getName());
        p.put(ConsumerConfig.AUTO_OFFSET_RESET_CONFIG, "earliest");
        try (KafkaConsumer<String, String> consumer = new KafkaConsumer<>(p)) {
            consumer.subscribe(List.of(TOPIC));
            int got = 0;
            long deadline = System.currentTimeMillis() + 15000;
            while (got < 3 && System.currentTimeMillis() < deadline) {
                ConsumerRecords<String, String> records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500));
                records.forEach(r -> {
                    System.out.printf("[consumer] read key=%s value='%s' from partition=%d offset=%d%n",
                            r.key(), r.value(), r.partition(), r.offset());
                });
                got += records.count();
            }
        }
    }
}

I compiled it with javac -cp "libs/*" KafkaWalkthrough.java and ran it against the live broker. This is the real, unedited output:

[setup] created topic 'greetings' with 3 partitions
[producer] sent key=vishnu value='hello kafka' -> partition=0 offset=0
[producer] sent key=asha value='kafka is a log' -> partition=0 offset=1
[producer] sent key=ravi value='partitions scale reads' -> partition=0 offset=2
[consumer] read key=vishnu value='hello kafka' from partition=0 offset=0
[consumer] read key=asha value='kafka is a log' from partition=0 offset=1
[consumer] read key=ravi value='partitions scale reads' from partition=0 offset=2

Four honest observations from that output:

  1. All three keys hashed to partition 0. With only three partitions and three keys, that is chance, not a rule - other keys land in partitions 1 and 2. The guarantee is narrower: the same key always goes to the same partition.
  2. Offsets count up within a partition. 0, 1, 2 - the append-only log in action.
  3. The consumer replayed history. The producer had already finished and exited when the consumer started. Nothing was lost, because the topic stores messages; AUTO_OFFSET_RESET_CONFIG = "earliest" told the new consumer group to start from offset 0.
  4. Order is per-partition. The consumer got the messages in offset order. Across partitions there is no global order - another reason keys matter when order matters.

When Kafka is the right tool

  • Decoupling services: the producer does not know or care who consumes.
  • Buffering bursts: consumers catch up after a spike or an outage instead of dropping work.
  • Multiple independent readers: analytics, email, and search can each have their own consumer group over the same topic.
  • Replay: because messages persist, a new service can rebuild its state by reading from offset 0.

It is more machinery than a plain queue, so for one producer talking to one consumer with no replay needs, a simpler tool can be the better call. Kafka earns its keep when the log itself - durable, ordered per partition, readable by many groups - is what you need.

Sources

  • Apache Kafka documentation: introduction
  • Apache Kafka quickstart

Written with AI assistance; code examples were compiled and run against a real single-node Kafka 4.4.0 broker on JDK 21 before publishing. The animation is an illustration of the message flow, not a screen recording.

title: Cloud Security Posture Assessment: Finding Misconfigurations Before Attackers Do
description:
Understand cloud security posture assessment, how misconfigurations arise, and how to keep posture healthy over time.

Many cloud breaches do not involve clever exploits. They involve something left open: a storage container with public access, a database with no password, an overly generous role. A cloud security posture assessment is designed to find exactly this kind of problem and show how your settings compare with good practice.

What “posture” means

Security posture is the overall state of your defenses at a point in time. In the cloud, much of it comes down to configuration: how services are set up, who can access them, what is logged, and how data is protected. Because configuration can be changed in minutes, posture can shift just as quickly.

Why misconfigurations are so common

Several factors combine:

Speed. Teams deploy fast and may skip reviews.
Complexity. Providers offer hundreds of services, each with its own settings.
Defaults. Some defaults favor convenience over security.
Decentralization. Many teams have the ability to create resources.
Human error. A single checkbox can change exposure.
Temporary changes. A rule opened for testing never gets closed.

None of these indicate negligence. They are natural side effects of flexible platforms.

What a posture assessment looks at

The review compares live settings with benchmarks and internal standards. Typical areas:

Storage and database access permissions.
Encryption settings and key policies.
Network rules and public exposure.
Identity configuration and privileged roles.
Logging and monitoring status.
Patch and image status for compute.
Account-level settings, such as organization policies.

Benchmarks and standards

Assessors rarely invent criteria from scratch. Common references include CIS Benchmarks, provider best-practice guides, and regulatory control sets. Using recognized baselines makes results defensible and comparable across time.

Point-in-time versus continuous

A one-time assessment reveals the current state. It is valuable for establishing a baseline and finding serious issues quickly. But posture drifts. Continuous monitoring uses automated tools to check configurations repeatedly and alert when something changes.

A balanced approach often works best:

Run a full assessment to understand the baseline.
Fix high-risk issues.
Implement continuous checks for the most important rules.
Repeat deeper reviews periodically.

Reading the results sensibly

Posture tools can produce large numbers of findings. Not all are equally important. Prioritize using these questions:

Is the resource exposed to the internet?
Does it hold sensitive data?
Could the issue be combined with others to form an attack path?
Is there a simple fix?

A medium-severity issue on a public system holding customer data may deserve attention before a high-severity issue on an isolated sandbox.

Attack paths and combined risk

Individual misconfigurations are one thing. Combined, they can be more serious. For example, a publicly reachable virtual machine, running with an overly privileged role, in a network that can reach a sensitive database, forms a path. Good assessments highlight these chains instead of listing issues in isolation.

Reducing drift through guardrails

Prevention beats cleanup. Practical guardrails include:

Organization-level policies that block risky settings, such as public storage.
Infrastructure-as-code with automated checks before deployment.
Approved templates for common services.
Limited permissions to create or change high-risk resources.
Alerts when critical settings change.

Ownership

Findings stall when no one owns them. Tag resources with owners and teams so that issues can be routed quickly. Track fix times and share simple metrics, such as the number of open high-risk findings and average time to resolve.

Exceptions

Sometimes a risky setting is intentional, such as a public website bucket. Record these as documented exceptions with an owner, a reason, and a review date. This keeps reports clean and prevents repeated debate.

Measuring progress

Useful posture metrics include:

Percentage of resources compliant with the baseline.
Number of public-facing resources, and how many are justified.
Share of accounts with logging enabled.
Time to remediate critical findings.
Count of recurring issues, which signals a process gap.

Closing perspective

Posture is not a score to chase for its own sake. It is a practical view of how exposed you are right now. Regular assessment, sensible guardrails, and clear ownership keep small configuration errors from becoming large incidents.

title: NestJS 12.2: Why validationError.target Is Now undefined
description:
A NestJS app upgrades from @nestjs/core 12.1 to 12.2 — npm i @nestjs/core@latest @nestjs/common@latest, nothing else touched. The test suite stays green. In production, an audit log that has recorded every failed signup for months — the field that failed, the message, and the full payload the user actually submitted — starts writing submittedPayload: undefined on every single entry. No exception, no crash, no warning in the logs. The validation itself still works exactly as before: bad input still gets rejected with a 400. Only the forensic trail disappeared.

This is written against @nestjs/core 12.2.0 (verified 2026-10-20 via npm view @nestjs/core dist-tags and the official v12.2.0 release notes; 12.0.0 shipped 2026-08-27, and the 11.x line remains on the legacy npm tag at 11.2.7). The change described here — validationError.target defaulting to false — is listed by name in that release's "new defaults and behaviour changes" section, not inferred from a diff. It applies to the class-validator-based ValidationPipe only; it does not touch the newer StandardSchemaValidationPipe covered in an earlier episode of this series.

What you'll learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain exactly what target, value, and property each mean on a class-validator ValidationError, and which of them NestJS's own built-in exceptionFactory actually uses
  • State precisely why @nestjs/core 12.2 changed validationError.target's default to false, in the maintainers' own words
  • Fix a custom exceptionFactory that silently breaks on the upgrade, without just disabling the new default
  • Restore the pre-12.2 behavior deliberately, globally or per pipe, when you genuinely need it
  • Place this change correctly on the request lifecycle's pipes stage, and rule out the two other places it could be confused for a bug

Who this is for

You've registered a ValidationPipe — global or scoped — against class-validator DTOs at least once, and ideally you've written or read a custom exceptionFactory. If you haven't read this series' NestJS request lifecycle episode, it maps exactly where a pipe runs relative to guards, interceptors, and filters — useful background, but this article stands on its own.

Table of contents

  • The problem: an exceptionFactory that used to work
  • The mental model: target, value, and property are three different things
  • Stage 1: why 12.2 changed the default
  • Stage 2: fixing the broken exceptionFactory
  • Stage 3: restoring the old behavior on purpose
  • Stage 4: the quieter 12.2 changes riding along
  • Edge cases and gotchas
  • Best practices
  • FAQ
  • Cheat sheet
  • Key takeaways

The problem: an exceptionFactory that used to work

Here's the pipe registration behind the audit log in the intro, unchanged across the upgrade:

// main.ts
app.useGlobalPipes(
  new ValidationPipe({
    exceptionFactory: (errors) => {
      const first = errors[0];
      auditLog.record({
        field: first.property,
        message: Object.values(first.constraints ?? {})[0],
        // this line is what broke — quietly
        submittedPayload: first.target,
      });
      return new BadRequestException(errors);
    },
  }),
);

Before 12.2, first.target was the whole object class-validator had just validated — the full DTO instance built from the request body, every field included, whether it passed or failed. That made it an easy, if slightly lazy, way to log "here's exactly what the user sent" next to the one field that failed. After 12.2, with nothing else in the application touched, first.target is undefined. submittedPayload: undefined is syntactically valid, so nothing throws — the audit log entry is just worse than it was.

The mental model: target, value, and property are three different things

The mental model: a class-validator ValidationError is a small record for one failing property, and it can carry up to four separate pieces of information about that failure — and only one of them changed in 12.2:

  1. property — the name of the field that failed, e.g. "email". Always present. Unaffected by this change.
  2. constraints — a map of rule name to human-readable message, e.g. { isEmail: "email must be an email" }. Always present. Unaffected.
  3. value — the actual value that was submitted for that one field, e.g. "not-an-email". This is scoped to the failing property alone. Unaffected by the 12.2 change.
  4. target — not the field's value, but the entire object being validated, with every property, whether it passed or failed. This is the one @nestjs/core 12.2 now suppresses by default.

That distinction is the whole article: value tells you what was wrong with the one field that failed; target repeats the complete request body on every single error in the array. A DTO with three failing fields used to produce three ValidationError objects, each one carrying a full copy of the same object. NestJS's own source comment on the change states the reasoning plainly: "the target of an error is the whole object it was found in, so an exception factory that sends the errors would repeat that object." Repeating it isn't just noisy — it's also how a request body with a password field, a token, or any other sensitive value ends up duplicated into every validation error a naive exceptionFactory forwards to a client or a log.

Stage 1: why 12.2 changed the default

Before @nestjs/core 12.2, ValidationPipe didn't configure validationError for you at all — it passed your validatorOptions straight through to class-validator's validate(), and class-validator's own long-standing default includes target. Since 12.2, ValidationPipe.transform() builds that option itself, and your own setting — if you have one — wins:

// @nestjs/common's ValidationPipe, from 12.2.0 onward (simplified)
const errors = await validate(object, {
  ...this.validatorOptions,
  validationError: {
    target: false, // the new default
    ...this.validatorOptions.validationError, // your setting, if any, overrides it
  },
});

Key concept: this is a default you can always override, not a removed feature. If you never touch validationError, you now get target: false. If you explicitly configure validationError: { target: true } on your ValidationPipe, that object sits on top of the spread above and wins, on every version from 12.2 onward.

Stage 2: fixing the broken exceptionFactory

The honest fix usually isn't restoring target — it's noticing that target was the wrong tool for the job. The audit log wanted "what did the user submit," and that's exactly what value already gives you, scoped to the field that actually failed, with no risk of dragging unrelated fields (passwords, tokens) along for the ride:

app.useGlobalPipes(
  new ValidationPipe({
    exceptionFactory: (errors) => {
      const first = errors[0];
      auditLog.record({
        field: first.property,
        message: Object.values(first.constraints ?? {})[0],
        submittedValue: first.value, // scoped to this field — works on every 12.x
      });
      return new BadRequestException(errors);
    },
  }),
);

Key concept: value was never touched by the 12.2 change, on any version. If your exceptionFactory only needs to know what the failing field contained, switching from target to value fixes the bug today and keeps working on whatever the default does next.

If you genuinely need the whole object — reconstructing the full attempted request for a support ticket, say — read on.

Stage 3: restoring the old behavior on purpose

When the full object really is the requirement, say so explicitly instead of relying on an implicit default that already changed once:

app.useGlobalPipes(
  new ValidationPipe({
    validationError: { target: true }, // explicit — survives future default changes
    exceptionFactory: (errors) => {
      const first = errors[0];
      auditLog.record({
        field: first.property,
        message: Object.values(first.constraints ?? {})[0],
        submittedPayload: first.target, // present again, on purpose
      });
      return new BadRequestException(errors);
    },
  }),
);

Key concept: this is scoped to wherever you construct that particular ValidationPipe. A global pipe with validationError: { target: true } restores the old behavior app-wide; a route-scoped @UsePipes(new ValidationPipe({ validationError: { target: true } })) restores it only there, leaving the global pipe on the new, leaner default.

Stage 4: the quieter 12.2 changes riding along

target isn't the only ValidationPipe default the same release changed. Two more are worth knowing before you assume a 400 you're suddenly seeing is a bug in your code:

new ValidationPipe({
  // New in 12.2 — caps how long the combined message string can get.
  // Past this, extra messages are replaced with one "omitted" entry.
  maxErrorMessagesLength: 1_000_000, // this is already the default
});

The other: sending an array or a bare primitive where a validated class is expected now gets a 400 instead of silently passing an unvalidated value through. If a route's DTO is CreateUserDto and the body arrives as [1, 2, 3] or the string "oops", 12.2 rejects it at the pipe instead of letting it reach the handler shaped nothing like the DTO. Both changes ship in the same release and share the same spirit as the target default: stop assuming more than class-validator was actually asked to check.

Edge cases and gotchas

  • The built-in exceptionFactory was never affected. @nestjs/common's own default error formatter — the one ValidationPipe uses when you don't pass your own — only ever reads property and constraints to build its message array. If you've never written a custom exceptionFactory, this entire change is invisible to you.
  • Nested DTOs still carry children, not a nested target. A failure on address.zip produces a ValidationError with children: [{ property: 'address', children: [{ property: 'zip', ... }] }]; target suppression applies at every level of that tree the same way.
  • This is specific to class-validator's ValidationPipe. StandardSchemaValidationPipe (covered in an earlier episode) validates with a Standard Schema library's own ~standard.validate(), which has no target concept at all — nothing here applies to it.
  • A pipe constructed before you set the option doesn't retroactively pick it up. validationError is read once, in the constructor's resolved options — set it when you call new ValidationPipe({ ... }), not after.
  • Logging error.target to the console for local debugging is still fine. The change doesn't remove the data from the validation run itself — it only removes it from what reaches exceptionFactory by default. console.log statements inside your own services that build the object from the raw request body are unaffected either way.

Best practices

  • Default to error.value, not error.target, in any exceptionFactory you write. It's scoped to the one field that failed, was never affected by this change, and can't accidentally leak an unrelated sensitive field.
  • Never echo the full submitted payload back to the client in an error response, with or without this default — a validation error is exactly the response an attacker can use to fingerprint which fields your DTO expects.
  • Set validationError: { target: true } explicitly, and only, where you've confirmed you need it — an internal audit log or a support tool, never a response body a client sees.
  • Audit every custom exceptionFactory in the codebase before upgrading to 12.2, the same way you'd check for any other breaking default: grep -rn "exceptionFactory" src/ and look for .target on the result.
  • Pin the behavior you rely on, not the default. The target: true default existed for years and still changed once; writing it explicitly means the next default change can't surprise you again.

FAQ

Does this break validation itself, or just error reporting?

Just error reporting. Validation still runs exactly the same way, and the HTTP response code and the fact that invalid requests get rejected are unchanged. Only what a custom exceptionFactory can read off each error changed.

Will my app silently stop validating anything after this upgrade?

No. target being undefined has nothing to do with whether validation ran — it only affects what one specific field on the resulting error object contains.

Does error.value ever get suppressed the same way?

No. The 12.2 release notes and the pipe's own source only change the target default; value — the specific field's submitted value — is untouched on every 12.x version.

Is this in the official migration guide, or just the release notes?

It's listed in the v12.2.0 release notes under that release's own "new defaults and behaviour changes," since it's a minor-version default change rather than a major-version breaking change requiring a migration guide entry.

Can I set validationError.target per route instead of globally?

Yes — pass the option to a ValidationPipe instance scoped with @UsePipes() on a controller or a single handler, the same way any other ValidationPipe option can be scoped.

Cheat sheet

Task Code Notes
Check if your code is affected grep -rn "exceptionFactory" src/ Only custom factories reading .target are affected
Fix forward (recommended) Read error.value instead of error.target Scoped to the failing field; unaffected by this change
Restore old behavior, globally new ValidationPipe({ validationError: { target: true } }) Register once, in main.ts
Restore old behavior, one route @UsePipes(new ValidationPipe({ validationError: { target: true } })) Leaves the global pipe on the new default
Confirm the built-in factory is unaffected Don't pass exceptionFactory at all The default formatter only ever used property + constraints
target vs value target = whole submitted object · value = one field's value Only target changed its default in 12.2
Other 12.2 ValidationPipe defaults maxErrorMessagesLength (new), array/primitive → 400 (new) Same release, same "stop assuming more than was checked" theme 
// main.ts — explicit, upgrade-proof configuration
app.useGlobalPipes(
  new ValidationPipe({
    // Only set this if something genuinely needs the whole submitted object.
    // validationError: { target: true },
    exceptionFactory: (errors) => {
      const first = errors[0];
      return new BadRequestException({
        field: first.property,
        message: Object.values(first.constraints ?? {})[0],
        submittedValue: first.value, // not first.target
      });
    },
  }),
);

Key takeaways

  • @nestjs/core 12.2 defaults validationError.target to false on ValidationPipe — a deliberate change, documented in the v12.2.0 release notes, not a regression.
  • target is the entire validated object; value is the one failing field's value. Only target's default changed; value never moves.
  • NestJS's own built-in exceptionFactory never read target — this only bites a hand-written one, which is exactly why it fails silently instead of at boot.
  • Fix forward by reading error.value, or restore the old behavior deliberately with validationError: { target: true }, globally or per route.
  • This lives entirely in the pipes stage of the request lifecycle — guards, interceptors, and filters are untouched by it.

Ending

The bug in the intro was never really about NestJS removing something — it was about a default quietly doing less work on an app's behalf than it used to, in a way that compiles, ships, and only shows up as a slightly worse log entry months later. That's the same shape of risk every implicit default carries: it's free until the day it changes, and the fix is almost always the same one — write down what you actually need (error.value, not "whatever target happens to contain") instead of leaning on whatever the framework currently hands you.

Has a NestJS minor-version upgrade ever changed behavior you didn't know you were depending on? Drop it in the comments.
