title: HTML Semantic Tags Explained: header, nav, main, article, section and footer
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

HTML semantic tags are elements that clearly describe their meaning and the type of content inside them, for both browsers and people reading the code. Tags such as header, nav, main, article, section and footer tell everyone what each part of a page is for, without guessing from class names. A header is for introductory content, nav is for main links, main holds the primary content, article holds a self contained piece, section groups related content, and footer holds closing information. Using them makes your pages easier to read, more accessible for screen readers, and clearer for search engines.

What Are Semantic Tags, in Simple Words?

The word semantic simply means related to meaning. A semantic tag carries meaning in its name. When you see a nav element in code, you instantly know it contains navigation links. When you see a generic div element, you know almost nothing. It could be a menu, a product card, a warning box, or just a wrapper someone added at midnight and forgot about.

Before HTML5, developers built almost every layout with div elements and added class names like header or footer to explain them. That worked visually, but the browser had no idea what those boxes really were. HTML5 gave us proper elements with built in meaning, so structure is clear in the markup itself.

If you are still getting comfortable with how a page is put together, it helps to first understand the difference between HTML, CSS and JavaScript. HTML provides this structure and meaning, CSS styles it, and JavaScript adds behaviour. Semantic tags belong firmly to the HTML side of that team.

Why Semantic Tags Matter

First, accessibility. Screen readers use landmarks such as header, nav, main and footer to help users jump straight to the part they need, instead of listening to every link on every page. That is a real kindness, not just a technical detail.

Second, search engines read your structure to understand a page. Clear structure does not magically rank you first, and anyone who promises that is selling magic beans. It does make content easier to parse, which supports good SEO. Third, maintainability: six months later, main and article explain themselves, while a pile of div elements named box2-wrapper-final does not. Browsers can also use the structure for reader modes that pull out the main article cleanly.

The HTML reference page on MDN, developer.mozilla.org, which lists the semantic elements.

The Main Tags: header, nav and main

The header element represents introductory content for a page or a section. On a full page, it usually holds the logo, site title and search box. An article can also have its own header, with its title, author and publish date.

The nav element is for a major block of navigation links, such as the main menu or a table of contents. You do not need to wrap every small group of links in it. The full list of elements is documented in the HTML reference on MDN at developer.mozilla.org, which is worth bookmarking.

The main element holds the dominant, unique content of the page. There should be only one visible main per page, and it should not include repeated parts such as sidebars, logos or the main menu.

article, section and footer Explained

An article represents a complete, self contained piece that could make sense on its own if shared separately. Blog posts, news stories, reviews and comments are classic examples. A simple test helps: if you copied that block elsewhere and it still made sense, it is probably an article.

A section groups related content together, usually with its own heading. Use it to divide a long page into chapters, such as features, pricing and testimonials. If you are grouping things only for styling, a plain div is still the honest choice.

The footer holds closing information, such as copyright text, contact details and policy links. An article footer might hold the author bio or tags. Two helpful relatives are aside, for loosely related content such as a sidebar, and figure, which groups media with its caption.

A Complete Page Layout Example

Here is a small but complete page that uses all six tags together. Notice how the structure tells the story of the page before any CSS is added. Our guide to CSS Flexbox explained with examples is a good next step for styling it.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>My Simple Blog</title>
</head>
<body>
  <header>
    <h1>My Simple Blog</h1>
    <p>Notes on learning web development.</p>
  </header>
  <nav>
    <a href="/">Home</a>
    <a href="/about">About</a>
    <a href="/contact">Contact</a>
  </nav>
  <main>
    <article>
      <header>
        <h2>My First Post</h2>
        <p>Published on 6 November 2026</p>
      </header>
      <section>
        <h3>Introduction</h3>
        <p>This is the opening part of the post.</p>
      </section>
      <section>
        <h3>Main Points</h3>
        <p>This section holds the key ideas.</p>
      </section>
      <footer>
        <p>Written by a beginner developer.</p>
      </footer>
    </article>
  </main>
  <footer>
    <p>Copyright 2026 My Simple Blog.</p>
  </footer>
</body>
</html>

Notice that header and footer appear twice, once for the page and once inside the article, and that is perfectly valid. Also notice the heading order: h1, then h2, then h3. Keeping headings in order helps readers and assistive tools follow the outline.

Semantic Tags vs Generic div Elements

Div elements are not banned, and you do not need to delete every one of them in a panic. A div is still the right tool for a pure styling wrapper with no meaning. The point is to choose the semantic element when a clear one exists, and fall back to div only when none fits.

Need Semantic choice Generic div version
Top of a page or article header, meaning is clear to browsers and screen readers div with a class, meaning only in the class name
Main navigation links nav, announced as a navigation landmark div with a class, no landmark created
Primary page content main, one per page, easy to jump to div with a class, tools must guess its role
Independent piece of content article, can stand alone and be shared div with a class, relationship stays unclear
Thematic group with a heading section, groups related content clearly div with a class, grouping is visual only
Closing information footer, recognised as closing content div with a class, no built in meaning

The visual result can look identical in both columns. The difference is what the code communicates behind the scenes. MDN also explains grouping in its guide to content categories on MDN.

Common Mistakes and Good Habits

A common mistake is using section for everything. If a block has no heading and no real meaning, a div is cleaner. Another mistake is having more than one main, or placing the site header and menu inside main.

Avoid skipping heading levels just to change font size. Use CSS for size, and keep headings in order. Do not replace a button with a styled div either: a real button gives you keyboard support for free.

Good habits are simple. Sketch each page outline with header, nav, main and footer, then add article and section where content naturally splits. Ask whether the structure still makes sense with styling removed. If it does, you are on the right track.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do semantic tags change how a page looks?

No, not by themselves. Most semantic elements look like plain block boxes by default. You still use CSS to style them, just as you would style a div.

Can I use more than one header or footer on a page?

Yes. A page can have a header and footer for the whole page, and each article or section can have its own. Each one belongs to its nearest parent section.

How many main elements can a page have?

Only one visible main element per page. It must hold the unique, primary content of that page, not menus, logos or other repeated blocks.

Is a section better than a div?

Use section when you are grouping related content, usually with a heading. Use div when the group exists only for styling and carries no meaning of its own.

Do semantic tags help SEO?

They help search engines understand your structure more clearly, which supports good SEO. They are not a ranking shortcut, so combine them with helpful content and clear headings.

Conclusion

Semantic tags are a small habit with a long payoff. Use header for introductions, nav for major links, main for the unique content, article for self contained pieces, section for related groups, and footer for closing information. Your code becomes easier to read, your pages become kinder to assistive tools, and search engines get a clearer picture. Start with your next small page, write the outline first, and let the tags describe the content honestly. That is most of the job done.

title: TypeScript `const` Enums Are Deprecated: What to Migrate to and Why the Compiler Team Made the Call
description:
TypeScript const Enums Are Deprecated: What to Migrate to and Why the Compiler Team Made the Call

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

TypeScript const enums promised zero-runtime cost for constant values, but they broke isolated module compilation and caused runtime errors downstream. The compiler team deprecated them not because of theoretical purity, but because they caused production failures when developers mixed const enums with modern build tools like esbuild, swc, and Vite. A const enum in a library's .d.ts file becomes a landmine: the consuming project inlines values at compile time but ships code that expects those enum objects to exist at runtime. When versions drift between compile and runtime dependencies, conditionals take the wrong branch and silent data corruption follows.

The problem diagram shows the failure path:

const enum compilation breaks when compiler cannot see declaration file

The solution eliminates compile-time inlining and removes the dependency on cross-module information:

union types with as const provide type safety without runtime dependencies

TypeScript const enum deprecation warning in compiler output

The migration path depends on whether the enum appears in a library or application code. Libraries must remove const enums entirely because they cannot control how downstream consumers compile their code. Application code can migrate incrementally, starting with high-risk modules that interact with external dependencies.

Key Takeaways

  • Const enums fail in isolated module compilation because the compiler cannot access cross-file information to inline values, causing unresolved imports at runtime.
  • The TypeScript team deprecated const enums to prevent version drift bugs where compile-time values differ from runtime values, leading to wrong conditional branches and data corruption.
  • Union types with as const provide equivalent type safety without runtime objects, making them compatible with modern build tools that compile modules in isolation.
  • Libraries shipping .d.ts files with const enums force downstream consumers to disable isolatedModules, breaking compatibility with esbuild, swc, and other fast compilers.
  • The preserveConstEnums compiler option emits runtime objects but defeats the original zero-cost promise and creates inconsistent behavior between development and production builds.

The Technical Problems With Const Enums

Const enums operate by replacing references with literal values at compile time. When the compiler encounters Direction.Up, it substitutes the numeric literal 0 directly into the emitted JavaScript. This inlining removes the enum object from the output entirely, which sounds efficient until modules compile independently.

The TypeScript documentation on enums explains that const enums "are completely removed during compilation" and "members are inlined at use sites." The removal happens because the compiler treats the enum as a macro expansion rather than a runtime value.

const enum inlining requires cross-module visibility to substitute values

The inlining breaks when the compiler processes files in isolation. Modern build tools compile TypeScript modules independently to maximize parallelism. A module that imports a const enum from another file cannot inline the values because it never reads the declaring file. The import statement stays in the output JavaScript, referencing an enum object that was never emitted.

The failure mode appears when libraries publish ambient const enums in declaration files. A library's .d.ts file declares the const enum shape but provides no implementation. The consuming project's compiler sees the declaration and inlines values based on that snapshot. At runtime, the library's JavaScript code contains no enum object because the const modifier stripped it during the library's build. The consuming code executes with hardcoded values that may not match the library's current version.

Version drift amplifies the problem. A project compiles against version 1.2 of a library, inlining Status.Active = 5. The deployment runtime loads version 1.3 where Status.Active changed to 7. The compiled code still checks if (status === 5) but the library now returns 7 for active status. The conditional silently fails and the application continues executing on the wrong path.

The isolatedModules compiler option exists specifically to catch these situations. When enabled, TypeScript rejects code patterns that only work with whole-program compilation. The documentation states that isolatedModules "is fundamentally incompatible with ambient const enums" because inlining requires seeing the enum definition.

Build tools choose isolated module compilation for speed. The TypeScript 5.0 release notes introduced the verbatimModuleSyntax option to make module semantics explicit and predictable across different compilers. The new option removes import elision and treats all module syntax literally, which makes const enum inlining impossible.

The TypeScript team deprecated const enums because they require whole-program knowledge in an ecosystem moving toward isolated compilation. The tradeoff between zero-cost abstractions and compilation speed tilted decisively toward speed when developers started hitting production failures from version drift.

How Const Enums Break in Isolated Module Compilation

The breakage becomes concrete when examining actual compiler output. A const enum in one file and an import in another produces different JavaScript depending on whether the compiler processes them together or separately.

// constants.ts
export const enum Direction {
  Up = 0,
  Down = 1,
  Left = 2,
  Right = 3,
}

// movement.ts
import { Direction } from "./constants";

export function move(direction: Direction): string {
  switch (direction) {
    case Direction.Up:
      return "moving up";
    case Direction.Down:
      return "moving down";
    case Direction.Left:
      return "moving left";
    case Direction.Right:
      return "moving right";
  }
}

When TypeScript compiles both files together, the output for movement.ts replaces enum references with literals:

// movement.js (whole-program compilation)
export function move(direction) {
  switch (direction) {
    case 0: // Direction.Up
      return "moving up";
    case 1: // Direction.Down
      return "moving down";
    case 2: // Direction.Left
      return "moving left";
    case 3: // Direction.Right
      return "moving right";
  }
}

The constants.ts file emits nothing because the const enum disappears entirely. The JavaScript output contains no Direction object and no export statement. This works only because the compiler inlined the values before generating code.

When a build tool compiles movement.ts in isolation, it cannot inline the values because it never reads constants.ts. The output keeps the import statement:

// movement.js (isolated module compilation)
import { Direction } from "./constants";

export function move(direction) {
  switch (direction) {
    case Direction.Up:
      return "moving up";
    case Direction.Down:
      return "moving down";
    case Direction.Left:
      return "moving left";
    case Direction.Right:
      return "moving right";
  }
}

At runtime, the JavaScript engine tries to import Direction from constants.js. That file exports nothing because the const enum was stripped during the library's compilation. The import fails with an unresolved module specifier or imports an undefined value, causing the switch statement to match no cases.

Example of runtime error from const enum in isolated compilation

The isolatedModules documentation calls out this specific failure. The compiler option enables a check that rejects const enum imports from external modules. The error message reads: "Cannot access ambient const enums when the '--isolatedModules' flag is provided."

The ambient qualifier matters. An ambient const enum appears in a declaration file without an implementation. Libraries ship .d.ts files containing const enum declarations, expecting consumers to inline the values. The consumer's compiler sees only the declaration and has no way to verify the values match the library's runtime code.

The fix requires either removing the const modifier to emit a runtime object, or migrating to an alternative that works without cross-file inlining. The next sections cover both migration paths and when to use each one.

Migration Path 1: Union Types With as const

Union types combined with the as const assertion replicate const enum type safety without emitting runtime code. The pattern defines an object with as const to create literal types, then extracts a union type from the object's values.

// Before: const enum
const enum Direction {
  Up = 0,
  Down = 1,
  Left = 2,
  Right = 3,
}

// After: union type with as const
const Direction = {
  Up: 0,
  Down: 1,
  Left: 2,
  Right: 3,
} as const;

type Direction = typeof Direction[keyof typeof Direction];

The as const assertion tells the compiler to infer the most specific type possible. Without it, TypeScript widens the type to number. With as const, each property gets its exact literal type: 0, 1, 2, 3. The type extraction typeof Direction[keyof typeof Direction] produces the union 0 | 1 | 2 | 3.

union type extraction flow from const object to type parameter

Functions that previously accepted the enum type now accept the extracted union type. The type safety remains identical:

function move(direction: Direction): string {
  switch (direction) {
    case Direction.Up:
      return "moving up";
    case Direction.Down:
      return "moving down";
    case Direction.Left:
      return "moving left";
    case Direction.Right:
      return "moving right";
  }
}

move(Direction.Up); // type-safe
move(Direction.Down); // type-safe
move(5); // error: Argument of type '5' is not assignable to parameter of type '0 | 1 | 2 | 3'

The TypeScript compiler enforces that callers pass only the valid direction values. The compiled JavaScript contains a runtime object with the direction properties, making it compatible with isolated module compilation:

const Direction = {
  Up: 0,
  Down: 1,
  Left: 2,
  Right: 3,
};

function move(direction) {
  switch (direction) {
    case Direction.Up:
      return "moving up";
    case Direction.Down:
      return "moving down";
    case Direction.Left:
      return "moving left";
    case Direction.Right:
      return "moving right";
  }
}

The object exists at runtime, so imports resolve correctly even when modules compile in isolation. The tradeoff is a small runtime cost: the object occupies memory and requires a property access instead of using an immediate literal value. For most applications, the cost disappears in the noise of other object allocations.

String-valued enums migrate the same way:

// Before: string const enum
const enum LogLevel {
  Debug = "DEBUG",
  Info = "INFO",
  Warn = "WARN",
  Error = "ERROR",
}

// After: union type with as const
const LogLevel = {
  Debug: "DEBUG",
  Info: "INFO",
  Warn: "WARN",
  Error: "ERROR",
} as const;

type LogLevel = typeof LogLevel[keyof typeof LogLevel];

The union type becomes "DEBUG" | "INFO" | "WARN" | "ERROR", which the compiler treats as distinct literal types. The TypeScript handbook on enums notes that "an object with as const could suffice" for many enum use cases, and this migration proves the point.

The pattern works in libraries because it requires no special compiler behavior. A library exports the const object and the type, and consumers import both normally. No inlining happens and no cross-file dependencies exist. The module system handles the runtime object like any other export.

Migration Path 2: Plain const Objects

When type safety matters less than convenience, a plain const object without type extraction provides a simpler migration. The object still gets as const to freeze its type, but no union type extraction happens.

// Before: const enum
const enum HttpStatus {
  OK = 200,
  Created = 201,
  BadRequest = 400,
  Unauthorized = 401,
  NotFound = 404,
}

// After: plain const object
const HttpStatus = {
  OK: 200,
  Created: 201,
  BadRequest: 400,
  Unauthorized: 401,
  NotFound: 404,
} as const;

Functions accept number instead of the specific union type:

function handleResponse(status: number): void {
  if (status === HttpStatus.OK) {
    console.log("Success");
  } else if (status === HttpStatus.NotFound) {
    console.log("Resource not found");
  }
}

The compiler allows any number, not just the defined status codes. This loses type safety but matches the original const enum behavior more closely. Const enums with numeric values did not prevent passing arbitrary numbers either, they just provided autocomplete for the defined constants.

plain const object migration removes type extraction step

The JavaScript output includes the object exactly as written:

const HttpStatus = {
  OK: 200,
  Created: 201,
  BadRequest: 400,
  Unauthorized: 401,
  NotFound: 404,
};

function handleResponse(status) {
  if (status === HttpStatus.OK) {
    console.log("Success");
  } else if (status === HttpStatus.NotFound) {
    console.log("Resource not found");
  }
}

This pattern suits internal application code where the team controls all usage sites. The lack of type constraints speeds up refactoring because changing a value requires updating only the object definition, not every function signature that references it.

Libraries should prefer the union type approach. Exporting a plain object without extracted types gives consumers no guidance about valid values. The autocomplete shows the object properties but the type system accepts anything, leading to runtime errors when callers pass invalid values.

The const object approach also handles computed enum values better than union types. Const enums with expressions become cumbersome to migrate to unions:

// Before: const enum with computed values
const enum Permissions {
  None = 0,
  Read = 1 << 0,
  Write = 1 << 1,
  Execute = 1 << 2,
  ReadWrite = Read | Write,
}

// After: plain const object preserves expressions
const Permissions = {
  None: 0,
  Read: 1 << 0,
  Write: 1 << 1,
  Execute: 1 << 2,
  ReadWrite: (1 << 0) | (1 << 1),
} as const;

Extracting a union type here requires computing the expression results manually (1 | 2 | 4 | 3), which defeats the purpose of the named constants. The plain object keeps the expressions readable and maintains the relationship between combined flags.

Const Enums vs Regular Enums vs Modern Alternatives

The three approaches differ in runtime presence, type safety, and compatibility with modern build tools. The table summarizes the key distinctions:

Feature Const Enum Regular Enum Union Type with as const Plain const Object
Runtime object No Yes Yes Yes
Type safety Compile-time only Full Full None
Isolated modules Breaks Works Works Works
Bundle size impact None Small object Small object Small object
Reverse mapping No Yes No No
Library-safe No Yes Yes Conditional

comparison flowchart showing const enum versus modern alternatives

Regular enums emit a runtime object that supports reverse mapping. Numeric enums create a two-way mapping between names and values:

enum Direction {
  Up,
  Down,
  Left,
  Right,
}

console.log(Direction.Up); // 0
console.log(Direction[0]); // "Up"

The compiled JavaScript contains an immediately invoked function expression that builds the bidirectional object:

var Direction;
(function (Direction) {
  Direction[Direction["Up"] = 0] = "Up";
  Direction[Direction["Down"] = 1] = "Down";
  Direction[Direction["Left"] = 2] = "Left";
  Direction[Direction["Right"] = 3] = "Right";
})(Direction || (Direction = {}));

This flexibility comes with a larger bundle footprint. The generated code uses more bytes than a simple object literal. Most applications never use reverse mapping, making the extra code pure overhead.

Union types with as const provide the same compile-time type safety as enums without the reverse mapping machinery. The object literal approach generates minimal JavaScript and works identically across all compilers. The TypeScript 5.0 release notes mention that the verbatimModuleSyntax option makes module semantics predictable, and union types fit that predictability better than enums with their special compilation rules.

Plain const objects sacrifice type safety for simplicity. They work when the codebase treats the values as documentation rather than constraints. API response status codes often fall into this category because external services return arbitrary numbers anyway.

The migration path depends on the enum's role in the codebase. Enums used as discriminated union tags need full type safety and should become union types. Enums used as named constants can become plain objects. Enums with reverse mapping lookups should stay as regular enums.

What to Do With Existing Const Enum Code

Migrating a codebase with existing const enums requires assessing impact before changing code. The first step identifies where const enums appear and whether they cross module boundaries.

migration decision flowchart for const enum replacement strategy

Search the codebase for const enum declarations and catalog their locations. Distinguish between application-internal enums and enums exported from library packages. Internal enums can migrate gradually. Exported enums require immediate attention because downstream consumers may already be hitting compilation failures.

For libraries, the migration path is strict. Remove all const enums from published declaration files. The TypeScript documentation on const enums explains that const enums in .d.ts files create "subtle implications" and "pitfalls" for consumers. The practical implication is that consumers cannot use isolatedModules if they import your const enums.

The migration steps for a library:

  1. Replace const enum declarations with union types using as const
  2. Export both the const object and the extracted type
  3. Update internal code to use the new types
  4. Bump the major version because the change breaks consumers who directly accessed enum values
  5. Document the migration in the changelog

Application code has more flexibility. The preserveConstEnums compiler option provides a temporary bridge. When enabled, the compiler emits runtime objects for const enums instead of removing them entirely. This makes the code compatible with isolated module compilation while preserving the const enum syntax:

// tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "preserveConstEnums": true
  }
}

The output JavaScript now includes the enum object:

const Direction = {
  Up: 0,
  Down: 1,
  Left: 2,
  Right: 3,
};

The const enum keyword becomes equivalent to a regular enum in terms of output, but the TypeScript compiler still inlines references during type checking. This creates an inconsistency where development builds inline values but production builds use the runtime object.

The better approach for application code migrates const enums to union types one module at a time. Start with modules that interact with external dependencies or appear in the critical path. These modules cause the most visible failures when const enums break.

The migration preserves type safety by using the union type extraction pattern. Tests catch any mismatches where code passed invalid values that const enums silently accepted. Strict TypeScript configurations with strict enabled surface these issues immediately.

For large codebases, automated refactoring tools can handle the mechanical transformation. A codemod script searches for const enum declarations, generates the equivalent as const object and type extraction, and updates references throughout the codebase. The TypeScript compiler API provides the parsing and type information needed to build such tools.

The investment in migration pays off in build performance and reliability. Codebases that remove const enums can enable isolatedModules and use faster build tools. The reduction in compilation time often measures in seconds for medium-sized projects and minutes for large monorepos.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I still use regular enums without the const modifier?

Yes. Regular enums work correctly with isolated module compilation because they emit runtime objects. The TypeScript compiler team deprecated only const enums due to their specific inlining behavior. Regular enums remain a supported feature with no planned deprecation.

Does preserveConstEnums make const enums safe to use?

No. The preserveConstEnums option emits runtime objects but does not solve the version drift problem. If your library ships .d.ts files with const enums, downstream consumers still inline values at compile time based on your declaration file. The runtime object your library includes may have different values, causing the same silent failures const enums are known for.

Why not just ban const enums with a linter rule?

Linter rules prevent new const enums but do not address existing ones or const enums in dependencies. The TypeScript compiler deprecated const enums to signal that the feature causes real problems and the team will not fix edge cases. Migration to alternatives provides a permanent solution rather than piecemeal prevention.

Will regular enums eventually be deprecated too?

The TypeScript team has not announced plans to deprecate regular enums. The TypeScript handbook still documents enums as a standard feature alongside the as const alternative, giving developers a choice based on their needs. Const enums failed because they broke fundamental module system assumptions, not because enums as a concept are flawed.

How do union types handle bitwise operations like flags?

Union types cannot represent computed values in the type itself, so bitwise flag operations work better with plain const objects. Define the base flags as separate properties and combine them at runtime. The type system sees only the defined properties, not the computed combinations. This limitation makes plain objects more practical than union types for permission flags and similar use cases.

The Future of Enums in TypeScript

The TypeScript compiler team's decision to deprecate const enums reflects a broader shift toward compilation models that prioritize speed and simplicity over optimization tricks. Modern JavaScript bundlers and build tools achieve better performance through parallelization and caching than through aggressive inlining. The zero-runtime-cost promise of const enums mattered more when JavaScript environments were slower and every byte counted.

Union types with as const emerged as the recommended pattern because they align with JavaScript's object literals while providing TypeScript's type safety. The pattern requires no special compiler support and works identically whether the code compiles with tsc, esbuild, swc, or any future compiler. Developers can reason about the code's behavior without understanding const enum inlining rules.

Related posts on TypeScript's evolution cover adjacent deprecation decisions. The TypeScript 6 breaking changes guide discusses other features the compiler team phased out for similar reliability reasons. The TypeScript 6 final JavaScript release explains how new ECMAScript proposals influence TypeScript's feature set. The TypeScript decorators legacy to TC39 migration shows another case where TypeScript deprecated an experimental feature in favor of the standardized alternative.

Const enums served their purpose when build pipelines were simpler and projects rarely mixed compilers. The ecosystem has moved on. The migration to union types or const objects removes a source of subtle bugs and makes TypeScript codebases more portable across different build tools. Teams that complete the migration gain faster build times and fewer production surprises. The const enum deprecation pushes TypeScript toward patterns that scale with modern development workflows rather than fighting against them.

Hypervisor-enforced capabilities limit agents to specific actions without storing secrets in the workload. Initial releases cover scoped command execution and workload identity; credential-brokered API access will follow.

title: I checked 14 free cloud hosting platforms against their own pricing pages. 8 need no card.
description:
TL;DR: Fourteen free cloud hosting and deployment platforms, each checked against the vendor's own pricing or docs page on 26 September 2026. Eight need no card at all; the other six ask for one. The master table shows which sleep, which run Docker and what each free tier really includes, grouped into static hosts, container platforms, cloud provider free tiers and self-hosted options, with a decision framework at the end.

Last verified: 26 September 2026. Every number below was checked against the vendor's own pricing or docs page on that date. Three of the platforms in this list changed their free tier between February and June 2026, so older comparisons (including the March version of this page) are wrong in places.

Free cloud hosting still exists in 2026, but it comes in three different shapes, and most lists of free deployment platforms mix them up. Here is the two-minute answer.

  • Static site or portfolio: GitHub Pages or Cloudflare. Free, no credit card.
  • Frontend app: Vercel (non-commercial use only) or Netlify (now 300 credits a month).
  • Backend, API or Docker container, no credit card: SnapDeploy, Render, or Railway's Free plan. All three sleep or cap hours.
  • Backend with a card on file: Google Cloud Run or Azure Container Apps. Same allowance, real usage limits.
  • Free cloud server (a VM you manage): Oracle Cloud, now 2 Arm cores and 12 GB, card required.
  • Not free any more: Heroku, Fly.io, Glitch. Koyeb now asks for a card.

What changed since March 2026

  • Koyeb removed its card-free Hobby plan in February 2026; a valid card with a $29 pre-authorisation hold is now required, and sign-up defaults to the $29/month Pro plan.
  • Render replaced its plans on 23 April 2026: the free Hobby workspace now includes 5 GB of bandwidth a month instead of 100 GB. Free web services (750 hours) are unchanged.
  • Oracle Cloud cut the Always Free Arm allowance from 4 OCPUs / 24 GB to 2 OCPUs / 12 GB in June 2026, without an announcement; idle instances can be reclaimed.
  • Netlify moved all new accounts to credit-based plans on 4 September 2025: 300 credits a month, roughly 15 GB of bandwidth, and projects pause when credits run out.
  • Railway brought back a permanent Free plan on 27 August 2025: a 30-day trial with $5, then $1 of credit every month.
  • Vercel Hobby now keeps only the three most recent production deployments per project (16 September 2026).
  • Hugging Face Docker and Gradio Spaces need a paid plan since July 2026.

Master Comparison Table (verified 26 Sep 2026)

Platform Type Free tier Docker Credit card at sign-up Sleeps / restart
GitHub Pages Static 1 GB site, 100 GB/month soft limit, public repos only No No No
Cloudflare Pages / Workers Static + Workers Unlimited static requests, 500 builds/month, Workers 100k requests/day No No No
Netlify Static + Functions 300 credits/month (about 15 GB bandwidth), pauses at 0 No No No
Vercel Static + Functions 100 GB transfer, 1M invocations, 4 CPU-hours, non-commercial only No No No
SnapDeploy Container PaaS 4 containers, 100 hours/month, 10 deploys/day Yes No After 15 min idle, wakes in about 60 s
Render Container PaaS 750 hours/month, 512 MB, 5 GB bandwidth, Postgres expires after 30 days Yes No After 15 min idle, about 1 min
Railway Container PaaS $5 for 30 days, then $1/month; 1 project, 3 services Yes No (card for paid plans) No (opt-in)
Back4App Containers Container PaaS 256 MB, 0.25 shared CPU, 100 GB transfer Yes No Free container stops after 60 min per deploy
Koyeb Container PaaS 1 service, 512 MB, 0.1 vCPU; Postgres 5 h/month Yes Yes ($29 hold) After 1 h idle, 1–5 s
Google Cloud Run Serverless containers 180k vCPU-s, 360k GiB-s, 2M requests (request-based billing) Yes Yes Scales to zero
Azure Container Apps Serverless containers 180k vCPU-s, 360k GiB-s, 2M requests Yes Yes Scales to zero
AWS Lambda Functions 1M requests, 400k GB-s, always free Images up to 10 GB Yes Yes
Oracle Cloud VMs 2 Arm OCPUs, 12 GB total, plus 2 AMD micro VMs Yes (manual) Yes Idle VMs may be reclaimed
Coolify / CapRover / Dokku Self-hosted Free software; you pay for a VPS Yes Depends on the VPS No

Free Cloud Hosting, a Free Cloud Server, or a Free Deployment Platform?

People search for "free cloud hosting" and mean three different things. Knowing which one you need saves an afternoon.

Free cloud hosting for files and static sites. GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify and Vercel serve HTML, JavaScript and images from a CDN. No server runs for you. This is the only category where "free" has almost no catch.

A free cloud server. A virtual machine you log into and manage yourself. Oracle Cloud's Always Free tier is the only permanent one left with real resources, and it needs a credit card. The big cloud providers' free cloud computing services (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure) are allowances on specific services, not a free VM you keep forever.

A free deployment platform (PaaS). Also called a cloud deployment platform: you push code or a Docker image and the platform builds, runs and gives you a URL. SnapDeploy, Render, Railway and Back4App are the free PaaS and container hosting platform options that do not ask for a credit card.

Cloud Run and Azure Container Apps do the same job but require a card. This is the category the rest of this page ranks.

What "Free" Actually Means in 2026

Tier 1: Free for static sites, with limits worth reading — GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify and Vercel host static sites and frontends without asking for a credit card. The catches are new: GitHub Pages is only free in public repositories and forbids running a business on it; Netlify's Free plan is 300 credits a month and pauses your sites at zero; Vercel's Hobby plan is for non-commercial use only, and ads count as commercial.

Tier 2: Free containers with real limits — SnapDeploy, Render, Railway's Free plan and Back4App run a backend or Docker container with no credit card. Each one sleeps, caps hours, or caps resources; none of them is a production host for free.

Tier 3: Free only with a card on file — the free-tier cloud options from Google Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps, AWS Lambda and Oracle Cloud, plus Koyeb since February 2026. These free cloud services are real allowances, but you need a valid payment method and you are one misconfiguration away from a bill.

Tier 4: No longer free — Heroku (28 November 2022), Fly.io (allowances removed 7 October 2024; the trial is 2 machine-hours or 7 days), Glitch (hosting shut down 8 July 2025), Cyclic (2024) and Deta Space (2024). Hugging Face Docker Spaces joined this list in July 2026.

Category 1: Static Site Hosting

If your project is a static site, documentation page, portfolio, or frontend application, these are the best free cloud deployment options available.

GitHub Pages

Free for public repositories on GitHub Free: 1 GB site size, a soft limit of 100 GB bandwidth a month and 10 builds an hour, Jekyll built in or GitHub Actions for any generator, free custom domains with HTTPS. GitHub's docs say it is "not intended for or allowed to be used as a free web-hosting service to run your online business". Best for documentation and portfolios.

Netlify

Accounts created since 4 September 2025 are credit-based: the Free plan gives 300 credits a month with a hard limit. Bandwidth costs 20 credits per GB (so about 15 GB if you spend everything on bandwidth), each production deploy costs 15 credits, and all projects pause with a "Site not available" page when credits run out.

Serverless functions, deploy previews and custom domains with SSL are included. The old "100 GB, 300 build minutes" numbers only apply to accounts created before that date.

Vercel

The Hobby plan includes 100 GB of fast data transfer, 1 million function invocations, 4 CPU-hours of active compute and 360 GB-hours of memory a month (Fluid compute is the default since April 2025), 200 projects, 100 deployments a day and 50 domains per project. It is restricted to non-commercial personal use; adding ads or getting paid to build the site requires Pro. The obvious choice for Next.js.

Cloudflare Pages and Workers

Requests to static assets are free and unlimited, 500 builds a month, 100 custom domains per project, and the Workers free plan adds 100,000 requests a day plus a D1 database with 5 GB of storage. Cloudflare now says to start new projects with Workers (static assets included) rather than Pages; Pages still works and still accepts new projects.

Category 2: Container and PaaS Platforms

When your project needs a backend — database connections, server-side processing, WebSockets, or Docker containers — these platforms offer free tiers for deploying applications.

SnapDeploy

SnapDeploy deploys a GitHub repository (with or without a Dockerfile) or a public Docker image onto AWS Fargate. Free tier: up to 4 containers, 100 running hours a month, 10 deploys a day (5 per rolling 12 hours), 512 MB / 0.25 vCPU per container, no credit card.

Containers sleep after 15 minutes without traffic and wake in about 60 seconds when someone opens them in a browser. Custom domains, WebSockets and 24/7 uptime need Always-On, from $12 a month per container.

Managed databases are paid add-ons with a $1, 12-hour trial.

Render

750 free instance hours per workspace a month, 512 MB RAM and 0.1 CPU per web service, no credit card needed. A free service spins down after 15 minutes without traffic and takes about a minute to come back.

Since the April 2026 plan change the free Hobby workspace includes 5 GB of bandwidth a month, 500 build minutes and 2 custom domains. The free Postgres database has 1 GB of storage and expires 30 days after creation.

Dockerfile builds and WebSockets work on the free tier; free services cannot send outbound SMTP.

Railway

New accounts get a 30-day trial with $5 of usage, no card required. After that the account drops to the Free plan, reinstated on 27 August 2025: $1 of non-rollover credit a month, 1 project, 3 services, up to 1 vCPU and 0.5 GB RAM per service, 0.5 GB of volume storage and no custom domain.

Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB and Redis templates are billed from the same credit. Services do not sleep unless you turn the Serverless option on.

Hobby is $5 a month with $5 of usage included.

Back4App Containers

A free container with 256 MB RAM, 0.25 shared CPU and 100 GB of transfer, no card required. Back4App's official template notes say a free container runs for 60 minutes per deploy, so treat it as a demo host. The separate Backend-as-a-Service free tier gives a Parse database with 25,000 requests and 250 MB.

Koyeb

One free web service with 512 MB RAM, 0.1 vCPU and 2 GB of SSD, in Frankfurt or Washington only, plus a free Postgres database limited to 5 compute-hours a month. Since February 2026 an account needs a valid card (verified with a $29 pre-authorisation hold that is cancelled immediately) and sign-up defaults to the $29 a month Pro plan, which you can downgrade. The free instance scales to zero after an hour without traffic and wakes in 1 to 5 seconds.

Category 3: Cloud Provider Free Tiers

Google Cloud Run

Request-based services get 180,000 vCPU-seconds, 360,000 GiB-seconds and 2 million requests a month free, aggregated per billing account; instance-based services get 240,000 vCPU-seconds and 450,000 GiB-seconds instead. Deploys any Linux container image, or builds from source without a Dockerfile.

A billing account with a card or other payment method is required. Google publishes no cold-start figure for ordinary containers, so we do not either.

AWS Lambda

1 million requests and 400,000 GB-seconds a month, always free. Container images up to 10 GB are supported, but they must implement the Lambda runtime API and live in Amazon ECR, so this is a function model, not a container host.

Accounts created after 15 July 2025 choose a Free plan ($100 in credits, closed after six months or when the credits are gone) or a Paid plan; the Lambda allowance applies to both. A payment method is required.

Azure Container Apps

180,000 vCPU-seconds, 360,000 GiB-seconds and 2 million requests per subscription per month on the Consumption plan. An Azure account needs a phone number and a credit or non-prepaid debit card. Pick this over Cloud Run only if your team already lives in Azure.

Oracle Cloud Free Tier

Always Free now means 2 Arm OCPUs and 12 GB of RAM in total (one or two VM.Standard.A1 instances), plus up to two AMD micro VMs and 200 GB of block storage. The 4-OCPU / 24 GB allowance ended on 15 June 2026.

Oracle reclaims instances that stay under 20 percent CPU, network and memory for seven days, and "out of host capacity" errors are common in popular regions. A card is required at sign-up.

You are your own sysadmin: Docker, SSL, updates and monitoring are on you.

Category 4: Self-Hosted Platforms

Coolify

Open-source (Apache 2.0) and free to self-host on any VPS; the hosted Coolify Cloud costs $5 a month for two servers plus $3 per extra server. Docker and Docker Compose, automatic SSL, databases and backups. Turns a $5 to $10 VPS into a full deployment platform.

CapRover and Dokku

CapRover (Docker Swarm, one-click app templates, still actively released) and Dokku (MIT-licensed Heroku-style buildpacks on one server; Dokku Pro is a one-time $849) are both free software. Same trade as Coolify: a few dollars a month for a VPS and you do the operations.

Decision Framework: Which Free Platform Should You Use?

Static Site or Documentation

GitHub Pages for a public project, Cloudflare for anything that may get a traffic spike. Both are free with no payment method.

Frontend Application (React, Vue, Next.js)

Vercel for Next.js, as long as the site is non-commercial. Netlify if you can live inside 300 credits a month. Cloudflare Workers with static assets if you want no ceiling on requests.

Container Deployment or Backend Service, No Credit Card

SnapDeploy for a Dockerfile or GitHub repo that can sleep between visits; Render if you need 750 hours and a 30-day Postgres to prototype with; Railway's Free plan if $1 of credit a month covers a tiny always-on service.

Full-Stack Application With Database

Railway's trial for a short project, Render for a 30-day prototype, or self-host Coolify on a $5 VPS for anything that must live longer than a month. No platform on this list gives a free database that lasts.

Full Control and Maximum Resources

Oracle's two free Arm cores are still the most raw compute on the list, if you accept the card, the reclamation policy and the sysadmin work. Otherwise Coolify or CapRover on a VPS.

The Honest Truth About Free Cloud Deployment in 2026

The free tiers are shrinking, and the shrinkage now comes with card walls: Koyeb in February, Render's bandwidth in April, Oracle in June, Hugging Face in July. For static sites and frontends, free hosting is still abundant. For backends and containers, "free" means "sleeps, capped, or needs a card", and the honest way to use it is for demos, prototypes and side projects with real users only once the app pays for its own uptime.

Match your needs to the category and read the limits before you deploy. If you are looking for a Heroku alternative or want to stop paying for idle containers, the table above is the starting point. We re-check every row every 60 days; the date at the top tells you when it was last done.

Frequently Asked Questions About Free Cloud Deployment

Is there any truly free cloud hosting in 2026?

Yes. The best free cloud hosting for a static site is GitHub Pages (public repositories), Cloudflare Pages, Netlify's 300-credit Free plan and Vercel's non-commercial Hobby plan cost nothing and ask for no credit card.

For a backend or container, the free options are real but limited: SnapDeploy gives 100 running hours a month, Render 750 hours, Railway $1 of credit a month. None of them is meant to run a production app for free.

Which cloud provider has the best free tier?

It depends on what you run. For raw compute, Oracle Cloud's Always Free tier (2 Arm OCPUs, 12 GB RAM, credit card required) is still the largest.

For serverless containers, Google Cloud Run and Azure Container Apps offer the same 180,000 vCPU-seconds, 360,000 GiB-seconds and 2 million requests a month, both with a card on file. For functions, AWS Lambda's 1 million requests a month is always free.

If you do not want to give a card at all, the answer is Render, SnapDeploy or Railway rather than a cloud provider.

What is the best free deployment platform for a Docker container or backend API?

For a repository with a Dockerfile, SnapDeploy (100 hours a month, 4 containers, sleeps after 15 minutes idle, wakes in about a minute) and Render (750 hours a month, spins down after 15 minutes, about a minute to wake) are the two no-card choices with a real container runtime; either one works as a free deployment server for an API. Railway's Free plan works for a very small always-on service inside $1 of monthly credit. Koyeb still has a free instance but requires a card since February 2026.

Can I deploy to the cloud for free without a credit card?

Yes. GitHub Pages, Cloudflare, Netlify, Vercel, SnapDeploy, Render, Railway (trial and Free plan) and Back4App all create an account without a payment method. Google Cloud, AWS, Azure, Oracle and Koyeb require a card at sign-up; Fly.io lets you try for 2 machine-hours or 7 days, then needs a card to keep anything running.

Is there a free cloud server I can keep forever?

Only Oracle Cloud's Always Free VMs: up to two Arm instances sharing 2 OCPUs and 12 GB, plus two AMD micro instances, with 200 GB of block storage. You need a credit card, capacity in popular regions is often unavailable, and Oracle reclaims instances that sit under 20 percent utilisation for seven days. AWS accounts created after 15 July 2025 get credits for six months instead of a 12-month free VM.

Which free PaaS options are left now that Heroku has no free tier?

SnapDeploy, Render, Railway's Free plan and Back4App on the hosted side. If you want the Heroku workflow on your own $5 VPS, Dokku and Coolify are free software and give you buildpacks or Docker deploys without hour limits.

Do free tiers sleep, expire or get deleted?

Most do, in different ways. SnapDeploy and Render put idle services to sleep after 15 minutes and wake them when a visitor opens them.

Render's free Postgres expires 30 days after creation. Railway's trial lasts 30 days, then $1 of credit a month.

Back4App's free container runs for 60 minutes per deploy. Koyeb scales to zero after an hour.

Netlify pauses every site when the month's credits are used. Oracle reclaims idle VMs.

Read the sleep column in the table before you rely on any of them.

Is there free cloud hosting for startups and student projects?

A student project, portfolio or demo fits the free tiers well: GitHub Pages for the site, SnapDeploy or Render for the API. A startup with real users should not run on a free tier at all; the first paid step is cheap.

Railway Hobby is $5 a month, Render Starter $7, SnapDeploy Always-On $12 per container, and a Coolify VPS about $5. That is less than the time you lose to cold starts and expiring databases.
