title: Hackers Hide Linux Backdoor in Control Web Panel Server to Execute Commands Without Logs
description:
A backdoor has been found hiding in the web server that runs Control Web Panel (CWP), a free panel for managing Linux hosting servers, researchers at QiAnXin's XLab said this week.

The backdoored web server executes commands that attackers send via web requests, and those requests never appear in its access logs. Installing it takes root access, so the attackers must already control the server.

title: S3 Select in 2026: Why New Accounts Get MethodNotAllowed, and What to Use Instead
description:
SELECT * FROM S3Object s LIMIT 5

That was the query I expected to work. I had uploaded a tiny CSV to Amazon S3, checked its metadata, and previewed the contents. When I clicked Run Query in Buckets by Serverless Creed, I got this instead:

The specified method is not allowed against this resource.

Changing the SQL didn't resolve it. Running the equivalent operation through AWS CLI returned MethodNotAllowed too.

This post follows that investigation across four scenarios in Buckets v2.8.7 and v2.8.9. It also explains the S3 Select availability change behind a plausible diagnosis, and the alternatives I would consider for a new project in 2026.

What S3 Select was designed to do

S3 Select lets an application send a SQL expression against one S3 object and receive selected records instead of downloading the entire object first.

It supports a subset of SQL over CSV, JSON and Apache Parquet inputs, with CSV or JSON output. For example, an application could request particular employee fields or filter records by department.

The single-object scope matters. A query against S3Object isn't a query across a bucket or a database of related tables.

What changed on July 25, 2024

In its July 2024 announcement, AWS closed new customer access to S3 Select, effective July 25, 2024. Existing eligible customers can continue using it. AWS also stated that it did not plan to introduce new capabilities.

The distinction is eligibility to use S3 Select, rather than simply how old an AWS account is. An older account isn't automatically evidence of existing S3 Select access.

My observed MethodNotAllowed response is consistent with these availability restrictions. However, AWS Support did not independently confirm the test account's eligibility, and the error alone does not establish the exact cause.

That qualification matters throughout the tests below.

The CSV query in Buckets — TC-S3SEL-001

I created a CSV with six employee records and a header row. It was 166 bytes, uncompressed, and encrypted with SSE-S3 (AES256).

The upload, metadata verification and object preview succeeded. In the query dialog, I chose CSV input, None for compression, and CSV output, then submitted the query at the start of this post.


Detail crops from the same testing screenshot: the CSV settings and failure notification.

Buckets displayed the failure rather than query results. Being able to upload and preview the object established that those workflows worked; it did not establish that S3 Select was available.

SSE-S3 also wasn't inherently an incompatible choice: the SelectObjectContent API documentation supports server-side encrypted objects, including SSE-S3.

Reproducing it outside Buckets

I next used AWS CLI to separate the application interface from the underlying service operation. This is the equivalent command with generic resource names:

aws s3api select-object-content \
  --bucket example-test-bucket \
  --key data/report.csv \
  --expression "SELECT * FROM S3Object s LIMIT 5" \
  --expression-type SQL \
  --input-serialization \
    '{"CSV":{"FileHeaderInfo":"USE"},"CompressionType":"NONE"}' \
  --output-serialization '{"CSV":{}}' \
  --region us-east-1 \
  /tmp/select-results.csv

FileHeaderInfo: USE tells S3 Select to treat the first CSV line as a header. The operation and serialization options are documented in the AWS CLI reference.

My independent CLI attempt returned:

An error occurred (MethodNotAllowed) when calling the
SelectObjectContent operation: The specified method is
not allowed against this resource.


The independent CLI attempt returned the same error. Private resource and profile details are covered.

This was the strongest evidence in the investigation: the failure was reproducible without Buckets. It narrowed the investigation, while leaving the exact AWS-side reason unresolved.

Invalid SQL didn't produce a syntax error — TC-S3SEL-002

The next scenario was intended to check SQL error handling. I deliberately submitted:

SELECT FROM S3Object s

I received the same MethodNotAllowed response. Correcting the expression and retrying didn't change the outcome.


Invalid SQL produced the same service response as the corrected query.

The editor remained responsive and let me retry. But I did not verify how Buckets presents an actual SQL syntax error: no parser-specific response was observed. The test also cannot reveal AWS's internal order of request validation.

JSON reached the same boundary — TC-S3SEL-003

I then created an uncompressed JSON Lines file with five employee records, totaling 314 bytes. Buckets identified it as JSON. With JSON input and CSV output selected, I submitted:

SELECT s.name, s.department
FROM S3Object s
WHERE s.department = 'Engineering'


The JSON query also returned MethodNotAllowed; no matching records were returned.

The expression was intended to select names and departments for Engineering employees. That describes the query's intention, rather than an observed result. AWS rejected this request with the same error as the CSV request.

A clearer explanation in Buckets v2.8.9

During the later JSON testing, v2.8.9 gave a more useful explanation of the service restriction. It discussed possible S3 Select availability issues and retained the original AWS error code, response and request identifiers.

The explanation was careful about uncertainty: possible causes included account eligibility and unsupported resource types. The AWS API reference confirms that directory buckets and S3 on Outposts do not support this operation. Those are documented possibilities, not confirmed findings about my test environment.

The expanded response is visible in the BZIP2 screenshot below, with request identifiers covered. It helped explain why repeatedly rewriting the SQL might not resolve this particular failure.

What the compression controls proved — TC-S3SEL-005

Buckets offered None, GZIP and BZIP2 in its compression dropdown. I could select GZIP and BZIP2 successfully.


GZIP was selectable. Selecting an option does not compress the stored object.

I reused the existing uncompressed JSON object and selected BZIP2. No compression-specific mismatch warning appeared before submission. When I ran the query, AWS returned MethodNotAllowed again.


BZIP2 selected for an uncompressed object. The displayed explanation concerns S3 Select availability, not a detected compression mismatch.

The dropdown worked as a UI control. Actual AWS decompression and compression-mismatch handling were not verified. I cannot claim that Buckets detected the mismatch.

AWS's format requirements distinguish these cases:

Input Supported compression
CSV or JSON Uncompressed, GZIP or BZIP2
Parquet Columnar GZIP or Snappy; no whole-object compression

S3 Select also has a 256 KB SQL-expression limit and a 1 MB input/result-record limit. These constraints are separate from service eligibility. Proper compression testing would need working S3 Select access and correctly compressed fixtures as well as mismatch cases.

Separating service behavior from application behavior

These tests made the responsibility boundary clearer:

Responsibility AWS Buckets
Request setup Defines the API and supported formats Collects SQL and input/output options
Execution Evaluates the request and returns data or an error Submits the configured request
Diagnostics Returns the service code and response Displays the response and explains possible causes

The CLI reproduction supports treating this observed failure as an AWS service response rather than assuming a defect in the Buckets SQL editor. It doesn't certify every part of the application: successful execution, syntax-error presentation and compression processing still need verification in an eligible environment.

Amazon Athena as an alternative

For SQL over a dataset spanning many S3 objects, Amazon Athena is a more suitable direction. It is a serverless analytics service that queries S3 data using SQL, with broader analytical capabilities than S3 Select's single-object API.

In a common setup, the AWS Glue Data Catalog stores table metadata: column names and types, data locations, format information and partitions. A crawler can discover that metadata, or it can be defined manually. A crawler is optional; see the Glue catalog documentation.


Illustrative architecture. Glue supplies metadata; it is not an intermediate store for the source records.

After defining a suitable employee table, the equivalent analytical query could be:

SELECT name, department
FROM employees
WHERE department = 'Engineering';

This is an illustrative Athena query, not something successfully executed during these S3 Select tests. Moving to Athena requires table definitions, permissions and result configuration; it isn't just changing an API name.

Where the results go

With customer-managed results, Athena writes to an S3 location selected by the client or workgroup. An enforced workgroup setting takes precedence. For API calls, StartQueryExecution.OutputLocation supplies the client-side location; a console setting alone does not configure API calls. See result-location settings.

Alternatively, a workgroup can enable Athena managed query results. This removes the need to supply your own results bucket. Results are retained for 24 hours at no additional managed-results storage cost, then automatically deleted. This mode does not support query-result reuse.

Costs, limits and when I would process locally

AWS currently illustrates on-demand Athena SQL pricing at US$5 per TB scanned on its pricing page. Check the applicable Region and current rate before estimating a workload. Billing concerns data scanned, rather than just the rows returned. AWS documents rounding to the next MB and a 10 MB minimum per query in its cost-model guidance.

Other models include SQL Capacity Reservations, billed for compute capacity, and Apache Spark, billed for compute use. S3 storage, requests and applicable transfer charges remain relevant, including customer-managed results. Glue catalog usage can incur charges beyond its free allowance; optional crawlers and ETL jobs are billed separately under Glue pricing.

For larger datasets, partitioning, compression and columnar formats such as Parquet can reduce scans. Workgroup scan controls can help constrain query usage.

Athena still has service quotas, including regional concurrency and query timeouts, and a 262,144-byte query-string limit. Its SQL limitations include a 32 MB row/column size ceiling.

For my 166-byte CSV or 314-byte JSON fixture, I would usually download the object and filter it with Python, pandas or DuckDB. That avoids catalog setup for a tiny one-off task, though S3 requests, transfer and local resources still matter. Athena becomes more compelling when the dataset and repeated analytical work justify that setup.

What I learned

No scenario produced successful S3 Select query results. The useful findings were the independent CLI reproduction, the working input controls, and the clearer explanation in v2.8.9.

The lesson I will carry forward is to reproduce an unexpected service error outside the application before deciding which layer needs fixing. Here, that prevented a blocked execution test from becoming an unsupported claim about SQL or compression behavior.

My next article will follow the Glue, Athena and S3 Tables workflow: defining queryable data, running SQL, inspecting result storage and understanding the costs. Those are the next steps to test, rather than outcomes established here.

References

  • AWS: S3 Select availability announcement
  • S3 Select formats and limits · CLI reference
  • Athena User Guide · Pricing
  • Glue Data Catalog
  • Athena result locations · Managed results

title: How to Convert Any Webpage to Clean Markdown for RAG & Save 90% LLM Tokens in Node.js
description:
If you are building AI agents, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipelines, or feeding web content into vector databases (Pinecone, Chroma, Qdrant), you already know the big problem with web scraping: Raw HTML is a token killer.

A typical news article or documentation page weighs 500 KB to 1 MB. Most of that weight is bloated navigation menus, ads, tracking scripts, and cookie banners. Ingesting raw HTML directly into an LLM context window burns tens of thousands of tokens and confuses the model.

Here is a clean, lightweight way to parse any URL directly into clean, noise-free GitHub Flavored Markdown (GFM) in Node.js while cutting token consumption by ~90%.

The Problem with Sending Raw Web Content to LLMs

Consider fetching a long Wikipedia or news article:

// Raw HTML fetch
const html = await (await fetch("[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence)")).text();
console.log(html.length); // ~2,200,000 characters (~570,000 tokens!)

Sending 570k tokens into a model like GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet costs real money and easily blows past standard context windows.

The Solution: Extraction via Mozilla Readability & Turndown
To solve this for AI pipelines, I built MarkRAG API: a microservice in Node.js that fetches the page with realistic browser header emulation, extracts the core content using Mozilla's Readability engine (the same engine behind Firefox Reader View), and converts it into clean Markdown with tables and code blocks preserved.

It also calculates exact token metrics so you know how much context you saved:

import express from "express";

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

app.post("/api/rag/ingest", async (req, res) => {
  const { url } = req.body;

  try {
    const response = await fetch("[https://markrag-web-to-clean-markdown-and-rag-parser.p.rapidapi.com/v1/extract](https://markrag-web-to-clean-markdown-and-rag-parser.p.rapidapi.com/v1/extract)", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "X-RapidAPI-Key": process.env.RAPIDAPI_KEY,
        "X-RapidAPI-Host": "markrag-web-to-clean-markdown-and-rag-parser.p.rapidapi.com"
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        url: url,
        options: {
          strip_links: true, // Flattens links to plain text to save extra tokens
          cache: true        // Sub-2ms response for recurring URLs
        }
      })
    });

    const { data } = await response.json();

    console.log(`Title: ${data.title}`);
    console.log(`Tokens saved: ${data.metadata.tokensSaved}`);
    console.log(`Context reduction: ${data.metadata.savingsPercentage}%`);

    // Ingest clean data.markdown directly into your vector store or LLM prompt
    return res.status(200).json({
      title: data.title,
      markdown: data.markdown,
      tokens: data.metadata.estimatedTokens
    });

  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Extraction error:", error);
    return res.status(500).json({ error: "Failed to extract content" });
  }
});

Benchmark: Raw HTML vs Clean Markdown
Testing the API against the Wikipedia Artificial Intelligence article yielded these real numbers:

Raw HTML Size: ~2.2 MB (~572,000 tokens).

Clean Markdown Size: ~201 KB (~50,300 tokens).

Tokens Saved: 521,693 tokens.

Savings Percentage: 91.2%.

It strips all sidebar clutter, footers, and redundant scripts while keeping markdown headings (#, ##), bullet points, and code blocks intact.

Try it out for your AI agents
I published the microservice on RapidAPI with a free tier of 100 requests/month for developers and side projects:

👉 MarkRAG API on RapidAPI

rapidapi.com



If you are building LangChain, LlamaIndex, or custom RAG workflows, test it out with your target URLs and let me know how it handles them!

title: Nodejs Queue Handoff: Publish Durable Alerts So Offline Users Get Notified
description:
Nodejs Queue Handoff: Publish Durable Alerts So Offline Users Get Notified

Short answer: In a Nodejs application, queue the notification before trying to publish it; offline users still get notified because the durable inbox, rather than the live connection, owns delivery.

The important trade-off is simple: presence should be allowed to expire, while a notification should remain durable until the application records that it was delivered or acknowledged. Treating both as the same realtime message is how a shared workspace quietly loses the person who was offline when a comment arrived. Queue the notification as application state first, then attempt the live delivery; the live channel is an optimization, not the record of truth.

I design this boundary around an incident pattern rather than a transport demo. A collaborator edits a document, another collaborator is disconnected for 90 seconds, and the product must still show that mention later. A presence badge that says “online” after the lease expired is stale data. A mention that disappears because a socket was absent is a delivery bug. Those are different failures and deserve different storage and retry rules. In Nodejs, the event loop changes how the worker is scheduled, but it does not change this ownership decision.

That is the boundary.

Keep it boring.

The failure worth designing around is the gap between two acknowledgements. The application commits a notification intent, a worker claims it, and the live transport accepts the envelope. Before the worker can mark the row delivered, its process is restarted, the network path times out, or the connection disappears. On restart, the pending row is visible again. A design that assumes the first acceptance was final either loses the item or sends it twice; a design with a stable notification ID lets the client and server collapse the second attempt into the same user-visible event. This is why the queue record needs an ownership lease, why the consumer needs deduplication, and why “the socket was connected” is not an audit trail. The extra state is operational work, but it is work that can be inspected and repaired.

What should survive the disconnect?

The durable record needs an idempotency key, recipient, event type, a reference to the workspace object, creation time, and a delivery state. It does not need to preserve a socket. The queue worker can read that record after a reconnect, while the presence service can independently observe a heartbeat and replace the badge with “offline” when its lease ends.

That split also makes the user-visible contract honest. “Alex is online” is a current observation with a bounded freshness window. “Alex mentioned you in a document” is an application event with retention and read semantics. A transient connection can carry either signal, but it should not own either meaning.

The first trap is enqueueing only after a publish call succeeds. A broker or websocket gateway can accept a message and the process can still fail before the database transaction that records the notification commits. The opposite ordering has a different cost: a worker may publish twice after a timeout. At-least-once work plus an idempotent consumer is the defensible default here; exactly-once delivery is not a property I would infer from a successful network write.

How should a Nodejs queue publish alerts when users go offline?

The queue-first path gives the application a recoverable fact before it asks a connection to do something best-effort. In a real implementation, the comment transaction and notification intent should be committed together, or an outbox row should be committed in the same transaction. A separate worker claims pending rows, publishes a small envelope, and advances the row only after a defined acknowledgement. If the recipient has no active session, the worker leaves the item pending for inbox retrieval or a later live session.

Here is the critical part of that path in Go. The interfaces are deliberately generic because the contract matters more than a particular queue or realtime product.

package notify

import (
    "context"
    "time"
)

type Notification struct {
    ID        string
    Recipient string
    Workspace string
    Kind      string
    ObjectID  string
    CreatedAt time.Time
}

// Store and LiveTransport are adapters around durable storage and a live channel.
type Store interface {
    ClaimPending(ctx context.Context, limit int) ([]Notification, error)
    MarkDelivered(ctx context.Context, id string, at time.Time) error
    Release(ctx context.Context, id string, reason string) error
}

type LiveTransport interface {
    Publish(ctx context.Context, n Notification) error
}

func DeliverBatch(ctx context.Context, store Store, live LiveTransport, limit int) error {
    items, err := store.ClaimPending(ctx, limit)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    for _, item := range items {
        err := live.Publish(ctx, item)
        if err != nil {
            if releaseErr := store.Release(ctx, item.ID, err.Error()); releaseErr != nil {
                return releaseErr
            }
            continue
        }
        if err := store.MarkDelivered(ctx, item.ID, time.Now().UTC()); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    return nil
}

The worker must claim with a lease or equivalent ownership token. Otherwise two workers can process the same row concurrently. The receiver must also deduplicate by ID, because the publish acknowledgement and the delivery-state update are separate operations. A retry after the first succeeds can therefore produce a duplicate attempt, even though the user should see one notification.

This code intentionally does not mark a notification read. Delivery means the application handed the envelope to the live transport or made it available through the inbox contract. Read state belongs to an explicit user action, and it should not be guessed from a websocket acknowledgement.

What does an offline user actually receive?

An offline user needs a second path: on session establishment, fetch the unread durable notifications for that user and workspace, order them by the application timestamp, and then subscribe to new events. The ordering boundary matters. If the initial fetch and subscription are arranged carelessly, an event can land between them and be omitted from the client view. A cursor, sequence number, or transactional snapshot gives the reconnect path a point from which to resume.

Presence does not belong in that backlog. The client can request current presence after authentication and then listen for changes; it should not replay ten-minute-old heartbeats as though they were current. A useful rule is that a presence lease is valid only until its expiry plus a deliberately small clock-skew allowance. The exact interval is a product decision tied to network conditions and the cost of showing stale availability, not a universal constant.

For a shared workspace, I would keep the notification payload narrow: notification ID, workspace ID, event kind, object ID, and a revision or timestamp. The client can fetch authorized details rather than trusting arbitrary text embedded in a broadcast. Authorization is checked again on fetch, because a recipient’s access to a document can change while a notification is waiting.

Which failure should page the on-call engineer?

A dashboard showing “connected clients” is a weak answer. It can be green while the durable backlog grows, or red while every notification is being recovered through inbox reads. I want signals that expose the user contract: age of the oldest pending notification, retry counts by reason, claim lease expirations, duplicate suppression, reconnect fetch latency, and the proportion of live publishes followed by a valid acknowledgement. The alert question is blunt: what page fired, and which user-visible promise is currently at risk?

Keep the incident boundary explicit. A temporary live-channel outage should increase pending age and retries; it should not erase notifications. A storage failure should block creation of the durable intent and may need a higher-severity response because the system no longer knows what it owes. A presence stream failure should degrade the badge to an unknown or stale state rather than manufacture online users.

Testing should exercise the gaps between operations, not just the happy path. Insert failures after the durable write, after claim, after live publish, and before the delivery-state update. Reconnect a client between its initial inbox read and subscription. Send the same notification twice. Revoke workspace access while an item is pending. Those cases reveal whether the design has a recovery contract or merely a successful demo.

Where this advice stops applying

Queue-first delivery is the wrong shape for data that has no value after the connection closes, such as a typing indicator or a rapidly changing cursor. It is also insufficient for urgent external escalation, where a separate policy may require provider-specific acknowledgement, rate limits, and human escalation. For ordinary in-app mentions, task assignments, and review activity, durable intent plus a live hint is a reasonable boundary.

The decision is therefore not “which realtime transport is fastest?” It is “which state must remain true when nobody is connected?” Presence answers: very little, and only for a bounded lease. Notifications answer: enough to reconstruct an unread inbox. Once that distinction is encoded in storage, queue retries, reconnect reads, and observability all become easier to reason about.

Sources

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSocket

title: KI-Agent zur Fehlerbehebung: So baut man einen Agenten, der Bugs zuerst reproduziert
description:
KI-Agent zur Fehlerbehebung: So baut man einen Agenten, der Bugs zuerst reproduziert

Ein KI-Agent, der Bugs selbstständig behebt, funktioniert nur, wenn er eine Regel befolgt: keine Reproduktion, keine Lösung. Der Agent verwandelt den Bug-Report in einen Test, der aktuell fehlschlägt, patcht den Code auf einem isolierten Branch, führt diesen Test erneut aus – zusammen mit der gesamten Testsuite – und meldet sich erst zurück, wenn alles grün ist. Das Merging übernimmt weiterhin ein Mensch. Kann er den Bug nicht reproduzieren, bleibt er still.

Testen Sie Apidog noch heute

Das DeepSeek-Harness-Team stellte diese Idee am 1. November 2026 einem breiten Publikum vor – in einem Essay zum Design von Super-Agenten. Diese Anleitung macht daraus eine Pipeline, die Sie noch diese Woche bauen können: mit einer Reproduktion, die als API-Test vom Agenten selbst erstellt und im Terminal ausgeführt wird.

Warum „Agent, behebe das“ ohne Repro scheitert

Bittet man einen Coding-Agenten, einen Bug-Report zu beheben, erhält man meist einen souveränen Diff. Ob damit Ihr Bug behoben wird, ein eingebildeter Bug oder gar nichts – das lässt sich nicht erkennen.

Ohne Reproduktionsschritt gehen drei Dinge schief:

  • Der Agent rät die Ursache. Er wählt die plausibelste Zeile anhand der Fehlermeldung und bearbeitet sie.
  • „Behoben“ hat keine Definition. Der einzige Beweis ist die eigene Zusammenfassung des Agenten.
  • Regressionen schleichen sich ein. Ein Patch an einem gemeinsamen Validator kann einen Endpunkt reparieren und vier andere beschädigen.

Ein fehlschlagender Test löst alle drei Probleme: Er verankert den Bug, definiert „fertig“ und bleibt als Regressionstest in Ihrer Suite.

Woher „stillschweigend reproduzieren und beheben“ stammt

In „Exploring Super-agent Design“ beschreibt das DeepSeek-Harness-Team eine Richtlinie aus seiner eigenen Nutzergruppe: Meldet jemand einen Bug, versucht ein Agent, ihn im Hintergrund zu reproduzieren. Er äußert sich erst, wenn es eine bestätigte, einfache Lösung gibt. Andernfalls schweigt er.

Das Essay nennt das spekulative Ausführung und kombiniert es mit zwei Bausteinen, die Sie hier wiederverwenden. Worker erhalten je Aufgabe eine isolierte Session, sämtliche Tools und das stärkste Modell – und berichten an einen Router, statt mit Menschen zu sprechen. Ein Watchdog ist eine separate Session, die prüft, ob jeder Worker Fortschritte macht oder abdriftet.

Ein Vorbehalt: Das Essay beschreibt eine Architektur, keine ausgelieferten DeepSeek-Harness-Features. Teile davon stecken in einem Prototyp-Plugin, dsh-superagent-prototype, das laut den Autoren kein offizielles DeepSeek-Produkt ist. Zum Router-und-Worker-Bild siehe wie man einen Super-Agenten baut.

Die fünfstufige Agent-Pipeline zur Bugbehebung

Ein sich selbst reparierender Agent durchläuft jedes Mal dieselbe Schleife – mit zwei Schranken:

  1. Aufnahme: Bericht, die fehlschlagende Anfrage und die erhaltene Antwort einsammeln.
  2. Reproduzieren: Einen Test schreiben, der aus dem gemeldeten Grund fehlschlägt. Kein fehlgeschlagener Test, keine Lösung.
  3. Beheben: Den Code auf einem isolierten Branch oder Worktree patchen.
  4. Erneut ausführen: Der neue Test muss bestehen, ebenso die bestehende Suite.
  5. Übergeben: Einen Pull Request mit den Nachweisen öffnen – oder schweigen.

Schritt 1: Den Bug-Report aufnehmen

Ihr Agent kann „der Checkout ist wieder kaputt“ nicht reproduzieren. Geben Sie der Aufnahme eine feste Struktur:

Feld Beispiel Warum es wichtig ist
Endpunkt POST /orders Welcher Handler gelesen werden soll
Anfrage Body mit "coupon": null Die exakte Eingabe, die den Fehler ausgelöst hat
Tatsächliche Antwort 500, {"error":"internal"} Was der Test fehlschlagen sehen muss
Erwartete Antwort 201 mit einer Order-id Was der Test behauptet
Umgebung staging Wo die Repro läuft

Fehlen Felder, fragt der Agent einmal nach oder zieht die Anfrage aus den Logs. Error-Bodies, die den RFC-9457-Problem-Details folgen, helfen, weil der Fehlertyp in einer vorhersagbaren Form ankommt.

Schritt 2: Den Bug als fehlschlagenden API-Test reproduzieren

Das ist die Schranke. Der Agent wandelt den Aufnahme-Datensatz in einen Testfall mit zwei Assertions um – den erwarteten Statuscode und ein Feld, das die Antwort enthalten soll – und führt ihn gegen die echte Umgebung aus. Drei Ausgänge sind möglich:

  • Er schlägt aus dem gemeldeten Grund fehl. Sie haben eine Repro. Weiter geht’s.
  • Er besteht. Der Bug ist wie beschrieben nicht reproduzierbar. Loggen und stoppen.
  • Er schlägt aus einem anderen Grund fehl (Auth-Fehler, fehlende Daten, Timeout). Das ist eine defekte Repro, kein bestätigter Bug. Stoppen.

Nur der erste Fall schaltet eine Lösung frei. Das bedeutet „stillschweigend“ in der Praxis: Die anderen beiden erzeugen einen Log-Eintrag für diejenigen, die die Warteschlange prüfen – nicht eine Nachricht im Chat des Nutzers.

Schreiben Sie die Repro als API-Test, nicht als Unit-Test: Der Agent trifft dieselbe Schnittstelle wie der Nutzer, sodass er nicht versehentlich einen anderen Bug reproduziert.

Schritt 3: Den Code in einem isolierten Branch beheben

Sobald die Repro rot ist, erhält der Worker eine eigene Kopie des Codes. Ein git worktree ist die leichtgewichtigste Option: ein zweites Arbeitsverzeichnis auf einem neuen Branch, sodass die Änderungen des Agenten Ihr Checkout nie berühren. Führen Sie den Service daraus aus und verweisen Sie die Testumgebung dorthin.

Halten Sie zwei Einschränkungen streng ein. Die Lösung muss klein sein: Legen Sie ein Limit fest, etwa 3 Dateien oder 50 geänderte Zeilen, und behandeln Sie alles Größere als Meldung für einen Menschen. Und sie muss die Repro zielen: keine Refactorings, Umbenennungen oder Aufräumarbeiten – jede zusätzliche Änderung ist etwas, das Ihr Reviewer prüfen muss.

Schritt 4: Repro und gesamte Suite erneut ausführen

Die zweite Schranke hat zwei Teile. Zuerst führt der Agent denselben Testfall aus Schritt 2 unverändert erneut aus – und er muss bestehen. Hat der Agent die Assertions bearbeitet, um dorthin zu gelangen, scheitert die Lösung; Ihre Pipeline findet das heraus, indem sie die Testdatei vor und nachher vergleicht.

Zweitens muss die bestehende Suite grün bleiben. Eine Lösung, die einen Test grün und drei rot macht, geht zurück zu Schritt 3. Begrenzen Sie die Schleife zeitlich, etwa auf 3 Versuche oder 20 Minuten, dann stoppen und protokollieren, was versucht wurde. Hier beweist der Watchdog seinen Wert: Er kann einen Worker abwürgen, der immer wieder dieselbe Zeile bearbeitet oder in Dateien abdriftet, die die Repro nie berührt hat.

Schritt 5: Nur eine bestätigte, einfache Lösung übergeben

Sind beide Schranken grün, öffnet der Agent einen Pull Request mit Nachweisen, nicht mit einer Erzählung: der Bericht, der fehlgeschlagene Lauf, der Diff und der erfolgreiche Lauf samt Suite-Ergebnissen. Ein Mensch prüft und merged. Geschützte Branches stellen sicher, dass das Token des Agenten zwar Branches pushen, aber nie in main mergen kann. Scheitert eine Schranke, hört der Melder nichts; der Agent schreibt eine Log-Zeile und macht weiter.

Schutzmaßnahmen für einen sich selbst reparierenden KI-Agenten

Errichten Sie diese Zäune, bevor der erste unbeaufsichtigte Lauf startet:

Schutzmaßnahme Einstellung Was sie verhindert
Umfang Max. Dateien und Zeilen pro Lösung Neuschreibungen, die als Lösungen ausgegeben werden
Zeitfenster Max. Versuche und Minuten pro Bug Ausufernde Schleifen, die Tokens verbrennen
Zugangsdaten Nur Staging, keine Produktions-Schlüssel Eine Repro, die echte Orders schreibt
Merge-Rechte Branches pushen, nie mergen Ungeprüfter Code, der main erreicht
Test-Integrität Testdatei vor und nachher vergleichen Auf Erfolg gezäumte Assertions
Schweigen Keine nutzergerichtete Nachricht bei Fehlschlag Lärm und halb bestätigte Behauptungen

Zugangsdaten sind am wichtigsten: Eine Repro trifft die API tatsächlich – nutzen Sie also Staging oder lokale Testdaten.

Ihren Coding-Agenten die Repro mit Apidog CLI erstellen lassen

Schritt 2 ist das Herz der Pipeline – und genau dafür wurde die Apidog CLI gebaut. Ihr Coding-Agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor oder OpenCode) schreibt den Testfall als JSON, legt ihn in Ihrem Apidog-Projekt an und führt ihn im Terminal aus. Sie schreiben nur einen Prompt.

Einmalig einrichten:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog auth login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

Dann geben Sie Ihrem Agenten den Bug-Report und diesen [REDACTED PROMPT]
Here is a bug report for POST /orders in Apidog project .
Turn it into an Apidog test case that fails today: assert status 201
and that $.id exists. Run it against staging and confirm it fails for
the reported reason. If it does, fix the handler on a new worktree
branch until the same test passes, run the endpoint's other cases, and
open a PR with both JSON reports. If it doesn't reproduce, stop and log why.


Der Agent baut das Payload nicht aus dem Gedächtnis. Er liest das Schema, findet eine Kategorie, validiert seine Datei und legt den Testfall erst dann an:


bash
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog test-case category --project
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file repro-orders.json
apidog test-case create --project --file repro-orders.json


Die Datei, die er schreibt, sieht so aus (die IDs stammen aus Ihrem Projekt):


json
{
"name": "Repro: POST /orders with null coupon returns 500",
"apiDetailId": 123456,
"categoryId": 1,
"method": "post",
"path": "/orders",
"parameters": {},
"commonParameters": {},
"requestBody": {
"type": "application/json",
"data": "{\"items\":[{\"sku\":\"A-100\",\"qty\":1}],\"coupon\":null}"
},
"postProcessors": [
{ "type": "assertion", "defaultEnable": true, "enable": true,
"data": { "name": "status is 201", "subject": "httpCode", "comparison": "equal", "path": "", "value": "201" } },
{ "type": "assertion", "defaultEnable": true, "enable": true,
"data": { "name": "order id exists", "subject": "responseJson", "comparison": "exists", "path": "$.id" } }
]
}


Jetzt der rote Lauf, der den Bug beweist:


bash
apidog run --test-case --project -e -r cli,json --out-file repro-before


Der CLI-Reporter zeigt die fehlschlagende Status-Assertion bei einem 500, und `repro-before.json` landet in `apidog-reports/`. Nach der Lösung führt der Agent denselben Befehl mit `--out-file repro-after` aus, und beide Assertions bestehen. Diese beiden Dateien sind die Nachweise im Pull Request. Für Schritt 4 führt er jeden Testfall des Endpunkts aus, damit die Lösung keinen Nachbarn still beschädigen kann:


bash
apidog test-case run --project --endpoint -e -r cli,json




Fügen Sie `--upload-report` hinzu, um den Lauf in der Apidog-App anzuzeigen. Nach dem Merge bleibt der Repro-Testfall als Regressionstest in Ihrem Projekt, und derselbe `apidog run` mit `-r junit` lässt sich in CI einbinden, wie in [Apidog CLI in einer CI/CD-Pipeline ausführen](https://apidog.com/de/blog/apidog-cli-ci-cd-pipeline?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation) gezeigt. Weitere Setups finden Sie im [Apidog-CLI-Agenten-Workflow](https://apidog.com/de/blog/apidog-cli-agent-workflow?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation) und unter [Apidog CLI in Claude Code](https://apidog.com/de/blog/apidog-cli-in-claude-code?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation). Apidog Free deckt bis zu 4 Nutzer ab – Sie können also die gesamte Schleife ohne Bezahlplan ausprobieren.

## FAQ

### Kann ein KI-Agent Bugs wirklich ohne Menschen beheben?

Er kann viele einfache Bugs selbstständig reproduzieren, patchen und beweisen – aber er sollte sie nicht mergen. Behalten Sie einen Menschen beim Merging, und lassen Sie den Branch-Schutz das durchsetzen.

### Was, wenn der Agent den Bug nicht reproduzieren kann?

Er stoppt und protokolliert, was er versucht hat. Ein Bug, den er nicht reproduzieren kann, ist eine Lösung, die er nicht bestätigen kann – jeder Patch wäre ein Ratespiel. Ein Mensch ergänzt dann Details im Bericht oder schließt ihn.

### Wie verhindere ich, dass der Agent den Test so bearbeitet, dass er besteht?

Speichern Sie eine Kopie oder einen Hash des Testfalls, sobald er erstmals fehlschlägt, und vergleichen Sie, bevor Sie die Lösung akzeptieren. Halten Sie die Testdatei außerhalb der Pfade, die der Worker bearbeiten darf.

### Brauche ich DeepSeek Harness, um das zu bauen?

Nein. Das Essay beschreibt ein Design, und sein Prototyp-Plugin ist kein offizielles DeepSeek-Produkt. Jeder Coding-Agent, der Shell-Befehle ausführt, funktioniert – auch Claude Code in [GitHub Actions](https://apidog.com/de/blog/claude-code-github-actions?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation). Sehen Sie sich [an, was DeepSeek Harness ist](https://apidog.com/de/blog/what-is-deepseek-harness?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation), wenn Sie es dort ausprobieren möchten.

title: 버그를 잡아주는 AI 에이전트, 재현 단계부터 자동으로 구축하는 방법
description:
버그를 잡아주는 AI 에이전트, 재현 단계부터 자동으로 구축하는 방법

스스로 버그를 고치는 AI 에이전트는 단 하나의 규칙을 지킬 때 작동합니다: 재현하지 못하면, 고치지 않는다. 에이전트는 버그 리포트를 오늘 실패하는 테스트로 바꾸고, 격리된 브랜치에서 코드를 패치한 뒤, 해당 테스트와 전체 스위트를 다시 실행하고, 모든 것이 그린일 때만 보고를 돌려줍니다. 병합은 여전히 사람이 합니다. 버그를 재현할 수 없다면 에이전트는 조용히 넘어갑니다.

지금 Apidog 사용해 보기

DeepSeek Harness 팀은 2026년 11월 1일 슈퍼 에이전트 설계에 대한 에세이에서 이 아이디어를 많은 독자에게 선보였습니다. 이 가이드는 그것을 이번 주 안에 구축할 수 있는 파이프라인으로 바꾼 것으로, 재현은 에이전트가 직접 만들어 터미널에서 실행하는 API 테스트로 작성됩니다.

재현(repro) 없이는 “에이전트야, 이거 고쳐"가 실패하는 이유

코딩 에이전트에게 버그 리포트의 수정을 요청하면 보통 자신감 넘치는 diff를 받게 됩니다. 하지만 그것이 당신의 버그를 고친 것인지, 에이전트가 상상한 버그를 고친 것인지, 아니면 아무것도 고치지 않은 것인지 알 수 없습니다.

재현 단계가 없으면 세 가지 문제가 생깁니다:

  • 에이전트가 원인을 추측합니다. 에러 메시지에서 가장 가능성 높은 줄을 골라 수정합니다.
  • "수정됨"의 정의가 없습니다. 유일한 증거는 에이전트 자신의 요약입니다.
  • 회귀가 몰래 들어옵니다. 공유 validator에 대한 패치가 하나의 엔드포인트는 고치고 네 개는 망가뜨릴 수 있습니다.

실패하는 테스트는 이 세 가지를 모두 해결합니다. 버그를 고정하고, 완료(done)를 정의하며, 회귀 검사로 스위트에 남습니다.

“조용히 재현하고 수정한다”는 아이디어의 출처

"Exploring Super-agent Design"에서 DeepSeek Harness 팀은 자신들의 사용자 그룹에서 나온 정책을 소개합니다: 누군가 버그를 보고하면 에이전트가 백그라운드에서 재현을 시도하고, 확인된 간단한 수정책이 있을 때만 말을 건다. 그렇지 않으면 아무 말도 하지 않는다는 것입니다.

이 에세이는 이를 스페클레이티브 실행(speculative execution)이라 부르며, 여기서 재사용할 두 가지 요소와 짝을 이룹니다. 워커(worker)는 작업당 하나의 격리된 세션을 받고, 전체 도구와 가장 강력한 모델을 사용하며, 사람이 아니라 라우터에 보고합니다. 왓치독(watchdog)은 각 워커가 진전을 이루고 있는지, 아니면 방황하고 있는지 확인하는 별도의 세션입니다.

한 가지 주의할 점: 이 에세이는 아키텍처를 설명한 것이지 출시된 DeepSeek Harness 기능이 아닙니다. 일부는 프로토타입 플러그인인 dsh-superagent-prototype에 담겨 있으며, 저자들은 이것이 공식 DeepSeek 제품이 아니라고 말합니다. 라우터와 워커 구조에 대해서는 슈퍼 에이전트 구축 방법을 참고하세요.

5단계 버그 수정 에이전트 파이프라인

자가 수정 에이전트는 매번 동일한 루프를 두 개의 게이트와 함께 실행합니다:

  1. 접수(Intake): 리포트, 실패한 요청, 그에 대한 응답을 수집합니다.
  2. 재현(Reproduce): 보고된 이유로 실패하는 테스트를 작성합니다. 실패하는 테스트가 없으면 수정하지 않습니다.
  3. 수정(Fix): 격리된 브랜치나 worktree에서 코드를 패치합니다.
  4. 재실행(Re-run): 새 테스트가 통과해야 하고, 기존 스위트도 통과해야 합니다.
  5. 전달(Deliver): 증거와 함께 풀 리퀘스트를 열거나, 조용히 넘어갑니다.

1단계: 버그 리포트 접수

에이전트는 “결제가 또 깨졌어"라는 말만으로는 재현할 수 없습니다. 접수 단계에 고정된 형식을 부여하세요:

필드 예시 중요한 이유
엔드포인트 POST /orders 어떤 핸들러를 봐야 하는지
요청 "coupon": null이 포함된 본문 버그를 유발한 정확한 입력
실제 응답 500, {"error":"internal"} 테스트가 실패로 봐야 하는 것
기대 응답 주문 id와 함께 201 테스트가 단언(assert)하는 것
환경 staging 재현이 실행되는 위치

필드가 누락되면 에이전트는 한 번 묻거나 로그에서 요청을 가져옵니다. RFC 9457 problem details 형식을 따르는 에러 본문은 에러 타입이 예측 가능한 형태로 도착하기 때문에 도움이 됩니다.

2단계: 버그를 실패하는 API 테스트로 재현하기

여기가 바로 그 게이트입니다. 에이전트는 접수 기록을 두 개의 단언, 즉 기대하는 상태 코드와 응답에 포함되어야 할 필드를 가진 테스트 케이스로 바꾸고, 실제 환경에서 실행합니다. 세 가지 결과가 가능합니다:

  • 보고된 이유로 실패합니다. 재현이 확보된 것입니다. 다음으로 진행합니다.
  • 통과합니다. 설명된 대로는 재현되지 않는 버그입니다. 로그에 기록하고 중단합니다.
  • 다른 이유로 실패합니다 (인증 에러, 데이터 누락, 타임아웃). 그것은 깨진 재현이지 확인된 버그가 아닙니다. 중단합니다.

첫 번째 경우만 수정을 허용합니다. “조용히"라는 말의 실제 의미가 바로 이것입니다: 나머지 두 경우는 사용자의 채팅에 메시지를 보내는 대신, 큐를 검토하는 담당자를 위한 로그 항목만 남깁니다.

재현은 단위 테스트가 아닌 API 테스트로 작성하세요. 에이전트가 사용자가 사용한 것과 동일한 인터페이스를 호출하기 때문에, 우연히 다른 버그를 재현하는 일이 없습니다.

3단계: 격리된 브랜치에서 코드 수정하기

재현이 빨간불이 되면, 워커는 코드의 자체 사본을 받습니다. git worktree가 가장 가벼운 방법입니다. 새 브랜치에 두 번째 작업 디렉터리를 만드는 것이므로 에이전트의 수정이 당신의 체크아웃에 절대 영향을 주지 않습니다. 거기서 서비스를 실행하고 테스트 환경이 그곳을 가리키게 하세요.

두 가지 제약을 엄격하게 유지하세요. 수정은 작아야 합니다: 3개 파일 또는 50줄 변경 같은 한도를 정하고, 그보다 큰 것은 사람에게 넘길 보고로 취급합니다. 그리고 수정은 재현을 대상으로 해야 합니다: 리팩터링, 이름 변경, 정리 작업은 금지입니다. 모든 추가 변경은 검토자가 확인해야 할 항목 하나가 되기 때문입니다.

4단계: 재현 테스트와 전체 스위트 재실행하기

두 번째 게이트는 두 부분으로 구성됩니다. 먼저 에이전트는 2단계의 동일한 테스트 케이스를 그대로 다시 실행하며, 반드시 통과해야 합니다. 만약 에이전트가 통과하기 위해 단언을 수정했다면 수정은 실패합니다. 파이프라인이 테스트 파일의 실행 전후 diff를 비교해 이를 잡아냅니다.

둘째, 기존 스위트가 그린을 유지해야 합니다. 하나의 테스트를 그린으로 만들고 세 개를 빨간으로 만드는 수정은 3단계로 되돌아갑니다. 루프에 시간 제한을 두세요. 예를 들어 3회 시도 또는 20분을 넘기면 중단하고 시도한 내용을 기록합니다. 왓치독이 빛을 발하는 순간이 바로 여기입니다. 같은 줄만 계속 수정하거나 재현이 전혀 건드리지 않은 파일로 방황하는 워커를 종료시킬 수 있습니다.

5단계: 확인된 간단한 수정만 전달하기

두 게이트가 모두 그린이면, 에이전트는 이야기가 아니라 증거와 함께 풀 리퀘스트를 엽니다: 리포트, 실패한 실행, diff, 그리고 스위트 결과가 포함된 통과한 실행입니다. 사람이 검토하고 병합합니다. Protected branches를 사용하면 에이전트의 토큰이 브랜치를 푸시할 수는 있지만 main에 병합하는 일은 결코 못하게 됩니다. 어떤 게이트라도 실패하면 보고자는 아무런 소식을 듣지 못합니다. 에이전트는 로그 한 줄을 남기고 다음으로 넘어갑니다.

자가 수정 AI 에이전트를 위한 가드레일

첫 무인 실행 전에 이 울타리들을 세워두세요:

가드레일 설정 방지되는 것
범위 수정당 최대 파일 수와 줄 수 수정으로 둔갑시킨 전면 재작성
시간 제한 버그당 최대 시도 횟수와 시간 토큰을 태우는 무한 루프
자격 증명 staging 전용, 프로덕션 키 금지 실제 주문을 생성하는 재현
병합 권한 브랜치 푸시만, 병합 금지 검토되지 않은 코드가 main에 도달
테스트 무결성 테스트 파일의 실행 전후 diff 비교 통과하기 위해 단언을 수정하는 행위
침묵 실패 시 사용자에게 메시지 없음 소음과 반쯤 확인된 주장

자격 증명이 가장 중요합니다. 재현은 API를 실제로 호출하므로 staging이나 시드된 로컬 데이터를 사용하세요.

Apidog CLI로 코딩 에이전트가 재현을 만들게 하기

2단계가 파이프라인의 핵심이며, 바로 Apidog CLI가 만들어진 목적입니다. 코딩 에이전트(Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode)가 테스트 케이스를 JSON으로 작성하고, Apidog 프로젝트에 생성한 뒤 터미널에서 실행합니다. 당신은 프롬프트 하나만 작성하면 됩니다.

한 번만 설정하세요:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog auth login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

그런 다음 에이전트에게 버그 리포트와 이 프롬프트를 넘기세요:

Here is a bug report for POST /orders in Apidog project <projectId>.
Turn it into an Apidog test case that fails today: assert status 201
and that $.id exists. Run it against staging and confirm it fails for
the reported reason. If it does, fix the handler on a new worktree
branch until the same test passes, run the endpoint's other cases, and
open a PR with both JSON reports. If it doesn't reproduce, stop and log why.

에이전트는 기억에 의존해 페이로드를 만들지 않습니다. 스키마를 읽고, 카테고리를 찾고, 파일을 검증한 후에야 케이스를 생성합니다:

apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog test-case category --project <projectId>
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file repro-orders.json
apidog test-case create --project <projectId> --file repro-orders.json

에이전트가 작성하는 파일은 다음과 같습니다 (ID는 프로젝트에서 가져옵니다):

{
  "name": "Repro: POST /orders with null coupon returns 500",
  "apiDetailId": 123456,
  "categoryId": 1,
  "method": "post",
  "path": "/orders",
  "parameters": {},
  "commonParameters": {},
  "requestBody": {
    "type": "application/json",
    "data": "{\"items\":[{\"sku\":\"A-100\",\"qty\":1}],\"coupon\":null}"
  },
  "postProcessors": [
    { "type": "assertion", "defaultEnable": true, "enable": true,
      "data": { "name": "status is 201", "subject": "httpCode", "comparison": "equal", "path": "", "value": "201" } },
    { "type": "assertion", "defaultEnable": true, "enable": true,
      "data": { "name": "order id exists", "subject": "responseJson", "comparison": "exists", "path": "$.id" } }
  ]
}

이제 버그를 증명하는 빨간 실행입니다:

apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <projectId> -e <stagingEnvId> -r cli,json --out-file repro-before

CLI 리포터는 500에서 상태 단언이 실패하는 모습을 보여주고, repro-before.json이 apidog-reports/에 저장됩니다. 수정 후에는 에이전트가 --out-file repro-after로 동일한 명령을 실행하고 두 단언 모두 통과합니다. 이 두 파일이 풀 리퀘스트의 증거입니다. 4단계를 위해 엔드포인트의 모든 케이스를 실행해 수정이 조용히 이웃을 깨뜨리지 못하게 합니다:

apidog test-case run --project <projectId> --endpoint <endpointId> -e <stagingEnvId> -r cli,json

--upload-report를 추가하면 실행 결과를 Apidog 앱에서 볼 수 있습니다. 병합 후에는 재현 케이스가 회귀 테스트로 프로젝트에 남고, -r junit을 붙인 동일한 apidog run이 CI에 그대로 들어갑니다. 자세한 내용은 CI/CD 파이프라인에서 Apidog CLI 실행하기를 참고하세요. 추가 설정은 Apidog CLI 에이전트 워크플로와 Claude Code에서의 Apidog CLI를 확인하세요. Apidog Free는 최대 4명의 사용자까지 지원하므로 유료 플랜 없이 전체 루프를 시도해볼 수 있습니다.

FAQ

AI 에이전트가 정말 사람 없이 버그를 고칠 수 있나요?

많은 간단한 버그를 스스로 재현하고, 패치하고, 증명할 수 있지만 병합까지 해서는 안 됩니다. 병합은 사람이 담당하고, 브랜치 보호로 이를 강제하세요.

에이전트가 버그를 재현하지 못하면 어떻게 되나요?

중단하고 시도한 내용을 기록합니다. 재현할 수 없는 버그는 확인할 수 없는 수정이므로, 어떤 패치든 추측에 불과합니다. 이후 사람이 리포트에 세부 정보를 추가하거나 닫습니다.

에이전트가 테스트를 통과하도록 수정하는 것을 어떻게 막을 수 있나요?

테스트 케이스가 처음 실패했을 때 사본이나 해시를 저장하고, 수정을 수락하기 전에 비교하세요. 테스트 파일을 워커가 수정할 수 있는 경로 밖에 두세요.

이것을 만들려면 DeepSeek Harness가 필요한가요?

아니요. 에세이는 설계를 설명한 것이고, 그 프로토타입 플러그인은 공식 DeepSeek 제품이 아닙니다. 셸 명령을 실행할 수 있는 어떤 코딩 에이전트든 작동합니다. GitHub Actions의 Claude Code를 포함해서요. 거기서 시도해보고 싶다면 DeepSeek Harness란 무엇인가를 참고하세요.

title: Agente de IA que Corrige Bugs: Crie um que Reproduza o Problema Primeiro
description:
Agente de IA que Corrige Bugs: Crie um que Reproduza o Problema Primeiro

Um agente de IA que corrige bugs sozinho funciona quando obedece a uma regra: sem reprodução, sem correção. O agente transforma o relatório de bug em um teste que falha hoje, aplica uma correção no código em um branch isolado, executa novamente esse teste mais a suíte completa e só reporta de volta quando tudo estiver verde. O merge continua sendo feito por um humano. Se não conseguir reproduzir o bug, ele fica em silêncio.

Experimente o Apidog hoje

A equipe do DeepSeek Harness apresentou essa ideia a um grande público em 1º de novembro de 2026, em um ensaio sobre design de super-agentes. Este guia a transforma em um pipeline que você pode construir esta semana, com a reprodução escrita como um teste de API que seu agente cria e executa a partir do terminal.

Por que “agente, corrija isso” falha sem uma reprodução

Peça a um agente de codificação que corrija um relatório de bug e você geralmente receberá um diff confiante. Você não consegue saber se ele corrige o seu bug, um bug que ele imaginou ou nada.

Sem uma etapa de reprodução, três coisas dão errado:

  • O agente adivinha a causa. Ele escolhe a linha mais provável a partir da mensagem de erro e a edita.
  • “Corrigido” não tem definição. A única prova é o resumo do próprio agente.
  • Regressões passam despercebidas. Uma alteração em um validador compartilhado pode corrigir um endpoint e quebrar outros quatro.

Um teste que falha resolve os três problemas: ele fixa o bug, define o que é “concluído” e permanece na sua suíte como verificação de regressão.

De onde vem “reproduzir e corrigir em silêncio”

Em "Exploring Super-agent Design", a equipe do DeepSeek Harness descreve uma política do seu próprio grupo de usuários: quando alguém relata um bug, um agente tenta reproduzi-lo em segundo plano. Ele se manifesta apenas com uma correção confirmada e simples. Caso contrário, não diz nada.

O ensaio chama isso de execução especulativa e o associa a dois componentes que você reutilizará aqui. Os workers recebem uma sessão isolada por tarefa, todas as ferramentas e o modelo mais forte, e reportam a um roteador em vez de falar com humanos. Um watchdog é uma sessão separada que verifica se cada worker está progredindo ou se desviando.

Uma ressalva: o ensaio descreve uma arquitetura, não recursos já lançados do DeepSeek Harness. Partes dela vivem em um plugin de protótipo, dsh-superagent-prototype, que, segundo os autores, não é um produto oficial da DeepSeek. Para entender o panorama de roteador e worker, veja como construir um super-agente.

O pipeline de agente de correção de bugs em cinco etapas

Um agente de autocorreção executa o mesmo loop todas as vezes, com dois portões:

  1. Recepção: coletar o relatório, a requisição que falha e a resposta recebida.
  2. Reproduzir: escrever um teste que falha pelo motivo relatado. Sem teste que falha, sem correção.
  3. Corrigir: aplicar a correção no código em um branch ou worktree isolado.
  4. Reexecutar: o novo teste deve passar, e a suíte existente também.
  5. Entregar: abrir um pull request com as evidências ou ficar em silêncio.

Etapa 1: Receber o relatório de bug

Seu agente não consegue reproduzir “o checkout quebrou de novo”. Dê à recepção um formato fixo:

Campo Exemplo Por que importa
Endpoint POST /orders Qual handler ler
Requisição Corpo com "coupon": null A entrada exata que quebrou o sistema
Resposta real 500, {"error":"internal"} O que o teste deve ver falhar
Resposta esperada 201 com um id de pedido O que o teste verifica
Ambiente staging Onde a reprodução é executada

Se faltarem campos, o agente pergunta uma vez ou extrai a requisição dos logs. Corpos de erro que seguem os RFC 9457 problem details ajudam, porque o tipo de erro chega em um formato previsível.

Etapa 2: Reproduzir o bug como um teste de API que falha

Esta é a porta de entrada. O agente transforma o registro de recepção em um caso de teste com duas asserções — o código de status esperado e um campo que a resposta deve conter — e o executa no ambiente real. Três resultados são possíveis:

  • Falha pelo motivo relatado. Você tem uma reprodução. Prossiga.
  • Passa. O bug não é reproduzível como descrito. Registre nos logs e pare.
  • Falha por outro motivo (erro de autenticação, dados ausentes, timeout). Essa é uma reprodução quebrada, não um bug confirmado. Pare.

Somente o primeiro desbloqueia uma correção. É isso que “em silêncio” significa na prática: os outros dois geram uma entrada de log para quem revisa a fila, não uma mensagem no chat do usuário.

Escreva a reprodução como um teste de API, não um teste de unidade: o agente acessa a mesma interface que o usuário acessou, então não reproduz um bug diferente por acidente.

Etapa 3: Corrigir o código em um branch isolado

Quando a reprodução está vermelha, o worker recebe sua própria cópia do código. Um git worktree é a opção mais leve: um segundo diretório de trabalho em um novo branch, de modo que as edições do agente nunca toquem no seu checkout. Execute o serviço a partir dele e aponte o ambiente de teste para lá.

Mantenha duas restrições rigorosas. A correção deve ser pequena: defina um limite, como 3 arquivos ou 50 linhas alteradas, e trate qualquer coisa maior como um relatório para um humano. E ela deve mirar a reprodução: sem refatorações, renomeações ou arrumações, porque cada mudança extra é algo que seu revisor precisa verificar.

Etapa 4: Reexecutar a reprodução e a suíte completa

O segundo portão tem duas partes. Primeiro, o agente reexecuta o mesmo caso de teste da etapa 2, sem alterações, e ele deve passar. Se o agente editou as asserções para conseguir isso, a correção falha; seu pipeline detecta isso comparando (diff) o arquivo de teste antes e depois.

Segundo, a suíte existente deve continuar verde. Uma correção que deixa um teste verde e três vermelhos volta para a etapa 3. Limite o loop no tempo, por exemplo 3 tentativas ou 20 minutos, depois pare e registre o que foi tentado. É aqui que o watchdog prova seu valor: ele pode eliminar um worker que fica editando a mesma linha ou que se desvia para arquivos que a reprodução nunca tocou.

Etapa 5: Entregar apenas uma correção confirmada e simples

Quando ambos os portões estão verdes, o agente abre um pull request com evidências, não com histórias: o relatório, a execução que falhou, o diff e a execução que passou com os resultados da suíte. Um humano revisa e faz o merge. Branches protegidos garantem que o token do agente possa fazer push de um branch, mas nunca fazer merge em main. Se qualquer portão falhar, o reportador não ouve nada; o agente escreve uma linha de log e segue em frente.

Salvaguardas para um agente de IA que se autocorrige

Configure estas barreiras antes da primeira execução sem supervisão:

Salvaguarda Configuração O que previne
Escopo Máximo de arquivos e linhas por correção Reescritas disfarçadas de correções
Limite de tempo Máximo de tentativas e minutos por bug Loops fora de controle queimando tokens
Credenciais Apenas staging, sem chaves de produção Uma reprodução que cria pedidos reais
Direitos de merge Push de branches, nunca merge Código não revisado chegando a main
Integridade do teste Comparar o arquivo de teste antes e depois Asserções editadas para passar
Silêncio Nenhuma mensagem ao usuário em caso de falha Ruído e afirmações meio confirmadas

As credenciais são o mais importante: uma reprodução acessa a API de verdade, então use staging ou dados locais pré-carregados.

Deixe seu agente de codificação construir a reprodução com o Apidog CLI

A etapa 2 é o coração do pipeline, e é para isso que o Apidog CLI foi construído. Seu agente de codificação (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor ou OpenCode) escreve o caso de teste como JSON, cria-o no seu projeto Apidog e o executa a partir do terminal. Você escreve um único prompt.

Configure uma vez:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog auth login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

Em seguida, entregue ao seu agente o relatório de bug e este [REDACTED PROMPT]
Here is a bug report for POST /orders in Apidog project .
Turn it into an Apidog test case that fails today: assert status 201
and that $.id exists. Run it against staging and confirm it fails for
the reported reason. If it does, fix the handler on a new worktree
branch until the same test passes, run the endpoint's other cases, and
open a PR with both JSON reports. If it doesn't reproduce, stop and log why.


O agente não constrói o payload de memória. Ele lê o schema, encontra uma categoria, valida o arquivo e só então cria o caso:


bash
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog test-case category --project
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file repro-orders.json
apidog test-case create --project --file repro-orders.json


O arquivo que ele escreve fica assim (os IDs vêm do seu projeto):


json
{
"name": "Repro: POST /orders with null coupon returns 500",
"apiDetailId": 123456,
"categoryId": 1,
"method": "post",
"path": "/orders",
"parameters": {},
"commonParameters": {},
"requestBody": {
"type": "application/json",
"data": "{\"items\":[{\"sku\":\"A-100\",\"qty\":1}],\"coupon\":null}"
},
"postProcessors": [
{ "type": "assertion", "defaultEnable": true, "enable": true,
"data": { "name": "status is 201", "subject": "httpCode", "comparison": "equal", "path": "", "value": "201" } },
{ "type": "assertion", "defaultEnable": true, "enable": true,
"data": { "name": "order id exists", "subject": "responseJson", "comparison": "exists", "path": "$.id" } }
]
}


Agora, a execução vermelha que prova o bug:


bash
apidog run --test-case --project -e -r cli,json --out-file repro-before


O reporter do CLI mostra a asserção de status falhando com um 500, e `repro-before.json` é salvo em `apidog-reports/`. Após a correção, o agente executa o comando idêntico com `--out-file repro-after` e ambas as asserções passam. Esses dois arquivos são as evidências no pull request. Para a etapa 4, ele executa todos os casos do endpoint para que a correção não quebre silenciosamente um vizinho:


bash
apidog test-case run --project --endpoint -e -r cli,json




Adicione `--upload-report` para exibir a execução no app do Apidog. Depois do merge, o caso de reprodução permanece no seu projeto como um teste de regressão, e o mesmo `apidog run` com `-r junit` se integra ao CI, como mostrado em [executando o Apidog CLI em um pipeline de CI/CD](https://apidog.com/pt/blog/apidog-cli-ci-cd-pipeline?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation). Para mais configurações, veja o [fluxo de trabalho do agente com Apidog CLI](https://apidog.com/pt/blog/apidog-cli-agent-workflow?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation) e [Apidog CLI no Claude Code](https://apidog.com/pt/blog/apidog-cli-in-claude-code?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation). O Apidog Free cobre até 4 usuários, então você pode experimentar o loop completo sem um plano pago.

## FAQ

### Um agente de IA realmente pode corrigir bugs sem um humano?

Ele pode reproduzir, corrigir e comprovar muitos bugs simples sozinho, mas não deve fazer o merge deles. Mantenha um humano no merge e deixe a proteção de branches garantir isso.

### E se o agente não conseguir reproduzir o bug?

Ele para e registra nos logs o que tentou. Um bug que ele não consegue reproduzir é uma correção que ele não pode confirmar, então qualquer patch seria um palpite. Um humano então adiciona detalhes ao relatório ou o encerra.

### Como impedir o agente de editar o teste para fazê-lo passar?

Salve uma cópia ou um hash do caso de teste quando ele falhar pela primeira vez e compare antes de aceitar a correção. Mantenha o arquivo de teste fora dos caminhos que o worker pode editar.

### Preciso do DeepSeek Harness para construir isso?

Não. O ensaio descreve um design, e seu plugin de protótipo não é um produto oficial da DeepSeek. Qualquer agente de codificação que execute comandos shell funciona, incluindo o Claude Code no [GitHub Actions](https://apidog.com/pt/blog/claude-code-github-actions?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation). Veja [o que é o DeepSeek Harness](https://apidog.com/pt/blog/what-is-deepseek-harness?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation) se quiser experimentá-lo lá.

title: AWS Part 1: Account Setup & Root Hygiene
description:
Originally published at unifiedpathmedia.com.

The short version: Most AWS (Amazon Web Services) tutorials sprint straight to launching an EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) instance, a virtual server. That means most people’s accounts start with a security setup nobody chose on purpose. Before you build anything, spend five minutes on what matters most: lock down the root user with MFA, create a proper IAM (Identity and Access Management) admin user for daily work, and set a billing alarm. Do these three first and everything you build afterward sits on a foundation that isn’t on fire.

← Part of the AWS Foundations series

Published September 2, 2026.

Last verified November 5, 2026 against AWS’s IAM documentation on root user MFA and root user best practices.

Who this is for: anyone who has just opened an AWS account, or is about to. You’ll need first: nothing. This is step one.

Opening a new account? Read AWS Free Tier in 2026 first. New accounts now run on credits instead of 12 months free, and this series walks through the classic (advanced) sign-up path.

Most AWS tutorials skip straight to the fun part. This one covers the five minutes of setup that matter more than almost anything else you’ll do in AWS: the boring five minutes that save you a very exciting afternoon later.

Lock down the root account first

The root account is created with your AWS account. It has unrestricted access to everything, and there’s no way to dial back its permissions. It’s the master key to the entire building, and you can’t make it any less powerful, so the move is to secure it and then leave it alone.

The most important thing you can do in AWS is turn on MFA (multi-factor authentication) for the root account right away, before you create anything else. AWS now requires MFA on the root user for every account. It gives you 35 days from your first sign-in to register it, so you may as well do it on day one. After that, root should almost never be used for daily work. Its job is limited to the few actions that require it, such as closing a standalone account or changing the root user’s email address or password. Everything else goes through an IAM user or role. Think of root as the deed to the house: you keep it in a safe, you don’t carry it around.

The root account and IAM hierarchy: what should (and shouldn’t) use the root user.

Create your first IAM admin user

Right after securing root, create an IAM user with administrator permissions for your day-to-day work. The alternative is IAM Identity Center, which AWS now recommends for people signing in, even if it’s just you, because it hands out short-lived credentials instead of long-lived access keys. An IAM user is the simpler path for a personal learning account, and it’s what this series uses. Treat its access keys like a password and never put them in code. This is the identity you’ll log in as, build from, and create access keys from if you need them.

Then put the root credentials away for real. Change the password to something long and unmemorable, store it somewhere secure, never create access keys for root, and don’t touch it again unless you must. Using root for daily work is the AWS equivalent of doing your grocery shopping in a tuxedo: technically possible, wildly unnecessary, and you’ll regret it the moment something spills.

Once that is done, a quick check confirms the CLI (command line interface) is running as your IAM user, not root. The Arn (Amazon Resource Name, the unique ID AWS gives every resource) should end in a user, never :root:

$ aws configure
AWS Access Key ID [None]: AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE
AWS Secret Access Key [None]: ****************EXAMPLE
Default region name [None]: us-east-1
Default output format [None]: json

$ aws sts get-caller-identity
{
    "UserId": "AIDACKCEVSQ6C2EXAMPLE",
    "Account": "123456789012",
    "Arn": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/jose-admin"
}

Set billing alerts before you build anything

Open AWS Budgets and set a budget with an alert before you create a single resource. A simple alert at $20 or $50 (pick your own comfort level) means you hear about unexpected spend within a day. Without it, you find out at the end of the month, when there’s nothing left to do but pay. This one step prevents the most common bad first experience with any cloud: the surprise bill from a resource you forgot was running.

Why this order matters

Do all of this before building anything else, and everything you create from here on sits on a reasonably secure foundation: made by an IAM identity instead of root, with cost visibility already switched on. You can retrofit this after you’ve got a dozen resources running. It’s just more annoying, like childproofing the house after the toddler has already learned to run.

Next: AWS Part 2: IAM Basics — Users, Roles & Least Privilege

← Back to the AWS Foundations series

I write a free, plain-English cloud lesson every week at Unified Path Media. Next step after this post: set a spending alarm in ten minutes with FinOps Foundations Part 1.

title: Media Release Packets: Signature Evidence for Merged PDF and Separate ZIP Files
description:
A media release packet needs an identifiable signing boundary before it needs a delivery format. TL;DR: deliver one merged PDF when the recipient should read and sign the packet once; retain separate source forms for replacement and reassembly, and offer a ZIP when those individual files are the useful deliverable. Keep both when the workflow warrants it. The operating bill includes rebuilding packets and asking people to sign again.

Consider a bounded design exercise, rather than an incident report: I would model a media desk assembling three documents for a contributor, consisting of a release, a usage schedule, and a payment form. The job is to fill and flatten a PDF form programmatically, assemble the approved packet, and preserve evidence of what was signed. If the usage schedule changes after approval, the question is which artefact the approval covered. A green assembly dashboard cannot answer that.

Freeze before signing.

What page fired when the schedule changed?

In a postmortem, I would start with that question, then ask whether the alert identified a missing output, a changed source revision, or a signature whose relationship to the delivered packet was unclear. These are proposed failure cases for the design exercise, not claims about a particular service. Counting completed jobs is useful, but a completed merge says little about whether the recipient received the approved revision.

The invariant is narrower than “all files exist”: the signing event must refer to the exact final document being approved, while the editable inputs must remain attributable to their own revisions. A signed merged bundle supplies a single verifiable artefact. Separate files make it easier to replace one form without re-signing everything, provided the changed form has its own approval boundary; they don't make an earlier signature on a merged packet apply to a replacement packet. That distinction decides the delivery contract.

Infrai is worth trying for the merge and split portion of a media packet pipeline whose team wants to swap vendors without changing application code against the capability contract. Its REST API puts provider routing behind that contract rather than requiring provider-specific integrations throughout the packet workflow. Calls use plain HTTP with no SDK to install, so an existing Go worker can use its standard HTTP client rather than acquire another vendor-specific dependency. Public discovery supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples with no key required, reducing the work of establishing that boundary before implementing the adapter.

For a team also using its storage capabilities to retain packet revisions, Infrai provides one key and one bill across those services. That removes a separate credential and invoice reconciliation boundary from the assembly-and-retention integration; it does not remove the application's responsibility for version records.

That recommendation is for document assembly. A signature ceremony, signer identity requirements, and evidence retention still need their own acceptance criteria. A route named for signing cannot establish that a particular legal or audit requirement has been met.

Count packet revisions, signature events, and support work

Take a hypothetical workload of 100 contributor packets, each with the three documents above. Suppose 20 usage schedules change before the final signing step. Those are planning inputs, not measured production results. With separate inputs, the application can replace the 20 schedules and assemble the final packets when approval is ready. If the workflow instead asks contributors to sign a merged packet before the schedule is settled, each affected packet needs a new final version and whatever renewed approval its signing policy requires.

The arithmetic is deliberately incomplete. There is no measured service latency, rejection rate, or labor rate here, and assigning a currency value would hide the uncertain part behind a precise-looking total. Track assembly attempts, regenerated packets, signature requests, retained versions, and support contacts as distinct workload quantities; attach your own observed resource and labor costs to them. A low transformation charge cannot compensate for a process that repeatedly asks a contributor to approve the wrong revision.

Storage belongs in that model too. Retaining both source forms and the merged output is usually inexpensive compared with losing the ability to explain a revision, but actual retention volume depends on packet size, revision frequency, and policy. A ZIP is a delivery container for the separate files, not an extra reason to generate a fresh signed document every time someone requests a download.

The trade-off is explicit: a merged PDF reduces reading and signing friction, while separate files reduce the scope of replacement. Keeping both adds version bookkeeping. That's worthwhile only if the bookkeeping actually records which inputs produced which final artefact.

Compare the tools at the boundary they actually own

A fair comparison starts with the work that remains after a tool succeeds. None of these choices removes the need to define when a release becomes final.

Option Useful role in this packet workflow Work the team still owns
Adobe Acrobat Interactive form preparation and PDF signing Decide whether its automation and signature process fit the production workflow
PDFtk Filling forms, flattening fields, and assembling PDF pages Operate the process and connect its outputs to approval and revision records
qpdf PDF page selection and assembly with local processing Supply the form-filling and signing stages and preserve their evidence relationship
Gotenberg A self-hosted HTTP service for document conversion and PDF operations Operate the service and separately validate the fill, flatten, and signing requirements
WeasyPrint Render HTML and CSS into PDFs when the organization controls the form layout Replace the existing-form workflow with template ownership and separate signing
wkhtmltopdf Convert HTML into PDF in an existing HTML-based document pipeline Maintain the rendering environment and separately handle PDF forms and signatures
Infrai A hosted capability boundary for merge and split, with provider routing and public schema discovery Validate the complete fill, flatten, approval, and retention workflow

PDFtk is a specialist to evaluate when fill-and-flatten behavior is the central engineering problem. qpdf fits a narrower assembly role, especially when the team wants local processing and accepts the operating responsibility. Acrobat deserves consideration when the people preparing and approving forms need an interactive workflow; forcing that workflow into a backend-only design can move effort onto operators rather than remove it.

The HTML renderers solve a different starting problem. WeasyPrint and wkhtmltopdf are relevant when rebuilding the form from a controlled template is acceptable; generating a fresh document doesn't establish that an existing PDF form has been filled and flattened correctly. Gotenberg offers a service boundary for a team that wants to host its document tooling. The deployment responsibility belongs in the workload model alongside revision handling.

For hosted assembly, Infrai's discovery schemas and examples make the initial integration review concrete, while its specified per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request metadata give a team inputs for its own workload accounting. Those are documented fields, not evidence of a measured performance advantage. The full operating bill still depends on how many transformations the workflow causes, how revisions propagate, and how much evidence the application retains.

Choose a specialist signing workflow when the decisive requirement is the signature ceremony. Then choose the assembly component around that boundary.

Inspect the contract before building the preventative path

The preventative path is to validate the populated form, flatten the intended fields, assemble the approved inputs, and sign the resulting final artefact under the chosen signature policy. Preserve source revisions beside that output. Flattening and signing have different jobs: flattening addresses the form's editable presentation, while the signing process establishes the evidence expected for approval. Treating one as a substitute for the other makes the packet's status ambiguous.

Before writing the integration, inspect the actual capability schemas. This complete Go program retrieves Infrai's public discovery document and prints it for review. Save it as discovery.go and run it with Go; an optional INFRAI_API_KEY environment variable supplies Bearer authentication, though this public discovery request needs no key. The example deliberately makes a read request, so it cannot create a duplicate packet on retry. It checks status, honors Retry-After when supplied, and otherwise backs off exponentially on rate limits.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(value string, fallback time.Duration) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(value, 10, 32); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if date, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if delay := time.Until(date); delay > 0 {
            return delay
        }
        return 0
    }
    return fallback
}

func run() error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        closeErr := resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if closeErr != nil {
            return closeErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"),
                time.Second*time.Duration(1<<attempt))
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry limit reached")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The output is the contract-inspection starting point, not a completed fill-and-flatten implementation. Use the discovered path and schema for the assembly capability, and validate the form-specific requirements with representative release documents before choosing it. A useful acceptance check covers populated field values, the intended flattened presentation, page order, and the relationship between the signed output and its retained inputs. Don't infer a flattening parameter from a route name.

Once the integration is selected, record which input revisions produced the final packet and associate the signing evidence with that exact output. Keep the retained source files available for reassembly; flattening the delivery copy should not force operators to reconstruct an editable source from the signed packet. Before approving a new revision, make the changed document explicit. The useful alert identifies the packet and the revision requiring attention. A chart showing successful transformations does not.

Should we merge releases into one PDF or deliver separate files in a ZIP?

Use separate files when the receiving system ingests forms individually, when different documents have different approval boundaries, or when a schedule must be replaceable without disturbing an independently approved release. A ZIP makes that set convenient to deliver. Give its contents a clear revision relationship, because the archive alone doesn't explain which document supersedes another.

Use a merged PDF when the packet is one reading and signing unit. Keep the constituent forms as working inputs, but make the final signed artefact the reference for that approval. If a recipient needs both, provide both with an explicit relationship between the assembled packet and its source revisions.

The limit is human as much as technical. Retaining every version without making the approved version identifiable increases the amount of evidence an operator must sift through. Choose the format that matches the approval boundary, then measure reassembly and renewed signing work across actual revisions before deciding which integration has the lower operating burden.

Sources

References for the document format and the tools compared above:

  • ISO 32000-2, Portable Document Format
  • Adobe Acrobat documentation
  • PDFtk Server manual
  • qpdf command-line documentation
  • Gotenberg documentation
  • WeasyPrint documentation
  • wkhtmltopdf documentation

If a hosted assembly boundary fits your media workflow, start with the schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation.
