title: 168 of 169 Paid 'description' Fields Were Identical to the Free 'summary'. The Real Text Was 17x Longer
description:
I run a visa agency in Bali. The other half of my week goes into Apify Actors, and one of them reads Eventbrite search pages: you hand it a search URL or a city, it pages through the results and returns one row per event — name, dates with the time zone, venue with coordinates, category, tags, image. Switch on the detail pass and it also opens each event page for the ticket price range, the organizer and the description.

That detail pass costs the buyer a second charge per event. I spent today measuring what it actually buys, on two search pages: Bali, Indonesia and Berlin, Germany, a hundred-event cap each.

Bali returned 69 events across 4 pages in 28.0 seconds. Berlin returned 100 in 22.2 seconds. Then I diffed two fields that should never be the same — summary, which comes free from the search listing, and description, which the buyer pays for.

They were identical on 168 of 169 rows. The 169th had no description at all.

The meta tag is not the description

Eventbrite event pages carry JSON-LD, the schema.org/Event block search engines read. It has offers with lowPrice and highPrice, an organizer, start and end timestamps with the UTC offset — all genuinely useful, none of it on the search page. It also has a description. I read that field, shipped it, and called it "full description" in my own documentation.

It is the meta description. Capped at 140 characters, built from the first sentences of the listing — which is exactly what the search page already hands over as summary, for free.

Across those 69 Bali events, description averaged 108 characters. Three rows sat exactly at 140, the cap. The field was not wrong, it was just a duplicate the buyer was paying me to deliver twice.

The text the organizer actually wrote is in the same HTML I had already downloaded, a few kilobytes further down, inside the Next.js payload:

const m = html.match(/<script id="__NEXT_DATA__" type="application\/json">([\s\S]*?)<\/script>/);
const ctx = JSON.parse(m[1]).props.pageProps.context;
const mods = ctx.structuredContent.modules;   // [{type:'text', text:'<p>…'}, {type:'image', url:…}]

structuredContent.modules is the event body as the organizer built it — text blocks, images, the occasional video embed. Joining the text blocks and stripping tags gives the real thing. I refetched all 69 event pages and measured both sources on the same bytes:

JSON-LD description structuredContent text
Pages that had it 69 / 69 69 / 69
Average length 108 chars 1,841 chars
Longest 140 12,764
Rows where it was longer — 67 of 69
Rows with nothing at all 0 2

Seventeen times more text, median ratio 7.8x, from a request I was already paying for. The two empty ones are honest: those organizers wrote no body copy, so the Actor falls back to the meta description rather than returning null.

The control run after the fix, same search, 20 events: description identical to summary on 0 of 20 rows, median length 647, longest 11,838. Prices and currency still filled on 20 of 20 — I did not trade one field for another.

While I was in there, the same payload gave up eleven more fields that cost nothing extra, because they ride on the page already being fetched: durationMinutes (filled on 69 of 69), salesStatus, refundPolicy, ageRestriction (9 of 69), doorTime, parking, organizerEvents, organizerFollowers, organizerVerified, descriptionBlocks, and nextSessionAt.

currency is the organizer's currency, not the country's

Now the finding I cannot fix, only document.

All 69 Bali rows carry country: "ID". Their prices came back in eight currencies:

USD 44   AUD 10   GBP 8   EUR 3   SGD 1   MYR 1   NZD 1   HKD 1

Zero in rupiah. A dive trip in North Bali is priced 5299.5 HKD. A free Bitcoin meetup in Canggu is priced 0 GBP. A bracelet workshop in Bali is served from eventbrite.ch at 7.49 EUR. Those 69 events arrived across eight different Eventbrite domains — .com, .com.au, .co.uk, .sg, .ch, .fr, .ie, .hk.

This is not a parsing artifact. I checked both independent sources on the page — the JSON-LD priceCurrency and basicInfo.currency in the Next.js payload — and they agree on 69 of 69 rows. Eventbrite publishes the price in the currency of the organizer's account. A yoga teacher who registered in Sydney sells a Canggu sound bath in Australian dollars, and the site never converts.

Berlin is why nobody notices: 95 of its 100 rows are EUR, because Berlin events are mostly run by Berlin organizers. Bali is a destination — its events are sold by Australians, Brits, Singaporeans — so the same behaviour becomes obvious. If your search covers a tourist region, sorting those rows by priceMin sorts by nothing at all, and averaging them produces a number with no unit.

Two more things to distrust in the price fields. priceMin equals priceMax on 49 of 69 rows, which usually means one ticket type, not a one-price event. And priceMax is whatever the most expensive offer on the page is: the Bali Venture Capital World Summit reports 168.94 to 57662.15 EUR, a 341x spread, because the top of that range is a sponsorship package nobody attends as a guest.

A series row is one date out of hundreds

Eventbrite recurring events are a single search result. My rows flag them — isSeries, seriesId, occurrencesInSeries — and on the Bali page 36 of 69 rows were series, covering 1,568 dates between them. The biggest single row: 421 occurrences. A sound bath studio: 283.

So "69 events in Bali" and "69 things happening in Bali" are very different counts, and a weekly calendar built from the row's one date will keep rediscovering the same workshop. The new nextSessionAt confirms what that one date means — on all 8 series rows in my control run it matched startsAt exactly, i.e. it is the next session on sale. The other 282 are not in the row, and the search page does not have them.

Berlin again shows the contrast: 7 series rows out of 100, 14 occurrences total.

Two smaller traps from the same two runs. organizerName is null on 11 of 69 Bali rows — null in both page sources, because those organizers never set a public name; you get organizerUrl with a numeric id and nothing else. And one organizer, Eurasia Research, owns 9 of the 69 rows with near-identical academic conferences, so an unfiltered "events in Bali" list is 13% one seller. Date range of that list: 6 November 2026 to 29 October 2030. Only 40 of 69 fall in the current month.

Calling it 

{
  "startUrls": ["https://www.eventbrite.com/d/indonesia--bali/all-events/"],
  "maxEvents": 100,
  "includeDetails": true
}

A real row from today's run, trimmed:

{
  "type": "event",
  "eventId": "1991054633005",
  "name": "Chakras sound sanctuary - SOUND HEALING sessions | Sound bath Bali",
  "startsAt": "2026-11-06T14:00:00",
  "timezone": "Asia/Makassar",
  "isSeries": true,
  "occurrencesInSeries": 283,
  "nextSessionAt": "2026-11-06T14:00:00+08",
  "venueName": "ADDA YOGA CANGGU - Meditation | Breath | Sound",
  "city": "Kec. Kuta Utara", "country": "ID",
  "latitude": -8.643315, "longitude": 115.1427276,
  "category": "Religion & Spirituality",
  "priceMin": 29.89, "priceMax": 29.89, "currency": "AUD", "isFree": false,
  "organizerName": "ADDA YOGA", "organizerEvents": 700, "organizerFollowers": 19,
  "durationMinutes": 90, "refundPolicy": "custom", "salesStatus": "sales_ended",
  "descriptionBlocks": 11, "urgency": ["salesEndSoon"]
}

Note salesStatus: "sales_ended" on an event the search page listed as upcoming — 3 of 69 Bali rows were sold out or closed. That field did not exist this morning.

From Python, run and read in one call:

import requests
rows = requests.post(
    "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/lergassy~eventbrite-scraper/run-sync-get-dataset-items",
    params={"token": "apify_api_..."},
    json={"location": "Berlin, Germany", "dates": "this_weekend", "maxEvents": 200},
    timeout=600,
).json()
events = [r for r in rows if r.get("type") == "event"]
print(len(events), "events;", len({r["currency"] for r in events if r.get("currency")}), "currencies")

The Actor is Eventbrite Scraper. It bills per event row, with a second charge only if you ask for the detail pass; error rows are free and there is no start fee. The detail pass is also what the time goes on: the same Bali search finished in 8.2 seconds with details off and 28.0 seconds with them on, because that is 69 extra page loads.

When it is the wrong tool. There is no search across all of Eventbrite from the API side — you bring a search URL or a city, and Eventbrite's own search decides what exists. Past events are gone; search pages show upcoming only, so a history has to be accumulated by running on a schedule. Attendee lists, ticket inventory and sales numbers are not public and never will be. And one operational detail worth knowing: Eventbrite's WAF answers a flagged search request with HTTP 405, not 403 or 429 — from my own server the search page returns 405 while individual event pages return 200 all day. The Actor climbs a proxy ladder when that happens; if you are writing your own, treat a 405 on a GET as a bot check rather than a method error, which is what I spent an afternoon assuming.

title: Building an Embeddable, Zero-Dependency DevTools Panel for React & Next.js
description:
Debugging network requests and browser storage during development often forces you to constantly switch context—toggling native browser DevTools, sifting through noisy logs, or relying on heavy browser extensions that don't travel with your repository.

To solve this, I built React Dev Companion: an embeddable, zero-dependency developer tools panel designed specifically for React and Next.js applications.

🎯 Why React Dev Companion?

Most debugging tools fall into two categories:

  1. Full-blown Browser Extensions: Requires every developer on the team (and QA testers) to install specific extensions.
  2. Heavy External Panels: Adds bloated dependencies to your project bundle.

React Dev Companion runs directly inside your application during development, giving you instant client-side inspection without bundle bloat.

Key Capabilities

  • ⚡ Real-Time Network Interception: Intercepts outgoing window.fetch calls, logging HTTP methods, target URLs, and response statuses live.
  • 💾 Multi-Store Storage Inspector: View, inject, and delete keys across localStorage, sessionStorage, and cookies from a single unified panel.
  • 📦 Zero Dependencies: Ultra-lightweight footprint engineered for zero impact on application performance.
  • 🌐 Framework-Agnostic Support: Works out of the box with React SPAs (Vite, CRA) and Next.js (App Router / Client Components).

🛠️ How It Works Under the Hood

1. Non-Invasive window.fetch Interception

Rather than requiring wrapper functions around your HTTP client, React Dev Companion safely wraps window.fetch upon mounting. It streams response metrics to an isolated state container without altering original request promises or application flow:

const originalFetch = window.fetch;

window.fetch = async (...args) => {
  const [resource, config] = args;
  const method = config?.method || 'GET';
  const url = typeof resource === 'string' ? resource : resource.url;

  try {
    const response = await originalFetch(...args);
    notifyDevTools({ url, method, status: response.status });
    return response;
  } catch (error) {
    notifyDevTools({ url, method, status: 500 });
    throw error;
  }
};

2. Unified Storage Management

Browser APIs handle storage types inconsistently (localStorage vs string parsing for document.cookie). The Storage Inspector abstracts key management, enabling instant state invalidations and seamless standard cookie expiration handling.

🚀 Quick Start Guide

Installation

Install via npm, yarn, or pnpm:

npm install react-dev-companion

Next.js (App Router) Integration

Load the companion component conditionally in your root layout so it only runs during development:

'use client';

import { DevCompanion } from 'react-dev-companion';

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        {children}
        {process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development' && <DevCompanion />}
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}

Vite / React SPA Integration 

import React from 'react';
import { DevCompanion } from 'react-dev-companion';

export function App() {
  return (
    <div>
      <MainContent />
      {import.meta.env.DEV && <DevCompanion position="bottom-right" />}
    </div>
  );
}

🏭 Built with Modern Engineering Standards

React Dev Companion was built from day one following open-source best practices:

  • CI/CD Pipeline: Fully automated via GitHub Actions (Node 22).
  • Strict Commit Standards: Conventional Commits enforced via Husky & Commitlint.
  • Type Safety: Written 100% in TypeScript with strict mode enabled.

💬 Let's Build Together! (Call to Action)

This project is fully open-source and ready for community feedback!

  • ⭐ Star the repo on GitHub: Kickz1nn/react-dev-companion
  • 🤝 Want to contribute? Check out our CONTRIBUTING.md and grab a good first issue!
  • 💬 Feedback: What features or tabs would you like to see next? (e.g., React Query status inspector, Console log collector, or Performance timers?) Let me know in the comments below!

title: Automation Testing With Playwright Using JavaScript
description:
Automation testing is a critical part of software development that helps ensure the quality and reliability of your application. Playwright is a robust end-to-end testing framework that enables you to automate browser actions and interactions. This comprehensive guide will walk you through performing automation testing using Playwright in a Next.js application.

Playwright is a JavaScript library that provides a high-level API to automate browsers like Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit. It allows you to write browser automation scripts that simulate user interactions, navigation, form submissions, and more. Playwright's unique architecture provides a fast and reliable way to test web applications.

Setting Up a Javascript Project

Before we start writing tests, let's set up a Next.js project:

Create a new Javascript project:

mkdir my-js-project
cd my-js-project
npm init -y

This will create a new directory called my-js-project, navigate into it, and initialize a new Node.js project with default settings.

The -y flag in the npm init -y command is a shorthand for "yes". It automatically answers "yes" to all the prompts that npm init would normally ask you, thereby accepting all the default values for the project setup.

Install the Playwright dependencies:

npm install playwright

Writing Automation Tests with Playwright

Let's create a simple automation test for a javascript application. We want to test the navigation from the home page to a blog post page.

const { chromium } = require('playwright');

describe('Next.js Blog Automation Test', () => {
  let browser;
  let page;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    browser = await chromium.launch();
  });

  beforeEach(async () => {
    page = await browser.newPage();
  });

  afterAll(async () => {
    await browser.close();
  });

  it('should navigate to a blog post', async () => {
    await page.goto('http://localhost:3000');
    await page.click('a[href="/blog"]');
    await page.waitForSelector('h1');
    const pageTitle = await page.textContent('h1');
    expect(pageTitle).toContain('Blog Post Title');
  });
});

Let us see the components of the above code in a bit more detail.

When using testing frameworks like Jest, Mocha, Jasmine, or Playwright, the describe block is a fundamental organizational structure that helps group related test cases together. It provides a way to define a logical container for a set of tests with a common context or functionality. The describe block is primarily used to improve your test suite's organization, readability, and maintainability.

The beforeEach function is a part of testing frameworks like Jest and is used to set up a consistent and controlled environment before running each individual test case within a describe block. This is particularly helpful in maintaining a clean state and avoiding interference between test cases.

In testing, it's important to create a controlled environment for each test case to ensure that they run independently and reliably. Sometimes, tests require the same setup steps before execution. Instead of repeating the setup code in every test case, you can use beforeEach to define those common setup actions.

In automated testing, especially when using testing frameworks like Jest, you often encounter lifecycle functions that help you set up and tear down certain conditions before and after tests are run. One important lifecycle function is beforeAll.

The beforeAll function executes a block of code before all the tests within a test suite (also known as a test file or describe block) are run. This block of code typically sets up any common resources or configurations required for all the tests in that suite.

The afterAll function is a part of testing frameworks like Jest, and it is used to perform cleanup tasks or teardown operations after all the test cases within a describe block have been executed. It's the counterpart of the beforeAll function, which is used for setup operations before the test cases.

In testing, there might be scenarios where you need to perform cleanup tasks or reset the environment after all the test cases within a particular test suite have run. afterAll allows you to define these cleanup actions.

Enhancing API Testing with Playwright

Did you know that Playwright, commonly recognized for its powerful browser automation capabilities, can also be utilized for API testing? This versatile tool excels in web application testing and offers robust features to automate and validate API interactions. By leveraging Playwright for API testing, you can streamline your testing processes and ensure your APIs function as expected.

Writing Your First API Test

Let's start with a basic example. We'll test a simple REST API that returns user information.

  1. Start with creating a new file called apiTest.spec.js.

  2. Import Playwright:

const { test, expect } = require('@playwright/test');
  1. Write a Basic Test:

Here's a test that fetches user data from a hypothetical API endpoint.

test('GET user data', async ({ request }) => {
  const response = await request.get('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1');
  expect(response.status()).toBe(200);
  const userData = await response.json();
  expect(userData.id).toBe(1);
  expect(userData.name).toBe('Leanne Graham');
});

Breaking Down the Test

  • test: Defines a test case.

  • request.get: Sends a GET request to the specified URL.

  • expect: assertions to check if the response meets our expectations.

  • response.status(): Checks the HTTP status code of the response.

  • response.json(): Parses the response body as JSON.

Handling Different HTTP Methods

Playwright supports various HTTP methods. Here are examples of POST, PUT, and DELETE requests.

POST Request:

test('POST create new user', async ({ request }) => {
  const response = await request.post('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users', {
    data: {
      name: 'John Doe',
      username: 'johndoe',
      email: 'johndoe@example.com'
    }
  });
  expect(response.status()).toBe(201);
  const newUser = await response.json();
  expect(newUser.name).toBe('John Doe');
});

PUT Request:

test('PUT update user data', async ({ request }) => {
  const response = await request.put('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1', {
    data: {
      name: 'Jane Doe'
    }
  });
  expect(response.status()).toBe(200);
  const updatedUser = await response.json();
  expect(updatedUser.name).toBe('Jane Doe');

});

DELETE Request:

test('DELETE user', async ({ request }) => {
  const response = await request.delete('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1');
  expect(response.status()).toBe(200);
});

Handling Authentication

Many APIs require authentication. Here’s how to handle it in Playwright:

test('GET user data with authentication', async ({ request }) => {
  const response = await request.get('https://api.example.com/protected-resource', {
    headers: {
      'Authorization': `Bearer YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN`
    }
  });
  expect(response.status()).toBe(200);
});

Using Fixtures for Setup and Teardown

Fixtures help set up and tear down resources required for your tests. Here's an example:

test.describe('API tests with setup and teardown', () => {
  let userId;

  test.beforeAll(async ({ request }) => {
    const response = await request.post('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users', {
      data: { name: 'Test User' }
    });
    const user = await response.json();
    userId = user.id;
  });

  test.afterAll(async ({ request }) => {
    await request.delete(`https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/${userId}`);
  });

  test('GET created user data', async ({ request }) => {
    const response = await request.get(`https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/${userId}`);
    expect(response.status()).toBe(200);
  });
});

Running Your Tests

You can run your Playwright tests using the Playwright Test Runner. Add a script to your package.json:

"scripts": {
  "test": "playwright test"
}

Then, run your tests with:

npm test

Generating Test Depictions

Playwright Test generates reports by default. You can view the test results in the console, but you might want a more detailed report. Playwright provides a built-in HTML report. To enable it, add a playwright.config.js file in your project root:

module.exports = {
  reporter: [
    ['list'],
    ['html', { outputFolder: 'playwright-report', open: 'never' }]
  ],
};

Run your tests again.

After completing the tests, you'll find the HTML report in the playwright-report directory. To open it, run:

npm playwright show-report

This command opens the HTML report in your default browser, providing a detailed view of your test results.

Best Practices for Automation Testing

Here are some best practices to follow when writing automation tests using Playwright in a Next.js application:

  • Isolation: Each test should be independent and not depend on the state of other tests.

  • Use Data Attributes: Use data attributes in your components to make it easier to select elements in your tests.

  • Mock API Calls: Use mocking or stubbing to avoid making actual API requests during tests.

  • Assertions: Use meaningful assertions to verify the expected behavior of your application.

  • Page Objects: Create page objects or helper functions to encapsulate the interactions with specific parts of your application.

Continuous Integration with Playwright

Integrate your Playwright tests into your continuous integration (CI) pipeline. This ensures that your tests are automatically executed whenever you push code changes.

  1. Choose a CI platform like GitHub Actions, Jenkins, or Travis CI.

  2. Configure the CI pipeline to run the Playwright tests using Jest.

Playwright vs. Selenium: A Comparison

Feature Playwright Selenium
Language Support Javascript/TypeScript, Python, C#, Java Java, C#, Python, Ruby, JavaScript, Kotlin
Browser Support Chromium (Chrome, Edge), WebKit (Safari), Firefox Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge, IE, Opera
Installation and Setup Single package installation (includes browser binaries) Separate installations for WebDriver binaries
Speed and Performance Generally faster (uses DevTools Protocol) Slower (uses WebDriver protocol)
Parallel Testing Built-in support for parallel testing Requires additional configuration/tools (e.g., Selenium Grid)
APIs and Features Modern API, auto-wait, network interception, mobile emulation Mature API, similar features but more configuration
Community and Support Growing community, backed by Microsoft Established community, extensive documentation
Cross-Browser Testing Consistent results with the same API for all browsers It is possible but may have inconsistencies
Test Reporting Integrated reporting tools Requires additional tools/libraries (e.g., TestNG, JUnit)
Script Debugging Built-in tools for debugging (e.g., Playwright Inspector) Debugging through language-specific IDE/tools

Conclusion

Automation testing using Playwright in a Next.js application can help you catch bugs and ensure the quality of your software. Following the steps in this guide, you've learned how to set up a Next.js project, write automation tests, and integrate them into your CI pipeline. Remember to continuously update and expand your test suite as your application evolves.

title: Your AI agent draws a pretty layout. Make it structure the view first.
description:
You ask your AI agent for an order status page. It returns a polished card grid, a sparkline you never asked for, and a primary button that says "Explore insights." The status sits in the middle. There is no empty state. Error is a toast that vanishes. On a phone, cancel is gone.

The screen looks finished. The view was never defined.

Design Decision Method's fifth step is there to stop that. Step 5, structure each view, asks the agent to say what the view is for, what information people need to decide, which actions matter, and which states exist — before it invents a layout.

What step 5 asks for

For each important view, the method asks the agent to state:

  • its purpose
  • the information required to decide
  • the actions
  • the states that apply, including loading, empty, and error where they exist

It also asks the agent to keep essential information visible, and to adapt the layout to the device without dropping a capability the task needs.

That is the whole fifth step. A short definition of the view's job, then a layout that still does that job on a phone.

A worked example: order status on example.com

Say you run a small shop at example.com, and you ask your agent for the order status page. This is an illustration of how the procedure applies, not a case study or a measured result.

Without the method, the agent jumps to a familiar pattern: a dashboard-shaped page with charts, because status pages elsewhere often look like that. The order identity is secondary. Loading is a spinner with no context. Empty and error are afterthoughts.

With step 5 filled in first, the note might look like this:

Purpose: Show where one order is, what happens next, and what the customer can do about it.

Information required to decide: Order id, current status, last update, next step, items, and a path to support.

Actions: Track shipment (when a carrier link exists). Cancel while still allowed. Contact support. Back to orders.

States: Loading keeps the order context. Empty says this id has no order and offers a path back. Error keeps the order id visible and offers retry and support. The success path makes status and next step readable without a chart.

Device: Phone first. Cancel and support stay available; do not hide them behind a hover-only control.

Now the sparkline has nowhere to hide. "Explore insights" is out of scope. The layout still has to answer the purpose, surface the decision information, expose the actions, and cover the states.

Purpose before chrome

Agents are good at completing a visual pattern. They are less good at noticing that the pattern belongs to a different job. A monitoring dashboard and an order status page can both show numbers. Only one helps someone decide what to do about a single order.

Write the purpose first and the mismatch is obvious. Decorative metrics need a reason or they stay out. Essential information — status, next step, recovery — stays visible instead of being trimmed for whitespace.

Why this matters when you build with agents

A pretty first draft is easy to accept. The missing pieces are usually the ones that hurt later: empty, error, and the action that disappeared on a narrow viewport.

Structure each view puts those pieces in the first note. You can reject a layout that drops cancel on mobile, or never defines what happens when the order id is wrong.

The method does not claim this saves time. That has not been measured. What it does give you is a view definition you can check before the chrome hardens.

Keep it proportional

A one-line copy fix does not need a full view note. The method is a shared procedure, not mandatory for every small edit. When the change adds a screen, changes what people must see to decide, or could hide an action on a smaller device, spend the few lines.

Earlier steps give you context, a map when relationships matter, and a decision record for costly choices. Step 5 structures the views those decisions imply, instead of starting from a stock layout again.

Where this fits

Structure each view is step 5 of six: establish context, choose the visual system, map objects before layout, write a decision record, structure each view, then deliver and validate.

Try it

Design Decision Method is a lightweight design decision workflow for developers building interfaces with AI agents. It follows the open Agent Skills format and is MIT licensed. Install paths for Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and Codex are in the README.

  • Docs: https://frozonfreak.github.io/DesignDecesionMethod/
  • Repo: https://github.com/frozonfreak/DesignDecesionMethod
  • Design record template: https://github.com/frozonfreak/DesignDecesionMethod/blob/main/assets/design-record-template.md

title: Don't lazy-load the image people see first (Web HIG tip #15)
description:
Open your home page or a product page on a phone, on a slow connection. The headline and buttons show up, but the big hero image stays blank for a beat longer than everything else. Look at its markup and you'll often find loading="lazy", added to every <img> on the site by a template, a plugin, or a well-meant "lazy-load all images" change.

Web HIG tip #15 (Quick #84): Lazy-load below-the-fold media; never lazy-load the LCP candidate.

Why it matters

Lazy loading is a trade: the browser waits to fetch an image until it's close to the viewport. That's a win for images further down the page, and a loss for the one people see first:

  • Images far below the fold that nobody scrolls to never download, which saves data and leaves bandwidth for what's on screen
  • A lazy image's fetch can't start until the browser has laid out the page and worked out where the image sits, so a lazy hero image starts downloading later than it would have otherwise
  • The LCP candidate is usually the biggest image or text block in the first view. When it arrives late, the page looks unfinished, and Largest Contentful Paint gets worse
  • If the image URL only exists in JavaScript, for example a data-src that a script swaps in, the browser can't find it in the HTML at all until that script runs

The full HIG covers the image side of this in §2.1, Document Fundamentals, under responsive images: lazy-load non-critical images where appropriate, and avoid lazy-loading the LCP candidate and other immediately needed content. The LCP candidate SHOULD be discoverable early and MAY use fetchpriority="high" when appropriate. Quick #84 is Quick-only guidance, with no rule ID of its own. It pairs with Quick #83, which asks every image to declare its dimensions or aspect ratio, and with Quick #82's LCP target of 2.5 s or less.

The rule of thumb

Ask: will this image be on screen before anyone scrolls? If yes, don't lazy-load it.

This page looks fine on a fast laptop, but the hero waits for layout and for a script before it even starts downloading:

<!-- Hero: the LCP candidate, hidden from the browser until JS runs -->
<img class="lazy" data-src="https://example.com/img/hero.jpg" alt="">

<!-- Further down the page -->
<img src="https://example.com/img/team.jpg" alt="The team at the spring meetup">

Load the hero early and lazy-load what's further down:

<!-- Hero: a real src in the HTML, high priority, not lazy -->
<img src="https://example.com/img/hero.jpg"
     width="1200" height="600"
     fetchpriority="high"
     alt="A reader using the app on a phone">

<!-- Further down the page -->
<img src="https://example.com/img/team.jpg"
     width="800" height="533"
     loading="lazy"
     alt="The team at the spring meetup">

The page looks the same. The difference is when each image starts downloading.

Do this instead

  • Leave loading off the LCP image (the default is eager), give it a real src or srcset in the HTML, and consider fetchpriority="high". Browsers that don't support fetchpriority ignore it
  • Add loading="lazy" to images and iframes that sit well below the first view: long article bodies, comment sections, footers, embedded maps and video players
  • For a <video> further down the page, use preload="none" (or "metadata") and a poster image. loading="lazy" on <video> is newly specified but only some browsers support it so far, so treat it as a bonus, not the fix
  • In a carousel or gallery, load the first slide eagerly and lazy-load the rest
  • Give lazy images width and height (or a CSS aspect-ratio) so the page doesn't jump when they arrive
  • If the hero is a CSS background-image, the browser only finds it after the CSS has loaded. Use an <img> instead, or add <link rel="preload" as="image"> for it
  • The LCP element can be different on a phone and on a desktop. Check both layouts before you decide which images stay eager

Quick check for your app

Open your main pages (say, example.com and example.com/products) at a phone width and at a desktop width. In the browser's developer tools, find the LCP element in a performance recording, then check its markup: no loading="lazy", and a URL that's in the HTML rather than added by a script. Scroll down and watch the network panel: images further down should only start loading as you get near them. A tool can flag a lazy-loaded LCP image in a single lab run, but only checking the real LCP element on your own pages, at the widths people use, shows which image needs to load first.

The Web HIG is an open set of guidelines for how the web should behave, not a component library. Design systems define how it looks. The Web HIG defines how it behaves.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/frozonfreak/webhig/discussions/32
  • Hashnode: https://thewebhig.hashnode.dev/dont-lazy-load-the-image-people-see-first-web-hig-tip-15
  • Dev.to: https://dev.to/frozonfreak/dont-lazy-load-the-image-people-see-first-web-hig-tip-15-38k3
  • Bluesky: https://bsky.app/profile/sastha.bsky.social/post/3mzmmnfubak2p

title: The DreamHost Data Breach Sat in a Web File Manager for Two Months Before Anyone Noticed
description:
The DreamHost Data Breach Sat in a Web File Manager for Two Months Before Anyone Noticed

The DreamHost data breach, confirmed in a notification this week, ran from roughly August 2026 to October 23, 2026, nearly two months, through a vulnerability in the web-based File Manager tool at files.dreamhost.com. By the time it was discovered, attackers had collected FTP and SFTP usernames and passwords for everyone who had logged into that one tool during the window, plus webmail session credentials for an unspecified number of additional users.

Jump to what DreamHost says wasn't touched if you want the scope boundary first.

What Actually Happened

According to DreamHost's own breach notification, "an unauthorized third party accessed the server that runs our web-based File Manager at files.dreamhost.com," then "exploited a vulnerability in that software" to access FTP/SFTP usernames and passwords for individuals who logged into that File Manager between approximately August 2026 and October 23, 2026. BleepingComputer's reporting adds that webmail systems may also have been reached, exposing session information, including credentials, for a limited number of users.

DreamHost says the attack "appears deliberate," not an opportunistic scan that happened to land somewhere sensitive, and that staff worked to contain it fully once discovered. The company has not disclosed how many accounts were affected. BleepingComputer notes it contacted DreamHost multiple times asking for that number specifically and received no response.

What DreamHost Says Wasn't Touched

The scope boundary matters as much as what was exposed. DreamHost states it found no evidence that the attacker accessed control panel login information or customer billing and payment details, the latter of which is handled by an external provider rather than DreamHost's own systems. That's a meaningfully narrower blast radius than a full account-takeover scenario: FTP/SFTP credentials and webmail sessions are serious, letting an attacker potentially modify website files or read email, but a compromised control panel login would have gone further, toward DNS, billing, and account-level configuration changes across a customer's entire hosting footprint.

Why Two Months Is the Detail That Matters Most

A single vulnerable tool being exploitable is, unfortunately, routine. What makes this incident worth examining structurally is the detection gap: nearly two months between the earliest exposure and discovery on October 23, 2026. During that entire window, every FTP/SFTP login submitted through files.dreamhost.com was potentially being collected, which means the actual number of affected credentials likely scales with ordinary File Manager usage over two full months of customer activity, not a single moment of exposure.

DreamHost's remediation, once it found the issue, was conventional and reasonably fast: the company says it blocked the attacker's access, patched the vulnerable software, terminated active sessions for potentially affected users, and invalidated their passwords, then began offering a year of credit monitoring and identity theft protection through Equifax to affected individuals. None of that undoes the two-month collection window; it only closes it.

What This Means If You Use a Web-Based File Manager on Your Hosting Platform

Our verdict: this isn't a reason to distrust DreamHost specifically, whose public response once the breach was found followed a reasonable playbook. It's a reason to think about what a convenience feature, a browser-based file manager that holds your raw FTP credentials to let you drag and drop files, actually costs in attack surface, because that tool becomes a single point of compromise for every credential it ever processes, for as long as it stays vulnerable and undetected.

  • If you were notified, rotate your FTP/SFTP password immediately, even though DreamHost already invalidated it, and check for any webmail forwarding rules or filters you didn't create, a detail DreamHost itself recommends checking.
  • Audit whether any other accounts reuse the exposed FTP/SFTP or webmail password. A hosting credential that doubles as a password somewhere else turns a contained incident into a much wider one.
  • If a hosting platform offers a convenient web-based file manager as an alternative to direct FTP/SSH access, understand that convenience layer is itself attack surface, separate from and in addition to whatever protects your actual server. It's not inherently unsafe, but it is one more thing that has to stay patched, and this incident shows what two months of it not being patched looks like.

FAQ

What credentials were exposed in the DreamHost data breach?

FTP and SFTP usernames and passwords were exposed for anyone who logged into DreamHost's web-based File Manager at files.dreamhost.com between approximately August 2026 and October 23, 2026. Webmail session information, including credentials, may also have been exposed for a limited number of additional users. DreamHost says it found no evidence that control panel logins or billing and payment details were accessed.

How long did the DreamHost breach go undetected?

Approximately two months. DreamHost's notification states the unauthorized access began around August 2026 and was discovered on October 23, 2026, when the company identified and blocked the intrusion and patched the underlying File Manager vulnerability.

What should I do if I received a DreamHost breach notification?

DreamHost recommends checking your website files for unauthorized changes, reviewing webmail forwarding rules and filters for anything you didn't set up, and changing passwords on any other accounts where you reused the exposed FTP/SFTP or webmail credentials. The company has already invalidated affected passwords and is offering one year of credit monitoring through Equifax to notified individuals.

What We Checked Before Publishing

We pulled DreamHost's own breach notification as quoted directly by daily.dev and cross-referenced the timeline, scope, and remediation details against BleepingComputer's independent reporting. DreamHost has not disclosed the total number of affected accounts despite being asked directly, and we've left that figure unknown rather than estimating it.

I'm Rohit, founder of Krova Cloud: every Cube ships with full root access over SSH rather than routing file management through a separate web tool that has to independently hold and protect your credentials. That doesn't eliminate attack surface, every piece of software you run is something that can have a vulnerability, but it does mean there's one fewer centralized tool standing between an attacker and every customer's FTP-equivalent credentials at once. title: The Citrix XenServer Vulnerability Nobody Can Fully Explain Yet
description:
The Citrix XenServer Vulnerability Nobody Can Fully Explain Yet

The Citrix XenServer vulnerability disclosed November 3, 2026 lets an unauthenticated attacker on the management network compromise the host itself, according to Citrix's own bulletin. What Citrix hasn't published is how. No root-cause analysis, no technical mechanism, no exploit detail, just the outcome and a patch. For a flaw this severe, that gap is as newsworthy as the vulnerability itself.

Jump to the identifier confusion nobody has resolved if you want the strangest part first.

What Citrix Actually Disclosed

Cloud Software Group's bulletin CTX697256, published November 3, 2026, covers nine CVEs across XenServer 8.4 and XenServer 9. The headline issue, according to GBHackers' reporting, is CVE-2026-98432: "an unauthenticated attacker on the management network may compromise the host and/or any running Workload Balancing (WLB) or Conversion Manager appliances." A second flaw, CVE-2026-102703, may let a privileged user inside a guest virtual machine compromise the host, the exact boundary virtualization exists to hold.

Cyberpress's analysis is careful to separate the two by precondition: CVE-2026-98432 requires only management-network reachability and no credentials at all, while CVE-2026-102703 requires an attacker who already has elevated access inside a guest. The bulletin, per multiple outlets, "does not map individual identifiers to each outcome," so matching the remaining seven CVEs, which cover PXE network-boot compromise and guest Secure Boot bypass, to specific mechanisms isn't currently possible from public information.

The Identifier Confusion Nobody Has Resolved

Here's where the story gets genuinely strange. GBHackers reports that "CVE-2026-98432 shares the same identifier as a Linux kernel IPv4 TCP use-after-free vulnerability, which has a CVSS score of 9.8," a completely different technical description than Citrix's own management-network compromise narrative. SecurityOnline's advisory independently describes CVE-2026-98432 as "ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period," the Linux kernel description, not Citrix's.

Citrix itself has not indicated whether the two descriptions refer to the same underlying bug or are simply colliding identifiers, and GBHackers states plainly that "administrators should not assume a connection." That's an unusually direct editorial caution for a vulnerability disclosure, and it tells you something about how little public technical detail actually exists here: enough trackers are filling the gap with an unrelated CVE's description that distinguishing fact from identifier confusion is itself part of the job right now.

Even the Severity Rating Isn't Settled

Brandefense's patch ranking and GBHackers both note that Citrix rates the bulletin Critical, while Hong Kong's HKCERT rated it only Medium risk, listing denial of service and security restriction bypass as the impacts rather than full host compromise. Two credible sources, reading the same bulletin, arrived at materially different severity assessments. Neither is necessarily wrong; they may be weighting the unauthenticated-but-network-restricted precondition differently. But it means the "how bad is this, really" question doesn't currently have a single answer, only competing ones.

What's Actually Confirmed, Separate From the Noise

Strip out the identifier confusion and the severity disagreement, and the confirmed facts are narrower than the headlines suggest. No outlet, including Citrix's own bulletin, confirms active exploitation or a public proof-of-concept. Mallory's incident tracker states the bulletin "does not confirm active exploitation or identify an associated malware campaign." Exposure to the headline flaw depends specifically on management-network reachability, not unrestricted internet exposure, a meaningful limiting factor that several outlets flag explicitly rather than letting the Critical label stand unqualified.

What This Means for Anyone Running XenServer or Similar Hypervisors

Our verdict: patch now regardless of the unresolved identifier confusion or the severity disagreement, because an unauthenticated path to host compromise, even one gated by management-network access, is not something to wait on while vendors and trackers sort out the details. But don't let a Critical label substitute for understanding your own exposure: if your management network is genuinely isolated from anything an attacker could reach, your actual risk looks very different than the headline score implies.

  • Patch management-plane hosts first, per GBHackers' own recommendation, and update Workload Balancing to 2026.1.1 or later and Conversion Manager to 2026.2.0 if you run either.
  • Audit management-network isolation specifically, since Mallory's tracker is explicit that exposure "depends on management-network reachability, not unrestricted internet access." If that network is flat or reachable from general infrastructure, your real exposure is higher than the precondition suggests.
  • Treat CVE-2026-102703, the guest-to-host flaw, as the one that matters most in multi-tenant or hosting environments, where a guest administrator is, by definition, someone outside your own trust boundary. GBHackers calls this risk "highest in multi-tenant and hosting environments, where guest administrators may not be fully trusted," which is exactly the scenario a hosting provider can't simply patch around with network segmentation alone.

FAQ

What does the Citrix XenServer vulnerability CVE-2026-98432 actually let an attacker do?

According to Citrix's own bulletin, an unauthenticated attacker with access to the management network may be able to compromise a XenServer host, as well as any running Workload Balancing or Conversion Manager appliances. Citrix has not published a technical root-cause analysis or exploit details, and the bulletin does not confirm active exploitation in the wild.

Is CVE-2026-98432 the same vulnerability as a Linux kernel IPv4 bug with the same identifier?

That's unresolved. Some trackers have described CVE-2026-98432 using the technical details of an unrelated Linux kernel IPv4 use-after-free vulnerability that happens to share the same identifier. Citrix has not confirmed whether the two are related, and security researchers have explicitly cautioned against assuming a connection between them.

Does CVE-2026-102703 let a guest virtual machine attacker break out to the host?

Yes, under a specific precondition. Citrix's bulletin states that a privileged user inside a guest virtual machine may be able to compromise the underlying host. This requires the attacker to already hold elevated privileges within the guest; it is not an unauthenticated flaw like CVE-2026-98432, but it directly breaks the isolation boundary virtualization is meant to provide.

What We Checked Before Publishing

We pulled Citrix's own bulletin as reported directly by GBHackers and Cyberpress, cross-referenced the severity disagreement against Brandefense's and HKCERT's independent assessments, and confirmed the CVE identifier confusion across both GBHackers and SecurityOnline's independent advisories. We were not able to find a public technical root-cause explanation from Citrix itself for either headline CVE, and we've reported that absence directly rather than filling the gap with a tracker's unconfirmed description.

I'm Rohit, founder of Krova Cloud: every Cube runs its own kernel behind a per-cube jailer sandbox, so there's no shared management-network API standing between one customer's VM and every other tenant's host-level access. That doesn't mean a Firecracker-based hypervisor can't have its own version of this bug class.

It means the specific failure mode here, an unauthenticated path from management network to host, and a guest-privileged path from VM to host, is exactly the two directions isolation architecture has to hold against, every time, not just when a CVE forces the question. More debugging stories at debugly.dev.

title: How Others Test Cross-Zone Locally
description:
How Others Test Cross-Zone Locally

tc netem, Toxiproxy, Pumba, Chaos Mesh, LitmusChaos, zone labels in kind and k3d, Jepsen and Testcontainers: what each gives, a short config form for each, and an honest comparison with what we built.

👋 Hi, I'm Anton - a software engineer. These days I work on a platform: contracts, generated code, data paths and the tooling around them. Running notes live on my GitHub: github.com/brilliant-almazov.

Every claim about a tool below links to its own documentation, read for this article. Our side of the comparison is what part 3 built; our failure-scenario runs are still planned.

This is part 5 of the series on testing cross-zone, cross-datacenter and cross-provider behaviour on a laptop. Maybe you already do it better, maybe you'd do it another way - this is how it is going, and where it stops.

Five layers

Part 4, Placement In Every Trace, made every span say where it ran. Before going further with our own emulation, it is worth looking at what the world already uses. The tools sort into layers by where they act:

Layer Tools Acts on
kernel tc netem packets on a device
TCP proxy Toxiproxy, Testcontainers' Toxiproxy module one connection through a proxy
container Pumba a container's namespace, from outside
Kubernetes Chaos Mesh, LitmusChaos, zone labels in kind and k3d pods selected by labels
history Jepsen what the system did, checked afterwards

The lower the layer, the more it can do and the less it knows about your system. The higher, the more it knows and the more it needs installed.

tc netem

Everything network-shaped in this list ends at the kernel's netem sooner or later. It adds delay, jitter and loss to packets leaving a device (tc-netem(8)):

tc qdisc change dev eth0 root netem delay 100ms 20ms distribution normal
tc qdisc change dev eth0 root netem loss 0.3% 25%

The man page has one warning worth repeating: for TCP performance tests, netem should sit on the ingress of the receiver, not on the sender. On its own, netem knows nothing about which peer is which; that is up to the filters around it.

Toxiproxy

Toxiproxy is "a TCP proxy to simulate network and system conditions for chaos and resiliency testing" (Toxiproxy). The client connects to the proxy instead of the real service, and toxics are added to the proxy over an HTTP API on port 8474:

toxiproxy-cli create -l localhost:26379 -u localhost:6379 redis
toxiproxy-cli toxic add -t latency -a latency=1000 redis

The toxics are latency, down, bandwidth, slow_close, timeout, reset_peer, slicer, limit_data and packet_loss. That is a richer vocabulary than netem has, at one price: the client must be pointed at the proxy.

Pumba

Pumba does chaos and network emulation for containers on Docker, containerd and Podman (Pumba). It runs tc from a helper that joins the target's namespace, so the target image needs nothing:

pumba netem --duration 5m delay --time 3000 mydb
pumba iptables --duration 2m loss --probability 0.1 myapp

That is the same trick as our sidecar in part 3, packaged as a tool.

Chaos Mesh and LitmusChaos

In Kubernetes, network chaos becomes a resource. Chaos Mesh's NetworkChaos supports netem, delay, loss, duplicate, corrupt, partition and bandwidth, selects pods by label and has a direction of to, from or both (Chaos Mesh):

apiVersion: chaos-mesh.org/v1alpha1
kind: NetworkChaos
metadata: { name: delay-example }
spec:
  action: delay
  mode: one
  selector: { namespaces: [default], labelSelectors: { app: frontend } }
  delay: { latency: '20ms', jitter: '5ms', correlation: '0' }

LitmusChaos, a CNCF Incubating project, describes itself as "a Cloud-Native Chaos Engineering Framework with cross-cloud support" (Litmus). Its pod-network-latency experiment starts tc with netem inside the target, takes NETWORK_LATENCY, JITTER and DESTINATION_IPS or DESTINATION_HOSTS to aim at one peer, and can use Pumba as its library (pod-network-latency).

Zones in kind and k3d

Zones on a laptop cluster are node labels. kind takes them in the cluster config (kind); k3d takes them on the command line with a node filter (k3d):

# kind
nodes:
  - role: worker
    labels: { topology.kubernetes.io/zone: a }
  - role: worker
    labels: { topology.kubernetes.io/zone: b }

# k3d
k3d cluster create --agents 3 \
  --k3s-node-label "topology.kubernetes.io/zone=a@agent:0" \
  --k3s-node-label "topology.kubernetes.io/zone=b@agent:1" \
  --k3s-node-label "topology.kubernetes.io/zone=c@agent:2"

Then topologySpreadConstraints spread the pods. DoNotSchedule tells the scheduler not to place a pod that would break the skew; ScheduleAnyway places it anyway, preferring nodes that reduce the skew (Kubernetes):

topologySpreadConstraints:
  - maxSkew: 1
    topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
    whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
    labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: my-app } }

Labels and spread give zones as a scheduling fact. They give no distance: two "zones" on a laptop are as close as two processes.

Jepsen

Jepsen is at a different layer altogether. It "aims to improve the safety of distributed databases, queues, consensus systems" (Jepsen). While a test runs operations against a system, a nemesis process introduces faults, and a checker then analyses the recorded history for correctness (jepsen-io/jepsen). Network manipulation in its tests is typically done with iptables.

What Jepsen adds is not a better way to cut a network. It is a rigorous answer to "was the result correct", which every tool above leaves to you.

Testcontainers

For tests in code, Testcontainers wraps Toxiproxy as a module. A ToxiproxyContainer joins the same network as the service under test, a proxy is created in front of it, and toxics are added from the test (Testcontainers):

proxy.toxics().latency("latency", ToxicDirection.DOWNSTREAM, 1_100).setJitter(100);
proxy.toxics().bandwidth("CUT_CONNECTION_DOWNSTREAM", ToxicDirection.DOWNSTREAM, 0);
proxy.toxics().bandwidth("CUT_CONNECTION_UPSTREAM", ToxicDirection.UPSTREAM, 0);

A connection cut is bandwidth zero in both directions; removing the toxics restores it.

Side by side

What the world gives What we built
latency and loss netem directly; Pumba, Chaos Mesh, Litmus on top of it; Toxiproxy per connection the same netem, but every rule derived from one topology file, per pair of sites
zones node labels in kind and k3d, spread constraints the same in k3d, plus compose with a subnet per site and zone
continents and providers not a concept in any of these tools levels of the declaration, with link kinds derived from them
partitions Chaos Mesh partition, Jepsen's nemesis, Toxiproxy down iptables DROP on both sides, each cut remembering its cause
checking the result Jepsen's checker on the history QA thresholds declared; the runs are planned
what we lack bandwidth limits, a Jepsen-grade history check —

The honest summary: we did not invent a new way to delay a packet. Under the hood it is netem and iptables, like most of the list. What is ours is the model above them - one declaration of a planet, from which every rule, every placement and every chaos action is derived. None of the tools above has a continent or a provider as a concept.

What we would borrow

Two things, both from the top of the list. Toxiproxy's vocabulary - slow_close, reset_peer, limit_data - names failures that netem cannot express. And Jepsen's stance: a chaos run without a strict check of the result is a demonstration, not a test. Both are ideas, not plans yet.

What I do not claim

  • Not a ranking of these tools. Each is good at its own layer.
  • Not that our emulation does what Jepsen does. It does not check histories.
  • Not that any of our scenarios has run. They are planned.
  • Not completeness. These are the tools I read for this part, not all of them.

What of this is method

  • Know the layer of a tool. Kernel, proxy, container, cluster, history - each sees a different system.
  • Read the documentation, not the reputation. Every claim here has a link.
  • A cut is not a test. The check of the result is the test.

Cross-anything on a laptop - Part 5. Next: Every Verdict Carries A Trace.

If you use Toxiproxy in tests, which toxic found the most? If you run Chaos Mesh or Litmus, do you run it locally or only on a shared cluster? If you have run Jepsen, what did the checker catch that nothing else would? Which of these would you add to a laptop first?

title: I'm building an open-source messenger for developers: This is what I have learned so far
description:
Talking code in a regular chat app is frustrating. Snippets turn into walls of text. Pull request links get buried. And worst of all, people paste database URLs and API keys into chat, where they stay in the history forever.

So I started building Ack, an open-source messenger for developers.

What Ack does

Code blocks and diffs that look like they belong in an editor
Repo-linked rooms, so pull requests and CI results show up in the conversation

Secret vaults: the secret is encrypted in your browser and deleted after the recipient reveals it
Search that only finds people who have joined Ack, with an invite link for everyone else

Where it is today

Working now: sign in with GitHub, search for people who have joined Ack, send an invite link to anyone who hasn't, and chat one on one. Messages are stored in Appwrite and sync between devices. When a friend joins through your invite link, your chat opens automatically.

Still in progress: locking each conversation so only its two participants can read it, and making the secret vault delete the secret on the server, not just in the browser. Until both are done, please don't put real passwords or keys into Ack. Treat it as a test.

Using sample data for now: the pull request cards and the Reviews inbox. Real GitHub connections through a GitHub App come next.

Not built yet: voice and video calls and pair programming. They're designed, and they're switched off behind feature flags until they work for real.

Try it: https://project-ack.vercel.app
Repo: https://github.com/kingenious0/ACK

How I'm building it

I'm not a hand-coder, and I'm upfront about that. I research the idea, write a spec, hand it to an AI coding IDE, build in small phases, test each phase, and review what the AI produced. The stack is Vite, React 19, TypeScript, Appwrite for sign-in and the database, and Vercel for hosting. I have been doing this for about 2 years now and it is really helping me.

Three things I learned

1. A display name is not a username.
My first version guessed a person's GitHub handle from their display name, and the link led to a GitHub 404. Display name and login handle are different fields. The fix was to fetch the real profile from GitHub's API after sign-in and store GitHub's numeric user ID, which never changes.

2. Don't search all of GitHub.
I first let anyone message any GitHub username. That means messages can pile up for someone who never agreed to join, and a stranger can spam them. Now search only looks at people who have joined Ack. If someone isn't there, you get an invite link, and nothing is stored for them until they sign up.

3. Be honest about security from day one.
I removed "end-to-end encrypted" from the app because it wasn't true yet. Saying less and being right builds more trust than a big claim.

What's next

Real-time sync, connecting GitHub repos through a GitHub App so pull requests and CI results appear in chat, and then calls.

Thanks for reading. If you try Ack, tell me what breaks.

title: Access control belongs in the database, not the UI
description:
The most common access-control bug I see isn't exotic. It's this: the app hides a button, and the developer calls it done. But the data is still one crafted request away. If authorization only lives in the UI, it doesn't really exist.

So I push access control down to where the data actually is — the database — using Postgres row-level security (RLS). I've built this into a campus platform (Cendekia), an ISP operations portal, and a mining workforce app, each with several roles that must only ever see their own slice.

What RLS actually does

With RLS on, a table doesn't return rows a user isn't allowed to see — even if the query asks for them. The policy is attached to the table, so it holds no matter which screen, endpoint, or ad-hoc query does the asking. A student sees their own grades; a lecturer sees their classes; an admin sees the registry — and the rule is enforced by Postgres, not by remembering to add a WHERE clause in every handler.

That's the key shift: authorization becomes a property of the data, not a habit of the code. New endpoints inherit it for free. A forgotten filter can't leak anything, because the database refuses.

Two lessons from doing it for real

  • RLS has a performance cost — design for it. A policy is evaluated per row. On one production system a Supabase slowdown traced straight to missing indexes and per-row policy evaluation; I fixed it with a handful of well-chosen indexes and a policy rewrite. RLS is not free, but it is optimisable — treat the policy like the hot path it is.
  • Roles and regions compose. Real orgs aren't just "admin vs user." Access is role and scope (which region, which class, which site). Modelling that in the policy — rather than in scattered app logic — keeps it consistent as the app grows.

Then make the record refuse to lie

Access control decides who can read and write. The other half is making sure what was written can't be quietly rewritten later. For attendance and approvals in the mining app, the audit trail is append-only at the database level: Postgres triggers reject UPDATE and DELETE on those tables. The app can add facts; it cannot edit history. When payroll or a dispute depends on those records, "trust me, nobody changed it" isn't good enough — the database guarantees it.

The principle

Hiding a control is UX. Enforcing access in the database is security. Do the second one, index it properly, and back it with records the application isn't allowed to alter — then the guarantee holds no matter what the front end does.

title: Formalizing inverse problems in the age of AI: possibilities, pitfalls, and an invitation
description:
arXiv:2611.06962v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Proof assistants such as Lean check mathematical proofs down to the axioms, and AI agents have recently made writing such proofs cheap. We describe AutoIP, a Lean library in which classical linear regularization theory, together with the functional analysis it rests on, has been autoformalized by AI agents. A machine-checked proof certifies only the formal statement it proves, so the remaining human task is to confirm that each formal statement says what was intended. We organize the library around this task: a reviewer compares the formal statements with their natural-language counterparts and never needs to read a proof. Our experience is that the risks lie in the statements rather than in the proofs, and that simple automated tests on the statements can expose problems even in the established literature. We illustrate this with a textbook theorem whose hypothesis is more restrictive than asserted. We invite the inverse problems community to extend and build on the library.

title: KDASO: Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization for Liability Adjudication Tasks
description:
arXiv:2611.06972v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Liability adjudication tasks (e.g., legal charge determination) require analyzing event descriptions against domain-specific skills to determine whether a party should bear liability. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in this area by leveraging executable skills for interpretable reasoning, existing approaches face three critical limitations: skill libraries become stale as real-world scenarios dynamically evolve, skill descriptions often suffer from a semantic execution gap where LLMs deviate from intended expert logic, and growing skill collections exceed context budgets causing critical skill omission. To address these challenges, we propose Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization (KDASO), which continuously evolves a skill library through neighborhood-conditioned induction from recent adjudication data, execution-aligned refinement based on LLM trajectory analysis, and context-budgeted routing for scalable skill selection. Experiments across ride-hailing adjudication, legal liability determination, and logical reasoning judgment demonstrate that KDASO significantly outperforms current general-purpose and domain-specific baselines. KDASO further achieves 8.96% improvement when transferring skills to concept-similar scenarios and maintains consistent performance gains through continuous optimization, underscoring the high transferability and stability of generated skills.

title: BlockLock: Reproducible LLM Inference with Fixed Batch Geometry
description:
arXiv:2611.06977v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reproducible LLM inference requires that a request produces the same output regardless of the other requests in the batch. Existing solutions pay for this in different ways: batch-invariant kernels constrain every operator, and isolating prefill with fixed-shape decode ({our CoRun-style baseline}) gives up shared prefill compute and pads decode. We present BlockLock, which keeps shared batched prefill and pins only the numerical path of the protected request: it fixes the geometry that the request sees, with {two modes: BlockLock-Rows uses fixed-width rows and retains batched decode of all requests; BlockLock-Pack uses terminal-anchored packing with an isolated dummy segment, then extracts the protected request's KV state for target-only decode. Under a stated per-deployment contract, both modes preserve the target's output bitwise when its companions change.} Across five {dense} models (Qwen3-8B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-4B/12B-IT) and three single-GPU deployments (NVIDIA A6000, A100, and H100), we evaluate our approach on both tinyBenchmarks and BFCL{; we also include initial tensor-parallel experiments on two NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. Both modes preserve target sequences and Top20-logit bits in the reported tests.} At equal delivered work, {BlockLock-Rows} reduces latency by 53.5--55.0\% and improves throughput by 115.2--122.2\% relative to vLLM Batch-Invariant; compared with batch-invariant kernels, it needs no custom kernel implementations and constrains only the protected requests.

title: Resource-Efficient Reinforcement Learning Post-Training through Elastic Expert Parallelism
description:
arXiv:2611.06984v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning post-training improves the capabilities of large language models, but generating training responses is a major computational bottleneck. In mixture-of-experts models, workers that finish their assigned responses may remain occupied because their experts are still needed by workers processing longer responses. Consequently, approximately one-third of occupied worker time in the baseline occurs after local response generation finishes. Here we present FlexFloor, a system that enables earlier resource release during synchronous response generation while preserving the expert computation required by ongoing responses. FlexFloor jointly adapts response scheduling and the active group of workers. It uses historical response lengths and memory constraints to guide batching and prompt placement, then progressively releases workers while maintaining expert availability and correct communication. Compared with the verl baseline, FlexFloor generates approximately 65.40% more response tokens per unit of occupied computing time and increases response generation throughput by 52.74%, with little observed variation in rollout reward. By making reinforcement learning post-training more efficient, FlexFloor supports faster development and iterative improvement of large language models and AI agents.

title: The Two-Ledger Model: Transaction-Grain Cost Accounting for Multi-Agent AI Systems Across Clouds, Models, and Systems of Record
description:
arXiv:2611.06989v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Enterprises run business transactions through multi-agent AI systems spanning clouds, large language models (LLMs), orchestration harnesses, and systems of record. Finance receives AI cost only at settlement grain, aggregated by SKU and charge period. The business question (what did this order, claim, or case cost in AI?) cannot be answered from billing data, because providers never see enterprise transaction boundaries. The FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification (FOCUS) gives billing data one schema across providers but remains settlement-grain even as it adds AI token and requester attribution. We formalize this grain mismatch, derive seven requirements, and propose the Two-Ledger Model: a settlement ledger of FOCUS-conformant billing data joined to an attribution ledger of invocation-grain usage records built on OpenTelemetry GenAI telemetry. A layered correlation spine (trace context, A2A/MCP metadata, business-key correlation, probabilistic matching) assigns each record to its business transaction with recorded method and confidence; a versioned rate card prices usage in near real time; period reconciliation ties both ledgers to the invoice, and the unexplained residual identifies shadow AI. Costs are reported per order, claim, or outcome with agentic cost metrics. A simulation with known ground truth shows the spine sustaining cost coverage above 99% as trace propagation falls to zero, the reconciliation residual recovering planted unmetered spend within 0.24 percentage points while flagging provider billing errors, and mid-flight gating cutting p99 transaction cost by up to 61% at a 2-4% false-pause rate. We propose the attribution ledger as an invocation-grain FOCUS profile for standardization.

title: Autonomous AI Agents Systematically Diverge From Human Preferences in Proof Formalization
description:
arXiv:2611.06995v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems have ushered in a new age of proof abundance, but helping humans understand these proofs requires new attention to the differences in how AI agents and humans pursue a proof-making task. We present "simulated collaboration", a methodology that allows us to examine two key questions: (1) the relative attention AI agents pay to surface syntax or, conversely, deeper underlying semantics, and (2) how and where AI agent preferences for what to do next diverge from human preferences. On a set of nine major human collaborations in Lean with 4.7M definitions across more than 6K commits, we find that, over the course of proof construction, AI agents (1) are far more strongly drawn than humans to explicitly marked gaps; (2) show a relative aversion to densely connected proof centers and to complex or surprising proof goals; and (3) are relatively attracted to surprising proof bodies, which they tend to regularize toward baseline. Our results highlight important blind spots and potential interventions for future human-AI collaboration in mathematics.

title: Trust Responsive Runtime Authorization for Agentic AI with Empirical Characterization of Policy Behavior and Parameter Sensitivity
description:
arXiv:2611.06996v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The policy that converts runtime estimates of an autonomous agent's condition into operational authority is rarely specified or measured. We empirically characterize the Trust Responsive Authorization Policy (TRAP), which maps an Authorization Readiness Score (ARS), a weighted combination of runtime trust, operational stability, and contextual risk, onto discrete authorization levels through an asymmetric rule: escalation requires consecutive observations above a band edge plus a margin, while a sharp drop in readiness restricts authority at once. On one matched set of 100 Monte Carlo traces, we compare TRAP with static, trust-only, risk-only, and symmetric policies. Under abrupt degradation, TRAP restricts at onset and re-escalates sooner after recovery than the symmetric policy, with the highest and, descriptively, least variable stability among the adaptive policies, although more of its post-recovery escalations occur below the selected trust threshold. Paired bootstrap intervals exclude zero for the remaining differences. In one-factor sweeps, recovery time rises with the escalation margin and run length, shifts with the score weights, and is unchanged by the restriction threshold. In an exploratory post-freeze experiment, when the same degradation is spread over 5-20 intervals, TRAP restricts only on the 4 traces that retain a single-interval drop above that threshold; averaged over all 100 traces, it holds authority above what readiness supports for 15.9-18.9 of the 20 degradation intervals, against 0.8 under abrupt degradation and about 10 for the symmetric policy. Its restriction advantage therefore depends on degradation being abrupt. All reported values are traceable to the publicly available, versioned research release.

title: Adapting the Process of Adaptation: Darwinian, Lamarckian, and Agent-Directed Evolution in AI
description:
arXiv:2611.07048v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evolution has shaped intelligence for billions of years. Artificial intelligence (AI) now raises a striking possibility: intelligence may begin to direct its own evolution. As AI agents become capable of modifying and evaluating their own behavior, how quickly could they improve, and how can that improvement remain safe? We develop a theoretical framework comparing Darwinian, Lamarckian, and agent-directed evolution following environmental change. Darwinian evolution relies on natural selection, Lamarckian evolution adds inherited learning, and agent-directed evolution allows agents to generate and evaluate behavioral variants and choose how extensively to search. When learning is sufficiently effective, these mechanisms exhibit progressively faster adaptation. Generating more variants accelerates adaptation, while optimal search effort depends on learning ability, problem difficulty, and experimentation costs. However, an agent's ability to direct its improvement does not ensure that improvements are evaluated against the intended objective. When the evaluation target is misspecified, additional search accelerates convergence toward the wrong behavior, even as measured performance improves. In recursive self-improvement, such errors may persist across generations, posing challenges for AI safety. Independent evaluation and oversight must keep pace with autonomous AI development. The central challenge is not simply to accelerate the evolution of intelligence, but to preserve humanity's ability to guide its direction, limit its speed, and intervene when necessary.

title: Closed-Loop Agent Evaluation: Layered Measurement and Self-Calibration
description:
arXiv:2611.07051v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Once an agent is live, teams want to know whether it is doing its job, not just whether it throws errors. Yet most evaluation is one-off: a benchmark run, a look at traces, a single score. Its conclusions neither check themselves nor reach the agent. We propose closed-loop evaluation, an evaluation method for deployed agents. It models evaluation as performance estimation under biased raters and censored outcomes, and it requires every level's conclusion to trace back to atomic data and to be computed by versioned rules. The method covers four levels of analysis (span, trace, conversation and engagement), measures along a spine of Execution, Substance, Trajectory and Results, treats Conduct as a constraint throughout, and uses Provenance and Adjudication components to certify the evidence and the evaluators. Evaluator agents generated by an Agent Factory carry these components, each with a domain knowledge pack and an adapter harness. Two loops close the evaluation: an inner loop audits the evidence, rules and metrics themselves, and an outer loop uses per-component regression checks to drive agent improvement. We also give a pipeline that runs this process automatically. Using the business-analysis agent SharpInsight as a case and porting the method to public conversation data, we show how problems differ across levels and how evidence-and-rule judgment is more reliable than holistic scoring (ICC 0.86 vs. 0.81; kappa 0.81 vs. 0.63).

title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Epigraph-Form Guided Exploration
description:
arXiv:2611.07066v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Discovering cooperative behavior in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is challenging due to the combinatorial complexity of joint state-action spaces, which hinders the emergence of coordinated behaviors from trial-and-error alone. Intrinsic rewards are often used to aid discovery, but naively combining them with team objectives can distort the learning signal, compromising task performance. In this paper, we propose EFXPLORER, a constrained exploration framework that maximizes exploration objectives subject to a constraint that preserves established task performance. We solve the resulting problem using an epigraph reformulation that introduces adaptive exploration budgets. This approach separates intrinsic rewards from task objectives and regulates exploration through task feasibility. To further encourage diverse and temporally extended exploration, we incorporate a successor distance-based intrinsic reward that captures long-horizon dependencies. Empirically, our method outperforms strong baselines and induces novel cooperative strategies across SMAX, VMAS, and MPE benchmark suites.

title: When Verification Is Not Agreement: Cross-Agent LLM-to-Dafny Formalization
description:
arXiv:2611.07073v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A verified Dafny postcondition certifies that a formula holds, but it does not guarantee that the result was reached through genuine independent reasoning.
