title: Building a Deterministic Market-Data Replay Engine for Backtesting on QuestDB
description:
The first backtest I ever trusted turned out to be a liar. It showed a Sharpe north of 3, a drawdown curve that looked like a staircase going one direction, and fills so clean I should have known. The strategy bought when a signal fired and sold a few seconds later, and in the backtest it always sold at a price that existed only after the decision was made. I had joined my trades to a quote table on timestamp equality, and because my quote snapshots were sampled a hair later than my signal, every single fill borrowed a price from a moment that hadn't happened yet. The future was leaking in through a JOIN clause.

That bug cost me a weekend and a lot of embarrassment, and it taught me the thing that most people building strategy code never internalize: a backtest is a simulation of what you knew at each instant, and the hardest part is not the strategy logic, it's refusing to let the engine know anything it couldn't have known. This post is how I built a replay engine that enforces that discipline — on top of QuestDB, with a Spring Boot harness, using real captured order-book data instead of toy CSVs.

Why timestamp-equality joins lie to you

Market data does not arrive on a clock. A trade prints at 09:31:04.218734, the top-of-book quote that preceded it was set at 09:31:04.102881, and the next quote update lands at 09:31:04.251002. If you want to know the prevailing quote at the moment of the trade, you need the most recent quote at or before the trade's timestamp. Not the closest. Not the next one. The last one that already existed.

A naive JOIN ON trades.ts = quotes.ts almost never matches, so people "fix" it by rounding timestamps to the nearest second or by matching whichever quote sits closest in time, before or after. Rounding destroys ordering inside the second — exactly where equities microstructure lives. Matching the nearest quote regardless of direction quietly lets a quote that printed after the trade attach itself to that trade, so your fill prices are built from information the market hadn't produced yet. Both tricks flatter the equity curve, and you only find out how much when the strategy meets a live spread and the edge isn't there.

The operation I actually want is a temporal, backward-looking join, and in QuestDB it's spelled ASOF JOIN. Given a trade on the left, it reaches back to the latest quote whose timestamp hasn't passed the trade's timestamp — the quote that was standing when the trade printed, never a later one. That single "at or before" rule is the entire point-in-time guarantee, written as a join instead of as a page of defensive application code.

The capture pipeline underneath

Before any replay, you need data you trust. I run a live depth-capture service that ingests top-of-book (mbp-1) and trade events for a nine-name basket — AAPL, MSFT, NVDA, AMZN, TSLA, META, SPY, QQQ, and AMD — straight into QuestDB over the InfluxDB line protocol. The ingestion path writes nothing it didn't receive: no enrichment, no derived columns, no spread or mid computed at write time. It records exactly what came off the wire, with the exchange timestamp kept as the designated timestamp, plus a separate ingestion timestamp so I can measure capture latency afterward without tangling it up with event time.

On a normal session those nine names generate between 28 and 41 million rows, the bulk of it quote churn in SPY and NVDA. The reason I keep ingest_ts as its own column rather than trusting wall-clock-at-read is that it lets me answer a concrete question later: subtracting ts from ingest_ts across a full day, my median capture lag sits around 1.1 ms with a p99 near 6 ms — the socket-read-to-WAL-commit cost, nothing exotic. That number matters because it becomes the floor for the order latency I simulate.

The table that matters looks like this:

CREATE TABLE market_events (
    ts            TIMESTAMP,      -- exchange/event time, designated
    ingest_ts     TIMESTAMP,      -- when our capture wrote it
    symbol        SYMBOL CAPACITY 4096 CACHE,
    event_type    SYMBOL,         -- 'quote' or 'trade'
    bid_px        DOUBLE,
    bid_sz        LONG,
    ask_px        DOUBLE,
    ask_sz        LONG,
    trade_px      DOUBLE,
    trade_sz      LONG,
    seq           LONG            -- exchange sequence number
) TIMESTAMP(ts) PARTITION BY HOUR WAL;

Two choices on that table pay off repeatedly. The first is PARTITION BY HOUR. The 09:30–10:00 open is a different animal from the 12:00 lull — the opening hour alone can hold a quarter of the day's rows — and hour partitions let a replay of just the auction touch a handful of physical chunks instead of dragging the whole day off disk. I didn't take that on faith. On one AAPL session, a single-symbol trade-plus-quote scan over the 09:30–10:30 window ran in 0.6 s against PARTITION BY HOUR versus 2.9 s when I rebuilt the same table as PARTITION BY DAY and forced it to prune inside one giant daily partition. The second choice is carrying seq, the exchange sequence number: when two events land on an identical nanosecond stamp — which happens far more than you'd hope, especially during bursts — seq gives me a total order to break the tie. Determinism dies the instant two same-timestamp events can replay in different orders across two runs.

Partitions older than seven days get converted to QuestDB's Parquet tier (ALTER TABLE market_events CONVERT PARTITION TO PARQUET WHERE ts < dateadd('d', -7, now()), driven on a nightly cron). The trade is real and measurable: on my box a native QuestDB partition for a busy session sits around 2.1 GB, and the Parquet-converted version of the same partition lands near 430 MB — roughly a 5x reduction thanks to columnar compression on the heavily repeated symbol and side data. The cost shows up on first touch: a cold scan of a converted partition runs about 3–4x slower than the native one (the 0.6 s scan above becomes roughly 2.2 s cold, then warms back down once the OS page cache is primed). For replaying history I'll take that trade every day — I'm bounded by correctness, not by milliseconds. You can read more about how I think about storage and ingestion trade-offs in my projects.

Expressing point-in-time correctness in SQL

Here is the query at the heart of the whole engine. I take every trade in a session and attach the top-of-book quote that was prevailing at the instant each trade printed:

SELECT
    t.ts,
    t.symbol,
    t.trade_px,
    t.trade_sz,
    q.bid_px,
    q.ask_px,
    q.bid_sz,
    q.ask_sz,
    (q.ask_px - q.bid_px)                         AS spread,
    (q.bid_px + q.ask_px) / 2.0                   AS mid
FROM (
    SELECT * FROM market_events
    WHERE event_type = 'trade'
      AND symbol = 'AAPL'
      AND ts IN '2026-10-15'
) t
ASOF JOIN (
    SELECT * FROM market_events
    WHERE event_type = 'quote'
      AND symbol = 'AAPL'
      AND ts IN '2026-10-15'
) q;

The ASOF JOIN guarantees q is the newest quote whose ts is <= t.ts, so no future quote can glue itself to a trade. The strategy I'd fooled myself with was a dumb mean-reversion scalp on AAPL: when the last trade printed more than two spreads below the trailing 30-second VWAP, buy one lot, exit after 5 seconds or a half-cent of profit, whichever came first — tested over the 2026-09 to 2026-10 sessions in the capture. Under the old ts = ts equality join (which, because my quote snapshots were stamped a touch later than trades, kept handing the exit the next quote) it showed a Sharpe around 3.1. Re-run with ASOF semantics and a fill model that pays the prevailing ask on entry and bid on exit, the same strategy printed a Sharpe of 0.4. The 3.1 was the equality join leaking the exit quote backward; the 0.4 was the strategy's actual, unglamorous edge. Painful, but honest.

One subtlety is easy to trip over: the join only behaves if both sides are already in timestamp order. QuestDB gets you that for free on a timestamp-partitioned table, and crucially it does not check the ordering — feed it unsorted input and it returns a confidently wrong answer instead of an error. Worse, dropping an ORDER BY into an ASOF subquery can strip the designated-timestamp property off the intermediate result and break the join quietly. So I keep ASOF subqueries to plain WHERE filters and never re-sort inside them.

Streaming a day in event-time order

The SQL gives me correctness within a single joined view, but a replay engine has to do more than answer one query. It has to walk the entire session forward, one event at a time, in the exact order those events occurred, and hand each one to a strategy that is only allowed to see the past. That's the Spring Boot harness.

The core abstraction is an event stream pulled from QuestDB over a cursor instead of being loaded into memory. Forty-odd million rows won't sit comfortably in heap, and — the part that matters more — the moment a full day lives in a List, some well-meaning strategy author will index into it and read ahead. A cursor only moves forward, so the lookahead temptation never even exists. The data arrives one event at a time and is gone once consumed.

@Component
public class MarketEventReplayer {

    private final DataSource questDb;

    public MarketEventReplayer(DataSource questDb) {
        this.questDb = questDb;
    }

    /**
     * Streams every event for a session in strict event-time order.
     * seq is the tiebreaker so two events sharing a nanosecond
     * timestamp always replay in the same order across runs.
     */
    public void replay(LocalDate session, String symbol, EventSink sink) {
        String sql = """
            SELECT ts, event_type, bid_px, ask_px, bid_sz, ask_sz,
                   trade_px, trade_sz, seq
            FROM market_events
            WHERE symbol = ? AND ts IN ?
            ORDER BY ts, seq
            """;

        try (Connection c = questDb.getConnection();
             PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement(sql)) {

            ps.setString(1, symbol);
            ps.setString(2, session.toString());
            ps.setFetchSize(10_000);            // keep the cursor streaming

            try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
                while (rs.next()) {
                    sink.onEvent(MarketEvent.from(rs));
                }
            }
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            throw new ReplayException("replay failed for " + symbol
                + " on " + session, e);
        }
    }
}

The ORDER BY ts, seq is the determinism contract. Two runs over the same partition produce byte-identical event sequences. The setFetchSize keeps the JDBC driver from trying to haul the whole result set across at once; events trickle through as the strategy consumes them.

The strategy harness that cannot see the future

A strategy, in my framework, is an object that reacts to events and emits orders. The critical design rule is that the harness never passes a strategy anything but the current event and whatever state the strategy has already accumulated from past events. There is no getNextQuote(), no lookahead buffer, no "peek" method anywhere in the interface. The absence is the feature.

public interface Strategy {
    /** Called once per event, in strict event-time order. */
    List<Order> onEvent(MarketEvent event, BookState book);
}

public final class BookState {
    private double bidPx, askPx;
    private long   bidSz, askSz;
    private long   asOfNanos;   // event time of the last update applied

    void applyQuote(MarketEvent e) {
        this.bidPx = e.bidPx();
        this.askPx = e.askPx();
        this.bidSz = e.bidSz();
        this.askSz = e.askSz();
        this.asOfNanos = e.tsNanos();
    }

    public double mid() {
        return (bidPx + askPx) / 2.0;
    }

    public double spreadBps() {
        double m = mid();
        return m == 0 ? 0 : (askPx - bidPx) / m * 10_000.0;
    }

    public long asOfNanos() {
        return asOfNanos;
    }
}

BookState is the only market context a strategy gets, and it only ever reflects quotes that have already been replayed. When a trade event arrives, the book still shows the quote state from before that trade, which is exactly what the strategy would have seen live. The asOfNanos field is my paranoia made visible — if a fill simulator ever tries to use a price whose timestamp is ahead of the current event, I can assert against it and blow up the run rather than quietly bank a fantasy profit.

Deterministic fills, not optimistic ones

The other place backtests lie is the fill model. Assuming you always get filled at the mid, or that your market order executes at the quote you saw rather than the quote that exists when the order actually reaches the book, manufactures returns from nothing. My fill simulator takes the opposite stance: a market buy pays the ask that is prevailing when the order lands, after a configurable latency, and it eats through available size if the order is large.

@Component
public class FillSimulator {

    private final Duration orderLatency;   // decision -> book arrival

    public FillSimulator(ReplayProperties props) {
        this.orderLatency = props.getOrderLatency();  // e.g. 900 microseconds
    }

    public Fill simulate(Order order, BookState bookAtArrival) {
        long arrivalNanos = order.decisionNanos()
            + orderLatency.toNanos();

        // The book passed in is the state as of arrivalNanos, resolved
        // by the engine via ASOF semantics -- never the decision-time book.
        if (bookAtArrival.asOfNanos() > arrivalNanos) {
            throw new LookaheadException(
                "fill used quote from the future: book asOf="
                + bookAtArrival.asOfNanos() + " arrival=" + arrivalNanos);
        }

        double fillPx = switch (order.side()) {
            case BUY  -> bookAtArrival.askPx();
            case SELL -> bookAtArrival.bidPx();
        };

        long available = order.side() == Side.BUY
            ? bookAtArrival.askSz()
            : bookAtArrival.bidSz();

        long filledQty = Math.min(order.qty(), available);
        return new Fill(order.id(), fillPx, filledQty, arrivalNanos);
    }
}

The latency parameter is where a backtest earns or loses its credibility. Set it to zero and you're claiming your order teleports to the exchange, which is a claim no real system can make. I calibrate it against the capture latency I measured earlier — the gap between ingest_ts and ts in the raw table gives me a sober sense of how far behind the live world I actually operate. The LookaheadException is not decoration; it has fired during development and caught a bug where I resolved the arrival-time book with a closest-match instead of an as-of match. That exception has saved me from publishing nonsense twice. The habits here are close cousins of the ones I wrote about in transactional outbox and idempotent consumers — in both worlds, correctness means refusing to let the system act on information it shouldn't have or process the same thing twice.

Wiring it together with Spring configuration

The pieces assemble into a runnable backtest through ordinary Spring wiring. I keep the replay parameters in a typed properties class so a backtest is fully described by its configuration — same config, same data, same result, every time.

@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "replay")
public record ReplayProperties(
        LocalDate session,
        List<String> symbols,
        Duration orderLatency,
        boolean strictLookaheadChecks) {
}

@Service
public class BacktestRunner {

    private final MarketEventReplayer replayer;
    private final FillSimulator fills;
    private final ReplayProperties props;

    public BacktestRunner(MarketEventReplayer replayer,
                          FillSimulator fills,
                          ReplayProperties props) {
        this.replayer = replayer;
        this.fills = fills;
        this.props = props;
    }

    public BacktestResult run(Strategy strategy) {
        LedgerSink ledger = new LedgerSink(fills, strategy);
        for (String symbol : props.symbols()) {
            replayer.replay(props.session(), symbol, ledger);
        }
        return ledger.settle();
    }
}

Because BacktestResult is a pure function of ReplayProperties plus the strategy code plus the immutable QuestDB partition, two runs are reproducible to the cent. When a colleague says "I can't reproduce your numbers," the first thing I check is whether they're pointed at a partition that got rewritten — which is why I treat replayed partitions as append-only and never backfill a session after it has been used in a published result.

What the production reality actually costs

A few things I did not expect when I started. First, the single biggest performance lever was not JVM tuning, it was QuestDB partitioning granularity combined with fetch size — getting the cursor to stream rather than buffer turned a nine-minute replay into forty seconds. Second, SYMBOL columns in QuestDB are interned and cheap to filter, so per-symbol replay scans are far faster than the generic string-column intuition suggests. Third, the Parquet tier is genuinely fine for backtesting even though it is slower per scan — I am not latency-sensitive when replaying history, I am correctness-sensitive, and correctness is a property of the data and the joins, not the storage tier.

The discipline that matters most has nothing to do with any of the tooling. It is the willingness to make your engine throw an exception the instant it touches information from the future, and to keep that check on in production rather than switching it off because it's inconvenient. Every optimistic assumption you let slide — fills at the mid, zero latency, closest-quote joins — is a small loan against reality that gets called in the moment you trade live. I would rather have a backtest that reports a boring 0.4 Sharpe I can trust than a glamorous 3 that evaporates on contact. If you want to talk through the capture side or the strategy harness, reach me through my contact page, and there's more on the systems I've built across trading and fintech in my experience.

Go instrument your fill model with a lookahead assertion this week, point it at one real session, and watch what your "winning" strategy does when it can no longer see tomorrow's prices.

title: The JPA Field That Turns a Silent Lost Update Into a 409
description:
Originally published on my blog — read it there with the full context, code and updates.

Two people open the same post. Both edit it. Both save. One of the saves
disappears without a trace — no error, no warning, and the API answered
HTTP 200 for both of them.

That is the lost update problem, and it is the quietest data-loss bug in
read-modify-write APIs. I hit it while building my Spring Boot reference
service — a Spring Boot 3.5.16 (Java 21) REST API where editors create and
update posts from a browser page. The fix turned out to be one @Version
field on the JPA entity, one field on the request contract, and one
exception that the API layer maps to HTTP 409 Conflict. This post traces
that path through the actual code.

The problem: an edit that vanishes with no one to blame

Why does one editor's change disappear when two people save the same
record?

Follow the timeline. Editor A and editor B both fetch the same post.
A saves first: the row is updated and the API answers 200. B saves a
moment later: the row is updated again, this time over A's text, and
the API answers 200 again. Every request succeeded; every response told
its caller that their save is the state of the record. A's edit is
simply gone, and neither client has any way to know.

The failure is silent because it is normal read-modify-write behaviour,
not an anomaly. That is exactly why the bug survives in real systems, and
why it is worth fixing properly in something meant to demonstrate
engineering judgement.

What I tried first, and why it failed

My first sketch of the update flow was the obvious one: GET the record,
edit it, PUT it back with the new title and body and nothing else.

GET  /api/posts/{id}    # read the record
PUT  /api/posts/{id}    # write it back with a new title and body

The server loads the row, applies the update, and returns 200. It has no
way to notice that the row moved underneath the client between the GET
and the PUT — the read and the write are two unrelated requests, and
nothing in the contract connects them. The last write wins, and both
writers are told they succeeded.

A 200 is worse than an error here. An error at least tells the losing
client that something happened and gives them a reason to look. A 200
tells both clients that their save is the current state of the record,
which is a lie for one of them. The losing edit now exists nowhere — not
on screen, not in the database — and because the client believes it
saved, nobody goes looking for the data.

The fix: a @version field, a contract, and a conflict

The fix is five small parts, all of them in the reference service's source.

1. The entity carries a version column 

@Entity
@Table(name = "posts", indexes = @Index(name = "idx_posts_title", columnList = "title"))
@EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class)
public class Post {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue
    @UuidGenerator
    private UUID id;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 160)
    private String title;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 10_000)
    private String body;

    @Version
    private long version;
    // ...
}

@Version tells Hibernate to treat version as an optimistic lock. Every
UPDATE it generates becomes conditional:

UPDATE posts
SET title = ?, body = ?, version = version + 1, ...
WHERE id = ? AND version = ?

If the row's version no longer matches the value the statement was built
with, zero rows change and Hibernate rejects the flush instead of quietly
overwriting. The entity never bumps the counter by hand — the update
method only touches title and body; the version moves with the write
itself.

2. The version is part of the API contract

A lock is useless if the client cannot take part in it, so the version
travels through the API in both directions. The response record exposes
it:

public record PostResponse(UUID id, long authorId, String title, String body,
                           long version, Instant createdAt, Instant updatedAt) {
}

and the update request requires it back:

public record UpdatePostRequest(
        @NotBlank @Size(max = 160) String title,
        @NotBlank @Size(max = 10_000) String body,
        @NotNull @Min(0) Long version) {
}

The learning note next to UpdatePostRequest says it plainly: "the
expected version is part of the update contract, making optimistic
locking visible to clients."

3. The service checks it inside the transaction that owns the write 

@CachePut(cacheNames = "posts", key = "#postId")
@Transactional
public PostResponse updatePost(UUID postId, UpdatePostRequest request) {
    Post post = postRepository.findById(postId)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new PostNotFoundException(postId));
    if (post.getVersion() != request.version()) {
        throw new PostVersionConflictException(postId);
    }
    post.update(request.title().trim(), request.body().trim());
    return PostResponse.from(postRepository.saveAndFlush(post));
}

The load, the comparison and the save all happen inside one
@Transactional method, and that is the part that makes the check
honest: the version is compared against the row as it stands at write
time, not against a snapshot from an earlier request. If the read and
the write lived in different transactions, the check would compare
against a version the row has already left behind, and the whole scheme
would be theatre. The learning note on PostService names the rule:
"service methods centralize transaction boundaries, cache coherence, and
optimistic-locking rules." The service also runs with
spring.jpa.open-in-view: false, so no lingering session serves a stale
entity across requests — the row is re-read inside the writing
transaction.

The explicit check catches stale requests deterministically. The
@Version column still matters underneath: if another commit slips in
between the check and the flush, the conditional UPDATE affects zero
rows and Hibernate refuses the write anyway.

4. The handler maps the exception to a 409

The exception itself carries the message a client can act on:

public class PostVersionConflictException extends RuntimeException {

    public PostVersionConflictException(UUID postId) {
        super("Post %s has changed; fetch it again before retrying".formatted(postId));
    }
}

and the error boundary turns it into the right HTTP answer:

@ExceptionHandler({PostVersionConflictException.class, ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException.class})
ProblemDetail handleConflict(RuntimeException exception) {
    return problem(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "POST_VERSION_CONFLICT", exception.getMessage());
}

HttpStatus.CONFLICT is HTTP 409, and the response is a problem document
— a type URI, a stable machine code (POST_VERSION_CONFLICT) and a
human-readable detail. Mapping both our explicit exception and Spring Data JPA's ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException (thrown when Hibernate detects a race condition) guarantees that concurrent write collisions always return 409 rather than an unhandled 500. The service enables the framework's problem-details
support in its configuration (spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled: true),
so validation and every other error ride the same shape.

5. The whole path, end to end 

stale PUT /api/posts/{id}
  -> PostService.updatePost re-reads the row inside its transaction
  -> post.getVersion() != request.version()
  -> PostVersionConflictException: "fetch it again before retrying"
  -> ApiExceptionHandler.handleConflict
  -> HTTP 409, ProblemDetail with code POST_VERSION_CONFLICT
  -> the client knows its premise was stale

One @Version field, one version in the request contract, one
exception, one handler method. Nothing on the controller changed —
updatePost still looks like an ordinary PUT.

Why a conflict is the correct answer, not a retry

When two editors produce two different versions of the same record, the
server cannot know which intent is the one meant. Both saves are
legitimate from their authors' point of view, and replaying the stale
write just replays the same data loss.

The honest verdict is HTTP's own definition of 409: the request conflicts
with the current state of the resource, and the client is told exactly
how to resolve it — "fetch it again before retrying". The losing client
re-reads the record, sees the other writer's change, and a human decides
what to keep. The silent overwrite becomes a visible decision point,
which is the entire purpose of the exercise.

What the rest of the reference service proves

The version field is one layer of a small system, and the rest of it is
verifiable the same way — every row below is a class or a config file in
the repository, not a claim:

Layer What it does Where it lives
Caching Bounded Caffeine cache on single-post reads (max 500, TTL 10 min, both from config); @Cacheable on read, @CachePut on update, @CacheEvict on delete; GET /api/showcase/cache exposes requests, hits, misses and hit rate CacheConfig, CacheProperties, ShowcaseMetricsController
Security Stateless HTTP Basic with BCrypt; pages and read APIs are public, every mutation needs the EDITOR role; local defaults are a throwaway demo-editor/changeit account overridable via env vars SecurityConfig, application.yml
Errors Request records validate at the boundary; one @RestControllerAdvice returns consistent problem documents with machine codes — POST_NOT_FOUND (404), POST_VERSION_CONFLICT (409), VALIDATION_FAILED (400) with a field-error map CreatePostRequest, UpdatePostRequest, ApiExceptionHandler
Configuration Local profile runs an in-memory H2 database in PostgreSQL mode with ddl-auto: update and seeded sample posts; prod selects PostgreSQL, takes every credential from APP_* env vars and sets ddl-auto: validate application.yml, application-prod.yml
Tests One @SpringBootTest suite asserts the rendered Thymeleaf pages, unauthenticated 401s versus editor 201s, the VALIDATION_FAILED problem response, public search, and cache hits after repeated reads DemoApplicationIntegrationTest

Hardening This Pattern for Production Rollout

Two things change the moment this pattern moves to production. The project
README says both, and they are worth repeating as my own judgement.

First, schema management. I would add Flyway or Liquibase migrations
before ever setting ddl-auto to validate. The local development profile
uses update, which is convenient on a scratch database and dangerous as
a habit — production schema should be versioned code, not a side effect
of startup.

Second, secrets. The local editor account is intentionally a non-secret
demo account with default credentials. For anything real, I would keep
credentials in a managed secret store and refuse to boot without them,
instead of falling back to a default. The prod profile already takes
every credential from environment variables with no committed secrets —
that is the shape I would keep, minus the fallbacks.

The result

A stale update now returns HTTP 409 with code POST_VERSION_CONFLICT
instead of a 200 that silently discards the other writer's change. The
loss can no longer happen quietly: the failure is loud, actionable —
"fetch it again before retrying" — and the integration test suite asserts
the access and validation behaviour end to end.

The whole fix is one annotation on one field, plus plumbing that makes
the version part of the contract. If a record can be read by two people
at the same time, that field is the difference between a lost edit and a
conflict both clients can see.

I build Java/Spring back ends and full-stack web applications — REST APIs
with JPA, optimistic locking, caching, validation and integration tests,
from the browser page down to the database. If you have a form or a field
where edits keep quietly disappearing, tell me about it:
WhatsApp ·
me@hoelee.com ·
hoelee.com.

I write about self-hosted infrastructure, DevOps and the failures behind them at blog.hoelee.com.

title: Node.js Support Routing: Keeping Email and SMS Providers Replaceable
description:
For a Node.js contact form that routes customers to support queues, keep the queue decision and its evidence in your application, then put every email or SMS provider behind a small adapter. The best provider is the one you can remove without changing the routing policy.

Short answer: use SendGrid when email deliverability is the main concern, Twilio when SMS is the main concern, and Sendinblue when a smaller system needs both channels. Infrai is a reasonable option when one REST surface, one key, and one bill reduce the operational boundary around several backend services. None of these choices removes the need to model compliance evidence yourself.

The useful mental model is a ticket, not a message. A form submission becomes a routing decision, an evidence record, and only then a delivery request. That ordering matters when a provider changes, a recipient opts out, or an auditor asks why a message was sent.

What belongs inside the replaceable boundary?

Start with the facts your support team owns: the contact-form event ID, the selected queue, the destination class, the channel, the template revision, the consent decision, and the time of the decision. The adapter can add a provider name, request ID, and raw status. It should not decide whether a question belongs to Billing or Account Access.

I initially treated a common send() method as enough portability. It is not. Email and SMS have different consent rules, status vocabularies, cancellation behavior, and regional constraints. A common method is useful only if the evidence record keeps the distinctions that the method hides.

Here is the small contract I would put between the router and its delivery implementations. The example is intentionally provider-neutral. Its job is to make the migration boundary visible.

type Channel = "email" | "sms";
type Queue = "billing" | "account-access" | "general";

type NotificationIntent = {
  eventId: string;
  queue: Queue;
  channel: Channel;
  destination: string;
  templateRevision: string;
  body: string;
  consentRecordedAt: string;
};

type DeliveryAcceptance = {
  provider: string;
  providerRequestId: string;
  acceptedAt: string;
};

interface NotificationAdapter {
  send(intent: NotificationIntent): Promise<DeliveryAcceptance>;
}

async function notifyQueue(
  intent: NotificationIntent,
  adapter: NotificationAdapter,
  writeEvidence: (record: object) => Promise<void>,
): Promise<DeliveryAcceptance> {
  await writeEvidence({
    type: "notification.decided",
    eventId: intent.eventId,
    queue: intent.queue,
    channel: intent.channel,
    templateRevision: intent.templateRevision,
    consentRecordedAt: intent.consentRecordedAt,
    decidedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
  });

  const acceptance = await adapter.send(intent);

  await writeEvidence({
    type: "notification.accepted",
    eventId: intent.eventId,
    provider: acceptance.provider,
    providerRequestId: acceptance.providerRequestId,
    acceptedAt: acceptance.acceptedAt,
  });

  return acceptance;
}

That record says “the provider accepted the request.” It does not say “the agent read the message.” The distinction is the first migration rule: normalize only the facts that all providers really share, and retain provider-specific events beside the normalized record.

How should you compare email and SMS API providers for event notifications?

The comparison is less about a feature-count race than about where each service leaves work for your application.

SendGrid is a strong email-first choice. Its email API, competitive email API pricing, and deliverability features fit teams that need to operate transactional email carefully. It is not a single abstraction for a two-channel support router, so SMS policy and evidence mapping remain application concerns.

Twilio is the stronger SMS-first comparison. Its SMS API is designed for reliable global event notifications and gives a team a broad communications platform. If the contact form mostly sends email, that breadth can be more surface area than the workflow needs; the adapter should keep email-specific templates and compliance decisions separate.

Sendinblue is a sensible candidate for smaller usage that needs both email and SMS capabilities. The combined offering can simplify the initial channel decision. Check regional delivery, consent handling, and the event details available to your evidence store before calling that convenience portability.

The shared REST platform belongs in a different part of the comparison. As of the 2026-11-01 snapshot, its documented surface covers 295 routes across 20 modules, including 41 routes in the comm-email-sms group, behind one REST API, one key, and one bill. Public discovery returns capability schemas and runnable examples without requiring a key; the documented examples cover 10 languages. Those facts can reduce integration and account sprawl when the same Node.js service also needs unrelated backend capabilities.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the delivery adapter when a support platform values one operational boundary across backend services and wants to keep the provider request behind a discoverable REST contract. The second benefit is practical for migration work: the capability surface specifies an Idempotency-Key convention, so retry behavior can be made explicit at the adapter boundary. Keep queue routing, consent, and evidence storage in your own code.

Option Strongest fit What stays in the application Migration question
SendGrid Email-first support alerts SMS policy and cross-channel evidence Can the email event vocabulary map to your record?
Twilio Global SMS-first alerts Email policy and template governance Does the broader communications surface justify its boundary?
Sendinblue Smaller email-plus-SMS systems Regional and consent checks Which event details are available for audit?
Shared REST platform One REST boundary across backend services Queue rules, evidence, and polling Does its channel surface cover the workflow you actually need?

No row wins by itself. The adapter test does.

The second practical advantage is runtime freedom. A plain REST request needs no vendor SDK, so a Node.js worker, a small edge process, or a later service written in another language can use the same HTTP boundary. In this support workflow, that keeps the form router and the notification worker from inheriting different client libraries while the rest of the backend grows around the same 295-route surface.

That is a useful constraint.

There is a second, verified advantage here: the public discovery surface is self-describing, and every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. For an Infrai adapter, that means a team can inspect the email contract before wiring the form flow, then use plain HTTP from the runtime that owns the worker. No SDK migration is required when the notification worker moves out of Node.js. That matters because the queue decision is supposed to outlive the delivery client.

The evidence chain is worth making concrete. Suppose event contact-2026-1101-0042 is routed to Account Access at 09:14:03 with template revision support-v3. The first record stores those facts and the consent timestamp. The adapter then records the provider request ID at acceptance. A later status check can append the provider's event without rewriting the original decision. If a second provider is tested, it receives the same event ID and template revision, while only the adapter-specific request and status fields change. This is the difference between comparing providers at the boundary and comparing them by screenshots of their dashboards.

How do you test a provider switch before it hurts?

Use the same synthetic contact-form event against each candidate. Route it to a fixed queue, send one email, send one SMS, and record the request IDs. Then remove the adapter and rerun the routing test. If the queue decision changes, provider details have leaked upward.

The test should also inspect the exit path. Can a retry carry the same client-supplied idempotency key? Can a duplicate submission be distinguished from a retry? Can the record show consent and template revision before the provider call? Can the system tell acceptance from later delivery? A green API response answers only one of those questions.

For this adapter, the relevant email operation is POST /v1/email/send. Use the discovery document for the exact request schema instead of guessing fields in application code. The following snippet makes that boundary executable without inventing an email body: it fetches the public schema, uses the environment key convention, retries a rate-limited read once, and surfaces the response body for every other failure.

async function discoverEmailSend(): Promise<unknown> {
  let delayMs = 500;

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/email.send", {
      method: "GET",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY ?? ""}`,
      },
    });

    if (response.ok) {
      return response.json();
    }

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 2) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const waitMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1000
        : delayMs;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
      delayMs *= 2;
      continue;
    }

    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Discovery failed with HTTP ${response.status}: ${detail}`);
  }

  throw new Error("Discovery failed after retries");
}

The returned schema is input to the adapter, not to the queue router. For a retryable POST /v1/email/send, add a client-supplied Idempotency-Key, honor Retry-After, and preserve non-2xx response bodies. Keep it boring.

The same discipline keeps the adapter honest across providers. Do not flatten SMS cancellation and email scheduling into one pretend-common feature. Infrai has POST /v1/sms/cancel/{id}, while email scheduled sends have no cancellation route. That difference belongs in capability checks and evidence, not in a misleading universal interface.

What are the two objections to this design?

The first objection is latency: polling is less convenient than a push event. It is a valid objection. Neither the email nor SMS namespace provides webhook event pushes, so multi-channel orchestration that depends on real-time provider events is limited by polling. A system that requires webhook-driven state changes should prefer a specialist or direct competitor whose contract meets that requirement. This is the main trade-off, and it is a real reason not to choose the shared boundary.

The second objection is compliance coverage. A provider API is not proof of domestic compliance. Infrai's domestic email vendor is still pending, so it cannot be used as a domestic-compliance basis. There is also no hosted email OTP interface, no SMTP relay, and no voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channel. SMS geographic anti-abuse fences and per-country billing circuit breakers remain business-layer work.

Those limits make the choice clearer. SendGrid fits email depth. Twilio fits global SMS. Sendinblue fits a smaller dual-channel deployment. Infrai fits a team that values a single, discoverable REST boundary and explicit retry conventions, provided polling and channel gaps are acceptable.

For unsubscribe behavior, apply the policy that matches the message category and consult RFC 8058 for one-click email unsubscribe details. For the Infrai boundary, start with the email discovery schema, then hide that request shape behind the adapter.

References

  • SendGrid Mail Send API
  • Twilio Programmable Messaging API
  • Brevo API documentation
  • RFC 8058: One-Click Unsubscribe
  • Infrai email.send discovery schema
