title: When a Solana Feature Activates but Its Program Migration Fails
description:
Originally published on xroot.dev.

On Solana, a feature gate activating and the change it carries actually happening are two separate events. For most gates the difference never shows. For a gate that replaces a core program’s bytes, it can: the replacement runs once, at the epoch boundary, and if it fails, the gate stays active anyway.

SIMD-0690, merged on 26 October, adds a deliberate way for that replacement to fail: the runtime hashes the new program bytes and refuses to deploy them unless they match a hash shipped inside the validator. Agave implemented it on 29 October. On 2 November it queued the first migration that relies on it, p-ATA, a rewrite of the Associated Token Account program, and Firedancer followed on 3 November. We pulled the real p-ATA buffer from mainnet, hashed it the way both clients do, and replayed every way the activation can go through the loader Agave uses. The check works. It also depends on something no code enforces: the two clients agree only if the gates activate in the right order.

Activated is not the same as replaced

In the first bank of each epoch, Agave works out which feature gates have just activated, writes the activation slot into each gate’s account, and then runs the migrations tied to those gates. The p-ATA one is a single call, and its failure path is a log line:

if new_feature_activations.contains(&feature_set::replace_ata_with_p_ata::id())
    && let Err(e) = self.upgrade_loader_v2_program_with_loader_v3_program(
        &feature_set::replace_ata_with_p_ata::SPL_ASSOCIATED_TOKEN_ACCOUNT_PROGRAM_ID,
        &feature_set::replace_ata_with_p_ata::PROGRAM_BUFFER,
        feature_set::replace_ata_with_p_ata::BUILD_HASH,
        true,
        "replace_ata_with_p_ata",
    )
{
    warn!("Failed to replace SPL Associated Token Account with p-ATA buffer '{}': {e}", ...);
}

Every check runs before anything is written, so a failure changes nothing except the gate. The gate is now active, so it is never a new activation again and the call never repeats. The proposal says so in one line: on a mismatch, “the feature is still marked as activated, but the program data remains unchanged.” A retry means a new gate in a new release. That leaves four states a migration can be in:

Gate account does not exist — not submitted

Gate exists, no activation slot — pending, next epoch

Active, program under Loader v3 — migrated

Active, program under its old loader — activated, migration failed

What the hash check adds

A migration copies a Loader v3 buffer account, uploaded ahead of time, into the target program’s address. Before SIMD-0690, the runtime checked that the buffer existed, was owned by the upgradeable loader and deserialized as a buffer, then deployed whatever it held. Agave’s implementation adds one step between those checks and the deploy:

let buffer = Self::new_checked(bank, buffer_address)?;
let data = buffer.buffer_account.data();

let elf = &data[UpgradeableLoaderState::size_of_buffer_metadata()..];
let end_offset = elf.iter().rposition(|&x| x != 0).map_or(0, |i| i + 1);
let hash = solana_sha256_hasher::hash(&elf[..end_offset]);

if hash != expected_hash {
    return Err(CoreBpfMigrationError::BuildHashMismatch(hash, expected_hash));
}

Skip the 37-byte buffer header, drop trailing zero bytes, take SHA-256, compare. Only then does the deploy step load and verify the ELF in the runtime’s program environment. That step deliberately still accepts SBPF v0 programs “for core program migrations”, which matters here because the p-ATA ELF is v0.

What came before is the reason for the change. When p-token replaced SPL Token in place on 13 May 2026, the function that did it took a program address, a buffer address, a flag and a log name. There was no hash. A Loader v3 buffer always has a write authority (the loader refuses to remove it), so until the activation slot, any change that authority made to the buffer, as long as it still loaded and verified, would have become SPL Token. Our p-token explainer covers that migration. Agave’s SIMD-0690 change also turns the expected hash from an optional parameter into a required one, so every future migration must name its bytes, while the check itself waits for its own gate, core_bpf_hash_validation.

The real buffer, hashed

SIMD-0567 merged on 1 November at 11:02 UTC. Twenty-seven minutes later, the p-ATA buffer appeared on mainnet: 37 transactions in slots 464,075,848 to 464,075,854, between 11:30:19 and 11:30:21 UTC. No transaction has touched it since. We read its bytes and hashed them both ways:

Account size — 35,869 bytes

Loader v3 buffer header — 37 bytes, authority set

ELF — 35,832 bytes, SBPF v0

Trailing zero bytes — 15

SHA-256, zeros removed — 4e008052⁠…⁠7f7d9e

Agave, Firedancer and SIMD-0567 expect — 4e008052⁠…⁠7f7d9e

SHA-256 of the whole ELF — 8dc8d134⁠…⁠3605a4

The buffer matches. The 15 zero bytes are worth a second look, because they are not padding. The buffer holds exactly one ELF file, and the file itself ends in zeros: its last section header has an alignment of 1 and an entry size of 0. Hash the ELF as a file and you get a different value. The expected hash is defined over the stripped bytes, the way solana-verify computes it, so solana-verify get-buffer-hash reproduces it straight from the chain.

The header also shows the buffer’s authority is still set, to 8pEc9HbS…7pkzf. Until the gate activates, whoever holds that key can rewrite or close the buffer. Before SIMD-0690 a rewrite would have been deployed. Now it can only make the activation fail.

Seven ways the activation can go

To see the success and failure paths without a cluster, we built a harness around the real buffer bytes. It runs Agave’s check copied verbatim, Firedancer’s check ported from C, and the deploy step through solana-sbpf 0.26.0, the loader version Agave pinned at the commit we read, configured the way Agave’s migration path configures it. With the SIMD-0690 gate active, both clients give the same answer for every case:

Buffer as it is on mainnet — migrated

Plus 4,096 zero bytes — migrated, same hash

Minus its last 15 zero bytes — hash passes, loader rejects

One .rodata letter changed — hash mismatch

Instruction 17 immediate, 83 → 84 — hash mismatch

First opcode set to 0xff — hash mismatch

Buffer closed before activation — account not found

Every failure leaves the gate active and ATA exactly as it was. Two of the rows are worth a closer look.

The hash pins the content but not the length. A buffer missing its last 15 bytes hashes identically, because those bytes are zeros. It is still a broken ELF: its section header table now runs past the end of the file, and the loader stops with “Offset or value is out of bounds.” The check and the loader cover each other. Neither alone would catch both a substituted program and a truncated one.

The authority problem has changed shape rather than disappeared. A changed letter in a string constant and a changed constant in an instruction both pass the loader and the verifier. Only the hash notices them. The buffer’s authority can no longer decide what ATA becomes, but closing or rewriting the buffer before activation still decides that ATA does not change, and a retry then needs a new gate.

When the order slips, the clients split

The two clients compute the same hash, but they decide differently whether to compute it. Agave hashes only if core_bpf_hash_validation is already active and otherwise skips the check. Firedancer always passes the p-ATA hash and checks whenever one is passed. Its feature map says why: it “assumes this feature gate is activated for all migrations”, because the SIMD-0690 gate will activate first. The same harness, with the SIMD-0690 gate inactive when p-ATA activates:

Buffer as it is on mainnet — both migrate

One .rodata letter changed — Agave deploys, Firedancer refuses

Instruction 17 immediate, 83 → 84 — Agave deploys, Firedancer refuses

First opcode set to 0xff — both refuse, for different reasons

In the highlighted rows the clients finish the epoch’s first slot with different bytes at the ATA address, so they compute different bank hashes. Validators executing with Firedancer’s runtime would disagree with validators executing with Agave’s about the same block. Frankendancer, the hybrid, executes with Agave’s runtime, so the line falls between runtimes rather than client brands. Which software each validator runs is visible in gossip and in block footers.

None of this is a bug today. The buffer on mainnet matches, so the order makes no difference to the bytes that would be deployed. SIMD-0567 names SIMD-0690 as a dependency, and both clients document the order. Activating both in the same epoch is also safe: Agave installs the new feature set before it runs any migration, so the check is already on. But the order is a scheduling commitment, not a check in code. Anza’s activation guidelines fix a priority order and say exceptions will occur. The thing to watch is simple: gate FCsQnd4V…zp1u must be active no later than gate pata6uFa…ksx3. Neither gate account had been created on mainnet when this was written.

Telling the states apart

A failed migration leaves no transaction and no event on chain. The only direct record is a warning in each validator’s log. It can still be detected from three accounts, read in one call:

const FEATURE_OWNER = 'Feature111111111111111111111111111111111111';
const LOADER_V3 = 'BPFLoaderUpgradeab1e11111111111111111111111';

async function migrationState(rpc, gate, program, buffer) {
  const res = await fetch(rpc, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ jsonrpc: '2.0', id: 1, method: 'getMultipleAccounts',
      params: [[gate, program, buffer], { encoding: 'base64' }] }),
  });
  const [g, p, b] = (await res.json()).result.value;

  // Feature account: owned by the Feature program, byte 0 = Some(activated_at)
  const data = g?.owner === FEATURE_OWNER ? Buffer.from(g.data[0], 'base64') : null;
  if (!data) return 'gate not submitted';
  if (data[0] !== 1) return 'gate submitted, pending';
  const slot = data.readBigUInt64LE(1);

  if (p.owner === LOADER_V3) return `activated at ${slot}: migrated`;
  return `activated at ${slot}: MIGRATION FAILED (buffer ${b ? 'still there' : 'gone'})`;
}

// p-token:  activated at 419472000: migrated
// p-ATA:    gate not submitted

The two comments are the script’s output against mainnet, for p-token and p-ATA. Checking the owner of the gate account matters: a gate’s address can hold lamports in an ordinary system account before anyone submits it, and reading those as feature data would report nonsense. Our upgrades tracker follows which protocol upgrades are live.

When p-ATA does migrate, the program account at ATokenGP…8knL changes owner from BPFLoader2111… to BPFLoaderUpgradeab1e…, gains a program-data account and has no upgrade authority. SIMD-0567 adds that ATA cannot be invoked during the migration slot, because Loader v3 programs take effect one slot after deployment. Tools that decide whether a program is upgradeable by its loader will see the change.

Two smaller things in the code

The log reads backwards. The mismatch error is built as BuildHashMismatch(hash, expected_hash), with the buffer’s hash first, but its message labels the first value “Expected”. For our altered-letter buffer, the warning prints:

Invalid build hash. Expected: 7c10bb1d…a3b147e730, Got: 4e008052…674e7f7d9e

The value after “Expected” is what the buffer holds, and the value after “Got” is what the validator expected. The labels have been this way since the error was introduced in April 2025. Anyone diagnosing a failed migration from logs should swap them.

A panic fixed in passing. The 2025 version of this check searched for the last non-zero byte across the whole account, header included. When the program bytes were all zero, as in a buffer created but never written, that search could land inside the 37-byte header and produce a slice that ends before it starts. Our harness reproduces the panic for a header with no authority, and for an authority whose last byte is zero. On a real cluster it would have stopped every validator at the activation slot. The SIMD-0690 commit fixed it under the line “strip trailing zeros from ELF bytes only”. It was never reachable on mainnet: the only migration that ever passed a hash before then was the slashing program’s, whose gate was never created on mainnet, and Agave removed it in June 2026. Firedancer’s version never had the problem.

What this does not show

The harness replays the checks and the loader on real bytes. It does not run a cluster through an epoch boundary. The deploy column uses Agave’s loader for both clients; Firedancer has its own loader, which we did not run. The altered buffers are our edits, not anything seen on chain. We checked the on-chain buffer against the published hash but did not rebuild p-ATA from source with solana-verify. We read mainnet only, not testnet or devnet.

Program Migrations: Questions People Actually Ask

Can a Solana feature gate be active while the program it was meant to replace is unchanged?

Yes. A core program migration runs once, inside the first bank of the epoch in which its feature gate activates. If any check fails, the runtime logs a warning and moves on: the feature account records its activation slot and the target program keeps its old bytes. Nothing retries, because the gate is never newly activated again. A second attempt needs a new feature gate in a new validator release.

What exactly does SIMD-0690 hash?

The program bytes in the source buffer account: everything after the 37-byte Loader v3 buffer header, with trailing zero bytes removed, hashed with SHA-256. The result must equal a hash compiled into the validator next to the feature gate. solana-verify computes executable hashes the same way, so solana-verify get-buffer-hash reproduces the value from the chain.

Is the p-ATA buffer on mainnet the one Agave expects?

Yes. The buffer at pataAAkF439TTjwRqmxRkTTEfZemRdoriXusez4PQ6S hashes to 4e008052…7f7d9e, the value in Agave’s replace_ata_with_p_ata gate, in Firedancer’s constant and in the SIMD-0567 text. It was created and written in 37 transactions on 1 November 2026 and has not been written since.

Do Agave and Firedancer run the hash check the same way?

They compute the same hash but differ on when they check it. Agave checks only once the SIMD-0690 gate, core_bpf_hash_validation, is active. Firedancer always checks the p-ATA hash and records that it assumes the SIMD-0690 gate activates first. If p-ATA activated before SIMD-0690 with an altered buffer, Agave would deploy the altered bytes, Firedancer would refuse them, and the two clients would compute different bank hashes.

How do I check whether a migration actually happened?

Read three accounts. The feature account is owned by the Feature program and holds an activation slot once active. The target program is owned by BPFLoaderUpgradeab1e… after a successful migration. The source buffer is consumed on success. An active gate with the program still under its old loader means the migration failed.

The one-line version

SIMD-0690 makes a core program migration deploy the reviewed bytes or nothing. A failure leaves the gate active and the program unchanged, and Agave and Firedancer agree on which happened only if the hash-check gate activates first.

The last in-place swap is in SPL Token was replaced in place, the prefunded-account rule p-ATA builds on is in SIMD-0312’s CreateAccountAllowPrefund, and how to tell which client built a block is in reading the block footer.

Sources: SIMD-0690 at commit eac20f29; SIMD-0567 at 93cdf03a; Agave #16077 and #16524 (source read at 9260869d); Firedancer #12680 (37c65819); the buffer and gate accounts read from mainnet with getAccountInfo, getMultipleAccounts and getSignaturesForAddress. Scenario results are from our own harness.

title: Token-2022 v12: What Changed for Rust Developers
description:
Originally published on xroot.dev.

On 28 October the Token-2022 repository released v12. It rewrites the program on Pinocchio, roughly halving the compute cost of a transfer, and publishes seven crates with breaking version bumps. The program every Solana wallet and exchange calls did not change: all three clusters still run v11.1.0, byte for byte.

So for now, “v12” means Rust crates. We diffed the v11.1.0 and v12.0.0 tags, read the deployed program on mainnet, devnet and testnet, and resolved both versions with Cargo. What follows is what breaks for Rust code, what does not, and how to tell when the new program actually ships.

Published is not deployed

The deployed Token-2022 binary carries a security.txt that names the release it was built from. Read it from the program-data account and hash the same bytes, and you know exactly what a cluster runs:

Mainnet — program@v11.1.0, since 23 Oct

Devnet, testnet — program@v11.1.0, since 23 Sep

SHA-256, all three — 5e888b29⁠…⁠6413d9

v11.1.0 verified build — 5e888b29⁠…⁠6413d9

v12.0.0 binary on any cluster — none

Mainnet took v11.1.0 on 23 October at 15:39 UTC, a month after devnet and testnet. The v11.1.0 release notes carry a deployment section, a verifiable-build hash and an audit link. The v12.0.0 notes list changes only. Until a v12 build is verified and deployed, every Token-2022 instruction on chain runs the v11.1.0 code, whatever crate version your project depends on. To check for yourself:

import base64, hashlib, json, struct, urllib.request

RPC = "https://api.mainnet-beta.solana.com"
PROGRAMDATA = "DoU57AYuPFu2QU514RktNPG22QhApEjnKxnBcu4BHDTY"  # Token-2022's program-data account

def rpc(method, params):
    req = urllib.request.Request(RPC, json.dumps({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": method,
                                 "params": params}).encode(), {"content-type": "application/json"})
    return json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req))["result"]

data = base64.b64decode(rpc("getAccountInfo", [PROGRAMDATA, {"encoding": "base64"}])["value"]["data"][0])
slot = struct.unpack_from("<Q", data, 4)[0]          # last deploy slot
elf = data[45:].rstrip(b"\x00")                     # 45-byte header, zero padding stripped
tag = elf.find(b"source_release\x00") + 15
print("deployed at slot", slot)                      # 460497271
print("source_release ", elf[tag:elf.index(b"\x00", tag)].decode())   # program@v11.1.0
print("sha256         ", hashlib.sha256(elf).hexdigest())             # 5e888b29…6413d9

The Pinocchio rewrite, and the savings still waiting

Pull request #1469 replaces the SDK entrypoint with Pinocchio’s and switches the processor from AccountInfo to Pinocchio’s AccountView, the zero-copy view of the input buffer. It is the same move that made p-token cheap for the original token program. The pull request reports these instruction counts from its own tests:

transfer — 1,444 → 719 CU

transfer_checked — 1,782 → 856 CU

initialize_account — 1,822 → 614 CU

initialize_mint — 1,347 → 553 CU

mint_to — 1,262 → 545 CU

burn — 1,372 → 638 CU

close_account — 1,219 → 535 CU

These are the pull request’s measurements from its instruction-count tests, not ours, and extensions add their own cost on top. They become real only when a v12 binary is deployed. Until then, a transfer of any Token-2022 asset on mainnet costs what v11.1.0 charges.

What breaks in Rust

Most Rust code depends on spl-token-2022-interface, the crate with instruction builders and account layouts. Its builders and state types did not change. The breaks are in four places.

1. The processor signature

In the spl-token-2022 program crate, Processor::process changed from &[AccountInfo] to &mut [AccountView]. Test suites that run Token-2022 as a native processor, with processor!(spl_token_2022::processor::Processor::process), stop compiling on 12.0.0. Load the program’s binary into the test instead, or keep the test on 11.

2. The zk-ops feature is gone

#1524 removed zk-ops, a default feature its own manifest said to remove “once the underlying syscalls are released on all networks”. It gated the confidential-transfer and confidential mint-and-burn processors, which are now always compiled in. A manifest that still names the feature does not build. We asked Cargo to resolve both versions with it:

# spl-token-2022 = { version = "=11.1.0", default-features = false, features = ["no-entrypoint", "zk-ops"] }
#   resolves

# spl-token-2022 = { version = "=12.0.0", default-features = false, features = ["no-entrypoint", "zk-ops"] }
error: failed to select a version for `spl-token-2022`.
package `featcheck` depends on `spl-token-2022` with feature `zk-ops` but `spl-token-2022` does not have that feature.
help: available features: no-entrypoint, test-sbf

3. Two interface helpers take AccountView

In spl-token-2022-interface 4.0, alloc_and_serialize and alloc_and_serialize_variable_len_extension now take &mut AccountView. They grow an account and write an extension into its TLV data; Token-2022 itself uses them for its token-metadata and token-group extensions, and a program that stores TLV data the same way can call them too. Callers holding an AccountInfo need to move to Pinocchio’s types or stay on interface 3.

4. The zero-knowledge types moved a major version

The interface re-exports its proof types from solana-zk-elgamal-proof-interface, now 1.0.0 instead of 0.1. Its confidential builders take those types, for example ProofLocation<CiphertextCommitmentEqualityProofData>. Proof data built against the old crate will not type-check. The confidential stack moves together: interface 4.0, proof-generation and proof-extraction 0.7, and solana-zk-sdk 8.

Instruction builders — unchanged

Mint and account layouts — unchanged

onchain CPI helpers — still AccountInfo

Processor::process — AccountView

zk-ops feature — removed

Confidential transfers: new call, same keys

Changing how confidential keys are derived would be the dangerous kind of break: a wallet that derives different keys can no longer decrypt balances it already holds. zk-sdk 8 changed the derivation API, but not the keys. In 7.0.1, derive_confidential_keys(signer, seed) signs "solana-conf-bal/v1" ‖ seed. In 8.0.1, STANDARD_DERIVATION_MESSAGE is defined as that same "solana-conf-bal/v1", so the seedless call signs the same bytes the old empty-seed call did.

// zk-sdk 7 (Token-2022 v11 stack)
let (elgamal, ae) = derive_confidential_keys(&signer, b"")?;

// zk-sdk 8 (v12 stack): the seed parameter is gone; seeded keys use
// derive_confidential_keys_with_seed(&signer, seed)
let (elgamal, ae) = derive_confidential_keys(&signer)?;

// zk-sdk 8 takes a solana-signer v4 Signer. Signers from the Agave 4.3 stack
// are v3, so sign the standard message yourself (same keys):
let signature = signer.try_sign_message(STANDARD_DERIVATION_MESSAGE)?;
let (elgamal, ae) = derive_confidential_keys_from_signature(&signature)?;

The last pattern is the one Token-2022’s own CLI and client tests now use, per #1584. zk-sdk 8.0.1 depends on solana-signer 4.0.0, while 7.0.1 used 3.0.0, and a v3 keypair does not satisfy the v4 trait.

Two smaller fixes ride along. The interface documentation listed the multisig accounts for confidential mint and burn wrongly, naming the mint twice and dropping the token account. The builders and the IDL that generates the JavaScript client were already right, so only hand-written integrations that followed the comments are affected (#1509). And spl-token-client 0.21.0 no longer builds proof-record transactions that exceed the packet limit when a memo, nonce or compute-budget instruction is added (#1550).

An upgrade order that works

Every crate in the release took a breaking version bump, so nothing moves until you change a version requirement: Cargo will not pick 12.0.0 to satisfy "11". When you do move:

Builders and account reads only — interface 3 → 4

Token-2022 as a native test processor — load the binary

A manifest that names zk-ops — delete the feature

TLV account helpers — move to AccountView

Confidential transfers — upgrade the stack together

None of this changes what happens on chain. The mint and account layouts did not change, and the instruction builders encode every instruction exactly as interface 3 did.

What this does not show

We did not build or run v12, so the compute figures are the pull request’s. Our Cargo check covered dependency resolution, not a compile of downstream code. Where we say a signature or type changed, we read it from the tagged source. The deployment facts come from each cluster’s program-data account, and a later upgrade would show up there first.

Token-2022 v12: Questions People Actually Ask

Is Token-2022 v12 live on Solana mainnet?

No. Mainnet, devnet and testnet all run the same v11.1.0 binary: its embedded security.txt says source_release program@v11.1.0 and its hash matches the v11.1.0 verified build, 5e888b29…. Mainnet was upgraded to it on 23 October 2026. v12.0.0 was published as Rust crates on 28 October, and its release notes have no deployment or verification section.

Will upgrading the spl-token-2022 crate to 12.0.0 break my build?

Only if you use the program crate itself. Processor::process now takes &mut [AccountView] instead of &[AccountInfo], so registering Token-2022 as a native processor in tests no longer compiles, and the zk-ops feature no longer exists, so a Cargo.toml that names it fails to resolve. Instruction builders, state parsing and the onchain CPI helpers are unchanged.

Does solana-zk-sdk 8 change my confidential transfer keys?

No. zk-sdk 8’s derive_confidential_keys(signer) signs STANDARD_DERIVATION_MESSAGE, which is the constant "solana-conf-bal/v1", and zk-sdk 7’s derive_confidential_keys(signer, b"") signed the same bytes. The keys are identical; only the function signature changed, and seeded derivation moved to derive_confidential_keys_with_seed.

How much cheaper is Token-2022 v12?

According to the instruction-count tests in the pull request that moved the program to Pinocchio, transfer falls from 1,444 to 719 compute units and transfer_checked from 1,782 to 856, roughly half. None of that applies on chain until a v12 binary is deployed.

How do I check which Token-2022 version a cluster runs?

Read the program-data account DoU57AYuPFu2QU514RktNPG22QhApEjnKxnBcu4BHDTY, skip its 45-byte header and trailing zero bytes, and read the source_release field of the embedded security.txt. Hashing the same bytes with SHA-256 gives the value solana-verify reports for a verified build.

The one-line version

v12 is a Pinocchio rewrite that halves transfer costs, but for now it exists only as crates: it breaks native test processors, the zk-ops feature and two TLV helpers, keeps confidential keys identical, and changes nothing on chain until a verified v12 binary replaces the v11.1.0 that every cluster runs.

For the extensions themselves, see pausable and permissioned burn and how confidential transfers compare.

Sources: the v12.0.0 and v11.1.0 releases and the tagged source (1bc00fa5, 8867f751); pull requests #1469, #1524, #1584, #1509 and #1550; the solana-zk-sdk 7.0.1 and 8.0.1 crate sources; and the Token-2022 program-data account on mainnet, devnet and testnet.

title: One Solana Slot, Multiple Banks: Fork-Aware Geyser Indexing
description:
Originally published on xroot.dev.

Your Geyser plugin buffers account updates by slot and writes a slot to the analytics tables when the slot is rooted. For as long as a slot meant one bank, that was correct. In October, Agave’s accounts database finished a migration whose stated purpose is to let “multiple banks with the same slot” exist side by side.

A bank is one replay of one block. When a node replays a slot twice, both replays stream their account writes and transactions to every Geyser plugin as they execute, and only one of them is ever finalized. The interface has been naming the bank behind each update since version 4.3.0. An indexer that keys by slot alone merges the two, and the abandoned bank’s data reaches the finalized table.

Here is where the second bank comes from, what a plugin is and is not told, what a slot-keyed indexer commits wrongly, and the bank-keyed buffer that fixes it, with tests that show both.

A slot is not a bank

A slot is a position in time: the window one leader has to produce a block. A bank is a node’s execution of a specific block at that position, with its own account changes, its own transaction results and its own ID. The Solana SDK says it plainly: a BankId “is unique even if the slot number of two different slots is the same”.

Agave’s accounts database used to assume the opposite inside its write cache, the in-memory layer that holds a bank’s account writes until its slot is rooted and flushed. Between late September and the end of October, one Agave engineer moved it from slot keys to bank keys:

BankId becomes its own type (#15620) — 2 Oct

Ancestors carry (slot, bank ID) (#15857) — 8 Oct

Write cache rekeyed by bank ID (#16102) — 20 Oct

Roots added by bank (#16262) — 23 Oct

Purge by bank ID (#16360) — 27 Oct

Flush and freeze by bank ID (#16447, #16459) — 28 Oct

Slot-to-bank map removed (#16497) — 28 Oct

Purge deferred to bank drop (#16508) — 31 Oct

The two highlighted changes say what the series is for. #16360 switched purging to bank IDs “so multiple banks with the same slot can exist in the write cache”. #16497 removed the last lookup by slot, after which the cache “no longer asserts one bank per slot: banks at the same slot each keep their own cache, and removing a bank removes only its own cache.” Before the series, the old bank’s cache had to be purged inline before the slot could be created again. #16508 moved that purge to the background and measured it falling from about 2 milliseconds to about 100 microseconds.

Where the second bank comes from

Three paths in Agave’s replay stage clear a bank and let the same slot be replayed into a new one.

  • Switching to the cluster’s version of a block. A leader can produce more than one version of a block for its slot. Under Alpenglow, live on mainnet since 21 October, votor tells replay when the version the cluster certified differs from the one the node replayed. Replay repairs the cluster’s version, then clears its own bank for that slot and every descendant and replays again. The same slots come back with new bank IDs.
  • Fast leader handover. The first slot of a leader’s four-slot window may start on an optimistic parent, before the previous leader’s last block is settled. If the leader then switches parents, the block carries an UpdateParent marker, and replay clears the in-progress bank and recreates it from the marker’s position in the block.
  • The leader’s own optimistic bank. On the producing side, the same handover clears the bank the leader started building and replaces it.

The second and third paths are fast leader handover, and replay’s restart path checks the FastLeaderHandover11111111111111111111111111 feature, which has not been activated on mainnet. The first needs only a leader that produced two versions of a block, which is rare, but the path is live today. The write-cache series is what lets these replays happen without the old bank’s cache being torn down first.

What a Geyser plugin is told, and what it is not

Since agave-geyser-plugin-interface 4.3.0, the callbacks that carry data name the bank they came from. In version 6.0.0, the current one on 31 October:

update_account_for_bank — slot + bank ID, every write

notify_transaction_for_bank — slot + bank ID, every transaction

update_bank_status · Rooted — bank ID + parent, once per rooted slot

update_slot_status · Dead — slot only, no bank ID

notify_entry_update_parent — cleared bank ID, entry plugins only

bank cleared to switch block versions — no callback at all

Three things in that table decide how an indexer has to be built.

Discards are mostly silent. The only notice of a cleared bank is the UpdateParent entry notification, and the plugin manager sends it only to plugins that enable entry notifications, which most account indexers do not. A bank cleared to switch block versions produces nothing at all. By the time either happens, the bank’s writes and transactions have already been delivered.

Finality is per bank, and ordered. When votor roots a block, the RPC tracker sorts the newly rooted chain by slot and reports each slot once, with its bank ID and with the previous root as its parent. The chain arrives contiguous: a slot between a rooted slot and its reported parent was never rooted. And a bank’s Rooted arrives after its data. Account writes are delivered synchronously while the bank replays, before it can freeze. Transactions travel through a separate service, but the root notification waits on that service’s declared work before it is processed.

Old plugins are blind. The slot-only callbacks were deprecated in 4.3.0, and each new bank-aware method’s default implementation forwards to its old counterpart, dropping the bank ID on the way. A plugin that still implements only update_account keeps compiling and keeps receiving data, with no way to tell two banks of one slot apart.

What a slot-keyed indexer commits

To see the failure without a validator, we fed the event sequence these paths produce to two small indexers in Rust. One buffers by slot and commits a slot when it is rooted. The other buffers by slot and bank ID. Slot 104 is replayed twice: bank 5 executes transactions a and b, writing account X to 70 and account Y to 1, and is then cleared. Bank 6 executes transaction c, writing X to 90, and is rooted.

// bank 5: the version that is abandoned
ix.transaction(104, 5, sig(0xa));
ix.account(104, 5, w(X, 70, 2));
ix.transaction(104, 5, sig(0xb));
ix.account(104, 5, w(Y, 1, 3));
// bank 6: the version the cluster finalizes
ix.transaction(104, 6, sig(0xc));
ix.account(104, 6, w(X, 90, 4));
ix.rooted(104, 103, 6);

// slot-keyed: Y = 1 is "finalized", slot 104 has 3 transactions
// bank-keyed: no Y, slot 104 has 1 transaction (c), X = 90

The slot-keyed indexer commits a value for Y that never existed on the finalized chain, and counts three transactions in a block that has one. Volume, fee and activity tables built on it are inflated by exactly the abandoned bank’s work.

It does get X right, and only by luck. Both banks wrote X, and the higher write_version happened to belong to bank 6, because the clearing paths remove the old bank before the new one replays. Swap the arrival order and a third test shows the slot-keyed indexer committing the abandoned value. Nothing in the interface promises that order, and the write-cache series exists to make same-slot banks cheaper to keep around.

Key by bank, commit on the rooted bank

The fix is a different buffer key and one rule at root time:

pub struct BankKeyed {
    pending: BTreeMap<(Slot, BankId), Pending>,
    pub finalized: Finalized,
}

impl BankKeyed {
    // update_account_for_bank / notify_transaction_for_bank
    pub fn account(&mut self, slot: Slot, bank_id: BankId, w: AccountWrite) {
        self.pending.entry((slot, bank_id)).or_default().write(w);
    }

    // update_bank_status(slot, parent, Rooted, bank_id): one call per newly
    // rooted slot, in slot order, parent = the previous root. Every bank
    // buffered in (parent, slot] is decided now: keep the rooted one.
    pub fn rooted(&mut self, slot: Slot, parent: Slot, bank_id: BankId) {
        let decided: Vec<_> = self
            .pending
            .range((parent + 1, BankId::MIN)..=(slot, BankId::MAX))
            .map(|(key, _)| *key)
            .collect();
        for key in decided {
            let p = self.pending.remove(&key).expect("key was just listed");
            if key == (slot, bank_id) {
                p.commit(slot, &mut self.finalized);
            }
        }
    }
}

The range does two jobs. It drops other banks at the rooted slot, the same-slot case, and it drops banks at slots the chain skipped, an ordinary abandoned fork, because a slot between a root and its reported parent will never be rooted. Banks above the rooted slot stay buffered until their own turn. Handling notify_entry_update_parent is optional: it lets a cleared bank’s buffer go early, but correctness rests on the rooted bank ID, the one signal every plugin receives.

Six tests pin both behaviours down. Two show the slot-keyed indexer committing the abandoned bank’s data, one of them through arrival order alone. The others show the bank-keyed buffer handling the same-slot case, an abandoned fork at a skipped slot, descendants of the root that must stay buffered, and the early discard. Inside a bank, the highest write_version per account is its final state, and that rule is still correct. It just has to be applied per bank, not per slot.

What this does not show

The tests replay event sequences derived from Agave’s source. They are not a captured Geyser stream from a validator, and we have not measured how often a mainnet node clears a bank today. With fast leader handover inactive, only the block-version switch can do it on mainnet, and that needs a leader to have produced two versions of a block.

The ordering guarantees in section 03 come from reading the notification paths, not from a fault-injection test. And a Dead status still names only a slot. A plugin that must react to a dead bank, rather than simply never committing it, cannot tell from that call which of a slot’s banks died.

Same-Slot Banks: Questions People Actually Ask

Can two Solana banks have the same slot?

Yes. A bank is one replay of one block, and Agave gives every bank a unique bank ID even when two banks share a slot. Under Alpenglow a node replaces its bank for a slot when the cluster settles on a different version of that block, and fast leader handover adds a second way once its feature activates.

Does Geyser tell a plugin which bank an update came from?

Since agave-geyser-plugin-interface 4.3.0, yes: update_account_for_bank, notify_transaction_for_bank and update_bank_status all carry a bank_id. The older slot-only callbacks are deprecated, and the default bank-aware methods forward to them without the bank ID.

How does an indexer know which bank was finalized?

Agave reports every newly rooted slot through update_bank_status with SlotStatus::Rooted and the rooted bank’s ID, in slot order, with the previous root as the parent. Commit only that bank, and discard every other bank buffered between the parent and the rooted slot.

Is buffering by slot until the slot is rooted enough?

No. A slot-keyed buffer merges every bank that ever replayed the slot, so accounts written only by an abandoned bank and transactions executed only in it reach the finalized table. Key the buffer by slot and bank ID.

Does Agave notify a plugin when it discards a bank?

Not in general. A bank cleared by fast leader handover produces an UpdateParent entry notification, but only to plugins that enable entry notifications. A bank cleared to switch to the cluster’s version of a block produces no notification at all. The rooted bank ID is the only signal every plugin gets.

The one-line version

A slot can have more than one bank, Geyser streams all of them, and only the bank named in the Rooted status is the finalized one. Key the buffer by slot and bank ID, and implement the _for_bank callbacks.

The pipeline this buffer belongs in is the subject of ingesting the Solana firehose with Rust, and the certificates that decide which bank is rooted are in Alpenglow finality in numbers. What a block says about its own producer is in which client built each block.

Sources: Agave master at commit 5817ebe009, the merge of #16508: replay_stage.rs, update_parent.rs, optimistically_confirmed_bank_tracker.rs, entry_notifier.rs and transaction_status_service.rs; pull requests #16360, #16497 and #16508; the GeyserPlugin trait in agave-geyser-plugin-interface 6.0.0; and solana_clock::BankId. The feature account FastLeaderHandover11111111111111111111111111 does not exist on mainnet.

title: One Lamport Can Break Consensus: Solana’s Integer Inflation
description:
Originally published on xroot.dev.

Once an epoch, every Solana validator computes how many lamports of inflation to mint, adds them to the chain’s capitalization, and folds the result into its bank hash. Today that calculation runs in floating point, with a powf in the middle of it.

SIMD-0607, written by engineers from both Anza and Firedancer, replaces every floating-point step with integer arithmetic specified down to the order of its divisions. Agave merged the implementation on 30 October behind a feature gate. We copied the specification’s Rust into a test harness to check its claims and to measure the problem it fixes. Two mathematically identical float formulas for the same reward disagreed by one lamport in 62 of 60,000 epochs. The integer path cannot disagree with itself.

Why one lamport is a consensus failure

Capitalization is part of the state every validator hashes. If two clients compute the same epoch’s reward and land one lamport apart, their capitalizations differ, their bank hashes differ, and the network has a disagreement no vote can fix. The proposal’s motivation is exactly that: these values “must be computed identically by all validator clients, without relying on IEEE-754 behavior or platform math-library functions such as powf.”

Basic float operations are deterministic. Exponentiation is not specified to the last bit, and the inflation rate is 0.08 × (1 − taper)^year. To see how much that matters, we computed the legacy epoch reward two ways that are equal on paper, (1 − taper).powf(year) and exp(year × ln(1 − taper)), for 6,000 epochs in each of five slot-time regimes and both tapers:

Capitalization 10¹⁸ lamports — 62 of 60,000 rewards differ

Capitalization 6.2 × 10¹⁷ lamports — 47 of 60,000 rewards differ

Size of every difference — 1 lamport

About one epoch in a thousand, the truncation that turns a float reward into lamports lands on the other side of an integer. That is not a claim that Agave and Firedancer compute different rewards today. It is the reason neither should depend on how a math library rounds the last bit.

The integer schedule

Rates are integers over RATE_SCALE = 10^15, so 8% is 80_000_000_000_000. Decay factors are integers over 2^64, a finer scale because a factor very close to one is multiplied by itself across hundreds of millions of slots. The per-slot factor is derived, not tabulated: a 32-term series for the logarithm of the taper and a cubic approximation of the exponential, then a binary exponentiation whose order and flooring are fixed:

fn decay_per_slot(ns: u128, taper_num: u32, taper_den: u32) -> Option<u128> {
    // -ln(1 - taper) = ln(taper_den / (taper_den - taper_num)), scaled by 2^64
    let annual_exponent =
        approximate_logarithm(taper_den, taper_den.checked_sub(taper_num)?)?;
    let slot_exponent = annual_exponent.checked_mul(ns)? / YEAR_NS;
    approximate_exponential(slot_exponent) // 2^64 * exp(-x), cubic
}

fn pow_decay_floor(mut base: u128, mut n: u64) -> u128 {
    let mut result = DECAY_SCALE;
    while n > 0 {
        if n & 1 != 0 { result = mul_decay_floor(result, base); }
        n >>= 1;
        if n > 0 { base = mul_decay_floor(base, base); }
    }
    result
}

// rate   = max(TERMINAL_RATE, floor(anchor_rate * decay / 2^64))
// annual = floor(capitalization * rate / 10^15)
// reward = floor(annual * slots_in_epoch * ns_per_slot / YEAR_NS)

Every step floors, every multiplication is checked, and an overflow is an error the validator must turn into a panic. The specification forbids wrapping, saturating or substituting a value, and it forbids falling back to floating point.

Its numbers, reproduced to the lamport

The proposal publishes how far the integer schedule drifts from the floating-point one: the largest difference in a single epoch’s reward over 6,000 epochs, at a capitalization of 10¹⁸ lamports, across the 400, 350, 300, 250 and 200 ms slot regimes. Running its functions verbatim against its stated float baseline:

15% taper, largest difference — 5,923 lamports (spec: 5,923)

30% taper, largest difference — 1,061 lamports (spec: 1,061)

Where the 15% worst case falls — 350 ms, epoch 1,282

Where the 30% worst case falls — 400 ms, epoch 509

32-term logarithm vs 200 terms — identical, both tapers

Both drift figures match exactly. So does the claim that 32 terms of the logarithm series are enough: for the 15% and 30% tapers, the 32-term sum and a 200-term sum are the same integer, to the last of 2⁶⁴ units. The drift is the price of the change, at most a few thousand lamports of an epoch’s reward. A relative difference below 7 × 10⁻¹¹ buys a reward every client computes identically.

Overflow, and why it panics

With 128-bit intermediates, the reward arithmetic stays valid up to a capitalization of about 18.4 trillion SOL, a thousand times beyond the 18.4 billion SOL a 64-bit lamport count can hold at all. The checks that can fail in practice are the invalid inputs: a zero slot duration, or a taper of 100% or more, return an error before any arithmetic.

The panic rule is deliberate. A validator that cannot compute the reward exactly as specified is safer stopped than running on a number the rest of the cluster did not compute. That is the same reasoning as the proposal itself, applied to its own failure path.

The activation order with SIMD-0550

SIMD-0550 doubles the yearly disinflation from 15% to 30%. Its original design kept issuance continuous by recomputing the stored initial rate at activation, initial = anchor / (1 − 0.30)^year, with powf. Our earlier post on SIMD-0550 described that design. An amendment merged on 29 October replaced it: SIMD-0607 must activate first or at the same boundary, the anchor is computed with the integer 15% schedule including its terminal clamp, and the 30% integer taper applies from the activation slot. Agave rekeyed the SIMD-0550 gate in the 4.4.0 release.

Anchor rate, activation at year 6 (illustrative) — 3.0172%

Rate zero slots after activation — 3.0172%

Rate one year later — 2.1120%

Naive governor formula, 0.08 × 0.70⁶ — 1.5% (terminal floor)

The anchor works: at zero elapsed slots the decay factor is exactly 2⁶⁴, so the rate does not move. The trap is for anyone reading the stored governor. After activation it reports initial = 0.08 and taper = 0.30, and the textbook formula built from those two numbers, which measures decay from genesis, lands on the 1.5% floor while the chain is minting at about 3%. Forward curves should start from getInflationRate, not from getInflationGovernor.

Where it stands

Agave’s implementation, #16355, merged on 30 October behind the remove_runtime_float_ops gate. Neither that gate nor SIMD-0550’s has been activated on mainnet. When SIMD-0607 does activate at the boundary into epoch E+1, rewards earned in epoch E are still paid with the legacy calculation, and the integer path starts with rewards earned in E+1.

What this does not show

We ran the specification’s code, not Agave’s implementation of it, and compared against the float baseline the specification states rather than against a running validator. The two float paths in section 01 are a test of sensitivity, not a measurement of any client. The year-6 activation in section 05 is illustrative, at constant 400 ms slots; the real anchor depends on the slot-time history up to the activation slot.

Integer Inflation: Questions People Actually Ask

Why does Solana want to remove floating point from inflation?

Inflation rewards are added to capitalization, which is part of the bank hash. If two validator clients compute an epoch’s reward one lamport apart, their bank hashes differ. Floating-point exponentiation depends on the math library, and mathematically identical float formulas can round to different lamport amounts. SIMD-0607 specifies the whole calculation in integers so every client gets the same number.

How large is the difference between the integer and floating-point schedules?

At most 5,923 lamports per epoch for the 15% taper and 1,061 for the 30% taper, over 6,000 epochs and five slot-time regimes at a capitalization of 10^18 lamports, a relative difference below 7.03 × 10^-11. We reproduced both figures exactly from the specification’s code.

What does SIMD-0607 have to do with SIMD-0550?

SIMD-0550 doubles the disinflation rate from 15% to 30% a year. Since an amendment merged on 29 October 2026, it must activate after or together with SIMD-0607: the anchor rate at activation is computed with the integer 15% schedule, and the 30% integer taper applies from there. The stored inflation governor keeps initial 0.08 and switches taper to 0.30.

Can I compute Solana’s inflation rate from getInflationGovernor?

Not after SIMD-0550 activates. The governor will report initial 0.08 and taper 0.30, but the rate decays from the activation anchor, not from genesis, so initial × (1 − taper)^years gives the wrong answer. Read getInflationRate, which the node computes.

Is SIMD-0607 active on mainnet?

Not as of 30 October 2026. Agave merged the implementation that day behind the remove_runtime_float_ops feature gate, which has not been activated on mainnet.

The one-line version

Floating point lets two correct implementations disagree by a lamport about once in a thousand epochs; SIMD-0607 trades a few thousand lamports of drift per epoch for a reward every client computes identically, and SIMD-0550 now waits for it.

The faster disinflation itself is in Solana’s inflation will decay twice as fast, how those rewards reach stake accounts is in when staking rewards arrive, and why two independent clients matter at all is in which client built each block.

Sources: SIMD-0607 as amended at commit 2934dbeb; the SIMD-0550 amendment; Agave #16355 (commit 9bcf93e368) and #16499. Measurements are from the specification’s functions run in our own harness.

title: Solana Geo Leader Schedule: Location Pays, Splitting Doesn’t
description:
Originally published on xroot.dev.

Under Alpenglow’s fast leader handover, the gap between two leaders is mostly the time a block takes to cross from one to the next. Today’s schedule picks leaders at random, so that crossing is often an ocean. SIMD-0675 proposes to reorder the schedule so that leaders near each other go one after another.

In review, Dean Little raised the obvious worry: that the reordering “appears to incentivize sybils”, letting validators use geography, “or even just a self-attestation of geography”, to line up their leader rotations “with better-than-random odds”. Two days later, the author of the proposal’s parameter analysis answered that splitting stake barely moves the odds, 7.146% to 7.147% in one example, because “the majority of the ‘upside’ for extractors (compared to random) is already given by the schedule design.”

We rebuilt the reordering in Rust from the specification to check both statements. The reviewer is right about splitting: it changes nothing, not even one window. But the second half of the sentence is the finding. The upside the schedule hands out depends on where an operator’s stake sits, and an honest operator in the right region gets back-to-back windows five to seven times as often as today, without splitting or lying about anything.

Bins, radii and runs

The base schedule is computed exactly as today, one stake-weighted random leader per four-slot window. SIMD-0675 then walks it in order and drops each leader into a bin:

  • Radius. Every validator has a radius, the smallest distance around it that holds STAKE_FLOOR (10%) of all stake. Dense places get small radii, isolated ones large radii. Locations are self-reported, through SIMD-0674.
  • Bins. A leader joins a random open bin whose anchor is within the larger of the two radii, or opens a new bin if none is.
  • Runs. When a bin holds RUN_LENGTH leaders, it is shuffled and written out as a block of consecutive windows. The proposal says 3; reviewers have argued for 7.

Every validator keeps exactly the windows it would have had. Only their order changes. With 200 ms slots, a run of three windows is 2.4 seconds of block production from one area of the map.

for &l in base {
    let near: Vec<usize> = (0..bins.len())
        .filter(|&i| {
            let a = bins[i].anchor;
            dist2(&vs[l], &vs[a]) <= r[a].max(r[l])
        })
        .collect();
    let bi = if near.is_empty() {
        bins.push(Bin { anchor: l, members: vec![l] });
        bins.len() - 1
    } else {
        let i = near[rng.roll(near.len())]; // one roll per join
        bins[i].members.push(l);
        i
    };
    if bins[bi].members.len() == run_length {
        let mut b = bins.remove(bi);
        rng.shuffle(&mut b.members); // Fisher-Yates
        out.extend(b.members);
    }
}
// end of epoch: shuffle the open bins, shuffle each one, append

The model, and a check against the proposal

Our implementation follows the specification’s pseudocode line for line: the radius, the nearness test, one random draw per join, Fisher-Yates within a run and a shuffled flush at the end of the epoch. Two simplifications are deliberate. The random generator is SplitMix64 rather than the specified ChaCha20, which changes which schedule comes out but not its statistics. And the network is stylized: about 800 validators with lognormal stake across 19 metros. Asia holds 10.4% of stake, the figure in the parameter analysis published on solana.com; the European and North American split and the metro mix are our assumptions. Latency between leaders uses the analysis’ estimate, 1.5 times the great-circle distance at 200 km per millisecond. Each scenario is 108,000 windows, an epoch, averaged over five seeds.

Mean handover, random schedule (SIMD’s figure) — 37.3 ms (36.2)

RUN_LENGTH 3 — 18.2 ms (17.0)

RUN_LENGTH 7 — 11.6 ms (10.8)

The proposal’s simulation, on the real stake distribution of epoch 1038 and measured round-trip times, is in brackets. Our stylized network lands within about a millisecond at every run length, which is close enough to trust it for the question it was built for: who gets consecutive windows.

Splitting stake changes nothing

We gave one operator 3% of stake as one validator in Frankfurt, then as six validators of 0.5% each in the same place. The two schedules were identical, window for window, at every run length.

That is not a statistical tie, it is structural. The base schedule gives the six the same windows the one would have had. The radius of a location is computed from all the stake there, so it is the same. And a bin only ever asks about locations and radii, never identities. Sybils at one address are invisible to the reorder, which is the reviewer’s 7.146% to 7.147% taken to its limit.

Splitting across regions is worse than useless for an extractor. The same 3% spread over Frankfurt, Ashburn and Singapore led two windows in a row 4.2% of the time at RUN_LENGTH 3, against 7.6% for the operator that stayed in one place.

Location changes a lot

Consecutive windows under one operator are the precondition for multi-block MEV: two windows are eight slots in which one party orders every transaction. We measured how often an operator’s window is followed by another of its own, under today’s random schedule and under the reorder. Columns are random, then RUN_LENGTH 3, then 7.

1% operator, Frankfurt — 1.06% → 2.56% → 3.31%

1% operator, Tokyo — 1.06% → 5.31% → 7.66%

3% operator, Frankfurt — 3.15% → 7.56% → 9.22%

3% operator, Tokyo — 3.15% → 15.10% → 19.10%

3% split over three regions — 3.15% → 4.18% → 4.90%

Under random, the chance is the operator’s stake share, wherever it sits. Under the reorder, a run is filled from nearby stake, so the chance tracks the operator’s share of its region instead. Three percent of all stake is a modest slice of Europe and a large slice of Asia, the smallest region that still forms bins of its own at a 10% floor. The same operator in Tokyo gets back-to-back windows 4.8 times as often as today at RUN_LENGTH 3, and 6.1 times at 7, twice what it would get in Frankfurt.

Nobody lied and nobody split stake. This is the schedule working as designed, and it is the reviewer’s point stated with a location attached: the upside comes from the design, and the design pays most to the largest operator in the smallest self-contained region. The solana.com analysis already notes that Asia sits just above the floor, at 10.4%, “with very little margin”. Our numbers say the margin is also where consecutive control is cheapest.

And lying about it

The attack the proposal’s authors model is a validator that declares an isolated location, so that no one else joins its bins. The solana.com analysis uses the most isolated point it could find, in the South Pacific, and reports that at RUN_LENGTH 7 lying is worth 0.28 extra consecutive windows to a validator with 4.07% of stake, the largest today, and 1.69 to one with 10%.

4.07% operator, back-to-back, truthful in Frankfurt — 4.23% → 10.13% → 12.15%

4.07% operator, back-to-back, declares South Pacific — 4.23% → 32.34% → 41.59%

10% operator, back-to-back, truthful in Frankfurt — 10.05% → 21.72% → 25.98%

10% operator, back-to-back, declares South Pacific — 10.05% → 65.11% → 83.19%

Measured the analysis’ way, as the expected run remaining from one of the liar’s windows, our model puts the gain from lying, against the same operator in Frankfurt, at 0.58 windows for the 4.07% validator and 2.43 for the 10% one, both at RUN_LENGTH 7. That is higher than the analysis’ figures, which come from the real map, where a few validators in Argentina and Australia can still reach the isolated point. The direction is the same: lying pays a little below the floor and a lot at it, which is why STAKE_FLOOR is pinned at 10%.

The proposal’s own location-fibbing table shows lying rarely improves a validator’s latency. It was never meant to. The reason to lie is the run, not the handover.

What it means for the parameters

RUN_LENGTH moves every number above. Going from 3 to 7 buys 6.6 milliseconds of mean handover in our model and raises back-to-back control for every operator we measured. The proposal’s authors prefer 3 for exactly this reason; the analysis finds a knee at 7 and calls 3 “the conservative choice”. Reviewers suggested handling Sybils outside the protocol, by raising the validator admission ticket or by detecting misreported locations, and the authors agreed that detection is probably possible.

Neither remedy touches the effect in section 04. A ticket prices the number of validators, and the location-driven gain needs only one. Detection catches false locations, and the Tokyo operator’s location is true. If the concern is consecutive control by honest operators, the levers are the run length and the floor, and the floor is already pressed against Asia’s share.

What this does not show

The network is stylized, so the exact percentages belong to it; the mechanism, that consecutive control tracks local rather than global share, does not depend on the split we chose. Back-to-back windows are a precondition for multi-block MEV, not a measure of its value, which the analysis also stresses. The random generator differs from the specified one. And SIMD-0675 and SIMD-0674 are open proposals, last amended on 22 October, so the constants may still change.

Geo-Aware Leader Schedule: Questions People Actually Ask

What is Solana’s geo-aware leader schedule?

SIMD-0675, an open proposal, keeps today’s stake-weighted random leader schedule and then reorders it: leaders that are geographically close are grouped into runs of RUN_LENGTH consecutive leader windows, so the handover between them is short. Every validator keeps exactly as many windows as before.

Does splitting stake into several validators help under SIMD-0675?

Not at one location. The reorder sees a validator’s location and stake, not its identity, so six validators in one city with a combined stake behave exactly like one. In our model they produced identical schedules, window for window.

Where does the geo-aware schedule give an operator more consecutive windows?

Where its share of the local stake is large. A run is filled from nearby stake, so an operator’s chance of leading two windows in a row tracks its share of its region. In our model a 3% operator in Tokyo got back-to-back windows 15% of the time at RUN_LENGTH 3, against 3% under today’s random schedule and 7.6% in Frankfurt.

Can a validator lie about its location to get consecutive leader slots?

Yes, and the proposal’s parameter analysis measures it: a validator that declares an isolated location ends up alone in its bins. The analysis puts the gain at 0.28 extra consecutive windows for a 4.07% validator at RUN_LENGTH 7, rising sharply once the liar holds STAKE_FLOOR, 10% of stake, which is why STAKE_FLOOR sits at 10%.

Is SIMD-0675 live on mainnet?

No. As of 26 October 2026 it is an open proposal, as is SIMD-0674, the location registration it depends on. Its parameters, especially RUN_LENGTH, are still being debated between 3 and 7.

The one-line version

SIMD-0675 halves handover latency and does not reward Sybils, but it turns local stake share into consecutive leader windows, and the smallest region that forms its own bins is where a large operator gains the most.

The consensus this schedule feeds is in Alpenglow finality in numbers, the admission ticket reviewers proposed raising is in the 2,000 validator seats, and the stake-weighted QoS that follows the leader is in stake-weighted QoS, with the formula.

Sources: SIMD-0675 and SIMD-0674 as amended on 22 October 2026, with their review threads to 26 October; the parameter analysis on solana.com, by Umberto Natale, 14 October 2026. Results are from our Rust model of the reorder, described in section 02.

title: Solana CPI Overhead: From 90-Byte Accounts to 4-Byte Indices
description:
Originally published on xroot.dev.

Every cross-program invocation on Solana starts with the calling program copying information the runtime already has. For each account it forwards, the program builds an account meta and an account info, then hands both arrays to a syscall that reads them back. SIMD-0670 proposes to replace all of that with a 4-byte index.

SIMD-0670, merged on 24 October with status Review, adds sol_invoke_signed_v2 next to today’s invoke. To see what it saves, we wrote a small Pinocchio program that prepares the same CPI both ways and ran it in solana-sbpf, the virtual machine Agave runs programs in, counting every instruction up to the syscall. The v2 path costs about a third as much per account, falls to a constant 17 to 20 compute units when the account list is fixed, and avoids a stack limit that today’s path hits before its own documented maximum.

Where the 90 bytes come from

A program receives its accounts as a serialized buffer and, to call another program, has to describe the accounts it forwards twice. The Rust interface takes an AccountMeta per account, a 32-byte address plus two flags, and an account info; the proposal counts 34 and 56 bytes for them. The C interface, which Pinocchio uses, replaces the address with a pointer, so its meta is 16 bytes with padding, and its account info is 56:

Rust ABI, as the proposal counts it — 34 + 56 = 90 bytes

C ABI (Pinocchio): meta + CpiAccount — 16 + 56 = 72 bytes

SIMD-0670: CpiAccount — 4 bytes

The new record is an index into the caller’s own instruction accounts plus the two flags. The runtime already holds those accounts, so it looks them up instead of reading copies:

#[repr(C)]
pub struct CpiAccount {
    pub account_index: u16, // index in the current instruction
    pub is_writable: u8,
    pub is_signer: u8,
}

pub fn sol_invoke_signed_v2(instruction_addr: u64, signers_seeds_addr: u64, signers_seeds_len: u64);

One naming trap: Pinocchio’s CPI module, solana-instruction-view, already has a type called CpiAccount. That one is the 56-byte account info. The proposal’s CpiAccount is the 4-byte record.

What preparing a CPI costs, measured

Our test program forwards N accounts to a callee in four ways: Pinocchio 0.11.2’s stack path (invoke_signed_with_bounds), its heap path for larger calls, v2 descriptors filled from the account flags, and a v2 descriptor list fixed at compile time. We built it with platform-tools v1.57 and ran it in solana-sbpf 0.26.0, configured as Agave configures it, with inputs serialized the way Agave serializes them. A stub syscall records the instruction count when the program reaches the CPI, and the count for reaching any syscall with the same accounts is subtracted. One executed instruction is one compute unit.

8 accounts: v1 · v2 · v2 fixed — 529 · 171 · 17 CU

16 accounts — 1,011 · 316 · 18 CU

32 accounts — 1,969 · 606 · 20 CU

56 accounts, v1 stack — 3,411 CU

64 accounts: v1 heap · v2 · v2 fixed — 4,319 · 1,179 · 17 CU

128 accounts — 8,543 · 2,332 · 18 CU

254 accounts: v2 · v2 fixed — 4,602 · 20 CU

Today’s path costs about 60 compute units per account on the stack and about 66 on the heap. The v2 path, filling each descriptor from the account’s flags, costs about 18. When a program always forwards the same accounts, the descriptor list can live in read-only data, and the cost stops depending on the number of accounts at all.

The proposal’s own benchmark, a Pinocchio program calling a program that logs how many accounts it received, reports different absolute numbers: from 1,376 to 1,174 compute units at 8 accounts, and from 2,813 to 1,267 at 64. The shape is the same. Today’s path grows with every account. The proposed one barely moves.

The stack limit comes before the documented one

A Solana program function gets a 4 KiB stack frame. Pinocchio allows up to 64 accounts on its stack path, which is 3,584 bytes of 56-byte account infos. Its CPI helpers are #[inline(always)], though, so that array lands in the caller’s frame next to the caller’s own 16-byte metas:

56 accounts, v1 stack — runs

60 accounts, frame estimate — 4,416 bytes, crashes

64 accounts, frame estimate — 4,672 bytes, crashes

254 accounts, v2 descriptors — 1,016 bytes

cargo-build-sbf prints a frame-overflow error for the 60- and 64-account versions but still produces the binary. At run time both stop with an access violation in the stack frame. A program that needs more accounts moves to the heap path, which allocates 72 bytes per account: 9,216 bytes of the default 32 KiB heap at 128 accounts, Pinocchio’s ceiling. With v2 the whole list of 254 accounts fits in about a quarter of one frame.

What the proposal leaves unchanged

Only the program’s side gets cheaper. The runtime still translates every account, applies the same privilege checks and charges the same compute: the proposal keeps the per-account charge at 34 bytes, because the runtime reads the same information either way. Old programs keep working, since today’s syscall is not changed or removed.

Indices also mean a program can only forward accounts that are already in its own instruction. That is true of today’s invoke as well, which needs an account info the program can only get from its input, so nothing a program could do before is lost.

Where it stands

The proposal is merged with status Review. Agave’s implementation was open as #15979 at the time of writing, and a new syscall also needs a feature gate before mainnet programs can call it. Program libraries will need a v2 path of their own; our test declared the syscall by hand. For a busy program the saving adds up: compute units are what priority fees are priced against, and a router that forwards dozens of accounts on every call pays the per-account cost every time.

What this does not show

We measured the program’s preparation only. The syscalls were stubs, so the runtime’s CPI work and the callee are not included. The numbers are for one program built with one toolchain. Other code, including Anchor’s, will differ, though not in shape. The v2 syscall was not running anywhere we could test, so we checked that our descriptors matched the proposal’s layout rather than that a runtime accepted them.

CPI Overhead: Questions People Actually Ask

What does SIMD-0670 change about Solana CPIs?

It proposes a second invoke syscall, sol_invoke_signed_v2, that describes each account passed to a cross-program invocation with a 4-byte record: the account’s index in the caller’s own instruction plus writable and signer flags. Today a program passes two records per account, an account meta and an account info: 90 bytes through the Rust interface by the proposal’s count, 72 through the C interface Pinocchio uses. The runtime’s CPI logic and its compute charge stay the same; only the program-side preparation shrinks.

How many compute units does SIMD-0670 save?

In our measurement inside Solana’s VM, preparing a CPI the way Pinocchio does today costs about 60 compute units per forwarded account (529 for 8 accounts, 1,969 for 32). Filling v2 descriptors from the accounts costs about 18 per account (171 and 606), and a descriptor list fixed at compile time costs 17 to 20 regardless of size. The runtime’s own CPI charge is not included and does not change.

What is the maximum number of accounts a Solana CPI can forward from the stack?

With Pinocchio 0.11.2’s stack path, our test program ran with 56 forwarded accounts and failed with a stack access violation at 60 and 64. Each account costs 72 bytes of the 4 KiB stack frame, and Pinocchio inlines its account array into the caller. With SIMD-0670’s 4-byte descriptors, 254 accounts take 1,016 bytes.

Is sol_invoke_signed_v2 available on mainnet?

No. SIMD-0670 was merged on 24 October 2026 with status Review, and Agave’s implementation was an open pull request at the time of writing. Like every new syscall it needs a feature gate before programs can call it on mainnet.

Does sol_invoke_signed_v2 change CPI security?

The proposal says the security surface is identical: the runtime applies the same privilege checks and compute metering, and it still charges as if each account were 34 bytes. A program can only reference accounts that are already in its own instruction, which is also true of today’s invoke.

The one-line version

SIMD-0670 lets a program forward an account to a CPI with a 4-byte index instead of 72 to 90 bytes of copies, cutting preparation from about 60 compute units per account to about 18, or to a constant 20 for a fixed list, and keeping 254 accounts inside one stack frame.

Pinocchio itself is the library behind p-token, where the same idea of not copying what the runtime already has made the token program several times cheaper.

Sources: SIMD-0670 at commit c9ec366a; Agave #15979; Pinocchio 0.11.2 and solana-instruction-view 2.1.0; solana-sbpf 0.26.0. Measurements are from our own test program and harness.
