title: A LangGraph SQL agent that only sees the tables it needs
description:
Most text-to-SQL agents paste the whole schema into every prompt. On a real database, most of it is tables the question never touches, and you pay for them on every call.

I added a small LangGraph example to schemagate that does it differently. It has four nodes:

  1. select_schema: SchemagateRetriever picks the few tables the question needs. This step runs offline, with no model call.
  2. write_sql: the model writes one SELECT using only those tables.
  3. run_sql: the agent runs the query. If it fails, the error goes back to the model once.
  4. answer: the model answers in one sentence from the returned rows.

On the bundled 42-table demo database:

Question Schema tokens sent
Which customers owe us money? 489 vs 2,199 (78% fewer)
How many orders did each carrier ship? 706 vs 2,199 (68% fewer)
Which products are below their reorder level, and in which warehouse? 563 vs 2,199 (74% fewer)

All three answers were correct with Claude Haiku. On databases with 50+ tables the saving reaches about 91%. The selection also respects roles: a table the caller can't read never appears in the prompt.

pip install langchain-schemagate langgraph langchain-anthropic tiktoken
python examples/langgraph_sql_agent.py

To use your own database, swap demo_catalog() for Catalog().bootstrap("postgresql://...").

schemagate is #1 on the BIRD Mini-Dev leaderboard (SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL), is listed in LangChain's official retriever integrations, and is Apache-2.0.

Example: examples/langgraph_sql_agent.py

title: Berrypicking still beats the single answer for search, even in the world of AI
description:
In 1989 Marcia Bates showed that people search by gathering, shifting, and revising as they go. Her ideas explain what AI still misses and what is still relevant from research done 47 years ago.

Much of what product teams are learning about artificial intelligence search, an information scientist wrote down before the web existed. Marcia J. Bates spent her career at UCLA studying how people search and her 1989 paper, The Design of Browsing and Berrypicking Techniques for the Online Search Interface, argued that real searches wander, change shape, and collect value in pieces.

She aimed it at library databases that assumed one query and one best result; AI turns this on its head.

The chat box makes the same assumption, only faster.

Bates is still relevant in the age of artificial intelligence, arguably more than ever. Large language models changed what a system can answer but they didn’t change how a person goes about asking, which still means starting vague, learning while reading, and changing direction midway.

I had the pleasure of meeting her at the IA Summit in Chicago in 2018 — she most politely asked if we could have lunch and I brought a few others. It became a great conversation where I still learned concepts that I apply today, and they are incredibility relevant to what we’re doing with AI back when my company was only applying machine learning.

I’ve used her concepts to frame search and artificial intelligence summarization in legal tech software. Anyone designing search or summarization should be thanking her.

Five of her ideas hold up, each tied to a decision you’re making now.

Support Evolving Searches

Bates built the berrypicking paper as an attack on the classic retrieval model, which treats a search as one query matched once against a database to produce one best set of results.

Her objection fit in one line: “typical search queries are not static, but rather evolve.”

People begin with one reference or a narrow slice of a bigger topic, read what comes back, and let each find reshape the question.

She named the bit-at-a-time collecting after picking huckleberries scattered through a forest. Marti Hearst later made the model a standard reference for interface designers in Models of the Information Seeking Process.

The need itself shifts as the person learns, and that separates berrypicking from search methods that look similar from the outside:

  • Known-item lookup. You know what you want, such as a fact or a file, and one query finds it or doesn’t. You can accomplish this usually in a single term.
  • Iterative refinement. You rephrase to hit a fixed target, the job Gerard Salton’s relevance feedback automated. The words change, but the need doesn’t.
  • Browsing. You glimpse, sample, and pick within one place. Bates treated it as one move inside a larger search, not the same thing.
  • Berrypicking. The need evolves, and the answer arrives in pieces from many sources rather than as one final set.

That last difference is why a successful search is so hard to define:

  • The classic model let researchers score one result set for precision and recall.
  • A berrypicking search has no single set to score, and Bates called knowing when to stop one of the fundamental problems of search strategy.
  • A thumbs-up on one chat answer measures the last berry, not the picking.

Sometimes what matters most is what isn’t found.

An empty patch tells a berrypicker something, whether it’s no earlier case on point, no conflicting clause in a contract, or no research on a question. A system that always produces a confident answer hides that signal, because it never lets the absence show.

The chat window rewards the user who already knows exactly what they want, which is the user who needs the least help.

Language models repeat the classic assumption.

In LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation, a 2025 study of more than 200,000 simulated conversations, every top model tested did worse when a task arrived in pieces, with an average drop of 39 percent across six tasks. The models guessed early and didn’t recover.

The design job is to support the person whose question is still forming. Show what has shifted since the first prompt, and let people revise early assumptions without starting over.

Bates even sketched the tooling in 1989: a temporary store where searchers could flag findings as they went.

Expose Search Tactics

A decade earlier, Bates published Information Search Tactics, which won her field’s best paper award the following year. A tactic, in her definition, is a move made to further a search.

She named 29 of them in four groups, including these:

  • Check. Compare the current search against the original request.
  • Pinpoint. Narrow to the most precise terms.
  • Parallel. Broaden with synonyms and related terms.
  • Trace. Mine what you’ve already found for new terms.
  • Record. Track the trails you followed and the ones you meant to revisit.

Her premise was that naming a tactic makes it easier to reach for. Reference librarians used many of these moves without names, which left beginners no easy way to learn them.

The web repeated the problem.

People had to learn to search like Google, stripping questions down to two or three keywords and adding quotes or a minus sign when results went wrong. They’re doing the same with chat now, working out by trial and error which phrasings get a useful answer.

A blank prompt box ships with none of them, so people improvise.

Nielsen Norman Group documented one improvisation in Accordion Editing and Apple Picking: Early Generative-AI User Behaviors.

Users copied part of an earlier response into a new prompt by hand, because the interface gave them no other way to point at it. It’s berrypicking with copy and paste as the only tool.

That’s a search behavior, because chat and search are closer than they look. In both, a person puts a need into words, the system matches it against stored information, and the person judges what comes back and tries again.

Retrieval-augmented assistants run a search behind the scenes and summarize the results, so the biggest difference is the shape of the reply: a list of links in one, a paragraph in the other.

Everything Bates learned about searching also applies to chatting in spades.

Missing controls matter most for experts, who read a bad result set as a clue rather than a verdict. They tighten, exclude, widen, and re-sort in small passes until the set matches what they meant, and they decide when it’s done. In Investigating the Querying and Browsing Behavior of Advanced Search Engine Users, Ryen White and Dan Morris found marked differences between people who used query operators and those who didn’t, in how they queried, clicked, browsed, and fared.

Faceted search is the interface version of those moves.

In a study reported in Hearst’s chapter Integrating Navigation with Search, 91 percent of 32 art history students preferred a faceted image interface to a plain one, even though it was slower.

A chat reply hides exactly those facets and filters, when most of Bates’s 29 tactics could become buttons nobody has to phrase.

Choose the Automation Level

In 1990, Bates asked the question every agent team is now answering under deadline: Where Should the Person Stop and the Information Search Interface Start? Her answer was a scale.

  • At level 0 the system offers no help.
  • Level 1 explains possible moves
  • Level 2 carries them out on command
  • Level 3 watches the search and suggests next steps
  • Level 4 runs the whole search, either explaining its choices or just returning results.

In product terms, the levels are easy to spot:

  • Level 1 is a help panel that lists search operators
  • Level 2 is a filter that runs when you click it
  • Level 3 is a “did you mean” correction or a suggested follow-up question.
  • Level 4 is the research agent that disappears for several minutes and comes back with a finished report.

She argued that research had fixated on level 4, while many searchers wanted the speed of automation and control of strategy. Jakob Nielsen called generative tools AI: First New UI Paradigm in 60 Years in 2023, describing a reversal of the locus of control in which users state the outcome and the computer picks the method.

Bates had mapped that reversal decades earlier, and put most of the useful ground short of the far edge.

Most AI products jump straight to level 4 and call the result an agent. That’s not right.

Skipping the middle skips the levels where trust gets built. People defer to the machine even when it’s wrong, which I document in the Automation Bias entry on UX Guidelines, a reference site I maintain. Pick the level per task, and let people move the dial.

Fix the Content Layers

Her 2002 paper The Cascade of Interactions in the Digital Library Interface lists the layers under any search experience: infrastructure, content, metadata, indexing, and the search engine, with the interface and the person at the top.

Decisions at each layer ripple upward, and good interface design can’t rescue weak choices further down.

Swap “digital library” for “retrieval-augmented assistant” and little changes. Above the model is the chat window your team keeps polishing. Below it are document stores, chunking rules, and permissions someone set up years ago for another purpose. Good metadata is what sets context for the model, telling it what a document is, who it applies to, and whether it’s still current. The demo runs on 20 clean documents, and production meets a decade of duplicate policies and unlabeled drafts.

A semantic layer goes a step further.

It defines what terms mean and how they relate, so “customer,” “client,” and “account holder” resolve to the same thing, and the model works from shared definitions instead of guessing.

Bates proposed something close to this in 1986: a cluster thesaurus that gathered every variant of a concept under one entry, so a search on any term could reach them all.

A fluent answer built on a bad index is still a bad answer.

Gartner predicted in Lack of AI-Ready Data Puts AI Projects at Risk, a February 2025 release, that through 2026 organizations will abandon 60 percent of artificial intelligence projects that lack ready data. That’s a forecast, but the same release reported that 63 percent of organizations lacked the right data practices or weren’t sure they had them.

This is the uncomfortable part for designers. The quality of a search result, or of a generative answer, is the user experience, and no polish around it makes up for a weak one.

Your influence has to reach down the cascade into labeling and indexing, and Bates argued the specialists for every layer had to design together.

Design for Browsing

Bates returned to browsing in 2007 with What Is Browsing — Really? A Model Drawing From Behavioural Science Research. Browsing, she argued, is a series of glimpses: you take in a field of view, select something, examine it, then keep it or drop it, and repeat.

She traced it to the exploratory behavior animals use to find food and shelter, which is why nobody needs to be taught how.

Similarly, I’ve been through 65 airports, partly to see how cities tell people where things are. The good terminals let you take in the whole hall at once, spot the sign you need, and change course without asking anyone. That’s the opposite of waiting at the information desk for one answer.

Generative search is quietly moving people toward the desk.

Pew Research Center tracked the browsing of 900 U.S. adults in March 2025 and reported that Google Users Are Less Likely to Click on Links When an AI Summary Appears in the Results. Visits with a summary led to a result click 8 percent of the time, against 15 percent without one, and sessions ended outright on 26 percent of summary pages versus 16 percent elsewhere.

Some of that is the summary doing its job. Some is a person who never glimpsed the source they didn’t know to ask for. So keep the scene around the answer, with neighboring sources and related threads, so the glimpse still has somewhere to land.

Conclusion

None of these ideas came from studying artificial intelligence. They came from watching people in libraries, card catalogs, and early online databases, and that’s exactly why they hold.

The technology between a person and the information keeps changing. The person mostly doesn’t.

Read together, Bates’s five ideas make one argument. Search is something people do over time, using moves they choose, at a level of control they want, on top of layers they never see. Their eyes do more of the work than any query. Every piece of that is a design decision, and most current products make it by default.

She also left what I’d call the berrypicking test for any assistant on your roadmap. Does it expect the question to change, or punish the change? Does it name the moves, or make people invent them? Can the person choose how much the system decides, and does anyone own the content underneath? Is there still room to look around?

The single answer is impressive. It’s also the classic model she spent decades arguing against, with better grammar. The teams that do best with this generation of tools will design for the berrypicker, the searcher whose question hasn’t settled yet.

Action Items

  • Show question history. Keep a visible summary of what the person has asked so far, and let them edit an earlier question without starting a new chat.
  • Add refine controls. Put buttons for narrowing, excluding, broadening, and checking against the original request next to every answer, so nobody has to phrase those moves as a prompt.
  • Set automation per task. Decide which tasks the system only suggests on and which it can run by itself, and give people a setting to change that.
  • Fix metadata first. Tag documents with type, owner, date, and status, define shared terms in a semantic layer, and show the sources behind every answer, including when nothing relevant was found.

Resources

  • Information and the Information Professions, Selected Works of Marcia J. Bates, volume I (Ketchikan Press, 2016). Her essays on what information is, including “Fundamental Forms of Information” and “The Invisible Substrate of Information Science.”
  • Information Searching Theory and Practice, Selected Works, volume II (Ketchikan Press, 2016). Collects “Information Search Tactics” and “What Is Browsing — Really?” along with her work on search techniques.
  • Information Users and Information System Design, Selected Works, volume III (Ketchikan Press, 2016). Includes the berrypicking paper and her 1990 paper on how much a search system should do for the person.
  • Understanding Information Retrieval Systems: Management, Types, and Standards (Auerbach Publications, 2012). A reference volume she edited on how retrieval systems are managed, the main types, and the standards behind them.
  • Marcia J. Bates Home Page. Her UCLA page, with free copies of many of the papers cited in this piece.

Berrypicking still beats the single answer for search, even in the world of AI was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Native is a floor, not a ceiling
description:
With AI, a polished look costs nothing. Native brings what can’t be drawn, and it moves with the system, one step ahead of what imitates it.

An AI assistant helped me write this. The ideas, the experience and the final edit are mine.

In June 2025, Apple introduced Liquid Glass, the new material of iOS 26. In its WWDC session on UIKit, the company put it plainly: “Your apps get this new appearance as soon as you recompile with the new SDK.” Bars, sheets, popovers and controls: most of what comes from the system frameworks changed at once, without a designer touching it.

Apps that drew their own controls got nothing. The next day, the Flutter team replied on GitHub that it was not developing Apple’s new design in its Cupertino library, the one that imitates iOS, for now. Its documentation presents drawing your own controls as a benefit: a Flutter app “looks and feels the same on all versions of the OS, even if the OS changed the implementations of its controls.” When iOS 26 shipped on September 15, 2025, that promise of stability had turned into a visible lag. The team has since moved its libraries out of the core framework to move faster, and says work is underway on Liquid Glass, but as of November 5, 2026, the issue is still open.

I worked with that choice for a long time, for the same reasons. Drawing your own controls means owning your rendering, on every version of the system. The price is that lag at every change. As long as a polished look took work, the price was worth paying: that work is what set an app apart.

AI changes the math. A polished look now takes one prompt, and generated interfaces converge in visual appearance and layout. I wrote elsewhere about why everything ends up looking alike, what people call slop; there I called apparent quality the floor, and AI now hands it to everyone. Native is a floor of another kind, the one an image doesn’t give you. Native components don’t make an app beautiful. They keep it from looking fake, and they move with the system.

AI draws the picture of native

Since October, I have been asking several AI models to design app screens, for a study I will publish soon. They imitate the system, under certain conditions, and only what can be seen.

The first condition is naming the device. Ask for a mobile app without saying which, and you get a generic screen that doesn’t really follow either iPhone or Android. Write “iPhone”, and the switches do have the shape of iOS switches. Add the instruction to follow the platform’s current conventions, and they fix a few more things that have a name: the green of the switches, the back chevron. But a year after iOS 26 shipped, the iOS they draw is still mostly the old one. The floating tab bar and the sheets detached from the edges, the iOS 26 design, only show up with that instruction, and rarely.

My explanation: an AI learns from what already exists, and the old iOS had years to fill the web. The system, meanwhile, moves every year, a little and sometimes a lot. On iOS, a native app follows by recompiling; an imitation stays stuck on the day it was copied. It’s the counterfeit copying last year’s collection, when the fashion house has already moved on to the next one.

A study published this spring points the same way. Researchers had three AI design tools generate 138 mobile screens, without mentioning iOS or Android. The models have learned “the visual syntax of contemporary mobile interfaces”, they write: navigation conventions are almost always there. But that success, in their words, “appears to be pattern-driven rather than principle-driven”, and they report a significant gap between visual and functional usability: help, error prevention and error recovery are often missing.

What the image doesn’t show

Imitating is already a lot. But the floor is mostly behavior. The back gesture that works everywhere. The share sheet everyone recognizes. The confirmation that, on iOS 26, grows out of the button that opened it. The sheet that rises from the bottom and that you dismiss with a swipe. A screenshot shows, at best, the picture of it.

Apple says it in the branding page of its guidelines: when you use components people already know, the experience feels “immediately reliable and familiar”. A familiar control does what you expect it to.

In 1998, with desktop software, John Satzinger and Lorne Olfman showed that commands that change from one application to the next make users take more actions, while a different visual appearance tends to make them more accurate. What matters is that the way you act stays the same.

It’s like the grammar of a language: everyone shares the same one, and nobody calls it slop. Slop is the stock phrase you’ve read a hundred times.

UIKit controls also come with built-in accessibility, and system components with text that scales to the size the user picked and a layout that flips for Arabic or Hebrew. On Android, the Compose documentation says that “most accessibility support is provided with little or no additional work” by its components, Material included. A control redrawn by hand has to rebuild all of that, and nothing guarantees it will: Kate Owens, at Deque, describes a custom slider that VoiceOver “skipped over entirely and never focused”.

Louie Mantia, a former Apple icon designer and a sharp critic of Liquid Glass, put it this way in 2025, about icons: “Everyone can look decent without actually being decent.” A generated mockup can draw an alert that looks like the iOS one without saying that the iOS one should be used. Rebuilt by hand, however faithfully, it only gives the app the picture of the floor.

The more apps get built from generated mockups, the more of them will look native without being native. That’s why, in my view, native matters more today than it did yesterday. The risk lies in the copied mockup: when an AI writes the code of a native project, it can call the real components. It can also produce native slop: the real components, all left at their defaults, and nothing of the brand around them. It works and it follows the system, but it looks like every other app.

On iPhone, the difference shows

You might think users see none of this. The only controlled experiment I found that pits a native app against its cross-platform version says they do see a difference, on iPhone, as soon as they can compare.

In 2014, Esteban Angulo and Xavier Ferré had thirty-seven people test two versions of the same app, fourteen of them on iPhone. One was native, the other built with Titanium, a cross-platform tool. Asked which version best matched their idea of an app for their phone, iPhone users picked the native one 86% to 7%. On Android, the gap was much smaller: 52% to 39%.

On iPhone, the seven people who had tried the cross-platform version first found it typical of iOS; among the seven who tried it after the native one, only four did. The gap mostly shows by comparison. But the cross-platform version also displayed native components, and a different team had designed it: the study can’t tell what made the difference. Nor does it say what it’s worth in ratings or sales, and a study of nearly 12,000 Android apps concludes that native and hybrid apps (web apps in a native shell) do equally well in ratings.

The ceiling is elsewhere

Native fixes the fake, not the alike. Standing out from other apps is still the brand’s job, and the floor doesn’t prevent it. In 2019, on UX Collective, Reza Bigdeli, an Android developer, answered designers who find standard components “cheap”. His advice: follow the platform’s guidelines, and keep creativity for the web. I follow him on the floor; for the rest, an app can have a strong identity without leaving its platform’s conventions.

Apple itself doesn’t reward a single style. In 2023, its Design Awards honored Flighty and Duolingo the same year. Flighty won in the Interaction category, which rewards interfaces “perfectly tailored to their platform”. Its founder, Ryan Jones, wanted the app to work so well that it would feel “almost boringly obvious”. Duolingo, on the other hand, is a highly stylized interface, which Apple still praises for its “best-in-class design” and “easy-to-follow UI”.

For Apple, “even a highly stylized interface can be approachable if it maintains familiar behaviors and patterns.” A WWDC26 session describes an app in two layers: bars and controls rely on what people already know, the content carries the brand, and the whole rests on a “baseline of platform familiarity”. That boundary is what a generated mockup doesn’t show.

Where to spend the effort

What comes from the system: navigation, back, sharing, confirmations, sheets, controls, text size. You don’t redraw them by default: Apple advises keeping custom work for the places where it has the “biggest impact”, and warns that a utility control remade by hand can make an app look less native, or even dated. Specify them by name, so nobody rebuilds them as a picture.

What comes from the brand: the content, the typography of headings (which should also follow the size the user picked), illustration, the tone of the copy, the moments where the app surprises. That’s where the identity budget gets spent. Apple even warns against too much brand: a brand color used everywhere dilutes its impact.

When the mockup comes from an AI, name the device and its current conventions in the prompt, then review that split first. Anything that looks like a system control should at least behave like one, and the safest bet is that it is one. The rest can be as free as you like: that’s where an app stops looking like the others.

Cover image: Apple’s design kits for iOS 27, the system components every app gets. Image: Apple Developer.

Mathieu Poli is Head of Frontend Engineering at GoodBarber and writes about frontend engineering, product design and AI.

Native is a floor, not a ceiling was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: JWT Authentication Explained: A Token You Can Verify Without a Database
description:
Ayesha manages a small online shop. Each morning she checks yesterday's paid orders and marks parcels ready to ship. Her dashboard talks to a small Node.js API, and every request has to answer one question first: is this really Ayesha? The usual answer is a session stored on the server, but that means a database lookup on every request, and it breaks when the API grows a second server. A JSON Web Token, a JWT, answers the same question without the lookup. The token carries who the caller is, and the server checks the token's signature instead of asking a database. This post builds that check with nothing but Node.js built-in crypto, and shows where it breaks if you use it carelessly.

What I would check before using it

My judgement, from building small APIs for years, is this: a JWT is the right call when several services need to check who is calling without sharing a database, and the wrong call when you need to cancel access instantly. The first check is revocation. A token stays valid until it expires, and there is no way to cancel it early, so a stolen token keeps working until its expiry time passes. The honest fix is a short lifetime, fifteen minutes to an hour. If you need a logout button that works everywhere at once, use sessions, because a JWT on its own cannot do that.

The second check is what goes inside the token. The payload is only encoded, not encrypted, so anyone who gets the token can read it. Keep it to an id, a name, and a role, and never put a password or anything else sensitive in there.

The third check is the secret. The whole scheme rests on one secret string that signs every token. It must be long and random, it must live in an environment variable rather than in the code, and every service that verifies tokens must use the same one. A short secret such as "secret" can be guessed offline by trying candidates against a captured token.

The fourth check is size. The token travels on every request, usually in an Authorization header, so keep the payload small.

The verdict, in short: use a JWT for short-lived access tokens in this shop API, with a one-hour expiry and a payload holding only an id, a name, and a role. Do not use it where instant logout matters.

A worked example that is not a toy

The worked example is the shop's login flow. Ayesha logs in, the API issues a token that says she is user-1042, a shop manager, valid for one hour. Her dashboard then sends that token with every request, and the API verifies it before returning any orders. The token has three parts, separated by dots: a header saying which algorithm signed it, a payload with the claims, and a signature. Both functions below were run with Node.js built-in crypto only, no packages installed.

const crypto = require('node:crypto');

const SECRET = 'demo-secret-do-not-use-in-production';

function base64url(input) {
  return Buffer.from(input).toString('base64url');
}

function signToken(payload, secret) {
  const header = { alg: 'HS256', typ: 'JWT' };
  const encodedHeader = base64url(JSON.stringify(header));
  const encodedPayload = base64url(JSON.stringify(payload));
  const data = encodedHeader + '.' + encodedPayload;
  const signature = crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret).update(data).digest('base64url');
  return data + '.' + signature;
}

function verifyToken(token, secret) {
  const parts = token.split('.');
  if (parts.length !== 3) throw new Error('malformed token: expected three parts');
  const [encodedHeader, encodedPayload, signature] = parts;
  const data = encodedHeader + '.' + encodedPayload;
  const expected = crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret).update(data).digest();
  const actual = Buffer.from(signature, 'base64url');
  if (actual.length !== expected.length || !crypto.timingSafeEqual(actual, expected)) {
    throw new Error('invalid signature');
  }
  const payload = JSON.parse(Buffer.from(encodedPayload, 'base64url').toString('utf8'));
  if (payload.exp && Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) > payload.exp) {
    throw new Error('token expired');
  }
  return payload;
}

Issuing the token at login and verifying it on the next request gave this real output:

eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJ1c2VyLTEwNDIiLCJuYW1lIjoiQXllc2hhIiwicm9sZSI6InNob3AtbWFuYWdlciIsImlhdCI6MTc5MzkxMjI4NywiZXhwIjoxNzkzOTE1ODg3fQ.BW4Av2PoMZMpM82x_3g4F7VNWODbf4u2z9t4hZig8f8
Decoded payload: {"sub":"user-1042","name":"Ayesha","role":"shop-manager","iat":1793912287,"exp":1793915887}
Access granted for Ayesha (role: shop-manager)

The header and payload are readable once decoded; the signature is what makes the token trustworthy. The iat and exp numbers are seconds since 1 January 1970, from the real run, so yours will differ.

Now the part the tidy tutorials skip: something goes wrong. A curious user copies the token, changes one character in the payload, and sends the edited token back. The signature was computed over the original payload, so it no longer matches the edited one, and the check refuses it:

Rejected: invalid signature

That is the whole security of the scheme in one line. The signature covers the header and the payload together, so any change to either part breaks it. The same check also catches a token verified with the wrong secret, which fails with the same message, and an expired token, which fails differently:

Rejected: token expired

The fix is already in the function above, and it is a matter of order: verify the signature first, then read the payload, then check the expiry before trusting anything it says. A version of the check that skips the expiry test is worse than useless, because it looks secure while accepting tokens that should be dead. Running the expired token through such a version proved it:

Accepted anyway: {"sub":"user-1042","name":"Ayesha","role":"shop-manager","iat":1793905087,"exp":1793908687}

The token had expired an hour before the check, and the careless verifier let it through. The lesson is that a JWT is not a magic string. It is a signature plus an expiry date, and both have to be checked every time.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

1. Trusting the payload before verifying the signature. The payload is only base64url encoded, so anyone can decode it without the secret. If your code reads the role from the payload without checking the signature, an attacker can set the role to "admin" in their own token. The fix: verify the signature first, then read the payload.

2. Using plain base64 instead of base64url. Node's Buffer.toString('base64') produces +, /, and = padding, which break inside a URL or a header, and encoding the same payload with plain base64 gave a string ending in ==. The fix is to use the base64url encoding for tokens.

3. Skipping the expiry check. A verifier that never looks at exp accepts tokens forever, as the run above showed. The fix is the exp comparison in the function above, run on every request.

4. A weak secret, or a different secret in each service. Verifying the real token with a different secret failed with "invalid signature", which is also what happens when two services drift apart. Worse, a short secret such as "secret" can be guessed offline against a captured token. The fix is one long random secret, at least 32 characters, in an environment variable, shared by every service that verifies tokens.

Where this leaves you

A JWT is a signature check, not encryption. The signature proves nobody changed the token, and the expiry date limits how long a stolen one stays useful. Keep tokens short-lived, keep payloads small and free of secrets, and keep the signing secret long, random, and out of the code. The test is simple. Take the token from the run above, change one character, and watch it get rejected, then check that your own verifier also rejects an expired token. The next step is to move the secret into an environment variable, add a login route that issues the token, and put the verify function in front of the orders route.

Further reading

  • RFC 7519, JSON Web Token (JWT)
  • RFC 8725, JSON Web Token Best Current Practices
  • Node.js crypto documentation

Originally published at https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/jwt-authentication-explained-token-you.html

title: Password Reset Emails: API Sending for High Deliverability and Compliance Evidence
description:
Short answer: For password reset emails and high-deliverability verification sending, use the /v1/email/send API when its region, retention, and processor terms satisfy your compliance review.

An e-commerce signup email has two jobs that are easy to confuse: get a verification link to the buyer, and leave enough evidence to explain what happened later. The second job changes the API decision.

Use /v1/email/send for the single transactional send, but keep consent, token generation, expiry, and compliance records in your own system. A delivery API can move the message; it cannot, by itself, prove the region where every processor handled the data, how long message content was retained, or that a deletion request reached every downstream system. For a password-reset flow, the same boundary applies.

Infrai fits this narrow part of the workflow when one REST boundary, one key, and one bill across backend services are operationally useful. Its public discovery surface also exposes capability metadata and runnable examples without a key, which makes the integration inventory easier to inspect before a compliance review.

Should this API handle password reset emails and verification sending?

The answer is yes only when the provider boundary is acceptable. Here is a minimal Python client that sends an application-owned JSON payload, retries a rate limit with Retry-After, and supplies an idempotency key. It deliberately leaves message fields in INFRAI_EMAIL_PAYLOAD, because the route's verified existence does not make an undocumented request schema safe to invent.

import json
import os
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request


api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
payload = os.environ["INFRAI_EMAIL_PAYLOAD"].encode("utf-8")
request = urllib.request.Request(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/send",
    data=payload,
    method="POST",
    headers={
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": os.environ["INFRAI_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY"],
    },
)


for attempt in range(4):
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
            if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                raise RuntimeError(f"send failed: HTTP {response.status}")
            print(json.loads(response.read()))
            break
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
        if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
            detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            raise RuntimeError(f"send failed: HTTP {error.code}: {detail}") from error
        delay = int(error.headers.get("Retry-After", "0"))
        time.sleep(delay if delay > 0 else 2**attempt)

Keep the idempotency key stable for the same internal event. A new key on every retry can turn a transient delivery problem into duplicate recovery mail.

What evidence must the signup flow produce?

Start with the evidence model, not the vendor feature list. For each verification request, record an internal event ID, account ID, purpose, template version, creation time, expiry time, and the provider request ID returned by the send operation. Store the recipient as a protected identifier or a keyed digest where the investigation does not require the raw address. The link token belongs in a separate short-lived store; putting it into a general-purpose audit record creates a needless credential-retention problem.

This is a trade-off, not a checklist. A longer retention window makes support investigations easier, while a shorter one reduces the blast radius of an exported event table. Decide the window from your policy and document it. Do not infer it from an API's default behavior.

The region question is similarly precise: where is the application data stored, where is the message content processed, and where are delivery and abuse-prevention logs retained? Those are different locations and often different processors. SPF is part of sender authorization, not proof of regional processing or deletion; RFC 7208 describes the former boundary clearly.

Which boundary belongs to the sending API?

A useful design divides responsibility into three layers. Your application owns the account event, token lifecycle, consent record, and deletion workflow. The sending service owns the accepted request and its delivery pipeline under its published processor and retention terms. Your compliance process owns the evidence that connects those layers without copying the entire message body into an audit system.

That division also exposes limits that marketing pages tend to blur. The email capability has no hosted email OTP interface, so a fallback code flow needs to be built by the application. It has no SMTP relay. Event retrieval is pull-based rather than webhook-driven, which means a polling job must reconcile provider events with your internal event ID; real-time orchestration should not be assumed. Scheduled email has a scheduled_at field, but there is no email cancellation route, so do not make cancellation a promise in the user experience.

For a domestic compliance decision, do not treat a pending Tencent email vendor as evidence that domestic processing is available. Ask for the actual region and processor commitments that apply to the account and route you will use. If those commitments are mandatory, the specialist provider remains the safer choice until the paperwork is explicit.

Why do the obvious provider comparisons miss the real risk?

SendGrid, Mailgun, and Postmark are credible products to evaluate, but they answer different parts of the question. SendGrid is a broad transactional and marketing email platform, so it can suit teams that want one larger email program. Mailgun is often evaluated by engineering teams that care about programmatic sending and operational controls. Postmark is positioned around transactional delivery, which makes it a natural comparison for verification and reset messages. None of those labels, by themselves, establishes a region, retention period, deletion propagation rule, or processor contract for your exact account.

The comparison should therefore be explicit:

Option Reason to evaluate Evidence boundary to verify
SendGrid Broad email program and mature sending surface Which data is retained for transactional messages, and which processors handle it?
Mailgun Developer-oriented sending and domain operations Can your required region and deletion request path be documented for the selected service?
Postmark Transactional-message focus What delivery, bounce, and abuse logs remain after message deletion?
Infrai One REST API, one key, and one bill across backend services Which region, retention, and processor terms apply to the email route and its vendors?

The last row is where Infrai can be useful, but the distinction matters. Its unified surface removes key and invoice sprawl when the same backend also uses other capabilities, and its public discovery surface exposes capability metadata and runnable examples without a key. That reduces integration inventory. It does not turn a multi-provider delivery chain into a single legal processor, and it does not supply a domestic compliance guarantee.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the single verification or password-reset send when your team wants one REST boundary and one operational account across backend services, provided your compliance review accepts the email route's documented region and processor terms. Choose SendGrid, Mailgun, or Postmark instead when their specialist controls or contract language meet a requirement that the unified layer cannot satisfy.

A small rollout with a hard stop

Ship the flow in stages. First, generate and expire the token inside the application. Second, version the template and write the internal audit event before calling the sender. Third, send through /v1/email/send and persist the provider request ID without storing the token in the provider-facing audit record. Finally, poll for events and reconcile them to the internal event ID. Treat every poll result as evidence to normalize, not as a replacement for your own audit trail.

Before production, make the compliance review answer five questions in writing: the processing regions, each relevant processor, message and event retention, deletion propagation, and the owner of the fallback OTP flow. If one answer is “we will find out after launch,” the rollout is not ready.

The practical answer is narrower than “which API has the highest deliverability.” Choose the sender whose deliverability controls and evidence boundary fit the account workflow. For a unified backend boundary, start with the email API documentation and verify the contractual details before committing the data path.

Sources

References:

  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework
  • SendGrid Email API
  • Mailgun API documentation
  • Postmark developer documentation
  • Infrai documentation

title: Delayed Webhook Retries: A Guide to Rate Limits and Idempotency Explained
description:
Short answer: let the queue own delay, and let the Node.js worker own rate limits, idempotency, and the final retry decision for a renewal reminder webhook.

That split keeps a business deadline visible while preventing a recovering customer endpoint from being buried under a retry storm.

The mental model is small:

Before: a failed HTTP call immediately schedules another HTTP call.

After: the worker records the attempt, applies a client-side limit, and publishes the next attempt with exponential backoff. The queue carries time. The worker carries policy.

This matters for a delayed renewal reminder because the reminder is a business event, not merely a failed network request. A duplicate reminder is annoying. A missed reminder may be expensive. The right design makes both outcomes observable.

For a bounded delayed task, Infrai fits at the queue boundary: its public discovery surface exposes the capability and runnable examples before a key is required, so a team can inspect the REST contract before adding an SDK. One key and a plain HTTP surface can reduce credential and client-library decisions around this small worker.

There is a trade-off. Infrai is not a workflow engine, has no native debounce or throttle, and does not provide a DAG or fan-out join primitive. If the renewal flow grows into a multi-step business process, Temporal or Inngest is the more natural place to model that orchestration.

What should retry, and when?

Retry transient failures: timeouts, connection resets, and HTTP 429 or 5xx responses. Treat most 4xx responses as a permanent failure unless the target's contract says otherwise. A malformed payload will not become valid because it waited 30 seconds.

Use exponential backoff with a ceiling. For example, delay = min(60 * 2 ** attempt, 3600) gives delays of 60, 120, 240 seconds, then caps at one hour. Add jitter so several reminders created together do not wake the endpoint at the same instant. Keep the business deadline in the message and stop retrying after that deadline or an explicit attempt limit.

The queue should be configured for retry-on-failure and exponential backoff. For a delayed task, publish the next attempt through publish_batch when several retries are ready at once. Batch publishing reduces request overhead, but it does not remove the need for per-target pacing. A batch is an efficient transport operation, not a rate-limit policy.

One hard boundary is seven days for a delayed message. A renewal reminder farther away needs a separate timer or a cron trigger that puts work into a queue later. A long worker run has the same shape: use the scheduler to trigger queue work, then let a worker consume it; do not treat a single cron execution as an unlimited process. Cron executions are capped at 900 seconds.

How do rate limits and duplicate delivery fit together?

Standard queues are at-least-once. The worker must assume that a message can be delivered again, even after a successful webhook call. FIFO deduplication helps only inside its five-minute window, which is shorter than many retry schedules.

Here is the part worth making boring: use a stable event ID as the idempotency key, and make the receiving endpoint store or enforce that key. The retry attempt number can change. The event ID cannot.

type WebhookJob = {
  eventId: string;
  targetUrl: string;
  body: string;
  deadlineMs: number;
  attempt: number;
};

const sleep = (ms: number): Promise<void> =>
  new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function deliverWebhook(job: WebhookJob): Promise<"delivered" | "retry" | "failed"> {
  const delayMs = Math.min(60_000 * 2 ** job.attempt, 3_600_000);
  if (job.attempt > 0) await sleep(delayMs + Math.floor(Math.random() * 1_000));

  const response = await fetch(job.targetUrl, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "content-type": "application/json",
      "idempotency-key": job.eventId,
    },
    body: job.body,
  });

  if (response.ok) return "delivered";
  if (response.status === 429 || response.status >= 500) {
    if (Date.now() < job.deadlineMs) return "retry";
  }
  return "failed";
}

type RetryMessage = {
  body: string;
  delay_seconds: number;
};

async function publishRetryBatch(
  queue: string,
  messages: RetryMessage[],
  idempotencyKey: string,
): Promise<void> {
  const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish_batch", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "authorization": `Bearer ${process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY}`,
      "content-type": "application/json",
      "idempotency-key": idempotencyKey,
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({ queue, messages }),
  });

  if (response.status === 429) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "1");
    await sleep(Math.max(1, retryAfter) * 1_000);
    throw new Error("Queue publish was rate limited; retry the idempotent batch");
  }
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Queue publish failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
  }
}

In production, place a token bucket or equivalent limiter around the fetch call. The limiter should be keyed by target, or by target plus credential, rather than shared across unrelated customers. Honor a Retry-After response when it is present. A 429 with a ten-second server instruction should not be followed by a locally chosen one-second delay.

The batch call uses an idempotency key because publishing is a write. Generate that key once for the logical retry batch and reuse it when the publisher retries; the function accepts that stable key from the message record. Keep delay_seconds at or below 604800. The same rule applies to the queue call as to the webhook: check the status and carry the real error forward.

This snippet deliberately returns a decision instead of silently republishing work. The consumer can acknowledge a delivered or permanent failure, and publish a new message with an incremented attempt for retry. That acknowledgement boundary is important: acknowledge too early and a process crash loses the reminder; acknowledge too late and the same reminder may run twice. The endpoint's idempotency check is what makes the second case safe.

Keep message bodies below 256 KB and retention at or below 30 days. Store a reference to larger reminder data elsewhere. Acknowledged messages are deleted, so this queue is not a Kafka-style replay log with multiple consumer groups. Keep an application-level delivery record if support staff need an audit trail.

Which queue fits this integration?

The choice depends on where you want the integration contract to live.

Option Useful fit Important boundary
RabbitMQ Explicit consumer acknowledgements, dead-lettering, and mature routing controls You operate a broker and must design its topology and operational lifecycle
BullMQ A Node.js-centered worker with Redis-backed delayed jobs and familiar JavaScript ergonomics Redis becomes part of the durability and operations story; downstream webhook idempotency is still yours
Amazon SQS Managed queues, visibility timeouts, and an established dead-letter workflow Delays, FIFO deduplication, and throughput controls follow SQS semantics; the worker still handles endpoint rate limits
Inngest Event-driven functions with retry and step-oriented application workflows It is a workflow product, so its model is broader than a small queue adapter and brings its own execution semantics
Temporal Durable, long-running orchestration with explicit workflow state It is a specialist workflow runtime; operating and modeling it is more work than a single delayed webhook needs
Infrai scheduling A plain REST integration when discovery, credentials, and a small queue surface matter It is not a DAG or workflow engine, has no native debounce or throttle, and standard delivery still requires consumer idempotency

RabbitMQ is the stronger choice when routing and acknowledgement semantics are the product of the system. BullMQ is attractive when the team already operates Redis and wants the worker and job model close to Node.js. SQS is a sensible managed option when AWS operations and IAM are already settled.

Infrai is worth trying for teams that want to discover the queue capability and runnable examples through a self-describing REST surface, then wire one credential into a delayed-webhook worker without adding another SDK-specific surface. Its second practical advantage here is a consistent idempotency convention for write operations, which reduces integration decisions around retrying queue publishes; it does not replace the receiver's idempotency key.

My decision rule is simple: choose the specialist whose routing, workflow, or operational guarantees you need. Choose the REST queue surface when the job is a bounded delayed task and reducing integration friction matters more than advanced orchestration.

What will surprise you in the first production test?

The first surprise is usually not the backoff formula. It is endpoint behavior under duplicates. Test a response that succeeds, then make the consumer crash before acknowledgement. Deliver the same event again and verify that the receiver returns a safe duplicate result without performing the renewal action twice.

Keep it explicit.

The second surprise is observability. Measure delivery age, attempt count, response class, rate-limit pauses, and time until the deadline. Monitor endpoint responsiveness during retries. A queue depth chart alone cannot tell you that every target is returning 429, nor can it prove that a reminder was delivered before its deadline.

Keep the retry record small and explicit: event ID, target, attempt, next delivery time, last status, and deadline. When a message reaches its limit, send it to a dead-letter path or durable failure store for inspection. Do not keep retrying a permanently rejected payload because the queue makes repetition easy.

The useful test is a timeline, not a happy-path request. Start with a failed attempt, inject a 429 and its Retry-After, restart the worker before acknowledgement, and then release the endpoint. The expected result is one business action, a visible retry history, and no burst that violates the target's contract.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the scheduling documentation at https://docs.infrai.cc. Keep the worker policy in your codebase, where the business deadline and target-specific rate limit can be reviewed alongside the reminder logic.

References

  • Infrai official documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • RabbitMQ consumer acknowledgements: https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • Amazon SQS visibility timeout: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html
  • BullMQ delayed jobs: https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/jobs/delayed
  • Inngest function retries: https://www.inngest.com/docs/features/inngest-functions/retries
  • Temporal workflows: https://docs.temporal.io/workflows

title: Transactional Email API Service Offers: 3 Marketplace Checks for Valid Suppression
description:
Short answer: choose the transactional email API service that offers durable event identity, bounded retries, and exportable suppression evidence; compare price only after those controls pass.

Evidence is the product boundary.

Treat the cheapest transactional email API as the one that can prove, for every rejected marketplace recipient, why the address was suppressed and when that decision can be revisited. A low sending rate is irrelevant if your system keeps retrying a permanent bounce or cannot show consent and suppression evidence during an audit.

My decision rule is three-part: separate provider delivery events from marketplace recipient state, classify failures before retrying, and retain an append-only evidence record. That gives a welcome-email flow a defensible boundary without making price the architecture.

What must the system prove?

The application is a marketplace sending a welcome or transactional message after account creation. Its difficult case is not the first successful send. It is the address that bounces, the mailbox that accepts and later complains, and the retry worker that knows less than the original request.

The invariants are strict:

  • A permanent recipient failure suppresses future sends for that address and purpose.
  • A transient failure can be retried under a bounded policy, with an idempotency key.
  • Every state change records the event identifier, recipient ID, classification, source, timestamp, and policy version.
  • The sending path never treats an accepted response as proof of inbox delivery.

The failure boundary sits between delivery telemetry and business intent. A provider can report a bounce; only the marketplace can decide whether a particular welcome message is still allowed. SPF is one part of sender authorization, not a substitute for that decision record.

This is the useful answer to the cost question: compare evidence and failure semantics first, then compare quotas and operational cost among options that meet them.

Which transactional email API service offers defensible evidence?

There are three reasonable implementation shapes. They solve different problems, so putting them in a single cheapest-API ranking is misleading.

Option Strength Boundary to verify Evidence question
Direct HTTPS submission to a delivery API Fast integration and clear request IDs Event schema and webhook authenticity vary Can events be replayed and correlated to one message?
SMTP relay behind a mail adapter Familiar operational boundary and broad protocol support SMTP responses are not the whole lifecycle Where do asynchronous bounce details land?
Self-hosted submission plus a separately operated MTA Maximum control over logs and retention Deliverability operations become your team’s job Can you demonstrate authorization and suppression?

The comparison axis is compliance evidence, not a promotional feature checklist. For each option, ask for retention period, event identity, retry semantics, webhook signing, export path, and deletion behavior. Record the answers with the architecture decision. Documentation that cannot answer those questions is a risk signal even when the endpoint is inexpensive. The trade-off is straightforward: a hosted service offers less control over retention, while self-hosting offers more control at the cost of operating deliverability.

How should the critical path classify a bounce?

The application should make suppression an explicit state transition. Do not infer it later from a dashboard export. Here is a transport-neutral adapter boundary; the actual delivery mechanism can be replaced without changing recipient policy.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from enum import Enum

class Outcome(Enum):
    ACCEPTED = "accepted"
    TRANSIENT = "transient"
    PERMANENT = "permanent"

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DeliveryEvent:
    message_id: str
    recipient_id: str
    outcome: Outcome
    provider_event_id: str
    observed_at: datetime
    policy_version: str

def apply_delivery_event(event: DeliveryEvent, store) -> None:
    # A unique event key makes webhook retries harmless.
    if store.has_event(event.provider_event_id):
        return
    store.append_event(event)
    if event.outcome is Outcome.PERMANENT:
        store.suppress(event.recipient_id, "welcome", "permanent_delivery_failure", event.observed_at)
    elif event.outcome is Outcome.TRANSIENT:
        store.enqueue_retry(event.message_id, datetime.now(timezone.utc))

The example intentionally does not turn every negative event into suppression. A temporary refusal and a nonexistent mailbox need different controls, and classification must come from a documented policy mapped to the delivery event. Keep the raw event as well as the normalized outcome. Normalization makes queries usable; raw data preserves evidence when the mapping changes.

A useful fixture includes one permanent bounce, one temporary failure delivered twice as a webhook, one accepted submission with no later event, and one recipient already suppressed before a send request. The expected result is one suppression, one bounded retry, one idempotent no-op, and one blocked send. That distinction matters.

Why keep suppression in the marketplace?

A provider-managed suppression list can protect one account or sending stream, but the marketplace owns the relationship between a recipient, a purpose, and a consent record. A user may be allowed to receive a security notice while unsubscribed from promotional mail. A global email flag loses that distinction.

Store suppression locally with a reason code, source event, first-seen time, last-seen time, and review policy. Use a stable internal recipient ID rather than placing a raw address in ordinary logs. Hashing can reduce exposure, but it does not automatically make data anonymous; retention and access rules still matter.

The outbound worker checks suppression immediately before submission, because state can change after a message enters a queue. It also writes the decision and transport result under one correlation ID. That is the point where a reviewer can follow the path without trusting a screenshot.

Expose counts by classification, purpose, domain family, and policy version. Alert on an unusual rise in permanent failures or on a missing event stream. Do not alert only on provider availability: a healthy API with a broken webhook consumer can quietly produce repeated sends.

The rejected design and its valid use case

I would reject “send first, reconcile a nightly bounce file” for welcome mail. It creates an interval in which an invalid recipient can be retried, and it makes an audit depend on a batch that may have lost ordering or correlation. It is hard to explain why a specific send was permitted at a specific time.

That design still has a valid use case for backfill and low-priority reporting when sending is already blocked by a local suppression check and the batch is treated as secondary evidence. It is not a good primary control for transactional delivery.

The same reasoning applies to price comparison. An endpoint that lacks durable event identity, usable exports, or clear webhook authenticity can move work into your application and compliance process. Count that work before choosing it. A service with weak event retention is unsuitable for an audit-heavy workflow, even if its submission path is convenient.

Choose the delivery option that meets the evidence contract, then measure total operational burden across submission, event ingestion, suppression, retries, retention, and incident review. For a marketplace, the cheapest safe path is the one that makes invalid-recipient decisions repeatable and explainable.

References

  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework (SPF): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • RFC 5321, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5321
  • RFC 3463, Enhanced Mail System Status Codes: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3463
  • RFC 8058, Signaling One-Click Functionality for List Emails: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8058
  • OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html

title: Docraft: Turn Pasted AI Responses into Word, PDF and HTML Files, Locally in Your Browser
description:
AI chats are great at producing structured text, but getting that text into a clean, shareable document is still a chore. Docraft is a Chrome extension that turns a pasted AI response into an editable Word file, a styled PDF, or a standalone HTML page in a couple of clicks.

Everything runs locally in your browser. There's no server, no account, no analytics, and no AI API behind it.

GitHub: https://github.com/abmdevx/docraft

What it does

Paste your text into the popup, optionally set a title, and export. When you need more control, open the full workspace.

  • Compact popup for fast paste-and-export
  • Full workspace with an editor, a live document preview, and document settings
  • Three export formats: Word (.docx), PDF, and HTML
  • Markdown-aware parsing that detects headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, code blocks, quotes, links, and inline formatting
  • Light and dark documents: a white page, or a near-black page with white text, for Word and PDF output
  • Document controls: font, size, page size, orientation, margins, title, and page numbers
  • Optional table of contents in all three formats
  • Multi-paste ZIP batches: add several responses, choose a format for each, and download them together
  • Math in PDFs: KaTeX renders supported LaTeX formulas as crisp images

Privacy by design

People paste a lot of sensitive text into AI tools, so the extension asks for as little as possible:

  • Only the storage permission is required
  • clipboardRead is optional and requested only when you use the Paste action
  • No host permissions at all
  • Pasted content isn't saved unless you enable "Remember my draft"
  • Pasted HTML is treated as literal text and is never rendered with innerHTML
  • Only validated http, https, mailto, and tel links become active

Tech stack

  • React + TypeScript for the popup and workspace UIs
  • Tailwind CSS for styling and Vite for building
  • Chrome Manifest V3
  • A Markdown parser feeding separate Word, PDF, and HTML exporters
  • Automated tests for the parser, the exporters, and the UI
  • The open-source Carlito font embedded so PDFs match Calibri's metrics

Known limitations

  • PDF fonts cover Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, and many symbols. CJK and complex scripts such as Arabic or Indic scripts may not render fully, and Docraft warns you after export when characters are unsupported.
  • Preview page breaks are estimates.
  • Landscape mode is manual, and wide tables are scaled with smaller type.

Try it

Docraft installs from source for now:

git clone https://github.com/abmdevx/docraft.git
cd docraft
npm install
npm run build

Then open chrome://extensions, enable Developer mode, choose Load unpacked, and select the generated dist/ folder.

It's MIT licensed, so feedback, issues, and stars are all welcome: https://github.com/abmdevx/docraft

What would you want from a tool like this? Let me know in the comments.

title: SQL Challenge: Extract the Year and Month From a Date
description:
94 SQL Challenge: Can You Extract the Year and Month From a Date?

Imagine your manager asks you to prepare a monthly sales report.

The report should show how much revenue the business generated in each month.

Your "orders" table contains complete dates, such as "2026-01-15".

How would you group these orders month by month?

Let's look at the data.

orders

order_id order_date amount
101 2026-01-05 5000
102 2026-01-15 3000
103 2026-02-10 7000
104 2026-02-20 4000
105 2026-03-12 6000

Your Challenge

Write an SQL query to:

  1. Extract the year from "order_date".
  2. Extract the month from "order_date".
  3. Calculate total sales for each month.
  4. Group the results by year and month.
  5. Sort the results by year and month.

Think before you scroll!

The SQL Solution

SELECT
EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) AS year,
EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date) AS month,
SUM(amount) AS total_sales
FROM orders
GROUP BY
EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date),
EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date)
ORDER BY year, month;

Expected Output

year month total_sales
2026 1 8000
2026 2 11000
2026 3 6000

Why is this useful?

Monthly sales reports are common in real projects.

You can use the same approach to find:

  • Monthly revenue
  • Customer registrations
  • Employee joining trends
  • Monthly order volume
  • Business growth over time

One Important Thing to Remember

Don't group only by month if your table contains data from multiple years.

For example, January 2025 and January 2026 are different reporting periods.

Always include the year along with the month.

Your Turn: Can you write the same query using "YEAR()" and "MONTH()"?
